en: The sages said:
How did Sanatkumāra explain all the dharmas to the high-souled Nārada, and how did those two meet?
O Sūta, tell us this: in what place did those two exponents of the Veda stand while they sang the hymn to Hari?
Sūta said:
The high-souled Sanaka and others were the mind-born sons of Brahmā;
they were all free from possessiveness and egoism, for they were perpetual celibates.
I shall state their names: Samaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, Vibhu, and he who is remembered as Sanātana. (NarP 1.2.4)
Those great-souled ones were devotees of Viṣṇu, devoted to meditation upon Brahman;
they resembled a thousand suns, were true to their word, and were seekers of liberation.
Once, as they set out for the assembly hall of Brahmā on the summit of Mount Meru,
those twice-born ones beheld on their path the Gaṅgā, the river born from the foot of Viṣṇu.
Beholding her, they became eager to bathe in the waters of the Sītā;
in the meantime, the divine sage, the seer Nārada, arrived there.
O best of the twice-born, having seen his elder brothers who had returned, he approached them;
seeing them intent on bathing, he paid homage with palms joined in reverence. (NarP 1.2.8)
Endowed with loving devotion, one should recite the names of the qualities of the Enemy of Madhu:
Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta, Ananta, Vāsudeva, Janārdana.
O Lord of sacrifice, O Person of the sacrifice, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, homage be to you!
O lotus-eyed one, O beloved of Kamalā, O progenitor of the Gaṅgā, Keśava;
O Lord of gods who reclines upon the ocean of milk, Dāmodara, homage be to you!
O Śrī Rāma, Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Aniruddha, Vāsudeva, O stainless Murāri! O Unborn One, protect us constantly from all fear.
Having thus loudly uttered the name of Hari and bowed to those sages who were his elder brothers,
he sat near them and, filled with joy, bathed together with them.
And they, having bathed and performed the funeral rites for Sītā in that water which purifies the world,
were cleansed of all taints regarding the gods, seers, and ancestors.
Having crossed over and performed their own customary duties such as the twilight prayers, O twice-born ones,
they engaged in various discourses centered upon the qualities of Nārāyaṇa.
When the sages had performed their morning rites on the delightful bank of the Gaṅgā,
Nārada posed his question amidst various narrations and stories.
Nārada said:
"O best of sages, you are all omniscient and devoted to the worship of the Blessed One;
you are all eternal Lords of the universe and Blessed Ones."
"I ask you, who are devoted to uplifting the world and have shown friendship toward the distressed: therefore, O Blessed Ones, tell me, O wise ones, what are the characteristics of a Buddha."
By whom this entire world, both moving and unmoving, was brought forth—
he whose foot-water is the Gaṅgā, how can that Hari be known?
And how does the threefold action of human beings arise together with its fruit?
O givers of honor, tell me the characteristics of knowledge and of austerity as well.
"Or even the honoring of a guest—by which Viṣṇu is pleased; such secret matters that cause gratification to Hari, O Lords, you ought to tell me in truth, having shown me favor. (NarP 1.2.20)
Śaunaka said: Salutations to the supreme deity, who is higher than the highest and beyond even the subtlest;
who dwells in both the high and the low, and who possesses attributes as well as being devoid of them.

Salutation to Viṣṇu, who is free from illusion, whose nature is self-consciousness, who is without beginning, who possesses universal forms, the Lord of Yogins, the embodiment of Yoga, and the one who is attainable through Yoga.
To the one who is knowledge, who is accessible through knowledge, who is the sole cause of all knowledge;
to the Lord of knowledge, who is the object of knowledge, the knower, and the perfection of consciousness.
Salutations to the one who is meditation itself, who is to be reached through meditation, and who removes the afflictions of the meditator;
to the Lord of meditation, whose own form is the object of meditation for the wise and the meditator.

To that unborn, ancient, true Lord of Praise, who is endowed with the power of the Sun, Moon, Fire, Brahmā, and the gods, as well as the hosts of Siddhas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Nāgas— to Him I am perpetually bowed.
I worship that unborn Lord, who is the creator of the worlds in the form of Brahmā, the protector in the form of Viṣṇu the twice-born, and who,
known as Rudra at the end of the aeon, lies upon the serpent-bed.

I take refuge in that primordial Viṣṇu, the Lord who, when his name was invoked, liberated Gajendra from the terrible grip of the crocodile, and who shines resplendent in his own supreme station. NarP_1,2.27 //

I eternally take refuge in Him alone, who is Śiva in form for those devoted to Śiva, who is Viṣṇu in form for those meditating on Hari, and who is the cause of their respective bodies according to their prior volitions.

I perpetually bow down to that Vāsudeva, the slayer of Keśin and the destroyer of Naraka, who as a child supported the mountain with the tip of his arm, and who delights in the sport of lifting the earth.
I meditate upon that unborn Lord, who, descending in the form of the fierce Man-lion, tore asunder the stone-like hardness of the Daitya’s chest and protected his own devotee Prahlāda.

I bow to that Supreme, Ancient Person, who is designated as the Self, though not defiled by ether and the other elements; who is stainless, eternal, and the reality beyond measure; the creator of the world, yet free from all karma.
I worship that primordial Self, the one Lord who abides through his various manifestations as Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Anila, Vāyu, mortals, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and hosts of gods. 1.2.32.
Since all this, which is diverse, has indeed arisen from Him, abides in Him, and will eventually return into Him—Him I have gone for refuge. (NarP 1.2.33)
I have gone for refuge to him who, though abiding in manifold forms, is perceived here as free from attachment; he is unattached and perfectly complete.
I have gone for refuge to that Supreme, Pure Lord who, though dwelling within the heart, is not known by those whose selves are deluded by Māyā. (NarP 1.2.35)
For those who have desisted from all attachments and whose souls delight in the yoga of meditation, the self of knowledge shines everywhere; I have gone for refuge to that.
During the churning for the nectar of immortality,
he took refuge in that tortoise for the sake of the welfare of the gods, who placed Mount Mandāra upon his back as a support.
I bow to that Vārāha, who, as the infinite one, lifted the earth from the ocean with his tusk-like sprout and stood here supporting this entire world.
I bow to that Nṛsiṃha who, while protecting the Daitya Prahlāda, indeed struck down [Hiraṇyakaśipu] by tearing open his chest, which was as hard as a stone.
Having attained the ground of Vairocana and having transcended it with his two feet as far as the realm of Brahmā, I bow to that unconquered one who stands above the gods even from his feet.
I bow to that son of Jamadagni, who, through twenty-one offenses committed by Haihaya, became the destroyer of the lineage of the Kṣatriyas.
I bow to Rāmacandra, who manifested in four forms, surrounded by monkeys,
and who destroyed the army of the Rākṣasas.
I worship that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who, having assumed two forms and removed the burden of the earth, withdrew his own lineage.
I worship that Lord, the stainless and pure one, whom they perceive within themselves as the self that completely fills the three worlds, beginning with the earth.
I bow to him who, at the end of the age, having pierced through the wicked and the pure with his sharp, excellent blade,
established the Dharma at the beginning of the Kṛta age.
O Pāṇḍavas, his forms are many such as these;
it is not possible to enumerate them even in millions of years—him I worship.
O lords of sages, since even the gods, asuras, and Manus are unable to reach the ultimate limit of the greatness of His name, how could a mere child like me worship Him? (NarP 1.2.47)
How can I, of meager intellect, praise him by whose mere hearing of the name even men who have committed great sins attain purification? (NarP 1.2.48)
In whatever way their name may be proclaimed or even heard, sinners shall become purified; through faith, they shall attain liberation.
I have gone for refuge to Him whom the yogis, having cast off all impurities, perceive as the embodiment of knowledge by establishing the self within the Self. (NarP 1.2.50)
The followers of Sāṅkhya perceive Hari as the one who brings completion and end to all things;
I worship that primordial god, the undecaying one whose form is knowledge.
I bow to Hari, the Lord who consists of all beings, the peaceful one, the seer of all, the thousand-headed deity, whose essence is pure existence.
I bow to that ageless Lord who devours whatever has been and whatever is yet to be— the world of the moving and the unmoving,
extending ten fingers' breadth.
I bow again and again to the God who is subtler than the subtle, unborn, greater than the great, and more secret than the secret. (NarP 1.2.54)
I bow to that Supreme Person, the Lord, who—whether meditated upon, remembered, worshipped, heard of, or even merely saluted—bestows his own abode. 1.2.55.
Thus praising the Supreme Lord, the lords of sages— Sanandana and the others, together with Nārada— their eyes clouded by tears of joy, approached Him who is the source of all refuge.
Whoever, having risen early in the morning, recites this hymn to Puruṣa,
becomes purified of all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Hymn to Viṣṇu Performed by Nārada," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Nārada.
Nārada said:
How did the all-pervading Primal God create Brahmā and the others in the beginning?
Therefore, O Sanaka, tell me this, since you are omniscient.
Śrī Sanaka said:
Nārāyaṇa is imperishable, infinite, all-pervading, and untainted;
by him this entire world, consisting of the stationary and the moving, is pervaded. (NarP 1.3.2)
At the beginning of creation, Mahāviṣṇu, who is self-luminous and identical with the universe,
presiding over the differentiation of the qualities (guṇas), brought forth the triad of forms.
O Sage, in ancient times, for the purpose of creation, the Lord brought forth from his right limb Prajāpati, and from his middle, the station known as Rudra, the bringer of the world's end.
For the protection of this world, some say that from his left side arose the imperishable Viṣṇu, whom they call the primordial god Śiva, ageless and eternal;
others called him Viṣṇu, and some spoke of him as Brahmā, the ever-true.
The supreme power of Viṣṇu, which impels the activity of the world, is that which consists of the nature of both existence and non-existence; it is celebrated as both knowledge and ignorance.
When the universe is perceived as distinct from Mahāviṣṇu,
then indeed ignorance becomes fully established as the cause of suffering.
O Nārada, when the limiting adjuncts such as the knower and the knowable perish,
that intellect which consists of the single realization of all things is designated as "knowledge" (vidyā).
This Māyā of Mahāviṣṇu is distinct [from Him] and bestows worldly existence;
yet, if perceived through the intellect of non-difference, it brings about the destruction of worldly existence.
All this, including the most excellent, has arisen from the power of Viṣṇu;
for all this is distinct from Him—whatever moves and whatever does not move.
Just as space is perceived as divided by limiting adjuncts,
so too is this entire world perceived as such through its connection with the limiting adjunct of ignorance.
O Sage, just as Hari pervades the universe, so too does his power;
just as the power of burning resides within a coal, pervading its own substrate.
Some call her Umā, others Lakṣmī;
still others call her Bhāratī, Girijā, and Ambikā. (NarP 1.3.13)
She is known as Durgeti, Bhadrakālī, Caṇḍī, and Māheśvarī;
she is Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrī, and Śāmbhavī.
The supreme sages speak of her as Brāhmī, as Vidyā and Avidyā, as Māyā, and likewise as Prakṛti and Parā. 1.3.15.
The supreme residual power of Viṣṇu, which effects the creation and other processes of the universe,
remains pervading the world in both manifest and unmanifest forms.
Primordial Matter (prakṛti), the Spirit (puruṣa), and Time (kāla)—such is the established order;
these three together have become the single cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
By him, assuming the form of Brahmā, this entire universe was brought into being;
therefore, he is called the eternal God who is higher than the highest.
The god who provides protection is eternally so designated;
he is the Supreme Person who provides protection for all the worlds. (NarP 1.3.19)
Higher than that is that which is imperishable, the supreme state.
He is the imperishable, devoid of qualities, pure, perfect, and eternal;
he who is known as beyond time, the object of meditation for yogis, and higher than the highest.
The Supreme Self is supreme bliss, devoid of all limiting adjuncts;
He is the ultimate reality, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who is to be known solely through knowledge.
That which is indeed pure and supreme, yet joined with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), is called "the embodied one" (dehī) by the deluded—alas, what a mockery of ignorance! (NarP 1.3.23)
That supreme, pure God, through the differentiation of the qualities such as *sattva*,
assumes three forms, becoming the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
O Sage, he who is that Brahmā, the creator of the world, born from whose navel-lotus [the universe arose], is himself the very self whose nature is bliss; therefore, there is no other besides him.
The Supreme Lord is indeed the inner controller, pervading the universe, the witness of all, and untainted; He abides in both distinct and non-distinct forms. (NarP 1.3.26)
His power is Mahāmāyā, who sustains the expansion of the universe; because she is the primary cause of the world's origin, she is called Prakṛti by the wise.
At the beginning of creation, when Mahāviṣṇu was intent upon creating the worlds, he became threefold:
as Prakṛti (Nature), Puruṣa (the Spirit), and Kāla (Time).
Those whose selves are cultivated perceive that which is designated as Brahman—
the pure, supreme abode, that highest step of Viṣṇu.

Thus, Maheśvara is pure, imperishable, and infinite; he is the embodiment of time, the embodiment of qualities, the substratum of qualities, the primordial creator of the worlds, and the all-pervading Lord.

When the primordial nature (Prakṛti) became agitated within the World-Teacher known as Puruṣa, the Great One (Mahat), which is Intellect (Buddhi), manifested; from that, the Ego (Ahaṃkāra) arose. (NarP 1.3.31)
And from ego-consciousness arise the subtle elements and the sense organs; indeed, from the subtle elements were born the gross elements for the sake of the world. (NarP 1.3.32)
O son of the one whose nature is the lotus-born, space, wind, fire, water, and earth successively serve as the causes for each one [of the subsequent elements]. (NarP 1.3.33)
Then the Lord Brahmā, the sustainer of the world, created beings of the nature of darkness (tāmasa),
namely creatures belonging to the animal kingdom, such as beasts, birds, and wild animals.
Considering even that creation of the gods to be ineffective,
the one born from the lotus (Brahmā) then fashioned the eternal human creation from the primordial source.
Then [he created] the sons beginning with Dakṣa, who were intent on the means of creation:
"By these sons, this world—including gods, asuras, and humans—is pervaded. (NarP 1.3.36)
Bhūr, bhuvar, svar, as well as mahar, jana,
tapa, and satya— these worlds are situated above Satyaloka.
O best of Brahmins, there are Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala,
Mahātala, and below that, Rasātala.
And Pātāla—thus there are exactly seven netherworlds (pātālas) in succession below. He created the lords of the worlds within all these worlds. (NarP 1.3.39)
And he fashioned the principal mountain ranges and rivers, as well as all the means of subsistence for the inhabitants of those respective worlds, according to what was appropriate.
In the center of the earth stands Mount Meru, the refuge of all the gods;
at the edge of the earth lies the Lokāloka mountain, and in between them are the seven oceans.
O best of Brahmins, there are six islands, and on each island are the principal mountain ranges;
there are also famous outer rivers, and the people resemble the immortals.
Those named Jambū and Plakṣa, as well as Śālmala, Kuśa,
Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara— all these are lands of the gods.
These continents are surrounded by oceans of salt water,
sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water, each equal in size to the one it encircles.
These islands and oceans, extending from the east toward the north,
should be known as being double the width of each preceding one, up to the Lokāloka mountain.
That which lies north of the salt ocean and south of the Mādrī [mountain] should be known as Bhārata-varṣa, which bestows the fruits of all actions.
O Nārada, here they perform three kinds of actions,
and their fruit is experienced according to the sequence of wealth in this land of enjoyment.
But in Bhārata, O best of Brahmins, whatever action is performed, whether auspicious or even inauspicious,
its fruit is exhausted as it is experienced by living beings elsewhere.
Even today, the gods desire birth on the land of Bhārata,
for it possesses a vast, imperishable, stainless, and auspicious merit that has been accumulated.
When shall we obtain birth in the lands of Bhārata, the best of regions?
When, through great merit, shall we go to the supreme state?
"Either by various gifts, or by sacrifices, or by austerities, we shall attain Hari,
the Lord of the World, who is eternal bliss and free from all ailment."
O Nārada, there is no one equal to him in the three worlds who, having reached the land of Bhārata, becomes devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu. (NarP 1.3.52)
Or one who is habitually devoted to the chanting of Hari's glories, or even one who is beloved by His devotees;
or one who possesses pure vision and is known even by the great gods.
One who is constantly devoted to the worship of Hari, whether performing the worship or praising Him,
and who partakes of the food remaining from the devotees' meal, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
He who utters "Nārāyaṇa," "Kṛṣṇa," or "Vāsudeva," being devoted to non-violence and other virtues and possessing peace, is worthy of homage even by the highest of the gods.
He who constantly remembers "Śiva," "Nīlakaṇṭha," and "Śaṅkara," and is ever devoted to the welfare of all beings, is declared by the gods to be worthy of worship.
One who is devoted to the guru, meditates upon Śiva, is intent on the conduct of his own stage of life,
free from envy, pure, and skillful— he too is worthy of worship by the lords of the gods.
One who acts for the welfare of brahmins, possesses faith in the duties of the social orders,
and is constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas— such a person should be known as a sanctifier of the assembly.
He who perceives no difference in the Lord of Gods, whose nature is both Nārāyaṇa and Śiva, sees everything as eternally Brahman; what then need be said of those such as us?
Patient toward cows, practicing celibacy, avoiding the censuring of others,
and possessing the virtue of non-possessiveness— that Nārada is worthy of worship by the gods.
Averse to faults such as theft, grateful, truthful in speech, pure,
and devoted to helping others— he is worthy of worship by gods and asuras alike.
He who possesses the inclination to hear the meaning of the Vedas, as well as to hear the Purāṇas,
and even to associate with the virtuous, is worthy of being saluted by the best of the gods.
Endowed with faith, one performs these and many other such deeds in the land of Bhārata; and our very relationship [with him] is likewise so. (NarP 1.3.63)
Among these, he who does not direct even one toward himself is a fool of evil deeds; there is no other more senseless than him. (NarP 1.3.64)
Having obtained birth in Bhārata, one who is utterly averse to virtuous deeds is like one who,
having drunk from a jar of nectar, resorts instead to a vessel of poison.
O Sage, he who does not purify himself through the duties proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti is a destroyer of his own self and the foremost among sinners.
O Lord of Sages, he who, having reached the land of action, does not practice the Dharma, is declared by those who know the Vedas to be the lowest of all.
He who abandons virtuous action and performs evil deeds is like one who,
having rejected the wish-fulfilling cow, seeks out the milk of a thorny plant.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, even the gods beginning with Brahmā— fearing the exhaustion of their own enjoyments— praise this region of the land of Bhārata.
Therefore, this most excellent Bhārata-varṣa should be known as the most meritorious;
it is difficult even for the gods to attain, and it bestows the fruits of all actions.
And in this meritorious region, whoever is intent upon virtuous deeds—
no one equal to him exists in the three worlds.
Any man born here who is intent on exhausting his own karma—he, though disguised in human form, is Hari; of this there is no doubt.
One who desires the supreme fruit of the world should perform actions without sloth;
for it is taught that by offering the fruit of those actions to Hari with devotion, that fruit indeed becomes imperishable.
If one is dispassionate even toward the fruits of actions, one should perform some work and dedicate that well-done deed, saying: "May Hari be pleased with me."
The worlds up to the realm of Brahmā grant rebirth;
one who is greedy for the fruits of actions attains those, but one who is not attains the supreme state.
One should perform the rites prescribed in the Vedas for the satisfaction of the Lord;
one who desires to renounce according to his stage of life attains the imperishable state.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, one should perform action according to the prescribed rule;
however, one who is devoid of the conduct proper to his own stage of life is declared by the wise to be fallen.
A Brahmin devoted to righteous conduct flourishes through the splendor of his spiritual power (*brahmatejas*);
O Nārada, Viṣṇu is pleased with him when he is endowed with devotion.
He who, having obtained birth in Bhārata, does not deliver himself,
is cooked in a terrible hell until the moon, sun, and stars cease to exist.
Dharma has Vāsudeva as its highest goal; austerity has Vāsudeva as its highest goal;
knowledge has Vāsudeva as its highest goal; the ultimate refuge has Vāsudeva as its highest goal.
The entire world, both moving and unmoving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, has Vāsudeva as its essence; nothing exists apart from him.
He alone is the Creator and He alone is the Destroyer of Tripura; He alone takes the form of the sacrifice of both gods and asuras.
He alone is this entire cosmic egg; there exists nothing else whatsoever that has a separate nature apart from Him.
Beyond this there is nothing else whatsoever; than this there is nothing subtler nor anything greater.
For by Him all this manifold world is pervaded—one should bow down to that God of gods who is ever-present.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Creation, the Excellence of Bharatavarṣa, and the Geography of the Earth," in the first quarter of the Pūrvabhāga of the Śrī Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
All religious duties are preceded by faith and bestow the fruits of one's desires.
Everything is accomplished through faith; indeed, Hari is pleased by faith.
Devotion must be performed through devotion alone, and likewise, ritual actions must be performed with devotion;
for, O best of the twice-born, actions devoid of faith do not succeed.
Just as light has become the cause of activity for living beings,
even so devotion is the supreme cause of all spiritual accomplishments.
Just as water is considered the life-force of all the worlds,
so devotion is held to be the life-force of all spiritual accomplishments.
Just as all living beings depend upon the earth for their livelihood, so too should one accomplish all tasks by relying upon devotion. 1.4.5
One who possesses faith attains the Dharma; one who possesses faith shall obtain the goal. Through faith desire is accomplished; one who possesses faith shall attain liberation.
O best of sages, the Blessed Lord Hari is not pleased by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, if they are devoid of devotion.
Even thousands of millions of crores of gold, equal in weight to Mount Meru,
when given by one devoid of devotion, leads only to the destruction of wealth.
Whatever austerity is performed without devotion is merely the withering of the body;
whatever oblation is offered without devotion is like an offering cast into ashes.
Whatever action a person performs, even if it is as small as an atom, provided it is done with faith—that indeed becomes eternal and yields its fruit for men. (NarP 1.4.10)
O Brahmin, even if one performs a thousand horse-sacrifices as prescribed by the Vedas, all of that is fruitless if it is devoid of devotion.
Devotion to Hari is remembered as being like the wish-fulfilling cow for men;
yet, while it exists, alas, the ignorant drink the poison of worldly existence! 1.4.12.
O son of Aditi, in this essence-less cycle of existence, these are the essences:
association with the devotees of the Blessed One, devotion to Hari, and forbearance. (NarP 1.4.13)
Know, O Brahmā, that whatever action—be it devotion, giving, or other deeds—is performed by those whose minds are possessed of envy, is fruitless; for Hari remains exceedingly distant from them.
For those who are intent on drinking [the nectar of] worldly splendor, whose souls delight in hypocritical conduct,
and who perform actions falsely— for them, Hari is exceedingly far away.
And for those who inquire about the great dharmas while speaking falsely to them,
whose minds lack devotion toward the dharmas, Hari is very far away.
The Dharma is established in the Veda, and the Veda is the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
but for those who are devoted to lack of faith therein, Hari is very far away.
He whose days come and go devoid of Dharma does not truly live, even though he breathes like a blacksmith's bellows.
The eternal goals of human life, known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, are indeed accomplished by those possessed of faith, O son of Brahmā; not otherwise.
Indeed, he who is devoted to the worship of Hari without transgressing his own proper conduct goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, which the wise behold.
O Lord of Sages, he who, devoted to meditation on Hari, performs the duties prescribed by the Vedas appropriate to his own stage of life, attains the supreme state. (NarP 1.4.21)
Dharma originates from right conduct, and Acyuta is the lord of Dharma;
Hari is always worshipped by one who is endowed with the conduct appropriate to his stage of life (āśrama).
He who has fallen away from his own proper conduct is to be known as an outcast, even if he has mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches; for he is excluded from ritual action.
Whether one is devoted to the service of Hari or intent on meditation upon Hari,
if he falls away from the conduct prescribed for his own stage of life, he is called fallen.
O best of the twice-born, neither the Veda, nor devotion to Hari, nor even devotion to Maheśvara can purify a fool who has fallen from right conduct.
O Brahmin, visiting fields of merit, resorting to sacred fords, or performing various sacrifices— none of these protect one who has abandoned right conduct.
Through right conduct heaven is attained; through right conduct happiness is attained;
through right conduct liberation is attained; what is there that cannot be obtained through right conduct? (NarP 1.4.27)
O most excellent one, for all modes of conduct and indeed for all yogas,
devotion to Hari is likewise held to be the primary cause.
"Viṣṇu, the bestower of the fruits of desired objects, is worshipped through devotion alone;
therefore, devotion is sung of as the mother of all the worlds. (NarP 1.4.29)
Just as all living beings live by depending upon their mothers,
so do all righteous people live by relying upon devotion.
O son of Aja, when one who is devoted to the conduct of his own stage of life becomes a devotee of Hari,
there is no one equal to him in the three worlds.
Through devotion, actions are perfected; Hari is pleased by those actions. When He is pleased, knowledge arises; from knowledge, liberation is attained. (NarP 1.4.32)
Devotion indeed arises through association with the devotees of the Blessed One;
that association is attained by men through previously accumulated meritorious deeds.
Devoted to the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life, longing for devotion to the Blessed One,
and liberated from defects such as desire, those virtuous ones are teachers of the world.
O Brahmā, this supreme eightfold yoga is not attained by those who have not disciplined themselves;
yet if it should be attained, one must recognize that it is the merit acquired in previous births. (NarP 1.4.35)
The sins accumulated in the past truly come to destruction for one who attains the company of the virtuous; indeed, that [company] does not occur otherwise.
For the sun destroys external darkness during the day with its web of rays;
likewise, the virtuous always destroy inner darkness with the rays of their well-spoken words.
Rare in this world are those men who long for devotion to the Blessed One;
for him whose association with such persons occurs, there is indeed eternal peace.
Nārada said: What are the characteristics of the Bhāgavatas, and what actions do they perform?
Of what nature is their world? Tell me all that in accordance with reality.
For you are a devotee of Rameśa, the God of gods, the wondrous one;
you are capable of describing these matters, and there is no other superior to you.
Sanaka said:
Listen, O wise Brahmin, to the supreme secret that the Lord of the World, released from his yogic sleep, spoke to the intelligent Mārkaṇḍeya.
He who is Viṣṇu, the supreme light, the god of gods, the eternal creator of the world, whose nature is Śiva-Brahman.
At the end of the eon, having seized the cosmic egg in his fierce form,
when the world has become a single ocean and all things mobile and immobile have perished— (NarP 1.4.43)
The Blessed One, Hari himself, the soul of all that remains, reclines upon a banyan leaf,
his body-hairs adorned by the countless births of Brahmās and other beings.
Purified by the cool waters of the Gaṅgā flowing from the tip of his big toe,
the Lord is subtler than the subtlest, yet he is nourished by the swallowing of the cosmic egg.
Reclining upon the banyan leaf,
the illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya remained in that place, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, endowed with all powers, and beholding the divine sports of the Great Lord.
The sages said:
"O sage, we have heard from of old that at that most terrible time, when all things mobile and immobile had perished, Hari alone remained."
When the world had become a single ocean and all things, both mobile and immobile, had perished,
for what purpose was he left remaining by Hari, who devours everything?
O Sūta, a supreme curiosity indeed prevails within us here; for who among living beings could ever feel indolence toward drinking the nectar of Hari’s glory? 1.49.
Sūta said:
There was a highly fortunate sage renowned as Mṛkaṇḍu;
that great ascetic performed intense penance at the great holy site of Śālagrāma.
O Brahmin, reciting the eternal Brahman for ten million ages,
he remained without food, endowed with patience, true to his promise, and having conquered his senses.
Beholding all beings as his own self, free from desire for sense-objects,
devoted to the welfare of all beings, and self-controlled, he performed most great asceticism.
Then all the gods, Indra and the others, fearing his heat,
went for refuge to the Supreme Lord, the unblemished Nārāyaṇa.
Having reached the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, the inhabitants of the triple heaven praised the Lord of the gods, the lotus-navelled teacher of the world.
The gods said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Imperishable One, O Infinite One, protector of those who have come for refuge!
Protect us, who have sought your shelter, as we are terrified by the ascetic power of Mṛkaṇḍu.
Victory to you, O Lord of the lords of gods; victory to you, the wielder of the conch and the mace!
Victory to you whose nature is the world; victory to you, the cause of the universe!
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, O Purifier of the worlds! Salutations to you, the Protector of the world; salutations to you, the Witness of the world. (NarP 1.4.57)
Homage to you who are attainable through meditation; homage to you who are the cause of meditation;
homage to you whose form is meditation; homage to you who are the companion of meditation.
Salutations to you, the slayer of Keśin, the slayer of Madhu, the Supreme Self;
salutations to you who take the form of the earth and other elements, and salutations to you whose form is pure consciousness.
Homage to the Eldest, to the Pure, to the One devoid of qualities yet the soul of all qualities; homage to You who are formless, whose nature is self-manifest, and who possess manifold forms.
Homage to the God who is the friend of Brahman, and to Him who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins;
homage again and again to Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, who acts for the benefit of the world.

Homage to Him who has the syllables *hi*, *kṣa*, *ma*, and *ga* as His essence; homage to Him who possesses the forms of Brahmā and the other gods; homage to Him who takes the form of the Sun and the other luminaries; homage to the consumer of the sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
Homage to the eternal one, worthy of worship, whose singular form is perpetual bliss;
homage to the destroyer of suffering when remembered; again and again, homage, homage!
Having thus heard the praise of the gods, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Kamalā, bearing the conch,
the discus, and the mace, appeared before their very eyes.
With eyes like the petals of a full-blown lotus, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
adorned with every ornament, and his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Wearing yellow garments, gentle, with a golden sacred thread,
he was being praised by the best of sages and surrounded by his foremost attendants.
Seeing him, those hosts of gods, their own splendor eclipsed by his brilliance,
paid homage with joy, prostrating themselves with the eight limbs of reverence.
Then the Blessed One, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, being pleased, spoke to the gods who were bowing down, headed by Indra: NarP_1,4.68 //
The Blessed One said:
"O gods, I know the mental anguish of yours arising from the penance of Mṛkaṇḍu; that sage, the foremost among the virtuous, does not afflict you."
O best of gods, whether endowed with prosperity or even beset by calamities, virtuous people do not harm others in any way, even in their dreams.
Even while being constantly oppressed by the enemies known as the sense-objects, how could a wise person, failing to provide protection for himself, harbor hatred toward others? (NarP 1.4.71)
For how could a human being, who is oppressed by what are called the three types of suffering,
be capable of playing with others, O best of beings?
He who constantly harms others through action, mind, or speech, and is perpetually possessed by desire and the like, is called one of deluded intellect. (NarP 1.4.73)

O best of beings, that mortal who acts for the welfare of the world, who is free from death, and who is devoid of envy and fear, is proclaimed by the virtuous as "Amātra" both here and hereafter. (NarP 1.4.74)
One who is full of doubt is always miserable; one free from doubt attains happiness.
Go to your own homes at ease; he will not play with you.
"And I am your protector; dwell at your ease.
Having thus granted them this boon, he who possesses the luster of the Atasi flower [disappeared].
Even as the gods were looking on, he vanished right there;
with their souls satisfied, the hosts of deities returned to heaven as they had come.
But to Mṛkaṇḍu as well, Hari, being pleased in spirit, appeared in person—
that formless, supreme Brahman, self-luminous and stainless.
Seeing him, who resembled an *atasī* flower, was clad in yellow garments,
was free from decay, and bore divine weapons, Mṛkaṇḍu was filled with wonder.
Opening his eyes from meditation, he beheld before him Hari,
whose face was serene, who was peaceful, the sustainer of all, and possessed of universal splendor.
With his body bristling with horripilation and his eyes filled with tears of joy,
he prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before the eternal God of gods.
Washing his feet with tears born of joy and placing his folded hands upon his head, he began to offer praise.
Mṛkaṇḍu said:
Salutations to the Supreme Lord, whose form is the supreme Self; who is higher than the highest, beyond the beyond, and more remote than the remote;
who is the shoreless shore, the benefactor of others, salutations to him who is beyond all and the one who carries others across.

I worship that supreme Lord worthy of praise, who is free from conceptual constructions such as name and genus, whose nature is distinct from defects such as sound, and who, though possessing many forms, remains untainted.

I worship the primordial Lord, the first one worthy of praise, who is to be known by the gods, the ancient Puruṣa whose nature is the world beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha, the incomparable one who feels compassion for his devotees. NarP_1,4.85.
I bow to Him, the supreme purifier who brings an end to saṃsāra, whom those free from all defects, devoted solely to meditation, devoid of longing, and with delusion ceased, behold.

I seek refuge in Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the suffering of those who remember him, the protector of those who have come for shelter, the one served by the world, the abode of the universe, the Supreme Lord, and the source of compassion. (NarP 1.4.87)
Thus praised by that great seer, the Blessed One Viṣṇu,
the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace, attained supreme satisfaction.
Having embraced the sage with his four long arms, the god, out of supreme affection, said: "O you of noble vows, choose a boon."
"I am pleased with that austerity and with your hymn, O sinless one.
Choose whatever boon you desire in your mind, O observer of noble vows."
Mṛkaṇḍu said:
O God of gods, Lord of the world, I have achieved my purpose; of this there is no doubt, for it is remembered that the sight of you is difficult to obtain for those devoid of merit.
Even Brahmā and the others do not perceive him, nor do the yogins of firm vows,
nor those most righteous, nor even those initiated, who are free from passion and devoid of envy.
I behold that supreme abode; what other boon than this could I choose?
By this alone, O Janārdana, bearer of the world, I have achieved my life's purpose.
O Acyuta, having seen those who, by the mere remembrance of his name, go to that supreme state even if they are great sinners—what wonder is there? (NarP 1.4.94)
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, you have spoken the truth; I am pleased with you, O wise one.
Indeed, my sight shall never be in vain."
"The gods always say that Viṣṇu is one whose family consists of his devotees;
I shall protect that very principle, for a man should not speak untruth. (NarP 1.4.96)
Therefore, being pleased by your asceticism, I shall enter into your state as a son—
endowed with all virtues, long-lived, and possessed of a beautiful form.
O best of sages, when I am pleased, what is impossible to achieve in the three worlds for that family into which I am born—a family that indeed attains liberation? (NarP 1.4.98)
Having spoken thus while the sage Atri was looking on, the God of gods vanished; and Mṛkaṇḍu devoted himself once more to his ascetic penance.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Life of Mārkaṇḍeya," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, occurring in the context of the description of devotion.
Nārada said:
"O Brahman, how did that Blessed One become the son of Mṛkaṇḍu?"
And what did Hari, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, do then? Tell that.
And it is heard in the Purāṇas that the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya beheld the Vaiṣṇava illusion during the dissolution of the one who lives for a long time.
Sanaka said:
Listen, O Nārada, as I shall recount this eternal narrative concerning the sage Mārkaṇḍeya, which is filled with devotion to Viṣṇu.
At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, O best of men, that Mṛkaṇḍu married a wife and,
joyful, tranquil, self-controlled, and having accomplished his purpose, he lived the life of a householder.
His wife was pure and skillful, eternally devoted to her husband;
she was a faithful wife in thought, word, and deed.
In due time, she conceived a fetus born from a portion of Hari’s splendor;
at the end of ten months, she gave birth to a son, the supreme among the radiant.
Seeing his son endowed with auspicious marks, that seer was exceedingly pleased;
he had the birth ceremony performed according to the prescribed rites for the sake of prosperity.
There that boy grew like the moon in the bright fortnight;
then, in his fifth year, he was initiated with great joy.
O best of Brahmins, he imparted the Vedic instruction concerning the dharma:
"My son, the twice-born must always be saluted and properly honored according to the prescribed rules."
Having worshipped the Sun three times a day by offering water and handfuls of flowers,
one should perform the Vedic rites preceded by the study of the Vedas.
Hari is always to be worshipped through celibacy and austerity;
that which is forbidden, such as looking at or conversing with [unfit persons], must be avoided. (NarP 1.5.11)
One should always dwell with the virtuous who are devoted to Viṣṇu;
one should not harbor hatred toward anyone, but should act for the welfare of all.
"Sacrifices, Vedic study, and giving of gifts must always be performed by you, my son.
Thus was Mārkaṇḍeya, the lord of sages, instructed by his father.
The highly fortunate Mārkaṇḍeya, compassionate and devoted to righteousness, constantly practiced dharma while always meditating upon Hari.
Self-possessed and true to his word, with a splendor like that of the sun,
he was self-controlled, tranquil, a man of great wisdom, and skilled in the meaning of all principles.
The wise Mārkaṇḍeya performed austerities for the sake of pleasing the Great Acyuta; thus was the Lord of the World propitiated by him.
The Imperishable One (Acyuta) granted a boon to the author of the Purāṇasaṃhitā.
The sage Mārkaṇḍeya performed supreme austerity for the sake of pleasing Acyuta;
therefore, the sage Mārkaṇḍeya is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
A long-lived and great devotee of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods,
Janārdana displayed his own power when the world had become a single ocean.
To show it to him, Hari did not withdraw that expanded form;
for the wise son of Mṛkaṇḍu was fully endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu.
Mārkaṇḍeya remained in that most terrible water like a withered leaf,
staying there as long as Hari himself lay asleep.
I shall state its measure; listen as I speak of time.
It is proclaimed to consist of fifteen *nimeṣas*. (NarP 1.5.21)
O son of Brahmā, thirty *kāṣṭhās* should be known as one *kalā*;
thirty *kalās* should be known as one *kṣaṇa*, and five of those are recorded as one *ghaṭikā*.
Two of those [nāḍīs] make one muhūrta; thirty of those make a day;
and thirty days, together with two fortnights, constitute a month. (NarP 1.5.23)
A season (*ṛtu*) consists of two months; three of those are known as a solstice (*ayana*);
two of those constitute a year (*abda*), which becomes a single day for the gods.
They say that the northern course is day and the southern course is night;
by a human month alone, a day of the ancestors is said to be measured.
Therefore, at the conjunction of the sun and the moon, the supreme Kalpa should be known;
twelve thousand divine years constitute a divine Yuga.
Two thousand divine yugas constitute two Brahmā-kalpas for humans;
a Manvantara consists of one hundred and seventy-one such divine yugas.
O sage, by these fourteen [periods], a day of Brahmā is completed;
as long as the duration of the day is, so long is the night proclaimed to be.
O best of Brahmins, at that time the three worlds do not perish;
hear now what its measure is in terms of thousands of human years. (NarP 1.5.29)
O Sage, four thousand yugas constitute a day of Brahmā;
likewise, his month and year are to be understood in the same manner.
O brahmins, according to his view, a period of two parārdhas constitutes a single day of Viṣṇu; his night is likewise proclaimed to be of equal duration.
The son of Mṛkaṇḍu remained there like a withered leaf;
in that terrible watery expanse, sustained by the power of Viṣṇu,
he stood in the presence of Hari, meditating upon his own supreme self.
Then, when the time had arrived, released from his yogic sleep,
he created this world of moving and unmoving beings in the form of Brahmā.
Having seen the waters withdrawn and the universe created, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu was filled with wonder and,
supremely delighted, prostrated at the feet of Hari.
Placing his joined palms upon his head, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya praised Him whose singular form is eternal bliss with pleasing words.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: I bow down to the thousand-headed god Nārāyaṇa, the untainted Vāsudeva, the supportless Janārdana.
I bow down to Janārdana, who is immeasurable, undecaying, eternal, whose singular form is perpetual bliss, inconceivable, and indefinable.
I bow down to Janārdana, the supreme, eternal syllable, who is without eyes yet the source of the universe, who consists of all principles, and who is peaceful.
I bow down to Janārdana, the ancient Puruṣa, the perfected one, the sole vessel of all knowledge, the form that is higher than the highest.
I bow down to Janārdana, the supreme light, the highest abode, the ultimate purifier, the supreme state, who is of one and the same form in all things.
I bow down to Janārdana, who is eternal bliss and pure consciousness, the supreme state beyond the highest, the all-encompassing, the ancient, and the most excellent.
I bow down to that Janārdana, who possesses qualities and is devoid of qualities, who is peaceful, beyond illusion yet the master of illusion, who is formless and yet possesses many forms.
I bow down to that primordial god, the Lord Janārdana, wherein he creates, maintains, and destroys the universe.
O Supreme Lord, supreme bliss, compassionate toward those who have come for refuge; save me, O ocean of mercy! Thus, salutations be unto You. (NarP 1.5.44)
To the lord of brahmins, Mārkaṇḍeya, the teacher of the world, who was thus offering praise,
the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace spoke with supreme affection.
The Blessed One said:
"Those in the world who are devotees of the Lord and whose minds are fixed on the Lord—
of them I am pleased, without a doubt, and I protect them at all times."
O best of the twice-born, I myself am always present in a concealed form;
I constantly protect the worlds in the guise of devotees of the Blessed One.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "What are the characteristics of those who are born as Bhāgavatas, and by what action do they become so?
Since I am filled with curiosity, I desire to hear this."
The Blessed One said: "O best of sages, listen to the characteristics of the Bhāgavatas;
for it is not possible to describe their power even in ten million years."
Those who are beneficial to all living beings, free from envy and devoid of malice, pure,
desireless, and peaceful— they indeed are the supreme devotees of the Lord.
Those who do not cause suffering to others through action, mind, or speech,
and who possess the virtue of non-possessiveness, are indeed remembered as Bhāgavatas.
Those whose minds are characterized by goodness when listening to sacred discourses, who are devoted to Him and devoted to Viṣṇu—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas. (NarP 1.5.52)
Those best of men who perform service for their mother and father with the same devotion as they would toward Gaṅgā and Viśveśvara are indeed the most excellent devotees of the Lord.

Those who are devoted to the worship of the gods, and those who are remembered as practitioners of that [worship], who rejoice upon seeing the ritual offering—they indeed are the most excellent Bhāgavatas. (NarP 1.5.54)
Those who are intent on serving those who observe vows and ascetics,
and who are free from censuring others— they are the best of the Bhāgavatas.
Those best of men who speak words beneficial to all,
and who perceive the virtues in the world— they indeed are remembered as Bhāgavatas.
Those best of men who see all beings as they do themselves,
remaining equal toward enemies and friends, are indeed the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
Those who expound the Dharmaśāstras, those who delight in truthful speech,
and those who serve the virtuous— they indeed are the most excellent Bhāgavatas.
Those who expound the Purāṇas, those who listen to them in that manner,
and those who are devoted to their speaker— they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas.
Those men who constantly perform service to cows and Brahmins,
and those who are devoted to pilgrimages to sacred fords, are indeed the most excellent Bhāgavatas.
Those men who, seeing the prosperity of others, rejoice,
and those who are devoted to the name of Hari— they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas.
Those who delight in planting groves, those who protect ponds,
and those who construct lakes and wells— they indeed are the most excellent devotees of the Bhagavān.
Those who construct tanks, those who perform hundreds of sacrifices to the gods,
and those who are devoted to the Gāyatrī— these indeed are the most excellent Bhāgavatas.
Those who, upon hearing the names of Hari, rejoice with exceeding joy and have their bodies covered in horripilation— they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas.
Those men who, upon seeing a grove of Tulasī, offer their salutations,
and whose ears are marked by its wood— verily, they are the best among the devotees of the Lord.
Those who feel satisfaction upon smelling the fragrance of *tulasī*, and those who [smell] the clay from its roots—they indeed are the best of *bhāgavatas*. (NarP 1.5.66)
Those who are devoted to the conduct of their respective stages of life, likewise those who honor guests,
and those who expound the meaning of the Vedas— they indeed are the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
Those who are dear to Śiva, those who are devoted to Śiva, those who delight in the worship of Śiva’s feet,
and those who wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)— they indeed are the supreme devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatottama).
And those who utter the names of Hari and the high-souled Śambhu, and who are adorned with rudrākṣa beads, they indeed are the best of the Bhāgavatas. (NarP 1.5.69)
Those who worship Mahādeva with seasonal sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
or who worship Hari with supreme devotion— they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas.
Those who have mastered the scriptures and speak for the sake of others,
and who possess virtue in all circumstances— they indeed are remembered as Bhāgavatas.
Those who proceed with equanimity toward Śiva, the Supreme Lord, Viṣṇu, and the Supreme Self— they indeed are remembered as Bhāgavatas.
Those who are devoted to the service of the fire of Śiva, who delight in the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra,
and who are intent on meditation upon Śiva— they indeed are the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
Those who are devoted to the gift of water, as well as those devoted to the gift of food,
and those devoted to the Ekādaśī vow, are indeed the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
Those who are devoted to the gift of cows, those who are devoted to the gift of daughters,
and those who perform service for my sake— they indeed are the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
O Brahmin, these few Bhāgavatas have been proclaimed here;
even by me, they could not be fully described even in hundreds of millions of years.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, you too should always be well-behaved,
a refuge for all beings, self-controlled, gentle, and devoted to dharma.
Furthermore, practicing all righteousness until the end of the age and remaining devoted to meditation on my form, you shall attain supreme nirvāṇa.
Thus, having granted a boon to his own devotee, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, that Lord of Gods, a treasury of compassion, vanished right there.
The highly fortunate Mārkaṇḍeya, who was always devoted to the worship of Hari,
practiced the supreme dharma and performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rites.
In the great field of Śālaprāma, he performed supreme austerity;
having exhausted his karma through meditation, he attained the ultimate Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, one who acts for the benefit of all living beings and worships Hari will undoubtedly obtain whatever he desires in his mind. (NarP 1.5.82)
Sanaka said:
"O best of the twice-born, all this that was asked by you has been narrated—the majesty of devotion to the Blessed One. What else do you wish to hear?"
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Mārkaṇḍeya," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having heard the majesty of devotion to the Blessed One, Nārada was indeed pleased.
He questioned Sanaka again, who had reached the further shore of both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom.

Nārada said: O you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of the scriptures, please tell me truly, out of supreme compassion, that which is the best of all sacred fields and likewise the best of all holy fords.
Sanaka said:
Listen to the supreme secret concerning the interval between Brahmās, which brings about all prosperity,
destroys evil dreams, is meritorious, righteous, sin-removing, and auspicious.
This should be constantly heard by sages as a means for warding off malevolent planets, pacifying all diseases, and increasing one's lifespan. (NarP 1.6.4)
The supreme sages declare that the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is the best of all fields and likewise the most excellent of all sacred fords.
At the sacred ford where the waters are white and black, Brahmā and all the other deities,
as well as the sages and the Manus, resort there, desiring merit.
The Gaṅgā is to be known as the meritorious river because it originates from the foot of Viṣṇu;
O Brahman, the Yamunā is born from the Sun, and their confluence brings auspiciousness.
O Sage, Gaṅgā is remembered as the destroyer of suffering and the most excellent of rivers;
she brings about the destruction of all sins and the eradication of all calamities.

O great sage, among all those meritorious fields upon the surface of the earth that lie as far as the edge of the ocean, that which is known as Prayāga should be known as the most meritorious of them all.
There, the Creator performed a sacrifice for the Lord who is the husband of Ramā,
and likewise all the sages performed various kinds of sacrifices.
Whatever merits belong to all the ablutions at sacred fords, they are not worth even a sixteenth part of the merit from an ablution with a single drop of the Gaṅgā.
Even one who, standing a hundred yojanas away, should say "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," would be liberated from sins; how much more so one who has performed an ablution in the Gaṅgā?
The goddess born from the foot of Viṣṇu, who dwells upon the head of the Lord of the Universe, is to be served by the sages; O God, how much more so by common folk?
That which is worn on the forehead by the best of men should be known as the eye; it blazes intensely, pierced through its center and below.
What supreme thing can be said to be greater than this bathing, which yields great merit, is difficult even for the inhabitants of heaven to attain, and bestows conformity with Viṣṇu? (NarP 1.6.15)
Where even sinners, having bathed, are freed from all sins,
mount great celestial chariots and proceed to the supreme state.
Having bathed there, high-souled ones indeed deliver thousands of their paternal and maternal lineages and proceed to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who remembers the Gaṅgā twice a day has bathed in all sacred fords;
he has dwelt in all holy places—of this there is no doubt.
Seeing a man who has bathed there, even a sinner becomes a partaker of the heavenly realm;
by the mere touch of my body, he shall become the foremost among the gods.
The earth originating from the root of the Tulasī plant, as well as that produced from the feet of the twice-born and that arising from the Gaṅgā, leads the worlds to the state of being like Acyuta.
The Gaṅgā, Tulasī, and unwavering devotion to Hari are extremely difficult for men to obtain; so too is devotion toward one who proclaims the Dharma. (NarP 1.6.21)

A person endowed with devotion, having placed upon his head the clay originating from the footprint of the speaker of the True Dharma, as well as that from the Ganges and from the root of the Tulasī plant, and likewise the word of Viṣṇu— NarP_1,6.22.
"When shall I go to the Gaṅgā? When shall I behold her?"—even he who desires thus shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin, even by Viṣṇu, let alone by others, it is not possible to describe the greatness of the Gaṅgā even in hundreds of years; what is the use of further words?
"Oh, how wonderful it is that this illusion deludes the entire world, for indeed people go to hell even while the Gaṅgā stands right before their eyes! (NarP 1.6.25)
The severance of the suffering of saṃsāra is proclaimed by the name of Gaṅgā;
likewise, devotion to Tulasī is [the means] for one who proclaims the glory of Hari.
Whoever should utter even once these two syllables, "Gaṅgā," being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who travels three yojanas along the Ganges is indeed liberated from all sins and attains the world of the Sun.
This most meritorious river Gaṅgā, when served with devotion during the signs of Aries,
Libra, Capricorn, and Cancer, purifies the entire world.
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇā, Revā, Sarasvatī,
Tuṅgabhadrā, Kāverī, Kālindī, and likewise the Bāhudā.
O best of the twice-born, among such sacred fords as the Vetravatī, the Tāmraparṇī, and the Sarayū,
the Gaṅgā is remembered as the most preeminent.
Just as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, established by pervading the entire world,
so too is this Gaṅgā all-pervasive, destroying all sins.
"Aha! How is it that this Gaṅgā, the mother of the world and purifier, who sanctifies the world through bathing, drinking, and other such acts, is not resorted to by men? (NarP 1.6.33)
Vārāṇasī is renowned as the most excellent of holy places among all holy places, and the most excellent of sacred fields among all sacred fields; it is frequented by all the gods.
Those two ears alone are truly blessed with great learning for those learned men who have heard of Kāśī here more than once. (NarP 1.6.35)
Those best of the twice-born who remember this sacred site, Avimukta,
have all their sins shaken off and indeed go to the world of Śiva.
Even if one stands a hundred yojanas away, if one should remember Avimukta,
then even if filled with many sins, one goes to the state that is free from ailment.
O noble one, he who remembers Avimukta at the time of the departure of the vital breath shall also be liberated from sin and attain the state of Śiva.
Having enjoyed in heaven the merit born from remembering Kāśī,
and at its conclusion having become a sole ruler upon the earth, one who reaches Kāśī becomes a partaker of liberation.
What is the use of saying much more regarding the virtues of Vārāṇasī?
For those who even utter the name of Kāśī, the fourfold aim of human life is not far off.
O twice-born ones, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is even more excellent than Kāśī;
by the mere sight of it, men attain the supreme goal.
When the sun is situated in Capricorn, the Gaṅgā— wherever she may be plunged into—
purifies the world through bathing, drinking, and so forth, leading it to the city of Indra.
How can the greatness of Gaṅgā be fully proclaimed, she whom Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, constantly honors in the form of a *liṅga*? 6.43.
Hari assumes the form of the Liṅga, and Hari assumes the form of the Liṅga;
there is not even the slightest difference between them, and it is only the person of dull intellect who perceives a distinction between the two.
In the God who is without beginning or end, known by the names Hari and Śaṅkara,
sinful people, submerged in the ocean of ignorance, create divisions.
"That god who is the soul of the worlds and the cause of all causes—at the end of the age, they declare this to be Hari bearing the form of Rudra. (NarP 1.6.46)
Rudra indeed protects the entire world in the form of Viṣṇu;
he creates it in the form of Brahmā; at the end, Hara is this triad itself.
That man who creates a distinction between Hari, Śaṅkara, and even Brahmā,
goes to a most dreadful hell.
He who perceives Hara, Hari, and the Creator as having one and the same form attains supreme bliss; this is the essential purport of all the scriptures.
There, Janārdana— He who is beginningless, omniscient, the primordial creator of the worlds, and all-pervading— remains eternally present in the form of the *liṅga*.
The Lord of Kāśī is called the Liṅga-Jyotirliṅga;
by beholding Him, the best of men attains the supreme light.
By him who has performed the circumambulation of Kāśī, the purifier of the three worlds,
the entire earth— with its continents, oceans, and mountains— has been traversed.
The stainless images of Śiva— whether made of clay, wood, stone, or inscribed on a surface— and likewise those of Acyuta (Viṣṇu), in them Hari is truly present.
O twice-born ones, wherever there is a grove of *tulasī*, wherever there is a forest of lotuses,
wherever there is the recitation of the Purāṇas— there Hari is ever present.
The speaker of the Purāṇa-saṃhitā is called Hari;
for men who practice devotion to him, it is as if they were bathing daily in the Gaṅgā.
O twice-born one, devotion to hearing the Purāṇas is equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā;
and the devotion toward its speaker is remembered as being comparable to Prayāga.
He who rescues the world submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra by narrating the ancient dharma is celebrated as Hari.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no teacher equal to one's mother;
there is no deity equal to Viṣṇu; and there is no reality higher than that of the Guru.
As the Brāhmaṇa is the best among the social classes, as the moon is among the stars,
and as the ocean is among rivers, so is the Gaṅgā remembered as supreme.
There is no kinsman equal to peace; there is no austerity superior to truth;
there is no gain greater than liberation; and there is no river equal to the Gaṅgā.
The supreme name of the Gaṅgā is a forest fire to the wilderness of sin;
the Gaṅgā removes the disease of worldly existence, therefore she should be served with diligent effort.
Both the Gāyatrī and the Jāhnavī are remembered as removers of all sins;
one should know that twice-born man who is devoid of devotion to these two to be fallen.
Gāyatrī is the mother of the meters, and Jāhnavī is the mother of the world;
both of them have become the cause for the destruction of all sins. (NarP 1.6.63)
For one whose Gāyatrī is pleased, the Gaṅgā becomes pleased;
those two, joined with the power of Viṣṇu, accomplish all desires simultaneously.
These two most excellent [teachings] proceed for the sake of benefiting all the worlds, appearing in the form of fruits consisting of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, which are themselves stainless.
Gāyatrī and likewise the Jāhnavī are exceedingly difficult for men to obtain;
so too are devotion to Tulasī and pure, sattvic devotion to Hari.
Oh, how fortunate is the Gaṅgā! She is remembered as the destroyer of sins;
when seen, she bestows the world of Hari; when drunk, she grants the state of similarity [to the Divine];
and where men who have bathed go to the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu.
Nārāyaṇa, the sustainer of the world, Vāsudeva, the eternal one,
bestows the fruits of desired objects upon those devoted to bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Even that best of men who is sprinkled with the water of the Gaṅgā,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme state.
Merely by serving that drop, he who was born of the lineage of Sagara cast off his demonic nature and attained the supreme state.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gaṅgā," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Nārada said:
Who was it in the lineage of Sagara that was indeed liberated from the state of being a Rākṣasa?
"O best of sages, who was Sagara? You should explain that to me."
Sanaka said:
Listen, O tiger among sages, to the supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā,
by the mere touch of whose water the lineage of the ocean was purified.
O Brahmin, he has gone to the station of Viṣṇu, the most excellent of all the worlds.
In the solar dynasty there was one named Bāhu, the son of Vṛka;
devoted to righteousness, he ruled the entire earth according to dharma.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other living beings were established by him, the lord of the people, each in their respective duties. (NarP 1.7.4)
He performed horse sacrifices with seven priests on the seven continents;
he gratified the gods of the earth with cattle, land, gold, garments, and other gifts.
He subdued his adversaries at will according to the science of polity; he considered himself to have achieved his purpose by warding off the afflictions of others.
O Sage, because people in that kingdom always offer pleasing sandalwood and oblations,
and are adorned with divine ornaments, they are happy.
The earth yielded crops without being ploughed, and was endowed with fruits and flowers.
The lord of gods rained upon the earth at the proper times; under that lord of sages, the subjects—who had previously been devoted to unrighteousness—were protected by dharma.
Once, a great lack of self-respect arose in that king, which destroyed all his prosperity; it was accompanied by malice and caused by the loss [of his kingdom].
"I am the king, the powerful protector of all the worlds and the performer of great sacrifices; who else is more worthy of worship than I? (NarP 1.7.11)
"I am wise and illustrious; all my enemies have been conquered by me.
I am a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and I am proficient in the treatises on ethics. (NarP 1.7.12)
"Invincible and possessing unimpeded sovereignty, who else on earth is superior to me?"—in one thus preoccupied with egoism, envy toward others arises. (NarP 1.7.13)
O Lord of Sages, from that envy arose desire in that king:
"While these [sages] remain here, a man will undoubtedly meet his destruction. (NarP 1.7.14)
Youth, the abundance of wealth, power, and lack of discernment—each one alone leads to misfortune; how much more so where all four are present?
Great envy has arisen within him, which is hostile to the world, destructive to his own body, and a destroyer of all prosperity. (NarP 1.7.16)
O observer of noble vows, know that if prosperity should arise in a mind possessed by envy, it is like the contact of wind with a fire of chaff. 1.7.17.
For those whose minds are possessed by envy, who behave with hypocrisy,
and who delight in harsh speech, there is no happiness either in this world or in the next.
For those whose minds are possessed by envy and who always speak harshly,
even their beloved wife, their sons, or even their kinsmen become enemies.
He who, having gazed upon another's wife, forms a longing for her, is an axe for the destruction of his own prosperity; of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.7.20)
O Sage, that man of evil intellect who, seeing the welfare of all, would make an effort for the destruction of his own well-being, would be committing a great folly.
O twice-born one, a man who desires the loss of friends, children, home, fields, wealth, grain, and even cattle, should constantly practice malice.
Then, for that undisciplined man whose mind was possessed by malice,
there arose powerful enemies— the Haihayas and the Tāla-jaṅghas.
For whom Lakṣmī’s Lord is favorable, his good fortune increases;
for whom He is turned away, his good fortune diminishes.
O Nārada, sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, houses, and so forth remain only as long as the Lord of Fortune gazes with a compassionate side-long glance.
O best of Brahmins, even fools, the blind, the deaf, and the dull-witted, as well as the brave and the discerning, become praiseworthy if they are looked upon by Mādhava.
The good fortune of that person whose character is marked by envy and the like surely declines;
there is no doubt in this matter, especially regarding hatred toward living beings. (NarP 1.7.27)
O best of sages, whatever man constantly harbors hatred toward anyone whatsoever, all his spiritual merits perish.
Viṣṇu turns his face away from him in whom envy increases;
from him, wealth, grain, and land will certainly depart. (NarP 1.7.29)
The absence of egoism destroys discernment, and from a lack of discernment, calamities surely arise for living beings; therefore, one should abandon the absence of egoism. (NarP 1.7.30)
For that king whose mind is possessed by envy and who harbors the sense of "I," destruction will come with extreme speed at the hands of his enemies.
He was defeated by his enemies, the Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas, for one continuous month in a most terrible battle.
But that Bāhu, though distressed by his pregnant wife,
attained supreme satisfaction upon seeing that great lake there.
And observing his state of mind, which was filled with malice, those birds dwelling in the tree remained hidden, thinking, "This is a great marvel. (NarP 1.7.34)
"Alas, what misery! Alas, a terrible form has appeared here! saying "We shall enter our dwelling with haste," those birds spoke thus. (NarP 1.7.35)
Having plunged into the lake together with his two wives and his son,
the king drank the water that bestows happiness and took refuge at the foot of a tree.
When that arm had departed for the forest, the subjects, protected by him alone, disregarded his faults and cried out, "Alas! Shame! (NarP 1.7.37).
Whether he be a mortal endowed with virtues or one who is more learned than all others, O twice-born one—
even if he is possessed of every prosperity, one devoid of virtue is censured by people.
No death in the worlds is found equal to ill-repute; when Bāhu went to the forest, the people who were once devoted to him attained supreme contentment, as if their fever had vanished.
Having endured much reproach, O best of the foremost of the twice-born, you remained in the forest like one dead,
and having destroyed [your] karma, you attained fame in the world.
There is no death equal to ill-repute; there is no enemy equal to anger;
there is no sin equal to censure; there is no intoxicant equal to delusion.
There is no infamy equal to malice; there is no fire equal to desire;
there is no snare equal to passion; there is no poison equal to attachment.
Having lamented thus in many ways, his arms were utterly distressed;
due to the torment of his mind and his aged limbs, he became like one who was old.
After a long time had passed near the hermitage of Aurva,
that Bāhu, seized by disease, died, O best of sages.
Then his wife, the youngest, who was pregnant and afflicted by grief,
lamented at length in many ways and set her mind on following him in death.
Having gathered the firewood and constructed a funeral pyre, she, being deeply distressed,
placed that Puru upon it and prepared to ascend it herself.
In the meantime, O wise one, the sage Aurva, a treasury of splendor,
perceived all of this through supreme meditative absorption.
The lords of sages, who know the three times— past, future, and present—
and who are free from malice, behold all with the eye of wisdom, O great ascetics.
By his asceticism, that sage— a mass of splendor equal in merit to Aurva—
reached that place where the virtuous Bāhupriyā was staying.
Seeing her prepared to ascend the funeral pyre, that best of sages spoke these words, which are rooted in Dharma. (NarP 1.7.50)
Aurva said:
"O virtuous one, beloved of the best of kings, do not commit such a rash act;
for within your womb dwells a universal emperor who will be the slayer of Śaṅkha."
Women with young children, those who are pregnant, those who have not yet reached puberty,
and women in their menses ascended the chariot along with the king’s son, while inauspicious thoughts arose within him.
The highest authorities have declared atonement for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
however, there is no atonement even for one who is a hypocrite, a slanderer, or a killer of an embryo.
O lady of virtuous vows, there is no atonement for an atheist, for one who has committed a heinous sin, for one who neglects dharma, or even for a betrayer of trust.
Therefore, O beautiful one, you ought not to commit this great sin;
all this suffering that has arisen shall come to an end.
Having been addressed thus by the sage, that virtuous woman, placing her trust in his grace,
lamented, afflicted by extreme sorrow, as she struck her husband’s feet with her hands.
Aurva, who was proficient in the meaning of all the scriptures, spoke to her again:
"Do not weep, O daughter of the king; you shall attain supreme prosperity."
O noble lady, let not the deceased be cremated by the virtuous today with weapons in hand;
therefore, casting aside your grief, perform the duties appropriate for this occasion.
Whether one is wise or foolish, poor or endowed with prosperity, ill-behaved or well-conducted—for all, death is equal in every respect. (NarP 1.7.59)
Or likewise in other cities; here, however, wretchedness exceeds all else.
Whatever ancient karma exists, that alone is joined with one here;
I consider destiny alone to be the cause in this matter, for people are possessed of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Whether in the womb, in childhood, in youth, or even in old age, O lotus-faced one, living beings must come under the sway of death. (NarP 1.7.62)
Govinda kills and protects beings who are subject to the power of their own karma;
yet the ignorant plant the rumor [of his cruelty] toward those beings who are merely the instruments of causes.
Therefore, O lady of noble vows, abandon sorrow and be happy;
perform your duties toward your husband and remain steadfast through discernment.
This body is seized by a multitude of sufferings and diseases;
it is a mere semblance of happiness, full of afflictions, and bound by the noose of karma.
Thus, that one of great intelligence caused various tasks to be performed for him;
and having abandoned her grief, that slender and modest woman spoke to the lord of sages: (NarP 1.7.66)
What is surprising in this, that the virtuous desire the fruit of the welfare of others?
For trees do not bear fruit upon the surface of the earth for the sake of their own enjoyment.
He who, having recognized the sufferings of others, awakens them with virtuous words,
is indeed Viṣṇu established in goodness, for he abides in what is beneficial.
He who suffers with the suffering of others and rejoices in the joy of others—
he alone is the Lord of the worlds, Hari, assuming a human form.

The virtuous have indeed declared that the sacred scriptures were heard by the wise for the sake of liberating others from suffering and for the destruction of the suffering of all beings. (NarP 1.7.70)
Where the virtuous engage, there suffering does not afflict;
for where the sun prevails, how could there be darkness? (NarP 1.7.71)
Having spoken thus, she performed other rites for her husband on the bank of that lake according to the procedure prescribed by the sage.
While the sage remained there, the king, blazing like the lord of the gods,
emerged from the midst of the funeral pyre and, ascending an excellent celestial chariot,
attained the supreme abode after bowing to Aurva, the lord of sages.
Whether they are burdened by great sins (mahāpātaka) or burdened by minor offenses (upapātaka),
those who are beheld by the Great Ones surely attain the supreme state.
O best of beings, if a person of meritorious soul beholds that corpse, its ashes, or even its smoke, he attains the supreme goal.
O Nārada, having performed the funeral rites for her husband and gone to the hermitage of the sage, she, together with her co-wife, rendered service to him.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gaṅgā," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
"O lord of sages, thus were those two wives of Bāhu [united] at the hermitage of Aurva."
Every day, they performed service with a spirit of devotion.
O twice-born one, when half of the rainy season had passed, Queen Jyeṣṭhā conceived an evil thought toward the prosperity of her co-wife.
Then that wicked woman gave poison to her younger sister;
however, due to her service to the sage, the poison did not exert its power at all.
By means of applying ointments and other services, he properly attended to the sage day after day;
through that exhausted meritorious karma, [he attained his goal].
Then, when three months had passed,
she who was free from sin through her service gave birth at an auspicious time to a son accompanied by poison.
Aho! What sin in this world would association with the virtuous not destroy? Or what supreme happiness is there for men of meritorious deeds that it does not provide? (NarP 1.8.6)
Whatever sin has been committed through knowledge or ignorance, and whatever else has been done by others—all that is swiftly destroyed by service to the great-souled ones. (NarP 1.8.7)
Even one who is dull-witted attains honor on the surface of the earth through association with the virtuous,
just as even a mere fraction of the cool-rayed moon was accepted by Śambhu.
For association with the virtuous always bestows supreme prosperity upon men, both in this world and the next; therefore, O Lord of Vidyādharas, the virtuous are most worthy of worship.
"O lords of sages, who is capable of describing his great virtues?
That he, having entered the womb, should have digested poison for three months—oh, how wonderful! (NarP 1.8.10)
Seeing his son together with Sagara, that sage, a treasury of splendor,
performed the birth-rites and gave him the name Sagara.
His mother affectionately nurtured the young Sagara,
and likewise the lord of sages performed for him the rites of the tonsure ceremony and the investiture of the sacred thread.
Knowing the sacred mantras, he taught him treatises suitable for a king,
seeing that Sagara had become capable and had somewhat outgrown his childhood.
O Sage, that lord of sages bestowed all the scriptures and weapons like mantras; Sagara was thoroughly instructed by that showerer of boons.
That Sagara, who was powerful, righteous, grateful, virtuous, and wise,
