and who likewise knew the dharma, daily brought to the sage of immeasurable splendor water with kuśa grass and flowers, along with other offerings.
Once, that Sagara, a treasury of virtues, having prostrated before his mother, spoke with palms joined in reverence and full of humility.
Sagara said:
"O mother, where has my father gone? What is his name, and from which lineage is he descended?
Tell me all of that, for I have a great curiosity to hear it. (NarP 1.8.17)
Those in this world who are deprived of their father, though living, are like the dead.
He whose father, though poor, is still present is like the Lord of Wealth;
he who has neither mother nor father finds no happiness.
Just as a fool devoid of dharma is censured both in this world and the next, so too is the life of one who lacks mother and father, who is ignorant and undiscriminating,
who is childless, and who is indeed burdened by debt, all in vain.
As a night without the moon, as a lake without Brahmā, as a woman without a husband, so is a child without a father. (NarP 1.8.21)
Just as a living being deprived of Dharma, just as a householder deprived of his duties, or just as a Vaiśya deprived of his cattle, so is a child without a father. 1.8.22.
Speech devoid of truth, an assembly lacking virtuous men, austerity without compassion, and a child without its father—[these are all like a forest without a lion]. (NarP 1.8.23)
Just as a forest is without trees, just as a river is without water, and just as a horse is without its bridle, so is a child without his father. (NarP 1.8.24)
Just as a man in this world who has no other [relative] than his mother is most wretched, so too is a son deprived of his father, filled with manifold suffering. (NarP 1.8.25)
Having heard this spoken by her son, she sighed in distress and reported everything that had occurred to him exactly as it happened, when he questioned her.
Having heard that, Sagara became enraged, his eyes bloodshot with anger, and he then made this vow: "I shall slay my enemies. (NarP 1.8.27)
Having circumambulated the sage and prostrated before his mother,
he was sent forth by that very sage and departed, O eloquent one.
Having emerged from the mountain hermitage of Aurva, the truthful and pure Sagara approached his own family preceptor Vasiṣṭha, filled with joy.
Having prostrated before that distinguished and high-souled guru,
he reported everything to him who perceives all through the vision of knowledge.
By that very sage, King Sagara obtained the Aindra, Vāruṇa, Brāhma, and Āgneya weapons,
as well as a sword and a bow like a thunderbolt.
Then, permitted by him, Sagara, filled with joy and honored with blessings,
immediately set forth after bowing down to him.
With a single bow alone, that hero sent his adversaries—
along with their sons, grandsons, and hosts— to dwell in heaven.
And those enemies of his, covered by the continuous stream of fire from the arrows released from that bow,
some were destroyed, while others, terrified, fled away.
Some, with disheveled hair, stood upon anthills;
some ate grass, and others entered the houses naked.
The Śakas, the Yavanas, and likewise other rulers of the earth,
longing for their lives, quickly sought refuge with Vasiṣṭha.
Jitakṣiti, the son of Bāhu, immediately learned through his spies that his enemies were near their preceptor, and he soon reached the presence of the teacher.
Hearing that the son of Bahu had arrived, the sage Vasiṣṭha immediately warded them off in order to protect those who had sought refuge and to carry out what his disciple had requested.
He made the Śabaras, Yavanas, and those with hanging hair into shaven-headed ones;
he made them all blind, bearded, shaven, and excluded from the Vedas.
Seeing that they were almost entirely slain by that sage Vasiṣṭha, Sagara, smiling, spoke to his own guru, the treasure-house of asceticism: NarP_1,8.40.
Sāgara said:
"O Guru, you protect these men of evil conduct in vain;
I shall by all means slay those who have seized my father's kingdom."
One who is capable should disregard those who obstruct the true Dharma;
for such a person is undoubtedly the cause of total destruction.
Considering the entire world to be their kinsman, the wicked [behave so];
yet if they are deprived of power, they resort to extreme goodness.
Alas! Wicked men of defiled minds perform deeds born of illusion only so long as their power remains strong. (NarP 1.8.44)
One who desires his own welfare should not place trust in the servitude of enemies, the friendship of courtesans, or the virtuous nature of snakes. (NarP 1.8.45)
Those very teeth which the wicked constantly display while laughing,
they quickly show when their own power has failed.
First, the treacherous ones speak harshly with their tongues;
likewise, those weak women utter words that are exceedingly piteous.
One who desires his own welfare and is skilled in the meaning of the treatises on ethics should maintain goodness and equanimity, yet never place trust in the wicked. (NarP 1.8.48)
One who places his trust in a wicked person who bows in feigned devotion, in a friend who practices deceit, or in a corrupt wife, is as good as dead; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, do not protect these who act like tigers in the form of cows;
by slaying all these wicked ones through your grace, may I enjoy the earth.
Having heard those words, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, being well-pleased, touched Sagar’s body with both hands and spoke as follows: ||| NarP_1,8.51 |||
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one! You speak the truth, O observer of noble vows.
Nevertheless, by hearing my words, you shall attain supreme peace."
"These were previously placed by me as obstacles to your vow;
tell me, what fame can arise from killing those who have already been slain? (NarP 1.8.53)
O Lord of the Earth, all living beings are bound by the noose of karma;
yet they are already struck down by their own sins—why do you strike them again?
The body, however, is produced by sin and is destroyed by the very same transgression;
for the Self is indivisible due to its perfection—this is the certainty of the scriptures. (NarP 1.8.55)
For living beings are merely the instruments for the enjoyment of the fruits of their own actions;
actions have destiny as their root, and this world is dependent upon destiny.
For the self is indeed indivisible and its protector is ill-trained; tell me, what can be accomplished by men who are thus rendered powerless? (NarP 1.8.57)
The body is born of evil and functions through evil alone;
knowing this to have its root in evil, how can you be intent on destroying it?
Although the Self is pure, when residing in the body, it is called "the embodied one" by the wise;
therefore, O King, this body is undoubtedly the root of sin.
"O son born of a Kṣatriya, what fame will there be for you, the slayer of one whose body is the root of sin? Having decided this, you did not kill them, my son. (NarP 1.8.60)
Having heard these words of his preceptor, he ceased from his anger;
then, O sages, he touched Sagara, his son, with his hand.
Then Atharvanidhi, together with sages of firm vows, performed the royal consecration of that high-souled Sagara.
And he had two wives, Keśinī and Sumati, the daughters of Kāśyapa and Vidarbha, O best of sages. (NarP 1.8.63)
Seeing the kingdom firmly established, the sage Aurva, a treasury of asceticism, returned from the forest, spoke with the king, and departed for his own hermitage. (NarP 1.8.64)
Once, at the request of that king’s two wives,
the sage Aurva, who was a knower of the Bhārgava mantras, granted a boon for the sake of offspring.
Having remained absorbed in meditation for a moment, the Lord of Sages, who knows the three periods of time, spoke these words to Keśinī and Sumati, gladdening them: NarP_1.8.66.
Aurva said:
"O highly fortunate lady, choose as you desire for the sake of offspring: either one son to continue the lineage, or six sons, or many."
Then, O Nārada, having heard those words of the sage Aurva,
Keśinī chose one son as the cause for the continuation of her lineage.
O best of sages, Sumati had sixty thousand sons,
while Keshini’s son was named Asamanja.
But Asamañja performed deeds like one of deranged conduct;
seeing him, all the oceans became troubled in their minds.
Knowing that his childish nature was thoroughly corrupted, the king,
the son of Bahu, duly reflected upon the contemptible act of his son.
Alas! The company of the wicked is indeed most painful in this world;
for fire is struck by smiths merely through contact with iron.
Aṃśumat was the son of Asamañjas;
he was learned in the scriptures, virtuous, righteous, and devoted to the welfare of his grandfather.
All the oceans are ill-behaved and cause affliction to the world;
they constantly become obstacles for those who perform religious observances.
All those oblations that had been offered in sacrifices according to the rules by the twice-born,
the denizens of heaven consumed them all after having rejected [the rightful recipients].
Having brought Rambhā and other celestial nymphs from heaven along with their husbands,
the oceans indeed enjoy them, having seized them by the hair with force.
Having gathered flowers from the *pārijāta* and other trees, those wicked men,
devoted to the drinking of liquor, adorn their own bodies with them.
They destroyed those of virtuous conduct and annihilated those of good behavior;
and those exceedingly wicked ones, though powerful, began to fight with their friends.
Seeing this, the gods, led by Indra and afflicted with extreme grief, engaged in profound deliberation for the sake of destroying that arrow. (NarP 1.8.79)
Having thus determined that Kapila was dwelling within the depths of Pātāla, all the gods, assuming concealed forms, went to the Lord of the God of Gods.
Then the gods, having bowed down like a staff upon the ground before him who was meditating on the Self by means of the self as the singular form of the Supreme, praised him.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you, the yogin; salutations to you who are devoted to Sāṅkhya and Yoga;
salutations to Viṣṇu, who has assumed a human form, the victorious one."
Salutations to the devotee of the Supreme Lord, who acts for the sake of favoring the worlds,
who is like a forest fire to the wilderness of saṃsāra, and who is a bridge for the protection of Dharma.
Homage again and again to you, the great one who is free from passion;
protect us, who have come to you for refuge, as we are oppressed by the oceans.
Kapila said:

"Those who desire here the destruction of their fame, strength, wealth, and lifespan—they alone bring harm to the worlds; there is no wonder in this, O most excellent of those who have found the path."
But he who wishes to oppress innocent people, O gods, should be known as one devoted to the enjoyment of sin in all the worlds. (NarP 1.8.86)
He who constantly oppresses others by deed, thought, or word is swiftly struck down by destiny itself; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
"In just a few days these oceans will come to destruction"—
so was it spoken by that great-souled sage Kapila.
Having bowed to him according to custom, the denizens of heaven departed for the celestial realm.
In the meantime, Sagara, together with Vasiṣṭha and other great sages,
began to perform the unsurpassed sacrifice known as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Then the Lord of the Gods, having seized that very sacrificial horse which had been yoked for the sacrifice,
established it in Pātāla, where Kapila resides.
When the horse had been stolen by Śakra, who was concealed in form, the sons of Sagara,
filled with great wonder, searched the worlds beginning with the earth.
Having failed to see the path to truth, they prepared to go to the netherworld (pātāla);
each one of them individually dug into the surface of the earth for a distance of one yojana.
They scattered the excavated earth along the shore of the ocean;
by that means, all the sons of Sagara entered the netherworld (pātāla).
Intoxicated with pride and deprived of their senses, they searched for the horse there.
There he saw the Great-Souled One, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns—
Kapila, absorbed in meditation— and the horse in his presence.
Then all of them, enraged upon seeing the sage, rushed forward with great speed and,
intent on killing him, fell upon him.
"Let him be slain! Let him be slain! Let him be executed! Let him be executed! Let him be hidden! Let him be seized quickly!"—thus they said to one another. (NarP 1.8.97)
Those who have stolen the horse through their virtuous nature, like Baka, are intent on meditation; yet there are wicked people in the world who create a great clamor.
Uttering these words, they laughed at Kapila, the lord of sages,
while restraining the entire collection of their senses within the self.
Kapila, though established among them, did not understand their karma.
Those whose deaths were near, their minds destroyed, kicked the sage with their feet, while others seized Buhu.
Then, having abandoned his meditative absorption, that sage, filled with wonder, spoke in a voice profound with emotion to those who were causing distress to the world: NarP_1.8.102.
For those intoxicated by the pride of power, for the hungry, for those possessed by desire,
and for those deluded by egoism, discernment never arises.
The earth always blazes by the mere presence of its treasure;
what wonder is it, then, that men blaze after having consumed that very same treasure? (NarP 1.8.104)
What is surprising in this, that wicked people afflict the virtuous?
Even the currents of rivers cast down trees growing upon their banks. (NarP 1.8.105)
Wherever prosperity, youth, or even Sarasvatī resides,
there misfortune, old age, and even stupidity constantly arise.
Aha! Who is able to describe the greatness of gold?
How wonderful it is that, due to the similarity of their names, even the thorn-apple (dhattūra) bestows intoxication! 1.8.107.
If a wicked person should possess prosperity, that very prosperity becomes destructive to the world;
just as wind is to a fire, or as venom is to a serpent.
Alas! One who is blinded by the intoxication of wealth does not see even though he sees;
if he does see, he sees only what is harmful—of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the enraged Kapila emitted fire from his two eyes;
that fire reduced all the oceans to ashes in an instant.
Seeing the fire born from his eyes, the inhabitants of the netherworld,
thinking it to be an untimely dissolution of the world, cried out, overcome with grief.
Scorched by that fire, all the venomous serpents and Rākṣasas quickly entered the ocean; for the anger of the virtuous is indeed unbearable.

Then, having approached the sacrifice of that monarch at that time, the messenger of the gods spoke as follows regarding everything that had occurred concerning the Yakṣas: NarP_1.8.113: "Then, having arrived at the sacrifice of that king, the messenger of the gods spoke this, concerning all that had indeed transpired regarding the Yakṣas."
Having heard these words, the all-knowing lord Sagara, greatly delighted, said: "The wicked have been disciplined by fate. (NarP 1.8.114)
Whether it be a mother, a father, a brother, or even a son—
whoever commits unrighteousness is considered an enemy.
But one who is devoted to unrighteousness and acts in opposition to all the world—know him to be the supreme enemy; this is the conclusion of the scriptures. (NarP 1.8.116)
Even upon the loss of his sons, Sagara, the lord of sages, did not grieve;
for the destruction of the wicked is a cause for the encouragement of the virtuous.
Because of the traditional law stating that those without sons have no entitlement to perform sacrifices,
the Lord indeed made that grandson, Aṃśumat, his own son.
Furthermore, he appointed Sudhīvan, the son of Asamañja and the best among those skilled in speech,
to the task of bringing back the horses, for he was a knower of their essential nature.
Having gone to the entrance of that cave and beheld that bull among sages,
Kapila— a mass of splendor— he prostrated himself before him with his eight limbs touching the ground.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he stood before Vinaya and spoke to the eternal God of gods, whose mind was tranquil.
Aṃśumat said:
"O Brahmin, forgive that misconduct which was committed by my paternal uncles;
for the virtuous are devoted to helping others and have forgiveness as their very essence. (NarP 1.8.122)
The virtuous show compassion even toward beings who are wicked;
for the moon does not withhold its moonlight from the house of a *caṇḍāla*.
Even when being oppressed, a virtuous person brings happiness to all;
like the moon being devoured by the gods, he bestows supreme satisfaction.
For even when split or cut, sandalwood produces its fragrance entirely through its own scent; in the same way, a person of noble character acts for the benefit of all.
O Supreme Person, the lords of sages, who know your virtues through your patience, austerity, and conduct,
recognize you as one born to govern the worlds.
Homage to you, O sage Brahmā; homage to you who are the embodiment of Brahman. Homage to him whose character is devotion to Brahman, and who is intent upon meditation on Brahman. (NarP 1.8.127)
Thus praised by him, the Sage, with a serene countenance, then said:
"Choose a boon; I am pleased with you, O sinless one. (NarP 1.8.128)
When the sage had spoken thus, Aṃśumat prostrated himself before him and addressed him,
saying, "Lead our ancestors to the world of Brahmā."
Then, being highly pleased with her, the sage spoke respectfully:
"Having brought the Gaṅgā, your grandson will lead your ancestors to heaven."
The river Gaṅgā, whose waters are meritorious, brought down by your grandson,
shall indeed lead these men, cleansed of their sins, to the supreme state.
"O child, lead this horse to where the sacrifice may be completed.
Having reached the presence of the Grandfather (Brahmā), he reported what had occurred regarding the horse.
Having performed that sacrifice with that animal together with the Brahmins, Sagar propitiated Viṣṇu through austerity and attained the abode of Hari.
From Aṃśumat was born a son renowned as Dilīpa;
from him was born Bhagīratha, who brought the Gaṅgā down from heaven.
O Sage, Brahmā, pleased by the ascetic penance of Bhagīratha, gave Gaṅgā to Bhagīratha; he then reflected upon how she might be sustained.
Then, having propitiated Śiva and brought the celestial river to the earth through his power,
he purified his ancestors by touching them with its waters and led them to heaven.
In the lineage of Bhagīratha was born a king named Sudāsa,
whose son was Mitrasaha, renowned throughout all the worlds.
Having assumed the body of a Rākṣasa due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha,
that King Saudāsa was released from it by bathing in a drop of the Gaṅgā and became a man once again.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gaṅgā," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
How was the excellent king Saudāsa cursed by Vasiṣṭha?
How could he become pure again by being sprinkled with drops from the Gaṅgā? || NarP_1,9.1 ||
"O brother, you ought to tell me all of this in its entirety—
the auspicious narrative of Gaṅgā— for those who hear it and for those who speak it."
Sanaka said: Saudāsa, who was a knower of all duties, omniscient, virtuous, and pure,
enjoyed the entire earth, pleasing his subjects like a father.
Just as this great earth was formerly protected by Sagara through his virtuous conduct,
so too has it been protected by him, who acts without contradicting any of the dharmas.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of all sovereign powers,
he enjoyed the earth as a youth for thirty-eight thousand years.
Once, King Saudāsa, devoted to the sport of hunting, entered the forest together with his army, which had been thoroughly cleared by his ministers.
Harassed there by the Niṣādas and killing herds of deer,
he, who knew what was right, reached the river Revā while overcome by thirst.
O Sage, having bathed there and performed his daily rites, the son of Sudāsa ate with his ministers and stayed there for that night.
Then, having risen at dawn and performed his morning rites,
he wandered together with his ministers in the forest on the banks of the Narmadā.
Wandering alone from forest to forest,
the lord of the earth drew his arrow back to his ear and pursued a black antelope.
Having left his army far behind, that king, mounted on horseback,
followed the deer and saw two tigers staying in a cave, engaged in sexual union.
Leaving the back of the deer, he went face-to-face with the two tigers;
by means of his bow and a drawn arrow, that expert in the science of archery [faced them].
He struck that tigress down with an arrow whose tip was sharp and its joints smooth;
as she fell, the tigress was thirty-six yojanas in length.
With a roar as terrible as a flash of lightning, the Rākṣasī became deformed;
seeing his beloved fallen, that enemy, the tiger-Rākṣasa, [attacked].
Having said, "I shall take retaliatory action," he then vanished;
but the king, agitated by fear, assembled his army in the forest.
Relating all those events, the son of Sudāsa returned to his own city,
yet he remained apprehensive of the deeds of that *rākṣasa*.
From that time forward, O Nārada, he completely abandoned hunting;
and when a great deal of time had passed, the king performed the horse sacrifice.
With a serene soul, he began [the sacrifice] together with Vasiṣṭha and the other lords of sages;
there, having offered oblations to Brahmā and the other gods according to the prescribed rites.
Having completed the sacrifice and bathed, Vasiṣṭha emerged as a snātaka;
at that moment, the Rākṣasa, whose wife had been harmed by the king,
arrived filled with rage to take revenge upon the monarch.
When that guru had departed, the rākṣasa immediately assumed the guise of Vasiṣṭha;
approaching the king, he said, "I shall eat meat; I desire it," so he spoke. (NarP 1.9.20)
Having once again assumed the guise of a cook and having cooked human flesh for him to eat,
the king remained standing, holding a vessel of water, awaiting the arrival of his preceptor.
Then Saudāsa, full of humility, respectfully presented that meat, placed in a golden vessel, to his teacher who had arrived there. (NarP 1.9.22)
Seeing him, the Guru was amazed and thought, "What is this? (NarP 1.9.23).
Perceiving with supreme concentration that it was human flesh, he thought:
"Alas! This king's immorality is such that he has given me something unfit to be eaten."
Thus, having fallen into a state of despondency, the sage became filled with indignation:
"O Lord of the Earth, this food has indeed been given for my destruction! (NarP 1.9.25)
Therefore, let this very food be yours as well;
for human flesh is the food of Rākṣasas alone, and it has been given to you by me.
"Therefore, O King, go back to your state as a Rākṣasa, for that is the food to which you are accustomed.
While he was pronouncing this curse, Saudāsa trembled with fear.
"Command us yourself," he said, trembling;
thus addressed by him, Bhūriśravas, the son of Vasiṣṭha, reflected.
Having learned through his divine vision that the king had been deceived by the Rākṣasa,
the king also took up water and prepared to curse Vasiṣṭha.
Seeing her husband, who was endowed with great vows, prepared to curse his teacher and once again filled with rage, Madayantī then replied to her beloved: (NarP 1.9.30)
Madayantī said:
"O heir of the Kṣatriyas, you ought to restrain your anger.
Whatever karma must be experienced by you, that has been obtained; there is no doubt in this."
That man of dull intellect who, having shown disrespect to his guru, speaks with a roar of defiance (*huṃ*), shall become a terrifying *rākṣasa* in a waterless forest. (NarP 1.9.32)
"Those who have conquered their senses, conquered their anger, and are devoted to serving their gurus go to the abode of Brahmā; this is the certainty established in the scriptures. (NarP 1.9.33)
Thus addressed by her, the king abandoned his anger and rejoiced with his wife;
he then reflected within himself, "Where shall I cast the water? (NarP 1.9.34)
"Wherever that water is sprinkled, it will certainly become ashes"—thinking thus, he himself poured that water at his own feet. (NarP 1.9.35)
Merely by the touch of its water, his two feet became mottled;
from that time forward, he became widely known as Kalmāṣapāda.
Then the wise Kalmāṣapāda, though urged on by his beloved,
was overcome with fear in his mind and prostrated at the feet of his preceptor.
And he, skilled in policy, having sought refuge with him, spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"Forgive everything, O Blessed One; no offense has been committed by me. (NarP 1.9.38)
Having heard that, the sage sighed sorrowfully and spoke to the king;
he indeed reproached himself for being devoted to a lack of discernment.
For lack of discernment is the supreme state of all calamities;
one devoid of discernment in this world is nothing but a beast—of this there is no doubt.
"Surely this deed was committed by the king while he was unaware; for I am ignorant and devoid of discernment, such that I might commit sin. (NarP 1.9.41)
Whether he be anyone at all, one who is disciplined by discernment attains liberation;
whereas one who lacks discernment, whoever they may be, attains no liberation.
Having thus spoken to himself, the sage replied to the king:
"This shall not be permanent; it will last for twelve years. (NarP 1.9.43)
Having been sprinkled with drops from the Gaṅgā and having indeed cast off your demonic body,
you shall regain your former form and enjoy this earth.
With the knowledge produced by the sprinkling of that drop, one's impurities are removed.
Devoted to the service of Hari, you shall attain supreme peace.
Having said, "It shall bring you auspiciousness," Vasiṣṭha, the knower of the Atharva-veda, departed for his own hermitage;
the king, however, filled with grief, remained there, having entered that Rākṣasī's body.
Afflicted by the particular pangs of hunger and thirst, and constantly devoted to anger, he,
terrifying with the luster of a dark night, wandered through the lonely forest.
There he ate various kinds of deer, humans, reptiles, birds, and monkeys that were fit for consumption. (NarP 1.9.48)
Furthermore, with many bones, with corpses of yellowish-red hue,
and with the blood-stained hair of the dead, the earth became variegated and terrifying.
Having made the earth, which extended for hundreds of yojanas, extremely distressed during three seasons, he thereafter departed for the depths of the forest.
There too, he constantly and perpetually consumed human flesh;
he went to the bank of the Narmadā, which is frequented by sages and perfected beings.
Wandering along the bank of the Narmadā, that one who causes terror to all the worlds beheld a certain sage sporting with his beloved.
He rushed toward the sage, who was tormented by the fire of hunger,
and seized him with great force, as a hunter seizes a fawn.
Seeing her own husband held in the hands of the night-stalker, the Brahmin woman placed her joined palms upon her head and spoke, trembling with fear: NarP_1,9.54.
The Brahmin woman said:
"O tiger among kings, protect me who am overwhelmed by fear!
O you who are dearer than life, fulfill my heart's desire by granting [me] my life."
O Mitraśaha, you are indeed born of the Solar dynasty;
you are no Rākṣasa. Therefore, protect me, who am helpless, in this desolate forest.
A woman who is bereft of her husband is like one dead even while living;
nevertheless, O crusher of enemies, what can I say regarding this premature widowhood?
I know neither my mother nor my father, nor any kinsman;
my husband alone is my supreme kinsman and my highest life.
O Lord of Men, you who know all duties and how women ought to conduct themselves— protect me, who am without kinsmen and have young children.
"How shall I live, bereft of my husband in this desolate forest?
I am the daughter of the Blessed One; save me by granting me a husband. (NarP 1.9.60)
"There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of life," so say those of great wisdom; therefore, grant me the gift of life.
Having spoken thus, she fell at the feet of that Rākṣasa;
yet, even though he was thus entreated by the Brāhmaṇī, the Rākṣasa [addressed] the twice-born man.
Just as a tiger might forcibly devour a young black antelope that it has not eaten before.
Then, having lamented in many ways, his devoted wife,
provoked to anger, cursed the king who had been struck down by a previous curse.
"Since you have forcibly harmed my husband while he was intent on sexual pleasure, therefore you too shall meet your death upon encountering a woman. (NarP 1.9.64)
Having spoken thus, the Brahmin woman, enraged, again uttered another curse:
"Since my husband has been devoured by you, may you certainly become a Rākṣasa! (NarP 1.9.65)
Having heard those two curses uttered by her, that night-stalker,
filled with fury, cast forth a mass of burning coals out of anger.
O wicked one, why have you bestowed two curses in vain?
For a single offense, only one curse was appropriate for me.
"Since you, O wicked woman, cast this further curse upon me,
therefore go this very day to the womb of a Piśāca, accompanied by your son."
Thus, having been cursed by that very [Brahmin] into the state of a Piśāca, she then became afflicted by hunger; accompanied by her offspring, the terrifying woman wailed piteously with a loud voice.
The Rākṣasa and the Piśācī, crying out in the desolate forest,
went along the bank of the Narmadā to the grove frequented by Rākṣasas.
Having shown indifference toward his guru and having assumed a demonic form, a certain person who opposes the world remains there, tormented by a continuous stream of suffering. (NarP 1.9.71)
Seeing the Rākṣasa and the Piśācī who had come to the banyan tree, the Brahmarākṣasa dwelling in that tree, filled with great anger, spoke: ||| NarP_1,9.72 |||
"For what purpose have you two come, O terrible ones, desiring my abode? By what sin were you born in such a state? Tell me for certain."
Having heard those words of hers and having reported everything that he himself had done, Saudāsa then spoke this to him.
Saudāsa said: "Tell me, O illustrious one, who are you? What indeed did you do in the past? Out of great affection for my friend, you ought to tell me all of that. (NarP 1.9.75)
Whosoever, even if he be a friend, commits a deception with a wicked mind,
he indeed eats the fruit of his sin for ten thousand ages of suffering.
The sufferings of all living beings are extinguished by the sight of a friend;
therefore, a wise person should never harbor malice toward friends.
O Nārada, having been addressed thus by Kalmāṣapāda, the Brahmarākṣasa dwelling in the banyan tree, filled with joy, spoke these words of dharma.
The Brahmarākṣasa said: "In former times, I was a Brāhmaṇa of Māgadha, a master of the Vedas,
known by the name Somadatta, and devoted to righteousness."
"O illustrious one, being intoxicated by my learning, my youth, and my wealth,
I displayed indifference toward my guru and have thus attained such a state."
"Defeated and excessively distressed, I find no happiness at all;
yet by me, O Brahmins, hundreds and thousands have been devoured. (NarP 1.9.81)
Constantly devoted to hunger and thirst, tormented within by internal heat,
he is perpetually intent on eating flesh and constantly causes terror to the world.
Disrespect toward the guru bestows the state of a rākṣasa upon human beings; indeed, this has been experienced by me myself, therefore a fortunate person should not act in such a way. (NarP 1.9.83)
Kalmāṣapāda said:
"What kind of person is declared to be a guru? Who was praised by you previously?
Tell me all of that in its entirety, for my curiosity is great. (NarP 1.9.84)
The Brahmarākṣasa said:
"There are many gurus who are worthy of worship and should be honored with respect;
I shall describe those who have passed away—listen with a one-pointed mind, O sage."
He was a teacher of the Vedas, one who understood the logic and meaning of the Vedas,
a speaker of the Shastras, a proponent of Dharma, and an instructor in the science of ethics.
He is the expounder of the instructions on mantras, the commentator, the one who dwells in the Vedas, and likewise the one whose heart is established therein;
he is the instructor of vows, the protector from fear, and indeed the giver of food.

O best of friends, the father-in-law, the maternal uncle, the elder brother, the father, as well as the initiator (upanetā), the procreator (niṣektā), and the performer of sacraments (saṃskarttā) [are all gurus]. (NarP 1.9.88)
For these are declared to be gurus; they are to be honored and saluted with reverence.
Kalmāṣapāda said:
"Many teachers have been mentioned; among these, which is the best?
Are they all equal, or is there a distinction? Tell me that exactly as it is."
The Brahmarākṣasa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! I shall tell you that which you have asked:
the narration of the greatness of the guru, as well as its hearing and approval."
It bestows the highest good upon all; therefore, I shall speak of it now.
These are always worthy of equal honor; there is no doubt in this matter.
Nevertheless, listen; I shall declare the determination of the essence of the scriptures, as well as [the views] of the teachers of the Vedas and those who compose explanations of the mantras.
The father and the teacher of the Dharma are remembered as especially venerable; O protector of the earth, hear now who among these is the most preeminent guru.
I shall declare to you that which was spoken by those who know the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures:
he who, being wise, recites the Purāṇas endowed with dharma.
That which severs the bonds of saṃsāra is supreme;
the fruits of worshipping the deities consist of those actions worthy of divine worship.
And they arise from the Purāṇas; therefore, O King, those Purāṇas are the deities here, containing the essence of the meaning of all the Vedas. (NarP 1.9.97)
The sages declare that he who makes an effort to cross over the ocean of worldly existence is the supreme teacher (paramo guru) as taught by them. (NarP 1.9.98)
"One should listen to the Purāṇas," so said the author of the division of the scriptures;
and he declared, O Lord of the Earth, that all dharmas are contained within the Purāṇas.

Logic, O one of great intelligence, is the cause for debate; policy is the means for success in this world; and the Purāṇas are indeed for the sake of happiness both here and in the hereafter. (NarP 1.9.100)
He who constantly listens to the Purāṇas with devotion shall possess a stainless intellect and become ever more devoted to dharma.
From hearing the Purāṇas, auspicious devotion arises toward the Lord of Śrī;
O King, for those men who are devotees of Viṣṇu, their intellect is directed toward dharma.
Through dharma, sins are destroyed and pure knowledge arises;
for those who desire the fruits of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Those who know the past have declared that one should listen to the Purāṇas;
however, I [have heard them] from the sage Gautama, the omniscient one who speaks the truth.
Once, on the delightful bank of the Gaṅgā, I, who was learned in the meaning of all dharmas,
went there to perform worship of the Supreme Lord.
Even though he had approached me, I did not offer him my salutation;
yet he was peaceful, possessed of great wisdom, a descendant of Gautama, and a treasury of splendors.
Those who find joy in performing the rites prescribed by mantras—yet by whom the god Śiva, the teacher of the entire world, has not been worshipped by me; (NarP 1.9.107)
"He who has committed contempt toward his guru—whether knowingly or even unknowingly—he was assigned to the state of a Rākṣasa. (NarP 1.9.108)
The wisdom, learning, wealth, sons, and activities of that very man quickly perish—he who performs service for his gurus with devotion. (NarP 1.9.109)
"O King, the wise say that his prosperity would become yours;
yet by that curse, I am consumed within by the fire of hunger. (NarP 1.9.110)
"O best of kings, I do not know when I shall attain liberation," said this lord of night-stalkers while staying in that banyan tree, O chief of brahmins.
Through the discourse on the Dharmaśāstras, the sin of those two came to an end. In the meantime, a certain brahmin, exceedingly righteous, arrived.
Born in the land of Kaliṅga, he was known by the name Garga;
carrying the water of the Gaṅgā on his shoulder, he praised the Lord Viśveśvara.
With the hairs on their bodies bristling with joy, they sang his names;
and seeing that the sage had arrived, both the Piśācī and the Rākṣasa [acted].
Having said, "May he ferry us across," they ran forward with their arms raised;
but hearing his name being proclaimed by him, the rākṣasas stood at a distance, unable to overpower him, and spoke as follows: NarP_1,9.115 //
O Brahmin, O highly fortunate one, salutations to you, the Great-Souled One!
By the greatness of the glorification of your name, this Rākṣasa has been driven far away.
"O Brahmin, previously we have devoured thousands of millions of brahmins; yet the armor of your name protects you from this great danger. (NarP 1.9.117)
"O friends, by the mere hearing of his name, even we Rākṣasas have attained supreme peace, indeed through the majesty of Acyuta. (NarP 1.9.118)
In every way, O illustrious one, you are grown over by passion and the like;
protect us from this accumulation of sins with the sprinkling of the waters of the Gaṅgā.
The wise proclaim that he who, becoming another's servant for Hari, delivers himself,
shall deliver all beings.
Having abandoned the name of Hari, the medicine for the terrible cycle of existence,
by what means could liberation be obtained, which is difficult to attain everywhere?
Just as one attempting to cross by means of an iron boat sinks into the water,
how can those who have not performed meritorious deeds help others to cross?
Oh, how great is the conduct of the noble ones, which brings happiness to all the world, just as the storehouse of digits (the moon) exists for the joy of all people! (NarP 1,9.123)
O best of the twice-born, whatever sacred and purifying holy sites exist upon the earth,
all of them are not equal to even a single drop of the Gaṅgā.
Even a drop of Ganges water the size of a mustard seed, if mixed with a fragment of a Tulasī leaf, purifies twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
Therefore, O illustrious Brahmin, skilled in the meaning of all scriptures,
protect us, who are doers of evil deeds, by the offering of the water of the Gaṅgā.
Having heard this supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā as recounted by those Rākṣasas,
that best of the twice-born was filled with wonder.
Such is the devotion even of these toward Gaṅgā, the mother of the world;
how much more so for the great ones, who are endowed with merit and the power of knowledge?
Then, having determined the Dharma with his mind, that best of brahmins,
devoted to the welfare and purity of all, attains the supreme state.
Then the Brahmin, overcome with compassion, sprinkled upon those Rākṣasas water from the Gaṅgā that had washed away their sins, mixed with Tulasī leaves.
The Rākṣasas, sprinkled by him with drops the size of mustard seeds,
wiped away their demonic nature and became like gods.
They approached the Brahmin with perfect composure,
and those bulls among the gods became as radiant as ten million suns.
Bearing the marks of the conch, discus, and mace, and having attained a form similar to Hari’s,
they went to the abode of Hari while praising the Brahmin correctly.
But King Kalmāṣapāda, having resumed his own form,
fell into deep anxiety upon seeing those who had attained liberation.
While that king was afflicted with great sorrow, Sarasvatī, in a concealed form,
spoke these great words rooted in Dharma in a profound voice.
"O King, O highly fortunate one, you ought not to go to sorrow; O King, at the end of your portion, great welfare shall also be yours. (NarP 1.9.136)
Those who have shaken off their sins through virtuous deeds and are devoted to the worship of Hari go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.9.137)
Those who are endowed with compassion for all beings, who set forth upon the path of Dharma,
and who are devoted to the worship of their gurus, go to the supreme state.
Having heard what was thus spoken by Bhāratī, the best of kings attained peace of mind and recalled the words of his preceptor.
Extremely delighted, he praised that guru and Hari,
and reported everything regarding his previous conduct to that brahmin.
Then, O Vamuna, having prostrated before the Kalinga king according to the prescribed rite and uttering the names of Viṣṇu, the king immediately departed for Vārāṇasī.
Having bathed there in the Gaṅgā for six months and having beheld Sadānīra,
Mitrasaha was liberated from the curse uttered by the Brahmin woman.
Then, having reached his own city, O best of sages, he was consecrated by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha and protected his own kingdom.
Having protected the entire earth and enjoyed pleasures without a wife,
that best of kings obtained progeny from Vasiṣṭha and attained liberation.

O best of the twice-born, it is not surprising that a man who praises, hears, or remembers the virtues of Vārāṇasī belonging to Viṣṇu, or who drinks from the Gaṅgā, shall become liberated. (NarP 1.9.145)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, it is not possible for even the lords of the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— to reach the further shore of Gaṅgā’s greatness.
Merely by remembering his name, a person is liberated from millions of great sins and goes to the abode of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.9.147)
Whenever the name "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" is uttered even once,
at that very moment one is liberated from sin and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the majesty of Gaṅgā, in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said: She who is born from the tip of Viṣṇu’s foot is called Gaṅgā.
Tell me, brother, how that [knowledge] arises, if I am worthy of your favor.
Sanaka said:
Listen, O sinless Nārada, I shall tell you of the origin of the Gaṅgā; it bestows merit and destroys the sins of those who speak of it and those who hear it. (NarP 1.10.2)
The sage Kaśyapa was the progenitor of Indra and the other gods;
he had two wives, the daughters of Dakṣa, namely Diti and Aditi.
Aditi is the mother of the gods, and Diti is the mother of the Daityas;
their sons, O Brahmin, were each desirous of conquering the other.
They are always preceded by the gods, for which reason they are proclaimed as *daityas*;
the first *daitya* was the powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu, the son of Diti.
His son was the great Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas;
his son was Virocana, who was devoted to the twice-born.
His son was Bali, possessed of great splendor and majesty;
he became the commander of the army for the Daityas, O Sage.
Endowed with great power, he enjoyed this earth;
having conquered the entire world, he set his mind upon conquering heaven.
O Lord of Sages, he possesses tens of millions and hundreds of thousands of elephants, and just as many horses and chariots;
for every single elephant there are five hundred foot soldiers—how can his most excellent army be described?
The two ministers named Kumbhāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa were the foremost among ten million ministers;
Bāṇa, the eldest of Bali’s hundred sons, was equal to his father in valor and prowess.
Bali, intent on conquering the gods, set out accompanied by a vast army;
with his banners and fans, he caused the ocean of the sky to recall the lightning flashing amidst its waves.
Having seized the city of Vṛtra’s enemy, the foe of the gods blocked it with Daityas who were as formidable as lions;
and likewise, the gods, led by Vajrapāṇi, sallied forth from the city for battle.
Then there commenced a terrible battle between the gods and the Daityas,
resembling the roar of clouds at the end of an aeon, and tumultuous with the sound of the drum *ḍiṇḍima*.
In that exceedingly terrible battle, the Daityas released showers of arrows upon the host of the gods,
and the gods [did likewise] upon the Daitya armies.
"Seize! Tear asunder! Break! Cut! Kill!
Strike!"—such was the great clamor that arose from those speaking among the two armies.
With the sounds of autumnal kettledrums, with the lion-roars of the enemies of the gods, with the clanging of chariots, and with the whizzing sounds of arrows; NarP_1,10.16 //
With the neighing of horses, the trumpeting of elephants,
and the twanging of bows, the world became composed entirely of sound.
Seeing the entire world amidst the fire produced by the impact of arrows released by the gods and asuras, he thought it was an untimely dissolution of the universe.
The army of the enemies of the gods, bearing a multitude of flashing weapons,
shone like a night covered with clouds and streaked with flickering lightning.
In that battle, those swift-moving enemies of the gods crushed the mountains and the earth-protectors with their most terrible iron arrows, as if they were mere straw.
Some struck elephants with elephants and chariots with chariots;
some, however, struck horses with horses and afflicted them with maces and staffs.
Some, struck by the iron clubs, fell into the mire of blood;
others, their life-breaths having departed, took refuge in celestial chariots.
Those Daityas who were then forcibly slain by the gods in battle attained the state of gods and rushed against the sons of Diti.
Then the hosts of Daityas, enraged and being struck severely by all [the gods],
being exceedingly fierce, struck back at the gods with many kinds of weapons.
With stones, slings, swords, axes, and tomara-spears; with clubs, daggers, lances, discuses, and spikes.
With pestles, goads, plows, and likewise with spears, with javelins,
stones, slings, nooses, and blows from the palms and fists.
The battle grew tumultuous with spears, *nālīka* and *nārāca* arrows, and missiles launched from slings, as well as by chariots, horses, elephants, and foot soldiers.
And the gods hurled various weapons at the Daityas;
thus there was a most terrible battle for eight thousand years.
Then, when the army of the Daityas had increased, the inhabitants of heaven were defeated;
terrified, they all fled, abandoning the world of the gods.
Concealed in human form,
Vairocana, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa, wandered upon the surface of the earth throughout the three worlds.
Possessing great strength, his prosperity increased through unimpeded sovereignty;
thus he enjoyed himself and, intent on pleasing Viṣṇu, he performed horse sacrifices.
He also established his sovereignty in heaven and likewise his status as a guardian of the quarters for the sake of pleasing the gods by means of those sacrifices performed by the twice-born.
In all those sacrifices, that king of the Daityas consumed the sacrificial oblation;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, seeing her own sons, was exceedingly distressed.
Thinking, "I am living here in vain," she went to the Himavat mountain,
desiring sovereignty for Śakra and the defeat of the Daityas.
Devoted to the meditation on Hari, she performed extremely difficult austerities;
for some time she remained seated, and after that, she stood. (NarP 1.10.35)
Then, for a very long time, she stood on one foot; thereafter, for some time, she remained on the tips of her toes alone.
Then she subsisted on fruits, and after that, she fed upon withered leaves.
Then, having become like a reservoir of water, abstaining from food even in the form of air, she meditated upon the Self by means of the self as the mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
O Nārada, she performed that difficult penance for a thousand divine years;
hearing of that penance which was hard to endure, the illusory Daityas [approached] Aditi.
Assuming the forms of deities, they spoke, prompted by Bali:
"O Mother, for what purpose do you perform this penance that withers the body? (NarP 1.10.39)
If the Daityas know [this], then great suffering will arise;
therefore, one should abandon this cause of bodily emaciation which abounds in misery.
The wise do not praise meritorious deeds that are accomplished through great exertion;
rather, those intent on the means of dharma must protect their bodies with utmost care.
Those who neglect their own bodies would be destroyers of themselves;
therefore, remain at ease, O blessed one, and do not distress us, your sons.
O Mother, people who are deprived of their mothers are as good as dead, there is no doubt;
whether it be cows, other animals, or even trees, they too are like that where there are no cows.
Those who are deficient in means find no happiness at all; they are like the dead—whether they be poor, or diseased, or even one who has gone to a foreign land. (NarP 1.10.44)
Merely by the sight of his mother, he obtains supreme joy,
whether it be regarding food, water, wealth, or beloved women.

Sometimes a person goes away without taking leave of his mother; yet there is no one for whom it is better to go to the forest than where there is no mother at home who is devoted to dharma, a virtuous woman who holds her husband as her very life.
Just as dharma devoid of devotion to Nārāyaṇa, wealth deprived of righteous enjoyment,
and a home lacking a wife and sons, so too is a mortal man who is bereft of his mother.
"Therefore, O Goddess, protect your daughter who is afflicted by suffering!
Though addressed thus by the Daityas, Aditi did not waver from her meditative absorption.
Having spoken thus, all the asuras, filled with rage, gazed upon her who was intent on meditating on Hari and formed the resolve to kill her.
Resounding like clouds at the end of an eon, their eyes bloodshot with rage, they emitted fire from the tips of their fangs; it consumed the forest in an instant.
Extending for a hundred yojanas and teeming with various living beings,
it consumed those Daityas who had gone there to attack.

She alone remained as the mother of the gods; for a hundred years, her mind was fixed on Acyuta, and she was protected by Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana, the slayer of Daityas who is compassionate toward his own kin.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Bali’s Defeat of the Gods during the Origin of the Gaṅgā," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"O brother, what you have told me is indeed most wonderful!"
Having released Aditi, how did that fire burn them in an instant?
The Great Being is the cause of extraordinary wonder from the very beginning;
for the lords of sages, the virtuous ones, are indeed devoted to instructing others.
Sanaka said:
Listen, O Nārada, to the greatness of those whose souls are devoted to the love of Hari; for who is capable of obstructing holy men who are intent on meditation upon Hari? (NarP 1.11.3)
Wherever one is devoted to Hari-bhakti, there Brahmā, Hari, Śiva,
the gods, the Siddhas, and the lords of sages— those most excellent beings— reside eternally.

O highly fortunate one, Hari dwells in the hearts of those whose minds are peaceful and who are devoted to the name of Hari; how much more so, then, in the hearts of those whose souls delight in meditation?
Whether one is devoted to the worship of Śiva or intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu,
wherever he dwells, there indeed resides Lakṣmī and all the deities.
Where one is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, there fire does not cause harm;
indeed, neither kings nor thieves nor diseases exist there.
Pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍa-grahas, and likewise bālagrahas,
as well as ḍākinīs and rākṣasas, do not afflict one who worships Acyuta.
But those beings such as *bhūtas* and *vetālas* who delight in tormenting others perish where a true devotee is intent upon the worship of Hari’s Lakṣmī—
one who has conquered his senses, is beneficial to all, and is devoted to righteous deeds.
Wherever he dwells, there indeed are all the sacred fords and the deities.
Wherever yogis remain for even a moment or half a moment, right there all blessings reside; that is a sacred ford, that is a grove of asceticism.
Since all calamities perish by the mere utterance of his name—
whether through hymns of praise or acts of worship— what need is there to mention the power of meditation?
Thus, O Brahmin, that forest together with the asuras was burnt by that fire;
yet Aditi was not burnt at all, being protected by the discus of Viṣṇu.
Then, with a serene countenance and eyes as broad as lotus petals,
he appeared near her, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
With the radiance of his teeth slightly visible as he smiled, illuminating the quarters of the sky,
he touched the beloved of Kaśyapa with his auspicious hand and spoke.
The Blessed One said: "O Mother of the Gods, I am pleased, having been propitiated by you through your ascetic penance.
You have been weary for a long time; may it be well with you, and there is no doubt that your desire shall be fulfilled."
"Choose a boon; I shall grant whatever is pleasing to your heart.
Do not fear, O blessed and highly fortunate lady; certain prosperity shall come to pass."
Having been addressed thus by the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, Aditi, being pleased, prostrated before him who brings happiness to all the worlds and offered praise. (NarP 1.11.18)
Aditi said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Janārdana who pervades all!
You are the cause of the world’s activity through the differentiation of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest. (NarP 1.11.19)
Salutations to you, the Great Soul, who possesses many forms and yet is formless;
who has a single form that is all forms; who is devoid of qualities, yet whose very self is the qualities.
Homage to you, the Lord of the World, whose form is supreme wisdom,
who is endowed with affection for those devoted to you, and whose very nature is auspiciousness.
I bow to that primordial Puruṣa, the God, whose incarnate forms the lords of sages worship, for the sake of accomplishing my purpose. (NarP 1.11.22)
I bow to that cause of the world, who is equal and free from guile— the one whom the Vedas do not know and whom even the wise do not know.

I pay homage to him who is worshipped by all, whose vision is wondrous, who is the cause of the world’s form and the world’s origin, and who is like an illusion to those afflicted by calamities. NarP_1,11.24 //
I bow to that husband of Kamalā, whose devotees— having their heads protected by service to the pollen of his lotus feet— attained supreme perfection.
I bow to Him who is the companion of His devotees, whose greatness even the gods headed by Brahmā do not truly know, and who is exceedingly near to His devotees.
O God, that ocean of compassion who forms an attachment for himself toward those who are peaceful and free from attachment—that God is indeed devoid of attachment. (NarP 1.11.27)
I bow to the Lord of Sacrifice, who is established in sacrificial rites,
the bestower of the fruits of sacrifice, and the awakener of the performance of sacrifice.
I bow to that witness of the world, by whose mere utterance of His name even the sinful Ajāmila attained the supreme abode. (NarP 1.11.29)
I bow to that teacher of the world, the guide of the universe, who is Mahādeva in the form of Hari and Janārdana in the form of Śiva.
I bow to that Leader of all, whose supreme nature even the lords of gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know, being bound by the noose of his māyā.
I bow to that witness of knowledge, whose true existence transcends all means of valid cognition, and who, though dwelling within my own heart, appears as if far removed to those who are unworthy.
From his mouth the Brāhmaṇa was born; from his two arms the Kṣatriya arose;
from his thighs the Vaiśya was produced; and from his feet the Śūdra was born. (NarP 1.11.33)
From his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun was born;
from his mouth Agni and Indra were born, and from his breath Vāyu arose.

Salutations again and again to you, who take the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas; whose essence is the attainment of the true tones; and who possess the form of the six limbs [of the Veda]. NarP_1,11.35 //
You are Indra, you are the purifier, you are Soma; you are Īśāna, you are Antaka; you are Agni and Nirṛti, you are Varuṇa, and you are Divākara.
The gods and the immovable beings, the piśācas and the rākṣasas,
the mountains, the siddhas and the gandharvas, the rivers, the earth, and the oceans.
You alone are the Lord of the worlds, you who are higher than the highest;
O God, everything is your form—therefore, let there be eternal salutation to you.
O protector of the helpless, O omniscient one, whose form is like that of Bhūta and Indra;
O Janārdana, protect my sons who are being tormented by the Daityas!
Having thus praised the god and bowed to him again and again, the mother of the gods, her breasts washed by tears of joy, spoke with palms joined in reverence. (NarP 1.11.40)
I am to be favored by you, O Lord of Gods, O Cause of all things from the beginning;
grant prosperity free from thorns to my sons, the denizens of heaven.
O Inner Controller, whose form is the universe, O Omniscient Supreme Lord!
What is unknown to You, O Śrīśa? Why do You urge me on, O Prabhō?
Nevertheless, O Lord of Gods, I shall speak to you that which pleases my mind:
I am a mother whose son is in vain, for I am tormented by the Daityas.
I do not wish to harm them, for they too are my sons;
O Lord of the Gods, grant prosperity to my sons without killing them.
Thus addressed, the Lord of the gods, having again attained a state of joy, spoke with respect to the Mother of the Gods, gladdening her, O Brahmin. (NarP 1.11.45)
The Blessed One said: "I am pleased, O Goddess; may it be well with you. For I shall indeed become your son, since such affection for the sons of one's stepmother, O Goddess, is difficult to find."
But those men who recite the hymn composed by you shall possess excellent prosperity,
and their sons shall never decline.
He who behaves with equanimity toward his own son or the son of another shall have no grief for a son; this is the eternal dharma.
Aditi said: "O Lord, I am capable of bearing you— the Supreme Primordial Person,
whose body hairs are innumerable cosmic eggs, the Lord of all, and the Cause of all."
O Lord, how can we comprehend that Lord of the gods, whose power even the Vedas and all the deities do not know? (NarP 1.11.50)
O God, how can I bear You within me—the unborn Lord, subtler than the subtlest, higher than the highest, the Supreme Person? (NarP 1.11.51)
If even one who is joined with great calamities is liberated merely by the recollection of his name, how could such a god deserve birth among common folk? (NarP 1.11.52)
Just as the boar, the fish, and others were your incarnations, O Lord, so too is this one; who can know your activity, O Sovereign of the Universe? (NarP 1.11.53)
Bowing at the lotus of your feet and intent upon the remembrance of your name, O God, I meditate on you alone;
do as you wish.
Sanaka said:
Having heard the words spoken by her, Janārdana, the God of gods, granted fearlessness to the mother of the gods and spoke these words: NarP_1,11.55 //
The Blessed One said:
"O illustrious lady, what you have spoken is true; there is no doubt in this matter.
Nevertheless, O auspicious one, listen as I shall speak that which is more secret than the secret."
Those devotees of mine who are free from passion and hatred, who are intent on me, who are devoid of malice and hypocrisy—they constantly carry me [within them]. (NarP 1.11.57)
Those who are averse to harming others, devoted to the worship of Śiva,
and intent on listening to my stories, indeed carry me constantly within them.
O Goddess, women who are devoted to their husbands, whose very lives are dedicated to them, and who have abandoned all other attachments, constantly carry [the world] upon themselves.
He who is intent on serving his mother and father, devoted to his gurus, fond of guests, and acts for the welfare of the Brahmins—he always carries me. (NarP 1.11.60)
Those who are constantly devoted to sacred fords, likewise intent upon the company of the virtuous,
and whose nature is to favor the world— they always carry me within them.
Those who abstain from helping others, who turn their backs on the wealth of others,
and who are not lustful toward the wives of others— they always carry me.
Those who are always devoted to the worship of Tulasī, those who are intent upon my names,
and those who are constantly dedicated to the protection of cows— they carry me.
Those who have desisted from accepting gifts, who likewise turn away from the food of others, and who are givers of food and water—they indeed carry me constantly. (NarP 1.11.64)
But you, O Queen, whose life is your husband, virtuous and devoted to the welfare of all beings—
having obtained the state of being your son, I shall fulfill your heart's desire.
Having spoken thus to Aditi, the mother of the gods,
the God of Gods gave her a garland that reached her throat and granted her fearlessness, and then vanished.
With a joyful heart, that daughter of Dakṣa, the delighter of the gods,
having bowed to the beloved of Kamalā, returned once more to her own abode.
Then Aditi, the highly fortunate one, honored by the world, being well-pleased,
gave birth at the proper time to a son who was venerated by all the worlds.
One should meditate on the one known as Vāmana, who bears the conch and the discus, who is peaceful, who dwells in the center of the lunar mandala,
and whose hands hold a jar of nectar and curd-rice.
Hari, who resembles a thousand suns, whose eyes are like blooming lotuses,
who is adorned with all ornaments, and who wears yellow garments.

Knowing that Hari, who is worthy of praise by hosts of sages, joined with them, and the sole leader of all the worlds, had appeared, Kaśyapa, overwhelmed with joy, bowed down with palms joined in reverence and began to offer hymns of praise. (NarP 1.11.71)
Kaśyapa said:
Salutations, salutations to you, the cause of all; salutations, salutations to you, the protector of all;
salutations, salutations to you, the leader of the immortals; salutations, salutations to the destroyer of the Daityas.
Homage, homage to Him who is dear to His devotees; homage, homage to Him who delights the virtuous;
homage, homage to Him who destroys the wicked; let there be homage to that Lord of the World. (NarP 1.11.73)

Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇa, who has assumed a dwarf form for a specific purpose, whose prowess is immeasurable, and who wields the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the sword, and the mace; let there be salutation to that Supreme Person.
Homage to the one whose dwelling is the ocean of milk; homage be to the one seated upon the noble lotus of the heart!
Homage to the one of immeasurable radiance like the sun and other luminaries; repeated homage to the one who has come as the narrative of merit!
Salutations, salutations to the one with eyes like the moon; let there be salutations to you, the bestower of the fruits of sacrifice.
Salutations to the one resplendent with the limbs of sacrifice; salutations to you, the beloved of the virtuous.
Homage to the cause of the cause of the world; homage be to you who are devoid of sound and other sensory objects.
Homage be to you, the bestower of divine bliss; homage, homage to you who dwell within the minds of your devotees.
Homage be to you, the destroyer of darkness; homage be to you, who are devoid of sound and other sense-objects.
Homage be to you, the destroyer of darkness, the bearer of the Mandara mountain.
Homage be to you, named Yajñavarāha; homage to the rending of Hiraṇyākṣa.
Homage be to you who assumed the form of a dwarf; homage be to you, the ender of the Kṣatriya lineage!
Homage be to you, the crusher of Rāvaṇa; homage be to you, the elder brother of Nanda’s son!
Salutations to you, O Beloved of Kamalā; salutations to you, the bestower of happiness.
To you, who destroy suffering upon being remembered, I offer salutation after salutation again and again.
O Lord of sacrifice, you who are the arrangement of sacrifice and the destroyer of obstacles to sacrifice;
O you whose form is sacrifice, whose nature is sacrifice, I worship you, the limb of sacrifice. (NarP 1.11.81)
Thus praised, that Lord of Gods, Vāmana, the purifier of the worlds, [was moved].
Laughing, he spoke, increasing the joy of Kaśyapa.
The Blessed One said: "O child, I am pleased; may it be well with you, O one honored by the gods!
Before long, I shall fulfill every desire of your heart."
Thus, in two successive births, I became the slayer of your sons;
even in this birth, I likewise destroy your supreme happiness.
In the meantime, the Daitya Bali,
joined by his preceptor Kāvya and by the lords of sages, commenced a great sacrifice of long duration.
At that sacrifice, Viṣṇu, accompanied by Lakṣmī,
was summoned by the sages who discourse on Brahman for the purpose of accepting the oblation.
While the great sacrifice of the Daitya, whose sovereignty was fully expanded, was in progress,
that young brahmin Vāmana took leave of his mother and father and departed.
Delighting the world with a smile, Vāmana, who is affectionate toward his devotees,
appeared before Bali like Hari himself come in person to consume the sacrificial oblation.
Whether he is ill-behaved or well-behaved, dull-witted or even learned,
Hari is always present within the heart of whoever is endowed with devotion.
Seeing the dwarf approaching, the sages, whose eyes were the faculty of knowledge,
recognized him as the god Nārāyaṇa and rose up together with their assembly.
Having understood this, the preceptor of the Daityas spoke to Bali in private:
"The wicked carry out their tasks without even considering their own sister. (NarP 1.11.91)
Śukra said:
"O gentle Lord of the Daityas,
Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a dwarf and become the son of Aditi, is indeed the one who has seized your fortune."
O Lord of Asuras, he will come to your sacrifice; through you, nothing at all should be given to him. Listen to my opinion, O wise one! (NarP 1,11.93)
The notion of "self" brings happiness, and the notion of "teacher" especially so; the notion of "other" leads to destruction, while the notion of "woman" causes total ruin.
But he who acts for the benefit of one's enemies must especially be slain.
Bali said: "O Guru, you should not speak thus, for it contradicts the path of dharma.
What boon could be greater than this, that Viṣṇu himself accepts [the offering]?"
The wise perform sacrifices for the purpose of pleasing Viṣṇu;
if He is the direct enjoyer of the oblation, who on earth could be superior to Me?
O Teacher, even by a poor person, whatever little is given to Viṣṇu becomes a supreme gift, and it becomes inexhaustible when bestowed. (NarP 1.11.98)
Even when remembered with supreme devotion, the Supreme Person purifies;
if worshipped by anyone in any manner whatsoever, he grants the highest goal.
Hari removes sins even when remembered by those with wicked minds;
for fire indeed burns even when touched unintentionally.
He on whose tip of the tongue reside these two syllables,
"Ha-ri," attains the world of Viṣṇu, from which a return [to this world] is difficult to obtain.
The wise have declared that he who, free from passion and other afflictions, constantly meditates upon Govinda, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
O highly fortunate one, whatever oblation is offered into the fire or even to a Brahmin out of devotion to Hari, by that Viṣṇu is pleased.
"I, however, perform this supreme sacrifice for the sake of pleasing Hari;
if Viṣṇu comes of his own accord, I shall have achieved my purpose, there is no doubt. (NarP 1.11.104)
While the lord of the Daityas was speaking thus, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a dwarf,
entered the sacrificial ground, which was as beautiful as a blazing fire.
Seeing him, who possessed the luster of ten million suns and was beautiful with well-proportioned limbs,
Vāmana suddenly stood up and received him with palms joined in reverence.
Having offered him a seat and washed his feet, he,
together with his family, bore the one in the form of Vāmana upon his head, experiencing supreme joy within himself.

Having offered the *arghya* according to the prescribed rites to Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the universe, the serpent king, his body bristling with hair and his eyes filled with tears of joy, spoke: NarP_1,11.108 //
Bali said:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my life-breath has become fruitful;
today my life is fruitful; I have achieved my purpose, there is no doubt. (NarP 1.11.109)
A rain of unfailing nectar, exceedingly difficult to obtain, has descended upon me;
for by your mere arrival, there is a great festival without effort.
And all these sages have achieved their purpose; of this there is no doubt.
For that austerity which was performed by them in the past has today borne fruit, O Lord. (NarP 1.11.111)
I have attained my goal, I have attained my goal, I have attained my goal—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you; salutations again and again!
"My mind is filled with great enthusiasm, thinking, 'By your command, I shall accomplish your task'; therefore, O Lord, give me your orders. (NarP 1.11.113)
Thus, while the consecrated Urukṛśa was laughing, Vāmana said:
"Give me land measured by three paces to stand upon for my ascetic penance."
Having heard this, Bali said: "I did not ask for a kingdom, nor a village, nor even a city, nor wealth; what have you done? (NarP 1.11.115)
Having heard that, Viṣṇu, the sustainer of all bodies, spoke to Bali,
as if generating detachment in one whose kingdom was about to fall.
The Blessed One said: Listen, O Lord of Daityas, I shall declare that which is the most secret of secrets.
Tell me, what is accomplished by worldly objects for those who are free from all attachments?
But meditate on me as the inner controller of all beings;
O Daitya, everything here exists within me—tell me, what else remains to be accomplished? (NarP 1.11.118)
For those who are free from passion and hatred, who are peaceful, who have abandoned deceit,
and whose very nature is eternal bliss— what else is to be accomplished by them through wealth?
For those of peaceful mind who see all beings as themselves and perceive everything as non-different from their own self—who is the giver, and what is given? 11.120.
"It is determined in the scriptures that this earth belongs to the Kṣatriya lineage;
all who abide by his command attain supreme happiness. (NarP 1.11.121)
The sages have declared that a sixth part of the army should be given to the king;
however, this great earth must be bestowed upon the Brahmins with every effort.
The greatness of the gift of land has never been equaled in the past, nor will it ever be;
there is no doubt that the giver of land attains supreme Nirvana.
By giving even a very small amount of land to a learned Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires,
one attains the world of Brahmā, from which a return to this world is difficult to find.
The giver of land is declared to be a giver of everything; the giver of land shall partake in liberation.
That should be known as the supreme gift, which destroys the life-force of all sins.
Whether one is joined with a great sin or joined with all sins,
by giving a plot of land ten cubits in extent, one is liberated from all evils.
He who gives land to a worthy recipient obtains the fruit of all possible gifts;
there exists nothing equal to the gift of land within the three worlds.
O Bali, I am not able, even in hundreds of years, to describe the fruit of the merit of one who bestows land upon a Brahmin who is destitute of a livelihood.
O Lord of Daityas, he who gives even a small piece of land to one who is devoted to the worship of the gods but destitute of livelihood, is Viṣṇu himself; of this there is no doubt.
He who gives land endowed with sugarcane, wheat, beans, betel-nut trees, and so forth, is Viṣṇu himself; of this there is no doubt.
By giving even a small amount of land to a poor Brahmin who is destitute of livelihood yet has a family, one attains union with Viṣṇu.
By giving a field of one āḍhaka to a brahmin who is devoted to the worship of the gods,
one obtains the fruit arising from bathing for three nights in the Gaṅgā.
Listen to the fruit that one obtains by giving a *droṇikā* of land to a Brahmin who is destitute of a livelihood and devoted to virtuous conduct. (NarP 1.11.133)
Whatever fruit a man obtains by performing hundreds of horse-sacrifices at the Ganges tirthas according to the prescribed rites, he obtains that same fruit in its entirety here.
Listen as I describe the merit of him who gives a khārikā of land to a poor brahmin; pay attention as I speak. (NarP 1.11.135)
Having performed thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices on the banks of the Ganges, one certainly obtains that same fruit.
The gift of land is proclaimed as a great gift, a supreme gift;
it pacifies all sins and bestows the fruit of liberation.
In this regard, O Lord of the Daitya lineage, I shall relate an ancient legend;
listen, for by hearing it with faith, one obtains the fruit of the gift of land. (NarP 1.11.138)
In the past, O Balarāma, during the Brāhma Kalpa, there was an excellent twice-born man of great intelligence named Bhadramati, who was poor and lacked a means of livelihood.
By him all the scriptures, including the Vedas, were heard day and night;
and the Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras were heard in their entirety.
He had six wives, renowned as Śruti, Sindhu,
Yaśovatī, Kāminī, Mālinī, and Śobhā.
O best of Asuras, while these were being cooked, there were two hundred and forty sons of his, all of whom were constantly hungry.
Possessing nothing yet noble-minded, seeing his beloved children afflicted by hunger while he himself was likewise tormented by hunger, he lamented with his senses overwhelmed.
Fie upon a birth devoid of fortune! Fie upon a birth destitute of wealth!
Fie upon a birth devoid of Dharma! Fie upon a birth devoid of renown!
Fie upon the birth and sovereignty of a man who has many offspring but is devoid of virtue!
Oh, how wonderful are virtue, gentleness, learning, and birth in a noble family! (NarP 1.11.145)
For one submerged in the ocean of poverty, none of this is glorious—not beloved sons and grandsons, nor kinsmen and brothers. (NarP 1.11.146)
And all disciples and men alike abandon that which is devoid of sovereignty;
whether he be an outcaste or even a twice-born, it is only the fortunate one who is honored.
In this world, a poor man is reviled by people like a corpse;
whereas one endowed with wealth—whether he be cruel or even gentle—is highly esteemed. (NarP 1.11.148)
Whether one is devoid of virtues or possesses them, whether one is a fool or a scholar—if one is endowed with the quality of sovereignty, one is certainly worthy of honor; of this there is no doubt.
Alas, poverty is suffering, and therein hope is the giver of extreme pain;
men overcome by hope experience inexhaustible suffering. (NarP 1.11.150)
Those who have hope as their servant are the servants of the whole world;
but for those whose servant is hope, the world serves them.
For in this world, pride is said to be the inexhaustible wealth of the great;
when that pride is destroyed by the enemy known as despair, there is poverty.
Even one who knows the meaning of all the scriptures appears like a fool when he is poor;
for those seized by the great crocodile of destitution, who is there to grant liberation?
Alas, what suffering! Alas, what suffering! Alas, what suffering is poverty!
And therein, even more, the abundance of sons and wives is a source of extreme misery.
Having spoken thus, Bhadramati, who had reached the further shore of the meaning of all treatises,
then reflected in his mind upon another dharma that bestows sovereignty.
Having determined that the gift of land is the most excellent of all gifts,
he who approves of such a gift has himself performed it in the past.
The gift of land is proclaimed to be the supreme giver of the highest Dharma, bestowing the fruits of all desires, and the most excellent among all gifts. (NarP 1.11.157)
"Whatever a man has given most dearly cherished, by giving that he becomes equal [to the recipient]," having thus resolved, the wise and firm-minded Bhadramati gave his strength. (NarP 1.11.158)
He went to the city named Kauśāmbī, accompanied by his wife, children,
and draft animals, to the eminent brahmin named Sughoṣa, who was endowed with all forms of prosperity.
Having gone there, Sughoṣa, who was devoted to the Dharma, requested five cubits of land from Bala; and Bala, that householder, looked upon him.
With a delighted mind, having worshipped him thoroughly, he said this: "O one of auspicious intellect, I have achieved my purpose; my birth has become fruitful. (NarP 1.11.161)
"O twice-born one, my lineage has been purified by your grace," having said this and having honored him, Sughoṣa, who was devoted to dharma, [departed]. (NarP 1.11.162)
The high-minded one gave him five *hasta*s of land—the holy earth belonging to Viṣṇu, the earth protected by Viṣṇu. (NarP 1.11.163)
"By this mantra, O Lord of Daityas, Sughoṣa [offered] that earth to the best of the twice-born, saying: 'May Janārdana be pleased with me by means of this gift of the earth.'"
Having worshipped him with the thought that he was Viṣṇu, the brahmin Bhadramati gave away that much of the earth,
which had been requested by the wise one.
Sughoṣa, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage, bestowed [the land] as a gift of earth upon a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who was a devoted follower of Hari and a householder.
He took refuge in the abode of Viṣṇu, having gone to which one does not grieve;
and from there, Bhadramati also requested prosperity for Bali.
He remained in the abode of Viṣṇu with his family for ten thousand yugas,
and likewise, having stayed in the abode of Brahmā for ten million yugas.
Having attained the station of Indra, he remained there for five kalpas;
then, having returned to the earth, he was endowed with all sovereign powers.
Remembering his past births, the illustrious Bhadramati enjoyed supreme pleasures;
thereafter, O Daitya, he became free from desire and devoted to Viṣṇu.
He bestowed the earth upon the Brahmins who were destitute of livelihood;
to him, Viṣṇu, with a gracious soul, granted unsurpassed sovereignty over the principles (tattvas).
O Lord of Daityas, you who are devoted to all dharma, you granted me supreme liberation while I was accompanied by ten million of my lineage. (NarP 1.11.172)
"I shall practice austerities for the sake of liberation; grant me the earth consisting of three paces.
Thereupon, the son of Virocana was seen holding a water-filled jar.
Knowing that he was obstructing the flow of water, Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, took up the earth in order to give it to the Brahmin Vāmana.
He placed that poem, like a tip of darbha grass held in his hand, upon the arrow;
at the tip of the darbha grass, there appeared a great scripture with a radiance equal to ten million suns.
The exceedingly fierce Brahmā, whose intellect is unfailing and who is eager to swallow the eyes of Kāvya,
arrived with his single eye, having [already] consumed the Asuras of the Bhṛgu lineage.
