And saying, "Behold," he pointed with the tip of a blade of darbha grass that was like a weapon;
Bali gave the earth, measured by three paces, to Mahāviṣṇu.
Then that Viśvātman, Hari, whose body is the universe, grew as far as the world of Brahmā; he measured out the earth with two of his feet.
Radiant with these footprints extending as far as the shell of the Brahma-egg,
he split the cosmic egg in two, piercing it from the tip of his big toe.
Through those channels, the external water arrived in many streams—
the pure, world-purifying water that had washed the foot of Viṣṇu.
That water, which was the abode outside the egg of Brahmā and existed in the form of a stream, was pure and supreme; it purified the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
And that which is practiced by the assembly of the virtuous fell upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Having witnessed this wondrous deed, the hosts of deities headed by Brahmā,
as well as the sages and the Manus, praised him, overwhelmed with joy.
The gods said: "Obeisance to the Supreme Lord, whose form is the supreme Self; to the one higher than the highest, who assumes forms that are not other [than Himself];
to the Self of Brahman, whose intellect is devoted to Brahman; obeisance be to You, whose nature is unimpeded action. (NarP 1.11.184)
O Supreme Lord, O Supreme Bliss, O Supreme Self, O One higher than the highest!
O Soul of all, whose form is the universe, O You who transcend all means of knowledge, salutations to You!
Salutations to you who have eyes on all sides, salutations to you whose arms are on all sides;
salutations to you whose head is on all sides, and salutations to you whose movement is on all sides.
Thus praised by Brahmā and the other inhabitants of heaven, the eternal God of gods, Mahāviṣṇu,
granted them fearlessness and rejoiced.
He bound the Daitya Virocana’s son, who was his equal in power;
then, recognizing that Bali had sought refuge, he granted him the netherworld (rasātala),
and the gatekeeper there became devoted to him.
Nārada said: In Rasātala, what did Mahāviṣṇu provide as food for the son of Virocana, who was in that terrible place filled with the fear of serpents?
Sanaka said:
That oblation which is offered into the fire without being consecrated by mantras,
and that which is given to an unworthy recipient— that is a terrible means of enjoyment.
Whatever oblation has been offered, whatever gift has been received, and whatever meritorious deed has been performed by one who is impure—
all that is fit for enjoyment there [in hell], yet it yields the fruit of falling downward.
Thus Viṣṇu, having granted freedom from fear to Bali together with the asuras, gave the netherworld (rasātala) to him and bestowed the third heaven upon all the gods.
Being honored by hosts of immortals, praised by great seers,
and sung of by Gandharvas, he again assumed the form of a dwarf.
Having witnessed this great deed of the sage who speaks of Brahman, they,
with smiling faces, paid homage to one another and to the Supreme Person.
Viṣṇu, who is the self of all beings, having assumed the form of a dwarf and deluding the entire world, entered the forest for the sake of ascetic penance.
Such is the power of that goddess Gaṅgā, who has her origin in the foot of Viṣṇu;
by the mere remembrance of her, one is liberated from all sins.
But whoever should read or even hear this majesty of the Gaṅgā in a temple or on a riverbank shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Origin of the Gaṅgā and the Greatness of the Gaṅgā," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. Nārada said:
"I have heard the greatness of the Gaṅgā, which fulfills desires and destroys sins."
Now, O brother, tell me the characteristics of the recipient of a gift and of the giver.
Sanaka said:
For all social classes (varṇas), Brahmā is the supreme preceptor;
one who desires the infinity of their gift should give those [offerings] to him.
A Brāhmaṇa may accept gifts from all sources, being free from fear;
however, the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya should never accept such gifts.
A gift given to one who is fierce, one who is childless, one who delights in deceitful conduct,
and also to one who abandons his own duty, becomes fruitless.
Even for one who delights in another's wife, who covets another's wealth, or who points out the constellations [for gain], that which is given becomes fruitless. (NarP 1.12.5)

A gift given to one whose mind is possessed by envy, who has committed a transgression, who is deceitful, or even to one who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, becomes fruitless.
What is given to one who is constantly intent on begging, to a harmful person, to a wicked man,
or to a seller of liquor, becomes fruitless.
O Brahmin, that which is given to one who sells the Vedas, or likewise to one who sells the Smṛtis, or to a seller of Dharma, becomes fruitless. (NarP 1.12.7–8)
That which is given to one whose livelihood is through song, to one whose wife is unchaste,
and to one who torments others, becomes fruitless.
To one who lives by the sword, one who lives by ink, a temple-priest, a village priest, or a washerman—if a gift is given to such as these, it becomes fruitless. 1.12.10.
Even if given to one who cooks for others, to a poet, to a slanderer, or to one who eats what is forbidden to eat, a gift becomes fruitless. (NarP 1.12.11)
That which is given to those who eat the food of Śūdras, to those who burn the corpses of Śūdras,
and to those who eat the food of outcasts (paṃśula) becomes fruitless.
A gift given to Viṣṇu who sells his name, to one who has abandoned the performance of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā),
or to one consumed by accepting improper gifts, becomes fruitless.

What is given to one who is habituated to sleeping during the day, likewise to one who engages in sexual intercourse, or even to one who eats at the two junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), becomes fruitless. (NarP 1.12.14)
A gift given to one who is guilty of a mortal sin, who has been abandoned by kinsmen and relatives, or who is a *kuṇḍa* or a *gola*, becomes fruitless. (NarP 1.12.15)
What is given to one who is deceitful, to a reviler, to one who is negligent,
to one conquered by women, or to one who is exceedingly wicked, shall be fruitless.
What is given to one who consumes liquor and meat, to a libertine, to one who is excessively greedy, to a thief, or even to a slanderer, becomes fruitless. (NarP 1.12.17)
O best of the twice-born, one should neither accept gifts from nor speak with those who are addicted to evil and are always censured by the virtuous;
O Nārada, even to one devoted to good deeds, a gift should be given with effort.
That gift which is given with faith and likewise offered to Viṣṇu, or even that which is requested by a worthy recipient, shall be the most excellent gift. (NarP 1.12.19)
O Nārada, that gift which is given to a worthy recipient with a view toward the next world or even this world is called "optional" (kāmya) and is considered mediocre.
Furthermore, a gift given with pride, for the sake of harming another, or even by an improper method;
given while angry, without faith, or to an unworthy recipient—that gift is considered middling. (NarP 1.12.21)

The best among those who know the Vedas have declared that [worship] performed for the gratification of one's strength is inferior, that performed for the accomplishment of one's own ends is middling, and that performed for the sake of pleasing Hari is supreme.
Wealth has three destinies: it may lead to generosity, enjoyment, or destruction.
O Brahmin, wealth that one gives but does not enjoy is a cause of destruction;
wealth has dharma as its fruit, and dharma is that which brings satisfaction to Mādhava.
Do not even trees live for the sake of others in this world,
since those trees perform the work of others with their roots and fruits?
O Brahmins, if humans do not act for the sake of others, then they are as good as dead;
for those mortals who do not perform the work of others, neither with their bodies nor with their wealth, are truly dead.
Whether by thought or even by word, they are to be known as the most wicked of evildoers. In this regard, I shall relate an ancient history; listen, O Nārada, according to the truth. (NarP_1,12.27)
In this [work], the characteristics of generosity and the other perfections have been fully proclaimed, together with the majesty of the Gaṅgā, which destroys all sins. (NarP 1.12.28)
[This is] the dialogue between Bhagīratha and Dharma, which is a cause of merit. King Bhagīratha was born in the lineage of Sagara.
He ruled this earth with its seven islands and its oceans,
ever devoted to all righteous duties, true to his word, and full of majesty.

In beauty, that king was like Kandarpa; he was wise and possessed the vigor of a sacrificer; in fortitude he was equal to the Snowy Mountain (Himavat), and in righteousness he was like Dharma himself.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, having reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures, possessed of every prosperity, he brings joy to all, O Sage. (NarP 1.12.32)
Always diligent in hospitality, devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva,
he was valiant, a treasury of virtues, friendly, compassionate, and wise.
O best of the twice-born, having learned that the king was such as this, Dharmarāja once came to see Bhagīratha.
The king honored the King of Dharma who had arrived according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures; then Dharma spoke to him: "Dharma said to him: (NarP 1.12.35).
The King of Dharma said:
"O King, best among those who know the dharma, you are renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having heard of your fame, O Dharmarāja, I have come to see you."
The gods, who delight in asceticism and cherish exalted virtues, desire to behold one who is devoted to the true path, truthful, and intent on the welfare of all beings.
O King, wherever fame, policy, and prosperity exist,
there the virtuous qualities and the divine beings invariably dwell.
"Oh, King of great fortune, how beautiful is your conduct!
Because it is for the benefit of all beings, such as this is difficult even for those like me to find. (NarP 1.12.39)
Having prostrated before Dharma who had spoken thus, Bhagīratha, filled with humility and rejoicing, addressed him in gentle words: NarP_1,12.40.
Bhagīratha said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, impartial observer, Lord of the Gods!
Moved by supreme compassion, please tell me that which I ask."
What kind of dharmas have been proclaimed? What worlds belong to those endowed with dharma? How many torments have been proclaimed, and for whom are they said to exist?
O illustrious one, you ought to explain to me in detail all those who are to be honored by you, and likewise those who are to be disciplined.
The King of Dharma said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great intelligence! Your mind is pure and exalted.
I shall proclaim dharma and adharma according to their true nature; listen with devotion. (NarP 1.12.44)
Many kinds of dharmas have been proclaimed as bestowing the worlds of merit;
likewise, innumerable torments of terrible appearance have been proclaimed.
It is not possible to describe this in detail even in tens of thousands of years;
therefore, I shall speak of it in brief as a demonstration of what is dharma and what is adharma.
In the same way, a gift given to one who has undergone great suffering is proclaimed to be of great merit;
likewise, a gift given to one who knows the inner self becomes inexhaustible.

Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who, having given [a well], causes it to be established for a householder, one learned in the scriptures, a Vedic scholar, or one endowed with virtues. (NarP 1.12.48)
Accompanied by ten million kinsmen on both his mother’s and father’s side, that twice-born man,
having entered the abode of Viṣṇu, rejoices there for an entire kalpa.
The dust particles of the earth may be counted, and the drops of rain may be counted;
but even by the Creator himself, the fruits of the life of a Brahmin cannot indeed be counted.
The Brahmin is proclaimed to be the embodiment of all deities; who is capable of describing the merit of one who provides him with his livelihood? (NarP 1.12.51)
He who constantly performs what is beneficial for Brahmins has performed all sacrifices;
he has bathed in all sacred fords, and by him all austerity has been practiced.
He who urges the Brahmins toward their supreme livelihood by saying, "Let him give," also obtains that same fruit; what is the use of much further talk?
Whether one constructs a pond oneself or through another,
no one with a lifespan of even a hundred years is able to describe the full measure of its merit.
O King, if even a single traveler drinks the water of a pond, all the sins of the maker of that pond are destroyed; of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.12.55)
Even if a man stays on land for only a single day while the water is on the ground,
he is liberated from all sins and shall dwell in heaven for a hundred years.
Any mortal who, being capable, provides assistance according to his power to construct a pond,
he too obtains that fruit, as does the one who instigates the work when satisfied.
Whoever throws a handful of earth or mustard seeds outside a pond or similar body of water shall remain in heaven for a hundred years, liberated from tens of millions of sins.
O best of kings, he with whom the deities or his gurus are pleased shall partake in the merit of the tank; such is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Thus, O best of kings, I shall relate a humorous tale to you here;
by hearing which one is liberated from all sins, of this there is no doubt.
In the land of Gauḍa, there was a king named Vīrabhadraka, who was extremely famous,
a great adversary [of his enemies], learned, and always a worshiper of Brahmins.
He was endowed with Vedic learning, scriptural knowledge, and noble family traditions, and possessed friends and wealth;
his illustrious queen was named Campakamañjarī.
The great ministers of that king, who were skilled in discerning the true nature of things, always made determinations regarding all matters according to the treatises on dharma.
"He who explains penance, medical treatment, astrology, or the determination of dharma by means of the science of destruction (vināśāstra) is called a slayer of a Brahmin. (NarP 1.12.64)
Having thus resolved in his mind, the king always listens to the dharmas proclaimed by Manu and others from his teachers according to the prescribed rule.
In the realm of that king, who protected his country according to dharma, not even the lowliest person acted unjustly.
A state of equality with heaven, bringing auspiciousness through good governance, had arisen;
and once that king was in a great forest on a hunt.
Surrounded by his ministers and others, he wandered about like the midday sun;
for there, by fate, he was utterly exhausted from a hunt that had yielded nothing.
O King, as he was returning from the lake, the sight of the lake arose before him;
then, seeing the lake dried up, he reflected there: NarP_1,12.69.
"What is this lake on the peak of the mountain, and by whom was it created? How might there be water here, so that this king may live? (NarP 1.12.70)
Then, O best of kings, the thought occurred to him regarding the excavation:
having dug a pit one cubit deep, he reached water. (NarP 1.12.71)
When that water was drunk, the king attained satisfaction,
as did the minister named Buddhisāgara, O lord of the earth.
That ocean of wisdom, skilled in matters of dharma and worldly affairs, said to the king:
"O King, this lotus pond was formerly filled with rainwater. (NarP 1.12.73)
"Today the thought has arisen in me to build a rampart around this city;
therefore, O sinless Lord, may you be pleased and grant me your permission. (NarP 1.12.74)
Having heard these words of the minister, the best of kings,
that monarch, rejoiced exceedingly and prepared to perform the rite himself.
Then, by the king's command, that Buddhisāgara also joyfully appointed him to that auspicious task among the ministers.
The most meritorious one prepared to turn the lake into an ocean,
extending fifty bows in width and length on all sides.
He constructed a lake with bottomless sands, its stones firmly bound together;
having fashioned that lake, he reported everything to the king.
O King, from that time forward, all the forest-dwellers and thirsty travelers there obtained auspicious water. (NarP 1.12.79)
Once, at the end of his own lifespan, that minister Buddhisāgara died and went to the world of me, O Lord, the Teacher of the World.
For that purpose, I questioned Dharma, the author of the script of righteousness; Citragupta then reported all of that deed to me.
Moreover, he himself is the instructor of the king in matters of dharma;
therefore, he is worthy to ascend the chariot of dharma here.
O King, when Citragupta had spoken thus, I commanded the ocean of intelligence to ascend the celestial vehicle known as Dharma.
Then, O King, after some time, that King Vīrabhadraka died and went to my abode, where he paid homage to me with great joy.
But there, O King, I also questioned him about his entire karma; Citragupta then recounted the dharma born of the lake.
Then I correctly enlightened the king; listen as it was told:
"O protector of the earth, on the plateau above a mountain of sand lies another [region]. (NarP 1.12.86)
O best of kings, after that cock had dug two finger-breadths deep into the water with its beak, at another time, that boar [did the same]. (NarP 1.12.87)
He dug a hole one cubit deep with his own beak,
and then another was made by Kālyā, measuring two cubits.
O Great King, when that water had remained in the lake for two months, it was drunk by small forest-dwelling creatures who were overwhelmed by thirst. (NarP 1.12.89)
Then, at the end of the rainy season, O observer of noble vows, a trench three cubits deep was dug by Gajatāna, and there was an abundance of water therein.
That water remained there for three months, and while it was being consumed by forest-dwelling creatures,
you arrived at that place immediately after the drying up of the water.
O King, when a month has passed there, you should dig for water at the *hasta* [asterism];
then, O ruler of men, by the instruction of that minister, you [shall obtain it]. (NarP 1.12.92)
A great body of water arose there, dug out to a depth of fifty bow-lengths;
it was then firmly bound together with stones and became a vast lake.
Furthermore, trees beneficial to all the world were planted there.
O Lord of the World, by their respective merits these five have ascended this righteous celestial chariot; you too should ascend it.
Having heard these words, that king, the lord of the earth,
ascended that celestial chariot as the sixth king, sharing in my portion.
Thus, all this fruit produced by a tank has been recounted to you;
having heard this, one is liberated from sin from birth until the end of death. (NarP 1.12.96)
That person who, endowed with faith, hears or recites what has been explained,
shall likewise obtain the entire merit arising from the construction of the lake.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of Dharma," in the first quarter of the Pūrvabhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Dharmarāja said:
"He who constructs a temple for a deity, or even causes one to be constructed..."
Listen now to the fruit of the merit of that [person], whether it be Śiva’s or even Hari’s.
Accompanied by a hundred thousand million kinsmen on both his mother’s and father’s side, he remains indeed in the abode of Viṣṇu for three kalpas; of this there is no doubt.
Listen as I declare the merit that belongs to that man who constructs a temple for a deity out of clay alone. (NarP 1.13.3)
Having assumed a divine body and mounted an excellent celestial chariot, he remains in the abode of Viṣṇu for three kalpas; of this there is no doubt.
Listen as I declare the merit that belongs to that man who constructs a temple for a deity even out of clay alone. (NarP 1.13.5)
Having assumed a divine body and mounted an excellent celestial chariot,
he shall dwell in the station of Viṣṇu for three kalpas and then proceed to the city of Brahmā.
Having remained there for two kalpas, he shall dwell again in heaven for one kalpa;
thereafter, he will be born into a family of yogins, endowed with compassion.
One who, having resorted to the Vaiṣṇava yoga, attains eternal liberation;
for one who constructs [an image] with wood, the fruit shall be twofold.
With bricks it is threefold, but with stone it is fourfold;
with crystal stones, however, it should be known as ten times greater.
Compared to those [merits], protecting a temple, a pond, or a village would be a hundredfold greater; by means of gold, it would become ten millionfold greater for one who protects such a place.
O King, by performing service for a temple through plastering, sprinkling, and decorating it, one’s merit becomes a hundredfold greater than that of the original builder. (NarP 1.13.11)
Whatever one should constantly perform with devotion, its merit is infinite—even if those meritorious deeds are undertaken for wages or out of necessity. (NarP 1.13.12)
Those upholders of the earth go indeed to the eternal station of Viṣṇu;
O King, half the fruit of a tank is proclaimed for a pond.
The fruit of [digging] a well is known to be one *pada*; that of a large pond (*vāpī*) is measured at eight *karas*;
the fruit of a canal (*kulyā*) is said by the Lord of the Earth to be a hundred times that of a large pond.
"One who possesses wealth should perform [the worship] with stones, while a person lacking anything should do so with clay;
the fruit of these two shall be equal," so said the Lotus-born One.
A wealthy person should give a city, while one who possesses nothing should give a mere cubit of land; those learned in the Vedas declare that the fruit for both of them is equal.
If a wealthy man constructs a tank as a means to achieve merit, and a poor man constructs a well, their merit is proclaimed to be equal. (NarP 1.13.17)
He who causes a hermitage to be built that benefits many living beings goes to the world of Brahmā, accompanied by three generations of his lineage.
O King, whether it be a cow, a Brahmin, or whoever else it may be,
one who stands for even half a moment in their shadow leads that person to heaven.
O King, those who establish groves, those who build temples for the gods,
and those who construct tanks and villages, are honored together with Hari.
O lords of men, hear now the fruit of the merit of those who establish a flower garden for the benefit of all the world, or for the sake of the deities. (NarP 1.13.21)
There, for as many years as there are leaves and flowers [on that tree], he rejoices in heaven together with ten million members of his lineage.
Those who construct ramparts for him and provide enclosures of thorns go to the abode of Brahmā, the sole lord of the ages.
O Lord of Men, O King, listen as I describe the fruit of merit for those who perform the planting of the *tulasī* plant. (NarP 1.13.24)
O King, endowed with sixty million lineages on both the mother’s and the father’s side,
he shall dwell in the abode of Nārāyaṇa for more than a hundred kalpas.

Listen now to the fruit of the merit of one who wears the vertical *puṇḍra* mark made from the clay at the root of a *tulasī* plant, or with *gopīcandana*, or even with clay from Citrakūṭa, or indeed with clay from the Gaṅgā. (NarP 1.13.26)
Mounted upon a supreme celestial chariot, with his deeds being sung by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, he rejoices in the intoxication of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, as many leaves as have fallen from the roots of the *tulasī* plant,
so many sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed.
He who sprinkles even a mere handful of water upon the *tulasī* shall dwell together with the Lord who resides in the Ocean of Milk for as long as the moon and stars endure.
He who gives even a single tender leaf of *tulasī* to the Brahmins goes to the abode of Brahmā, accompanied by three generations of his lineage.
He who offers śāla blossoms or tulasī leaves shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu until the dissolution of all beings.
He who causes a fence of thorns or even a wall to be constructed likewise rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for twenty-one generations.
O Lord of Men, he who worships the lotus feet of Hari with the tender leaves of Tulasī shall not return again from the world of Viṣṇu.
He who bathes Hari with milk on the twelfth day or the full moon day rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu, along with ten million members of his lineage.
He who bathes Keśava with even a single *prastha* measure of milk shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu, accompanied by tens of millions upon tens of millions of his kinsmen.
O King, that man who bathes Viṣṇu with a prastha of ghee on the twelfth day attains union with Hari, along with ten million members of his lineage.
Whoever causes a bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) to be performed for Viṣṇu on the eleventh day shall attain union with Him after ten million times ten thousand births.
O best of kings, on the eleventh, the full moon day, or the twelfth, one should bathe Viṣṇu with coconut water; hear now the fruit of that act.
O best of kings, liberated from the sins accumulated over ten lifetimes,
he rejoices together with Viṣṇu along with two hundred families.
O King, he who bathes Keśava, the Lord of Gods, with sugarcane juice shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu together with his ancestors numbering one hundred thousand.
Having bathed Govinda with flower-water and likewise with scented water, one who worships Hari with devotion shall attain the station of Viṣṇu.
He who bathes Mādhava with water filtered through a cloth,
being liberated from all sins, rejoices together with Viṣṇu.
Whoever bathes Hari with milk and other substances at the time of the sun's transit shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu together with three hundred generations of his ancestors.
On the fourteenth day, the eighth day, or on the full moon day of the bright fortnight.
On the eleventh lunar day, on Sunday, on the twelfth, on the fifth lunar day,
during solar and lunar eclipses, and on the anniversaries of the Manvantaras and Yugas.
When the sun rises at midday during Puṣya, on a Sunday; likewise when Rohiṇī coincides with a Wednesday;
and similarly when Śani (Saturn) is in Rohiṇī, or when Aśvinī coincides with a Tuesday.
On a Saturday when the moon is in Śatabhiṣaj or Bharaṇī, at the conjunction of Bhṛgu and Revatī, as well as on a Wednesday in Anurādhā, and likewise on a Sunday in Śravaṇa; NarP_1,13.47 //

And likewise, when the moon is in the constellation Śravaṇa conjoined with the asterism Hasta, when Jupiter is present, on the eighth lunar day of Mercury, in the month of Āṣāḍha, and during the auspicious Vināyakī festival; NarP_1,13.48 //
One who is peaceful, restrained in speech, and pure should bathe Viṣṇu with milk, or even with ghee, honey, or curd; hear now the fruit of that act. (NarP 1.13.49)
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices and being freed from all sins, O King,
he shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu together with three hundred generations of his ancestors.

Having attained right there that knowledge which is difficult even for yogins to obtain, O King, one attains liberation from which a return [to worldly existence] is difficult to find again. (NarP 1.13.51)
O King, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight falling on a Monday,
by bathing Śiva with milk, one shall attain union with Śiva.
Having bathed Śiva with devotion even with coconut water on the eighth lunar day or on a Monday, one attains union with Śiva.
O King, on the fourteenth or the eighth day of the bright fortnight, having bathed Śivā with ghee and honey, one shall attain equality with her. (NarP 1.13.54)
Having bathed Viṣṇu or Śiva in this manner with sesame oil,
he goes to a state of similarity with that deity, together with his ancestors who are virtuous beings.
He who bathes [the deity] with even the juice of the Śivamiśra plant with devotion shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa, together with his ancestors and descendants.
O highly fortunate one, on the twelfth day at the time of rising, one should bathe the Liṅga with ghee or milk; hear now from my words the fruit of that act.
O King, a man liberated from the sins committed throughout ten thousand births shall uplift his lineage numbering in the tens of millions and attain the state of Śiva.
O King, having worshipped Viṣṇu with perfumes and flowers on the lunar day sacred to Viṣṇu,
one is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten thousand births and goes to His abode.
The man who worships Viṣṇu or Śivā with a lotus flower goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
Having worshipped Hari with *ketakī* flowers and Śiva with *dhattūra* flowers at night,
one is liberated from sin and shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu for a *yuga*.
O Great King, by worshipping Hari with campaka flowers and Śaṅkara with arka flowers, one shall attain the same world as those respective deities.
Or by offering guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter as incense to Śaṅkara or Viṣṇu with devotion, a person is liberated from all sins.
O best of kings, by offering a lamp filled with sesame oil to either Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara,
a man obtains all his desires.
Whoever offers a lamp with ghee to Śaṅkara or to Viṣṇu is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
O King, listen now to the fruit obtained by lighting a lamp for Mahāviṣṇu or even for Śiva with ghee, oil, or indeed any other substance. (NarP 1.13.66)
Freed from all sins and endowed with all sovereign powers,
he attains residence in the same world as those respective [deities] for three generations of his lineage.
Whatever food is most dear to one, by giving that very thing to the Lord Viṣṇu,
one goes to that very station, accompanied by forty generations of one's lineage.
Whatever object is most dear to oneself, one should cause that to be given to a Brahmin;
he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
O King, one becomes pure by the gift of gold for the sake of an embryo-killer;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to that of food and water.
The giver of food is declared to be the giver of life, and the giver of life is the giver of everything;
for, O best of kings, the fruit of all gifts belongs to the giver of food.
The giver of food goes to the abode of Brahmā accompanied by ten thousand generations;
it is certain in the scriptures that for him there is no returning again.
O best of kings, the gift of water is known to provide immediate satisfaction;
for this reason, it has been declared by the exponents of the Vedas to be superior even to the gift of food.
Whether one is joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) or even joined with minor sins (upapātaka), one who gives water is liberated from them; so said the Lotus-born One.
They say that the body is born of food, and they know that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are also born of food;
therefore, O Lord of the Earth, the giver of food should be known as the giver of life.
O King, since there is no gift that brings such satisfaction as food, which bestows the fruit of all desires, therefore, O protector of the earth, there is no gift equal to food on this earth.
O best of kings, those born in the family of one who gives food do not see a hell for a thousand years;
therefore, the giver of food is preeminent.
The man who, filled with devotion, performs an oil massage for the feet of a guest,
has effectively bathed in all sacred fords, preceded by a bath in the Gaṅgā.
O Great King, he who performs an oil massage for Brahmins has effectively bathed more than eight hundred times in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.
That protector who, out of love, protects those Brahmins who are afflicted by disease,
shall dwell in the city of Vaikuṇṭha for a yuga, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
O protector of the earth, Viṣṇu, with a gracious soul, bestows all desires upon him who protects a theatrical arena or a diseased man.
He who protects one afflicted by disease through thought, deed, or word, being himself freed from all evils, attains all his desires. (NarP 1.13.82)
O protector of the earth, to him who indeed gives a dwelling to a Brāhmaṇa,
the Lord of the Gods, being pleased, bestows his own world.
He who gives a milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda goes to the abode of Brahmā, which is exceedingly difficult for others to attain.
O wise one, even if one were to receive a milch cow from others and then give it away, I am not able to describe the fruit of his merit. (NarP 1.13.85)
O protector of the earth, he who gives a milch cow of the Kapila breed to one learned in the Vedas becomes Rudra himself, freed from all sins.
Whoever should give a cow with two faces (one at each end) to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas,
no one is able to calculate his merit even in hundreds of years.
O King, listen as I shall tell you the fruit of his merit according to the truth:
on one side are all the sacrifices, complete with the most excellent sacrificial fees.
O protector of the earth, he who protects the life of a living being terrified on one side— specifically a brahmin overwhelmed by fear— is performing a great act of preservation.
He who gives clothing has bathed in all sacred fords and is consecrated in all sacrifices;
the giver of a maiden goes to the abode of Rudra, and the giver of a daughter goes to the station of Brahmā.
He who gives a daughter adorned with ornaments to one who knows the supreme self goes to the abode of Viṣṇu along with his entire lineage.
Endowed with a hundred lineages, O King, he shall go to the abode of Rūhyaṇa on the full moon day of Kārttika, or indeed on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha.
One should release a bull for the sake of pleasing Śiva; hear now the fruit of that act:
liberated from the sins accumulated over many births, one comes to possess the form of Rudra.
Having marked a buffalo with the Śiva-liṅga, he who releases it rejoices together with Rudra as the lord of his family. (NarP 1.13.94)
O best of kings, he who gives betel-leaf according to his ability shall not experience the world of torment, O most excellent of monarchs. (NarP 1.13.95)
Viṣṇu, with a gracious soul, grants him long life, fame, and prosperity;
likewise, the Ocean of Milk, the Giver of Clarified Butter, the Giver of Honey, and the Giver of Curd [bestow their gifts].
He is glorified in the heavenly world for ten thousand divine years.
O best of kings, the giver of sugarcane goes to the abode of Brahmā.
The giver of perfumes, who bestows the fruit of merit, goes to the abode of Brahmā;
and the giver of jaggery and sugarcane juice likewise goes to the Ocean of Milk.
A man who gives water to soldiers goes to the unsurpassed world of the Sun;
by the gift of knowledge, a person attains union with Mādhava.
The gift of knowledge, the gift of land, and the gift of a cow are the most excellent of all;
through recitation, driving [the cow], and milking, they truly deliver one from hell.
Among all forms of giving, the gift of knowledge is preeminent;
by the gift of knowledge, O best of kings, one attains union with Viṣṇu.
Indeed, by the gift of fuel, a man is liberated from minor offenses;
the gift of a Śālagrāma stone is proclaimed as a great gift.
The gift of a *liṅga* is likewise remembered as that which, when given, one attains liberation;
it yields the same fruit that a man obtains by the gift of ten million cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*).
One obtains that fruit through the gift of a *liṅga*; of this there is no doubt. By the gift of a *śālagrāma* stone, the fruit is twice as great as that. (NarP 1.13.104)
O Lord, that man who gives a gift to one known as Viṣṇu himself, who exists in the form of a stone at Śālagrama, attains the state of a householder.
O best of kings, by the gift of gold endowed with gems, the certain fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā arises for him, O supreme monarch. (NarP 1.13.106)
Since it is remembered that through great gifts one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
a person may attain supreme liberation by the gift of a ruby.
By the gift of a diamond, a human being attains the world of Indra;
by the gift of coral, one shall attain the world of Rudra.
By the gift of vehicles one goes [to the world of the Moon], and by the gift of pearls, to the world of the Moon;
by the gift of lapis lazuli one reaches the world of Rudra, as does the giver of topaz.
By the gift of a ruby, one enjoys happiness everywhere;
O King, one attains the presence of horses for a long time. (NarP 1.13.110)
By the great gift of an elephant, one obtains all desires;
by the gift of a vehicle, one goes to heaven seated upon a celestial chariot.
By the gift of a buffalo, one certainly conquers death; of this there is no doubt.
By the offering of grass to cows, one shall attain the world of Rudra.
The lord of the earth who bestows salt attains the world of Varuṇa;
those devoted to their own duties and conduct, and intent on the welfare of all beings, [attain the same].
Free from hypocrisy, devoid of malice, devoted to instructing others, free from passion and envy, they go to the abode of Brahmā.
Those who are devoted to the worship of Hari’s feet go to the abode of Hari;
they delight in the company of the virtuous and are ever-striving in noble deeds.
Those who turn away from slandering others, and who are constantly intent on doing what is beneficial for Brahmins and cows, go to the abode of Hari.
Those who turn away from union with the wives of others do not see the abode of Yama;
they have conquered their senses and subdued their appetites, being patient toward cows and possessed of excellent conduct.
Those among the Brahmins who are of a forgiving nature go to the abode of Hari,
as do those who serve the sacred fire and likewise those who serve their gurus.
Those who are devoted to serving their husbands do not indeed partake in the cycle of worldly existence;
they are always intent on the worship of the gods and have Hari as their supreme refuge.
O best of kings, those who refrain from accepting gifts and cremate the corpse of a helpless Brahmin attain the supreme state.
O lord of men, they always obtain the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices by means of leaves,
flowers, fruits, or even water.
Listen to the fruit obtained by one who worships a *liṅga* devoid of ritual practice:
traveling in a celestial chariot, he is praised by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas.
"By bathing a liṅga with even a mere mouthful of water, O protector of the earth, one attains proximity to Śiva," so said the Lotus-born One. (NarP 1.13.123)
The wise person who worships a linga that has been neglected with flowers undoubtedly attains the merit born of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices. (NarP 1.13.124)
O Lord of Men, by worshipping even an empty linga with foods to be chewed, foods to be swallowed, or fruits, one shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
O descendant of Akrūra, he who worships Viṣṇu even without formal worship attains union with Śiva, from which there is no return.
O best of men, even by merely sprinkling water, that wise man who performs the sweeping of a temple attains the same world as Viṣṇu. (NarP 1.13.127)
O best of kings, he who repairs a shattered crystal liṅga shall indeed dwell in a Vaiṣṇava temple for as long as the age of dust (pāṃsayuga) endures.
O King, that man who [cleanses] even an area the size of a cow-hide within a temple is liberated from the sins accumulated over a hundred births.
That man who sprinkles a portion of the ground with water shall also attain heaven;
likewise, he who sprinkles the ground in a temple of the gods with scented water [attains the same].
Whoever should smear the temple of a deity with clay or products of minerals, it shall remain in the presence of the god for as long as a grain of rice lasts.
That mortal who constructs a temple for the gods using lime-powder rescues ten million members of his family and attains equality with the Slayer of Madhu.
Or one should make svastikas and other such designs; O King, he who arranges lamps in a temple of the deities gains infinite merit.
I am not able to calculate his merit even in hundreds of years—
he who would offer an unbroken lamp to Viṣṇu or to Śaṅkara.
For one who, having seen Śaṅkara or Viṣṇu worshipped, bows down to them, the fruit of a horse sacrifice is not difficult to obtain at every moment.
O King, having reached the abode of Viṣṇu, he rejoices there for ten thousand yugas by performing a single circumambulation of the Goddess, just as one does for the Sun.
Having performed [the rite] for Vināyaka three times and for Viṣṇu’s temple four times, one reaches that respective abode and rejoices for a hundred thousand aeons.
For one who performs circumambulation with a spirit of devotion toward Viṣṇu, as well as toward cows and the twice-born,
there is indeed an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step.
Whoever, having fully worshipped the Māheśvara Liṅga of Maheśvara at Kāśī, bows down to it,
for him there remains no further duty to perform, nor is he ever born again into the cycle of worldly existence.
Having performed the circumambulation of Śiva with his right side toward him according to the prescribed rule,
a man does not fall from heaven through the grace of Śaṅkara.
Having praised Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World and the one free from affliction, with hymns of praise,
one obtains all desires, whatever one wishes for in one's mind.
O protector of the earth, he who dances or sings with devotion in a temple of the deity becomes a partaker of liberation in the world of Rudra.
But those men who perform instrumental music in a temple of the deities,
they, mounted upon swan-vehicles, go to the abode of Brahmā.
Those who clap their hands in a temple of the gods are liberated from all sins and remain in celestial chariots for ten thousand ages.
As for those who cause the sound of bells to ring in a temple of the deities,
Śiva himself is not capable of describing their merit.
Listen to the fruit of merit for those who gratify the Lord of Gods with kettledrums, clay drums, paṭahas, murajas, and ḍiṇḍimas. (NarP 1.13.146)
Accompanied by hosts of celestial women and honored with all objects of desire,
they reach the heavenly world and rejoice for five kalpas.
O King, a man who sounds the conch in a temple of the deity is liberated from all sins and rejoices together with Viṣṇu.
A man who makes the sound of cymbals, bronze gongs, and other instruments in the temple of Viṣṇu,
being liberated from all sins, shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
That god Viṣṇu, who is all-seeing, whose form is knowledge, and who is stainless,
being fully contented, bestows the complete fruit of all dharmas.
O King, by the mere remembrance of that wielder of the discus, the god of gods,
all ritual actions indeed become fruitful.
The Supreme Self is the Lord of the World, the bestower of the fruits of all actions;
when constantly remembered by those who perform righteous deeds, He is the destroyer of all suffering.
Whatever is performed with Him as the objective is fit for infinity.
The objects of experience are Viṣṇu, and the fruits are Viṣṇu; the actions are Viṣṇu, and the enjoyer of the fruits is Viṣṇu.
The effect is Viṣṇu, and the instruments of action are Viṣṇu; therefore, there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from him.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Dharma," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Dharmarāja said:
[I shall describe] the dharma proclaimed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis for the social classes (varṇas) in their proper order.
I shall speak, O best of kings; listen to it with a concentrated mind.
I shall now declare the expiation for one who, while eating, should touch an impure person, an outcaste, or a fallen man, whether out of anger or through ignorance.
One should perform the penance for three nights or six nights according to the respective number;
by bathing at the three periods of the day and offering the five products of the cow to a Brahmin, one is purified.
But when the anus of a Brahmin who is eating should ever involuntarily discharge [feces], I shall tell you the purification for him in that state of being rendered impure by leavings. (NarP 1.14.4)
Having first performed purification, the twice-born man should afterwards touch water;
having fasted for a day and night, he becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one urinates while chewing food, or if urination occurs after having eaten,
one should fast for a day and night and offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire.
If at any time during a meal a Brahmin should become impure,
he should place that morsel on the ground, bathe, and thereby attain purity.
Having eaten that [food], one becomes pure after fasting for three nights;
however, having consumed all of it, one shall remain impure for three nights.
If one has not heard [the scriptures], there will indeed be vomiting; if one is unwell, one should mutter the *triśruta* [mantra].
For one who is healthy, three thousand recitations of the *gāyatrī* are the supreme purification.
If a twice-born man is touched by Cāṇḍālas or dog-cookers, or if he voids excrement or urine, [he must perform purification].
If one has eaten while remaining impure from food remnants, one should observe a fast for three nights;
likewise, if an outcaste should touch a woman in her courses or a woman who has recently given birth, one should likewise observe this penance.
"Śātātapa declared that purification occurs after three nights if a woman in her menses is touched by dogs, outcasts, or crows. (Narada Purāṇa 1.14.12)
One should remain pure while abstaining from food; one becomes purified by bathing at the proper time.
When two women who are menstruating happen to touch each other anywhere, [they must bathe].

One who has been touched by someone defiled by the *brahmakūrca* or by one who has consumed the *brahmakūrca*, or by one who has eaten leftovers, shall be purified by performing the *brahmakūrca* rite and bathing thereafter.
If one suspects conception during the fertile period, bathing is prescribed for the one who has engaged in sexual intercourse;
however, if one approaches a woman outside the fertile period, purification is like that required after voiding urine or excrement.
Both husband and wife would be impure when joined in sexual union;
however, upon rising from the bed, the woman becomes pure while the man remains impure.
A woman who, out of wickedness, fails to perform service for her husband's body shall be fined twelve [paṇas] and, if she persists, she shall be abandoned without any provision of wealth.
Those who abandon fallen kinsmen or relatives who deserve punishment shall be fined the highest amercement; for while a father may indeed become fallen through lust, a mother can never do so.

He who causes himself to be killed by means of such methods as hanging with a rope shall be purified by a penance involving sacrificial food once he is dead; if he survives, the fine is two hundred [paṇas].
The sons and friends of those who deserve punishment shall each be fined one paṇa;
thereafter, they shall perform the expiation as prescribed by the scriptures.

Those who have perished by water or fire, by hanging, or by falling; those who have died after renouncing the world or through fasting; those destroyed by poison or by leaping from a precipice, and those slain by the stroke of a weapon—[all these attain the supreme state].
Nor are these people fallen from their status or excluded from all society;
they are purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or by two Kṛcchra penances.
One who has resorted to both [practices] and fallen from the Pāpaśyāma and Cchabala hells shall be purified by two Cāndrāyaṇa fasts, provided he gives away a cow and likewise a bull.

If one is touched by one's own dog, jackal, monkey, and so forth, or by humans, except during sexual intercourse, one becomes pure immediately after bathing; this applies both during the day—at the two twilights—and at night.
But he who, out of ignorance, has somehow eaten the food of a Cāṇḍāla,
becomes purified after half a month by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
Having set fire to the house of a cow or a Brahmin, or having killed one by means of hanging or other such methods,
or likewise having cut the rope [of a suspended person], a twice-born man shall perform one *kṛcchra* penance.
Having eaten the food of a Cāṇḍāla or a Pulkasa, or having killed a woman,
one should perform a Kṛcchra penance for half its duration if done intentionally, and two Aindavas if done unintentionally.

A Brahmin who eats the food of Kāpālikas, likewise one who has sexual intercourse with their women, one who approaches those who should not be approached, one who drinks liquor, or one who eats meat; NarP_1,14.28 //
One who has undergone the penance of *parāk* is purified by the *maurvī* oblation;
this applies especially to the four types of perpetrators of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). (NarP 1.14.29)
Having entered the fire, they are purified; or else, by remaining at a great sacrifice, even one who has committed a secret sin becomes pure in this way after practicing for a month.
Or one may become pure by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta while submerged in water. A washerman, a leather-worker, an actor, and a basket-maker likewise [become pure]. (NarP 1.14.31)
Fishermen, Medas, Bhills, and Aśvas—these six are indeed remembered as the lowest-born (antyajas).
Having eaten their food, having gone to their women, having drunk from them, or having accepted a gift from them, [one becomes an outcast].
If one does so out of ignorance, one should perform half a *kṛcchra* penance and two *aindava* fasts;
this applies to the mother, the wife of a guru, a daughter, a sister, and a daughter-in-law. (Narada Smṛti 1.14.33)
Having united with her, he shall enter the fire; no other purification is prescribed for this.
The same applies to a queen, a female ascetic, a nurse, or even one of a higher caste.
Having approached a woman of the same lineage, one should perform two penances that are not difficult;
likewise for those women who belong to the father's lineage or the mother's lineage.
For approaching all types of women other than one's own wife, one should perform the Tapana penance for half a Kṛcchra;
likewise, the twice-born remove the sin incurred by approaching a prostitute.

Having committed adultery with the wife of his guru, a Brāhmaṇa who has taken an oath shall drink the juice of the *suta-tarpa* plant once and water infused with *kuśa* grass for five nights according to the prescribed rule.
Some desire the punishment for a member of a religious community (gongha), while others [desire it] for one who has broken his vow;
he who should cause a cow to fall by striking it with a blow exceeding a staff [is likewise liable].
One should purify that [offense] by performing the cow-vow (govrata) twice over as an expiation;
it should be as thick as a thumb and as long as an arm.
The "cow-stick" (godaṇḍa) is proclaimed to include the fresh grass and the guardian;
likewise, even if a fetus should be present when a cow is struck down, it is included.
One should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual case;
this is the expiation for the collective slaughter of cattle, as well as for their binding, confining, or causing them to suffer illness while being nourished.
If death occurs, he is tainted by that very cause;
whether he has fainted, fallen, or been struck by a staff thereafter.
Having risen, he should walk six steps or even fifteen;
or if he should take a morsel of food, or even drink water. (NarP 1.14.43)
For those whose every disease has been destroyed, no expiation exists,
even if cows have been struck down by painful clods of earth, stones, or weapons.
In that regard, an expiation is prescribed in the Śastra:
for killing wood, Sāntapana is declared; but for a clod of earth, Prājāpatya is prescribed.
If that [medicine] is on a stone, it is a *pāṣaṇa-kṛcchra* penance; if on a weapon, it is an *atikṛcchra*.
One should give medicine, oil, or food to cows and Brahmins.
If a transgression should occur while [medicine] is being given, there is no need for penance;
this applies likewise to the drinking of oil-based medicines and the consumption of medicinal substances.
And for the purpose of extracting a splinter, no expiation is prescribed, provided it is done by tying a cord around the calves' necks or by means of medicinal treatment. (NarP 1.14.48)
In order to conceal it in the evening, there is no fault in your anger or imprisonment;
moreover, he has hair only on his feet, and on two feet, only a beard. (NarP 1.14.49)
But when three-fourths [of the hair] remains, one should perform the *śikhāvarta* at the root;
having gathered all the hair together, one should cut it to a length of two finger-breadths.
In the same way, however, shaving the head is prescribed for women;
yet, shaving [the entire body] is not to be performed by a woman, nor is the vīrāsana posture prescribed for her.
Nor should one dwell in a cow-pen, nor follow a woman as she goes,
whether she be a king, a prince, or a learned Brahmin.
One should prescribe an expiation for them without requiring the shaving of their hair;
however, for the sake of preserving their hair, one should ordain that their vow be doubled.
When the vow is observed for double the duration, the sacrificial fee for the vow shall be doubled.
The sin of the killer is not destroyed, and the giver shall go to hell—those who prescribe a penance that is neither ordained by the Śruti nor the Smṛti. (NarP 1.14.55)
The king should punish those who violate the Dharma with a rod;
however, the king, deluded by passion, should not under any circumstances oppress these [virtuous ones].
That sin, having become a hundredfold, creeps back toward him alone;
therefore, when the expiation has been performed, he should provide a feast for Brāhmaṇas.
One should give twenty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for them;
[this applies even when] worms produced from grass have fallen among flies and other insects.
He should perform half a *kṛcchra* penance and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability;
having indeed performed the expiation, he should feed the best of the twice-born.
One should give a māṇika of gold, and then purification is prescribed;
if touched by Cāṇḍālas or Śvapacas at night, bathing is prescribed.
One should not dwell there even for a night; one becomes pure by immediate bathing.
However, if an ignorant person should dwell there at night through lack of discernment, [he must perform penance].
Then that sin of his is multiplied a hundredfold;
moreover, the constellations and the planets that rise above him [become adverse].
When these [waters] have been touched by their rays, one should perform a ritual bath in water;
this applies also to waters found within lakes, in anthills, in mouse-holes, in saline soil, and on paths.
Good clay should not be taken from a cremation ground or from what remains after purification;
rather, a Brahmin should diligently perform rites for his own welfare and for the benefit of others.
Through *iṣṭa* one attains heaven, and through *pūrta* one may attain liberation;
*iṣṭa* consists of the expenditure of wealth for sacrifice, while a reservoir is called *pūrta*.
And especially gardens, as well as temple courtyards, ponds, wells, tanks, and shrines for the deities; NarP_1,14.66.
He who retrieves what has fallen obtains the aforementioned fruit;
he should fetch the urine from a white cow and likewise the dung from a black cow.
The milk of a copper-colored cow is to be taken, and the curd of a white cow is prescribed;
the ghee of a tawny cow is to be taken, for it destroys even the greatest sins.
Having gathered all the materials individually with *kuśa* grass from the banks of sacred rivers,
one should raise them up with the *praṇava* alone, and [place them] with the *praṇava*.
Having stirred it with the *praṇava*, one should drink it with the *praṇava* itself, using a vessel made of copper or from the middle leaf of a *palāśa* tree. (NarP 1.14.70)
One should drink water infused with *kuśa* grass from either a lotus leaf or an earthen vessel when a birth-impurity has occurred and a second [birth] is imminent.
There is no fault in the second [case], for one is purified by the very first;
that which is born is purified by what is born, and likewise, that which is dead by what is dead.
In the case of a miscarriage during the fourth month, one should prescribe three days [of impurity].
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified in as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
once her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who has become menstruating is purified by bathing.
A woman falls from her own lineage at the seventh step of the marriage;
the performance of her *piṇḍa* and water offerings must be done by the lineage of her husband.
In the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), the intended recipient should be named twice for each individual rice-ball.
Three rice-balls should be given to six [ancestors]; thus, the giver does not become confused.
For a thousand years, her mother was enjoyed by her own husband as if by a fortunate deity;
likewise her grandmother and her great-grandmother were enjoyed by their own respective husbands.
In the [anniversary] year, however, one should perform an honoring of one's mother and father;
one should offer a Śrāddha without [invoking] the gods and present a single funeral cake (piṇḍa).
The wise should know that *śrāddha* is of five kinds: the daily (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the optional (*kāmya*), the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and the *pārvaṇa*. (NarP 1.14.79)

During an eclipse of a planet, at the transit of the sun, on a festival day, or at a pure abode, a man should offer three rice-balls; however, on the anniversary of the death day, he should offer only one.
An unmarried daughter does not share a separate *piṇḍa* or *gotra* during a period of impurity (*sūtaka*);
she falls from her own *gotra* only through the mantras of the marriage ceremony.

By whichever caste a woman is married, the impurity (sūtaka) resulting from her death becomes equal to that of her husband; likewise, this applies to the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) and the water libation (udaka).
When a marriage has been performed, she attains oneness with her husband during the four nights;
she likewise attains oneness with him regarding the funeral cake (piṇḍa), the lineage (gotra), and the birth-impurity (sūtaka).
On the first, second, third, or fourth day,
the collection of the bones should be performed by kinsmen who possess a sense of what is beneficial.
In the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, and likewise the ninth [day],
the collection of bones is prescribed for the castes in their proper order.
On the eleventh day after the death of a person, whoever releases a bull is liberated from the world of the departed and is glorified in the heavenly world.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should contemplate with the heart:
"May my ancestors come; may they accept these handfuls of water."
Having joined the two hands together and filled them with water,
one should lift up as much as would fill a cow's horn and cast it into the midst of the water.
Standing in water, facing south with a focused mind, one should pour water into the air;
for the sky is the abode of the ancestors, as is the southern direction.
The waters are declared to be the host of gods, and likewise the waters are the host of ancestors;
therefore, one who desires the welfare of the ancestors should offer water to them.
Water is always pure when it is heated by the rays of the sun during the day, by the stars and the wind at night, and by both of these during the two intermediate periods.
Water is always pure by its very nature; it remains ever pure even when in contact with impurity, whether contained in a vessel or situated upon the ground. It is eternally sacred.
A wise person should offer handfuls of water to the deities and the ancestors; however, for those who have died without having received the funeral rites, one should offer water on dry land.
O Śraddhā, at the time of the fire-oblation one should give with one hand;
at the libation (tarpaṇa) one should give with both hands—this is the established law.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Dharma and Peace," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Dharmarāja said:
"I shall proclaim the various types of sins, as well as the gross torments that correspond to them."
Listen with steadfastness, for from this [I shall describe] those terrible hells.
I shall describe those evil-minded sinners who are constantly cooked in the fires of hell, which yield terrifying results.
Tapanī, Vālukākumbha, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
Kumbhīpāka, Nirucchvāsa, Kālasūtra, and Pramardana.
The terrible forest of sword-leaves, the eater of saliva, the fierce cold,
the state of being a rat, the pit of fat, and likewise the river Vaitaraṇī.
They are devoured [there], as well as in the drinking of urine and in the very mire of excrement;
likewise in that Paśūla, that Paśila, and at the Śālmalī tree.
Likewise, there is the terrible Śoṇitakūpa, which feeds on blood;
and Svamāṃsabhojana, as well as Vahnijvālāniveśana.
A rain of stones, a rain of weapons, and likewise a rain of fire;
alkaline water, hot water, and even the drinking of molten iron balls.
Then there was the withering of the head, as well as the falling from Mount Marut;
likewise, the color of ashes and the feeding upon worms.
Alkaline liquid, drinking [it], wandering about, as well as being sawn apart,
being smeared with excrement, and even eating excrement.
The drinking of semen is most terrible, causing a burning sensation in all the joints;
the inhalation of smoke results in bondage with nooses and the application of various piercing pains.
There was indeed lying on beds of burning coals, as well as being crushed by pestles,
many wooden machines, as well as scraping and cutting.
Falling down and leaping up, striking with maces, staffs, and other weapons,
attacking with elephant tusks, and being bitten by various serpents.
Likewise, the sprinkling of cold water on the nose and the mouth, as well as the drinking of terrible alkaline water and the consumption of salt. (NarP 1.15.13)
The severing of tendons, the binding of sinews, the breaking of bones,
as well as the entry into cavities filled with alkaline water and the devouring of flesh.
The drinking of bile, which is most terrible, as well as the eating of phlegm, being cast down from the top of a tree, and likewise drowning within the water; NarP_1,15.15 //
He practiced the bearing of stones, lying upon thorns,
being bitten by ants, and even being tormented by scorpions.
Affliction by tigers, affliction by jackals, as well as being trampled by buffaloes, lying in mud, and being completely filled with foul odors. (NarP 1.15.17)
Frequently sleeping on one side, consuming very bitter substances, drinking excessively hot oil, and consuming very pungent things; NarP_1,15.18 //
Drinking decoction water, carving stones with that [water], bathing in excessively hot or cold water, and likewise gnashing one's teeth; NarP_1,15.19.
That milk is indeed their bed, and that very burden of iron is their bond;
O highly fortunate one, such tortures as these exist by the tens of millions.
"O Protector of the Earth, even in a thousand years I would not be able to describe what each of these sinners has obtained. (NarP 1.15.21)
I shall explain all of that; listen to me as I speak.
One who kills a Brahmin, one who drinks liquor, a thief, and one who violates the teacher’s bed— NarP_1,15.22.
These are the great sinners (mahāpātakin), and the fifth is he who associates with them:
one who pierces the boundary, one who cooks for no purpose, and one who constantly reviles Brahmins.

One who gives false instruction, one who sells the Vedas—these five are slayers of Brahman. He who, having invited a Brahmin with the words "I shall give you wealth and so forth," later says "I have nothing," him they call a slayer of Brahman. (NarP 1.15.24)
He who creates an obstacle for a Brāhmaṇa going for the purpose of bathing or for the purpose of worship is called a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
He who is devoted to flattery and praise, who delights in self-exaltation,
and who is likewise devoted to untruth, is proclaimed to be a slayer of a Brahmin.
One who approves of unrighteousness is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin,
as is one who delights in causing distress to others and one who points out the faults of others.
One who is devoted to hypocritical conduct is called a slayer of a Brahmin;
likewise, one who is constantly intent on receiving gifts and intent on the slaughter of living beings [is so called].
O King, one who consents to unrighteousness is proclaimed to be a slayer of a Brahmin;
indeed, O King, there are many kinds of sins equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
I shall now briefly declare the sins equal to drinking liquor:
eating from a communal feast and consorting with courtesans. (NarP 1.15.30)
Eating the food of an outcast is recorded as being equal to drinking liquor;
so too is the abandonment of one’s preceptor and eating at the shrines of the gods.
Association with a woman who drinks liquor is declared to be equal to drinking liquor itself;
likewise for a twice-born man who takes food from one who has struck him while he was a Śūdra.
He who, having been authorized by a Śūdra, performs the work of a servant, should be known as a drinker of liquor, excluded from all righteous dharmas. (NarP 1.15.33)
That lowest of men incurs a sin equal to the drinking of liquor;
such various kinds of sins are remembered as being equal to the drinking of liquor.
I shall declare the sin equal to stealing gold; listen:
[the theft] of bulbs, roots, and fruits, as well as of musk and scented powders. (NarP 1.15.35)
The theft of gems at all times is considered equal to the theft of gold;
likewise [the theft] of copper, iron, tin, bronze, clarified butter, and honey.
The theft of fragrant substances is declared to be equal to the theft of gold;
so too is the taking of betel nuts, water, and sandalwood.
The theft of the juice of leaves is remembered as equal to the theft of gold;
the abandonment of ancestral sacrifices and the neglect of religious duties [are likewise grave offenses].
Censuring ascetics and stealing foodstuffs as well as grains are recorded as equal to the theft of gold. (NarP 1.15.39)
The theft of a rudrākṣa is remembered as equal to the theft of gold;
likewise, sexual intercourse with a sister and sexual intercourse with one's son's wife [are equal to the same].

Sexual intercourse with a woman in her menses and the like is recorded in the Smṛtis as equal to violating the Guru’s bed; so too is approaching a woman of a lower caste and consorting with a woman who drinks liquor.
Sexual intercourse with another's wife is recorded as equal to violating the teacher’s bed;
likewise is sexual intercourse with a brother’s wife or consorting with the wife of a friend.
Approaching a woman who has placed her trust in one is remembered as equal to violating the teacher’s bed;
so too is performing ritual acts at the wrong time and approaching one’s own daughter. (NarP 1.15.43)
"Neglecting the Dharma, reviling the scriptures, and violating the teacher's bed—these and others like them, O King, are designated as the great sins (mahāpātaka). (NarP 1.15.44)
By forming an attachment to even one of these, one becomes equal to them;
for in whatever way these sins are committed, they are so described by the supreme sages.
Expiation is seen for those [sins] through the application of penances and the like;
but hear now, O King, regarding those sins that are devoid of penance. (NarP 1.15.46)
Equal to all sins and bestowing the great hells,
there may somehow be an expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
O lord of men, there is no atonement anywhere for one who hates a Brahmin, nor for a betrayer of trust, nor for those who are ungrateful.
There is no atonement anywhere for those who consort with Śūdra women,
whose bodies are nourished by the food of Śūdras, and whose souls delight in reviling the Vedas.
And for those who revile true discourses, there is no atonement either in this world or the next.
If a twice-born man enters a Buddhist temple even in times of great distress, no atonement for him is seen, even through hundreds of penances. (NarP 1.15.51)
Buddhists are declared to be heretics because they revile the Vedas;
therefore, a twice-born man should not look upon them, for they are excluded from the Dharma.
Whether knowingly or unknowingly, a twice-born man may enter the abode of a Buddhist;
yet if he does so with full knowledge, there is no atonement—this is the certainty of the scriptures. (NarP 1.15.53)
O Lord, because of the abundance of their sins, these lead to hell for ten million kalpas; other acts as well have been declared to be devoid of atonement. (NarP 1.15.54)
Listen to me as I describe their sins, which lead them to the hells.
Among them, those who committed great sins (mahāpātakin) reside individually for the duration of a yuga;
at the end of that period, having returned to earth, they become donkeys through several births among virtuous people.
Thereafter, their bodies shall become dogs for ten lifetimes;
for a hundred years they shall be dung-worms, and for twelve lifetimes they shall be serpents.
Then, O King, for a thousand births he was animals such as deer;
for a hundred years he was stationary beings, and thereafter he had the body of a monitor lizard.
Then, for six births, they become sinful Caṇḍālas; thereafter, for sixteen births, they belong to low castes such as Śūdras and the like.
Then, in two subsequent births, they will be afflicted by poverty and disease;
constantly intent on accepting gifts, they will thereafter go again to hell.
It is taught that those whose minds are possessed by malice fall into the Raurava hell;
having remained there for two kalpas, they become outcastes (cāṇḍālas) for a hundred births.
He who says "do not give" to cows or to Brahmins,
having passed through a hundred births as dogs, is born among the Cāṇḍālas.
Then, for three births, he takes the form of a crow, and after that, the form of a tiger;
at the end of that, he goes to hell for twenty-one yugas.
Listen now to the fruit of the evil deeds of those who are intent on reviling others, those who speak harshly, and those who create obstacles to acts of giving.
But the thieves were violently ground to powder by pestles and mortars; at the end of that period, they remained holding those stones for three years. (NarP 1.15.65)
Then, for seven years, those who have stolen the property of others are split by the *kālasūtra* [torture], lamenting their own cruel deeds.
There, they are continuously cooked in the limbs of hell by means of their own karma.
And hear now of the terrible hell for those who point out the property of others:
for as many as a thousand yugas, they must subsist on that very excrement as their food.
And their tongues are crushed with extremely cruel pincers;
breathless, they dwell in that most terrible place for half a kalpa.
And I shall describe to you the hell for those who lust after the wives of others;
there, their wives—possessing beautiful forms and adorned with ornaments—are made to fall by him.
They take their pleasure violently with whomever they please,
and they forcibly seize even a wise man out of fear of them.
And speaking of that deed, they lead those women—who, O protector of the earth, have abandoned their husband and taken another—to the hells in succession. (NarP 1.15.72)
But those who are masters of that milk-man, being endowed with strength, forcibly cast him down upon that bed of milk and take their pleasure for a long time. (NarP 1.15.73)
Then those women were released by them; having embraced a pillar blazing like fire, they remain there for a thousand years.
Then they undergo bathing in alkaline water and the consumption of alkaline water;
at the end of that, they experience all the hells for a hundred times a hundred years.
He who kills a brahmin, a cow, or a kṣatriya, the best of kings,
shall also endure all the torments during five kalpas.
Listen to the fruit for him who listens with respect to the great censure [of the virtuous]:
into their ears shall be driven a multitude of iron spikes.
Then, through those openings, intensely hot and pungent oil is poured in, and consequently, he falls into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
I shall declare the fate of those atheists who are averse to Hari and to Lord Hara:
for ten million years, they indeed consume salt.
And thereafter, O lord of men, those of evil deeds are likewise broken for an entire kalpa on the sandy shore of the Raurava hell.
Those lowest of men who look upon Brāhmaṇas with eyes of anger—
by a thousand needles produced from that [anger], their own eyes are pricked.
Then, O best of kings, those of evil deeds are drenched with streams of caustic water,
and thereafter they are pierced by terrible saws.
Now hear of the terrible hell for those who betray trust, those who violate established boundaries, and those who greedily covet the food of others.
Constantly eating their own flesh while being devoured by dogs, they dwell for a full year in each and every one of the hells.
Listen to me regarding those who delight in receiving gifts, those who are readers of the stellar constellations, and those who eat the food of temple-priests. NarP_1,15.85 //
O King, those who were always addicted to sensual enjoyments and were possessed by sin are constantly cooked in these torments until the end of the kalpa, remaining in suffering.
Then, tormented by the Kālasūtra hell, they are filled with oil;
thereafter, they undergo bathing in alkaline water and must consume urine and excrement.
At the end of that, having reached the earth, they become Mleccha tribes;
those who delight in causing distress to others go to the Vaitaraṇī river.
Those who have abandoned the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) indeed go to the state of consuming saliva;
one who abandons spiritual practice (upāsanā) shall go to the Raurava hell.
O King, listen to what happens to those who collect taxes from Brahmin villages:
they are cooked in these torments until the moon and stars perish.
That excellent king who imposes excessive taxes upon villages shall,
along with his thousand kinsmen, suffer in hell for five kalpas.
O King, he who consents to the collection of taxes from a village of Brahmins is himself the perpetrator of a thousand acts of Brahmin-slaughter. (NarP 1.15.92)
That man who [engages in sexual intercourse] with one who is not his wife, with one of low birth, or with an animal, shall dwell in the most terrible Kālasūtra hell for four yugas.
One who is a great sinner by discharging semen shall become a consumer of semen;
having then reached a pit of fat, he remains there for six hundred divine years.
O King, a man who brushes his teeth on a day of fasting becomes a consumer of semen and is censured in all the worlds.
He who abandons his own duty and is a heretic goes to the terrible Vyāghrapakṣa hell for four *yugas*; he is called a heretic by the wise.
The fruit resulting from association with them would be in vain; both of them would be exceedingly sinful, and for thousands of millions of eons, they would successively fall into hells.
O King, those who steal the property of the gods and those who misappropriate the property of their gurus partake of an evil deed equal to the penance for killing a Brahmin.
Those who seize the wealth of the helpless and those who harbor hatred toward the helpless shall dwell in hell for thousands of millions of eons.
Now, listen with a well-composed mind as I describe the fruit of the sin of those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas in the presence of women and Śūdras. (NarP 1.15.100)
With their heads downward and feet upward, pinned between two pillars,
they remain there constantly for as long as a Brahma-year, perpetually addicted to drinking smoke.
He who discharges the bodily waste into water or in a temple incurs a most terrible sin equal to that of killing an embryo.
Listen to the fruit of the sin of those who cast away teeth, bones, hair, or nails in the abode of the immortals, or who discard the remains of food in water. NarP_1,15.103 //
Impaled on spears and pierced by plows, crying out in piteous lamentation,
they are intensely tormented in the exceedingly dreadful boiling of superheated oil.
Those who perform [such acts] undergo a succession of sufferings and then go to other [lower realms];
likewise for one who destroys a Brahmin or a sandalwood tree.
O King, he who seizes the property of a Brahmin goes to a terrible hell as long as the moon and stars exist; it brings suffering both here and in the hereafter.
Listen to the fruit of the sin of him who gives false testimony, which leads to the destruction of his prosperity in this world and to hell in the next. (NarP 1.15.107)
He undergoes all the torments for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
here his sons perish, and on the next day as well.
Those mortals who are excessively lustful and those who speak falsehoods experience the Raurava hell, and thereafter other hells as well, in succession.
In their pleasure, they are filled with leeches resembling serpents;
thus for sixty thousand years, they are then sprinkled with caustic water.
Those who are addicted to meat eaten in vain go to the Pit of Caustic Mud;
from there they are struck down by elephants as if falling from Mount Marutprapātana.
At the end of that [period], O Lord of Men, those who do not approach their own wives during the proper season are born with deficient limbs. (NarP 1.15.112)
He goes to the terrible Raurava hell and incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin,
he who, though capable, does not restrain one seen engaged in improper conduct.
That sin they both share equally, and both go to hell;
having calculated the sins of the wicked, they assign [the punishment] to others and receive [its fruit] themselves.
O King, those who attribute sin to one who is sinless incur a guilt equal to that of the sinner; if they further revile him, their guilt is doubled. (NarP 1.15.115)
He goes to a terrible hell for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure;
and for those sinners who are being censured, half of their sin is destroyed.
But he who, having undertaken vows, abandons them before completing them,
shall experience agony in the Sword-Leaf Hell and be born on earth with impaired limbs.
A man who obstructs other vows being undertaken by others goes to the terrible Śloṣmabhojana hell, which causes extreme suffering.
For one who shows partiality toward justice and the instruction of Dharma,
there is no further atonement even through ten thousand penances.
One who eats what should not be eaten, having consumed excrement mixed with food, will thereafter always be born in the womb of a *caṇḍāla* and become an eater of cow-flesh. (NarP 1.15.120)
By insulting Brahmins with harsh words, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having experienced all manner of torments, he becomes a Cāṇḍāla for ten births.
