But if someone should create an obstacle when a gift is being given after a dispute has been settled,
he must perform a vow equal to that for the killing of a Brahmin.
He who, having stolen wealth for his own sake, bestows it upon others, is a thief destined for hell; the fruit of that act belongs to the one whose wealth it was.
O King, by failing to give after having made a promise, a man becomes a consumer of saliva;
and one who is intent on censuring ascetics goes indeed to the state of a stone-fly.
Those who destroy groves go for twenty-one eons;
thereafter, they all experience every kind of torment in succession as food for dogs.
O King, hear now the destiny to which those who destroy temples, reservoirs, and flower gardens go. (NarP 1.15.126)
In all these various torments they are indeed cooked separately; thereafter, they become worms in excrement for twenty-one kalpas.
And thereafter, O King, he will be born for a hundred lifetimes in the womb of a Cāṇḍāla,
among those who destroy villages, burn them down, and plunder them.
I am not able, even with my own life, to prescribe the great sin of those who eat the remnants of others' meals and those who are intent on betraying their friends.
For those who have severed the worship of the ancestors and gods, or who stand outside the path of the Vedas, there are intense torments lasting as long as the moon and stars endure. (NarP 1.15.130)

O Lord of the Earth, for those who have gone to the realms of the wicked and for those who have departed from the Dharma, there are thus many kinds of torments for the evildoers, O King. (NarP 1.15.131)
O Lord, O King, I am not able to calculate the number of those [beings], nor of those women, nor of the sins, nor of the torments, nor even of the dharmas. (NarP 1.15.132)
Who in this world, other than Viṣṇu, is capable of enumerating the number of all these sins according to the prescriptions of the Dharmaśāstras? (NarP 1.15.133)
When penances have been performed, the heap of sins is destroyed;
these penances should be carried out in the presence of the Lord of Kamalā.
And for the fulfillment of deeds that are deficient or excessive:
the Gaṅgā, Tulasī, the company of the virtuous, and the chanting of Hari’s names. (NarP 1.15.135)
For freedom from envy and non-violence—indeed, all these destroy sin;
for actions dedicated to Viṣṇu truly become fruitful.
Actions not offered [to the Lord] are like substances cast into ashes;
this applies to the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and desire-driven (kāmya) rites, as well as whatever else is a means to liberation.
Everything offered to Viṣṇu becomes endowed with goodness and fruitful;
supreme devotion to Hari destroys all the life-force of sins for men.
O best of kings, that devotion should be known as eightfold— resembling a forest fire to the wilderness of sin— and it is divided into the tamasic, rajasic, and sattvic types.
And that worship of the Lord of Śrī which is for the purpose of destroying another, O King,
is the lowest form of tamasic devotion, because it possesses the nature of a wicked person.
But that woman of tamasic nature who worships Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, with a deceitful mind, like an unchaste woman toward her own husband, is merely mediocre. (NarP 1.15.141)

O protector of the earth, seeing those devoted to the worship of the gods, if one worships them out of envy or rivalry, that devotion is considered the highest form of *tāmasī* (dark) devotion. NarP_1,15.142 //
If one who desires wealth, grain,
and so forth should worship the Lord endowed with supreme faith, that is remembered as the lowest form of the rājasa sacrifice.
She who worships Mādhava with supreme devotion, dedicating it to him whose fame is renowned throughout all the worlds— that [worship] is considered the middling *rājasa* type.
O Lord of the Earth, that devotion by which one worships Hari with the goal of attaining the state of *sālokya* and so forth is proclaimed as the highest form of *rājasa* devotion. (NarP 1.15.145)
But he who, endowed with supreme faith, prays to a deity for the sake of exhausting his own committed sins, that [worship] is remembered as the lowest form of *sāttvika* worship.
But he who, endowed with faith, performs service with the thought, "This is dear to Hari," that [faith] is sattvic and middling. (NarP 1.15.147)

O King, he who worships the Lord of Śrī with the understanding that it is according to scriptural injunction, like a servant—that is considered the foremost among forms of devotion, the supreme *sāttvika* devotion. (NarP 1.15.148)
When a person, having performed even a small act of honoring Hari,
becomes satisfied through absorption in Him— that is the highest of the high forms of devotion.
"He who constantly perceives: 'I alone am the supreme Viṣṇu; this entire world is within me'—him one should know as the most excellent of the excellent."
Thus, devotion is of ten kinds and it brings about the severance of saṃsāra;
even among those, sattvic devotion bestows the fruit of all desires.
Therefore, O protector of the earth, you who desire to conquer the cycle of existence,
you should practice devotion to Janārdana in accordance with your own duty.
Viṣṇu is not pleased with one who abandons his own duty and lives by devotion alone; He is pleased only by right conduct.
Among all the scriptures, right conduct is considered the foremost;
dharma originates from right conduct, and the Imperishable Lord is the master of dharma.
Therefore, devotion to Hari should be practiced without contradicting one's own duty;
for even religious duties yield no happiness to those who are devoid of right conduct.
Devotion devoid of one's own duty is also proclaimed to be as if unperformed;
that which was asked by you further has all been explained by me. (NarP 1.15.156)
Therefore, being devoted to dharma, worship Janārdana;
by worshipping Nārāyaṇa, who is more subtle than the subtlest, you shall attain eternal happiness.
Śiva is indeed Hari directly, and Hari himself is Śiva;
the wicked person who perceives a difference between the two goes to ten million hells.
Therefore, perceiving Viṣṇu and Śiva as equal, worship them;
for one who creates division attains suffering in this world and in the next.
O lord of men, O wise one, listen attentively as I tell you the purpose for which I have come into your presence; pay heed to it. (NarP 1.15.150)
"O King, those ancestors of yours, who were sinners because they committed suicide, dwell in hell, having been consumed by the wrath of Kapila."
Lift them up, O illustrious one, by the act of bringing the Gaṅgā;
for the Gaṅgā, O lord of the earth, surely destroys all sins.
O best of kings, even hair, bones, nails, and staves,
once touched by the water of the Gaṅgā, lead one to the abode of Viṣṇu, even if they have been reduced to ashes.
O King, he whose bones or ashes are cast into the Gaṅgā by men departs,
liberated from all sins, to the abode of Hari.
O King, whatever sins have been described by you,
those actions are destroyed by being sprinkled with drops from the Ganges.
Sanaka said:
Having spoken thus to the great king Bhagīratha, that righteous soul, the King of Dharma (Yama), immediately vanished from sight, O tiger among sages.
But that king, possessed of great wisdom and having mastered the meaning of all the śāstras,
entrusted the entire earth to his ministers and departed for the forest.
Then, having gone from the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa on the Snowy Mountain (Himavat),
he reached the peak covered in snow sixteen yojanas to the west.
Having performed austerities, he brought down Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Bhagīratha’s Effort to Bring the Gaṅgā through the Instruction of Dharmarāja," in the first quarter of the section on Dharma within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
Having reached the Himavat mountain, what did the lord of the earth do?
How did you bring the Gaṅgā? You ought to tell this to me.
Sanaka said: O sage, the great king Bhagīratha, wearing matted hair and bark garments,
while traveling to the Himalaya mountain for asceticism, reached the bank of the Godāvarī.
There, in the great forest, they beheld the excellent hermitage of Bhṛgu,
teeming with black antelopes and frequented by herds of elephants.
Resounding with the cries of wandering bees, teeming with warbling birds,
filled with herds of roaming boars, and shimmering with the waves of yak-tail manes.
It was frequented by flocks of dancing peacocks and deer,
filled with large trees that had grown tall, and was visited with reverence by the daughters of sages.
It was rich with *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, surely adorned with *hintāla* trees,
and beautified by *mālatī*, *yūthikā*, *kunda*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *vaṭa* trees.
The son of Bhṛgu entered the hermitage, which was filled with blossoming flowers, frequented by throngs of sages, and resounded with the great chanting of the Vedas and Shastras.
There he beheld the sage Bhṛgu, who was proclaiming the supreme Brahman and the code of conduct to his circle of disciples, and who resembled the sun in his splendor.
Then he prostrated before the best of Brahmins by grasping his feet and other such acts;
Bhṛgu, for his part, performed hospitality for him with due honor.
Having performed the rites of hospitality, the king, with palms joined in reverence, spoke with humility to that bull among sages, the supreme Ṛṣi Bhṛgu.
Bhagīratha said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, expert in all scriptures,
I, fearing worldly existence, ask you about the cause for the liberation of human beings."
O Best of Sages, O Omniscient One, tell me that action by which the Blessed One is pleased; I am worthy of your favor, O Ascetic. (NarP 1.16.12)
Bhṛgu said:
"O King, your desire is known; for you are the best among the meritorious.
Otherwise, how would you be able to uplift your entire lineage?"
O protector of the earth, whoever— be they anyone at all— desires to uplift their own lineage through auspicious deeds, one should know him to be Hari himself, assuming human form.
O King of kings, listen with a well-composed mind as I shall explain that ritual by which the Lord of Gods bestows desired fruits upon men. (NarP 1.16.15)
O King, be devoted to truth and likewise refrain from violence;
always be intent on the welfare of all beings, and never speak an untruth.
Abandon association with the wicked; cultivate the company of the virtuous.
Perform meritorious deeds day and night, and remember the eternal Viṣṇu.
Perform worship of Mahāviṣṇu and attain unsurpassed peace;
conquer the twelve-syllable and eight-syllable mantras, and there will be welfare.
Bhagīratha said:
"O Sage, what is declared to be truth that is beneficial to all beings?
What is declared to be falsehood? And who are the wicked people?"
What kind of people are said to be virtuous (sādhu), and what is merit (puṇya) like? How is Viṣṇu to be remembered, and what is his worship like? (NarP 1.16.20)
O Sage, skilled in the knowledge of reality, what kind of peace is said to be [attained], and what is the eight-syllable mantra? And what is the twelve-syllable one, O Sage? (NarP 1.16.21)
"Having shown me supreme compassion, you ought to explain everything.
Bhrigu said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Your intellect is unsurpassed."
O King, I shall tell you all that I have been asked by you;
for the wise say that speaking according to the facts is truth. (NarP 1.16.23)
Indeed, that [teaching] must be spoken by those devoted to the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma;
having personally understood the place, time, and other factors, it should be taught without contradicting them.
That speech which is uttered by the virtuous is called truth;
for it is that which produces no affliction for any living beings whatsoever.
O King, that is declared to be non-violence (ahiṃsā), which bestows all desires; it acts as an aid in the performance of actions and serves as an obstacle to what should not be done.
Indeed, those skilled in the Dharma declare that it is for the benefit of the entire world;
for one who discriminates between dharma and adharma, speech consists of following the inclinations [of others]. (NarP 1.16.27)

That indeed should be known as falsehood; it is opposed to all that is beneficial. Those in the world who are hateful, foolish, and whose intellects delight in the wrong path [are its followers]. (NarP 1.16.28)
O King, those who follow the path of the Vedas through their discernment of dharma and adharma should be known as the virtuous; whereas those excluded from all dharma are to be known as wicked men.
The virtuous are proclaimed to be those who are devoted to the welfare of all the world;
whatever promotes devotion to Hari is cherished by the good.
That which generates joy for oneself is proclaimed as merit;
this entire world is Viṣṇu, and Vāsudeva is the cause of all.
I am Viṣṇu; they know that the knowledge of which is the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu, who embodies all the gods, I worship him according to the prescribed rite.
Thus, whatever faith one possesses is proclaimed as devotion to Him;
Viṣṇu is composed of all beings, the perfect and eternal.
The cognition that arises through such non-differentiation is proclaimed as equanimity;
O King, equanimity toward enemies and friends is likewise mastery.
Contentment with whatever is obtained by chance is proclaimed as true peace.
All these are declared to bestow the perfection of austerity upon men.
The eight-syllable great mantra, which destroys all sins, is the cause for the swift destruction of the entire mass of evil deeds. (NarP 1.16.36)
O Indra among kings, I shall declare to you that which is the sole means for achieving the goals of human life,
which is pleasing to Viṣṇu, and which bestows all perfections.
One should recite "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" preceded by the praṇava, and after that, having uttered "Namo Bhagavate Vāsudevāya. (NarP 1.16.38)
O Great King, the twelve-syllable mantra beginning with the Praṇava has been proclaimed;
O King, the fruit of both the eight-syllable and the twelve-syllable mantras is equal.
Equanimity has been taught regarding both worldly involvement and withdrawal;
[one should meditate on] Nārāyaṇa, who is peaceful, free from disease, and the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace.
The Lord, whose left lap is occupied by Lakṣmī, likewise grants fearlessness with his hand;
he wears a crown and earrings, and is adorned with various ornaments.
The god, adorned with a shining garland of kaustubha gems, his chest marked with the śrīvatsa,
wearing yellow garments, and saluted by gods and asuras.
One should meditate upon Him who is without beginning or end, the bestower of the fruits of all desires,
the inner controller, whose form is knowledge, the perfect and eternal.
All this that you have asked about has been fully explained, O King.
May it be well with you; go now to attain success in your asceticism as you please.
Thus addressed by Bhṛgu, the supreme ṛṣi,
the protector of the earth attained the highest joy and retired to the forest for asceticism.
Having reached the Himavat mountain at a delightful and holy place,
in the great sacred field of Nādeśvara, he performed an exceedingly difficult penance.
The king bathed three times a day, subsisted on roots, tubers, and fruits,
honored his guests, and was constantly devoted to the performance of fire oblations.
Beneficent toward all beings, peaceful, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa,
he was a worshiper of Hari three times a day with leaves, flowers, fruits, and water.
Having spent such a great length of time in this manner, remaining exceedingly steadfast,
he subsisted on withered leaves while meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa.
Becoming devoted to breath control, the most righteous king then began to perform austerities while remaining without breathing.
Meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who is tranquil and unconquered,
he remained intent on holding his breath for sixty thousand years.
From the mouth of that king, a terrifying fire was born;
seeing it, all the deities were struck with fear, scorched by the flames.
Having reached the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, where Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, resides, the lords of the thirty gods approached him and praised the God of gods,
the protector of those who have come for refuge.
The gods said:
We bow to Viṣṇu, the sole lord of the world, the supreme master who removes all the afflictions of those who remember him;
he who is pure by nature, whose being is perfectly full, and whom the knowers of truth describe as having knowledge for his very body.

He who is always to be meditated upon by the great-souled practitioners of yoga, who performs the work of the gods through bodies assumed at will, whose very nature is the world, and who is the primordial Lord of the universe— to that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), we bow.

We bow to that Lord Viṣṇu, the praiseworthy, ancient Puruṣa, by the mere chanting of whose name all the sins of the wicked go to their destruction; we bow for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human life.

We bow indeed to that Lord of the Thirty-three, who is the soul of Time and the embodiment of the goals of human existence; by whose splendor the sun and other luminaries shine, yet his instructions are never transgressed.
The creator of the world, born from the lotus, the destroyer Rudra, and the Brahmins with the Vedas purify the worlds;
therefore, we have come for refuge to that primordial god, the locus of all qualities, the teacher of all, and the one worthy of protection.
We bow down to the God who is the best of the best, the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, whose footstool is worshipped by gods and demons,
who is the cause of the fulfillment of the resolves of true devotees, and who is to be known solely through wisdom.

We bow down to the Lord, who is without beginning, middle, or end, unborn, the Supreme Ruler, the destroyer of the darkness called beginningless ignorance; whose nature is a mass of pure existence, consciousness, and supreme bliss, and who is devoid of form and other such attributes.
We bow down to that Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, the infinite Lord, clad in yellow garments, served by the lotus-born Brahmā and others;
beloved of sacrifice, the performer of sacrifice, pure, the most excellent of all, and immutable.
Thus praised by the gods, Indra and the others, Mahāviṣṇu then reported the conduct of that royal sage to the gods.
Then, having comforted the gods and granted them fearlessness,
Anañjana went to where the royal sage Nārada was performing austerities.
The Lord who bears the conch and the discus, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss,
the teacher of all the worlds, became manifest before that king.
Having seen that lotus-eyed one, who illuminated the horizons with his splendor, who resembled an *atisī* flower, and was adorned with shimmering earrings; (NarP 1.16.65)
He bore a face with glossy, curly locks like a curved lotus, radiant and brilliant with a crown;
he wore the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and was adorned with a forest garland.
With his neck bowed, the king prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before the one with long arms and noble limbs, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the Lord of the World.
Filled with extreme joy, his hair standing on end and his voice faltering, he cried out repeatedly, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Śrī Kṛṣṇa! (NarP 1.16.68).
To him, Viṣṇu— the inner controller, the teacher of the world, the Lord who brings all beings into existence— being filled with compassion and with a gracious soul, spoke.
The Blessed One said: "O highly fortunate Bhagīratha, your desire shall be fulfilled;
your ancestors will come to my world."
O King, praise Śambhu, who is another form of myself, with hymns according to your own ability;
he will immediately fulfill every one of your desires.
But he who seized the moon when it approached as a śūraṇa root—therefore, one should propitiate Īśāna, the praiseworthy bestower of happiness, with hymns of praise. (NarP 1.16.72)
O King, this god, who is without beginning or end and the bestower of the fruits of all desires,
will immediately grant you prosperity when he is worshipped by you.
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, Acyuta, the Lord of the gods and Master of the worlds, vanished; and that king also rose up.
"O best of the twice-born, is this a dream or is it reality?
Having attained such wonder, the king was struck with amazement and thought, 'What shall I do? (NarP 1.16.75)
Then, a voice spoke loudly from the sky to him whose mind was bewildered:
"This is clearly true; you ought not to harbor doubt. (NarP 1.16.76)
Having heard that, the protector of the earth, intent on devotion, praised Īśāna, the cause of all things and the king of all deities.
Bhagīratha said:
I bow to the Lord of the World, the destroyer of the suffering of those who prostrate;
to the God who is beyond the reach of the means of valid cognition, the Sovereign whose essence is the Praṇava.
I bow to the one whose seed is fierce, who is the unborn and eternal form of the world, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction, the universal-formed Virūpākṣa.
I bow to that increaser of nourishment whom the lords of yogis declare to be devoid of beginning, middle, and end, infinite, unborn, and immutable.
Homage to the Lord of the World, the Deceiver, the Universal Deceiver;
homage be to the Blue-necked One, and homage to the Lord of Creatures.
Homage to the one who holds a skull in his hand, homage to the Lord of the Noose;
homage to the one beyond all conceptual construction, homage to the Lord of Beings.
Homage to you who hold the Pināka bow in hand; homage to you who hold the trident in hand;
homage to you who hold a skull in hand, and who bear the noose and the mallet.
Salutations to you who are all beings; salutations to you who hold a bell in your hand. Salutations to the five-faced deity; salutations to the Lord of the sacred fields.
Salutations to the mountain-dweller who is the primordial sustainer of all beings,
whose form consists of manifold forms, who is devoid of qualities, and who is the Supreme Self.
Homage to the presiding deity of the sacrificial gift, homage to the Lord of the hosts;
homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, homage to the Lord of gold. (NarP 1.16.86)
Salutations to you, O Hiraṇyaretas; salutations to you, O Hiraṇyabāhu.
Salutations to you whose nature is meditation; salutations to you, the witness of meditation.
Salutations to you who abide in meditation; salutations to you who are attainable through meditation, by whom this entire universe, resplendent with all things moving and unmoving, [is pervaded].
It was produced by the primary person (pradhānapuruṣa), like rain from a cloud.
The knowers of reality declare him to be self-luminous, the Great Soul, the supreme eternal light, the Sun for those who behold men.
To Umākānta, Nandikeśānta, Nīlakaṇṭha, Sadāśiva,
Mṛtyuñjaya, Mahādeva, the all-pervading Lord who is higher than the highest.
I bow to that Supreme Cause, whose nature is the Śabdabrahman;
salutations to you, Kapardin, and salutations indeed to Sadyojāta.
To him who arises from existence, who is pure, the eldest and the youngest;
to Manyu, to Iṣa, to the Lord of the sacrifice, and to the thread of the ritual.
Salutations be to you, the great-souled one, who are the nourishment, the lord of the quarters, time, and the one of terrible form, whose seed is fire. // NarP_1,16.94 //

From which the oceans, rivers, and mountains; the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas; the stationary and the moving, the great and the small; the non-existent and the existent, the living and the lifeless [all proceed]. (NarP 1.16.95)
I am born [to worship] those lotus feet of the Lord of Yogins, who is the inner self of all, formless, and the Sovereign;
I bow again and again to that one independent one, who is both the possessor of qualities and the quality itself.
Thus praised, Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
manifested himself before the king who was intensely engaged in ascetic penance.
Five-faced and ten-armed, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
three-eyed and of noble limbs, he has a serpent as his sacred thread.
The god with a broad chest, possessing a splendor like that of the snowy mountain,
wearing an elephant hide as his garment, with lotus feet worshipped by the gods.
Having seen him, O Nārada, he fell prostrate like a staff upon the ground at his feet;
then, rising suddenly with palms joined in reverence before Śiva, he stood there.
He prostrated before Mahādeva while chanting the name Śaṅkara;
and Śaṅkara, the moon-crested one, having perceived the king’s devotion, [appeared]. (NarP 1.16.101)
He said to the king, "I am pleased; choose a desired boon.
I have been thoroughly gratified by you through this hymn as well as through your ascetic penance. (NarP 1.16.102)
Thus addressed by the god, the king, his mind filled with satisfaction,
spoke with palms joined in reverence to the Lord of the lords of the worlds.
Bhagīratha said: "O Maheśvara, if I am worthy of being favored by you through the granting of a boon,
then bestow Gaṅgā for the sake of the liberation of my ancestors."
Śrī Śiva said:
"Gangā has been granted by me to you; she is the supreme goal for your ancestors, and she shall grant you supreme liberation. Having spoken thus to him, Śiva vanished.
Trembling with matted locks, Gaṅgā— the sole purifier of the worlds—
following Bhagīratha, purified the entire universe as she went along.
From that time forth, O sage, that goddess became renowned throughout the three worlds as Bhāgīrathī— the stainless one who removes all impurity.
The Gaṅgā, the best of all rivers, flooded that region where the sons of Sagara had previously been consumed by their own sin.
When the ashes of the oceans were flooded by the Gaṅgā,
those who were submerged in hell were immediately uplifted and freed from their sins.
Those very same people who were previously tormented by Yama while he was crying out in distress,
were now comforted by him when they were drenched with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having ascertained that the sins of the sons of Sagara had departed, Yama,
with a joyful mind, bowed to them, honored them according to the prescribed rites, and spoke to them.
"O princes, you have been liberated from this most dreadful hell; ascending these celestial chariots, go now to the abode of Viṣṇu!"
Thus addressed by Yama, those great-souled ones, freed from all taint,
assumed divine bodies and attained the world of Viṣṇu.
Such is the power of that Gaṅgā, who originated from the tip of Viṣṇu’s foot;
she is renowned throughout all the worlds as the destroyer of great sins.
Whoever reads or even hears this meritorious narrative, which destroys great sins, shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
But he who shall recite this meritorious narrative before Brahmins goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which there is no return.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Bringing of the Gaṅgā by Bhagīratha," in the first quarter of the Pūrvabhāga of the Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, within the section on the Greatness of the Gaṅgā.
The Sages said:
"Well done, O highly fortunate Sūta! By you, who are of a most compassionate nature..."
The supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā, which destroys all sins, has been proclaimed.
O Sūta, having heard the greatness of the Gaṅgā, what did Nārada, who has the vision of the gods, ask again of Sanaka, the best of sages?
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to exactly what was spoken by the celestial sage Nārada in response to his question; that I shall now relate.
Having heard this supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā, consisting of various narratives and histories, the son of Brahmā again asked this with reverence: NarP_1,17.4 //
Nārada said:

"O Sage, oh, how exceedingly blessed is this merit-filled essence of my own good deeds! I have heard from you, the compassionate one, this desired and holy greatness of Gaṅgā’s son, whose meaning is fully revealed and which destroys all sins."
Those virtuous ones who worship Viṣṇu well, striving indeed for their own sake and for the sake of others,
forcefully awaken the mind that is utterly deluded by various teachings and then become serene.
Therefore, tell me of the vows of Hari, by the performance of which Viṣṇu attains pleasure;
for the compassionate one bestows devotion upon those who worship him, and liberation is indeed known to be his handmaid.
Mukunda grants liberation to those who worship Him and are devoted to vows, ritual offerings, and meditation;
yet, having considered the great effort involved in serving His devotees, He does not grant the yoga of devotion to anyone else.

O best of sages, O giver of honor, you are a devotee of Viṣṇu; therefore, please explain at that time the karma that leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to liberation, which brings delight to Hari.
Sanaka said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of sages! You are a devotee of Puruṣottama, since you repeatedly ask about the deeds of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow."
I shall proclaim to you the vows that bring benefit to the world;
by means of these, Hari is pleased and likewise grants freedom from fear.
For him with whom the Blessed One Janārdana, whose emblem is the sacrifice, is pleased,
there arises happiness in this world and the next, as well as an increase in his ascetic merit.
"By whatever means possible, those who are devoted to the worship of Hari go to the supreme abode; so have the great seers declared. (NarP 1.17.13)
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight at the beginning of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
a man endowed with faith, having fasted, should properly worship the one who reclines upon the waters.
Having bathed and put on white garments, and having first performed the cleansing of the teeth,
[one should worship] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
Restraining his speech with a spirit of devotion, he should worship Hari, the best of sages;
he should also worship Viṣṇu, saying, "Salutations to you, O Keśava."
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of ghee and sesame seeds into the fire,
one should keep a vigil at night near a Śālagrāma stone.
One should bathe the healthy Nārāyaṇa with a prastha of milk,
and [worship] Keśava with songs, musical instruments, and offerings of food, both solid and soft.
One should worship with devotion three times a day together with Mahālakṣmī;
then, having risen at dawn and performed the appropriate duties, [one should continue].
In this manner, restrained in speech, self-controlled, and pure, one should worship as before,
offering milk-rice mixed with ghee and accompanied by coconut fruits.
With this mantra, one should devotedly give [the gift] along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin:
"May the god Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, be the bestower of all prosperity. (NarP 1.17.21)
By the offering of *paramānna*, may he be the bestower of my desired goals;
thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability, together with one's kinsmen.
"Having become devoted to Nārāyaṇa, one should eat oneself while restrained in speech"—thus he who performs this supreme worship of Keśava with devotion. (NarP 1.17.23)
Having fasted on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa, he shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Paiṇḍarīka sacrifice. (NarP 1.17.24)
With a restrained mind, one should worship Hari with the mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," bathing him with milk and offering milk-rice as a food-oblation.
One should keep a vigil at night, intent on worship during the three periods of the day,
with incense, lamps, food offerings, perfumes, and beautiful flowers.
One should worship Hari with grass, songs, instrumental music, and hymns;
and one should give to a Brahmin krisara-rice along with ghee and a sacrificial fee.
Nārāyaṇa— the self of all, the lord of all worlds, the omnipresent, the eternal— becomes pleased by the gift of kṛśara rice.
Having bestowed this supreme gift upon a Brahmin with this mantra, he should feed the twice-born according to his ability and then eat himself along with his kinsmen. (NarP 1.17.29)
Thus, one should worship with devotion the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
he shall obtain in full the fruit of eight Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, having fasted as before, one should offer eight oblations of clarified butter while reciting: "Salutations to you, O Mādhava! (NarP 1.17.31).
Then, one should bathe Mādhava with milk according to the previously mentioned measure,
and worship him with flowers, perfumes, and unbroken grains (akṣata) with a mind full of attentiveness.
One should keep a vigil at night, endowed with devotion as before;
and having performed the morning rites, one should worship Mādhava once again.

One should indeed give a *prastha* of sesame seeds to a Brahmin, accompanied by mantras, along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and a garment, for the sake of liberation from all sins. (NarP 1.17.34)
May Mādhava, the self of all beings and the bestower of the fruits of all actions,
grant all desires through this great gift of sesame seeds.
Having given this with this mantra to a Brahmin while endowed with devotion, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability, remembering the Lord Mādhava. (NarP 1.17.36)
O Sage, he who thus performs this vow of offering sesame seeds with devotion shall obtain the full fruit of a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, having fasted, the observer of the vow should worship [the deity], saying: "Salutations to you, O Govinda. (NarP 1.17.38)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds mixed with ghee,
the pure devotee should bathe Govinda with milk according to the previously mentioned measure.
One should keep a vigil at night and likewise perform worship during the three periods of the day;
then, having completed the morning rites, one should worship Govinda once again.
And one should give a *vrīhi* measure of rice, along with a garment and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), to a Brahmin, saying:
"Obeisance to Govinda, Lord of All, Beloved of the Gopīs! (NarP 1.17.41)
"Be pleased by this gift of grain, O Teacher of the World!
Having thus properly performed the vow, one is freed from all sins. (NarP 1.17.42)
A man who fasts on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra obtains the complete merit born of the Gomedha sacrifice. (NarP 1.17.43)
One should worship as before with the mantra, "Salutation be to you, O Viṣṇu," and bathe Viṣṇu with milk according to the previous measure, or according to one's capacity.
In that same manner, O Brahmin, one should bathe the image with a prastha of ghee;
having performed a vigil at night, one should worship the goddess as before.
Then Tātaka, having risen at dawn and completed his morning rites,
offered one hundred and eight oblations mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
One should indeed give an āḍhaka of rice along with a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin;
for Mahāviṣṇu, who is the giver of life and beloved by all, exists in the form of the vital breaths.
"May Janārdana be pleased with me by this gift of one āḍhaka of rice.
Having performed this with devotion, a man is freed from all sins. (NarP 1.17.48)
By fasting on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha and worshipping Madhusūdana, one shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Atyagniṣṭoma sacrifice. (NarP 1.17.49)
Endowed with devotion, one should bathe the Lord of Gods with *droṇa* milk;
there, a vigil should be observed along with worship performed at the three times of day.
"Salutations to you, O Slayer of Madhu," he should say, and offer clarified butter according to his capacity;
having thus praised Madhusūdana one hundred and eight times according to the prescribed rule.
Indeed, being free from evil, he shall obtain the fruit of eight horse-sacrifices by fasting on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha. (NarP 1.17.52)
One should bathe Trivikrama with milk measuring one āḍhaka, and endowed with devotion, one should worship him with the mantra: "Obeisance to Trivikrama. (NarP 1.17.53)
One should indeed offer one hundred and eight oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa);
having kept a vigil at night, one should again perform worship.
Having given twenty cakes along with a sacrificial fee to a Brāhmaṇa, [one should pray]:
"O God of gods, O Protector of the world, O Supreme Lord, be gracious! (NarP 1.17.55)
"Having accepted the gift, become the bestower of what I desire.
One should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability, or eat oneself while remaining silent. (NarP 1.17.56)
O Brahmin, he who thus performs this supreme Traivikrama vow shall become free from sin and obtain the fruit of eight human sacrifices.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the observer of the vow, having fasted and subdued his senses,
should first bathe the image of Vāmana with milk according to the prescribed measure.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of *dūrvā* grass and clarified butter while reciting "Salutations to Vāmana," one should keep a vigil and worship Vāmana once again.
And with devotion, one should offer curd-rice accompanied by coconut fruit and a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin who is habituated to the worship of Vāmana.
Vāmana is the bestower of wisdom; Vāmana always abides in all things.
Because Vāmana delivers us from this [world], salutations again and again to Vāmana.
Having given curd-rice with this [mantra], one should feed the twice-born according to one's ability;
by doing so, one obtains the fruit of a hundred agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the observer of the vow,
having fasted, should bathe Śrīdhara with milk mixed with honey.
"Salutation be to Śrīdhara"—with these words, one should worship him in due order with perfumes and other offerings;
O Sage, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of *pṛṣadājya*.
Having kept a vigil during the night, one should again perform worship;
and an unsurpassed *āḍhaka* of milk should be given to a Brahmin.
O best of Brahmins, one should indeed give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of gold earrings along with a garment, using this mantra for the fulfillment of all desires. (NarP 1.17.66)
O Lord of gods, who reclines upon the ocean of milk, Beloved of Ramā, Master of the world!
Be well-pleased by this offering of milk, you who bestow all happiness.
Because it bestows happiness, the observer of the vow should feed Brahmins according to his ability;
by doing so, he shall obtain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having fasted on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada,
one should bathe Hṛṣīkeśa, the teacher of the world, with a droṇa measure of milk.
A person should worship with the words, "O Hṛṣīkeśa,
salutations to you," and should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with sacrificial porridge mixed with honey.
Having performed the vigil and other rites, he should then give to the knower of the Self one and a half āḍhakas of wheat as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), along with gold according to his capacity.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations to you, the sole cause of all the worlds;
grant me all happiness through the gift of wheat.
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability, and one should eat oneself while remaining restrained in speech;
thus liberated from all sins, one obtains the fruit of the Brahmamedha sacrifice. (NarP 1.17.73)
Having fasted on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina,
one who is pure should devoutly bathe Padmanābha with milk.

"Salutations to Padmanābha; one should perform a fire sacrifice according to one's capacity with sesame, rice, barley, and clarified butter, and worship Him according to the prescribed rite. (NarP 1.17.75)
Having completed the vigil at night, one should perform the worship again;
one should give a *kuḍava* of honey to a Brahmin along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Obeisance to you, Padmanābha, the grandfather of all the worlds;
be well-pleased by this offering of honey, O bestower of all happiness.
Thus, the wise person who performs the Padmanābha-vrata with devotion certainly obtains the fruit of a thousand Brahma-sacrifices.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one who has fasted and subdued his senses should offer milk in the measure of an āḍhaka, and an equal amount of ghee.
One should bathe [the deity] with devotion, saying "Salutation to Dāmodara," and having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds mixed with honey and clarified butter.
One should remain self-controlled and keep vigil, intent on worship during the three periods of the day;
in the morning, one should worship the Lord with beautiful lotus flowers.
Furthermore, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with sesame seeds mixed with ghee;
and one should devotedly give food consisting of the five kinds of delicacies to a brahmin.
O Dāmodara, O Jagannātha, O cause of all causes!
Protect me, O Lord, out of compassion, for you are the protector of those who have come for refuge.
Having given this gift to a learned Brahmin who maintains a household, he should also give a sacrificial fee according to his ability and feed other Brahmins as well. (NarP 1.17.84)
Having duly performed the vow in this manner, he should eat together with his kinsmen;
he enjoys a fruit twice that of thousands of horse-sacrifices.
O best of sages, he who observes this supreme Dvādaśī vow for a full year in this manner goes to the highest state. (NarP 1.17.86)
Whether for one month or two months, he who acts with devoted intent shall obtain each respective fruit and attain the station of Hari.
O Lord of Sages, having completed a full year, the observer of the vow should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having bathed in the morning according to custom, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth,
he should wear white garlands and garments, and be anointed with white perfumes.
One should have a divine pavilion constructed, square and very beautiful,
equipped with bells and chowries, and adorned with the sound of tinkling bells.
Adorned with flower garlands, shining with canopies and banners,
covered with white cloth, and decorated with rows of lamps.
In the center of that, one should properly construct a Sarvatobhadra [mandala] well-adorned;
upon it, one should place twelve jars filled with water.
With a single cloth purchased at the toll-house and properly purified,
one should cover all the jars provided with the five jewels.
O twice-born ones, the devotee observing the vow should have the deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa fashioned from gold,
silver, or likewise from copper.
The self-controlled practitioner should place that image upon the water-pot,
O best of the twice-born, or else its value in gold according to his own capacity.
In all religious observances, the wise man should avoid deceit regarding his wealth;
if he should practice such deceit, his lifespan and his riches will come to ruin.
Filled with devotion, one should first bathe the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who reclines upon Ananta and is free from all affliction, with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should perform the ritual services using names beginning with Keśava;
at night, one should keep a vigil through means such as listening to the Purāṇas.
Having conquered his sleep and subdued his senses, he should observe the fast correctly and worship the God three times a day with the full extent of his available means.
Then, having risen at dawn and completed his morning rites,
he had the twice-born perform a thousand oblations of sesame seeds with the *vyāhṛtis* for the sake of the poet.
Then one should worship the God in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
thereafter, one should perform the recitation of the Purāṇas before the God.
One should give to twelve Brahmins curd-rice and milk-porridge,
likewise accompanied by ten cakes, along with ghee and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O God of gods, Lord of the world, whose form is the grace bestowed upon devotees;
accept this offering, O Kṛṣṇa, and become the granter of all desires.
Having offered this gift, the practitioner, standing with palms joined in reverence,
places his knees upon the ground and, bowing low out of humility, makes his request.
Homage, homage to you, O King of the kings of gods; homage be to you, O God, abode of the world!
Grant me today the fulfillment of my fruit; homage be to you, the Supreme Person.
Thus he should pray to the Brahmins and to the god Puruṣottama;
and he should indeed offer the arghya-water to the god who is accompanied by Mahālakṣmī.
O Lord of Lakṣmī, salutations to you who dwell in the Ocean of Milk;
O Lord of Gods, accept this water offering together with Lakṣmī, O Prākṣa.
I bow to that Infallible One, by whose remembrance and by whose utterance of His name, whatever is deficient in austerities, sacrifices, ritual acts, and the like, immediately attains completeness.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods regarding all that pertains to the vow, the self-restrained practitioner should present the image, together with the sacrificial fee, to the preceptor.
Thereafter, he should feed the Brahmins and give them a sacrificial fee according to his capacity;
then, remaining silent, he himself should eat, surrounded by his kinsmen.
"In the evening, one should listen to the story of Viṣṇu together with learned men"—
the man who acts in this way performs the vow of the twelfth day (Dvādaśī).
O Nārada, he attains all desires both here and in the next world;
accompanied by three hundred generations of his kin and freed from all sins,
he dwells in the abode of Viṣṇu, where having gone, he does not grieve.
O Brahmin, that man who hears this supreme Dvādaśī vow,
or even causes it to be recited, shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Mārgaśīrṣa Śukla Dvādaśī Vrata," in the first quarter of the Pūrvabhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
O best of sages, listen as I describe another excellent vow.
It is meritorious, removing all sins and destroying all suffering.
It bestows the fruits of all desires for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise for women; it grants the fruit of all religious observances.
The Pūrṇimā-vrata is righteous, it destroys ill-fated sounds, wards off malevolent planets, and is renowned throughout all the worlds;
by its performance, a heap of tens of millions of sins is pacified. (NarP 1.18.3)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the full moon day, being self-controlled and pure,
one should perform a bath according to custom, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Wearing white garments, pure and restrained in speech, having entered the house,
washed his feet, and sipped water, he should remember the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed the daily worship of the deity, he should thereafter worship the god Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa with a spirit of devotion, preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
Devoted to worship, the observer of the vow should perform the rite with invocations, seats, and so forth, as well as with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, reciting "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa."
With songs, instrumental music, dances, the recitation of Purāṇas,
and hymns of praise, the performer of the vow, being well-composed, should worship the God.
Having prepared a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) one cubit (aratni) in size before the deity, one should install the fire there according to the domestic ritual tradition (gṛhyamārga).
Having performed the offerings up to the portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), one should satisfy [the deity] with the Puruṣasūkta.
Likewise, one should offer oblations with sesamum seeds and ghee at the feet.
One should diligently perform the fire-oblation (homa) one, two, or even three times according to one's capacity, for the sake of the cessation of all sins. (NarP 1.18.10)
Having completed all the rites, such as the expiation (prāyaścitta), according to the rules prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra,
he should diligently recite the Śānti-sūkta after performing the fire-oblation (homa) according to the injunctions.
Afterwards, having approached the deity, one should again perform worship;
likewise, endowed with devotion, one should offer the fast to the deity.
"O Lotus-eyed God, having remained without food on the full moon day by your command, I shall eat on the following day; be my refuge."
Having thus addressed the gods, one should likewise offer the arghya to the Moon;
having knelt upon the ground, one should do so while holding white flowers and unbroken grains of rice.

"O you who were born from the ocean of milk, O lord who are the progenitor of the three lineages of Aṅgiras, accept this *arghya* offered by me, O Lord, leader of Rohiṇī. Having thus presented the *arghya* to the Moon, one should then pray with palms joined in reverence: NarP_1,18.15: "O you who were born from the ocean of milk, O lord who are the progenitor of the three lineages of Aṅgiras, accept this *arghya* offered by me, O Lord, leader of Rohiṇī. Having thus presented the *arghya* to the Moon, one should then pray with palms joined in reverence.
Standing facing the east and beholding the moon, O Nārada.
Homage to you, the possessor of white rays; homage to you, the king of the twice-born.
Homage to you, the lord of Rohiṇī; let there be homage to you, the brother of Lakṣmī.
Then, having conquered his senses, being thoroughly purified and avoiding the company of heretics, he should keep a vigil by means of listening to Purāṇas and other such activities.
Then, in the morning, he should perform his customary rites according to the rules;
he should again worship the God with full elaboration, according to his means.
Then, having fed the Brahmins according to his ability, the man, being self-restrained,
should eat himself along with his kinsmen, servants, and others, maintaining silence.
Thus, having fasted on the full moon day of the months beginning with Pauṣa,
one should worship the unborn Nārāyaṇa, endowed with devotion.
Having performed it thus for one year, on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana); I shall describe its procedure to you. (NarP 1.18.22)
One should have a divine pavilion constructed, square and highly auspicious,
adorned with flower garlands and resplendent with canopies and banners.
It was strewn with many cloths, adorned with networks of small bells,
and covered with mirrors, chowries, and water-pots.
In the center of that, O twice-born one, one should place a water-filled jar adorned with five colors, upon which is a *sarvatobhadra* diagram.
Having covered the jar with a very fine cloth, beautifully adorned with gold,
silver, or likewise with copper, O twice-born one,
and having fashioned the deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, one should place it upon that [jar].

Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and worshipped him in due order with perfumes and other offerings, one whose senses are restrained should offer food offerings such as eatables and drinks with devotion.
One should likewise keep a vigil, endowed with perfect faith;
on the following day at dawn, one should worship Viṣṇu according to the rules as before.
An image endowed with wealth and skill should be presented to the preceptor;
one should feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity, and if one has the means, without restraint. (NarP 1.18.29)

One should perform the gift of sesame seeds with composure according to one's ability; and a wise person should duly perform the sesame oblation (tilahoma) within a colored mandala according to the rules.
Having thus properly performed the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow, a man,
endowed with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, shall enjoy great pleasures in this world.
Freed from all sins and accompanied by ten thousand members of his lineage,
he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for yogins to attain.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Vrata on the Full Moon of Mārgaśīrṣa," in the section on Vratas within the first quarter of the ancient *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanaka said:
I shall now describe another vow known as Dhvajāropaṇa (the Raising of the Banner).
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and is the cause of pleasing Viṣṇu.
He who performs the supreme hoisting of the banner in the temple of Viṣṇu is honored by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others; what is the use of further words?
The fruit obtained by one who gives a thousand *bhāras* of gold to a householder is equal in measure to the merit of the act of planting a dhūpa tree.
Bathing in the Gaṅgā is unsurpassed and equal to the hoisting of the victory banner;
alternatively, it is like service to Tulasī or the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
"O twice-born one, oh, how unprecedented! Oh, how unprecedented! Oh, how unprecedented is this rite that removes all sins, known as the *dhvajāgra-ropaṇa*! (NarP 1.19.5)
Indeed, whatever tasks there are in the rite of hoisting the banner, I shall describe them all; listen as I speak.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
a man who is self-restrained should diligently perform his bath, preceded by the cleansing of his teeth.
Eating but once a day and observing celibacy, the pure Brahmin, wearing washed garments, should sleep while remembering Nārāyaṇa before Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having risen at dawn, bathed, and sipped water according to the rules,
and having performed his daily obligatory rites, he should thereafter worship Viṣṇu.
Having performed the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*) together with four Brahmins,
one should perform the *nāndīśrāddha* rite for the ceremony of raising the flagstaff.
One should sprinkle the flagstaffs, which are covered with cloths, while reciting the Gāyatrī;
then one should worship the Sun, Vainateya, and the Moon in succession.
One should worship Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ upon the flagstaff with turmeric, akṣa seeds, ghee, perfumes, and so forth, especially with white flowers. (NarP 1.19.12)
Then, having indeed smeared a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) the size of a cow-hide,
and having established the fire according to one's own domestic ritual (svagṛhya), he should perform the rites in sequence, beginning with the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga).
One should offer milk-rice mixed with clarified butter one hundred and eight times,
reciting first the Puruṣasūkta, the Viṣṇornuka, and the Irāvatī hymns.
Then, O twice-born one, he should likewise offer eight oblations with "svāhā" to Vainateya, and then he should offer [the oblations] with the verses "somaṃ dhenum," "ud u tyaṃ," and so forth.
There, he should recite the solar mantras and various pacifying hymns according to his ability;
at night, being pure, he should keep vigil near Hari.
Then, having risen at dawn and completed his daily obligatory rites,
he should worship the God with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, following the sequence as before.
Then, with auspicious musical instruments, recitations of sacred hymns,
dances, and the chanting of the *Ratnaghaṭa*, one should carry the banner to the temple of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin, filled with joy and remaining well-composed, one should install the banner together with its supporting pole at the gateway or on the spire of the temple.

One should worship Hari with perfumes, flowers, incense, and parched grain; with delightful offerings of smoke and lamps; and with food offerings consisting of various kinds of eatables and delicacies. NarP_1,19.20 //
Having thus installed a beautiful and excellent banner in the temple, and having circumambulated it, one should recite this hymn of praise. (NarP 1.19.21)
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe.
May there be salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One.
I have taken refuge in Keśava, by whom this entire universe was born, in whom all things are established, and into whom they shall likewise go to their dissolution.
I bow to him whose supreme state even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know,
and whom even yogins do not perceive— he who has the form of primordial wisdom.
I bow to Him who possesses universal forms, whose navel is the intermediate space, whose head is indeed heaven, and whose foot became the earth.
I bow to him whose form is Brahman, whose ears are all the directions, whose eyes are the sun and the moon, and by whom the Ṛg, Sāma, and Yajur Vedas are perceived.
From whose mouth the Brahmins were born, from whose arms the kings arose,
from whose thighs the Vaiśyas were born, and from whose feet the Śūdra was produced.
They say that the Puruṣa is unborn, naturally stainless, pure, changeless, and untainted, merely through its association with Māyā. (NarP 1.19.28)
I bow to Viṣṇu, the Lord who reclines upon the ocean of milk, the infinite and unconquered, who is affectionate toward his true devotees and accessible through devotion.
I bow to Him who faces in all directions, by whom the elements such as earth, the subtle elements, and the senses— both subtle and gross— came into being.
I bow again and again to that which is the external supreme abode, the most excellent among all worlds,
devoid of qualities, and supremely subtle.
The yogis, who are firm in yoga, proclaim Him as the unchanging, unborn, pure Lord whose arms extend in all directions, the cause of all causes.
May that God Viṣṇu be gracious to me— he who is the inner self of all beings, who consists of the universe, who is devoid of qualities, and who is the Supreme Self.
Though dwelling in the heart, he remains distant to those whose souls are deluded by illusion;
yet to the wise, he is all-pervading—may that Viṣṇu be gracious to me.
May that Viṣṇu grant me his favor— he who is offered oblations with four, with four, with two, and indeed with five, and again with two and eight.
May that Viṣṇu, who is sought by the entire universe and who bestows the ultimate goal upon the wise, the performers of ritual action, and likewise upon men possessed of devotion, grant me grace.
May that Viṣṇu be gracious to me, whom the wise worship as those bodies which Hari assumes effortlessly for the sake of the welfare of the world.
May that Viṣṇu be gracious to me, whom the wise describe as the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is devoid of qualities yet the substratum of all qualities.
Having praised Viṣṇu in this manner, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas;
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor with sacrificial fees, clothing, and other offerings.
Endowed with devotion and a sincere disposition, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity,
together with one’s sons, mother, wife, and others, as well as oneself along with one’s kinsmen.

O Brahmin, one who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa should perform the breaking of the fast. Listen with a well-composed mind as I describe the meritorious fruit for him who performs this supreme rite of raising the banner. NarP_1,19.41 //
O best of Brahmins, as long as the cloth of the banner moves with the wind, so many nets of sins are destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Whether one is burdened by a great sin (mahāpātaka) or burdened by all sins,
by setting up a banner in the house of Viṣṇu, one is liberated from all sins.
O twice-born one, for as many days as the banner remains in the temple of Viṣṇu,
for that many thousands of yugas does one enjoy union with Hari.
Those righteous ones who rejoice upon seeing the raised banner are all liberated from tens of millions of great sins.
The banner raised in the temple of Viṣṇu, shaking its own cloth,
shakes off all the sins of the maker within half a moment.
That king of noble mind who, having consecrated you as a banner in the house of Viṣṇu, worships you constantly, goes to heaven by the path of the gods.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Hoisting of the Banner," in the section on Vows within the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures!
And you have stated that the bearing of this banner is the most excellent of all ritual acts.
O Sage, please describe in detail to me the life story of that one named Sumati, who was mentioned by you as being devoted to the raising of the banner.
Sanaka said:
Listen with a one-pointed mind to this ancient and meritorious history,
which destroys all sins, as it was told to me by Brahmā.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Sumati,
born of the Lunar dynasty, illustrious, and the sole leader of the continent Satpada.
He was righteous in soul, endowed with truthfulness, born of a pure lineage, and fond of guests;
he was possessed of all auspicious marks and adorned with every form of prosperity.
Always serving the stories of Hari, devoted to the worship of Hari,
intent on serving those who are devoted to Hari, and free from the sense of "I" and "mine."
Always devoted to honoring those worthy of honor, possessing an even-minded vision and endowed with virtues,
he was intent on the welfare of all beings, peaceful, grateful, and likewise possessed of renown.
O Sage, his wife was highly fortunate and endowed with all auspicious marks; she was devoted to her husband, regarding him as her very life, and was named Satyamatī.
Both that husband and wife were constantly devoted to the worship of Hari;
they were noble-minded, possessed the memory of their past lives, knew the truth, and were dedicated to the Supreme Reality.
Constantly devoted to the gift of food and dedicated to the gift of water, they constructed countless tanks, groves, embankments, and other such works.
But that Satyamati, ever pure while residing in the abode of Viṣṇu,
danced with extreme delight, charming and speaking with gentle words.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth [lunar fortnight], that illustrious king likewise raises up a beautiful and very extensive banner.
Thus, even the gods constantly praised that king, who was devoted to Hari, eternally skilled in dharma, and possessed of excellent wisdom and intellect.
Knowing that the couple were renowned throughout the three worlds and were experts in the knowledge of dharma,
Vibhāṇḍaka arrived with many disciples, desiring to see them.
Hearing that the sage Vibhāṇḍaka was approaching, the king went out to meet him together with his wife and his subjects in great numbers.
Once the sage had performed the rites of hospitality, was tranquil, and had accepted his seat, [Narada], sitting on a low seat with palms joined in reverence, spoke again to the muni.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, I have achieved my purpose by your arrival here.
The virtuous praise the honoring of the virtuous, which brings about the favor of the gods."
Where there is love for the great, there all prosperity shall be found;
the wise declare that this consists of splendor, fame, wealth, and sons. (NarP 1.20.18)
In that regard, O Sage, thieves increase day by day where the virtuous, O Lord, exercise great compassion. (NarP 1.20.19)

He who would place upon his head the dust from the feet of one worthy of being carried [on the shoulders] has bathed in all sacred fords; he is a meritorious soul—of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.20.20)
"My sons and my wife have been entrusted to you;
command me, O best of Brahmins—what dear service may I perform for you? (NarP 1.20.21)
Beholding King Vinayañcavana, that foremost of sages touched him with his hand and, filled with great joy, spoke to him affectionately.
The sage said:
"O King, everything that has been spoken by you is entirely worthy of your lineage;
everyone who is bowed down with humility attains great prosperity in this world. (NarP 1.20.23)
O best of kings, through discipline a mortal obtains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; what indeed is difficult for the great-souled to attain? (NarP 1.20.24)
"I am pleased with you, Bhāpāla, who have turned toward the true path.
May it be well with you always; now tell me that which I ask. (NarP 1.20.25)
There are many kinds of worship that bring satisfaction to the hands [of the deities];
among these, you should always remain ever-vigilant in the raising of the victory banner.
This virtuous wife of yours is also constantly devoted to dancing;
you ought to tell me the truth of this matter exactly as it is.
The king said:
"Listen, O Blessed One; hear all that you ask, for I shall tell it to you—the wondrous account of our conduct here in this world."
O best of beings, in the past I was a Śūdra named Mālini,
constantly devoted to evil paths and delighting in the deception of all the world.

A slanderer, one who hates the Dharma, a stealer of the property of the gods, a killer of cows, a killer of a Brahmin, a thief, and one who delights in the slaughter of all living beings; NarP_1,20.30 //
Constantly speaking harsh words, sinful, and devoted to courtesans—remaining thus for some time, he disregarded the great Ṛgveda. (NarP 1.20.31)
Abandoned by all his kinsmen, he came to the forest in misery;
there he constantly subsisted on deer meat and likewise lived as a plunderer of travelers.
Alone, he dwelt in a desolate forest full of suffering;
once, exhausted by hunger, afflicted by the heat, and parched with thirst.
In a lonely forest, I saw a dilapidated temple of Viṣṇu,
and near it, a great lake crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks.
O Lord of Sages, having reached that place covered by a mass of flowers from the surrounding forest,
I drank water there on its bank, my fatigue dispelled.
Having eaten the fallen fruits and thus dispelled my hunger,
I made that ruined abode of Viṣṇu my dwelling.
I constantly repaired its dilapidated and cracked joints; with leaves, grass, wood, and straw, I properly constructed the house. (NarP 1.20.37)
O Lord of Sages, for the sake of my mother-in-law, I wandered about that place;
there, established in the livelihood of a hunter, I killed many kinds of deer.
Having lived for twenty years, constantly maintaining his livelihood,
this virtuous woman, born in the Vindhya region, has now arrived.
Born of the Niṣāda clan, she was known by the name Viprā;
she was like a female cuckoo abandoned by her kin, sorrowful and with a worn-out body. (NarP 1.20.40)
Exhausted by hunger, thirst, and the heat, and grieving over her own misdeeds,
she arrived there by the turn of fate while wandering through the desolate forest.
Afflicted by the heat of summer outside and oppressed by mental anguish within, seeing her thus tormented by suffering, great compassion arose in me. (NarP 1.20.42)
"O Brahmin, I gave her water, meat, and wild fruits; once her fatigue had vanished, I questioned her as to who she was."
She related her own story; listen to that, O great sage:
"I am named Avakokilā, born of the Niṣāda clan."
And I am the daughter of Dāruka, dwelling on the Vindhya mountains; I am a constant thief of others' property and always a speaker of slander. (NarP 1.20.45)
Having spoken thus as a wanton woman, I was abandoned by my circle of kinsmen; thereafter, for some time, I was supported by my husband, though I was censured by the world.
By fate, he too has gone to the realm of Yama, leaving me here;
alone, wandering in this desolate wilderness, I am oppressed by sorrow.
"By fate I have come into your presence, and now I have been restored to life by you"—in this way she recounted all her own past deeds to him. (NarP 1.20.48)
Then, having adopted the state of husband and wife,
we two remained for ten years in that temple, subsisting on meat and fruit.
Once, O Sage, the two descendants of Raghu, intoxicated by the drinking of liquor and delighted by their consumption of meat, were in that temple in a state of extreme revelry.
Deluded and unaware that our garments had been stripped away, we performed a dance; we have both arrived simultaneously at the end of the enjoyment of our *prārabdha* karma. (NarP 1.20.51)
Then the messengers of Yama arrived, terrifying with nooses in their hands, in order to lead us—who were intent on dance—to the most agonizing torments of Yama. (NarP 1.20.52)
Then, O giver of honor, the Blessed One was pleased by this deed performed by me,
known as the restoration of the dwelling for the gods.
Intent on protecting his own devotees, he dispatched his own messengers;
those messengers of the God of gods bore the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Resembling a thousand suns, they all possessed beautiful four arms;
they wore crowns and earrings, were captivating, and adorned with forest garlands.
O Brahmin, they dispelled the darkness from the quarters with their own splendor,
[and they beheld] the terrifying servants of Yama, holding nooses in their hands and possessing fangs.
Those devoted to Kṛṣṇa spoke thus, exerting themselves to capture us both.
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"O cruel ones, of wicked conduct and devoid of discrimination,
release this sinless couple, who are dear to Hari!"
Discrimination is the primary cause of prosperity in the three worlds;
but he who perceives sin in the sinless, one should know him to be the lowest of men.
But he who perceives evil as non-evil—one should know him to be the lowest of the low.
The messengers of Yama said:
"What you have spoken is indeed true; however, these two are the worst of sinners.
Sinners are to be punished by Yama, therefore we shall take these two away."
For dharma is that which is established by the Vedas, while adharma is its opposite;
this distinction between dharma and adharma, we shall seek from Yama.
Hearing this, the messengers of Viṣṇu, possessed of great majesty and regarding unrighteousness as righteousness, became enraged and replied to those soldiers of Yama.
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"Alas, what a tragedy! Unrighteousness touches the assembly of those who perceive dharma, yet are utterly devoid of right discernment; for this is the great source of all calamities."
Since you have attained the status of overseers of hell without distinction from those who committed [other] sins,
for what purpose do you still exert yourselves today in committing further evils?
Even those who have committed great sins remain in the terrible hell until the exhaustion of their own karma, lasting as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars.
"Since I have not seen any atonement for previously accumulated sins, why should I perform sinful deeds again and again in vain? (NarP 1.20.67)
Dharma is established in the Vedas; it is truth, truth, there is no doubt.
However, we shall explain the dharmas practiced by these two exactly as they are.
"Released from sin and devoted to the service of Hari, let them be liberated by Hari as he protects them; release them without delay. (NarP 1.20.69)
She performed a dance and likewise the *dhvajaroṣaṇa* rite;
at the time of death, they both attained freedom from sin in the abode of Viṣṇu.
At the time of death, by merely hearing or even uttering their name just once, one attains the supreme abode; how much more so for those who are devoted to serving them?
Whether one is burdened by great sins (mahāpātaka) or even by minor offenses (upapātaka),
a person who serves Kṛṣṇa attains the supreme goal even at the end [of life].
Those who are devoted to the service of ascetics and devotees of Viṣṇu go swiftly to the supreme goal,
even if they are sinners.
He who stands for even a moment or half a moment in the temple of Hari goes to the supreme abode; what need is there to mention those who remain for twenty-one years?
These two, who constantly apply plaster and are devoted to sweeping, are always engaged in repairing what is worn out and decayed in the temple of Hari.
O you two who sprinkled water and offered lamps in the temple of Hari,
how is it that you two highly fortunate ones deserve to experience such torment?
Thus addressed, those messengers of Viṣṇu immediately severed our bonds,
placed us upon the foremost of celestial chariots, and departed for the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
There, O lord of sages, having attained proximity to the god of gods, the wielder of the discus, they enjoyed divine pleasures for that length of time.
Having enjoyed divine pleasures even there, they came to this earth;
here too, they obtained incomparable prosperity through the grace of service to Hari.
O sage, O Brahmin, even by serving Hari unintentionally, such a fruit has been obtained, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (NarP 1.20.80)
"By worshipping Viśveśa and Mādhava with a spirit of devotion according to our desire, we shall attain the supreme good"—this is the reason that has been set forth. (NarP 1.20.81)
O Lord of the Earth-dwellers, even an action performed involuntarily yields very great fruit; how much more so, then, one performed with faith?
Having heard this, that lord of sages, Vibhaṇḍaka,
praised the couple and departed for his own forest of asceticism.
Therefore, know this, O celestial sage: the service rendered to the God of gods, the wielder of the discus, is remembered as being like the wish-fulfilling cow for all beings.
But for those devoted to the worship of Hari, the eternal Hari himself bestows the supreme good, granting the fruit of all desires. NarP_1,20.85 //
Whoever reads or even hears this meritorious narrative, which destroys all sins, shall also attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Story of King Sumati," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
O Nārada, listen to another secret as it truly is.
The five-fold hymn to Hari, renowned throughout all the worlds, is difficult to obtain.
O Best of Sages, it wards off all suffering for both women and men; it is the primary cause of virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
It bestows all that is desired and grants the fruit of all vows;
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should remain with the senses restrained.
One should perform the rites beginning with bathing and preceded by the cleansing of the teeth;
having properly performed the worship of the deity as well as the five great sacrifices (mahādhvaras).
On that day, O Lord of Sages, one should observe the vow while remaining in a state of fasting; then, having risen at dawn on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one should proceed.
Having performed his bath according to custom, he should bathe Hari,
the Lord of the gods, in the temple of the Noble One (Ārya) with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship with supreme devotion, in due order, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
as well as with incense, lamps, food offerings, betel leaves, and circumambulations.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, one should utter this mantra:
"Homage to you, whose form is primordial wisdom; homage be to you, the giver of knowledge. (NarP 1.21.8)
"Salutations to you, O Śrava-paruṣa, the bestower of all perfections!
Having thus prostrated before Vāsudeva, the Lord of Gods and the benefactor of people," so it is said.
One should offer up the fast with the mantra that will be spoken:
"O Keśava, from this day forward, I shall remain without food for five nights. (NarP 1.21.10)
"O Lord of the World, by your command, be the granter of my desires.
Having thus made this offering to the God, he, with his senses subdued, observed a fast.
O twice-born one,
having conquered the senses, one should keep a vigil at night on the eleventh day, as well as on the twelfth, the thirteenth, and the fourteenth.
O Sage, the worship of Viṣṇu should be performed in this manner on the full moon day;
likewise, a vigil (jāgara) should be observed on both the eleventh and the full moon days.
The worship with the five nectars and other offerings is common throughout the five days;
however, on the full moon day, one should bathe Viṣṇu with milk according to one's ability. Furthermore, an oblation of sesame seeds should be performed, as well as the gift of sesame seeds.
Then, on the morning of the sixth day, having performed his own daily domestic rites and consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should worship Hari according to the prescribed rules.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins without restriction if one has the means;
then, with speech restrained, one should eat together with one's own kinsmen.
O Nārada, in this manner, from the month of Pauṣa until the end of Kārttika,
a man should perform the vow during the bright fortnight according to the previously described procedure.

In this manner, O twice-born one, the vow that destroys sin should be observed for one year; then, at dawn in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the observer of the vow should perform the concluding ceremony (*udvapanam*),
remaining without food on the eleventh day, just as before.
On the twelfth day, being well-composed, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having properly worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one who has conquered his senses should present a gift to the Lord of the Ṛbhus.
Milk-rice mixed with honey, combined with ghee and fruits,
joined with fragrant substances, placed in a full jar along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Lord of Sages, one should give a water-pot covered with cloth and endowed with five gems to a Brāhmaṇa who is a knower of the supreme self.
O Soul of all, Lord of all beings, eternal pervader of all,
O Mādhava, be well-pleased by this offering of supreme food.
Having given this milk-rice (pāyasa) to the Brahmins and then fed them,
he himself should eat with his kinsmen according to his capacity, remaining restrained in speech.
Whoever performs this vow known as the "Five Haris," there shall never again be a return for him from the world of Brahmā.
O twice-born one, those who desire supreme liberation should undertake this vow, which is like a forest fire to the wilderness of all sins. (NarP 1.21.26)
Whatever fruit one might obtain by giving away ten million cows,
that same fruit is obtained by men through this fast.
But he who, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, should hear this with devotion,
is liberated from millions of most terrible torments.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Five-Night Vow," in the section on vows within the first quarter of the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*, concerning the period from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa until the full moon.
Sanaka said:
"I shall describe another excellent vow; listen to it with a concentrated mind."
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and is beneficial to the entire world.
O twice-born one, one should perform this vow during the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, or likewise in the month of Āśvina.
During any one of these months, in the bright fortnight, having conquered his senses,
he should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sleep in the presence of Viṣṇu.
Then, having risen at dawn and completed his daily rites,
one who is self-controlled and free from anger should worship Viṣṇu with faith.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu along with learned scholars as is appropriate,
he should then make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), preceded by the recitation of "May there be well-being" (svasti-vācana).
