"O Keśava, from this day forward I shall remain without food for one month;
at the end of the month, I shall break my fast by your command, O God of gods. (NarP 1.22.6)
Obeisance to you whose form is austerity, O bestower of the fruits of ascetic practices;
grant me the fulfillment of my desires and ward off all obstacles.
Having thus offered this auspicious month-long vow to the god Viṣṇu,
one should then reside in the temple of Hari from that time until the end of the month.
One should bathe the Lord every day according to the rite of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
and one should maintain a lamp continuously in the temple of Hari during that month.
Every day he should chew wood derived from the apāmārga plant;
thereafter, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, he should bathe according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having bathed Viṣṇu, one should worship Him as before while remaining self-restrained;
filled with devotion, one should always feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity and give them a sacrificial fee.
Restraining his senses, he should eat together with his kinsmen;
in this manner, the observer of the vow should perform thirteen month-long fasts.
At the end of the year, he should give a cow as a sacrificial fee to one learned in the Vedas;
there, he should feed exactly twelve Brahmins according to the prescribed rule,
and he should also give a sacrificial fee according to his ability, as well as gold ornaments.
He who, with his senses restrained, performs three months of fasting,
enjoys twice the fruit of the Āptoryāma sacrifice.
O best of sages, he by whom the Pārāka penance has been performed four times shall obtain the supreme merit arising from the Aṣṭāśītoma sacrifice.
The man by whom this vow has been performed five times shall obtain twice the merit born of an Atyagniṣṭoma sacrifice, O Great-souled One.
He who, being well-composed, performs six months of fasting shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
A man who, abstaining from food,
performs month-long fasts six times over shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
O Lord of Sages, he who performs the Pāvāsānya fast for eight times during a month shall obtain fivefold the fruit of the sacrifice known as the Naramedha.
But the man who performs month-long fasts nine times over obtains threefold the merit born of the Gomedha sacrifice.
O best of sages, he who performs the Parāka penance ten times enjoys a fruit three times greater than that of the Brahmamedha sacrifice.
He who, with his senses restrained, performs eleven *parāka* penances,
attains the state of similarity to Hari, endowed with all enjoyments.
The man who, being self-restrained, performs thirteen *parāka* penances goes to supreme bliss, having reached which he does not grieve.
Those who are devoted to month-long fasts, intent on bathing in the Gaṅgā, and expounders of the Dharma-mārga are indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Fasting for a month should be performed by women without male protectors, by ascetics, by celibate students, and especially by those living in the forest.
Whether a woman or even a man, by performing this very difficult vow, one attains liberation, which is hard to reach even for yogins. (NarP 1.22.26)
Whether one is a householder, a forest-dweller, a practitioner of vows, or even a mendicant;
whether a fool or a scholar—having heard this, one shall partake in liberation.
One who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa, whether they hear or recite this meritorious account of the vow, is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Month-long Fasting Vow," in the section on vows within the first quarter of the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanaka said:
I shall now proclaim another vow, renowned throughout the three worlds.
It pacifies all evils and bestows the fruit of all desires.
O twice-born one, for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even for Śūdra women,
it bestows liberation upon those who perform it with devotion and is most dear to Viṣṇu.
The vow known as Ekādaśī bestows all desired objects upon men; it must be observed by all means, since it brings pleasure to both the Brahmins and Viṣṇu.
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight; he who eats on this day is most sinful here and shall go to hell in the next world. (NarP 1.23.4)
One who desires the fruit of the fast should abandon four meals:
two on the preceding day, one at night, and one during the middle of the day and night.
The man who desires to eat on the day of Ekādaśī undoubtedly desires to consume all manner of sins. (NarP 1.23.6)
O Lord of Sages, if one desires liberation, one should remain without food on the tenth, the eleventh, and the twelfth lunar days. (NarP 1.23.7)
O Brahmin, whatever sins there may be, including such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, they all reside dependent upon food, O Lord Hari; therefore,
if one desires liberation, one should remain without food on the Ekādaśī day.
O Lord of Sages, whatever sins there may be, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth, they all reside within food; therefore,
if one desires liberation, one should remain without food on the eleventh day.
And whatever evils there may be, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth.
O Brahmin, they remain dependent upon food during the day of Hari.
There may be some way to atone for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
however, for one who eats on the Ekādaśī day, there is no atonement whatsoever.
Whether one is burdened by great sins or joined with all manner of offenses,
by remaining without food on the eleventh day, one attains the supreme goal.
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) is of great merit and is most dear to Viṣṇu; it should be observed in every way by Brahmins who desire the severance of the cycle of worldly existence.
On the tenth day, having risen in the morning and performed the cleansing of the teeth,
one should bathe Viṣṇu according to the rules and worship him with the senses restrained.
On the eleventh day, one should remain without food and with the senses restrained;
devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, one should sleep in the presence of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, having bathed on the eleventh day and having properly worshipped Janārdana with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should then utter the following: NarP_1,23.14.
"O lotus-eyed one, having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat on the following day; O Acyuta, be my refuge. (NarP 1.23.15)
Having recited this mantra of the god of gods, the wielder of the discus,
one with a soul satisfied by a spirit of devotion should offer the fast.
The practitioner, restrained and observing the vow, should perform a vigil before the deity with songs,
instrumental music, dances, and the listening to Purāṇas and other such recitations.
Then, having risen at dawn on the twelfth day, the observer of the vow,
with his senses restrained, should bathe according to the rules and worship Viṣṇu.
Having bathed Janārdana with the five nectars on the eleventh day,
O Brahmin, one who bathes him with milk on the twelfth day attains union with Hari.
O Keśava, for me who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance, be gracious through this vow; becoming well-disposed, grant me the vision of knowledge.
Having thus informed Mādhava, O best of Brahmins, being well-composed,
one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability and likewise give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, having performed the five great sacrifices together with his own kinsmen, he himself should eat while maintaining silence.
Thus, he who, being self-restrained, performs the meritorious vow of Ekādaśī,
goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
Devoted to the vow of fasting and dedicated to the performance of religious duties,
he should never, under any circumstances, look upon Cāṇḍālas or those who have fallen from their caste.
One devoted to the vow of fasting should never, at any time, converse with atheists, those who have broken the bounds of propriety, revilers, or backbiters.

One who observes a vow should never speak with one who supports a woman born of a low-caste mother, nor with the husband of such a woman, nor with one who performs sacrifices for those for whom it is forbidden to sacrifice.
One who eats from a sacrificial pit, a singer, one who subsists on serving the gods, a physician, a composer of poetry, and one who opposes the gods and the twice-born; // NarP_1,23.27 //
One should not honor, even with mere words, a person who is greedy for the food of others, one who is devoted to another's wife, or even one who is intent on vows and fasts. (NarP 1.23.28)
Thus, being purified by these and other such means, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all,
one who becomes intent on fasting shall attain supreme perfection.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no teacher equal to one's mother;
there is no deity equal to Viṣṇu; and there is no austerity superior to fasting.
There is no mother equal to patience; there is no wealth equal to fame;
there is no gain equal to knowledge; and there is no father equal to the Dharma as a gain.
There is no kinsman equal to solitude, and no vow superior to Ekādaśī.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history.
This is the conversation between Bhadraśīla and his father Gulava.
Long ago, there was a sage named Gālava who was devoted to truth.
And he spoke on the bank of the Narmadā, a treasury of asceticism who was peaceful and self-controlled,
in a place thickly covered with many trees and frequented by elephants and Bhallas.
It was frequented by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Vidyādharas;
it was filled with bulbous roots, roots, and fruits, and was inhabited by throngs of sages.
A preeminent brahmin named Gālava made his residence there for a long time;
he had a self-controlled son known as Bhadraśīla.
The illustrious one was a rememberer of his former births, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa;
even during the time of childhood play, he was of auspicious character and great intelligence.
Having fashioned an image of Viṣṇu even from clay, one should worship it for a moment;
one should also awaken one's companions [to this truth]: "Viṣṇu is always to be worshipped by men. (NarP 1.23.38)
"Even the wise must observe the Ekādaśī vow.
O Lord of Sages, thus were those children enlightened by him.
Those highly fortunate ones, devoted solely to the worship of Viṣṇu, joyfully fashion an image of Hari from clay, whether individually or collectively, and worship it.
Bowing down to Viṣṇu, the auspicious-minded one, who is the Viṣṇu of all, spoke these words: "May there be well-being for all the worlds. (NarP 1.23.41)
Whether for a moment during play, or even for half a moment, one who resolves upon the Ekādaśī vow and offers it to Keśava, [attains the fruit]. (NarP 1.23.42)
Having thus observed such virtuous conduct in his son, the sage Gālava,
a treasury of asceticism, embraced him and questioned him, overcome with wonder.
Gālava said:
"O illustrious one of auspicious character, you are truly Bhadraśīla, O observer of noble vows! Your conduct is so auspicious that it is difficult even for yogis to attain."
Constantly devoted to the worship of Hari, intent on the welfare of all beings,
dedicated to the vow of Ekādaśī, and avoiding prohibited conduct;
free from enmity, free from the sense of "mine," peaceful, and solely absorbed in meditation upon Hari.
"How has such an intellect as this arisen in this child?
For devotion to Hari is indeed difficult to attain, even without the service of the great."
For the minds of these people, my son, naturally incline toward ignorance, desire, and action; how then can your conduct be so extraordinary?
Even among those who associate with the virtuous, devotion to the Blessed One arises only through the excellence of one's prior merit; at this, I have become filled with wonder. (NarP 1.23.48)
Filled with joy, I ask you: it behoves you, O best of sages, to explain this, just as Bhadraśīla was instructed by his father with these well-considered words.
Remembering his former births, virtuous in soul, and with a face beaming with joyful laughter,
he reported everything exactly as it happened and according to his vows to his father.
Bhadraśīla said:
"Listen, dear one, O best of sages, for I have experienced this myself in the past;
through the memory of my former births, I know what was spoken by Yama."
Having heard this, the highly fortunate Gālava, filled with wonder and moved by affection,
spoke to the high-minded Bhadraśīla.
Gālava said:
"Who were you previously, O highly fortunate one, and what was said to you by Yama?
Whose [son] were you, and for what reason? You ought to tell me all of that."
Bhadraśīla said:
"O father, in former times I was a king born of the lunar dynasty,
renowned as Dharmakīrti, and ruled by Dattātreya."
For nine thousand years I protected the entire earth;
likewise, many unrighteous acts as well as righteous ones were performed by me.
Then, intoxicated by prosperity, I committed much unrighteousness;
through association with heretics, I became a practitioner of heretical ways.
Although I had accumulated very many merits in the past,
being oppressed by heretics, I completely abandoned the path of the Vedas.
And all my sacrifices were destroyed by me through the employment of fraudulent stratagems;
yet, seeing that I was devoted to unrighteousness, the sons of Maheśa [punished me].
They always committed evil deeds, and a sixth part of that fell upon him;
thus he was one whose conduct was sinful and who was constantly devoted to vices.
Once, having become fond of hunting, I entered the forest with my army; there in the woods, I slew many kinds of wild animals. (NarP 1.23.60)
Overcome by hunger and thirst and exhausted, I reached the bank of the Revā;
scorched by the fierce heat of the sun, I performed my ablutions in the Revā.
His army unseen, he was alone and severely oppressed by hunger.
At that time, at the onset of night, I saw all those who lived in Revātīra, whoever they were, devoted to the vow of Ekādaśī.
And there, deprived of food and separated from my army, I remained alone with only my attendants, keeping watch throughout the night.
Exhausted by the fatigue of the journey and tormented by hunger and thirst,
I passed away at that very spot at the end of my waking state.
Then, bound by the messengers of Yama with their terrifying great fangs,
he was led along a path filled with many torments to the presence of Yama;
there he beheld Samavartin, whose face was formidable with fangs.
Then Kāli summoned Citragupta and spoke this to him:
"O wise one, tell me correctly the rules for his instruction."
O best of beings, having been thus addressed by Dharmarāja, Citragupta reflected for a long time and then spoke this again.
"He is indeed devoted to evil; nevertheless, listen, O Dharmaja:
by fasting on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight], he is liberated from all sins."
On this delightful bank of the Revā, having observed a fast on the day of Hari and performed a vigil and an upavāsa, he attained freedom from sin.
Whatever sins have been committed, even if they are very numerous,
all of them are indeed destroyed by the power of fasting.
Thus addressed by the wise Citragupta, the King of Dharma,
feeling compassion for me, prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before me.
There, Dharmarāja worshipped me with a spirit of devotion;
then, having summoned all his own soldiers, he spoke as follows: (NarP 1.23.73).
The King of Dharma said:
"Listen to my words, messengers; I shall speak what is most beneficial for you.
Bring before me those mortals who are devoted to the path of dharma."

Those who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, self-restrained, grateful, dedicated to the vow of Ekādaśī, and have conquered their senses—those peaceful ones constantly say, "O Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta, Hari, be our refuge!"—so quickly abandon [all else]. (NarP 1.23.75)

"Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta, Janārdana, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Padmeśa, Padmajapita, Śiva, Śaṅkara"—those who are peaceful, who desire the welfare of the entire world, and who have cast off all enemies, constantly utter these names; my instruction is that you should not abandon them.
O messengers, never abandon those who have offered their deeds to Nārāyaṇa, who practice devotion to Hari, who are intent on the path of good conduct, who serve their gurus,
who are devoted to giving to worthy recipients, who show compassion to the very poor, and who are constantly attached to the name of Hari.

O messengers, abandon those people who are free from association with heretics, who are steadfast in devotion to the twice-born, who are intensely eager for the company of the virtuous, who are hospitable, who possess equal regard for Śambhu and Hari, and who are intent on doing good to others.
Those who have avoided the service of the nectar of stories concerning Hari, and whose minds are not devoted to the constant remembrance of Nārāyaṇa.
"Bring those sinful ones, who are not gladdened by the sprinkling of the water from the feet of Virūpākṣa, to my house. (NarP 1.23.79)

O messengers, bring here those who are habitually abusive toward their mothers and fathers, those who hate the world, those who perform deeds harmful to well-wishers, those who are intent on coveting the property of the gods, those who cause the destruction of living beings, and those who are preoccupied with offenses.

"O messengers, bring here that man who is averse to the vow of Ekādaśī, of fierce character, devoted to public scandal, a reviler of others, the destroyer of the village, possessed of supreme enmity, and greedy for the wealth of Brahmins. (NarP 1.23.81)

Those men who are averse to devotion to Viṣṇu, who do not bow down to Nārāyaṇa—the protector of those who have sought refuge—and who do not go to the temples of Viṣṇu, are utterly foolish; bring them here by force, for they are devoted to extreme sin.
Thus it was heard that when Yama had thus rebuked me, I, consumed by remorse, remembered that censurable deed. (NarP 1.23.83)
Through remorse for my evil deeds and by hearing the true Dharma,
all my sins have there been eliminated without remainder.
Yama also bowed down before him, who was liberated from the remainder of his evil karma, who had attained a form resembling that of Hari, and who shone like a thousand suns.
Having seen this, those messengers of Yama, though fierce with fear, were struck with wonder and placed their supreme trust in what was spoken by Yama.
Then, having honored me, Kāla immediately dispatched me to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots.
Together with ten million celestial palaces endowed with all enjoyments,
O brahmin sage, he dwelt in the world of Viṣṇu by virtue of that karma.
Having remained in the station of Viṣṇu for thousands of koṭis of kalpas and hundreds of koṭis of kalpas, he subsequently went to the world of Indra.
There too, enriched with all enjoyments and honored by all the gods,
he remains in heaven for that length of time, and then descends to the earth.
"Even here, O best of sages, I have been born into your family as a devotee of Viṣṇu;
because I possess the memory of my former births, I know all this."
Therefore, I shall make an effort to worship Viṣṇu together with the boys;
previously, I did not realize that this was the Ekādaśī vow.
Through the power of recollecting my past lives, I have now understood this:
that this is indeed the fruit of the karma performed by myself in this very life.
"O Lord, what more need be said of those who perform the Ekādaśī vow with devotion?
Therefore, O chief of brahmins, I shall observe the auspicious Ekādaśī vow."
Those men who, desiring the supreme station, perform the worship of Viṣṇu day after day and observe the Ekādaśī vow with faith; NarP_1,23.95 //
"But for them, there is the abode of Viṣṇu, which bestows supreme bliss.
Having heard these words of his son, the sage Gālava was well-pleased.
He attained supreme satisfaction and was exceedingly delighted in his mind:
"My birth has become fruitful; my lineage has been purified. (NarP 1.23.97)
"Since you were born in my house as one devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu," he said,
his mind satisfied by the deeds of that son.
And he fully explained the procedure for the worship of Hari as it truly is.
"Thus, O best of sages, this has been related by me to you exactly as it is, both in brief and in detail. What else do you wish to hear? (NarP 1.23.99)

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Ekādaśī Vow," in the first quarter of the Purvabhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, within the narrative of vows.
Sūta said: Having heard this immeasurable, meritorious, and most excellent account of the day of Hari spoken by Sanaka, [the sages were filled with wonder].
Thus the son of Brahmā, filled with joy, spoke again concerning the essence of the vow, which brings peace to the flood of evil.
Nārada said: O sage, you who are skilled in the knowledge of ultimate truth, you have related everything—
the highly meritorious account of the vow— which, when properly observed, bestows devotion to Hari.
Now, O Sage, I wish to hear the rules for the conduct of the social classes (varṇas),
as well as the conduct for all stages of life (āśramas) and the rules for expiation (prāyaścitta).
O illustrious one, you who are skilled in the meaning of all principles,
you ought to explain all of this to me correctly, out of your supreme compassion.
Sanaka said:
Listen, O tiger among sages,
to how the imperishable Hari, who brings about the welfare of his devotees, is worshipped by those devoted to the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life.
I shall duly declare to you that which was proclaimed by Manu and others regarding the regulations for the social classes and stages of life; for you are a devotee of Adhokṣaja.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—these four alone are designated as the social classes (varṇas); among them, the Brahmin is superior.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are declared to be the three twice-born (dvija);
the status of being twice-born is attained by these three through their mothers and through the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
All duties (dharmas) must be performed by these castes according to their respective castes;
those who abandon the duties of their own caste are called heretics (pāṣaṇḍa) by the wise.
A twice-born man becomes accomplished by performing the rites prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*;
otherwise, he shall become fallen and excluded from all religious duties.
The duties of the respective ages (yugas) should be observed by these castes as is appropriate;
likewise, local customs should be adopted provided they do not conflict with the dharma of the Smṛtis.
One should practice dharma with effort through action, mind, and speech;
however, one should not practice even that which is consistent with dharma if it leads away from heaven or is despised by the world.
Undertaking sea voyages, carrying a water-pot, and likewise marrying daughters of women of a different caste—these [are forbidden] for the twice-born. (NarP 1.24.13)
The procreation of sons through the husband’s younger brother, the slaughter of an animal at the honey-mixture offering (*madhuparka*),
the eating of meat at a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), and likewise the stage of life of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).
The giving away again of a maiden to whom the *akṣata* rite has been performed;
lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*); and the human sacrifice (*naramedha*) and horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
The Great Departure, as well as the Gomedha sacrifice—
wise men say that these dharmas are to be avoided in the Kali age.
The local customs of various regions should be adopted by the people residing in those respective lands;
otherwise, one should be known as fallen and excluded from all righteous dharma.
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the general rites for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; listen to that with a concentrated mind.
He should give gifts to the Brahmins, likewise worship the gods with sacrifices,
beg for his livelihood, and likewise teach others.
A Brahmin who is constantly engaged in the water-libations should officiate at sacrifices for those worthy of performing them,
undertake the study of the Vedas, and likewise perform the formal consecration of the sacred fire.
One should maintain an even mind toward both types of external objects of perception;
one should act for the welfare of the entire world and utter gentle words. (NarP 1.24.21)
Approaching one's wife during her season is indeed praised for a Brāhmaṇa;
he should not speak anything harmful to anyone and should be devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu. (NarP 1.24.22)
O best of the twice-born, even a Kṣatriya should give gifts to Brāhmaṇas,
undertake the study of the Vedas, and likewise worship the gods with sacrifices.
He should indeed live by the profession of arms and protect the earth according to dharma;
he should carry out the punishment of the wicked as well as the protection of the virtuous. (NarP 1.24.24)
O best of the twice-born, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture,
and the study of the Veda are likewise proclaimed as the duties of the Vaiśya.
He should take a wife and practice his religious duties,
as well as engage in buying and selling with wealth derived from the crafts of artisans.
Even a Śūdra may give gifts and perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
he should be devoted to serving the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Likewise, he should approach his own wife during her fertile period;
being one who acts for the benefit of all the world, auspiciousness, and pleasant speech [are also required]. (NarP 1.24.28)
Absence of exertion, delight in the mind, forbearance, and lack of excessive pride—
these have been proclaimed by the sages as common to all social classes.
And all attain the state of a sage through the performance of duties appropriate to their own stage of life;
however, O twice-born one, in times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa may resort to the conduct of a Kṣatriya.
Even a Kṣatriya may resort to the livelihood of a Vaiśya in times of distress; however, a twice-born man must never resort to the livelihood of a Śūdra, even in extreme distress.
O best of sages, if a foolish twice-born man should resort to such [a practice], he would then become a Cāṇḍāla; this applies to the three castes: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Four stages of life have been declared; a fifth does not exist, O best of beings: the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant.
Through these four stages of life, the supreme Dharma is accomplished;
O best of Brahmins, Viṣṇu is pleased with one whose self is devoted to the yoga of action.
For one whose mind is free from longing and tranquil, who is devoted to his own duty,
he then goes to the supreme state from which he does not return again.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Right Conduct," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannārāyaṇa Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
I shall now specifically declare the rules for the conduct of the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas).
Listen to that, O best of sages, with an attentive mind.
He who abandons his own duty and practices the duty of another should be known as a heretic, excluded from all righteous laws.
The sacraments, beginning with the rite of conception, should be performed according to the rules of mantra;
for women, they should be performed at the proper times and according to the prescribed rites, but without the use of mantras.
The parting of the hair (sīmantakarma) is recommended for the first time in the fourth month;
one may also have it performed in the sixth, the seventh, or even the eighth month.
When a son is born, the father, having bathed with his clothes on, should perform the birth-rite (jātakarman) and the Nāndīśrāddha,
preceded by the recitation of the Svasti-vācana.
One may perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha with gold or even silver;
however, he who performs it with ordinary food becomes equal to a Caṇḍāla.
Having performed the *abhyudayika* śrāddha at the end of the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the father, remaining silent, should perform the naming ceremony for his son according to the prescribed rule.
O best of Brahmins, one should not give a name that is indistinct, devoid of meaning, excessively long, composed of too many syllables, or likewise contains irregular phonemes.
In the third year, or in the fifth, sixth,
seventh, or even eighth year, one should perform the tonsure ceremony according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.

If, due to the influence of fate, the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony (*garbhādhāna*) have been neglected, a *pādakṛcchra* penance must indeed be performed; for the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), one should prescribe half of that.
The initiation (*upanayana*) of a young student (*baṭuka*) should take place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth];
they also consider the period up until the sixteenth year to be a secondary time for it.
The wise declare that for a Kṣatriya, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) takes place in the eleventh year from conception, with the time limit extending until the twenty-second year.
The initiation for all [castes] is declared to take place in the twelfth year from conception;
the wise say that it may extend up to the twenty-fourth year as a secondary option.
If a twice-born man should transgress this time-limit, one should know him to have fallen from the Sāvitrī; one must never speak with him.
O Brahmin, if the primary time for the initiation (*upanayana*) of a twice-born has passed,
he should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve years, followed by a *cāndrāyaṇa*,
and having performed two *sāṃtapana* penances, he may then carry out the rite.
One should know that if it falls otherwise, even the performer becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
The girdle of a Brahmin is to be known as made of muñja grass, while that of a Kṣatriya is a bowstring.

The skin of the sheep (*āvī*) is to be known as that of the Vaiśya; likewise, listen to what is prescribed for the deer-skin: the skin of the black antelope (*aiṇeya*) for the Brāhmaṇa, and the skin of the Ruru deer (*raurava*) for the Kṣatriya. (NarP 1.25.17)

The staff of a Vaiśya should be known to be made of Āmra wood; I shall now describe the appropriate punishments in their proper order: for a Brāhmaṇa a staff of Palāśa is prescribed, and likewise for a king (Kṣatriya) one of Udumbara.
The staff of a Vaiśya should be known as made of Bilva wood; hear from me its dimensions:
that of a Brāhmaṇa should reach the hair, and that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead.
The wise have declared that the staff of a Vaiśya should reach the tip of his nose;
likewise, I shall describe the garments for the Brāhmaṇas and the others in their proper order.
O Brahmin, the dyed garments prescribed for a twice-born man who has been initiated are saffron, madder-red, and turmeric-yellow; he should be devoted to the service of his guru.
Until the completion of his study of the Vedas, the religious student (brahmacārī) shall dwell in the house of his teacher;
he should bathe in the morning and carry fuel-sticks, kuśa grass, fruits, and other such items.
O Lord of Sages, O best of Munis, one should daily bring for the sake of the Guru the sacred thread, the deerskin, and the staff, every single morning.
If [the manuscript] is lost or damaged, one should take a new [copy] from the oral tradition and cast the damaged one into water;
they say that the livelihood of a student of sacred knowledge (varṇin) should consist solely of food obtained through alms.
With his senses restrained, he should fetch alms from the house of a Vedic scholar;
for a Brāhmaṇa, the request should begin with "bhavat" (be so pleased), and for a king, it should have "bhavat" in the middle.
The speech regarding the collection of alms was declared by Bhava for the sake of the people;
having conquered his senses, he performed the fire-ritual every evening and morning according to custom.
A student (brahmacārī) should perform daily the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña) and the libation (tarpaṇa);
one who neglects the fire-ritual (agnikārya) is declared by the wise to be fallen.
One who is devoid of the Brahmayajña is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin;
he should perform the worship of the deities immediately following service to his guru.
He should always eat food obtained as alms, never eating the food of a single person;
having conquered his senses, he should bring alms from the houses of blameless Brahmins.
Having offered it to the guru, he should eat while restraining his speech, following the guru’s permission;
[he should likewise avoid] honey, women, meat, salt, betel, and the cleansing of the teeth.
One should avoid eating leftovers, sleeping during the day, as well as sandals, perfumes, garlands, and ointments. (NarP 1.25.31)
One should avoid sporting in water, as well as dancing, singing, and instrumental music; likewise, one should avoid slander, causing distress, idle chatter, and the application of collyrium.
One should avoid association with heretics and contact with Śūdras;
one should be habitually inclined to offer salutations to elders in the proper order.
There are three types of elders: those advanced in knowledge, those advanced in austerity, and those advanced in age;
that teacher who wards off internal and external sufferings is the true guru.
According to the instruction of the Vedic scriptures, one should first offer salutation to him;
for at the time of salutation, a twice-born man should indeed say, "I am so-and-so."
A Brahmin should never, under any circumstances, salute Kṣatriyas and others who are atheists, who have transgressed the bounds of conduct, who are outcasts, or who act as priests for a village.
One should never salute a thief, a gambler,
a heretic, an outcast, one who has lost his caste, nor one who lives by the stars or astrology.
Likewise, one should never offer salutation to an outcaste,
nor to one who is insane, deceitful, fraudulent, running, or impure.
One should not offer salutations to one who has anointed their head while reciting prayers, nor to one who is quarrelsome, fickle, vomiting, or standing in the middle of water. (NarP 1.25.39)

One should not salute a woman carrying alms-food while she is lying down, nor one who has killed her husband, one who is menstruating, an adulteress, a woman who has recently given birth, or one who has caused an abortion.
One should never salute a woman who has committed a sin against her husband, nor one who is fierce (caṇḍī),
whether in an assembly, in a sacrificial hall, or even in temples dedicated to the gods.
Indeed, each individual act of salutation destroys previously accumulated merit, as well as ancestral rites, vows, charity, and the worship of deities. (NarP 1.25.42)

One should not offer salutation to one who is performing a sacrifice or a libation; likewise, one should not respond with a salutation to one who, having been saluted, does not return the greeting. (NarP 1.25.43)
He should not be saluted; he is to be known as being just like a Śūdra.
Having washed his feet and sipped water, he should always remain facing his teacher.
Having clasped his feet, the discerning student should study [the Veda] on the Aṣṭakā days, on the fourteenth day, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, and likewise on the Parvan days.
On the twelfth day of the month of Śravaṇa, as well as on the second day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should honor the best of Brahmins at Mahābharaṇya.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, on the ninth day of Āśvina, when the sun is surrounded by a halo, or when a learned Vedic scholar has arrived at one's house— NarP_1,25.47.
Likewise when a Brahmin has been bound, during a great quarrel,
at twilight, when clouds are thundering, or during unseasonable rain.

O Brahmin, likewise when there is the falling of meteors and thunderbolts, when a brahmin has been insulted, O divine sage, and on the anniversaries of Manu and the other progenitors, as well as on all four anniversaries of the Yugas; NarP_1,25.49 //

No twice-born man who is eager for the fruits of all his actions should study on the third day of the bright fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, nor on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada. (NarP 1.25.50)
The ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika and the fifteenth lunar day in Māgha—
these are declared to be the beginnings of the Yugas (yugādi), which cause what is given to be inexhaustible.
I shall also proclaim Manu and the others; listen with a well-composed mind:
the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika joined with the asterism Akṣa (Aśvinī), and the twelfth day of the bright fortnight [in the same month]. NarP_1,25.52 //
The third day of the month of Caitra, as well as that of Bhādrapada;
the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and the auspicious fifth day of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha,
the new moon of Phālguna, and the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa.
The fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha are declared to be the beginnings of the Manvantaras; gifts given on these occasions yield inexhaustible merit.
The twice-born should perform the śrāddha on the anniversaries of the Manvantaras and the Yugas,
as well as when invited to a śrāddha or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
O Sage, one should never study during either of the two solstices, nor during an earthquake, nor when the throat is constricted, nor on an ill-omened day.
O Nārada, for all such times of non-study,
the progeny, wisdom, fame, and fortune of those utterly deluded who nevertheless study [the Vedas] are destroyed.
Yama himself cuts short one's lifespan, strength, and health;
know that he who studies on a day forbidden for study is a slayer of Brahman.
One should not converse with that outcaste, nor should one dwell together with him;
O Nārada, some say this applies to the Kuṇḍa and Golaka, as well as to those who are mentally deficient and the like.
And some say that the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) may be performed for his sons and others;
however, he who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits, [is at fault]. (NarP 1.25.61)
He should be known as equal to a Śūdra; he is a guest dear to hell.
A Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas may nevertheless adopt right conduct.
He does not obtain the fruit of his conduct; he is just like a Śūdra.
This applies to the obligatory, the occasional, the optional, and whatever other Vedic ritual action there may be.
For a Brahmin who has not studied, everything becomes fruitless;
Viṣṇu, who consists of the Śabdabrahman, is the Veda itself, visibly borne upon the tongue.
Then, that Brahmin who studies the Vedas shall obtain all his desires.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Duties such as Vedic Study within the Dharmas of the Castes and Stages of Life," in the first quarter of the Pūrvabhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
Until the completion of the acquisition of the Vedas, one must remain disciplined in service to the guru.
Then, having been authorized by him, he should perform the formal taking possession of the sacred fire.
Having studied the Vedas, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Vedāṅgas, O twice-born one,
and having given the teacher his fee, he may enter the householder stage of life.
A twice-born man should marry a maiden who is endowed with beauty and charm, possessed of virtues, born of a noble family, of excellent character, and a follower of dharma.
A wise twice-born man may marry a maiden who is fifth in descent from his mother and likewise fifth from his father; otherwise, he becomes one who violates the bed of his guru.
A wise man should not marry a woman who is diseased, who has round eyes, who is born into a family of disease, who has excessive hair, no hair, or sparse hair, or who is talkative.

A wise man should not marry one who is prone to anger, nor one who is stunted, nor one with a long body, nor one who is deformed, nor one with missing or extra limbs, nor one who is insane, nor one who is malicious.
One should not marry a woman who has thick ankles, long shanks, a masculine build, or who possesses the characteristics of a beard, nor one who is hunchbacked.
One should not marry a woman who laughs excessively for no reason, who always dwells in another's house, who is quarrelsome, fickle, or cruel. (NarP 1.26.8)
A wise man should never marry a woman who eats excessively, has protruding teeth, thick lips, a gurgling voice,
is extremely dark, or is red-complexioned and deceitful.

One should not marry a woman who is habitually weeping, pale in complexion, or contemptible; nor one afflicted by palpitations, labored breathing, and the like, or one who is excessively prone to sleep.
A wise man should not marry a woman who speaks what is useless, who is devoted to the hatred of the world, who delights in slandering others, or who is a thief.
A wise man should by no means marry a woman with a long nose, one who is deceitful, one whose body is adorned [only for show], one who is arrogant, or one who behaves like a heron.
If one should marry a girl who, due to her childhood, does not understand her own nature,
he should abandon her entirely once he recognizes that she possesses the qualities of eloquence and maturity.
A woman who is always harsh toward her husband and sons,
and who is entirely devoted to others, he should abandon in every way.
O best of sages, marriages are to be known as eightfold, beginning with the Brāhma;
each preceding one is to be considered superior, and in the absence of the former, the latter is to be accepted.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura;
the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca is considered the eighth.
O Brahmin, the best of the twice-born is indeed eligible for marriage through the Brāhma rite, or through the Daiva rite;
some, however, declare the Ārṣa rite as well.
O Brahmin, the five marriages beginning with the Prājāpatya are not censured;
however, in the absence of the former, a wise man should indeed perform the latter.
He should wear two sacred threads along with an upper garment,
as well as golden earrings and a pair of washed clothes.
With his limbs smeared with unguents, having trimmed his hair and nails, and being pure,
he should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water.
One who is pleasing to behold should wear a stainless turban, a parasol, sandals, and shoes, as well as flowers, garlands, and fragrant scents.
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas and should conduct oneself according to traditional custom;
one should never eat the food of others and should avoid speaking ill of others.
One should not step with one foot upon the other, nor should one cross over what has been left as food scraps.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together.

A twice-born man should not pass around a venerable object or a temple with his right side turned away (apasavya) during the worship of deities, the rinsing of the mouth, bathing, vows, śrāddha rites, and other such ceremonies. (NarP 1.26.24)
One should not have disheveled hair, nor likewise wear only a single garment;
one should not mount a camel vehicle and should avoid harsh speech.
A Brahmin should not approach another’s wife, should avoid backbiting,
and should not pass to the left of cows, sacred trees, fire, or mountains.
One should avoid a crossroads, a sacred tree, a natural pool, and likewise a king;
one should also avoid envy, malice, and sleeping during the day.
One should not speak of the sins of others, nor should one proclaim one's own merit;
one must strictly conceal one's own name, one's birth star, and one's pride.
A twice-born man should not dwell with wicked people, nor should he listen to that which is contrary to the scriptures; furthermore, he should take no delight in liquor, gambling, or singing.
Having touched a moist bone, as well as food-leavings, a Śūdra, an outcaste (patita), a snake, or a dog, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Having touched a funeral pyre, the wood for a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, an outcaste,
or a temple-priest (devalaka), one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
The shadow of a lamp, a bed, or a body; the water from a sieve;
a goat, a sheep, or a cat; and dust—these may take away one's good fortune. (NarP 1.26.32)
One should avoid from afar the wind from a winnowing basket, the smoke from a funeral pyre, eating the food of a Śūdra, and association with the husband of a Śūdra woman.
One should always completely avoid reflecting on the meaning of false scriptures, biting one's nails or hair, and likewise sleeping naked.
One should not smear the body with oil remaining from anointing the head;
one should not eat impure betel leaf, nor should one awaken a sleeping person.
One who is impure should not tend the sacred fire, nor worship the gurus or deities;
nor should one drink water with only the left hand or with the mouth alone.
O Lord of Sages, one should not step on the shadow of the guru, nor should one disobey his command;
likewise, one should not revile yogis, brahmins, those observing vows, or ascetics.
A twice-born man should never speak of the vital secrets of others;
and on the new moon and full moon days, he should perform the sacrifice according to the prescribed rule.
The twice-born must perform the *upāsana* sacrifice both morning and evening;
one who abandons the *upāsana* is called a drinker of liquor by the wise. (NarP 1.26.39)
A twice-born householder should perform the Śrāddha rite during the solstices, at the equinoxes, on all four Yugādi days, on the new moon day, and during the fortnight of the ancestors (Pretapakṣa).
O Nārada, on the days sacred to Manu and others, on the clay-heating days, on the Aṣṭakās, and when the new grain has arrived,
a householder should perform the Śrāddha.
When a learned Vedic scholar arrives at his house, during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
or at sacred sites and holy places, a householder should perform a śrāddha ceremony.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations for the ancestors—
all these become fruitless if performed without the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
Some do not accept the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) or Tulasī at a Śrāddha ceremony;
therefore, such futile practice should be abandoned by twice-born men who seek their own welfare.
These and other such duties, impelled by the path of the Smṛti, should be performed correctly by the twice-born; they bestow the fruits of all actions.
Viṣṇu is pleased with those who are always devoted to his service;
O best of the twice-born, when Viṣṇu has attained a state of grace, what is there that cannot be accomplished?
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Study of the Vedas and Other Duties of the Householder," in the first quarter of the Pūrvabhāga of the Śrī Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said: O best of sages, I shall now describe the conduct of the householder.
By reciting this, all sins are destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, O Brahmin, and having arranged his hair, he should reflect upon his livelihood that does not conflict with the goals of human existence.
During the day and at the twilights, with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) placed over the ear, one should void urine and feces facing north; however, if it is at night, one should face south.
Having covered his head with a cloth and having concealed the earth with grass,
the twice-born man should carry a single piece of wood in his hand while observing silence.
On a path, in a cow-pen, on the bank of a river, near a pond or a house,
likewise in the shade of a tree, in a wilderness, or in the vicinity of fire.
In a temple, as well as in a garden, on ploughed ground, at a crossroads, in the presence of Brahmins, and likewise in the vicinity of cows, gurus, and women; NarP_1,27.6 //
One should not void excrement or urine in husks, charcoal, or potsherds, nor likewise in the midst of water, or in other such places.
Effort must always be made regarding purity; the twice-born is said to have purity as his very root.
For one devoid of pure conduct, every ritual action is fruitless.
Purity is said to be twofold:
external and internal; external purification is achieved through earth and water, while internal purity is the purification of one's disposition.
Having held his penis and stood up, he should take earth for the purpose of purification;
however, he should not take earth dug up by mice or the like, nor that which has been turned over by a plow.
One should not fetch even earth from ponds, wells, or tanks;
rather, one should perform purification with effort by taking auspicious earth.
One application of earth should be applied to the penis, or three to the two testicles;
the wise declare this to be the purification for the voiding of urine.
One application of clay should be applied to the penis, five to the anus, ten to both hands, six to the feet, and three to each foot; thus the applications of clay should be given separately.
This is the purification for the voiding of excrement, intended to remove odor and residue;
this same purification for a householder is doubled for students of sacred knowledge.
O best of sages, for forest-dwellers it is threefold, and for ascetics it is fourfold; in their own place, purification is complete, but on the road it is half, O most excellent sage.
There is no restrictive rule for one who is ill, and likewise for one in great distress;
a wise person should perform purification that removes odors and stains.
For women who have not been initiated, purification lasts until the removal of odor and stain;
for all those established in vows, however, purity is prescribed to be like that of an ascetic.
O Lord of Men, this very same rule is declared for widows as well;
having thus performed the purification, one should thereafter remain well-composed.
Facing either east or north, with his senses controlled, he should sip water three or four times—water that is free from odor, foam, and the like. (NarP 1.27.19)
O best of men, one should wipe the cheeks twice with the palm and the lips with the palm;
one should touch the two nostrils using the combination of the index finger and the thumb.
With the thumb and ring finger, the twice-born should touch his eyes and ears respectively; with the application of the little finger and the thumb, he should touch the region of the navel.
The wise man should touch his chest with the palms and his head with the tips of the fingers; he should also touch his shoulders either with the palms or with the tips of the fingers.
Having thus sipped water, O best of Brahmins, and attained unsurpassed purity,
he should then chew a tooth-stick made from a recommended tree, complete with its bark.
Having washed the twigs of the bilva, āsana, apāmārga, nimba, mārkava, and other trees with water, they should also be consecrated with the mantra.
O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us long life, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence.
A Brahmin should eat ten finger-breadths in thickness, equal to the tip of the little finger;
a Kṣatriya, nine finger-breadths; and a Vaiśya, eight finger-breadths in measure. (NarP 1.27.26)
O Lord of Sages, a Śūdra [should use wood] measuring four finger-breadths, and a woman likewise;
in the absence of sacrificial wood, one should perform the rite with twelve mouthfuls of water.
The purification of the mouth should be performed with blades of grass and leaves;
taking them with the left hand, one should cleanse [the teeth] with the left incisor.
Having rubbed his teeth with a tooth-stick and washed them,
he should then scrape his tongue with those two blades, while keeping his senses under control.
Having washed it, he should throw it far away; then, having sipped water again as before, he should perform his bath in a pure body of water such as a river.
Having washed the bank and arranged the darbha grass, he should enter the water;
having bowed there to the sacred fords (tīrthas), he should invoke them from the solar disc.
O Viriñca, having prepared a maṇḍala with perfumes and other offerings and meditated upon the god Janārdana,
one should bathe while recollecting the meritorious mantras and sacred fords.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters! NarP_1,27.33 //
May the holy sites beginning with Puṣkara, as well as the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā,
O highly fortunate ones, always come to me at the time of my bath.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā,
and the city of Dvārāvatī should be known as the seven sacred abodes that bestow liberation.
Then, having recited the *adhamarṣaṇa* mantra and being immersed in the water as much as he desires,
and having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) which is a limb of the bath, he should sip water (*ācamya*) and offer the *arghya* with devotion.
Then, O Nārada, having meditated upon the Sun and emerged from the water,
he put on a fresh, washed garment and fastened the second one around him.

Having sat down upon a seat of kusha grass, O Brahmin, the twice-born man should commence the twilight rites; facing the northeast and having sipped water with the Gayatri mantra, he should perform the ritual.
Having consecrated the water with the mantra "Ṛtam," the wise man should again meditate upon its meaning;
then, having enveloped himself with that water and sprinkled it over himself.
Having made the resolve at the end of the *praṇava*, while recollecting the sages, meters, and deities,
he should sprinkle his head with the six *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) separately on the hands and the limbs;
having placed the Tāra at the heart, he should then place Bhūḥ upon the head.
One should place *bhuvaḥ* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *svaḥ* at the throat (*kavaca*), *bhūrbhuvaḥ* at the two eyes,
and likewise *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ* as the weapon (*astra*) mantra in the directions, while performing three claps of the hands (*tālatraya*).
Then, in the morning, he should invoke Sandhyā seated upon a lotus:
"Come, O boon-granting goddess, you who are three-syllabled and a speaker of Brahman! (NarP 1.27.43)
O Gāyatrī, mother of the meters, born from the womb of Brahman, homage be to you!
At midday, you are mounted upon a bull and clothed in white garments.
One should invoke Sāvitrī, who has Rudra as her source and is the proclaimer of Rudra;
at evening, however, she is mounted upon Garuḍa and clothed in yellow garments.
One should invoke Sarasvatī, whose source is Viṣṇu and who proclaims Viṣṇu,
while reciting the syllable Om, the Vyāhṛtis, and the three-footed Gāyatrī.
Having filled the head and the crest-lock and having constricted them,
one should exhale the air through the left middle finger in sequence during the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).

Thereafter, one should sip water twice: in the morning with the mantra "The Sun and... (Prātaḥ sūryaśca me), and at midday with "May the Waters Purify... (Āpaḥ punantu); in the evening, one should do so with "Agni and... (Sāyam agniśca me).
Then one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having recited "sumitriyā naḥ," one should touch the water to the nose.
Having driven away the host of enemies, one should strike Drupada on the head; and by means of this, having performed the *adhamarṣaṇa* rite, one establishes both *ṛta* and *satya*.
Moving within by means of the mantra, one should drink water only once;
thereafter, one should offer perfume, flowers, and a handful of water to the Sun according to the prescribed rule.
O celestial sage, having cast [the water], one should stand before the Sun with hands joined in the *svastika* gesture;
with arms raised and then lowered, respectively, during the three periods beginning with dawn.
One should mutter this triad— "ud u tyam," "citraṃ," and "taccakṣuḥ"—
as well as other mantras dedicated to the Sun, Śiva, and Viṣṇu, O Nārada.
One should pray with the mantra "Thou art splendor, thou art Gāyatrī" to the greatness of Savitṛ;
then, having repeated the limbs three times, one should meditate upon the Śaktis as being of that same nature.

May Gāyatrī— the daughter who is the personification of the Rigveda, whose face possesses the luster of the rising moon, who holds the water-pot, the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), and the spoon (*sruva*) in her hands, who wears a rosary of beads on her four faces as Brahmā, who is worshipped with the tinkling sound of gems during the sport of riding the swan, and who is adorned with ornaments— always grant us the abundance of prosperity.

May Rudrāṇī, possessed of fresh youth, three-eyed, clad in tiger-skin garments, and adorned with a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a garland, a crest-lock, a rosary, and bracelets, grant us the glory of fearlessness.

May Sāvitrī, whose form is the Yajurveda, be meditated upon—she who rides a bull, has a white body, and joyfully bears on her head a mass of matted hair shining like a streak of lightning and a crescent moon.
And let that blessed Sarasvatī be meditated upon—clad in yellow garments, dark-complexioned with a dark body, her limbs radiant above the waist, the consort of Viṣṇu;
seated upon Garuḍa, resplendent with ornaments such as jeweled anklets, armlets, and necklaces, and holding in her hands the conch, discus, mace, and lotus—may she grant us prosperity. (NarP 1.27.57)
Having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] while standing in the morning and at midday;
likewise, seated in the evening, with devotion and a mind focused upon that.
The goddess [Gāyatrī], which has a thousand as its maximum, a hundred as its middle, and ten as its minimum;
which consists of three feet, is endowed with the *praṇava*, and proceeds from the sequence of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.

O Sage, for one observing a vow or for an ascetic, the recitation should consist of the six-syllable mantra or the *saṃpuṭa* form; for a householder, it should be the seven-syllable mantra—such is the manner of recitation.
Then, having recited [the mantra] according to one's ability and having offered it to Savitṛ,
one should cast two handfuls of water toward Gāyatrī and Savitṛ with joined palms.
Then, having dismissed her with the mantra "O Brahmin woman, go northward," she was respectfully sent forth by Hari, who is the Lord of Brahmā.
Having paid homage with palms joined in reverence to these and to the deities of the directions,
he should perform his subsequent duties, beginning with the morning rites, according to the prescribed rules.
O divine sage, a householder should perform his bath in the morning and at midday; a forest-dweller should do so as well, while an ascetic should bathe three times a day.

O Lord of Sages, for those afflicted by diseases and the like, as well as for travelers, the Brahma-yajña is prescribed to be performed only once; thereafter, with darbha grass in hand, one should perform it.
If the duties prescribed for the day have been left undone through negligence,
one should perform them in their proper order during the first watch of the night.
That twice-born man who, being of deceitful intellect, does not worship at the twilights when no calamity exists,
should indeed be known as a heretic, excluded from all dharma.
But he who, being skilled in deceptive reasoning, abandons the rites of twilight worship and the like— one should know him to be the foremost among great sinners.
Those twice-born ones who speak [thus] while having abandoned the twilight prayers and other rites go to terrible hells for as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist.
Then he should perform the worship of the gods and the Vaiśvadeva offering according to the rules;
therein, he should duly honor a guest who has arrived with food and other offerings.
But when they have arrived, one should speak sweet words to them;
one should honor them with water, food, bulbs, and roots, or by the gift of a house.
When a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he transfers his own misdeeds to that person and departs taking away their merit.
They say that a guest who has arrived from another village, whose lineage and name are unknown, is a Vipaschit; one should honor him as if he were Viṣṇu.
Every day, he should satisfy one resident of his own village who is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) and devoted to Viṣṇu, with food and other offerings, intending it for his ancestors.
One who abandons the five sacrifices is called a "Brahma-eater" by the wise;
therefore, one should perform the five sacrifices every day with great effort.
The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to all beings, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to Brahman— these are declared to be the five sacrifices.
Accompanied by his servants, friends, and others, he himself should eat while maintaining silence;
he should partake of the food offered by the twice-born and never reject the vessel.
Having placed his feet upon his own breath (his lap) and having put on half a garment,
one who eats what has been vomited by the mouth is called a drinker of liquor by the wise.

One who eats again after having already eaten half [his meal], and one who eats sweetmeats and fruits [at improper times], as well as one who consumes salt directly, is said to be a consumer of cow-flesh. (NarP 1.27.79)
During the *apośāna* rite, the sipping of water (*ācamana*), and while consuming foodstuffs today, a twice-born brāhmaṇa should not make a sound; by doing so, he becomes a denizen of hell.
One should eat wholesome food while restrained in speech, not scattering the food about;
before eating, one should perform the *apośāna* rite with the mantra: "Thou art the under-layer of nectar. (NarP 1.27.81)
"Thou art the covering of nectar"—with these words, one should drink water once at the end of the meal;
having offered the oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇa) and others, and having sipped water, one should proceed with the meal. (NarP 1.27.82)
Then, O best of Brahmins, having sipped water for purification, one should be intent on reflecting upon the scriptures,
even at night, according to one's ability, through [moderation in] lying down, sitting, and eating.
O Sage, a householder should thus perform good conduct every day;
when he abandons such conduct, then he becomes one who requires expiation.
O best of men, seeing his own body defiled by Pālita and the others,
he should either entrust his wife to his sons and go to the forest alone, or go together with her.
He should bathe at the three periods of the day, wear his nails, beard, and matted hair long,
sleep on the ground, remain celibate, and be devoted to the five great sacrifices.
Constantly subsisting on fruits and roots, likewise devoted to the study of the Vedas,
compassionate toward all beings, and having Nārāyaṇa as his supreme refuge.
One should avoid flowers and fruits grown in villages;
one should eat only eight mouthfuls and should not eat at night.
One in the stage of life of a forest hermit (vānaprastha) should completely avoid oil,
as well as sexual intercourse, sleep, and likewise idleness.
The forest-dweller should constantly meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands,
and he should perform austerities such as the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should endure cold, heat, and the like, and always attend to the sacred fire, once detachment has arisen toward all worldly objects in the mind. (NarP 1.27.91)
At that very time, O Brahmin, he should renounce; otherwise, he would become fallen.
He should be devoted to the study of Vedanta, peaceful, self-controlled, and one who has conquered his senses.
One should always be free from aversion, free from egoism, and free from the sense of "mine," endowed with virtues such as tranquility, and devoid of desire and anger.
A twice-born ascetic should be either naked or wear a worn-out loincloth, and he should have a shaven head;
he should be impartial toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor.
A renunciant should dwell for one night in a village and likewise for three nights in a city;
he should always subsist on alms and must not eat the food of a single person.
A mendicant should wander for alms at the house of an irreproachable twice-born man who has no embers left in his fire, who has finished his meal, and who is free from disputes.
One who bathes at the three periods of the day, is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa,
and has conquered his self and subdued his senses, should constantly recite the Praṇava.
If an ascetic should ever become greedy and eat food from only one house,
no atonement for him is seen, even through ten thousand penances.
O Brahmin, if an ascetic, out of greed, becomes intent on nourishing his own body,
he should be known as equal to a Caṇḍāla, despised by those of all castes and stages of life.
One should contemplate the Self as the divine Nārāyaṇa, who is free from disease,
beyond dualities, devoid of possessiveness, peaceful, transcending illusion, and free from envy.
It is imperishable and complete, whose singular form is eternal bliss;
it is the stainless nature of knowledge, the supreme, eternal light.
One should meditate upon the Self, which is changeless, without beginning or end, the cause of the consciousness of the universe, devoid of qualities, supreme, and higher than the highest.
One who has conquered the senses should recite the sentences of the Upaniṣads, contemplate the meanings of the Vedānta, and always meditate upon the thousand-headed God.
Thus, the ascetic who is devoted to meditation and free from envy attains supreme bliss, the eternal, highest light.
The twice-born who thus performs the duties of the stages of life (āśrama) in their proper sequence goes to the supreme abode, having reached which he does not grieve.
Those who are devoted to the conduct of their caste and stage of life, who are free from all sins,
and who are intent upon Nārāyaṇa, go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Householder, Forest-Dweller, and Renunciant within Good Conduct," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
"Listen, O tiger among sages, to the supreme procedure for the Śrāddha."
Having heard which, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
On the day before the anniversary of the death, having bathed and observed a single meal,
he should sleep on the ground, remain celibate, and invite Brahmins for the night.
The performer of a śrāddha should avoid brushing the teeth, chewing betel, anointing with oil, sexual intercourse, medicinal herbs, and the food of others. (NarP 1.28.3)

One who performs a *śrāddha* and one who partakes in it should likewise avoid traveling on a journey, quarreling, anger, sexual intercourse, carrying a burden, and sleeping during the day. (NarP 1.28.4)
If one who has been invited to a *śrāddha* engages in sexual intercourse, he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and goes to hell as well. (NarP 1.28.5)
At a śrāddha ceremony, one should engage a brahmin who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), devoted to Viṣṇu,
steadfast in his own conduct, tranquil, and born of a noble family.
Free from passion and hatred, skilled in the meaning of the Purāṇas,
knowing the Trimadhu and Trisuparṇa mantras, and supremely compassionate toward all living beings.
He was devoted to the worship of the gods, proficient in the principles of mindfulness,
endowed with the truth of Vedānta, and dedicated to the welfare of all the world.
One who is grateful, endowed with virtues, devoted to serving his teacher,
intent on instructing others, and likewise engaged in the exposition of the true scriptures.
O Lord of Sages, these Brahmins indeed should be appointed at a śrāddha;
I shall now describe those who are to be avoided at a śrāddha—listen to them with full attention. (NarP 1.28.10)
One with deficient limbs, one with extra limbs, a miser, as well as one who is diseased, a leper, one with deformed nails, one with long ears, and one who has broken his vows; NarP_1,28.11 //
One who lives by reciting the names of constellations, a cremator of corpses, a proponent of false doctrines, a reviler, and likewise a wicked temple-priest; NarP_1,28.12 //
One who is a reviler, intolerant, a rogue, and likewise a village priest; one who is devoted to false scriptures and one who subsists on the food of others.
One who is the son of a *vṛṣalī*, a nourisher of a *vṛṣalī*, and indeed the husband of a *vṛṣalī*;
likewise, a *kuṇḍa* and a *golaka*, as well as one who performs sacrifices for those for whom it is forbidden to sacrifice.
He is a hypocrite in conduct, a shaven-headed mendicant in vain, intent upon the wives and wealth of others,
devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, and turned away from devotion to Śiva.
Those who sell the Vedas, as well as those who sell their vows, those who sell the Smṛtis, and likewise those who sell the mantras; NarP_1,28.16 //
Singers, authors of poetry, those who subsist on medical treatises, one intent on reviling the Vedas, and one who sets fire to villages or market-towns; NarP_1,28.17 //
Likewise, one who is excessively lustful, a seller of liquids,
and one devoted to fraudulent schemes should be avoided with great effort at a śrāddha.
One should invite [the Brahmins] either on the previous day or on that very day;
the invited Brahmin should be a celibate student who has conquered his senses.
O best of beings, at a *śrāddha*, one should grant an invitation and show favor;
with *darbha* grass in hand and senses subdued, one should invite a wise twice-born man. (NarP 1.28.20)
Then, having risen at dawn and completed his morning rites,
the wise man should perform the śrāddha ceremony at the time known as kutapa.
When the sun begins to grow dim at the eighth period of the day, that time is called *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.
The afternoon was designated as the time for the ancestors by the Self-Existent One;
therefore, the oblation to the ancestors (kavya) must be offered at that very time by the best of the twice-born.
O best of sages, that poetic composition which is offered with material gifts at an improper time should be known as belonging to the Rākṣasas; it does not reach the ancestors.
But if a poem is presented in the evening, it becomes demonic;
the giver falls into hell, and the consumer likewise goes to hell. (NarP 1.28.25)
O Brahmin, if the duration of the lunar day (tithi) on the anniversary of death should measure only one daṇḍa,
the wise man should perform the śrāddha when it occurs within the afternoon (aparāhṇa).

If the lunar day of the anniversary of death falls within two afternoons, it should be observed on the earlier one when there is a decrease; likewise, when there is an increase, it should be performed on the later one.
If a lunar day (tithi) extends into the evening on the second of two consecutive days,
that later one is renowned as the correct time for the recitation of poetry.

O Lord of Sages, some say that the gift of poetry should be made on the preceding day when two muhūrtas remain; however, this opinion is not held by everyone regarding the giving of poetry. (NarP 1.28.29)
O best of the twice-born, when those invited Brahmins have assembled,
he whose soul has been purified by penance should seek their permission.
Having been duly authorized for the sake of the *śrāddha*, he should again invite Brahmins—
two for the sake of the Viśvedevas and three for the sake of the ancestors, according to the rule.
For the sake of the deities and for the sake of the ancestors, he should invite one person for each;
being duly authorized, he should cause two mandalas to be prepared for the purpose of the śrāddha.
The square [mound] belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, the triangle to the Kṣatriya;
the circle should be known as that of the Vaiśya, while for the Śūdra there should be mere sprinkling with water.
In the absence of Brāhmaṇas, however, one may appoint a brother or even a son, or even oneself; but one must not appoint a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Vedas.

Having washed the feet of the Brahmins and made them perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should seat them and perform their worship according to the rules, while remembering the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
In the midst of the Brahmins and likewise at the doorway,
the performer should scatter sesame seeds while reciting the verse beginning with "apahatāḥ."
Having said, "This is the seat for the Viśvedevas," one should offer barley and blades of *darbha* grass,
and furthermore, one should grant the invitation (*kṣaṇa*) for the gods.
In the case of the "imperishable seat" (akṣayyāsana), the genitive case is prescribed; for the invocation (āvāhana), the accusative is traditionally taught.
In the giving of food (annadāna), the dative should be used; the remaining cases are traditionally taught as being used in the sense of the compound (saṃpud).
Having placed two vessels provided with blades of darbha grass,
he should then pour water into those vessels with the verse "śanno devī".

Having scattered barley with the words "Thou art barley," and having offered fragrant flowers while remaining silent, he should then invoke the gods with the verse beginning "The All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ)."
With the mantra "yā divyā," one should, being composed, offer the arghya;
thereafter, one should worship with perfumes, leaves, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Having been authorized by the gods, he should likewise worship the hosts of ancestors;
with darbha grass mixed with sesame seeds, he should always provide them with a seat.
The twice-born should place three vessels for the *arghya* offering as before;
having poured water with the verse "śanno devīḥ," he should scatter sesame seeds with the mantra "tilosi. (NarP 1.28.43)
Having invoked the ancestors with the two verses beginning with "uśantaḥ," the wise man, being composed,
should offer the arghya water as before with the mantra "yā divyāḥ."
O best of men, one should worship according to one's means with perfumes, leaves, flowers, incense, lamps, garments, and ornaments. (NarP 1.28.45)
Then, having taken the first portion of food mixed with ghee, the wise man,
saying "I shall offer this into the fire," should seek permission from them.
O Sage, even when unasked, Brāhmaṇas should say, "I shall do it," or "I will have it done";
they should likewise say, "Do it," "Let it be done," or simply "Do so."
Having established the domestic fire according to the procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, he should utter: "Svadhā! Adoration to Sāma and Pitṛmat! (NarP 1.28.48).
Or here, the wise man should offer oblations like those in the Pitṛyajña, either with the mantra "To Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā! Obeisance! or ending with "svāhā. (NarP 1.28.49)
By these two oblations alone, the satisfaction of the ancestors becomes inexhaustible;
however, in the absence of fire, the offering is prescribed to be made into the hand of a Brahmin.
O twice-born one, one should perform [the rite] according to custom, either with the hand or with fire;
for when the Pārvaṇa rite has arrived, the fire should not be kept at a distance.
Having established the fire and performed the necessary rites, the one who has completed his duty should then dismiss it;
O Brahmin, this is to be done if the fire has moved far away when the Pārvaṇa ceremony has arrived.
On the anniversary of the death, when it has arrived, one should have the śrāddha performed according to the rules by brothers who are twice-born and maintain the sacred fires,
even if one's own fire has gone far away.
In the same way, the brothers there remained even by the worldly fire;
though their brother was standing nearby, they were at a distance as far as the objects of their worship.
If one should offer oblations either in the fire or even in the hand, he is indeed a sinner;
some twice-born ones, however, desire [this] when the fire for worship is situated at a distance.
Having done that, he should scatter [the remains] into the vessels of the Brahmins while remembering Hari;
he should honor the Brahmins with foods to be chewed, foods to be eaten, foods to be licked, and foods to be tasted.
Then, being composed in both respects, he should perform the dismissal of the food with the words:
"May the highly fortunate Viśvedevas of great power come hither."
"May those who have been appointed to this *śrāddha* be attentive," thus one should pray to the gods with the verse beginning "O gods... (ye devāsaḥ). NarP_1,28.58.
Likewise, O Brahmins, he prayed to the ancestors with the verse beginning "And others," for the sake of the formless and the formed ancestors who possess radiant splendor.
I always pay homage to those who proclaim [the truth], whose eyes are the wheel of yoga;
having thus paid homage to the ancestors, one who has Nārāyaṇa as his supreme goal— NarP_1,28.60.
O Karna, one should offer that oblation to Viṣṇu;
thereafter, all those Brahmins, the twice-born, should eat while remaining silent.
Someone laughs and says, "That should be the sacrificial oblation for the Rākṣasa;
and according to custom, honey, meat, and so forth should be offered. (NarP 1.28.62)
Restrained in speech and holding their vessels, they should praise the cooking and other preparations;
yet, if any Brāhmaṇa engaged in the Śrāddha should drop his vessel, [they should act accordingly].
He should be known as a destroyer of the *śrāddha*; he falls into hell if he touches one another while the Brahmins are eating.
Without discarding that food, the performer, devoted to faith, should eat and then recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times while the Brahmins are eating.
One should remember the god Nārāyaṇa, who is infinite and unconquered,
as well as the Vaiṣṇava mantras that destroy demons, and especially those dedicated to the ancestors.
And he should recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta, as well as the three Nāciketa hymns,
the Trimadhu, the Trisuparṇa, the Pāvamāna hymns, and the Yajus formulas.
One should likewise recite the common [texts] that bestow merit,
as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and indeed the Dharmaśāstras.
O twice-born one, he should mutter these [mantras] for as long as the Brahmins are eating;
and when the Brahmins have finished eating, he should likewise scatter the *vikira* offering.
One should speak regarding the remaining food and indeed recite the Madhu-sūkta;
then, O Nārada, having washed one's own feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) properly.
When the Brahmins have sipped water for purification, one should then offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas);
thereafter, one should perform the recitation for well-being (svastivācana) and the offering of water for imperishability (akṣayyodaka).
Having given [the gift], one should remain composed and likewise perform the salutation to the Brahmins;
