those twice-born ones who pronounce "svasti" without moving the vessel [are to be honored].
For one year, their ancestors become eaters of leftovers,
[being addressed] with such Smṛti-prescribed phrases as, "May our givers prosper," and so forth.
One should receive their words of blessing, then offer salutations;
and according to one's ability, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with betel leaf mixed with fragrance.
Then, having brought forward the overturned vessel, one should utter the word *svadhā*;
with the verse beginning "In strength after strength" (*vāje-vāje*), one should dismiss the ancestors and the gods. (NarP 1.28.75)
The one who eats and the one who performs the *śrāddha* should abstain from sexual intercourse on that night;
likewise, they should diligently avoid Vedic study and travel.
A traveler, one who is ill, one who is destitute of wealth,
and likewise one whose wife has died, may perform an *āmāśrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food) or one with gold.
In the absence of ritual materials or the absence of twice-born guests, one should cook only food;
a wise man should perform the fire-oblation with the *paitṛka* hymn.
O Brahmin, if one is utterly devoid of offerings, one should, according to one's own ability, offer grass to cows;
or, having bathed according to the rules, one should perform the offering of sesame seeds and water.
Alternatively, in a lonely forest, the wise man should weep very loudly, saying, "I am poor and a great sinner. (NarP 1.28.80)
The mortal who performs a *śrāddha* but does not offer libations to the ancestors on the following day causes his lineage to perish and incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Lord of Sages, those mortals who perform the śrāddha with faith do not suffer the interruption of their lineage; they become truly successful. (NarP 1.28.82)
Those who honor the ancestors in the śrāddha ceremony have thereby worshipped Viṣṇu;
when that Lord of the World is satisfied, all the deities are satisfied.
The ancestors, the deities, as well as the gandharvas and apsarases,
the yakṣas, the siddhas, human beings, and indeed the eternal Hari himself.
By whom this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has been produced;
therefore, the eternal Viṣṇu is both the giver and the enjoyer of everything.
O Brahmin, whatever exists and whatever does not exist, both the visible and the invisible—all that should be known as consisting of Viṣṇu; nothing other than that exists.
The Blessed One is the support of the universe, the self of all beings, the imperishable,
whose nature is beyond comparison, and who partakes of the offerings to gods and ancestors.
Janārdana, who is designated as the Supreme Brahman, is indeed the one;
the eternal Viṣṇu is both the doer and the instigator of all.
Thus, O best of sages, this supreme rite for the Śrāddha has been described by me;
for those who perform it in this manner, their sin is instantly dissolved. (NarP 1.28.89)
If an excellent twice-born man recites this with devotion at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
his ancestors are satisfied and his progeny increases.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Performance of Śrāddha," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
I shall now declare the determination of lunar days (tithis) as well as the procedure for the purification of the mind.
Listen to that, O best of sages, from which the accomplishment of one's actions arises.
O twice-born one, whether it be a vow prescribed by the Vedas (śrauta) or the Smṛtis (smārta), a gift, or any other Vedic rite—
none of these bears fruit when the lunar dates are not determined.
The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, the full moon, the fourteenth, the new moon, and the third day are [auspicious] for fasts, vows, and the like. (NarP 1.29.3)
Those [tithis] pierced by the subsequent [day] are praised, but those joined with the preceding [day] are not to be accepted;
the sixth tithi pierced by Nāga (the seventh) and the excellent fifth tithi pierced by Śiva (the fourth).

The tenth day pierced by the eleventh should never be observed as a fast; likewise, one should not fast on the new moon, the full moon, the sixth lunar day, or the day of the ancestors (the fourteenth).
One who observes a lunar day that is "pierced" by the preceding one is reborn in hell; this applies to the fourteenth and the fifth days when they are pierced in the dark fortnight.
Some say that the third and likewise the ninth [lunar days] are praiseworthy;
however, for all religious observances and the like, the bright fortnight is distinguished as superior.
The afternoon should be taken as the morning, since it is more excellent;
for if the morning lunar day is not available for the observances and other rites.
When the sun has risen, two muhūrtas should be accepted;
for the vow of *nakta*, the lunar day (*tithi*) that extends through the evening (*pradoṣa*) is always to be accepted.
One should observe the fast under the lunar mansion upon which the sun sets,
in the performance of a vow prescribed by the conjunction of a lunar day and a lunar mansion.
The lunar day (tithi) that extends through the evening (pradoṣa) should be accepted; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
That lunar day which extends through the asterism (nakṣatra) below midnight (ardharātra) [is to be taken].
O best of sages, in the case of a vow prescribed for a specific lunar mansion (nakṣatra), that very [mansion] which occurs on both days should be accepted if it spans the two days across midnight.
That merit is said to be associated with the lunar day (tithi) and the asterism (nakṣatra) that should be accepted;
this applies when both the asterism and the lunar day coincide during two midnight periods.
In the case of waning, the former [tithi] is recommended; likewise, in the case of waxing, the latter should be used.
A lunar day (tithi) that extends across two midnight points, conjoined with a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) and a weekday (ghasa), [is to be observed].
If the first [lunar day] is devoid of waning or waxing, and likewise the next;
if the Mūla [nakṣatra] is mixed with Jyeṣṭhā, and Rohiṇī is conjoined with Agni (Kṛttikā).
The elder [lunar day] conjoined with Maitra destroys progeny and so forth;
thereafter, the lunar days (tithis) become auspicious for the performance of rites during the day.

Among all night-vows, the conjunction with the night is preeminent; that lunar day which is proclaimed as meritorious through its conjunction with a specific constellation is especially so when it occurs at night.
In that [observance], however, the vow must be performed; indeed, that very day should be observed by the wise.
For the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī vow, the day that extends until sunrise should be accepted.

During solar and lunar eclipses, recitation and other rites should be performed for as long as the eclipse lasts; however, at all transits of the sun (saṃkrāntis), the time is declared to be a period of merit.
For those performing bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and other rites there, the fruit is inexhaustible;
that is to be known as the Karkaṭaka transit, the southern solstice.
The wise know that for thirty *ghaṭikās* prior [to the sun's entry], it is a time of merit,
as it is in Taurus, Scorpio, Leo, and likewise in Aquarius.
In the case of Libra and Aries, the first eight muhūrtas are to be taken for bathing, recitation, and other rites,
both before and after [the solar transit].
O twice-born one, ten ghaṭikās in the signs of Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius should be known as bringing inexhaustible merit to that which is given.
The sixteen ghaṭikās following [the moment of transition] should be known as bestowers of merit;
they call the transit into Capricorn by the name "northern course" (uttarāyaṇa).
And thirty *parās* and forty *ghaṭikās*, as before;
if the sun and the moon are to be grasped as having set. (NarP 1.29.25)
Having bathed, O best of Brahmins, one should eat on the following day when the lunar disc is pure;
Sinīvālī is known as that [lunar day] on which the moon is visible, and Kuhū as that on which the moon has disappeared.
The new moon day (amāvāsyā) is declared to be of two kinds by the learned who desire to follow the path of dharma:
it should be observed as Sinīvālī by the twice-born who maintain the sacred fires during the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha).
If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) extends across two afternoons, it should be observed by women, Śūdras, and likewise by those who maintain the sacred domestic fire (vānaprasthas).
In the case of a waning moon, the former [lunar day] should be observed; likewise, in the case of a waxing moon, the latter should be performed.
If the new moon (amāvāsyā) is understood to occur after midday, [it belongs to the preceding day].
It is known as *bhūtaviddhā* by those who are experts in the scriptures and filled with wonder;
however, according to the doctrine of absolute destruction (*atyantakṣaya*), it does not occur on the following day if it falls in the afternoon.
In that regard, the lunar day (tithi) that extends into the evening is the one to be accepted for Sinīvālī;
likewise, when there is a decrease [of the tithi], it is the one extending into the evening that is to be taken.
Sinīvālī is always to be preferred for the performance of the śrāddha rite;
however, when there is an excessive increase in the lunar days, one should avoid the tithi pierced by the fourteenth day (bhūta).
The *kuhū* (new moon) occurring in the afternoon is suitable for rites pertaining to the ancestors;
however, when there is an increase in the subsequent day, those [moments] joined with the [preceding] lunar day (*bhūta*) must be abandoned.
On the following day,
if the new-moon lunar day (amāvāsyā) extends across both halves of midday, it should be observed by the best of the wise during the afternoon.
In that regard, one may choose either the first or the latter [lunar day] according to one's desire.
O virtuous ones, I shall now describe the *anvādhāna* in its entirety.
O best of sages, one should perform the sacrifice on the first day of the lunar fortnight;
the first three quarters of that first day constitute the fourth part of the full moon (parvan).
That time is to be known as the hour for sacrifice, declared by the wise to be at dawn;
and both the new moon and the full moon should occur at the two midday periods.
O best of Brahmins, on the very next day, the immediate time (sadyaḥkāla) is prescribed.
In the case of the first two [types of *tithi-kṣaya*], the wise hold that it occurs on the following day after the *saṃgava* period;
in the case of *tithi-kṣaya*, the time for the rite should be known as the current day (*sadyaḥ*) or the following day.
The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) should be observed by all, avoiding the tenth day (Daśamī);
for when joined with the tenth, it destroys the merit acquired over three lifetimes.
If even a single digit (kalā) of Ekādaśī is perceived on the twelfth day,
and the twelfth day exists on the thirteenth day, that [Ekādaśī] is remembered as the superior one.
When the Ekādaśī is complete and pure, and the Dvādaśī is observed,
and the Trayodaśī lasts until the end of the night— in such a case, I shall state the definitive rule.
The former [observance] should be performed by householders, and likewise the latter by ascetics;
for householders desire worldly success, whereas the lords among ascetics seek liberation.
If the breaking of the fast can be obtained on the twelfth part (kalā) of the day,
then even if the Ekādaśī lunar day is pierced by Daśamī, that Ekādaśī should be observed as a fast.
If there should be two Ekādaśīs, one on the Śukla (bright) and the other on the Kṛṣṇa (dark) fortnight,
the former is prescribed for householders and the latter for ascetics.
If on the twelfth day there is any conjunction with the tenth,
it is proclaimed by all that, in the case of a loss of a day (dinakṣaya), it is indeed the second [lunar day] alone.
Even if the Ekādaśī is pierced [by the preceding day], it should be accepted provided that the Dvādaśī does not follow;
even if it is unpierced, it is indeed forbidden if the Dvādaśī follows.
When Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī remain at the end of the night and Trayodaśī begins,
there is the merit of twelve Dvādaśīs if the ritual breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is performed on the Trayodaśī.
If even a single digit (kalā) of Ekādaśī exists on the day of Dvādaśī, and whether or not Dvādaśī exists on the day of Trayodaśī, [the fast should be observed]. (NarP 1.29.49)
Even when there is a doubt regarding the Ekādaśī, for householders the preceding day should then be observed;
likewise, by those without sons and by widows, the subsequent day should indeed be taken.
When the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is complete and pure, and there is nothing [of it] on the twelfth day (dvādaśī),
yet the twelfth day exists on the thirteenth day— how should one act in that case?
In this matter, the former lunar day (tithi) should be observed by householders, while the latter should be observed by ascetics;
some say that out of devotion one should fast on the second day as well.

When the Ekādaśī is overlapped [by the previous day] and is not perceived on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), and the dvādaśī exists on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī)—in that case alone, others [hold]. NarP_1,29.53.
The pure twelfth day (dvādaśī) is to be observed as a fast by everyone without a doubt;
some, however, say it should be the preceding day, but that opinion is not correct.
On the transit of the sun, on Sundays, and likewise during eclipses of the moon or sun,
a householder with sons should neither break his fast nor observe a fast.
On a Sunday, on the day of the full moon or the new moon, on the fourteenth or eighth day of the lunar fortnight during the day,
or on the eleventh day for a full day and night— having eaten on these occasions, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
During a solar eclipse, one should not eat in the morning, nor likewise during the first three watches of the night; if one should eat, he would become equal to a drinker of liquor.

O best of sages, if an eclipse of the moon or sun occurs during the preparatory rites (anvādhāna) or within the sacrificial offering (iṣṭi), the performers of the sacrifice must perform an expiation (prāyaścitta) in that case.
O twice-born one, during an eclipse of the moon, one should offer oblations with the verse beginning "Soma is the tenth," with the verse "Āpyāyasva," and also with the verse "Somapāstas."
During a solar eclipse, one should offer oblations with the mantras "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam," "ā satyena," and "ud vayaṃ tamasas pari";
these three mantras have been declared.
Having thus determined the lunar day according to the path of the Smṛtis, the wise man who performs his vows and other rites shall obtain imperishable fruit.
The Dharma is established in the Vedas; by means of Dharma, Keśava is pleased. Therefore, those who are devoted to Dharma go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Those who desire to perform actions other than the Dharma are indeed of the nature of Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, the disease of worldly existence never afflicts them at all.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of Lunar Days and Other Matters," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
"O Nārada, listen now as I shall describe the rules for expiation."
One whose self is purified by expiation shall obtain the fruit of all actions.
O Sage, whatever action is performed by those who lack expiation is declared to be entirely fruitless; it is frequented by Rākṣasas.
Those who desire the fruit of all dharmas should consult Brāhmaṇas who are free from lust and anger and are experts in the treatises on dharma.
O best of Brahmins, expiatory rites performed by those who are averse to Nārāyaṇa do not purify them,
just as rivers cannot cleanse a vessel that has held liquor.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these are the perpetrators of the great sins (mahāpātakin), and the fifth is one who associates with them.
But he who lives for a year with those [outcasts], sharing their beds, seats, and food, should be known as fallen from all religious rites.
Having killed a Brahmin through ignorance, one should wear rags and grow matted hair;
for one who has intentionally killed a Brahmin, he should even carry a skull.
In the absence of that, O best of sages, one should take a skull or some other such object and,
holding it upon the staff of his banner, become a forest-dweller.
Subsisting on forest-grown food, he should dwell there for one night with moderate eating;
he should properly perform the twilight devotions and practice bathing at the three times of day.

One should avoid [worldly] pursuits such as studying and teaching; one should constantly remember Hari. One should always remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) and avoid perfumes, garlands, and the like.
He should dwell at sacred fords and likewise in holy hermitages;
if he cannot subsist on forest products, he should practice begging for alms in a village.
One devoted to Hari should thus observe this vow for twelve years;
by doing so, even a slayer of a Brahmin attains purity and becomes fit for ritual action.
In the midst of his vow, he may even be destroyed by wild animals or by diseases;
or for the sake of a cow, or for the sake of a twice-born man, he may even renounce his own life.
Or else, he may give ten thousand excellent cows to the best of the twice-born;
by performing any one of these, the slayer of a Brahmin shall attain purification.
Having killed a consecrated Kṣatriya, one must indeed perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa,
or else enter the fire, or likewise throw oneself from a mountain peak.
Having killed a consecrated Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the vow twice over;
and for the killing of an Ācārya or others, the vow is said to be fourfold.
"Having killed even a mere Brahmin, one should perform the vow for a year;
thus, O twice-born one, has the rule for expiation been declared for a Brahmin.
For a Kṣatriya, it is said to be twofold, while for a Vaiśya, it is recorded as threefold."
The wise declare that a Śūdra who kills a Brāhmaṇa deserves to be impaled on a stake.
"It is the settled rule among the scriptures that the king alone must administer instruction;
however, for the killing of Brāhmaṇa women, the penalty shall be half, and for the killing of a maiden, it shall be a quarter. (NarP 1.30.19)
Having killed those who have not been initiated, one should likewise perform the *pādavrata* penance;
but having killed a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six years.
Having killed a Vaiśya, one should perform this for three years; having killed a Śūdra, for one year;
having killed the wife of one consecrated for sacrifice, for eight years; and likewise for killing a Brāhmaṇa woman.
By performing the vow for the murder of a Brahmin, one certainly becomes pure;
however, O best of sages, the rule for expiation applies everywhere.
The wise have declared that for the elderly, the sick, women, and children, half [of the penance] is prescribed.
Surā is to be known as threefold: that distilled from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that from honey (mādhvī). (NarP 1.30.23)
O Nārada, O Sage, it may be drunk by members of the four castes as well as by women;
among these, milk, ghee, or cow-urine—whichever one [is available]—should be used. (NarP 1.30.24)
Having bathed and wearing wet clothes, being self-restrained and recollecting Nārāyaṇa,
one should make the water resemble molten iron and then drink it.
One should drink it from a vessel of iron or of steel, or else from a vessel of copper; having drunk it from such a vessel, one shall go to death. (NarP 1.30.26)
One who drinks liquor becomes pure [only] in this manner; no other purification is desired.
However, if a twice-born man drinks liquor through ignorance, thinking it to be his own substance, he must perform penance.

If one should drink liquor for the sake of medicine in order to cure a disease, he must perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin correctly, while remaining free from its external marks. NarP_1,30.28 //
For him, there must again be the initiation ceremony (upanayana) as well as two Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
likewise for one who has drunk water from a vessel touched by liquor or from the contents of a liquor jar.
They say that eating the moon is equal to drinking liquor,
as are [eating] the fruits of the palmyra, the breadfruit, the grape, and those produced from the date palm.
Mādhuka, śaila, māriṣṭa, maireya, that which is produced from coconut,
gauḍī, mādhvī, and surā— liquor is thus remembered as being of eleven kinds.
A Brahmin should never drink any one of these;
however, if a twice-born man should drink any one of them through ignorance, [he must perform penance].
Furthermore, his initiation ceremony must be performed again;
likewise, he shall undergo that penance (kṛcchra) whether [the theft was committed] in the presence [of the owner], in their absence, by force, or by stealth.
The taking of another's property is called theft by the wise;
the standard measure for gold has been defined by Manu and others.
I shall speak; listen, O best of brahmins, to the means for the practice taught by Prāyaścitti:
it is seen in the midst of the rays of the sun as they enter through a lattice window.
The wise say that a particle the size of a *trasareṇu* is called "dust";
eight *trasareṇus* make a *niṣka*, and three of those make a *rājasarṣapa*.
Three mustard seeds from Mathurā make one *tarkṣya*; six of those are said to be a *yava*.
Three *yavas* make one *kṛṣṇala*, and five of those are traditionally known as a *māṣa*.
"Nārada, sixteen māṣas shall constitute one suvarṇa;
having unknowingly consumed the property of a Brāhmaṇa, one must perform penance for twelve years as previously described."
But for one who has killed a preceptor, a performer of sacrifices, or those most devoted to dharma, he must perform the vow for the murder of a Brahmin, even if he lacks the skull-emblem.
Having stolen gold from Vedic scholars who are twice-born, one should act in this manner:
filled with remorse, one should smear one's entire body with ghee.
If a Kṣatriya who has stolen the property of a Brāhmaṇa undergoes remorse and is burned while covered with dried cow-dung, he is liberated from the sin of theft.
He gives again in that very same manner; hear from me the procedure for that:
having performed the *sāṃtapana* penance there, followed by twelve days of fasting.

O divine sage, he attains purification; otherwise, he would become fallen, as in the case of [illicit intercourse with] a woman who is a relative, a seated woman, a human female, a cow, land, and so forth. (NarP 1.30.43)
For stealing gold that is equal in weight to a *suvarṇa*, half the penance is prescribed; having stolen gold equal to a *trasareṇu* in weight, one who is composed should perform [the following].
By two proper breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), a human being is thoroughly purified;
one should perform three breath-restraints while holding a weight equal to a niṣka.

And four breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) performed for the duration of one *rājasa-r̥ṣapa* [weigh] the same as stealing gold the size of a white mustard seed (*gaurasarṣapa*), O wise one. (NarP 1.30.46)
Having bathed according to the rules, a twice-born man shall recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times;
by this, he becomes purified from the theft of gold even as small as a barley grain.
Having recited the Mother of the Vedas from evening until morning,
one who has stolen even as much gold as a *kṛṣṇala* seed must perform the *Sāṃtapana* penance.
For stealing gold weighing one *māṣa*, an expiation is prescribed:
by eating barley cooked in cow's urine for one year, one becomes pure.
O Lord of Sages, having committed the theft of a full measure of gold, one should,
with a concentrated mind, perform the vow for the murder of a Brahmin for twelve years.
But for the act of stealing silver when it is less than a suvarṇa in measure, one should properly perform the Sāṃtapana penance; otherwise, one becomes fallen.
O Sage, having stolen silver weighing from four niṣkas up to ten niṣkas, a wise man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
For one who steals silver worth ten *diśatis* or more,
two *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts are prescribed as the means for purifying that sin.
For stealing more than one hundred up to one thousand [units], three Cāndrāyaṇas are prescribed;
for theft exceeding one thousand, one should perform the vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
For stealing vessels made primarily of bell-metal or brass, as well as those of magnetite,
when the value is one thousand niṣkas, the Parāka penance is prescribed.
The penance for those who steal gems is declared to be the same as that for stealing gold;
now the penance for those who violate the teacher’s bed is proclaimed.
Having approached his mother or even her co-wife out of ignorance, he himself shall cut off his own testicles while proclaiming his sin. (Narada Purāṇa 1.30.57)
Holding his testicle in his hand, he should indeed go toward the southwest direction;
while traveling on the road, he should never consider whether it is pleasant or painful.
If one sees someone departing, one should follow them until they reach the end of their life;
or, proclaiming one's sin, one should even cast oneself from a mountain peak. (NarP 1.30.59)
But for one who, without deliberation, has sexual intercourse with a woman of his own caste or a woman of a higher caste,
he should, with a concentrated mind, perform the twelve-year vow prescribed for the killing of a Brahmin.
By practicing with an uninitiated woman, or likewise with a woman of his own caste who is superior,
the best of the twice-born attains purification by being burnt with a fire of dried cow-dung.
If he desists from intercourse with his mother even before the emission of semen, he shall perform the vow for killing a Brahmin; if there is emission of semen, he shall perform the rite for arson.
One who has ceased from discharging semen upon women of his own caste or of a higher caste shall perform the vow for killing a Brahmin for nine years, being entirely devoted to Viṣṇu.
If he approaches his father’s Vaiśya wife, he should perform the vow for six years;
if he approaches his Guru’s Śūdra wife, he should perform the vow for three years.

If one, deluded by lust, should approach his mother’s sister, his father’s sister, the wife of his teacher, the wife of his father-in-law, the wife of his paternal uncle, his maternal aunt, or his own daughter; NarP_1,30.65 //
One should perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin according to the prescribed rules for two days;
however, if it occurs many times on a single day, the penance lasts for three years.
If one year has passed, he becomes pure by performing a vow;
if three days have passed, he would be purified by being consumed by fire, and not otherwise.
He who, out of lust, approaches a woman of the Cāṇḍāla caste, a Puṣkasī, a daughter-in-law, a sister, the wife of a friend, or the wife of a disciple— NarP_1,30.68.

O Lord of Sages, he who kills a Brāhmaṇa unintentionally should perform the vow for the slaughter of a Brāhmaṇa for six years; however, he who does so intentionally should practice the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
The expiation for association with those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) is now declared;
one whose self is purified by such expiation shall obtain the fruit of all ritual acts.
Whosoever should have contact with any of these four types of slayers of Brahmins,
he shall attain purification by performing the specific penance prescribed for each, without a doubt.
He who, out of ignorance, performs the *pañcarātra* rite at these places of confluence (*saṃgama*) should properly perform the *kāyakṛcchra* penance; otherwise, he would become fallen.
In the case of association with those twelve causes [of impurity], the Mahāsāṃtapana penance is prescribed;
having formed such an association for half a month, one should observe a fast for twelve days.
If sexual intercourse occurs once a month for three lunar months, a *parāka* penance is prescribed;
however, having engaged in it for six months, one should perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
If the duration of association is slightly less than a year, one should observe the vow for six months;
and this is declared to be threefold according to the sequence of knowledge when there is association.
Having killed a frog, a mongoose, a crow, a boar, a mouse, as well as a cat, a goat, a sheep, a dog, and likewise a cock; NarP_1,30.76 //
A Brahmin should perform the Kṛcchrārdha penance for killing a horse, and he should perform the Atikṛcchra for killing an elephant;
for killing a goat, the Jāpyakṛcchra is prescribed, and for killing a cow, the Parāka is traditionally taught.
The wise have observed that no purification whatsoever exists for the intentional killing of a cow,
nor for [the consumption of] drinks, beds, seats, and the like, nor for flowers, roots, and fruits.
For the theft of various kinds of food and edibles, purification is achieved through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
this applies likewise to the theft of dry wood, grass, trees, and molasses.
For killing leather, clothing, or horn, there shall be a three-night fast;
the same applies for killing a *ṭiṭṭibha*, a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), a swan (*haṃsa*), or a water-fowl (*kāraṇḍava*).
The owl, the crane, the partridge, the water-fowl, the parrot, the blue jay, the heron, the crocodile, and the tortoise; NarP_1,30.81 //
Having killed any one of these,
or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Prājāpatya vow consisting of fasting for twelve days.

It is declared that for eating the leavings of a Śūdra, or [the food of] a woman in her menses, a Caṇḍāla, or likewise one who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), three Cāndrāyaṇas are prescribed.

Having touched a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, one who is impure from eating, or a washerman and the like, one should bathe with one's clothes on and likewise consume clarified butter.
O twice-born one, having touched any one of these while eating, if it occurs through ignorance, the pure-souled man should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.

O twice-born Nārada, purification from the consumption [of forbidden food] occurs through fasting for three nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as through bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth, and by abstaining from eating. NarP_1,30.86.
Whoever should hear or speak even the sound of any one of these, he must vomit up the food he has eaten, bathe, and likewise fast.
On the second day, having consumed clarified butter, one becomes pure, O Nārada; even if she should hear a thunderclap during the beginning or middle of her vow, she remains so. (NarP 1.30.88)
One should recite the Mother of the Vedas one thousand and eight times;
for among all sins, the greatest sin is the reviling of the twice-born and the gods. (NarP 1.30.89)
O Nārada, according to all the scriptures, there is no atonement for one who has not seen [it],
even for those acts declared by the wise to be equal to the great sins (mahāpātaka).
One should indeed perform atonement for them in this manner according to the rules;
he who performs these atonements while being solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa [is purified].
His sins are destroyed; otherwise, he would fall.
This applies to one who is liberated from passion and the like, and is endowed with remorse.
Endowed with devotion toward all beings and intent upon the remembrance of Viṣṇu,
whether one is burdened by great sins or burdened by all possible transgressions, [one is purified].
One who is devoted to Viṣṇu should be known as truly liberated from all evils,
for he possesses a mind directed toward Nārāyaṇa— the beginningless and endless one, whose form is the universe and who is free from all affliction.
But that mortal who remembers [him] is liberated from tens of millions of sins—whether he has remembered, worshipped, meditated upon, or even bowed down to him. (NarP 1.30.95)
Viṣṇu, who dwells in the hearts of the virtuous, surely destroys all sins—
even for one who worships Hari out of mere association or even through delusion.
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes to the abode of Hari;
by remembering Viṣṇu even once, the accumulations of afflictions are destroyed.
O Lord of Sages, the attainment of enjoyments such as those of heaven is inferred for him by the wise, who have obtained this human birth that is so difficult to attain.
Even there, devotion to Hari is proclaimed to be difficult to attain;
therefore, having obtained this rare human birth, which is as flickering as a flash of lightning— NarP_1,30.99.
One should worship Hari with devotion, the liberator from the bonds of the individual soul;
all obstacles perish and purity of mind arises.
When Janārdana is worshipped, one indeed attains supreme liberation;
for the eternal human goals known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa [are attained].
But for those devoted to the worship of Hari, these are accomplished; of this there is no doubt—[the world] that runs after children, wife, house, field, wealth, and grain.
Having obtained this human condition, O friend, do not give way to pride;
abandon desire, anger, greed, delusion, and likewise arrogance. (NarP 1.30.103)
Devoutly worship Hari; abandon slander and censure of others.
Setting aside all worldly activities, worship Janārdana.
The trees of the city of Death are already seen nearby,
as long as death has not yet arrived and as long as old age has not yet come.
As long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long should the wise man worship Hari; he should not place his trust in this perishable body.
Death is ever-present, and prosperity is extremely fickle;
the body is close to death—therefore, abandon pride.
Unions end in separation, and everything is fragile by its very nature;
knowing this, O illustrious one, worship Janārdana.
One's intention is indeed distressed, and liberation is exceedingly difficult to attain;
yet, even one who is burdened with great sins, if he worships Viṣṇu with devotion— NarP_1,30.109.
He too goes to the supreme state, reaching which one does not grieve;
O best of beings, all sacred fords, sacrifices with their constituent parts, and the Vedas [are surpassed by this].
These do not equal even a sixteenth part of the worship of Nārāyaṇa;
what indeed is the use of the Vedas, sacrifices, scriptures, or the frequenting of sacred fords?
For those devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, what is the use of austerities or even vows?

Those mortals who, having beheld the excellent Viṣṇu of infinite form manifest in all shapes— the one to be known through the Vedāntas and the physician for the disease of worldly existence— perform sacrifice, go to the abode of the Infallible One.

Having remembered the Friend—the beginningless Self, possessed of infinite power, the support of the universe, worthy of worship by the gods, whose nature is light, and known as the supreme Acyuta—a man attains Him. NarP_1,30.114 //
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Rules for Expiation," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O Sage, you have fully explained the rules regarding the castes and stages of life.
Now I wish to hear about the path of Yama, which is so difficult to traverse.
Sanaka said: Listen, O Brahmin, I shall describe the path of Yama, which is extremely difficult to traverse;
it bestows happiness upon those of virtuous character and brings fear to the sinful. (NarP 1.31.2)
O Lord of Sages, the width of the path of Yama has been stated by the ancient seers to be eighty-six thousand yojanas.
O twice-born one, those men who are devoted to giving go forth in happiness;
whereas men devoid of dharma go forth severely afflicted by suffering.
Exceedingly terrified and helpless, with parched throats, lips, and palates,
the sinners go along that path wailing piteously and at length.
They are being struck by the messengers of Yama with goads and other such weapons.
Running hither and thither, they travel that path with great suffering;
in some places there is mud, in some places fire, in some places a river of sand;
in some places there are trees in the form of forest fires, and in some places stones with sharp edges.
In some places there were thorny trees and mountains of stone difficult to climb;
there were caves of dense darkness and great enclosures of thorns.
Climbing to the top of an embankment, entering a cave, pebbles, clods of earth, and thorns as sharp as needles; NarP_1,31.9 //
In some parts of the path there was moss, in others rows of hollow bamboos;
in some places clouds thundered, and in others fevers increased.
Thus, O Nārada, sinners burdened by manifold afflictions go along,
wailing, weeping, and withering away.
Some sinners go along, restrained by nooses and dragged by hooks, while others are beaten from behind with staffs and weapons.
Some are dragged by nooses attached to the tips of their noses, others are bound with entrails;
carrying loads of iron, they indeed proceed with the tip of their penis [pierced through].
Some sinners go along carrying two iron plows on the tip of their noses, and others likewise carry them on their ears.
Some went stumbling along while being beaten, others likewise;
some were gasping excessively for breath, and some had their eyes covered by their hands.
On a path devoid of shade and water, they travel in extreme misery, grieving over their own actions performed both knowingly and unknowingly. (NarP 1.31.16)
But those, O Nārada, who are most righteous, charitable in nature, and wise,
being exceedingly endowed with happiness, go to the palace of Dharma.
O best of sages, those who give food indeed go happily while eating delicious food;
those who give water go happily drinking excellent milk;
and those who give buttermilk and curds certainly obtain the enjoyment of those very things.
O best of the twice-born, they are indeed givers of clarified butter, givers of honey, and givers of milk.
Those who drink nectar go indeed to the temple of Dharma;
those who give vegetables, those who eat milk-rice, and the giver of lamps who illuminates the quarters [attain the same]. (NarP 1.31.19)
O tiger among men, one who gives clothing goes clothed in divine garments;
one who formerly gave a city or a fort goes along the path being praised by the immortals.
By the gift of a cow, a man goes endowed with all happiness;
by the gift of land and a house, he likewise dwells in a celestial chariot possessed of every prosperity.
Surrounded by throngs of Apsarases, he sports and goes to the abode of Śiva;
O best of the twice-born, he is the giver of horses, the giver of vehicles, and the giver of elephants.
O best of sages, the giver of a bull indeed goes to the abode of Dharma by means of a celestial chariot endowed with all enjoyments, mounted upon that vehicle.
The man who gives fruit and flowers goes endowed with contentment;
the man who gives betel-leaf goes to the abode of the gods, filled with joy.
And that best of men who has performed service to his mother and father goes to heaven with a fully satisfied soul, being honored by those who dwell there.
He who performs service for ascetics who observe their vows,
and for the foremost of the twice-born, the Brāhmaṇas, shall go endowed with supreme happiness.
Endowed with compassion for all beings and honored by the immortals,
that twice-born man proceeds in a celestial chariot furnished with every enjoyment.
One who delights in the gift of knowledge goes being honored by the sons of Brahmā;
one who recites the Purāṇas goes being praised by the lords of sages.
Thus, those devoted to Dharma go happily to the abode of Dharma;
Yama, becoming four-faced and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword, [welcomes them].
He honors one who delights in meritorious deeds with perfect affection, as if he were a friend;
O best among the wise, you who fear the torments of hell! (NarP 1.31.30)
You have accomplished merit that brings happiness in this world and the next;
yet he who, having obtained a human birth, does not perform virtuous deeds [is lost].
He alone is the worst among sinners who commits suicide, having obtained this impermanent human birth, yet fails to accomplish what is eternal. (NarP 1.31.32)
He goes to a terrible hell; what else is more senseless than that?
For the body is of the nature of torment, utterly defiled by impurities and the like.
One who places trust in such a person should know him to be a destroyer of his own self.
Among all living beings, humans are the best; among them, those who live by their intellect are indeed the most excellent.
Among men, those with intelligence are the best; among intelligent men, likewise, the Brahmins;
among Brahmins, the learned; and among the learned, those whose intellects are perfected.
Among those who have perfected their intellect, the doers are superior; among doers, the exponents of Brahman;
and among the exponents of Brahman, likewise, he who is free from the sense of "mine" is said to be the most excellent.
Even beyond these, one who is constantly devoted to meditation is to be known as superior;
therefore, with every effort, one should practice the accumulation of Dharma.
A person who possesses righteousness is honored everywhere; of this there is no doubt.
Go to my abode, endowed with all enjoyments, by means of your own merits.
If there is any evil deed committed, you shall experience its fruit right here afterwards;
having thus honored him, Yama leads him to a happy rebirth.
Having summoned the sinners, he should threaten them with the staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa),
possessing the roar of the clouds at the dissolution of the world and the luster of a mountain of collyrium.
Possessing the brilliance of lightning, formidable and terrifying, he was endowed with thirty-two arms;
he was three yojanas in height, with red eyes and a long nose.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, eyes as fierce as those of a well-crocodile,
and accompanied by the fever of death and other ailments, Citragupta himself was fearsome.
Then all the messengers, as terrifying as Yama himself, roar;
thereafter, they speak to all those trembling sinners.
Lamenting their own deeds at the command of Yama, Citragupta says:
"O you sinners, of wicked conduct, utterly corrupted by egoism!"
For what purpose was this sin accumulated by you, who lack discernment, with minds full of pride and driven by the thirst for sensual desires? (NarP 1.31.45)
O people, for what purpose did you formerly perform those most heinous sins, committing them with extreme joy? (NarP 1.31.46)

In that very same way, one must experience the torments of hell; for what is the use of practicing extreme wickedness in vain, just as one has committed evil deeds for the sake of servants, friends, and wives?
Thus, by the power of karma, you have arrived here in extreme suffering;
those sons and others whom you nurtured have gone elsewhere.
That sin is yours alone; what cause for sorrow is there?
Indeed, very many sins were committed by you yourselves.
Since such sufferings have been obtained, for what purpose do you remain suffering here? You yourselves must investigate what was done by you in the past.
Why was it not considered that Yama will inflict punishment upon everyone—whether one is poor or foolish, or whether one is wise or endowed with prosperity? (NarP 1.31.51)
"Yama is known to be impartial toward both the cowardly and the heroic.
Having heard these words uttered by Citragupta, those sinners then [fell silent].
Terrified by [Yama’s] command, the cruel, fierce, and fearsome messengers, who carry out Yama's orders, remain silent while performing their own tasks.
Candālas and others forcibly cast them into the hells;
having experienced the fruit of their own evil deeds, they remain there at the end due to the residue of their sin.
"And having reached the surface of the earth, they become stationary beings and so forth.
Nārada said: "O Blessed One, O treasure-house of compassion, a doubt has arisen in my mind. (NarP 1.31.55)
You are capable of cutting through that, for you are indeed our elder;
various types of dharmas have been proclaimed, as well as many sins.
The fruit of their long-term enjoyment has been described by you, the omniscient one;
indeed, at the end of a day of Brahmā, the destruction of the three worlds is proclaimed.
But at the end of two parārdhas, even the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) undergoes destruction;
as for the merits of village gifts and the like, O son of Vidhi, [they last] only until that time.
Great enjoyment is said to last for thousands of millions of kalpas;
yet for all worlds alike, there is destruction during the dissolution into primordial matter (prakṛti).
"Janārdana has been declared by you to be the one who alone remains;
this doubt has arisen in me, which you ought to dispel. (NarP 1.31.60)
"There is no exhaustion for him even in the great deluge, due to the equalization of the experiences of merit and demerit.
Sanaka said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! This is indeed the most secret of secrets."
I shall explain that which you have asked; listen with a well-composed mind.
Nārāyaṇa is imperishable, infinite, the supreme light, and eternal.
Pure, devoid of qualities, eternal, and free from illusion and delusion—
he who, though devoid of qualities, shines as if possessed of qualities, being the supreme bliss.
O Eternal One, through Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, You appear as if possessed of differentiation within these three who are differentiated by the limiting adjuncts of the qualities (guṇas).
Having joined with Māyā, he performs all the activities of the world;
in the form of Brahmā he creates, and in the form of Viṣṇu he protects.
And it was certain that he had previously devoured everything in the form of Rudra;
then, at the end of the dissolution, Janārdana arose in the form of Brahmā.
O best of Brahmins, he fashioned the universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving exactly as before,
establishing the stationary beings and others in their respective places.
Brahmā indeed makes all those various worlds exactly as they were before;
therefore, O best of beings, [the fruits] of both merits and sins committed [persist].
For the inexhaustible fruit of actions must necessarily be experienced;
an action that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
One must inevitably experience the fruit of whatever action has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
for the eternal and perfect Lord, who is the inner self of all worlds and consists of the universe, experiences the fruit of every action.
That god Viśvaṃbhara, established through the differentiation of qualities, creates, protects, and devours all this; he is the consumer of all, the imperishable one.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Deeds of Yama's Messengers," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
In this manner, living beings, bound by the fetters of karma, having experienced the enjoyment of merit in holy places such as heaven and elsewhere, pass away.

Having experienced the fruit of evil which is even more painful, and having exhausted his karma, he returns to this world by means of what remains and is born among those who are agitated by all fears and afflicted by the pain of death— among stationary beings and the like;
namely, trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, mountains, and grasses.
Known as the "Immovable Ones," they are completely enveloped by great delusion.

Regarding the state of stationary beings (*sthāvara*), seeds sown in the earth immediately upon being moistened with water, through the power of the collection of conditions for wholesome transformation (*susaṃskāra-sāmagrī*) and being cooked by internal heat, attain swelling;

from that, they reach the state of a root; from that root, the sprout arises; from that as well, leaves, stalks, and tubes arise; and within those stalks, they undergo flowering, and from them the production of flowers occurs. // NarP_1,32.2 //

Among those flowers, some are without fruit while others serve as the cause for fruit; when those flowers have reached maturity, the production of husks arises from the roots of those flowers. Then, by the power of the collection of conditions (*saṃskāra-sāmagrī*) of the sentient beings who consume them, and due to the proximity of the rays of the cool-rayed moon, the essence of that medicinal plant enters within the husks, attains the state of milk, and at its own time, assumes the form of rice grains.
By the power of the karmic impressions of living beings' enjoyments, they shall bear fruit within a year.

Even in the state of being stationary, while being consumed by monkeys and other creatures for a long time, they experience the sufferings of being cut, burned by forest fires, and afflicted by cold and heat, and then die.

Thereafter, becoming worms, they live for half a moment and die for half a moment, abounding in constant suffering; unable to prevent the oppression of powerful beings, they are mostly tormented by cold winds and the like, and are perpetually hungry.
Wandering amidst excrement, urine, and the like, they experience suffering.

Having come from that very place to the lotus-born Brahmā, they—tormented by powerful afflictions, filled with futile anxiety, constantly emaciated by hunger, wandering the forests, and even while among their mothers, distressed by sense-objects and beset by many sufferings such as wind and other elements—experience misery: in one birth eating grass, in another birth eating meat, impure substances, and the like, in another birth eating bulbs, roots, and fruits, and being intent on harming weak creatures. // NarP_1,32.5 //
Even among those born from eggs, such as birds that eat wind or flesh-eaters, there are those who consume impure things and are intent on harming others; they are constantly beset by much suffering.

Even when they enter the womb of domestic animals, they experience all manner of miseries, such as separation from their own kind, the burden of carrying loads, being bound with ropes and the like, and being beaten or made to pull ploughs and other implements.
Thus, having wandered through many wombs, they gradually attain human birth;
and some, due to a particular excellence of merit, even attain human birth by skipping over [the intermediate stages].

Furthermore, even in human birth, they do not experience the abundance of suffering arising from being born as leather-workers, outcasts, hunters, potters, dyers, water-carriers, blacksmiths, goldsmiths, weavers, tailors, ascetics with matted hair, bath-attendants, scribes, hired laborers, messengers carrying royal edicts, low servants, the poor, or those with missing or extra limbs;
nor do they experience the many sufferings such as feverish heat, cold, phlegm, abdominal tumors, pain in the feet, eyes, head, womb, or sides. // NarP_1,32.8 //

Even in the human state, when there is sexual union between a man and a woman, at that time, as soon as the semen enters the womb, the living being, by the power of karma, enters the womb along with the semen and begins to develop within the embryo consisting of semen and blood.
Through the entry of the vital principle (jīva), that embryo becomes a *kalala* in five days;
having reached the state of a *palvala* in half a month, it attains the size of a span (*prādeśa*) in one month. (NarP 1.32.10)

From that time forward, although it lacks consciousness due to the power of the vital wind (*vāyu*), it wanders about because it is unable to remain in one place within the mother's womb due to the unbearable heat and the state of being a hair-like embryo.
When the second month is complete, it attains the mere form of a human being; when the third month is complete, it attains the state of having limbs such as hands and feet;
when four months have passed, there is the full discernment of the joints of all the limbs; when five have elapsed, the nails become manifest;
when six have passed, the nails reach a state of clear definition, while the body is nourished by the umbilical cord and its limbs are drenched in impure urine.
Seeing himself dwelling within this loathsome body— defiled by the placenta and corrupted by blood, bones, worms, fat, marrow, sinews, hair, and the like—
and seeing his own self likewise so thoroughly defiled, and further seeing himself being scorched by the mother’s consumption of bitter, sour, salty, and excessively hot food, the embodied soul,
through the power of recollecting his previous birth and remembering the sufferings of hells previously experienced, is filled with inner anguish.
Being scorched by the dry urine, feces, and other secretions of his mother’s body, he thus perishes within the mind.

"Alas! I am an utter sinner. In my previous birth, through extreme attachment to servants, children, friends, wives, houses, fields, wealth, grain, and so forth, I committed great sins by seizing the property, fields, and other assets of others by means such as theft while they looked on, for the sake of maintaining my family; and being blinded by lust, I committed the abduction of others' wives and the like. By those sins, I alone must experience such hells."
Furthermore, having experienced great suffering among stationary beings and others, I am now being consumed by internal agony and external heat while enveloped by the fetal membrane.
The wife whom I nourished has gone elsewhere, under the power of her own karma.
Alas, how great is the suffering of embodied beings!
The body, however, has arisen from sin; therefore, one should not commit sin.
"For the sake of servants, enemies, and wife, other wealth was seized by me. (NarP 1.32.16)
Enveloped by the womb, I am consumed by that evil,
having previously seen the prosperity of another and being constantly tormented by envy.
"May this evildoer be consumed by the fire of the womb even now!
Having caused pain to others through body, mind, and speech, I alone am scorched by that sin and am exceedingly miserable."
Thus, while remaining in the womb, the creature laments in these many ways, either by itself, or...

Having comforted himself and, immediately after his birth, purified his mind through association with the virtuous and by hearing the deeds of Viṣṇu, he performed righteous acts; [he beheld] the pair of lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the inner self of the entire universe, who consists of truth, knowledge, and bliss, who has accomplished the liberation of the worlds through the power of His own energy, and whose lotus feet are worshipped by the multitudes of all gods, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, pannagas, munis, and kinnaras.

Having worshipped with devotion and having placed within his heart Him who is the cause of the destruction of the world, who is clearly revealed by the secret Upanishads of the Vedas, and who is the supreme refuge of all the worlds, he meditated in his mind: "I shall pass through this most painful house of the purificatory rites."

O Sage Nārada, because at the time of his mother’s delivery, the embodied being within the womb is tormented by the wind, causing pain to his mother as well, he is forcibly expelled through the path of the birth canal by the noose of karma and experiences the full extent of all agonies belonging to that single lifetime.
Therefore, having been crushed by the mechanism of the womb through that extreme suffering, once emerged from the womb, he falls into a state of unconsciousness.
But the external air revives it;

immediately upon the touch of the external air, although all the sufferings previously experienced while his memory was lost have ceased, he experiences extreme suffering because, due to the absence of cognition, he does not recognize them even as they are present.

Thus, having attained the state of infancy, the creature—his body smeared with its own filth and urine, though afflicted by internal and other pains—is unable to speak; tormented by hunger and thirst, when he cries, [people] give him the breast and so forth.
Thinking thus, they exert themselves.
Thus, experiencing manifold bodies and enjoyments as dependent upon others, he is unable to ward them off even from gadflies and the like.

Having reached the state of childhood, he constantly experiences such internal suffering as being beaten by his mother, father, and teacher; a habit of wandering about; playing in dust, ashes, mud, and the like; being perpetually engaged in quarrels; impurity; being occupied with many apparent activities and tasks that are ultimately impossible; and so forth. // NarP_1,32.26 //
Then, due to their youthful state, they are devoted to the acquisition of wealth, the preservation of what has been acquired, and are extremely distressed by its loss or expenditure;
deluded by *māyā*, with minds corrupted by desire, anger, and other passions, they are constantly intent on envy, dedicated to means for seizing the property and wives of others,
absorbed in contemplating means for maintaining sons, friends, wives, and so forth, defiled by vain egoism, and [anxious] regarding the illnesses and other misfortunes of their sons and kin.

When beings are afflicted by diseases and other such sufferings, having abandoned all concern for themselves, they themselves become overwhelmed by internal suffering in the presence of those tormented by illness and the like, and they experience anxiety in the manner that will be described. // NarP_1,32.27 //
Not even a single matter such as house or field was considered;
how could there be a livelihood for a family so prosperous? (NarP 1,32.28)
"I have no principal capital, and the rain does not fall;
where has my horse fled, and why have my cows not returned? (NarP 1.32.29)
My wife has young children, I am afflicted by disease and destitute; through lack of foresight my farming has failed, and my sons weep constantly. (NarP 1.32.30)
"My home is broken and ruined, my kinsmen have gone far away, and no means of livelihood can be found; O King, the oppression is most unbearable. (NarP 1,32.31)
"My enemies are rushing toward me; how shall I conquer them?
I am incapable of resolve, and these guests have arrived. (NarP 1.32.32)
Thus, utterly overwhelmed by anxiety and unable to ward off his own sufferings, he reproaches fate, saying: "Fie on destiny! For what purpose was I, devoid of fortune, created? (NarP 1.32.33).
Likewise, having reached old age, his vital essence diminished, his body afflicted by wrinkles, grey hair, and the like, and beset by the oppression of diseases;

with trembling limbs, tormented by labored breathing, coughing, and so forth, his eyes rolling and turbid, his throat choked with phlegm, and being reviled by his sons, wife, and others—agitated by the thought, "When shall I meet death? Upon my passing, will my sons and others [take] the house, fields, and other things acquired by me?"—[he remains thus].
How will they protect it, or to whom will it belong?
When his wealth has been seized by others, overwhelmed by the suffering of possessiveness— wondering how his sons and others will survive—
he sighs deeply; repeatedly remembering the deeds he committed during his own youth, yet momentarily forgetting them, he remains constantly haunted as death draws near.

Afflicted by disease and distressed by internal fever, he moves here and there from his bed to his couch for a moment; tormented by hunger and thirst, he begs with extreme wretchedness, "Give me even a little water. Yet, hearing those possessed by fever say that water is not beneficial for them, he harbors intense hatred in his mind and becomes dull-witted.

Then, unable to pull away his hands and feet and surrounded by weeping kinsmen, he is incapable of speaking; preoccupied with the thought, "To whom will my self-earned wealth and so forth belong?", his eyes clouded with tears and his throat gasping, his life-force departs from his body.
Being threatened by the messengers of Yama and bound with nooses, he experiences the hells and other realms as described before.
Just as metals are thoroughly purified in fire by means of the application of *āmalaka* and other agents,
so too all living beings are intensely refined until the exhaustion of their karma.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one afflicted by the heat of the forest fire of saṃsāra should practice supreme knowledge; through knowledge, one shall attain liberation.
Those men who are devoid of knowledge are proclaimed to be like beasts;
therefore, for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra, one should thoroughly practice supreme knowledge.
Having attained this human birth, which accomplishes all actions, who else could be more senseless than he who does not serve Hari? (NarP 1.32.41)
"O lords of sages, how wonderful! How wonderful! How wonderful!
While Kāmadeva Viṣṇu remains established [in his form], men indeed go to torment."
Alas! Even though Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who grants the fruits of all desires, is present, those devoid of knowledge are cooked in the hells.
While this body is transitory and flows with urine and excrement,
the ignorant, shrouded by great delusion, imagine it to be eternal.
That man who, having obtained this body which is loathsome due to its flesh, blood, and other constituents,
does not worship Viṣṇu— the one who cuts asunder the cycle of worldly existence— is a perpetrator of a heinous sin.
Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery! Alas, indeed, what folly!
Even a Caṇḍāla, O Brahmin, who is devoted to the meditation on Hari, is possessed of great happiness.
Seeing the filth of excrement, urine, and other impurities issuing from their own bodies,
why indeed do foolish, sinful men not feel revulsion?
Human birth is difficult to obtain and is sought even by the gods;
having attained it, a wise person should exert effort for the sake of the next world.
Endowed with knowledge of the inner self and devoted to the worship of Hari,
they attain the supreme state from which return is difficult to find.
He from whom this universe is born, by whom consciousness is attained,
and into whom it goes to its dissolution— he is the liberator from saṃsāra.
Having worshipped that Lord of Gods, who, though devoid of qualities and infinite, appears as if possessed of qualities, one is completely liberated from the cycle of worldly existence.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Forest of Existence," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, everything that was asked by you, the wise one, has been fully explained."
For those bound by the snares of saṃsāra, there are indeed very many sufferings.
O rich in asceticism, tell me: what is considered the cutter of this snare of saṃsāra? By what means might liberation be attained? Tell me that.
O best of sages, nets of karma are woven daily and intensely by living beings, and they are experienced as well; how can there be an end to them?
The embodied soul attains a body through karma; it is bound by desire.
Overcome by desire, one becomes subject to greed; from greed, one becomes intent on anger.
From anger, the destruction of dharma occurs; from the destruction of dharma, there is confusion of the intellect.
A man whose intellect is ruined commits sin once again. (NarP 1.33.5)
Therefore, tell me how one may abandon this body— the root of evil and devoted to sinful deeds— so that, casting it off, one may become a partaker of liberation.
Sanaka said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Your intellect is pure and powerful, since you desire the means for liberation from the sufferings of saṃsāra."
O observer of noble vows, by whose command Brahmā creates the entire world,
Hari protects it, and Rudra destroys it— he indeed is the bestower of liberation.

One should know that Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the one free from all affliction, who is the source of the power from which everything beginning with "I" and ending with the specific distinctions has arisen, is the bestower of liberation.
Having meditated upon that fierce and undecaying God, for whom all this is non-different—both that which moves and that which does not move—one is liberated from suffering. (NarP 1.33.10)
They declare that which is unchanging, unborn, pure, self-luminous, stainless,
consisting of the nature of knowledge, eternally blissful, and the means to liberation.
One should know that Hari, who bestows the eternal abode, is he whose forms of incarnation the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā worship.
Know that Truth which brings happiness— the Truth which those who have conquered their vital breaths, who have mastered their food, and who are ever devoted to meditation perceive within the heart.

Though devoid of qualities, he is the substratum of qualities; assuming a form for the sake of favoring the worlds, he dwells in the midst of space as the Full One—him they call the giver of liberation to men.
The overseer of all actions, who dwells in the heart of the embodied soul, who is incomparable and the support of all—that God one should go for refuge. (NarP 1.33.15)
The sages who perceive the ultimate reality call him Viṣṇu, the bestower of liberation, who at the end of the aeon withdraws everything and himself rests upon the waters.
He alone, who is worshipped with various sacrifices by those who know the meaning of the Vedas and understand ritual action,
is the bestower of the fruits of action and the giver of liberation to those whose actions are free from desire.

He who, assuming the forms of the deities and ancestors, partakes in the offerings of *havya* and *kavya* and other gifts—he is the unmanifest Lord; they call him the Sovereign who bestows liberation.
Whether meditated upon, saluted, or worshipped with devotion, he bestows the eternal abode; one should worship that compassionate one.
He who is the sole supreme Person, the support of all beings,
liberated from old age and death, the bestower of liberation— that imperishable one is Hari.
O Lord of Sages, those embodied beings who, having fully worshipped his lotus feet,
quickly attain immortality— they know him to be Puruṣottama.
It is bliss, the undecaying Brahman, the supreme eternal light;
it is that which is higher than the highest, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
They know that which is non-dual, devoid of qualities, eternal, without a second, incomparable, perfectly full, consisting of knowledge, and the means for attaining liberation. (NarP 1.33.23)
The yogi who always worships such a supreme reality through the application of the path of yoga attains the highest state.
The yogi who has completely renounced all attachments, who is endowed with virtues such as tranquility,
and who is free from desire and greed, attains the supreme state.
Nārada said:
"O best among speakers, tell me truly the means by which the perfection of yoga is attained by yogins through what specific action."
Sanaka said:
Those who contemplate the meaning of reality declare that supreme liberation is attainable through knowledge;
that knowledge has devotion as its root, and devotion likewise arises from those engaged in ritual action.
By whomsoever gifts, various sacrifices, pilgrimages to sacred fords,
and so forth have been performed throughout thousands of births, devotion to Hari shall arise in him.
The supreme, inexhaustible Dharma arises through even a slight fragment of devotion;
and by means of supreme faith, every sin is utterly destroyed.
When all evils have perished, the intellect becomes stainless;
that very intellect is designated by the term "knowledge" (jñāna) by the wise.
They say that knowledge bestows liberation; such knowledge belongs to the yogins.
Yoga, moreover, is declared to be of two kinds, distinguished as the yoga of action and the yoga of knowledge.
Without the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge is not accomplished for men;
therefore, one devoted to the yoga of action should worship Hari with faith.
These images of Keśava— known as Dvija, Bhūmi, Agni, Sūrya, Ambu, Dhātu, Hṛt, and Citra— are to be worshipped with devotion.
Averse to causing affliction by deed, mind, or speech,
one should therefore worship Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, endowed with devotion.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, celibacy,
non-possessiveness, lack of envy, and compassion are common to both types of yoga.
Having resolved in one's mind that the eternal Viṣṇu alone is the universe consisting of the moving and the non-moving, one should practice the two-fold yoga.
Those wise ones who regard all beings as themselves know the supreme state of the God of gods, the wielder of the discus.
If one whose soul is corrupted by anger and other vices should be intent on worship and meditation,
Viṣṇu is not pleased with him, since he is remembered as the Lord of Dharma.
If one whose soul is corrupted by desire and other passions should become intent on the worship of the deity,
he should be known as a hypocrite, equal to all evildoers.
If one who is devoted to austerity, worship, and meditation should become intent on malice,
then that austerity, that worship, and that meditation are indeed useless.
Therefore, a person intent on qualities such as tranquility and devoted to the yoga of action should properly worship Viṣṇu, who is the self of all, for the sake of liberation.
Devoted to the welfare of the entire world through action, mind, and speech,
one who worships the Lord of Gods— that is called *kriyā-yoga*.
He who praises Viṣṇu— Nārāyaṇa, the source of the world, the indwelling witness of all, and Hari— with hymns and other forms of praise, is called a practitioner of *karmayoga*.
Worship of Viṣṇu through fasting and other observances, as well as by listening to the Purāṇas and offering flowers and other articles, is declared to be *kriyā-yoga*.
Thus, for those who possess devotion toward Viṣṇu and whose minds are intent on the yoga of action,
all sins accumulated in previous births are indeed destroyed.
With a mind purified through the destruction of evil, one desires supreme knowledge;
for knowledge should be known as the giver of liberation—therefore, I shall tell you the means to attain it. (NarP 1.33.46)
In this world consisting of both the moving and the unmoving, which is both eternal and indeed impermanent,
the wise man should investigate thoroughly together with the virtuous who are experts in the meaning of the scriptures.
All objects are indeed impermanent, while Hari alone is remembered as eternal;
having abandoned the impermanent, one should take refuge in the eternal alone. (NarP 1.33.48)
One should likewise become detached from enjoyments both here and in the hereafter;
however, he who remains undetached continues to revolve in saṃsāra.
For that man who feels attachment toward impermanent things,
the cessation of saṃsāra never occurs.
One who desires liberation and is endowed with qualities such as tranquility should practice for knowledge;
for one devoid of qualities such as tranquility, knowledge is never perfected.
One who is free from passion and hatred, endowed with qualities such as tranquility,
and constantly devoted to meditation on Hari, is called a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu).
By these four means, one is said to possess a purified intellect;
devoted to compassion for all beings, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu as all-pervading.
"Nārāyaṇa stands pervading the entire universe, which consists of both the perishable and the imperishable"—O Brahmin, those who know this understand it to be knowledge born of yoga. (NarP 1.33.54)
Therefore, I shall now describe the means of yoga which turns one back from saṃsāra;
yoga is pure knowledge, and the wise know that knowledge to be the giver of liberation.
They say that the self is twofold, distinguished as the higher and the lower;
and the Atharvaṇa Śruti states: "Two Brahmans are to be known. (NarP 1.33.56)
The Supreme is said to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), while the other is endowed with egoity (ahaṅkāra). The realization of the non-difference between these two is designated as Yoga.

He who is the witness situated in the heart within the body composed of the five elements is called the "lower" (apara) by the virtuous; the Supreme Self (paramātman) is remembered as the "higher" (para).
They say the body is the field (kṣetra); that which resides therein is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
It is described as unmanifest, supreme, pure, and all-pervading.
But when the realization of the non-difference between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) occurs,
O best of sages, then the bonds of the lower self are severed.
The one, pure, imperishable, eternal Supreme Self, which pervades the universe,
appears as if possessed of diversity due to the differences in the consciousness of men.
That which is the one, non-dual, supreme, and eternal Brahman, praised by the Vedāntas— O twice-born, there is nothing higher than that.
For that Supreme Self, which is devoid of qualities, there is no action nor any object of action, nor form or color; nor indeed does it possess the state of being an agent or an enjoyer.
The source of all causes, the supreme radiance among all radiances—that which is beyond which nothing else exists—should be known for the sake of liberation. (NarP 1.33.64)

O twice-born one, that which consists of the Śabdabrahman—the Great Sayings (Mahāvākya) and so forth—and the knowledge arising from the inquiry into them, is the supreme means for liberation. (NarP 1.33.65)
To those devoid of right knowledge, the world appears as manifold;
but to those of supreme wisdom, O twice-born one, it is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
The one alone is supreme bliss, devoid of qualities, higher than the highest;
though immutable, he shines assuming many forms through the differentiation of consciousness.
Those possessed by illusion perceive duality within the Supreme Self through that very illusion;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, one who desires liberation should abandon illusion through yoga.
Māyā is neither of the nature of non-existence nor of the nature of existence, nor is it both;
therefore, it should be known as indefinable, that which causes the perception of duality to arise.
O best of sages, it is *māyā* itself that is understood by the word "knowledge";
therefore, the severance of ignorance occurs for those who have conquered their *māyā*.
The eternal, supreme Brahman is designated by the word "knowledge";
indeed, for the wise, the Supreme Self shines incessantly within the heart.
O best of sages, the yogi should destroy ignorance through yoga;
yoga is perfected by means of its eight limbs, which I shall describe to you according to their true nature.
The restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), as well as the postures (āsanas), O best of beings,
along with breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), and meditation (dhyāna) itself.
And concentration, O best of sages, along with the limbs of yoga in their proper order—
O Lord of Munis, I shall describe the characteristics of these in brief.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy,
non-possessiveness, freedom from anger, and freedom from envy— these are briefly declared to be the restraints (yamas).
Indeed, that which produces no affliction for any living beings whatsoever is called non-violence by the virtuous; it bestows the attainment of yoga.
O best of sages, they say that truth is the speaking of things as they truly are, through the discernment of dharma and adharma; now hear concerning non-stealing. (NarP 1.33.77)
The taking of another's property, whether by theft or by force, is called *steya* (theft) by the virtuous; its opposite is *asteya* (non-stealing).
The renunciation of sexual intercourse in all circumstances is proclaimed as *brahmacarya*;
by abandoning *brahmacarya*, even one possessed of knowledge becomes a sinner. (NarP 1.33.79)
He who has renounced all attachments yet engages in sexual intercourse should be known as equal to a Caṇḍāla, excluded from all social classes.
O Brahmin, for a man devoted to yoga who nevertheless harbors desire for sense-objects,
the sin of killing a Brahmin accrues to him merely by conversing with such a person.
If one who has renounced all attachments should again become attached,
he incurs the fault of a great sin through that attachment to those who are attached.
O Lord of Sages, the non-acceptance of material things even in times of distress is called non-possession; it brings about the perfect accomplishment of yoga.
Those who know the Dharma say that speaking with extreme harshness out of self-exaltation is anger; non-anger is the opposite of that.
Seeing others superior in wealth and other such things, the intense distress felt in the mind is called envy by the virtuous; the abandonment of that [envy] is indeed non-envy.
Thus, O best of the wise, the restraints (yamas) have been briefly declared;
I shall now speak to you of the observances (niyamas), so listen to them, O Nārada. (NarP 1.33.86)
Austerity, self-study, contentment, purity, worship of Hari,
and the performance of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyopāsana) are proclaimed as the primary observances (niyamas).
Where the emaciation of the body through the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such practices is performed,
that is declared by the virtuous to be austerity, the supreme means for accomplishing yoga.

O twice-born one, [I shall explain] the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Praṇava, of the twelve-syllable mantra, of the eight-syllable mantra, and of the collection of great sayings (mahāvākya). (NarP 1.33.89)
Recitation and self-study are declared to be the supreme means for accomplishing yoga;
for that fool who abandons self-study, yoga does not succeed.
Even without yoga, the destruction of sin occurs for men through the study of sacred texts (svādhyāya);
for the deities, being gratified by such studies, become truly propitious.
Recitation is said to be threefold: vocal, whispered, and mental;
and among these three, O best of Brahmins, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
The vocal recitation (japa) of a mantra is said to be that which is performed correctly with clear syllables and words; it bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
In the recitation of a mantra, the discernment of each word from the next is called *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation;
it is declared to be twice as superior as the former.
For having performed the investigation of each respective meaning within the sequence of syllables,
that mental recitation is declared to be the bestower of the perfection of yoga.
The deity is always pleased with one who praises them through recitation;
therefore, one endowed with the practice of self-study shall obtain all their heart's desires.
Contentment is proclaimed as being satisfied with whatever is obtained by chance;
a person devoid of contentment shall find no happiness anywhere. (NarP 1.33.97)
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
rather, desire increases, thinking, "When shall I obtain even more than this? (NarP 1.33.98).
Therefore, having abandoned desire, which causes the emaciation of the body,
