one should be devoted to dharma and content with whatever is obtained by chance.
Purity is traditionally taught to be of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal:
external purification is achieved through earth and water, while internal purity is the purification of one's disposition.
O best of sages, those various sacrifices performed by those devoid of inner purity do not bear fruit, like oblations cast upon ashes.
For those devoid of purity of being, every action is fruitless;
therefore, having abandoned all passion and the like, one should become happy.
Even if one has performed purification with thousands of loads of earth and ten million jars of water,
a person of wicked soul is considered equal to a Caṇḍāla.
But if one who is devoid of inner purity is intent on the worship of a deity,
that very deity destroys him, and he falls into hell.
He who, devoid of internal purity, practices external purification,
does not attain peace— like a decorated wine-vessel.
Those who undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords while devoid of purity of mind— the sacred fords do not purify them, just as rivers do not purify a vessel that once held liquor.
O best of sages, one should know that he who proclaims the teachings with his speech yet desires evil with his mind is the foremost among great sinners.
But those whose minds are purified, who perform that which is the unsurpassed Dharma alone—know that its fruit is inexhaustible and bestows happiness. (NarP 1.33.108)
He whose devotion to Hari is firm through action, mind, and speech, and through hearing praises and worship, is proclaimed as one who performs the worship of Hari.
The restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) have thus been briefly explained;
those whose minds are purified by these know that liberation is within their grasp.
With a steady intellect and senses conquered through the observances (yamas) and restraints (niyamas),
one should properly practice the posture (āsana), the supreme means for achieving yoga.
The lotus-seat, the auspicious cross-seat, the lion-seat, the cock-seat, the elephant-seat, the tortoise-seat, the vajra-seat, the boar-seat, and the deer-cloth seat.
The *krauñca*, the *nālika*, and the *sarvatobhadra*; the *vārṣabha*, the *nāga*, the *mātsya*, the *vaiyāghra*, and the *ardhacandraka*. 113.
The staff-wind posture, the mountain, the abyss, the mallet,
the crocodile, the triple-path, the wood, the pillar, and likewise the ear-opening.
The earth-seat (bhaumāsana) and the hero-seat (vīrāsana), which are the means for accomplishing yoga— indeed,
thirty postures have been described by the lords of sages.
Devoted to the service of his guru, having bound himself to one of these [vows],
the lay practitioner— transcending dualities and free from envy— shall conquer his vital breaths.
Facing either east, north, or even west,
one should conquer the vital breaths through practice in a place that is silent and devoid of people.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the wind residing within the body; its expansion and its restraint are called *prāṇāyāma*. It is proclaimed to be of two kinds. 118.
There is the "without-embryo" (agarbha) and the "with-embryo" (sagarbha); of these two, the latter is superior.
That which is devoid of victorious meditation (jayadhyāna) is "without-embryo," while that which is endowed with it is "with-embryo."
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), retention (kuṃbhaka), and likewise the voiding (śūnyaka)—
thus has breath control (prāṇāyāma) been declared to be fourfold by the wise.
The southern channel of living beings is celebrated as Piṅgalā;
she has the Sun as her presiding deity and is known as the womb of the ancestors.
The right channel, known as Iḍā, is called the womb of the gods;
know that the moon is its presiding deity, O best of sages.
Between these two, the *suṣumṇā* channel is traditionally taught;
it is known to be extremely subtle, most secret, and has Brahmā as its presiding deity.
One should exhale the breath through the left nostril; this is known as *recaka* because of the act of exhaling (*recana*).
One should fill [the breath] through the right nostril alone; this is known as *pūraka* because of the act of filling (*pūraṇa*).
Having restrained this [breath] which has filled one's own body, one does not release it;
it remains like a full jar—that indeed is renowned as kumbhaka.
One neither grasps nor abandons the wind situated within or without;
know that to be the true state of breath control (prāṇāyāma), called "the void" (śūnyaka).
The vital breath (prāṇa) must be gradually conquered like a rutting lordly elephant;
otherwise, indeed, terrifying great diseases arise.
The yogi, freed from all impurity, should gradually control the vital breath;
liberated from all sins, he shall attain the state of Brahman.
The lord of sages, having drawn back the senses that are attached to their objects, restrains them; this is known as withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
O twice-born one, even those great-souled ones who have conquered their senses, though they may be absorbed in meditation and emptiness,
go to the supreme Brahman from which a return is difficult to obtain.
But one who would be intent on meditation while the collection of his senses remains unsubdued—
one should know him to be a deluded soul, and for him, meditation is not perfected.
Whatever one perceives, one should perceive all that within oneself as being like the Self;
with the senses withdrawn, one should maintain that state—that indeed is *dhāraṇā*.
Having firmly withdrawn those [senses] into the heart through yoga, one whose collection of senses is conquered should meditate upon the supreme Self, the infallible sustainer of all.
Viṣṇu, who is the soul of the entire universe, the sole cause of all sorrow,
whose eyes are like the petals of a blooming lotus, and who is adorned with beautiful earrings.
The god had long arms and noble limbs, was adorned with every ornament,
wore yellow garments, and had a golden sacred thread.
The god who wears a garland of *tulasī*, who is resplendent with the *kaustubha* gem,
whose chest bears the *śrīvatsa* mark, and who is saluted by gods and demons.
In the eight-petaled heart-lotus, which is twelve finger-breadths in extent,
one should meditate upon the unmanifest Self, the pervasive Lord who is higher than the highest.
Meditation has been described by the virtuous as the one-pointedness of the mind;
by practicing meditation for even a moment, a person may attain supreme liberation.
Through meditation sins are destroyed; through meditation one attains liberation;
through meditation Hari becomes gracious; and through meditation all goals are accomplished.
Whatever form belongs to Mahāviṣṇu, one should meditate upon that with a concentrated mind;
by that meditation, Hari, his soul being pleased, indeed bestows liberation.
O best of beings, one should make the mind unwavering upon the object of meditation,
so that the states of meditation, the object of meditation, and the meditator utterly vanish.
Then, immortality arises from partaking in the nectar of knowledge;
through uninterrupted meditation, there shall be the realization of non-duality.
When one is endowed with the supreme bliss of deep sleep, with the senses stilled,
and remains steady like a lamp in a windless place, that is called samādhi.
O best of beings, in the state of meditative absorption, the yogi does not hear, does not see,
does not smell, does not touch, and says nothing at all.
But the Self—stainless, pure, whose form is being, consciousness, and bliss, and liberated from all limiting adjuncts—shines unwaveringly to the yogis. (NarP 1,33.145)
Although the supreme deity is devoid of qualities, he appears as if possessing qualities due to ignorance; however, upon the destruction of ignorance, he remains established exactly as before.
The supreme light, the immeasurable self, like a master of illusion among illusionists,
reveals the stainless Brahman to the wise man upon the destruction of that [ignorance].
The supreme light is one alone, without a second, and stainless;
it abides as the inner ruler within all beings.
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the eternal Self, the cause of the entire universe—
those foremost among the knowers of wisdom behold that which is purer than the purest, higher than the highest.
Established through the differentiation of phonemes from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*,
the beginningless Primordial Person is celebrated as the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*).
Pure, imperishable, eternal, full, situated in the midst of space, blissful, stainless, and peaceful—that is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman. (NarP 1.33.151)
In their hearts, yogis behold the eternal Supreme Self, which is changeless, unborn, and pure; it is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman.
I shall now describe another form of meditation; listen, O best of sages, for it is like a rain of nectar for men scorched by the sufferings of saṃsāra. (NarP 1.33.153)
One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, the supreme bliss, who is established in the Praṇava;
he is of the nature of sound, incomparable, and situated above the half-measure (ardhamātrā).
The syllable *a* is the form of Brahmā; the syllable *u* possesses the form of Viṣṇu;
the syllable *m* would be the form of Rudra; and the half-measure (*ardhamātra*) is of the nature of the Supreme Self (*parātman*).
Three measures have been declared, presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
their combination, O Brahmin, awakens one to the Supreme Brahman.
The supreme Brahman is the object of expression, while the syllable Om is traditionally known as its designator;
for, O twice-born ones, the relationship between the expressed and the expresser exists between these two only by way of figurative designation.
Those who constantly recite the *praṇava* are liberated from all sins;
and being fully engaged in its practice, they attain supreme liberation.
And while reciting the Praṇava mantra, which embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
one should meditate upon the stainless radiance within oneself, equal to ten million suns.
Whether in the form of a Śālagrāma stone or in the form of an image,
one should meditate in the heart upon whatever object is destructive of sin.
O Lord of Sages, this Vaiṣṇava knowledge which has been told to you—
having known this, the lord of yogis attains supreme liberation.
But whoever, being composed, should either hear this or even read it,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain the same world as Hari.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Yoga," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said: O great sage, all the limbs of yoga have been fully explained.
O Omniscient One, even now, let that which I ask be told.
"You have stated that yoga is accomplished only by those possessed of devotion;
and for whomsoever the Lord of All is pleased, for him there is eternal devotion. (NarP 1.34.2)
O omniscient sage, ocean of compassion, tell me that by which Janārdana, the Lord of all, the God of gods, is pleased. (NarP 1.34.3)
Sanaka said: O Brahmin, if you desire liberation, worship with your whole being Nārāyaṇa, the supreme deity, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Enemies do not harm him, nor do malevolent planets afflict him;
even Rākṣasas do not look upon the man who is devoted to Viṣṇu.
For one whose devotion to Janārdana, the God of gods, becomes firm, his spiritual merits are accomplished; therefore, those possessed of devotion are superior.
Those feet of men are fruitful which go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
those hands should be known as fruitful which are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Those eyes of men are truly fruitful which behold the Destroyer of Danu;
that tongue alone is called virtuous by the wise which is devoted to the name of Hari.
"Truth, truth, and again truth—I speak this while raising my arm:
there is no reality equal to the Guru; O bowing one, there is no deity higher than Keśava."
I speak the truth; I speak what is beneficial; I speak the essence again and again:
in this worthless cycle of existence, the only truth is the worship of Hari.
Having severed with the axe of devotion to Hari the very firm snare of saṃsāra, which bestows great delusion, become one who possesses ultimate happiness.
Their minds were united with Viṣṇu; their speech was devoted to Him as its ultimate goal;
and those ears of theirs, honored by the world, were filled with the essence of His stories.
O Nārada, constantly worship the God who is bliss, the imperishable, the void, beyond even the three states, and situated in the midst of space.
O tiger among sages, its location or its true nature can never be pointed out, nor can it be seen by those of unrefined self.
When that eternal inner controller exists joined with all the instruments of perception, he is called "the waking state" by the wise.
When this Self moves about at its own will, joined with the internal organs, it is called "waking"; indeed, when it is devoid of sleep, it is called "awake."
When this Self is devoid of form, it is not joined with external organs, nor likewise with internal organs; it is free from both merit and demerit.
For bliss that is liberated from all limiting adjuncts, devoid of qualities, and all-pervading—
the God consisting of the Supreme Brahman— is celebrated as deep sleep.
O best of Brahmins, this world of moving and non-moving beings is indeed composed of mental cultivation;
it is as flickering as lightning. Therefore, O lord of sages, take refuge in Janārdana.
The Lord of the worlds is pleased only with him in whom non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness abide.
Endowed with compassion for all beings and devoted to the worship of Brahmins,
the Lord of the World, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, was pleased with him.
He who delights in noble discourse and engages in noble discourse—
Lord Ramāpati is pleased with him, for he is in the company of the virtuous and free from the sense of "I."
Adhokṣaja is truly pleased with him who constantly chants the names of Viṣṇu even when distracted by hunger, thirst, stumbling, or other such conditions.
O Sage, may that woman who regards her husband as her very life and is devoted to the worship of her husband be pleased by the Lord of the World, who grants her his own abode.
But for those who are free from envy, devoid of egoism,
and devoted to the worship of the gods, Keśava is pleased.
Therefore, listen, O divine sage, and worship Hari constantly;
do not indulge in vain pride on account of this fortune that flickers like lightning.
The body is joined with death, life is exceedingly fickle,
wealth is seized by kings and others, and prosperities are momentary in their destruction.

Do you not see, O divine sage, that half of one's lifespan is destroyed by sleep, and how much of that lifespan is further consumed by eating and other such activities? How little of it remains truly gathered!
How much of his life has passed in childhood, how much has been spent in vain, and how much in the enjoyment of sense-objects; when will he finally practice the Dharma?
In childhood, one should engage in the worship of Acyuta even through old age;
therefore, while you are still young, perform your duties free from egoism.
O Sage, do not meet your destruction, submerged as you are in the abyss of saṃsāra;
for destruction is the abode of ruin and the supreme state of calamities.
Why should a man, with the notion that it is eternal, commit sin in vain for this body, which is the abode of enjoyments yet thoroughly defiled by impurities and the like? (NarP 1.34.32)
In this saṃsāra, which is devoid of essence, filled with various sufferings, and certainly crowded with death, one must not place any trust. (NarP 1.34.33)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, listen; I tell you this truth:
for the sake of ceasing the union with the body, [worship] Janārdana immediately.
Having abandoned pride as well as greed, and being free from desire and anger,
worship Viṣṇu constantly— you who have obtained this human state so difficult to attain.
O best of beings, after wandering through thousands of millions of births among stationary objects and other forms of existence,
human birth is somehow attained.
Even there, O best of beings, the perception of them as deities, the perception of them as gifts,
and likewise the perception of them as objects of enjoyment for men, is the fruit of austerity performed in previous births.
Having attained this human birth which is so difficult to find, whoever does not worship Hari even once—
who else is more foolish than that person, being dull-witted and insentient?
Having attained this human birth which is so difficult to find, those who do not worship Hari—where can there be any discernment for such extreme fools? (NarP 1.34.39)
The Lord of the World, when propitiated, bestows the desired fruit; who, being scorched by the miseries of saṃsāra, would not worship him? (NarP 1.34.40)
O best of sages, even a Caṇḍāla who is a devotee of Viṣṇu is superior to a twice-born;
whereas a twice-born man devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu is the lowest of outcasts.
Therefore, having abandoned desire and the like, one should worship the imperishable Hari;
for when He is satisfied, everything is satisfied, since Hari is omnipresent.
Just as every footprint is absorbed within the footprint of an elephant,
so too does the entire universe, with its moving and unmoving beings, dissolve into Viṣṇu.
Just as the world, with its moving and unmoving beings, is pervaded by space,
even so is this entire universe of the mobile and immobile pervaded by Hari.
For humans, death follows birth, and birth is indeed the means for death;
know that both of these are near at hand, and their destruction comes through service to Hari.
Janārdana, when meditated upon, remembered, worshipped, or even saluted, is the severer of the bonds of saṃsāra; who would not worship him?
O brahmin sage, by the mere utterance of whose name great sins are destroyed, and by worshipping whom a man becomes a partaker of liberation.
"O twice-born one, how wonderful! How wonderful! How wonderful indeed is this:
while Hari remains present, the world revolves in saṃsāra! (NarP 1.34.48)
O you whose wealth is asceticism, though I am being led away by the messengers of Yama and rendered powerless by the instruments of dharma, I shall speak this truth again and again.
As long as there is no impairment of the senses, and as long as disease does not afflict one,
for that very time should one worship Viṣṇu, if one desires liberation.
As soon as a living being emerges from the mother’s womb,
death itself becomes present; therefore, one should be devoted to dharma.
"Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery! Oh, how terrible it is that this body, having recognized its perishable nature, does not practice the Dharma at all! (NarP 1,34.52)
"Truth, truth, and again truth—raising up my arm, I declare this:
having abandoned deceitful conduct, one should worship Vāsudeva. (NarP 1.34.53)
Again and again I speak what is beneficial, O Nārada, raising my arms: Viṣṇu is to be worshipped with one's whole soul; likewise, malice and falsehood must be abandoned.
Mental anguish has its root in anger; anger is the bond of saṃsāra.
Anger causes the destruction of dharma; therefore, one should completely avoid it.
This birth has its root in desire; desire is the cause of evil;
desire is the destroyer of fame; therefore, one should utterly abandon it.
Avarice is remembered as the cause of all nets of suffering and the means to the hells; therefore, one should abandon it as well. (NarP 1.34.57)
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
therefore, having fully yoked it to the Supreme Self, one should become happy.
Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, of men!
While Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, stands present, they do not worship him, being arrogant with pride.
Without propitiating the Lord of the World, the sustainer of all and the infallible one,
how indeed can those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra reach the further shore?
"By the medicine that is the utterance of the names Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda, all diseases perish; I speak the truth, the absolute truth."
Those who constantly utter "Nārāyaṇa, Jagannātha, Vāsudeva, Janārdana," are indeed honored everywhere.
O best of sages, even the gods beginning with Brahmā do not know his power; go for refuge to him, O sage.
"Alas, the folly! Alas, the folly! Alas, the folly of the evil-minded, O Nārada! They do not recognize Viṣṇu, who resides within the lotus of the heart."
Listen, O tiger among sages; I tell you again and again:
Hari is pleased with those who possess faith, but not by wealth nor by kinsmen.
O best of beings, in birth after birth, those men who possess devotion to Viṣṇu shall have kinsmen, abundant wealth, and sons. (NarP 1.34.66)
This body is composed of the root of evil and is likewise devoted to sinful deeds;
knowing this, Janārdana should be constantly worshipped.
Sons, friends, wives, and many other riches shall belong to those who are devoted to the worship of Hari; of this there is no doubt.
One who desires happiness in this world and the next should constantly worship Hari;
one who desires unhappiness in this world and the next should be intent on censuring others.
Fie upon the birth of those devoid of devotion to Janārdana, the God of gods; and fie again and again upon that wealth which is empty of gifts to worthy recipients! 1.34.70.
O best of sages, that person whose body does not bow to Viṣṇu, the divider of karma, should be known as a mere mine of sins.
Know for certain that whatever wealth is guarded by one who is devoid of giving to worthy recipients is, in this world, effectively guarded by theft. (NarP 1.34.72)
Intoxicated by the flickering splendor of lightning and lacking even momentary stability,
they do not worship the Lord of the Universe, the liberator from the bonds of worldly existence.
Creation is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as divine (daivī) and demonic (āsuri).
That which is endowed with devotion to Hari is divine; that which is devoid of it is indeed demonic, O Great One.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, listen:
those who are devoted to Hari are the most excellent and renowned everywhere, for such devotion is very difficult to attain.
Keśava is pleased with those who are free from malice, who are devoted to the protection of others, and who are devoid of desire and the like.
But those who are devoted to serving Viṣṇu through sweeping and other such acts,
and who are intent on giving gifts to worthy recipients, go to the supreme state.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Devotion to Hari," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanaka said:
I shall speak again of the majesty of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods.
For those who recite or hear it, the mass of their sins is instantly destroyed.
Peaceful, having conquered the sixfold group of enemies, and rendered free from egoism through yoga,
they worship the imperishable one whose form is knowledge by means of the yoga of knowledge.
Those who have been purified by bathing at sacred fords, by vows, gifts, austerities,
and sacrifices, worship the imperishable Sustainer of All through the yoga of action.
Greedy, addicted to vices, and ignorant, they do not worship the Lord of the World; like fools who are neither subject to old age nor death, these worms of hell remain [in their state].
Intoxicated by the splendor of streaks of lightning and reviled by those who utter the sound "haṃ" in vain,
they do not worship the Lord of the World, the bestower of all prosperity.
By the grace of fate, some rare individuals are born here in this world devoted to the dharma of Hari, peaceful, serving the lotus feet of Hari, and intent on bestowing grace upon the world.
He who worships Hari with devotion through action, mind, and speech,
goes to the supreme abode, the most excellent of all worlds.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, which destroys all sins for those who recite it and those who hear it. (NarP 1.35.8)
I shall proclaim that life-story of Yajñamālin and Sumālin,
by the mere hearing of which one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
O Brahmin, in former times, during the Raivata Manvantara, there was a certain man known as Vedamālin, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (NarP 1.35.10)
Endowed with compassion for all living beings and devoted to the worship of Hari,
he became intent on acquiring wealth for the sake of his son, friends, and wife.
He engaged in the sale of forbidden goods as well as the sale of liquids;
he conversed with Caṇḍālas and others, and likewise accepted gifts from them.
He sold his ascetic merits and likewise sold his vows;
he undertook pilgrimages for the sake of others and caused them to be made for the sake of his wife.
O Brahmin, as time passed, two sons were born to him,
Yajñamālin and Sumālin, who were twins and exceedingly handsome.
Then their father, filled with great affection, nourished those two boys out of paternal love with many provisions.
Having diligently acquired wealth through many means, Vedamālin counted his own riches in order to know how much he possessed.
Having personally calculated thousands of millions of treasures, multiplied by millions upon millions, he was struck with wonder as he contemplated their wealth.
This wealth has been acquired through accepting gifts from the unworthy, by selling goods that should not be sold,
and by the sale of their own austerity and other such means.
Even now my unbearable craving has not attained peace;
for it desires countless pieces of gold, each equal to Mount Meru. (NarP 1.35.19)
"Alas! I consider this to be a great misery, the means for accomplishing all afflictions;
for one attains all desires, yet still longs for something else. (NarP 1.35.20)
The hair of one who grows old decays; the teeth decay as one grows old;
the eyes and ears grow old; yet craving alone remains ever youthful.
All my senses are becoming dull,
my strength has been destroyed by old age, and my thirst has become youthful once more.
He for whom there exists a painful hope is neither wise nor learned;
even one who is perfectly tranquil may become full of anger, and even an intelligent man may become utterly dull-witted.
Hope brings about the ruin of men and is like an unconquerable enemy;
therefore, a wise person should abandon hope if they desire eternal happiness.
Strength, splendor, fame, knowledge, honor, and old age,
as well as birth in a noble family— hope destroys all these with its extreme velocity.
This is said to be a marvel among men who are overcome by desire:
even a Cāṇḍāla who gives something has surpassed them. (NarP 1.35.26)
Alas! Those mortals who are overwhelmed by desire, possessed of great delusion and extreme arrogance, never recognize the suffering caused by contempt and the like. (NarP 1.35.27)
By me, too, this wealth was acquired through many hardships;
my body has grown old, and my strength has been taken away by decrepitude.
"From now on, I shall strive with devotion for the sake of the next world.
Having resolved thus, O best of Brahmins, he became devoted to the path of dharma.
At that very moment, he divided all that wealth into four parts;
he himself, however, took away two shares from the wealth he had acquired.
And he gave the remaining two shares to both his sons,
intending at that time to effect the destruction of the sins he had acquired himself.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, he constructed water-stations, ponds, and groves, as well as many temples for the gods, and he bestowed gifts of food and other necessities.
Having thus distributed his entire wealth, the devotee of Hari went to the forest at the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa to practice austerities.
There he beheld a most delightful hermitage frequented by sages,
adorned with clusters of trees laden with fruit and flowers.
It was graced by aged sages who were devoted to the contemplation of the scriptures, chanting the supreme Brahman, and intent upon its service.
There he beheld the sage named Saṃjña, surrounded by his disciples,
proclaiming the supreme Brahman and appearing as a mass of splendor.
Seeing the sage endowed with qualities such as tranquility, free from passion and the like,
and subsisting on withered leaves, Māli bowed down before him.
Knowing that he was coming,
O Sage, she prepared a worthy offering for him with bulbs, roots, fruits, and other foods, regarding him as Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed the rites of hospitality for him, Vedamālin, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low with humility, spoke to that best of speakers.
O Blessed One, I have accomplished what was to be done; my defilement has vanished.
O illustrious one, O wise one, uplift me with the gift of knowledge. (NarP 1.35.40)
Having been addressed thus by him, the eloquent and best of sages, knowing [the truth],
spoke with a smile to Guṇānvita, the son of Veda.
Jānitrī said:
"Listen, O tiger among brahmins, to the cause for cutting through the cycle of worldly existence;
I shall explain it in brief, though it is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined their selves."
Worship Viṣṇu eternally as the supreme; remember the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Never, at any time, utter slander against others or engage in backbiting.
O Mahāmati, always be devoted to helping others,
intent upon the worship of Hari, and abandon the company of fools.
Having abandoned desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, and having seen the world as being like yourself, you will attain peace.
Never at any time harbor envy or revile others;
abandon deceitful conduct, egoism, and harshness.
"Show compassion toward all beings and likewise serve the virtuous;
do not reveal the religious duties performed by you out of pride in your tail."
Seeing those intent on improper conduct, do not remain indifferent if you have the power [to act]; always honor your guests without causing hardship to your own family.
Worship Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, with leaves, flowers, fruits, or even with dūrvā grass and tender shoots, according to your desire.
Satisfy the gods, the sages, and the ancestors according to the prescribed rites;
O Vapra, be devoted to the service of the sacred fire in accordance with the rules.
Be constantly devoted to sweeping the temple of the deity,
and likewise perform the smearing [of the floor] with great concentration.
Always repair what is decayed, broken, or worn out in the temple of the gods; beautify the path and provide lamps in the sanctuary of Viṣṇu.
Or else, always worship Mādhava with bulbs, roots, and fruits, as well as with circumambulations, prostrations, and the recitation of hymns. (NarP 1.35.53)
Listen to the Purāṇas and likewise read the Purāṇas;
read the Vedānta as well, doing so every day according to your ability.
In this way, your knowledge will become the most supreme of the supreme;
through that knowledge, liberation from all sins will certainly occur. (NarP 1.35.55)
Thus enlightened by him, the high-minded Vedamālin,
who was constantly devoted to knowledge, attained a small portion of that knowledge.
Once, however, Vedamālin, impelled by a mere fragment of knowledge, reflected within himself: "Who am I? What is my action? What is mine? (NarP 1.35.57)
"How was my birth brought about? What is the nature of my form?"—thus intent on such inquiry, he remained unwearied day and night.

Having become uncertain in mind, that best of the twice-born, having returned to where the Veda was displayed, bowed down and spoke this again: NarP_1,35.59: "Having become uncertain in mind, that best of the twice-born, having returned to where the Veda was displayed, bowed down and spoke this again."
Vedamālin said:
"O Guru, best among the knowers of Brahman, my mind is utterly bewildered.
Tell me: who am I? What is my action? And how was my birth?"
Jānitrī said:
"Truly, truly, O noble brother, the mind is firmly resolved;
yet how can a mind driven by the wind of ignorance reach the state of true being?"
Even that which is expressed as "mine" is held to be an illusion;
for the wise, O learned one, the absence of ego is the nature of the mind, not of the self.
Furthermore, as for what you said regarding "Who am I?", since I am empty of birth and so forth, how indeed can I perform that? (NarP 1.35.63)
How indeed can I [describe] the Supreme Self, which is of incomparable nature, devoid of qualities, formless, and immeasurable? 35.64.
How can action be predicated of that which is the supreme light by nature, whose self is perfectly full and imperishable, and whose essential being is uninterrupted?
O Brahmin, how can action and birth be attributed to the self-luminous, eternal, infinite Supreme Self?
O twice-born one, there is nothing else here than that eternal, supreme Brahman, which is ageless, knowable through knowledge alone, perfectly full, and the highest bliss.
Knowledge derived from statements such as "That thou art" is the means to liberation;
once that uncontrived knowledge is established, everything becomes identical with Brahman.
Thus enlightened by him, O lord of sages, Vedamālin rejoiced,
beholding the imperishable Lord within his very self.
Having ascertained that "I am indeed Brahman—devoid of limiting adjuncts, self-luminous, and stainless"—he attained supreme peace. (NarP 1.35.70)
Then, having bowed to his preceptor, the lord of sages, Vedamālin remained constantly devoted to meditation, knowing that he would need him for the sake of worldly affairs.
After a long time had passed, O lord of sages,
Vedamālin reached the city of Vārāṇasī and attained supreme liberation.
Whoever reads this chapter or listens to it with a concentrated mind shall attain the severance of the bonds of karma and obtain happiness. (NarP 1.35.73)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Knowledge," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannārādīya Purāṇa*.
Sanaka said: "O best of sages, those two who were declared to be the sons of Vedamālin—"
Yajñamālin and Sumālin—the deeds of these two are now being told.
Of those two, the elder, Yajñamālin, divided the wealth accumulated by his father;
he then gave one portion to the younger brother as his share.
And Sumālī, O twice-born one, being constantly afflicted by calamities, caused all his wealth to perish through such means as theft and the like.
He was constantly devoted to song and instrumental music, addicted to the drinking of liquor,
lusting after the charms of courtesans, and became an adulterer.
When all the gold accumulated by his ancestors had been exhausted,
he seized the property of others and became devoted to courtesans.
Seeing Sumālin’s trident, the high-minded Yajñamālin became exceedingly distressed and spoke thus to his brother: ||| NarP_1,36.6 |||
"Enough, my younger brother, with this extremely wretched way of life in our family;
you alone have become a wicked soul, devoted to great sin. (NarP 1.36.7)
Having resolved, "I shall kill him," he seized his elder brother by the hair with sword in hand, despite the latter's repeated attempts to restrain him.
Then a most terrible and great clamor arose in the city;
and the enraged citizens bound that Sumālin.
For Yajñamālin, of immeasurable soul, having entreated the citizens in his distress and being overcome by brotherly affection, set them free from their bonds.
Furthermore, Yajñamālin divided his own wealth into two parts;
he took half for himself and gave half to his younger brother.
O Nārada, that extremely deluded soul Sumālī,
together with arrogant fools and Pāraśava Caṇḍālas, consumed that wealth as well.
The prosperity of the wicked is for the enjoyment of the evil;
though the neem tree be rich in fruit, it is enjoyed only by crows.
O Sage, Sumālī squandered that wealth given by his brother;
intoxicated by the drinking of liquor, he ate cow-flesh and other forbidden foods.
Abandoned by all his kinsmen, accompanied by a Cāṇḍāla woman,
and even harassed by the king, the Brahmin entered a desolate forest.
O Brahmin, Yajñamālin was wise and always devoted to dharma;
having his impurities removed through the company of the virtuous, he gave food without restraint.
O best of men, devoted always to righteousness, he diligently protected all the tanks and other works constructed by his father.
All the wealth of the high-souled Yajñamālin was bestowed away;
he was devoted to giving to worthy recipients and was one who set forth upon the path of dharma.
Oh, how the riches of the virtuous are for the enjoyment of the good!
The fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree is enjoyed by the immortals alone.
Having distributed his wealth for the sake of dharma, the high-minded Yajñamālin became constantly devoted to the proper service of the temple of Viṣṇu.
As time passed, those two reached old age;
both Yajñamālin and Sumālin died at the same time.
To this high-souled Yajñamālin, who was devoted to the worship of Hari,
Hari sent a celestial chariot attended by his own attendants.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, the high-minded Yajñamālin was honored by hosts of gods and praised by the lords of sages.
He was sung of by the Gandharvas and attended by hosts of Apsarases;
he was nourished by the Kāmadhenu cow and adorned with variegated ornaments.
Adorned with soft garlands of tulasī, that treasury of splendor,
while proceeding toward the divine abode of Viṣṇu, saw a man on the path.
Being dragged away by the messengers of Yama, tormented by hunger and thirst,
he has become a hungry ghost (preta), naked, miserable, and bound by nooses;
he runs hither and thither, wailing like one who is helpless.
And seeing Sudanta crying out, his heart was deeply pained.

Wearing a garland of sacrifices and endowed with compassion, he asked the messengers of Viṣṇu who were standing nearby, with palms joined in reverence: "Who is this being harassed by these soldiers? (NarP 1.36.28)
Then those messengers of Hari said to that Yajña of great majesty, "That one is your brother Sumālin, whose soul is evil. (NarP 1.36.29)
Having heard what was explained by Viṣṇu’s messengers, Yajñamālin was overcome with mental anguish; O Nārada, he questioned them once again.
"How may there be liberation for him from the accumulated stores of evil?
O you who are indeed my kinsmen, devise a means for this for me."
"Those learned in the Dharma say that friendship is formed by walking seven steps together;
the friendship of the virtuous is formed by seven steps, while that of the truly virtuous is formed by three. (NarP 1.36.32)
Even among those who are virtuous, may there be a mind of loving-kindness toward them at every step.
"Therefore, since you, my kinsmen, have come here to lead me away,
let it be said now so that even this brother of mine may be released."
Having heard the words of Yajñamālin, the compassionate messengers of Viṣṇu, their faces smiling once more, spoke to Yajñamālin, who was dear to Hari: NarP_1,36.35.
The messengers of Viṣṇu said: "O illustrious Yajñamālin, devoted to Nārāyaṇa,
we shall tell you a means that grants liberation from the love of Sumālin."
The very great deed that was performed by you in a previous birth, we shall relate in brief; listen to it with a concentrated mind.
In former times, you were indeed of the Vaiśya caste, known by the name Viśvaṅghabhara;
the sins committed by you were truly innumerable and incurable.
Devoid of the impressions of good karma and a source of discord for his parents,
he was once abandoned by his kinsmen, afflicted by the torment of grief and anguish.
Though tormented by the fire of hunger, he reached the abode of Hari;
at that time, rain fell there, and that place indeed became muddy.
By you, the mud was removed from that spot with the desire to remain there;
that place in the temple of Viṣṇu has been turned into a plastered surface. (NarP 1.36.41)
O twice-born one, while he was dwelling within that divine temple with you,
he was bitten by a serpent and met his death.
By the power of that merit and by the act of anointing [the image],
you have obtained birth as a brahmin and likewise unshakable devotion to Hari.
Having attained the presence of Hari for more than a hundred crores of kalpas,
and having dwelt here today and acquired knowledge, you shall go to supreme liberation.
"You wish to uplift your younger brother, the foremost of sinners;
O high-minded one, I shall tell you the means for that—listen."
"O illustrious one, by the merit arising from smearing the ground even as large as a cow's hide, lift up your brother, moved by compassion. (NarP 1.36.45)
Thus addressed by the messengers of Viṣṇu,
the great lord Yajñamālin gave that fruit to his brother for the sake of liberation from sin.
Sumālī, his impurities removed by the merit bestowed by his brother, became free from stain;
the messengers of Yama, however, abandoned him and fled.
O Sage, a celestial chariot endowed with all enjoyments then arrived immediately; having ascended that heavenly vehicle, Sumālī rejoiced.
O Brahmin, those two brothers, who were honored by the hosts of gods,
attained great joy as they embraced one another.
Adorned with garlands of sacrifice, Yajñamālin and Sumālin, being praised by great sages and sung of by Gandharvas, departed for the world of Viṣṇu.
O best of sages, having attained the sight of Hari,
Sumālī and Yajñamālī both dwelt there for one kalpa, filled with joy.
Having enjoyed many pleasures there, the high-minded Yajñamālin,
endowed with knowledge, attained supreme liberation right there.
But the highly fortunate Sumālī, filled with joy while staying in the world of Viṣṇu,
returned to earth once more and attained the state of a brahmin.
Born into an exceedingly pure family, virtuous, a master of the Vedas,
endowed with every prosperity, and solely devoted to the worship of Hari.
Chanting the names of Hari, he reached the bank of the Jāhnavī;
having bathed there in the Gaṅgā and beheld the Lord Viśveśvara, he [proceeded].
He attained the supreme station, which is difficult even for yogins to reach.
O Lord of Sages, you have thus described to me the greatness of the act of smearing [the ground].
Therefore, with every effort, the Lord of the worlds should be worshipped;
for even those who perform the worship of Viṣṇu but once, even without desire [for reward], [attain liberation].
For those who are devoted to the worship of Hari and honor him with the thought that he is Hari himself, the bondage of worldly existence never arises at any time.
O best of Brahmins, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are pleased with those who are devoted to Hari,
merely by the company of their companions.
Even one who has committed great sins is liberated from all evils,
as are those devoted to the worship of Hari and whose souls delight in the name of Hari.
Even those who are sinners attain the supreme goal if they are devoted to service.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Power of Service to Viṣṇu," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
O best of Brahmins, listen further to the majesty of the Lord of Kamalā.
In whom does joy not arise upon hearing the nectar of the stories of Hari?
For men blinded by sense-objects and whose minds are agitated by the sense of "mine," the single name of Hari alone is the destroyer of all sins.
One who does not bow even once to Viṣṇu, the remover of the sins of men—
one should know him to be a dog-eater (outcaste) and should never speak with him.
O best of the twice-born, that house which is devoid of the worship of Hari is indeed like a cremation ground; one should never enter it.
Those who are devoid of the worship of Hari, as well as those who hate the Vedas and are intent on hating cows and Brahmins,
are proclaimed to be Rākṣasas.
O best of Brahmins, whoever— be they anyone at all— is devoted to hating Brahmins,
their worship of Govinda shall become fruitless.
O highly fortunate one, that very worship which people perform for the sake of destroying the welfare of others quickly destroys the worshippers themselves. (NarP 1.37.7)
Those who are experts in the meaning of reality say that he who performs worship of Hari, yet commits sin, is himself a hater of Viṣṇu.
Those who are devoted to Viṣṇu, intent on bestowing grace upon the worlds,
and constantly engaged in righteous deeds, are considered by me to be forms of Viṣṇu himself.
Devotion to Viṣṇu arises through merits earned over half a crore of births;
how could a sinful thought arise in those who possess firm devotion to Viṣṇu? (NarP 1.37.10)
The sin accumulated over ten million births perishes in an instant for those whose souls are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu; how could they ever possess a sinful mind?
Those who are devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu are proclaimed to be outcasts (caṇḍālas);
yet even outcasts are indeed superior if they are devoted solely to Hari.
For men blinded by sense-objects, service to Hari is renowned as the destroyer of all suffering and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whatever man performs the worship of Viṣṇu, whether out of attachment, affection, fear, greed, or even ignorance, he enjoys imperishable happiness.
Whoever drinks even a single drop of the water from Hari’s feet has bathed in all sacred fords and shall become most dear to Viṣṇu.
The water from the Haripada is known to pacify untimely death, destroy all diseases, and still all suffering.
For those great-souled ones who have taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa, the supreme abode, the highest light among all lights, their liberation is indeed eternal.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history, which destroys all sins for those who recite it and for those who hear it. (NarP 1.37.18)
In former times, during the Kṛta age, there was a hunter named Gulika,
who was constantly intent upon seizing the wives and wealth of others.
Constantly intent on reviling others and likewise causing harm to living beings,
he killed Brahmins and cows by the hundreds and thousands.
O Brahmin, he was constantly intent on seizing the property of gods as well as the property of others; indeed, he was always the lord of the miserly.
By him many sins, exceedingly great, were committed;
it is not possible to state their number even in tens of millions of years.
Once that great sinner, who was like Death itself to his kinsmen,
[attacked] the city of the King of Sauvīra, which was endowed with all prosperity.
Adorned with women decorated with ornaments and with lakes of pure water,
it was embellished with market-stalls and resembled the city of the gods.
Seeing the beautiful temple of Keśava situated in the middle of that grove,
covered with golden domes, the hunter attained great joy.
"I shall take away many gold pieces from here," he resolved;
and the miserly man, greedy for theft, went inside his house.
There he saw Uttanka, the best of the twice-born, peaceful, skilled in the knowledge of the true meaning of reality,
devoted to the service of Viṣṇu, and a treasure-house of asceticism.
O Sage, seeing him alone, compassionate, free from desire, and intent on meditation— a creator of obstacles to his theft— the hunter [approached].
Desiring to seize the wealth of the god, that most reckless man,
arrogant with pride, began to strike Uttaṅka while brandishing his sword.
Having stepped upon his chest with his foot and seized his matted locks with his hand,
Uttaṅka, seeing the hunter intent on killing him, spoke to him.
Uttaṅka said:
"O good man, you will kill me, who am innocent, in vain.
What offense have I committed against you? Tell me that, O highly intelligent one! (NarP 1.37.31)
In this world, those who possess power administer punishment to those who have committed offenses;
for even virtuous people, O gentle one, do not slay sinners in vain.
Even when observing virtues residing in fools who are their adversaries,
virtuous people of peaceful mind do not engage in hostility.
Even when being provoked in many ways, that man who remains endowed with patience—
him they call the supreme man, always most dear to Viṣṇu.
A virtuous person, whose mind is intent on the welfare of others, does not harbor enmity even at the time of their own destruction;
like a sandalwood tree, even when being cut down, it makes the edge of the axe fragrant.
Alas! Fate is exceedingly powerful; it oppresses people in many ways.
For even one who is free from all attachments is indeed tormented by that evil-minded force.
Alas! In this world, people cause harm to others in many ways without any justification;
even one who is free from all attachments is oppressed by malicious folk.
Furthermore, they oppress the virtuous, but never those who are their equals.
In this world, hunters, fishermen, and slanderers are causeless enemies toward the deer, the fish, and the virtuous, who sustain themselves with contentment through grass and water.
Oh, how powerful is illusion! It deludes the entire world;
for the sake of son, friend, and wife, it joins everyone to suffering.
By seizing the property of others, you have supported your wife;
yet in the end, abandoning all that, you must indeed depart alone.
"My mother, my father, my wife, my children;
this is mine"—thus does the sense of "mineness" (mamatā) falsely afflict living beings. (NarP 1.37.41)
For as much wealth as one acquires, only that belongs to one's kinsmen;
however, both merit and demerit remain together with oneself in this world and the next, and no one else.
Those men by whom others were nourished with wealth acquired through both righteous and unrighteous means,
indeed consume clarified butter and food after offering it into the mouth of the fire at the deceased's funeral.
When a man departs for the next world,
neither merit nor demerit, nor wealth, nor sons, nor kinsmen follow him.
Desire increases for men who perform evil deeds;
desire diminishes for men who perform meritorious deeds.
People are indeed needlessly distressed in the constant acquisition of wealth and its preservation.
"What is destined to be, will surely come to be; what is not destined to be, shall not come to be.
For those whose minds are certain of this, anxiety does not trouble them at any time.
This entire world, both stationary and moving, is dependent upon destiny;
therefore, no one other than destiny knows birth and death.
Whatever is destined to happen will certainly come to pass, regardless of where one may be situated;
yet the world, perceiving this, exerts itself in vain.
Alas, what suffering for humans whose minds are agitated by the sense of "mine," who,
even after committing great evils, strive diligently to nourish others!
The kinsmen always enjoy all the wealth that has been acquired,
while the fool alone, by himself, reaps the fruit of that evil deed.
Having released that ṛṣi who was speaking thus, Gulika, overwhelmed by fear,
spoke with palms joined in reverence, saying "Forgive me" again and again.
By the power of association with the virtuous and by the mere presence of Hari, the sinner Lubdhaka, freed from sin and filled with remorse, spoke as follows: (NarP 1.37.53).
The great and very many sins committed by me have all perished, O best of Brahmins, simply from the sight of you.
"Alas! I am of evil mind and have constantly committed great sin.
How may there be atonement for me? To whom shall I go for refuge, O Lord? (NarP 1.37.55)
"Due to sins accumulated in previous births, I have attained the state of a hunter;
having created further nets of sin even here, what destiny shall I attain? (NarP 1.37.56)
"Alas! My life is swiftly coming to an end, yet many sins have been accumulated. I have performed no remedy for these; what will be my destiny, or what shall be my next birth? (NarP 1.37.57)
Alas, O Creator! Why did you create me, a hundredfold wicked one, and ever more sinful?
And how shall I, a doer of fierce deeds, experience the fruit of that sin throughout so many births?
Thus reproaching himself by himself at that time, the hunter,
tormented by the fire of inner remorse, immediately met his death.
Seeing that hunter fallen, the high-minded Uttaṅka, being full of compassion,
sprinkled him with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.
Through the touch of the water from Hari’s feet, the hunter was cleansed of his sins;
then, ascending a divine celestial chariot, he spoke thus to the sage: NarP_1,37.61.
Gulika said:
"O Uttaṅka, tiger among sages, you are my guru, O observer of noble vows;
by your grace, I have been liberated from the shroud of great sin."
O bull among sages, through your instruction my torment has vanished,
and likewise all my sins have been destroyed with extreme speed.
O Sage, because you have sprinkled the water from Hari’s feet upon me,
I have therefore been led by you to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
"I have been delivered from this sinful body by you, O Brahmin;
therefore, O learned one, I bow to you, and may you forgive what I have done."
Having spoken thus, he scattered divine flowers over the best of sages,
performed three circumambulations, and paid his respects.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot endowed with all desirable things and crowded with throngs of apsaras, he reached the abode of Hari.
Having seen this, Uttaṅka, that treasure-house of asceticism, was filled with wonder;
placing his joined palms upon his head, he praised the Lord of Kamalā.
Praised by him, Mahāviṣṇu granted him an excellent boon;
by that boon, Aṅka also attained the supreme state.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, in the section on the majesty of Viṣṇu.
Nārada said: "O highly fortunate one, what is that hymn? And how was Janārdana pleased?"
It has been told who the meritorious man was; what kind of boon did he obtain?
Sanaka said:
Then the brahmin Uttaṅka, devoted to the meditation on Hari, having witnessed the majesty of the water from the feet, praised him with devotion. (NarP 1.38.2)
Uttaṅka said:
I bow to Nārāyaṇa, the primordial god, the abode of the world, the sole kinsman of the universe;
to the Great One who bears the discus, the lotus, and the Śārṅga bow, I go for refuge to him who destroys the suffering of those who remember him.
I bow to that primordial god Viṣṇu, from whose navel-lotus the Creator (Brahmā) is born and who creates this entire collection of worlds, and by whose wrath Rudra arises and destroys the universe.

I have taken refuge in Viṣṇu— the Lord of Lakṣmī, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, who possesses manifold valor, the sole cause of all things, known through the Vedāntas, the Supreme Person, the Ancient One, and the treasury of splendor.
May the Lord— who is the imperishable Self, all-pervading, known as the Immovable, whose nature is knowledge, the refuge for those who know wisdom,
who is to be known solely through wisdom, beginningless, and whose form is both the individual and the universal— be gracious.
May the one of infinite power, who is devoid of the birth of qualities yet whose nature is pure quality, who is honored as the best among those who possess knowledge,
who is eternal, the supreme Self who removes the distress of those who have sought refuge, and who is an ocean of compassion, grant me boons.

O Supreme Self, you alone have entered that entire universe—which you yourself created according to its true nature through the distinctions of gross, subtle, and other specific forms—and which has you as its infinite essence; for there is nothing higher than you.
The virtuous perceive that which is your pure domain— devoid of illusion, devoid of the categories of qualities, stainless, immaculate, and immeasurable— which is designated as the ultimate reality.
Just as ornaments made of a single gold are perceived as distinct due to the difference in their limiting conditions (*upādhi*),
so too the one Lord alone appears as if divided among all beings, like the soul of an enemy army.
Those whose minds are deluded by illusion do not perceive even their own well-known self;
yet those very same people, when freed from illusion, behold that very form of the Self which is the soul of all.
I bow to the all-pervading, incomparable light known as Viṣṇu,
from whom this entire universe has arisen and in whom it is established.
Salutation indeed to that whose nature consciousness has emerged from,
which is immeasurable, without beginning, and whose form consists of both the support and the supported.
I bow to Vāsudeva, the supreme bliss consisting of pure consciousness,
the God who dwells in the cave of the heart and is served by yogis.
I bow to Him who is the primordial ground of all yogas, who abides as the *praṇava*,
whose essence is sound (*nāda*), who is the seed of sound, and who is the imperishable self of the *praṇava*.

I bow to Him who possesses true existence, consciousness, and bliss; to Him who wields the sharp discus, who is undecaying, the witness of this universe, and indeed beyond the reach of speech and mind. (NarP 1.38.16)
I bow to Viṣṇu, who is stainless, known as the infinite,
and whose form is the senses, the mind, the intellect, goodness, splendor, strength, and fortitude.
They say that both the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) have Vāsudeva as their essence;
they likewise say that [the Lord] is composed of both knowledge and ignorance, and is higher than the highest.
For those great-souled ones who have taken refuge in Him— who is without beginning or end, peaceful, the sustainer of all elements, and immutable— their liberation is indeed eternal.
To the most excellent, the most venerable, the giver of boons, the ancient, the eternal, the omnipresent, and the all-encompassing—
I bow again, I bow again, I bow again and again.
I worship that immeasurable Puruṣa, whose foot-water is the physician for the disease of sin, whose foot-dust brings about the attainment of purity, and whose name wards off evil karma.

I worship Him who is of the nature of existence, of the nature of non-existence, and of the nature of both existence and non-existence; who is immutable, distinct from all those, supreme, and more excellent than the most excellent.
Stainless, formless, full, and situated in the midst of space, it is the Supreme,
dwelling in the lotus of the heart beyond both knowledge and ignorance.
Self-luminous and indescribable, greater than the great and subtler than the subtle, unborn and devoid of all limiting adjuncts.
I have gone for refuge to that which is eternal, supreme bliss, the supreme Brahman, the ancient one, known by the name Viṣṇu, the abode of the universe.
I have gone for refuge to the Lord, whom those devoted to ritual action worship and whom yogis behold— the peaceful one, more worthy of worship than the most worshipful.
I bow to that omnipresent and imperishable Lord who stands pervading all this, whom the wise do not perceive, who is eternal, and who is superior to everything. 1,38.27.
That which, due to its conjunction with the internal organ, is called the "living soul" (jīva),
is celebrated as the "Supreme Self" (paramātman) when it is free from the effects of ignorance.

I bow down to the one who is higher than the highest, whose self is everything, who is the cause of all, the locus of the fruits of all actions, the most excellent, the one to be chosen, and the unborn.
I worship Hari, the omniscient, the all-pervading, the peaceful, the destroyer of all ends; the embodiment of knowledge, the treasury of knowledge, established in knowledge, the omnipresent Lord.
I bow to Murāri, the treasure-house of the Vedas, whose purpose is perfectly ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta;
who is the Lord of the three worlds, blazing like the sun and fire, the very embodiment of the Veda, and whose nature is that of the Supreme Lord.

I worship that Puruṣa, the Lord of all, who is omnipresent, the Great One, whose essence is the Vedas, the most excellent among those who know the Vedas; him who is inconceivable by speech or mind, possessed of infinite power, and known through knowledge alone.
I take refuge in that immeasurable one of perfect being, who protects the worlds through Indra, Agni, Kāla, Asura, Pāśi, Vāyu, Soma, Īśa, Mārtaṇḍa, Purandara, and the rest. 1.38.33.

I bow to the primordial one, who has a thousand heads, a thousand feet, a thousand arms, and a thousand eyes; who is worshipped by all sacrifices, who bestows contentment, and who possesses fierce valor.
I [bow to Him] who is the essence of time, the cause of the divisions of time, who transcends the three qualities (guṇas) yet knows the qualities,
who loves the qualities, who grants desires, who is free from attachment, beyond the senses, the enjoyer of the universe, and free from thirst.
I worship that which is effortless and supreme, unattainable even by the mind, consisting of both mind and food, firmly established,
appearing as a manifestation of consciousness, yet not composed of speech or vital breath.

He whose form, strength, and power there are not, whose deeds there are not, and whose measure there is not—whom even the gods, beginning with the Lotus-born Brahmā, do not know; how shall I satisfy that Self in its true nature?

O Ocean of Compassion, protect me, who have fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra—miserly, overwhelmed by delusion, bound by a hundred desires, a partaker of ill-repute, treacherous, ungrateful, ever impure, devoted to evil, and full of wrath; I take refuge in you again and again. (NarP 1.38.38)
Thus propitiated by him, the Lord of Kamalā, compassionate and a treasury of splendors, became manifest before his very eyes, O Bhagavān.
Resembling an *atasī* flower, with eyes like full-blown lotuses, wearing a crown and earrings, and adorned with necklaces and armlets; (NarP 1.38.40)
He bore the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, wore a golden sacred thread, and had a pearl set upon his nose, increasing the radiance of his body.
The god, wearing yellow garments and adorned with a forest garland,
his feet worshipped by the tender leaves of the *tulasī*, possessed great luster.
Seeing the one whose banner is Garuḍa, adorned with tinkling bells, anklets, and other ornaments,
the best of Brahmins prostrated himself like a staff upon the surface of the earth.
Then Uttaṅka, his mind focused on nothing else, bathed the feet of Hari with tears of joy while crying out, "O Murāri, protect me! Protect me! (NarP 1.38.44).
Having raised him up, Mahāviṣṇu, devoted to compassion, embraced that bull among sages and said, "Choose a boon, my child. (NarP 1.38.45)
"O best of beings, when I am pleased, there is nothing whatsoever that is unattainable for you.
Having heard these words spoken by the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi), Uttaṅka bowed again to Janārdana, the God of gods, and spoke to him. (NarP 1.38.46)
Why do you delude me, O Lord? What need have I for other boons, O God?
Let my devotion to You be firm, even throughout future births.

Whether I am born among insects, birds, wild animals, or reptiles, or even among *rakṣasas*, *piśācas*, or humans— wherever I may be born— by your grace, O Keśava, may I have unwavering and unswerving devotion toward you alone.
"So be it," said Lokeśa, and touching him with the edge of his conch shell, he bestowed upon him divine knowledge, difficult even for yogins to attain.
As the lord of sages was thus praising him, Janārdana, the God of gods, placed his hand upon the sage’s head and, with a smiling face, spoke these words.
The Blessed One said: "O best of the twice-born, always worship me through the yoga of action;
go to the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and you shall attain liberation."
The man who constantly recites this hymn composed by you shall attain all his desires and, at the end, become a partaker of liberation.
Having spoken thus to the brahmin, O sage, the descendant of Bhrigu vanished right there;
Uttaṅka then proceeded to the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Why should devotion always be practiced toward the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus?
Devotion to Hari is declared to be supreme, bestowing the fulfillment of all desires.
O Sage, Utanka, devoted to the yoga of action with a spirit of devotion,
constantly worshipped Mādhava in the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Endowed with both knowledge and discernment, with all doubts regarding duality severed,
he indeed attains that supreme state of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the gods to reach.
Whether worshipped, saluted, or even merely remembered, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World and the increaser of the strength of his devotees, bestows liberation.
Therefore, one who desires happiness in this world and the next should worship the god Nārāyaṇa, who is infinite and unconquered, endowed with devotion.
Whoever should read this narrative or listen to it with a concentrated mind,
he too, liberated from all evil, goes to the abode of Hari.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Majesty of Viṣṇu," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanaka said:
O best of Brahmins, listen further to the majesty of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
Oh, how the discourse on Hari destroys sin and bestows merit in this world,
especially for those who hear it, those who speak it, and those who are devoted to Him!
I bow down to those best of men who are delighted by tasting the flavor of devotion to Hari; by association with whom a person attains liberation.
But to those who are devoted to the worship of Hari and dedicated to the name of Hari—
whether they be of evil conduct or of good conduct— to them I offer constant salutations again and again.
O bull among men, he who wishes to cross the ocean of saṃsāra should indeed devote himself to the devotees of Hari, those who remove all sins.
Whether seen, remembered, honored, meditated upon, or even merely saluted,
Govinda delivers one from the ocean of existence so difficult to cross.
Salutations again and again to him who, whether sleeping, eating, walking, standing, sitting, or speaking, likewise meditates upon the name of Hari.
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for those whose souls are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu!
For them, liberation—which is difficult even for yogis to attain—is already within their grasp.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history,
which destroys all sins for both those who speak of it and those who hear it.
In ancient times, there was a protector of the earth born of the Lunar dynasty,
renowned as Jayadhvaja, who was devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
He was constantly devoted to sweeping the temple of Viṣṇu,
intent on offering lamps, and dedicated to compassion for all living beings.
Once, that protector of the earth constructed a temple to Viṣṇu on the delightful bank of the Revā river, adorned with various flowers.
There, that tiger among kings was always devoted to sweeping,
and he was especially intent on the offering of lamps, being a great lover of Hari.
Constantly devoted to the names of Hari, with his mind ever attached to Hari,
he was intent on prostrating himself and was dear to those who were devotees of Hari.
He had a priest known as Vītihotra,
who was filled with wonder upon seeing the conduct of Jayadhvaja.
Once, when that king, who was devoted to Viṣṇu, was seated,
Vītihotra, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, questioned him.
Vītihotra said:
O King, knower of the supreme dharma, devoted to the worship of Hari,
you are the best among men who possess devotion to Viṣṇu, O bull of the Bharata race.
"One who is constantly devoted to sweeping and likewise delights in the offering of lamps—
tell me that, O highly fortunate one, what fruit has been realized by you?"
You are always endowed with the excellence of preparing wicks and the excellence of providing oil, just as you were when you were engaged in sweeping the house of Viṣṇu, O auspicious one.
"There are indeed other rites that bring pleasure to Viṣṇu;
nevertheless, O illustrious one, why are you constantly intent upon these two?"
O Lord of Men, if you have affection for me, then tell me that which is known to you as the greatest merit of all, and which is most secret.
Thus addressed by the family priest, Jayadhvaja laughed,
bowed with humility, and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Jayadhvaja said: Listen, O tiger among Brahmins, to what was performed by me in the past;
because of my memory of former births, I know this which will cause wonder to those who hear it.
O Brahmin, formerly in the Kṛta age, during the Svārociṣa interval,
there was a lord of sages named Raivata, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
One who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, one who is always a leader of a village, a slanderer, a cruel person, and a seller of goods that should not be sold; NarP_1,39.25.
Due to his practice of forbidden actions, he was abandoned by his kinsmen;
he became poor and miserable, with broken limbs and afflicted by disease. (NarP 1.39.26)
Once, while wandering upon the earth, that twice-born man died on the bank of the Narmadā, afflicted by asthma and coughing.
O Sage, when he had died, his wife named Bandhumatī,
who was devoted to following her own desires, was abandoned by her kinsmen.
Born of her, I became a Caṇḍāla known as Daṇḍaketu; I was constantly devoted to great sins and intent upon hatred for Brahmins. (NarP 1.39.29)
He was greedy for the wives and wealth of others, a slayer of living beings,
and many cows, Brahmins, wild animals, and birds were killed by him.
He stole many pieces of gold equal in weight to Mount Meru;
he was constantly addicted to drinking liquor and repeatedly obstructed the royal highway.
Like the God of Death to creatures such as beasts, birds, and deer,
he was once tormented by desire and wished to go to his wife for sexual pleasure.
Seeing that the temple of Viṣṇu was empty, he entered it with his wife;
there at night, the lustful man lay down for the sake of enjoying Rāma.
O twice-born one, how much ground was wiped away by the edge of the brāhmaṇa’s own garment—how many particles of dust were swept clean there? (NarP 1.39.34)
At that very moment, O best of the twice-born, the sin committed during that lifetime reached its destruction; a lamp had been placed there for the sake of sexual pleasure.
By that [merit], my evil karma has also been entirely exhausted;
while this was occurring, the city guards indeed arrived at Viṣṇu’s abode.
"Thinking, 'This is a paramour,' they have indeed forcibly killed both me and her;
having slain us both, all those city guards have now retreated."
At that very moment, the four-armed messengers of Viṣṇu arrived,
wearing crowns and earrings, and adorned with garlands of forest flowers.
Impelled by those stainless messengers of Viṣṇu,
we ascended a divine celestial chariot endowed with every enjoyment.
Having assumed divine bodies, they went to the world of Viṣṇu;
O best of the twice-born, remaining there for more than a hundred Brahma-kalpas.
Endowed with divine enjoyments, they remained in heaven for that length of time;
thereafter, they were born in succession upon the regions of the earth among the ranks of the gods.
By the power of that merit, the lineage of the Yadus arose;
by that very same merit, my prosperity became unfailing and my kingdom free from thorns.
O Brahmin, having performed [this] for the sake of enjoyment, he thus attained the highest good;
as for those virtuous ones who perform it with devotion, their merit is not to be known by me.
Therefore, O best of beings, since I remember my past lives, I shall strive with supreme devotion in the constant sweeping [of the temple] and in the offering of lamps.
He who, alone and free from desire, worships the Lord of the World,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme state.
If one has attained this prosperity even by performing an act involuntarily,
how much more so through proper worship performed with devotion, goodness, and tranquility?
Having heard these words of the king, Vītihotra, the best of the twice-born,
attained infinite satisfaction and became devoted to the worship of Hari.
Therefore, O chief of Brahmins, listen: the imperishable Lord Nārāyaṇa grants liberation to his worshippers, whether through knowledge or even through ignorance.
All kinsmen are impermanent, and prosperity is never eternal;
death is ever-present, so one must practice the accumulation of dharma.
The ignorant world, being greatly arrogant, will vainly indulge in pride; for the body is subject to imminent ruin—what then can be said of grain and other such things?
Only those by whom merit has been fully accumulated over thousands of millions of births shall possess pure devotion for Janārdana, the God of gods.
Bathing in the Ganges is easily accessible, and likewise is the honoring of guests;
all sacrifices are easily performed, but devotion to Viṣṇu is very difficult to attain.
Service to Tulasī is difficult to obtain; association with the virtuous is difficult to obtain;
even compassion toward all beings is not easily found by just anyone.
Association with the virtuous, service to Tulasī, and devotion to Hari are difficult to attain.
Having obtained this human birth which is so difficult to attain, a wise person should not let it pass in vain;
for he should worship the Lord of the World, O best of the twice-born, for this is the very essence.
If a person desires to cross the difficult-to-traverse ocean of existence, let him be devoted to the worship of Hari; this alone is the elixir.
"O brother, take refuge in Govinda; do not delay, my dear one, for the city of Death is clearly visible nearby."
O best of Brahmins, if you desire worldly enjoyment, worship Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe and the cause of all causes.
Those great-souled ones who have taken refuge in the all-supporting, the source of all, the omnipresent inner controller, have achieved their purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Those who worship Mahāviṣṇu, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him, are to be revered, they are to be honored, and especially they are to be saluted.
Those devotees of Viṣṇu who, free from desire, worship the Supreme Lord,
go to the abode of Hari together with twenty-one generations of their lineage.
He who would give even water or a fruit to a high-souled devotee of Viṣṇu who is free from desire— he alone is beloved by the Blessed One.
But those who perform service for those devoted to Viṣṇu go to the realm of Viṣṇu until the dissolution of all beings.
Those who perform sacrifice free from desire for the sake of the devotees of Hari and for Hari himself—
they alone purify the entire world with the dust of their own feet.
In whosever house one devoted to the worship of the gods always dwells,
there all the gods as well as Śrī Hari reside.
O twice-born one, all auspicious things increase day by day in the house where Tulasī is worshipped and remains.
Wherever Keśava resides in the form of a Śālagrāma stone,
there the planetary spirits, ghosts, vetālas, and other such beings do not cause harm.
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, that is a sacred ford (tīrtha) and that is a grove of asceticism (tapovana),
because the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana is ever-present there.
O celestial sage, that house in which there is no worship of the Śālagrāma stone should be known as resembling a cremation ground, devoid of all auspiciousness.
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras, O twice-born one.
Likewise, all the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs are proclaimed to be the form of Viṣṇu.
Those who perform four circumambulations of Viṣṇu with devotion also go to the supreme abode, which destroys all karma.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Majesty of Viṣṇu," in the first quarter of the first part of the *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanaka said:
"O Sage, hereafter I shall proclaim the Vaiṣṇava manifestation."
By hearing it or reciting it, there shall be an immediate destruction of evil for those who do so.
In a former age, during the interval of Vaivasvata Manu, there was a very great conversation between Śakra and Bṛhaspati; I shall relate that, so listen attentively.
Once, enriched with all enjoyments, surrounded by gods,
and thronged by hosts of apsaras, he addressed Bṛhaspati.
Indra said:
"O Bṛhaspati, highly fortunate one, skilled in the meaning of all principles!
O Lord, what was the nature of the creation during the past kalpa of Brahmā?"
What is Indra said to be like? What are the gods remembered to be like?
And what is their activity like? You should explain this to me exactly as it is.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Śakra, the conduct of Vidhi on the previous day is not known by me;
even that of the present day appears difficult for me to discern."
Even Mānava is not capable of describing those who have passed away;
listen as I tell you today of him who knows them. (NarP 1.40.7)
In your city there dwells a certain man renowned as Sudharman,
who, having come here from the world of Brahmā, enjoys divine pleasures.
"He indeed knows this; listen as I tell it.
Having been addressed thus by his preceptor, Śakra was joined by him.
Surrounded by hosts of deities, he went to the Sudharma assembly hall.
O celestial sage, seeing the lord of the gods arrived accompanied by Bṛhaspati, he honored him respectfully according to his merit.

Having seen that supreme splendor, Śakra, honored by Sudharma, was filled with wonder in his mind and spoke with humility: NarP_1,40.12: "Honored by Sudharma, Śakra, having seen that supreme splendor, was filled with wonder in his mind and spoke with humility."
Indra said:
"O wise one, if you know the account of the past Brahmakalpa, then relate it; for this sacrificer has arrived to ask about this."
O you of excellent vows, tell us by what means you know the gods who have overcome sleep;
why is it that you, though dwelling in heaven, are superior even to us?
O scorcher of foes, O Lord, how has he become such as this through splendor, fame, renown, and knowledge, or through gifts or austerities?
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, Sudharmā then laughed and,
filled with humility, spoke of past events according to tradition.
Sudharmā said:
"O Śakra, a day of Brahmā is said to consist of a thousand cycles of the four yugas;
in a single such day, there are fourteen Manus."
Fourteen Indras have been proclaimed, as well as various distinct gods;
O Vāsava, this applies to all the Indras and to the Manus and others as well.
They are equal in splendor, fortune, influence, and strength;
I shall state their names—listen with a well-composed mind. (NarP 1.40.19)
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, then Svārociṣa,
as well as Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
Vaivasvata Manu, and Sūryasāvarṇi as the eighth;
the ninth is Dakṣasāvarṇi, who is devoted to the welfare of all the gods.
The tenth is Brahmasāvarṇi; after him is Dharmasāvarṇika;
then follows Rudrasāvarṇi, and after that Rocamāna is recorded.
The fourteenth Manu is declared to be Bhautya; these indeed are remembered as the Manus.
O bull among the wise, listen as I shall describe the gods and the Indras.
In the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, the gods were known as the Yāmas;
their Indra, the great lord, was known as Śacīpati.
And during the Svārociṣa interval, the Pārāvatas were the Tuṣita gods;
their lord of gods was named Vipaścit, endowed with every prosperity.
Likewise, the Sudhāmans, the Satyas, and the Śivas were the Prartadanas;
their Indra was Suśānti, as proclaimed in the third [Manvantara].
