The Sutās, Pārāharas, Sutyās, and Asudhiyas were likewise [their progeny]. Śiva was declared their Indra during the Tāmasa Manvantara;
the fifth, known as Vibhu, is celebrated as the Lord of the Gods (Devapati).
Listen likewise to the gods of the sixth [world-system], Amitābha and the others;
the noble deities and so forth have been described, and their Indra is Manojava.
In the Vaivasvata Manvantara, the gods beginning with the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras were present;
Indra was proclaimed as Purandara, endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
And the immeasurable gods, such as Sutapa and others, have been proclaimed;
by the power of their worship of Viṣṇu, Bali is remembered as their Indra.
In the ninth [chapter], the gods beginning with Pārādyas and the wonderful Indra are mentioned;
in the tenth, the deities beginning with Suvāsanā are proclaimed.
And there the Indra named Śānti is endowed with all enjoyments;
the gods beginning with Vihṛṅgṛma are also there, and their Indra is known as Vṛṣa.
Now listen as I tell you the account of the eleventh and twelfth [Manvantaras]:
the lord of the gods was named Kratu, and the deities were the Harinābhas.
Likewise, in the thirteenth interval, there were the gods beginning with Sutrāman;
among them, the very powerful Divaspati is proclaimed as their Indra.
In the fourteenth [Manvantara], the gods are the Ākṣuṣas and others, and Indra is remembered as Śuci.
Thus have those Manus, Indras, and gods been declared according to their true nature.
For one day of Brahmā, they enjoy their own authority.
In all the creations within the world-ages, creation is recorded as being of one kind;
though there are many creators, only the wise man knows their number.
"While I have remained in the world of Brahmā, many Brahmās have passed away;
O best of the twice-born, I am not able even today to calculate their number."
Listen to me regarding even the time spent after reaching the heavenly world:
four Manus have passed away, and my glory was exceedingly vast.
"O Lord, I must remain right here for hundreds of millions of eons;
after that, I shall go to the land of karma—listen to me."
O you of noble vows, I shall relate to you the deed performed by me in the past, which destroys all sins for both those who speak of it and those who hear it. (NarP 1.40.41)
"O Śakra, in the past I was a flesh-eating vulture, particularly wicked; I dwelt indeed upon a patch of ground, feeding on impure meat."
Once, O Lord, while I was standing on the rampart of Viṣṇu’s house,
I fell at evening in the courtyard of Viṣṇu’s residence, struck by the weapon of a hunter.
When my life-breath had reached my throat, the dog Bhaṣaṇa, greedy for flesh,
seized me with his mouth as he ran swiftly along with other dogs.
O Lord, though I was carrying you on my own face, I was terrified by other dogs;
thus, I went to circumambulate that temple of Viṣṇu.
The inner self, which pervades the universe, attained satisfaction through that very act;
he granted the supreme state both to me and to the dog.
O best of the wise, such a fruit was obtained even by one who merely went around [the shrine] keeping it to the right; how much more so, then, from proper worship?
Thus addressed by the high-souled Sudharma,
the king of the gods attained joy in his mind and became devoted to the worship of Hari.
Nevertheless, all the liberated beings who desire rebirth in Bhārata worship Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, who is free from all ailment;
and the hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā, constantly worship them.

How can there be a bond to fierce existence for those great-souled ones who are intent on the remembrance of Nārāyaṇa and have abandoned all possessions, even if they are greedy for union with Him, provided they are partakers of liberation?
Those men who, daily freed from all attachments, worship Nārāyaṇa whose vehicle is Garuḍa—
they, completely liberated from the multitude of all sins, go joyfully to the most auspicious abode of Viṣṇu.
Those men who, having transcended passion and knowing the higher and the lower, constantly remember Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the gods—
their minds, with their sins destroyed by that meditation, do not drink the milk from a mother’s breast again.

Those men who listen to the stories of Hari, whose faults have been removed, and whose consciousness is devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet—they purify the worlds through contact with their bodies or even by conversation; therefore, Hari alone is to be worshipped.
O twice-born one, wherever there are great souls of pure intellect devoted to the worship of Hari,
in that very place all is auspicious, just as water flows toward a low-lying spot.
Hari alone is the supreme kinsman; Hari alone is the supreme refuge;
therefore, Hari alone is to be worshipped, for he is the cause of consciousness.
O best of sages, for one who worships [the Lord], there shall arise the supreme good, which bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, is eternal bliss, and is free from all affliction.
But for those who worship Hari without desire and with pure minds,
Viṣṇu, being pleased in spirit, bestows all their desires.
O best of eminent sages, whoever hears this or reads it with a well-concentrated mind obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Thus has this fruit of the worship of Hari been fully explained to you, O twice-born one, both in brief and in detail; what else shall I tell you?
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the first quarter of the first part, concerning the majesty of Viṣṇu, in the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"O Sage, knower of the true meaning of reality, everything has been narrated by you."
Now I wish to hear the characteristics of the duration of the Yugas.
Sanaka said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise sage, benefactor of the world!
I shall proclaim the duties of the ages (yuga-dharmas), which are beneficial to all the worlds."
O supreme one, at a certain time Dharma attains growth,
and likewise, Dharma itself comes to destruction upon the surface of the earth.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four yugas;
O best of beings, they should be known to consist of twelve divine years each.
The Yugas, together with their morning and evening twilights, are indeed to be understood as equal in duration; so it has been stated by those who perceive the truth.
They say that in the first [period] was the Kṛta Yuga; then follows the arrangement of the Tretā;
thereafter they speak of the Dvāpara; and they know the Kali to be the last in sequence.
O Brahmin, in the Kṛta age, the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas were all remembered as being equal to the gods.
All were joyful and most righteous; there was no buying or selling there, nor was there any division of the Vedas in that age known as Kṛta.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were devoted to their own proper conduct;
they were always intent upon Nārāyaṇa and dedicated to austerity and meditation.
Free from defects such as desire and the like, devoted to virtues such as tranquility,
their minds intent on the means of dharma, they were devoid of malice and free from hypocrisy.
All were devoted to truthful speech, adhering to the duties of the four stages of life;
they were perfected in the study of the Vedas and were experts in all the sciences.
By means of action associated with the four stages of life and originating from Time,
those who are unattached to the fruits of their actions proceed to the supreme goal.
Nārāyaṇa is white in color and perfectly pure in the Kṛta Yuga;
I shall now proclaim the dharmas of the Tretā; listen with a well-composed mind.
O best of sages, in the Tretā age, Dharma turns pale;
Hari turns red, and people become somewhat afflicted by suffering.
All were devoted to the yoga of action and established in sacrificial rites;
they were committed to the vow of truth, intent on meditation, and always dedicated to contemplation.
O Lord of Sages, in the Dvāpara age, dharma exists on two feet;
Hari assumes a yellow hue, and the Veda is also divided.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, some among those there—
belonging to the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas— will be devoted to untruth and possessed of evil qualities such as passion.
Some perform sacrifices for the sake of heaven and liberation;
some desire wealth and other such things; and some possess defiled minds.
O best of brahmins, in the Dvāpara age, dharma and adharma become equal;
and through the power of adharma, the subjects likewise perish.
O Lord of Sages, some will be short-lived;
and seeing others devoted to merit, O Brahmin, they will practice envy.
I shall proclaim the condition of the Kali age; listen to that with a concentrated mind.
When the Kali Yuga has arrived, Dharma exists by means of only a single quarter.
Having reached the Tāmasa Yuga, Hari assumes a dark form;
yet whoever is righteous in soul performs the practices of sacrifice.
Whosoever is a virtuous soul devoted to the yoga of action,
everyone displays envy upon seeing that man who delights in the Dharma.
Vows and religious observances will perish, as will the sacrifice of knowledge and other such rites;
indeed, calamities will arise from the prevalence of unrighteousness.
In the Kali age, all people will be devoted to envy, intent on hypocritical conduct, and all living beings will have short lifespans.
Nārada said: O sage, you have described the duties of the ages in brief;
now speak of Kali in detail, for you are the best among those who know the dharma.
O best of sages, what will be the food and what will be the conduct of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras in the Kali age?
Sanaka said: Listen, O tiger among sages, you who bring benefit to all the worlds;
I shall describe the characteristics of the Kali age in detail and according to the truth.
All things perish when Kṛṣṇa has attained his dark state;
therefore, Kali is most terrible, a confluence of all sins.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras will turn their backs on dharma, and the twice-born will turn their backs on the Vedas.
All will be devoted to dharma in hypocrisy, likewise intent on malice;
they will be corrupted by false pride, devoid of truth, yet claiming to be wise.
And all of them dispute, saying, "I alone am superior";
for all those men are greedy for unrighteousness and likewise possessed by malice.
Therefore, in the Kali age, all will have short lifespans;
O twice-born one, because of the shortness of human life, there will be no acquisition of knowledge.
Due to the absence of the acquisition of knowledge, unrighteousness prevails once more; all subjects, intent on sin, perish through the transgression of the established order.
Likewise, the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas will become intermingled with one another;
deluded and devoted to lust and anger, they will be tormented by futile anxieties.
In the Kali age, all social classes will become equal to Śūdras;
the highest will fall to the state of the lowly, and likewise, the lowly will attain the state of the highest.
For kings who are devoted to wealth and act unjustly oppress their subjects with excessively imposed taxes. (NarP 1.41.37)
The twice-born will become bearers of the corpses of Śūdras;
even husbands, acting like paramours, will have sexual relations with the wives of others.
Sons will hate their father, and all women will hate their husbands;
everyone will be devoted to the wives of others and intent upon the wealth of others.
O Brahmin, in the terrible Kali age, all people are devoted to sin; they live by the meat of fish and even kill those who have no other means of livelihood. (NarP 1.41.40)
Those intent on finding fault with the virtuous will mock them;
they will plant medicinal herbs along the banks of rivers using spades.
The earth becomes barren, and the seed perishes like a flower;
women feel desire for the charms and character of courtesans.
Brahmins who sell the Dharma, women who sell their virtue, others who sell the Vedas, and twice-born men devoted to the conduct of Śūdras; (NarP 1.41.43)
They will seize the wealth of the virtuous and widows;
greedy for riches, the Brahmins will no longer observe their vows.
Abandoning the practice of dharma and addicted to vain talk,
the twice-born perform rites such as the ancestral śrāddha for the sake of hypocrisy.
The lowest of men bestow gifts only upon unworthy recipients, and they show affection toward cows solely for the sake of desiring their milk.
The base among men do not perform such rites as bathing and purification;
they bestow gifts only upon unworthy recipients.
O Brahmin, the minds of those who are intent on censuring the virtuous and likewise intent on censuring the Brahmins shall never become devoted to Viṣṇu.
When Kṛṣṇa has attained his dark state, wicked men— servants of kings seeking wealth— will beat the twice-born who perform sacrifices, even though those brahmins are devoted to their duties.
O Sage, in the terrible Kali age, all men will be devoid of charity;
even twice-born ones will accept gifts from those who are fallen.
Even during the first quarter of the Kali age, men will revile Hari;
and at the end of the age, no one at all will utter the name of Hari.
In the Kali age, the twice-born will be devoted to union with Śūdra women, greedy for the company of widows, and intent on consuming the food of Śūdras.
Having abandoned the Veda and the path of the righteous, those who follow the conduct of evil ways will become heretics,
revilers of the four stages of life.
And those base ones born from the feet, who do not perform service to the twice-born,
will adopt the dharma of the twice-born while wearing the marks of heretics.
Clad in saffron robes, with matted hair and smeared with ashes and dust,
they will proclaim the dharma of the Śūdras, being devoted to deceit and trickery.
Casting aside their own proper conduct, the twice-born will become evil-minded men who eat the food cooked by others; likewise, even Śūdras will become renunciants.
In that Kali age, O Sage, there will be those who live by bribery;
there will be heretics who are hypocrites regarding dharma, as well as base mendicants who carry skulls.
O best of the twice-born, when the twice-born are characterized by the destruction of dharma,
Śūdras will indeed ascend the highest seats and proclaim the dharmas.
These and many others— naked ascetics, those clad in red robes, and so forth—
will mostly be heretics who revile the Vedas.
In the Kali age, men will for the most part be skilled in song and instrumental music, relying on trivial doctrines, and will be destroyers of the Dharma.
Possessing little wealth, bearing outward signs in vain, and defiled by useless displays of pride,
those lowest of men will become plunderers of the property of others.
Constantly intent on receiving gifts, they follow the wrong path in the world;
all are devoted to praising themselves and likewise devoted to reviling others.
O Brahmin, in the Kali age, men will become betrayers of those who trust them, cruel, devoid of compassion and righteousness, and kinsmen of unrighteousness.
And at that time, O Brahmin, in the terrible Kali age, the maximum lifespan will be sixteen years; [a woman] will give birth when she is five years old.
Those aged seven or eight years are considered youths, and from then on they are old;
all of them abandon their own duties, being ungrateful and of broken conduct.
In the Kali age, the twice-born will constantly be beggars,
delighting in insulting others and rejoicing in the houses of others.
In that very state, people who delight in censure and place their trust in vain constantly cast blame upon their fathers, mothers, and sons.
Those who are greedy for evil speak of the teachings with their speech while harboring them in their minds; intoxicated by wealth, learning, and youth, they are destined for all suffering.
Afflicted by disease, thieves, and famine,
these excessively deceitful people prosper in vain, without reflecting upon their evil deeds.
Sinful people revile the one who leads the path of Dharma,
as do those who place their trust in vain toward one devoted to righteous deeds.
When the Kali age has arrived, there will be kings of Mleccha origin;
the Śūdras will be devoted to begging for alms, while the twice-born will be intent on serving them.
In this confusion of castes, there will be no disciple and no teacher, no son and no father, and likewise no wife and no husband.
When the Kali age has arrived, even those who are wealthy will become beggars,
and even the twice-born will become sellers of liquids.

Clothed in the mantle of dharma and wearing the garb of sages, those twice-born ones were devoted to the sale of forbidden goods and likewise practiced sexual intercourse with women who should not be approached.
O Sage, those twice-born who are intent on reviling the Vedas, who disparage the treatises on Dharma, and who live solely by the livelihood of a Śūdra, are worthy of hell.
In the Kali age, all mortals will be overcome by the fear of drought; with their eyes fixed upon the sky, they will be distressed by the terror of hunger.
Subsisting on bulbs, leaves, and fruits like men who steal by day,
they will save themselves when they are deeply distressed by drought.
Afflicted by desire, short of stature, greedy, and devoted to unrighteousness,
all people in the Kali age will have little fortune yet many offspring.
Women who are intent only on nourishing themselves, courtesans who delight in their own beauty,
disregard the words of their husbands and are always devoted to the houses of others.
Those of immoral conduct will always harbor a longing for the wicked;
women of noble families will become unchaste toward men.
Terrified by the fear of thieves and other dangers, people, being excessively oppressed by famine and the burden of taxes, construct wooden mechanical devices. (NarP 1.41.81)
In a land abundant with wheat and barley, they will go about distressed;
though placing [their hopes] in their hearts upon a taskless state, they urge forth auspicious words.
People maintain a state of kinship only until their own purpose is accomplished;
even monks are constrained by bonds of affection for friends and others.
Bhikṣus accept disciples on account of the condition of receiving food.
Furthermore, women who scratch their heads with both hands transgress the commands of their elders and husbands. (NarP 1.41.85)
When the twice-born become intent on conversing with heretics and associate with heretical people,
then the Kali age shall reach its height.
When the subjects no longer perform sacrifices and the twice-born do not offer oblations,
then indeed the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise.
O twice-born ones, there will be an increase in unrighteousness and even untimely death;
when all dharmas have perished, the world will fall into a state devoid of splendor.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, the true nature of Kali has been described to you;
for one who is devoted to Hari, this Kali does not cause affliction anywhere.
After that, they say that in the Kṛta age meditation alone is the means, in the Tretā age meditation as well,
in the Dvāpara age sacrifice alone, and in the Kali age charity alone.
That which is accomplished in ten years during the Kṛta age, in one autumn during the Tretā,
and in one month during the Dvāpara, is achieved in a single day and night during the Kali age.
What one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by performing sacrifices in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara,
that one attains in the Kali age simply by chanting the praises of Keśava.
And those men who chant the name of Hari day and night,
or who perform worship of Hari— the Kali age does not afflict them.
And those men who proclaim "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," whether they are free from desire or possessed of desire, Kali does not afflict them.
But those who are devoted to the names of Hari in this terrible Kali age, O twice-born one, they alone have accomplished their purpose; indeed, Kali does not afflict them.
And those who are intent on the worship of Hari and dedicated to the names of Hari—
They are indeed equal to Śiva; no deliberation need be made in this matter.
Meditating upon Viṣṇu, the support of the entire world and the embodiment of the ultimate reality, one does not perish when the terrible Kali age has arrived.
Oh, how exceedingly fortunate are those who worship Keśava even once,
now that the terrible Kali age has arrived, which is devoid of all righteousness!
In this Kali age, for those ritual acts prescribed in the Vedas that suffer from defects of deficiency or excess,
the remembrance of Hari alone is what provides their completion.
"O Hare! O Keśava! O Govinda! O Vāsudeva!
O you who pervade the universe!"—those who constantly utter these names are never afflicted by the Kali age.
"O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, O Rudreśa, O Nīlakaṇṭha, O Trilocana!"—
even those who mutter these names are not afflicted by the Kali age.
"O Mahādeva, Virūpākṣa, Gaṅgādhara, Mṛḍa, Avyaya!
Those Brahmins who speak thus have achieved their purpose; of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.41.102)
"O Janārdana, O Lord of the World, O Acyuta clad in yellow garments"—
those who utter even this much here have no fear of the Kali age.
In this world, O Brahmin, sons, wives, wealth, and the like are easily obtained by men; however, in this terrible Kali age, a devotee of Hari is difficult to find.
Those heretics who are devoid of action and faith, who revile the Vedas,
and who are devoted to unrighteousness, are not at all worthy of hell if they remember Hari.
For people who stand outside the path of the Vedas, who perform sinful deeds,
and who are devoid of purity of mind, expiation occurs only through the name of Hari.
"O twice-born one, this entire world, both moving and stationary, is dependent on destiny; it acts exactly as it is impelled by him."
Having performed all rites prescribed in the Vedas according to his ability,
one who is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa should offer them to Mahāviṣṇu.
Actions dedicated to Mahāviṣṇu, the Supreme Self,
attain perfection simply through the remembrance of Hari.
For those devoted to the worship of Hari, the bond of sin does not arise;
therefore, devotion to Hari is extremely difficult for the evil-minded to attain in this world.
Oh, those who are devoted to Hari in this terrible and fearsome Kali age—
they are fortunate and high-souled, for they are also benefited by the company of the virtuous.
O twice-born one, for those who are devoted to the remembrance of Hari and whose souls delight in the name of Śiva,
all their actions truly reach completion.
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for those whose souls delight in the name of Hari!
They are worthy of worship even by the gods of the three worlds; what is the use of further words?
Therefore, for the benefit of all the worlds, I declare this:
Kali shall never afflict those mortals who are devoted to the name of Hari.
The name of Hari alone, the name alone, the name alone is my life;
in the Kali age, there is truly no other way, there is truly no other refuge.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, having been thus enlightened by Sanaka, Nārada attained supreme peace and spoke this once again.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures, by you, whose nature is exceedingly compassionate, has been revealed the supreme, eternal Brahman, the light of the world. (NarP 1.41.117)
This alone is the supreme merit, this alone is the supreme austerity:
that one should remember the lotus-eyed Lord, the destroyer of all sins.
"O Brahmin, this manifold world has been revealed by you as being illumined by a single consciousness; how can I understand what you have said without an illustration? (NarP 1.41.119)
Therefore, tell me how Brahman was realized by you when you were instructed, so that my mind, which is currently sinking, may attain stability.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada,
Sanaka replied as follows, while recollecting the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Sanaka said: "O Brahmin, I shall be intent on meditation; ask Sanandana whatever you desire.
He is skilled in the Vedānta scriptures and, being honored by the supreme noble ones, he may dispel your doubts."
Having heard what was thus spoken by Sanaka, Nārada proceeded to question Sanandana regarding the dharmas of liberation.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Names," in the first quarter of the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O Brahmin, from where was this world, with its moving and non-moving beings, created?"
And at the time of dissolution, to what does he go? Tell me that, O Sanandana.
By whom was this world created— along with its oceans, its sky, its mountains, its clouds, its earth, its fire, and its wind?
How were the elements created, and how did the divisions of the social classes arise?
How do purity and impurity belong to them, and what is the rule for dharma and adharma?
"What is the nature of the life-force of those who live, and where do those who have died go? May your lordship explain to me everything regarding the transition from this world to that world."
Sanandana said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall relate this ancient history—
the scripture spoken by Bhṛgu to Bharadvāja when he questioned him.
Having seen the great seer Bhṛgu seated on the peak of Kailāsa, blazing with great splendor, Bharadvāja questioned him.
Bharadvāja said: O giver of honor,
how does the individual soul wander continuously through various wombs,
and how is its liberation from saṃsāra brought about?
And that Nārāyaṇa, the creator, who is himself the self-existent Lord—
he and [the other] always exist in the relationship of the served and the server.
Into Him, the Lord, all things mobile and immobile enter at the time of dissolution;
He is the delighter of the worlds, devoid of qualities, and stainless.
O Sage, how can that which is invisible and inconceivable be known by anyone?
How can this Supreme Self, which is difficult to follow due to the power of time, be understood?
How do the Vedas praise with such reverence that which is beyond the reach of thought?
How does the individual soul, by transcending its state as a living being, become one with Brahman through perfect union?
"I wish to hear this; tell it to me, O mine of compassion.
Thus was the Blessed One questioned by Bharadvāja regarding his doubt.
Then the great seer, who resembled Brahmā, told him everything.
Bhṛgu said:
"He who was formerly known as Mānasa, renowned among the great seers—" *Nārada Purāṇa* 1.42.13.
The God who is without beginning or end, likewise ageless and immortal among them,
is celebrated as the Unmanifest, eternal, undecaying, and immutable.
From whom all beings were created, and who are born and die—
He, the God, first created the one known by the name Mahat.
The Lord, the sustainer of all beings, is renowned as Ākāśa;
from Ākāśa arose water, and from water arose fire and wind.
Then, from the conjunction of fire and wind, the earth came into being;
thereafter, a divine lotus consisting of light was created by the Self-born One.
From that lotus arose Brahmā, the Ordainer, composed of the Vedas;
he is celebrated as Ahaṃkāra, the creator who has become the self of all beings.
He of great splendor is indeed Brahmā; these five elements are his:
the mountains are the joints of his bones, while the fat and marrow are the earth.
The oceans are his blood, and the sky is likewise his belly;
the wind is his breath, fire is his heat, and the rivers are his veins.
His two eyes are renowned as Agni and Soma, having the forms of fire and the moon;
the sky is his upward-pointing head, the earth his feet, and the directions his arms.
For he whose nature is inconceivable is difficult to know even for the perfected ones (siddhas), there is no doubt;
he is this very Lord Viṣṇu, renowned as Ananta.

Abiding as the self of all beings, he is difficult to be known by those of unrefined soul; he who is the creator of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and the source of the existence and dissolution of all beings— from him the universe arose, concerning whom I have been questioned here by you.
Bhagadatta said:
"What are the dimensions of the sky, the directions, the earth, and the wind? Cut through my doubt regarding these according to the truth."
Bhṛgu said:
"This sky is infinite, inhabited by perfected beings and deities;
it is beautiful, filled with various abodes, and within it, death is not found."
Above the path of ascent, however, one no longer sees the moon and the sun;
there, the gods are self-luminous, possessing the brilliance of the sun and the splendor of fire.
And even those of renowned power do not see the end of the sky;
tell me why this is so, O giver of honor—because of its inaccessibility and its infinity.
Furthermore, this immeasurable space was filled from above and above by self-luminous rays that were blazing forth, such that it was obstructed even for the gods.
At the end of the earth is the ocean; at the end of the ocean, darkness is said to be;
at the end of darkness, they say there is water; and at the end of water, indeed, is fire.
At the end of the netherworld (rasātala) is water; at the end of the water are the lords of serpents;
at the end of that is space again; and at the end of space is water once more.
Thus, the limit of the Blessed One’s measure and that of the waters are difficult to discern even for the gods, as are fire, wind, and water.
The colors of fire, wind, water, and the surface of the earth are indeed like space; they are distinguished only by the vision of reality.
And the sages recite in various scriptures how the measure [of the world] has been established for the three worlds and for the ocean.
Who could declare the means of knowledge for that which is invisible and inaccessible,
when even the movement of the perfected ones and the deities is limited?
Then, the name of that great-souled Mānasa, which was renowned as "Ananta" (the Infinite) and was truly commensurate with his nature, became known as incalculable.
But when that divine form diminishes and increases again,
who else could possibly know it, even if there were another such as he?
Then, from Puṣkara, there was born the omniscient Lord in embodied form—
Brahmā, the primordial creator of beings, consisting of dharma and unsurpassed.
Bharadvāja said:
"If Puṣkara was born first, then Puṣkara is the eldest;
yet you say that Brahmā is the first-born—this is indeed my doubt."
Bhṛgu said: "The very form of the Mental [Being] that has attained the state of Brahman— here,
for the purpose of providing a seat for that form, the earth is called a lotus."
The pericarp of that lotus is Mount Meru, rising high into the sky;
situated in its center, this Creator of the world brings forth the worlds.
Bharadvāja said: O best of the twice-born, how does that Lord Brahmā, situated in the midst of Meru, create the various emanations of progeny outside of it?
Bhṛgu said:
Through his mind, Mānasa created the various emanations of progeny;
for the sake of protecting living beings, he first created water.
Water was created first as the life-force of all beings;
by it the life-force of all beings increases, and by it all creatures flourish.
And because they do not perish even when abandoned, this entire world is pervaded by them:
the earth, the mountains, the clouds, and whatever else possesses form—all that is to be known as belonging to Varuṇa; for the waters solidified once again.
Bharadvāja said:
How was the water produced, and how were fire and wind?
And how was the earth created? In this matter, I have a great doubt.
Bhṛgu said:
O Brahman, formerly in the Brahma-kalpa, at a gathering of the celestial rishis,
a doubt concerning the origin of the worlds arose among those great-souled ones.
Relying on meditation and maintaining silence, those twice-born ones remained motionless,
having renounced food and vying with one another for a hundred divine years.
The speech consisting of Brahman reached the ears of them all;
there, the divine Sarasvatī manifested from the expanse of the sky.
The sky before him appeared motionless, infinite, and like a mountain;
with the moon, sun, and wind vanished, it shone as if fast asleep.
Then water arose, like a profound darkness within darkness;
and from that pressure of water, the wind rose up.
Just as the interior of a house appears soundless and without gaps,
yet when it is being filled with light, the wind makes it resonant with sound.
Likewise, when the sky is completely filled with water without interval,
the wind, having pierced the surface of the ocean, rises up with a roar.
Or the wind, arising from the pressure of the ocean, moves within these [spaces];
having reached its station in space, it does not attain tranquility.
From that friction of wind and water, there appeared a being of blazing splendor and great strength,
with flames rising upward, dispelling the darkness.
Fire, joined with wind, draws up water from the sky;
through contact with fire and wind, that water attains the state of density.
Of that [wind], another which remains out of affection falls into space;
having attained a state of condensation, it proceeds to become earth.
This earth should be known as that which is the source of all tastes, all fragrances, all oils, and likewise of all living beings; from her everything is produced.
Bharadvāja said:
These five elements, which the Lord created as objects to be guarded,
by which these worlds are enveloped and which are designated as the great elements (mahābhūtas).
When that one of great intelligence created thousands of beings,
how did the state of being a "being" subsequently come to be established within them?
Bhṛgu said:
"Immeasurable great things undergo origination;
therefore, this term 'great elements' (mahābhūta) is appropriately applied to them."
Movement is wind, space is the ether, heat is fire, fluidity is water, and here the solid aggregate is earth; thus the body is composed of the five elements.
Therefore, all that is stationary and moving is endowed with these five;
hearing, smell, taste, touch, and sight are designated as the sense organs.
Bharadvāja said:
"If mobile and immobile beings are all composed of the five elements,
why are the five constituent elements not seen in the bodies of immobile things?"
In trees— which are without heat, without movement, and solid in their true nature— the five elements are not found within their bodies.
They neither hear nor see, nor do they perceive smells or tastes;
nor indeed do they know touch—how then can those five elements exist?
Because it is not liquid, not fire, not earth, and not air;
because space is immeasurable and the stars are not composed of elements, there is no materiality [in them].
Bhṛgu said:
Even for dense trees, there is space; of this there is no doubt.
The manifestation of their flowers and leaves occurs constantly.
From heat, the leaf withers, as do the bark, the fruit, and even the flower;
it withers and also decays, for such a tactile sensation is found here.
Fruits and flowers are destroyed by the assaults of wind, fire, and lightning;
since sound is perceived by the ear, therefore trees hear.
A creeper entwines trees and moves all around them;
since there is no path that is unseen, therefore the trees see.
Likewise, through merits and demerits, as well as by various medicinal herbs and incenses, trees remain free from disease and are in bloom; therefore, they emit fragrances.
Because they experience pleasure and pain, and because that which has been cut regrows, I perceive a living soul in trees; they are not devoid of consciousness.
By that [wind], it takes up that water and digests the fire and wind;
from the transformation of food, moisture and growth are produced.
And in the bodies of all mobile beings, the five elements are individually differentiated, by which the body moves.
Skin, flesh, as well as bones, marrow, and sinew as the fifth—
this is the aggregate here in the body composed of earth.
For heat is fire, as well as anger, the eye, and warmth;
and that which fire generates—these are the five fiery elements within embodied beings.
The ear, the nose, as well as the mouth, the heart, and the stomach—
these five elements in the bodies of living beings arise from space.
Phlegm, bile, sweat, fat, and blood— thus water always exists in five forms within the bodies of living beings.
Through the prāṇa one is satisfied, and likewise through the vyāna one exerts oneself.
The *apāna* moves downward, while the *samāna* is situated in the middle;
from the *udāna* one breathes out and speaks the five [types of] sounds.
Thus, these five winds envelop the embodied being here.
The embodied being perceives the quality of fragrance from the earth and taste from the waters;
I shall now describe in detail the qualities of that fragrance as they have been set forth.
It is pleasant, with a pervasive fragrance, sweet, and even pungent;
it is diffusive, compact, unctuous, dry, and indeed clear.
Thus, the detailed expansion of the earth's fragrance should be known as ninefold;
through the eyes one perceives light, and through the wind one experiences touch.
Sound, touch, form, and taste are recorded as the qualities (guṇas).
Now I shall speak of the knowledge of taste; listen to me as I declare it. (NarP 1.42.84)
Taste has been declared by the sages of celebrated soul to be of many kinds:
sweet, salty, bitter, astringent, sour, and pungent.
This sixfold expansion is known as the water-element;
sound, touch, and form are said to be the three qualities of light.
The light perceives forms, and form is remembered as manifold:
short, long, thick, square, minute, and circular.
White, black, as well as red, blue, yellow, and likewise ruddy;
hard, sticky, smooth, slimy, soft, and harsh.
Thus, the light-element (jyotis) is traditionally held to have sixteenfold expansion;
therein, space (ākāśa) possesses a single quality, which is traditionally known as sound alone.
I shall explain in detail the various natures of that sound:
Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, and likewise Dhaivata.
The fifth should also be known as possessing the *niṣāda* [note];
this is declared to be the sevenfold quality arising from space.
Though he abides everywhere through his sovereign power— even within water and other elements—
he [perceives] the sounds of clay drums, kettledrums, conchs, thunder, and chariots.
Thus, sound of many kinds originates from space;
however, touch is the quality of wind, and touch is recorded as being of many types.
Hot, cold, pleasure, pain, oily, and clear; likewise rough, soft, smooth, light, and even heavy. (NarP 1.42.94)
Sound and touch are to be known as the two qualities of air;
thus, the quality of air is said to be elevenfold.
They say that sound is born of space, yet it is perceived along with these qualities of wind; whether it is unobstructed or not, its course is inconsistent.
And those elements are constantly nourished by those very elements;
water, fire, and air are ever awake within embodied beings.
These vital breaths (prāṇas), having pervaded the root of the body, remain here;
having reached the earth-element, they cause it to move, just as a powerful being does.
Fire, having resorted to the head, protects the body;
the vital breath (prāṇa), existing both in the head and in fire, performs its functions.
That living being is the self of all beings, that Puruṣa is eternal;
he is the mind, the intellect, the ego, the elements, and the objects of the senses.
In this way, he is protected everywhere here by the vital breaths; from behind, however, he is supported by the samāna breath as it follows its own respective course.
Resting upon the fire at the base of the bladder and the anus,
the apāna wind circulates, carrying away both urine and feces.
Those skilled in the knowledge of the inner self say that the one which operates in the three— effort, action, and restraint— is called udāna.
Furthermore, the wind that is likewise situated in all the joints within the bodies of human beings is taught as the *vyāna*.
The fire, spread throughout the arms and impelled by the samāna wind, exerts itself intensely while circulating the fluids, the breaths, and the humors.
Between the downward-moving breath (apāna) and the upward-moving breath (prāṇa), the fire, impelled by both prāṇa and apāna and supported by them, properly digests [the food].
From the mouth down to the anus, at its end is that which is designated as the rectum;
from there, the semen and all the channels of embodied beings are produced.
The convergence of the vital breaths (prāṇas) gives rise to the "conjunction" (sannipāta);
it should be known as the heat (ūṣman), which is fire, that digests the food of embodied beings.
The vital breath (prāṇa), carrying the force of fire, is struck back at the end of the rectum;
having moved upward, it again throws the fire upward.

The receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) is below the navel, while the receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya) is known to be above it; at the root of the navel, all the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the body are established.
Setting out from the heart, all the channels— extending horizontally, upwards, and downwards— carry the essence of food, impelled by the ten vital breaths.
This is also the path of yogis by which they go to that state—
those who have conquered fatigue, who are equanimous and steadfast, placing the Self upon the crown of their heads.
Thus, when the inhalation and exhalation of all embodied beings have been regulated,
the fire is perpetually kindled therein, like a fire placed within a cooking pot.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the World," in the second quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Bhṛgu and Bharadvāja.
Bharadvāja said: "If Vāyu, the lord of life, is indeed the wind that moves about,"
It breathes and speaks; therefore, the individual soul (jīva) is purposeless.
That state of heat which belongs to fire is perceived only by means of fire;
since fire itself consumes this [body], the individual soul (jīva) would then be purposeless.
When a living being is being slain, the soul is not perceived at all;
it is the vital air alone that abandons him, and his state of warmth perishes.
If the living being were composed of wind, or if its union were with wind,
it would perceive itself as being like a handful of air and would depart along with the qualities of the wind.
If there were union with him, or if one perishes because of him,
it would be like a vessel of water that has been separated from the great ocean.
Just as one who enters quickly into water or offers a lamp into fire would perish, so too does he perish. 43.6.
For life is established in this body through five supports;
there is no doubt that it does not exist in the absence of even one of these four.
Water perishes from lack of food; wind perishes from the suppression of breath;
the digestive fire perishes for the sake of breaking up the internal organs through fasting.
The earth itself withers through the afflictions of disease and wounds;
for when any one of these is oppressed, the entire aggregate meets its end.
When that [body] has reached the state of the five elements, what does the living soul follow?
Or what does the living soul distress? What does it hear, and what does it speak?
"This cow will deliver me when I am situated in the next world"—
when a creature dies after giving [this thought], whom will that cow deliver?
When the cow, the recipient, and the donor alike meet their destruction right here in this world, how can there be a reunion for them?
For one who has been devoured by birds, fallen from a mountain peak,
or consumed by fire, how can there be a return to life again?
If the root of a severed tree does not sprout again, where will one who has died come back to, even while still living? (NarP 1.43.14)
Only the living soul was created in the beginning;
that which revolves here perishes upon death, for from seed to seed, all perishes.
"O Brahmin, this doubt runs through my heart; dispel it, O Omniscient One, for I have indeed taken refuge in you. (NarP 1.43.16)
Sanandana said: Thus questioned by him at that time, O best of sages, that Bhṛgu, the son of Brahmā, spoke again for the sake of dispelling his doubt.
Bhṛgu said:
"The vital breaths do not belong to the living being who has been given away or for whom a ritual act has been performed;
rather, the living being goes to another body, while the physical frame simply falls apart."
The living soul does not depend on the body; when that [body] is destroyed, it does not perish, just as fire is seen even when the fuel has been consumed by the flames. // NarP_1,43.19 //
Bharadvāja said: Just as there is no destruction of that fire upon the exhaustion of its fuel,
so too that fire is not perceived once the fuel has been consumed.
"I know that it is extinguished, like a fire without fuel; for it has no destination, no measure, and no form. (NarP 1.43.21)
Bhṛgu said:
"At the conclusion of the use of the sacrificial fuel, that fire is no longer perceived;
I know it simply perishes when the fire is extinguished and lacks fuel."
He whose course, measure, or configuration cannot be perceived is like a fire that is no longer perceived once its fuel has been consumed.
For, because it has entered into space, it is difficult to grasp and is without support;
likewise, upon the abandonment of the body, the living soul remains like space.
It does not perish because of its extreme subtlety, just as light [does not vanish]; there is no doubt about this. For the fire sustains the vital breaths; let that be understood as the *jīva*.
For fire, which is sustained by the vital air, perishes through the suppression of the breath;
when that bodily fire has perished, the body consequently becomes insentient.
When fallen, one returns to the state of earth,
for the earth is the destination of all things that move as well as those that are stationary.
The wind follows space, and light follows it;
because these three are one, we two are established upon the earth.
Where there is space, there is wind; where there is wind, there is fire.
These should be understood as formless, yet they possess form when embodied within a body.
Bharadvāja said:
"O sinless one, if fire, wind, earth, ether, and water are present within embodied beings, what are the characteristics of the *jīva* therein? Please explain this to me."
In this body of living beings, which consists of five elements, delights in the five [senses], and is designated by the five consciousnesses, I wish to know what kind of soul (jīva) resides therein.
In this mass of flesh and blood, this accumulation of fat, sinews, and bones,
when the body is dissected, the living soul is not perceived at all.
If a body devoid of a living soul is composed of the five elements, then who experiences that pain—the physical or the mental suffering within the body? (NarP 1.43.33)
The living soul hears what is spoken through the two ears, yet it does not hear it when the mind is distracted; therefore, O Great Sage, the living soul is useless.
Everyone sees whatever is visible with the eye joined by the mind;
when the mind is distracted, the eye does not see even while seeing.
Under the sway of sleep, he no longer sees, nor smells, nor hears, nor speaks; furthermore, he does not perceive any touch.
Who here rejoices and who becomes angry? Who grieves and who is terrified? Who desires, meditates, hates, or utters speech? (NarP 1.43.37)
Bhṛgu said:
"In this regard, a single inner self (antarātman) sustains within that body which is common to the five [elements].
It perceives odors, tastes, sounds, touch, form, and whatever other qualities there may be."

The inner self, which pervades all limbs and manifests the five qualities within the body composed of the five elements, experiences both pains and pleasures here; however, upon separation from that [body], it no longer experiences the body.
When there is neither form nor touch, nor even the state of being in the fire, then,
when the fire of the body has been stilled, it perishes through the abandonment of the body.
All this is composed of water; for embodied beings, water is their very form.
Within that, the mental self is Brahmā, the creator of the worlds among all living beings.
Know that Self to be the essence of the welfare of all the worlds,
which dwells within the body like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf.

Know him to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), eternally devoted to the welfare of the world; know that darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva) are these qualities of the individual soul (jīva).
They say that the quality of the individual soul (jīva) is insentient, yet it moves and causes everything to move;
beyond this, those who know the field (kṣetrajña) say that he is the one who set the seven worlds in motion.
"There is no destruction of the living soul when the body is divided; the ignorant, not being sages, say this falsely.
The living soul, having passed beyond the body, proceeds; its separation from the body occurs at the end of its five-fold [life]."
Thus, he always moves hidden within all beings;
however, he is perceived by those who see reality with a sharp and subtle intellect.
Constantly applying himself during the first and last watches of the night, the wise man—
having obtained his food, with a purified self— beholds the Self within the self.
For by means of the serenity of mind, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, one whose self is serene, abiding in the Self, enjoys infinite happiness. (NarP 1.43.48)
The mental fire within bodies is designated as the *jīva*;
this is the creation of Prajāpati, according to the determination of the elements and the internal self.
In the beginning, Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, created only Brāhmaṇas,
who were produced from his own splendor and possessed a radiance equal to the sun and fire.
Then the Lord ordained truth, righteousness, and likewise the eternal Brahman, as well as proper conduct and purity for the sake of attaining heaven.
The gods, danavas, gandharvas, daityas, asuras, and mahoragas;
the yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, piśācas, and likewise human beings.
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—
Bharadvāja said:
if the caste is distinguished by the color of the four castes..."
Sweat, urine, feces, phlegm, bile, and blood flow from within all beings; why then is their appearance differentiated?
The species of mobile beings and stationary things are innumerable;
for those of such diverse colors, how can there be a definitive determination of color?
Bhṛgu said:
There is no distinction among the social classes; the entire world is composed of Brahman.
For it was created by Brahman in the beginning, and through its actions it attained the state of being the various classes.

Those twice-born ones who were fond of sensual pleasures, fierce, prone to anger, unkind, and reckless, who abandoned their own duties and whose limbs were stained with blood, attained the state of Kṣatriyas.
Those twice-born who, having adopted a livelihood dependent on cattle, subsist by agriculture and do not perform their own duty,
have indeed fallen to the state of Vaiśyas.
Devoted to violence and falsehood, greedy, and subsisting on all manner of occupations,
those twice-born who were blackened by a lack of purity fell to the state of Śūdras.
Thus, when the twice-born, though engaged in these various activities,
remain established in the system of dharma, their ascetic merit does not perish.
May they constantly uphold the Veda, as well as the vows and observances,
by which those who know it understand that the Veda was indeed created in the beginning.
Among them, there were various other twice-born ones here and there,
as well as Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, and diverse Mleccha tribes;
that creation is known as the "Mānasī" (mental), and it was devoted to the system of Dharma.
Bharadvāja said:
"O best of the twice-born, by what does one become a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra? O brahmin-sage, best among speakers, tell me that."
Bhṛgu said:

He who has been purified by the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony, who is pure, perfected through the study of the Vedas, and established in the duties pertaining to Brahman; ||| NarP_1,43.64 |||
One who is firmly established in purity and conduct, who practices knowledge correctly, who is dear to his guru,
who is constant in his vows, and who is devoted to truth— he indeed is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Truthfulness, generosity, non-malice, lack of cruelty, compassion, and mercy—
wherever these and austerity are observed, he is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa.
He who performs the duties born of the kṣatra class, is devoted to the study of the Vedas,
and delights in giving and receiving gifts— he indeed is called a kṣatriya.
One who quickly enters among cattle, is pure and takes delight in agriculture and trade,
and is accomplished in the study of the Vedas— he is designated as a Vaiśya.

One who constantly delights in eating all kinds of forbidden food, who performs all types of work, who is impure, who has abandoned the Vedas, and who is devoid of proper conduct— he indeed is known as a Śūdra.
If this mark were to exist in a Śūdra and were not found in a twice-born man,
then a Śūdra would truly not be a Śūdra, nor would a Brāhmaṇa be a Brāhmaṇa.
The restraint of greed and anger by every possible means,
as well as self-control, is the most purifying of all forms of knowledge.
One should avoid those two with all one's being, for they are intent on destroying one's welfare;
one should protect prosperity from constant anger, and one should protect ascetic merit from envy.
One should regard learning as devoid of honor or dishonor, but one should regard oneself as subject to negligence.
O twice-born one, he whose every undertaking is free from the bonds of desire,
and for whom everything has been offered in renunciation— he is a true renouncer and he is wise.
Non-violent toward all beings, he should live having attained a state of friendliness; having renounced all possessions, he should remain with a focused mind, his senses conquered.
The sage who is constant in austerity, self-controlled, and restrained in mind and thought, finds a state free from sorrow and fearless both in this world and the next.
By one desiring to conquer the unconquered and remaining unattached amidst attachments, whatever is grasped by the senses—that is established as the manifest (vyakta). 43.77.
That which is unmanifest should be understood as graspable by its signs yet beyond the senses;
it should be contemplated with unwavering faith, and one should fix the mind upon it with confidence.
One should restrain the mind with the vital breath, and hold the vital breath in Brahman; through non-attachment alone comes liberation, and one should not think of anything at all.
O Brahmin, one indeed attains the bliss of Brahman through detachment,
provided one is constantly engaged in purity and endowed with right conduct.
Compassion for all beings—that is the characteristic of the twice-born;
truthfulness, vows, austerity, and purity—truth indeed creates progeny.
The world is sustained by truth; by truth alone one goes to heaven. Untruth is the form of darkness; by darkness, indeed, one is led downward.
Those seized by darkness do not see; they are obscured by light and darkness.
They say that hell is indeed darkness, a most difficult light to perceive.
Both truth and falsehood are encountered by those who move within the world;
even therein, such a mode of conduct regarding truth and falsehood exists in the world.
Dharma and adharma, light and darkness, as well as suffering and happiness, along with physical and mental sufferings and pleasures that arise from what is not pleasure; ||| NarP_1,43.85 |||
Perceiving the world as created by the Lord, the wise are not deluded;
therein, the discerning person should strive for the sake of liberation from suffering.
For the happiness of living beings in this world and in the next is indeed impermanent;
it does not shine, just as the moonlight of the moon seized by Rāhu does not gleam.
Likewise, the happiness of beings who are overcome by darkness perishes.

That happiness is indeed said to be of two kinds: bodily and mental. In this world and in the next, the engagement with objects is undertaken for the sake of happiness; for there is nothing more distinguished than this, whether in this life or in the hereafter, other than the fruit of prior actions. That very desirable excellence is the source of the undertakings of the qualities of dharma and artha; its cause is their commencement, and these undertakings are for the purpose of achieving happiness.
Bharadvāja said: "Tell me this which you have stated: that it is the supreme state of happiness."
We do not accept that, for these sages are established in greatness.
This excellence of desirable qualities is not attained by those who do not cultivate them;
it is heard that even Brahmā, the creator of the three worlds, remains alone as a celibate ascetic in austerity, and does not apply himself to the pleasures of desire.
Moreover, the Blessed One, the Lord of the Universe and Consort of Umā, reduced Kāma, who was advancing against him, to the state of being bodiless.
Therefore, although it is held by great-souled ones on this earth, it does not yet manifest; for this excellence of qualities is not yet fully distinguished.

"I do not believe this of the Blessed One; yet you have said that women are the highest of pleasures. "For there are two kinds of worldly report regarding the arising of results: happiness is obtained from good deeds, and otherwise, suffering," so Bhṛgu said.
To this it is replied: "Indeed, darkness arises from untruth; then, seized by darkness, they follow only unrighteousness, and not [the truth]."
Those who are indeed obscured in this world by anger, greed, delusion, violence, falsehood, and so forth, do not attain happiness in the next world;

they are overwhelmed by various diseases, afflictions, and torments, and are tormented by the sufferings of killing, imprisonment, and distress, as well as by the pains caused by hunger, thirst, and fatigue,
and by terrifying physical sufferings caused by rain, wind, excessive heat, and extreme cold, and by those arising from the destruction and separation from kinsmen and wealth.
Those who are overcome by these—by mental anxieties, by physical ailments, and by others such as those caused by old age and death—[are bound].
In heaven there is no physical or mental [suffering], no old age, and no sin;
there is only eternal happiness. In this world, however, both happiness and suffering exist.
In hell, they say there is only suffering; that [suffering] is the supreme state.
The earth is the mother of all beings, and women are of that same nature.
"The male Prajāpati is known there as the seed consisting of splendor;
thus [he is] the creator of the world, of dharma, and of conduct. (NarP 1.43.98)

The sin committed is pacified by well-performed austerity, by the study of the Vedas, and by the oblation; through the oblation it is stilled, but in the study of the Vedas there is the highest peace.
They say that through giving one obtains enjoyments, and through austerity one attains heaven;
moreover, they declare that giving is of two kinds: for the sake of the next world and for this very world.

Whatever is given to the virtuous stands to one's credit in the next world; but that which is given to the wicked is enjoyed here [in this world]. One reaps a fruit corresponding exactly to the kind of gift that is given.
Bharadvāja said:
What is the practice of dharma for whom, or what is the characteristic of dharma?
Of how many kinds is dharma? You ought to explain that.
Bhṛgu said:
Those wise ones who are intent upon the performance of their own duty attain the fruit of heaven; he who acts otherwise is deluded.
Bharadvāja said:
"Regarding this system of the four stages of life (āśrama) established of old by the Brahman-sages,
you should tell me here their respective modes of conduct."
Bhṛgu said:
"In the past, the Blessed Brahmā, acting for the welfare of the world, prescribed four stages of life (āśramas) for the purpose of protecting the Dharma."

In that regard, they consider residence in the teacher’s house (gurukula) to be the very first stage of life (āśrama). Here, with his self fully restrained by purity, purificatory rites, observances, and vows, he worships the two twilights as well as the deities of the sun and fire. Having abandoned indolence, his inner self purified by saluting the teacher, practicing the Vedas, and hearing their recitation, he performs ablutions three times a day. With his inner self entirely dedicated to celibacy, tending the sacred fires, service to the teacher, and the constant offering of all alms-food and other requisitions, he dwells there.
He should not be contrary to the execution of the instructions of his guru, and he should be devoted to the study of the sacred texts obtained through the guru’s grace.
And on this point there is a verse:
"The twice-born man who, having propitiated his guru, obtains the Veda,
attains the fruit of heaven and his heart's desire is fulfilled."
Thus, they indeed call the life of the householder the second stage of life.
We shall fully explain all the characteristics of his proper conduct.
For those who have completed their studies, who observe virtuous conduct, and who seek the fruit of practicing dharma together with their wives, the householder stage of life is ordained.

For the attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure—the fulfillment of the three aims of life—is achieved here by means of irreproachable action. A householder should maintain his domestic life by acquiring riches through one of these means: by means of wealth obtained through the excellence of Vedic study, or that fashioned by Brahmanical sages, or that found in the ocean by means of water, or by wealth acquired through the practice of ritual restrictions and the grace of the deities.

For that is declared to be the root of all ascetic orders: those wandering mendicants who dwell in the teacher's family, as well as others who practice the dharma through prescribed vows and observances; even for them, the distribution of alms and offerings continues during the intervals.

And for forest-dwellers, there is the provision of material requisites; for these virtuous men are generally devoted to wholesome food and the study of the Vedas, and they wander the earth for the purpose of visiting sacred fords and seeing various lands.
For them, there is rising to meet them, approaching them, speaking words free from malice, providing comfort and honor, offering comfortable seats, comfortable beds, and the honoring of their meals.
And on this point there is a verse:
"The guest from whose house returns with his hopes frustrated, having given his own misdeeds to him, departs taking away his merit. (NarP 1.43.113)

Moreover, in this regard, the deities are gratified by sacrificial rites; the ancestors by the offering of funeral oblations; the sages by the study, hearing, and retention of sacred knowledge; and Prajāpati by the procreation of offspring.
On this subject there are two verses: "From all beings comes affection for one's offspring; likewise, from Vāyu come the ear and speech."
In this context, causing distress, striking others, and harshness are censured.
Disregard, lack of ego, and hypocrisy are indeed censured;
non-violence, truthfulness, and freedom from anger constitute the austerity belonging to all stages of life.

Moreover, there is the acquisition of garlands, ornaments, garments, ointments, and constant enjoyment of dance, song, instrumental music, and the pleasant sounds of the ear; the sight of beloved women with affectionate glances; and the enjoyment of various kinds of food—those to be chewed, swallowed, licked, drunk, and sucked. (NarP 1.43.117)
Contentment with one's own dwelling and the attainment of the pleasures of desire— when these three goals are constantly fulfilled through the virtues of the householder stage of life,
one experiences happiness here in this world and shall attain the destination of the virtuous.
For a householder who lives by gleaning grains, who is devoted to the performance of his own duty,
and who has renounced the pursuit of sensual pleasures, heaven is not difficult to attain.

Indeed, even the forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), following the dharma, wander about performing austerities at sacred fords, rivers, and springs in their own beloved forests, which are teeming with deer, boars, buffaloes, tigers,
and wild elephants.

Having abandoned the enjoyment of village clothing and food, they subsist on a varied and restricted diet consisting only of wild herbs, fruits, roots, and leaves; they remain standing or seated, sleeping on the earth, stones, gravel, pebbles, sand, or ashes; their bodies are covered with kasha grass, kusha grass, skins, or bark garments; they wear their hair, beards, nails, and body hair as they grow; they perform ritual ablutions at fixed times and carry out the performance of offerings and oblations at the prescribed hours.

Having found rest through gathering sacrificial wood, *kuśa* grass, and flowers, and through sweeping [the altars], their skin was cracked open by cold, heat, and wind; with their flesh, blood, skin, and bones completely withered by the performance of various observances and yogic practices, they remained devoted to fortitude and sustained their bodies through the application of spiritual essence (*sattva-yoga*).
But he who practices this disciplined conduct ordained by the Brahman-sages shall burn away his defects like fire and conquer worlds that are difficult to attain.
Furthermore, the conduct of the wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) is as follows:
having abandoned fire and attachment to wealth, wife, and possessions, and having cast off the bonds of affection for themselves, they wander forth;
regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, their intellects are unattached to the pursuits of the three aims of life.

Viewing enemies, friends, and neutrals with equanimity, they are free from malice toward beings—whether stationary, born from a womb, born from an egg, or born from sweat—and do not harm them through speech, mind, or physical actions.
Having no fixed abode, they wander among mountains, riverbanks, the roots of trees, and temples; or else they may join a caravan or enter a city or village.
They are devoid of anger, pride, greed, delusion, miserliness, hypocrisy, slander, arrogance, and violence.
And there are verses on this point:
"The sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings, for him no fear arises from any beings anywhere. (NarP 1.43.125)

Having established the Agnihotra within his own body, the Brahmin offers his body as an oblation into the fire of his own mouth with the sacrificial offerings obtained through alms; thus, kindled by that fire, he indeed proceeds to the worlds.
The twice-born who practices the stage of liberation (mokṣāśrama) as prescribed, pure and with an intellect disciplined by his own resolve,
attains the world of Brahman, being as utterly tranquil as a flame that has no fuel.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Conduct of Brāhmaṇas," in the second quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Bhṛgu and Bharadvāja.
Bharadvāja said:
"A world beyond this world is heard of, yet it is not perceived."
I wish to know that; your honor ought to explain it to me.

The sage said: On the northern side of the Himalayas, in a region endowed with all virtues and merit, there is a place called the Supreme World (Paraloka), which is holy, secure, and desirable. (NarP 1.44.2)
For there, men are free from evil deeds, pure, and utterly stainless;
they have abandoned greed and delusion, and are without affliction.
That region is like heaven, for there the auspicious qualities have been described;
death prevails only at the proper time, and diseases do not touch them.
There was no lust for the wives of others; people were devoted to their own wives. No one else was killed there, nor was there any greed for material possessions.
Indeed, there is no higher unrighteousness; of this there is no doubt, nor does it even arise.
Yet, the fruit of that which has been committed is perceived there directly.
Some, provided with vehicles, seats, and food, dwelling in palaces of pure faith, were surrounded by all objects of desire and adorned with golden ornaments.
For some, however, the mere maintenance of life is possible;
others maintain their lives only through great exertion. (NarP 1.44.8)
In this world, some men are devoted to righteousness while others are deceitful;
some are happy and some are miserable; some are destitute and others are wealthy.
In this world, fatigue, fear, delusion, and intense hunger arise, as well as greed for wealth, because of which the unwise are bewildered. (NarP 1.44.10)
The wise man who knows this is not defiled by evil; yet, deceit, fraud, theft, slander, and malice are accompanied by fear.
Harming others, violence, slander, and likewise falsehood—
he who indulges in these finds his austerity diminished.
But for the wise man who practices these [rules], his austerity does not increase;
for here there are manifold anxieties regarding the action of dharma and adharma.
This world is the field of action; having performed good or evil deeds here, one attains good through good deeds, and likewise, the opposite through evil.
In this regard, in former times, Prajāpati, the gods, and likewise the hosts of sages—
purified by their performed sacrifices and austerities— resorted to the world of Brahmā.
The northern region of the earth is the most meritorious and auspicious of all;
those people who perform meritorious deeds here are indeed born there.
If others desire honor even among the animal births,
or likewise others whose lifespans are exhausted, they perish upon the surface of the earth.
Addicted to devouring one another and possessed by greed and delusion,
they revolve right here and do not go toward the northern direction.
But those wise ones who, self-restrained and observing the vow of celibacy, worship their gurus,
understand the path of all the worlds.
Thus has this Dharma, fashioned by Brahmā, been declared by me in brief.
For he who truly understands both dharma and adharma in the world is wise.
Bharadvāja said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, tell me this: what is that which is called 'the inner self' (adhyātma) regarding a person here, and how is it that it is the inner self?"
Bhṛgu said: O brahmin-sage, regarding this which you inquire about as "the supreme self" (adhyātma),
I shall explain it to you, my son, for it is the most beneficial happiness.
The teachers have fully demonstrated that which is conjoined with creation and dissolution;
by knowing which, a person finds joy and happiness in this world. (NarP 1.44.23)
He shall obtain the fruit thereof, which is the welfare of all beings;
[namely] earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
The great elements are the origin and the dissolution of all beings;
from whence they were created, there indeed they go again to their absorption.
The great elements emerge from the beings like waves from the ocean;
and just as a tortoise extends its limbs and then withdraws them again, so do they.
In the same way, the Self of beings, the creator of beings, withdraws again the five great elements from all beings that have been created. (NarP 1.44.27)
Indeed, the individual soul does not perceive that [subtle body] correctly within the elements;
sound, the ear, and the bodily cavities—these three are born from the womb of space.
Touch, movement, and the skin are known as the triad of wind;
form, the eye, and digestion are said to be the threefold nature of fire.
Taste, moisture, and the tongue—these three are known as the qualities of water.
That which is to be smelled, the sense of smell, and the body—these three are the qualities of earth.
There are five great elements, and the mind is said to be the sixth;
O Bhārata, the senses and the mind are its perceivers.
They say that the seventh is the intellect (buddhi), while the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is the eighth.
Indeed, the ear is for the purpose of hearing, and the skin is traditionally taught to be for the purpose of touch.
The tongue is for the taking of flavors, the nose for the taking of scents, and the eye is for seeing; it is the mind alone that creates doubt. (NarP 1.44.33)
The intellect exists for the purpose of determination, while the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) stands like a witness;
he beholds everything that is above the soles of the feet, as well as what is below and above.
By this all-pervading one, every intermediate space here is filled;
it should be understood that the sense-faculties are entirely composed of persons.
Darkness, passion, and goodness—these states also depend upon that [intellect];
having understood this intellect, a person understands the past and future courses of all beings.
By observing in this way with composure, one attains supreme tranquility;
for by the qualities [of passion and the like], the intellect is destroyed, and from the intellect alone, the senses are also destroyed.
When the elements, with the mind as the sixth, are dissolved into the intellect, from where would the qualities arise?
Thus, all this—both the stationary and the moving—is composed of that alone.
It dissolves and it arises from that; therefore it is described in such a way.
That by which one sees is the eye; that by which one hears is called the ear.
They say that one smells with the nose; one perceives taste with the tongue;
one feels touch with the skin; and the intellect undergoes modification all at once.
That by which one desires something is then the mind (*manas*);
however, due to the presiding over of the intellect (*buddhi*), it is divided into five distinct objects.
They call those the senses; the invisible one presides over them.
Intellect resides in the person and operates within the three states of being.
Sometimes he attains joy, sometimes he grieves;
he never exists in a state of neither pleasure nor pain.
Thus, in the minds of men, it abides within three states;
yet this very nature of being transcends these three states.
Just as the ocean is the lord of rivers and the sea is the boundary of the shores,
so too does the intellect, having transcended its objects, abide within the mind through those very objects.
While living thus, the sage conforms to his own nature;
for that [nature] always causes all the sense-faculties to function.
Joy is *sattva*, sorrow is *rajas*, and anger is *tamas*—these three are they;
and whatever states exist in this world, all of them are indeed contained within these three.
Thus have all the meditations residing in the intellect been explained to you;
and all the sense organs must be conquered by the wise man.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas always reside within living beings;
these threefold perceptions are seen in all sentient creatures.
It is of three kinds, O giver of honor: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic.
The quality of sattva is characterized by the touch of pleasure; the quality of rajas is characterized by the touch of pain.
Endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas), you two become engaged in worldly affairs;
whatever may be joined with pleasure in your body or mind, [that belongs to me].
One should declare that state which proceeds from *sattva* to be such;
whereas that which is joined with suffering and is disagreeable to the self [is of a different nature]. (NarP 1.44.52)
Know, O best of sages, that when it is active, it is indeed *rajas*;
furthermore, when it is joined with delusion, it becomes unmanifest and uneven.
One should understand that state to be beyond reasoning and unknowable— a darkness characterized by exhilaration,
joy, bliss, happiness, or tranquility of mind.
These sattvic qualities manifest in some way or another:
discontent, remorse, grief, greed, and likewise forbearance.
These are the signs of passion (rajas) seen through the causes pertaining to the body:
contempt, delusion, negligence, sleep, and lassitude.
In some way or another, various qualities of darkness (tamas) prevail;
they consist of manifold corruption, reaching far, and are characterized by longing and doubt.
He whose mind is self-restrained is happy both in this world and after death;
he who perceives this distinction between the two subtle entities, the sattva and the kṣetrajña.
One creates the qualities, while the other does not create the qualities;
they are always joined together, like a gnat and an udumbara fruit.
These two would exist in mutual conjunction, and likewise for both;
by their very nature, they are always distinct yet conjoined.
Just as a fish and water are joined together, so too are those two;
the qualities do not know the Self, but the Self knows the qualities in every respect.
The witness of the qualities, however, likewise considers itself their creator;
through the excellence of the intellect, it employs the senses for the purpose of illumination.
The Supreme Self, like a lamp, creates the qualities while remaining inactive and unaware; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) indeed beholds the quality of sattva.
This is the constant association between these two, the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*;
yet there is no substratum whatsoever for either the *sattva* or the *kṣetrajña*.
The sattva creates the mind, but never the qualities; when he properly restrains their rays with his mind, [he attains liberation].
Then his self shines forth like a lamp burning within a jar—
the sage who has abandoned worldly action and is eternally delighted in the Self.
Therefore, having become the self of all beings, he shall go to the supreme goal,
just as a water-dwelling bird is not smeared by the water.
In this very way, one of perfected wisdom moves among living beings;
thus, a person should dwell with their own intelligence, realizing that this is simply the nature of things.
Neither grieving nor rejoicing, equanimous and free from envy,
he who is engaged through the application of contemplation constantly creates the qualities.
Just as a spider produces its thread, so should the qualities (guṇas) be understood as being like threads;
once destroyed, they do not return, and their cessation is no longer perceived.
The imperceptible is established through the perceptible by means of inference;
thus some determine it, while others maintain that it is cessation.
Having thoroughly considered both of these, one should resolve according to one's own understanding;
thus [should one untie] this firm knot of the heart, which consists of the deliberations of the intellect.
Having been liberated, one should dwell in happiness and not grieve, with all doubts severed;
just as people who are soiled attain purity by entering a full river.
Having plunged into it, O wise one, know that the piercing of ignorance is likewise; for he who knows the further shore of the great river is not tormented, whereas he who does not cross it is.
But the knower of reality does not suffer; rather, one who knows the lineage transcends [suffering].
Thus, those who know the supreme knowledge of isolation (*kaivalya*) regarding the inner self (*adhyātma*). NarP_1,44.75 //
