Thus, every wise man, having observed the coming and going of all beings with his intellect, gradually attains peace from that.
He for whom the threefold aim of life is understood, who, having observed it, renounces it,
who is endowed with mental inquiry, who perceives reality, and who is free from worldly longing— [he is a sage].
And the self cannot be seen within the senses individually,
for they are scattered here and there and are difficult to restrain by those who have not disciplined themselves.
By this alone one would become a Buddha; what other characteristic of a Buddha could there be?
For having realized this, the wise consider their task accomplished.
Therefore, the wise have no fear that which would be a very great fear for the ignorant;
for there is no superior state for anyone, since when a quality exists, it proclaims its incomparability.
He who acts without prior intention and burns away what was done in the past—for him, neither of those two is unpleasant; how then could it produce anything pleasant for him as he acts here?
People here praise worldly life and, by performing its duties, they produce that very life for themselves;
look there at those who are skillful—they do not grieve, even if fear arises, for their state is eternal.
Bharadvāja said: "O Brahmin, explain to me the yoga of meditation for the sake of attaining that state,
by knowing which a person is liberated from the threefold suffering."
Bhṛgu said:
"Indeed, I shall fully declare to you the fourfold yoga of knowledge,
knowing which the great seers here attain eternal perfection."
Just as they have practiced meditation, so do the yogis,
the great seers who are satisfied with knowledge and whose minds are directed toward nirvāṇa.
Once liberated from the defects of saṃsāra, they do not return again;
having exhausted the defects of birth, they are established in their own true nature.
Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, liberated, and without possessions, they are unattached,
free from fear and other such states, and bring peace to the mind.
There, through meditation, the sage should hold the mind—though it be afflicted—in one-pointed concentration;
sitting like a log of wood, with the collection of his senses withdrawn.
One should not perceive sound with the ear, nor should one feel touch with the skin;
one should not perceive form with the eye, nor likewise tastes with the tongue.
The knower of reality should abandon all fears through meditative concentration; the energetic one should not desire these things that agitate the fivefold group of senses.
Then, having withdrawn the group of five into the mind, the wise one should steady the wandering mind together with the five senses.
Wandering at will, without support, and fluctuating in strength across the five sense-doors—
the wise man should swiftly compose his mind upon the path of prior meditation.
When one draws together the senses and the mind itself, this is the first path of meditation described by me out of fear [of worldly existence]. // NarP_1,44.93 //
For him, that [knowledge], previously restrained, together with himself as the sixth,
will immediately flash forth across the ends of the ocean, like lightning from a rain-cloud.
Just as a drop of water on a leaf is unsteady and moves in every direction,
even so does his mind become when on the path of meditation.
Concentrated for a brief moment, it remains somewhat on the path of meditation;
yet again, the mind wanders onto the path of the wind and becomes like the wind itself.
Free from despondency, free from afflictions, free from weariness, and indeed devoid of envy,
one who knows the yoga of meditation should repeatedly compose the mind through meditative concentration.
Investigation, reflection, and discernment arise for the sage engaged in meditative concentration; this is the first dhyāna from the beginning.
Even when being afflicted by the mind, one should practice composure;
the sage should not fall into despondency, but should indeed act for his own welfare.
Just as heaps of dust, ashes, and dried cow-dung, when suddenly drenched with water, do not undergo complete saturation; (so it is with those who have not practiced meditation).
Just as a powder that is somewhat oily yet dry and unblessed gradually and slowly becomes completely infused, so too does that [practice] reach full cultivation.
In this very way, one should gradually cultivate the collection of the senses;
by withdrawing them step by step, they will be properly stilled.
O Lord of Sages, having first established the mind itself and the fivefold group [of the senses] upon the path of meditation, one attains tranquility through constant yoga.
Neither by human effort nor by any divine power will that happiness come to him which belongs to one whose self is thus restrained.
Endowed with that happiness, he will delight in the practice of meditation;
for in this way, yogis proceed to the stainless state of Nirvāṇa.
Sanandana said: O Brahmin, having been addressed thus by Bhṛgu, the powerful Bharadvāja,
whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma, was filled with wonder and honored Bhṛgu in return.
O wise one, O highly intelligent one, this origin of the world has been proclaimed to you in its entirety. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the second section of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, having heard the words of Sanandana concerning the dharma of liberation, [the sages asked:]
Then Nārada, the knower of reality, again asked about the sublime discourse on the supreme self.
Nārada said:
"O highly fortunate one, I have heard the scripture on liberation spoken by you;
yet no satiety arises in me even as I listen again and again."
O Sage, O Omniscient One, tell me how a living being is liberated from the bondage of ignorance, and likewise explain the dharma of liberation which is ever-relied upon.
Sanandana said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history concerning how Janaka,
the lord of Mithilā, attained liberation.
Janaka Janadeva, however, was the sovereign of Mithilā;
he was intent upon reflecting on the duties pertaining to the afterlife.
In his house, the teachers constantly dwell in the cremation ground,
demonstrating various doctrines while propounding diverse and deceptive views.
Regarding their state after death and their rebirth,
he remains firmly established in his conviction and is for the most part satisfied by the true nature of the self.
Thereupon, a great sage named Pañcaśikha, the son of Kapila,
having wandered over the entire earth, arrived at Mithilā.
He has fulfilled all the duties of renunciation, is firmly established in the determination of the knowledge of reality, is free from the pairs of opposites, and has destroyed all doubt.
The seers say that he who has dwelt among men out of desire,
seeking eternal and ultimate happiness so difficult to attain, is called one alone.
Those whom the Sāṃkhyas call Kapila, the supreme seer and Prajāpati,
I believe is he himself who makes himself known in that form.
The first disciple of Āsuri, whom they call Cirajīvin (Long-lived),
is he who performs a sacrificial session (*satra*) at Pañcasrotas for a thousand years.
Having approached the great circle of the followers of Kapila, which consists of five streams,
he taught the ultimate truth, which is unmanifest and abides in the state of the Puruṣa.
Endowed with sacrificial mantras and further strengthened by asceticism, the sage Asuri,
who perceived the body as a manifestation, attained the realization of the field and the knower of the field within the wise.
That single-syllabled Brahman which appears in manifold forms— Āsuri realized that imperishable one within that maṇḍala.
His disciple was Pañcaśikha, who had been nourished with human milk;
there was a certain housewife, a Brāhmaṇī named Kapilī.
Having become the son of that woman, he drank from her breasts;
thereafter, he obtained the status of Kāpileya and attained resolute wisdom.
The Blessed One has thus told me the origin of Kāpileya; [he explained] his status as the son of Kapila and his unsurpassed omniscience.
O Sage, Janaka, who knew the Dharma, having learned that [the king] was a man of knowledge,
approached him along with his ministers and a hundred teachers, and attempted to delude him with logical arguments.
But Janaka, deeply attached upon seeing Kāpileya,
left behind his hundred teachers and followed after him.
To him, who was supremely auspicious and bowed down in accordance with dharma,
he spoke of the supreme liberation which is prescribed as Sāṃkhya.
Having spoken of weariness with birth, he spoke of weariness with karma;
and having spoken of weariness with karma, he spoke of weariness with everything.
That for the sake of which there is association with dharma and the ripening of the fruits of actions— that delusion is unreliable, perishable, unstable, and transient.
When destruction is being perceived directly before one's eyes and witnessed by the world,
even one who asserts on the basis of scripture that "the supreme exists" is defeated.
For that which is non-self is death to the self; affliction is death, consisting of old age and disease.
To think of it as the self through delusion is considered an incorrect supreme view.
But if there were even such a thing as that which does not occur in the world—
that this king is ageless and immortal— then he would believe it to be so.
Regarding that which is characterized by non-existence, upon what basis could one assert the determination of worldly affairs, such as "it exists" or "it does not exist"? (NarP 1.45.27)
For direct perception is the foundation of these two, and indeed, the established conclusion (*kṛtānta*) is also their foundation;
for scripture is directly perceived, whereas a divergent conclusion amounts to nothing at all.
In this inference, wherever it may be formulated— even if one meditates upon it—
the view of the nihilists that the soul is distinct from the body remains established.
The scenting of ghee during its cooking within the calyx of a lotus, the recollection of past births, the magnet, the sun-crystal, and subsisting on water; NarP_1,45.30 //

The propitiation of hungry ghosts (pretas), spirits (bhūtas), and deities, as well as the cessation of rites for the deceased, is the established rule regarding the authoritative standard. // NarP_1,45.31 //
Indeed, whatever reasons there may be that reside in a material form do not apply here; for no commonality is perceived between that which is immaterial and that which is material.
Some say that ignorance, karma, and craving lead to rebirth;
yet when that mind subject to death has perished and been consumed by fire, [rebirth does not occur].

They say that another kind of delusion arises, which is the destruction of one's essence (*sattva*), when [another person] is perceived as different in appearance, birth, learning, and purpose. (NarP 1.45.34)
How could there be such an unconnected relationship as "he is in this"? And if this were so, what benefit would there be from the powers of knowledge, learning, and austerity?
Whatever action he has performed that is understood through commonality,
yet here in this very world he would suffer for it along with other ordinary people.
Whether one is happy or suffering, there is the discernment of what is seen and what is unseen;
for just as the body might be struck by pestles, it would come into existence once again.
Knowledge that is other than this is in vain, by which this [reality] is not perceived:
the seasons, the year, the Kali age, cold and heat, and likewise the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Just as he perceives those [limbs], such is the destruction of sentient beings;
one who is overwhelmed by old age is destroyed by death.
First, the weak perishes, just as the foundation of a house collapses;
[then] the sense faculties, the mind, the vital air, the blood, the flesh, and the bone.
They perish in succession and return to their own elements; furthermore, there would be a disruption of worldly affairs when the fruits of the merit of giving are about to arrive. (NarP 1.45.41)
"For that purpose, there are many well-considered reasons, such as the words of the Veda and worldly conventions. (NarP 1.45.42)
"Is this a hand? "It is not. No one can perceive it as such;
for those very people who are deliberating upon it, it appears clearly as they pursue it correctly.
Wherever the intellect dwells, there it decays like a tree;
in this way, all living beings are afflicted by both meaningful and meaningless sufferings.
They are dragged away by the scriptures, just as elephants are led by their keepers.
In the same way, many objects that bring happiness, when licked, become parched;
having encountered even greater suffering and abandoned their bait, they fall under the power of death.

For those who are subject to destruction and whose life is unstable, what use are kinsmen and the acquisition of mantras? He departs, leaving everything behind, and having gone, he does not return in an instant. (NarP 1.45.47)
Even earth, space, water, fire, and air always sustain the body;
having observed this, how could there be any attachment? For even though it is sustained by these, there is no peace for that which is subject to destruction.
Having beheld this statement free from worldly attachment, unerring, supremely stainless, and witnessed by his own self,
the king was struck with wonder and proceeded to question him further.
Janaka said:
"O Blessed One, if no consciousness exists after death for anyone,
then being thus, what will ignorance or knowledge do?"
O best of the twice-born, behold this which leads to the ultimate destruction of everything:
whether one is heedful or heedless, what difference will it make? (NarP 1.45.51)
For what purpose could non-attachment to the elements or attachment to those that are perishable be practiced? What certainty can there be here in reality?
Sanandana said:
The wise Pañcaśikha, calming once again with his words that parasol of the intellect which had become bewildered and distressed by darkness, spoke as follows. (NarP 1.45.53)
Pañcaśikha said:
"There is no doctrine of annihilation here, nor is there a doctrine of eternal existence;
for this [world] is merely a collection of body, senses, and mind."
The five elements—water, space, wind, fire, and earth—function in various ways, both individually and by depending upon one another, in their respective activities. (NarP 1.45.55)
They abide in those [elements] by way of their manifestation, yet they are separated from them by their own nature:
space, wind, heat, moisture, and that which is of the earth.
This body is a collection of five elements, yet it is not of a single nature;
knowledge, heat, and wind constitute the threefold composition of the body.
The sense-faculties and their objects, intrinsic nature, consciousness, and the mind, as well as inhalation and exhalation, transformation, and the elements— all these have emerged from here.
Hearing, touch, the tongue, sight, and likewise the nose—
these five sense organs are qualities preceded by the mind.
In that regard, the threefold volition associated with consciousness is constant;
it is what they call pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Sound, touch, and form—these three constitute the object of the body;
for these five, along with the [other] senses, are the virtuous qualities until death for the attainment of knowledge.
In those [states], there is the accomplishment of actions and the ascertainment of the meaning of all principles;
they call that supreme purity, the imperishable Great Intellect (*buddhi*). (NarP 1.45.62)
For one who perceives this collection of qualities as a self through incorrect views, endless suffering does not subside.
Since it has been seen that there is no self, the notions of "I" and "mine" do not exist;
upon what basis, then, does this continuous succession of suffering persist?
In that regard, a person of right conduct should listen to this unsurpassed treatise on renunciation; and when it is being spoken, it shall lead to liberation.
For indeed, the renunciation of all actions— even those prescribed as obligatory—
is always better than the suffering that brings darkness for those who are improperly disciplined.
When one renounces material objects, there are ritual acts; when one renounces enjoyments, there are vows;
through the renunciation of pleasure, there is austerity and yoga; and through the renunciation of everything, there is the attainment of liberation.
This non-dual path of universal renunciation has been shown for the sake of abandoning suffering; for in such a way, one would not fall into a miserable state.
Having spoken of the five organs of cognition, with the mind as the sixth,
I shall now describe the five organs of action, making them six in total.
The two hands are to be known as the organ of action; likewise, the two feet are the organ of locomotion.
The male organ is for procreation, and the anus is the organ of excretion.
Speech is for the purpose of specific sounds; thus they know it to be endowed with five [qualities].
In this way, he released these eleven through the mind at the time of birth.
The ear, sound, and the mind—these three are involved in the act of hearing;
likewise in the case of touch, likewise in the case of form, and the same applies to taste and smell.
Thus, these five triads are indeed qualities for the sake of perceiving that [object],
by which this threefold state arises through its various modes.
These three— the sāttvika, the rājasa, and the tāmasa—
are the threefold [modes] of the Vedas, through which that which accomplishes all things has spread forth.
Exultation, joy, bliss, happiness, and tranquility of mind—
whether arising from no cause or from some cause— this is the quality of sattva.
Dissatisfaction, remorse, grief, greed, and intolerance—these are the marks of *rajas*, seen whether they arise from a cause or without a cause. (NarP 1.45.76)
Lack of discernment, as well as delusion, negligence, sleep, and lassitude—
these various qualities of tamas manifest in some way or another.

And he who understands this wisdom of liberation and seeks the Self with vigilance is not smeared by undesirable fruits of action, just as a leaf is not wetted by water when sprinkled upon it. (NarP 1.45.78)
When he is released from the firm and various bonds caused by progeny as well as by the deities,
and when he abandons both suffering and happiness, then, liberated and free from marks, he attains the supreme goal.
Through auspicious rites established by the authority of the Vedas, he lies beyond the fear of old age and death;
when merit is exhausted, sin has departed, and the causal body and its fruit have perished.
Having thus resorted to the unmanifest, formless, and great void, those who are powerless perceive it;
just as a spider, when its web is exhausted, remains stationary even while moving about.
Thus liberated, he abandons suffering, casting it off like one seeking a clod of earth;
just as a ruru deer sheds its old horn, or as a serpent casts off its skin. (NarP 1.45.82)
Departing without looking back, thus liberated, he abandons suffering;
just as a bird, having left a fish falling into the water, flies away with power. (NarP 1.45.83)
For thus, having abandoned both suffering and happiness, he is liberated and, being signless, attains the supreme goal.

Having heard this state of immortality being spoken here by Pañcaśikha himself, and having fully comprehended its entire meaning, the king, his purpose certain, dwelt in supreme happiness, free from sorrow.
Moreover, it is said that when the King of Mithilā beheld his city consumed by fire, he sang:
"Indeed, nothing of mine here is being burnt," and so the protector of the earth spoke of himself.

For whoever recites this "Certainty of Liberation" by the Great Sage and constantly contemplates it in that manner, they will not experience calamities; remaining free from suffering, they are liberated, just as the King of Mithilā was upon encountering Kapila.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the second quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, having heard that supreme discourse on the spiritual self from the King of Mithilā, Nārada—
Then the noble-minded one again questioned Sanandana with affection.
Nārada said:
O Sage, ocean of compassion, please explain to me, who have sought refuge in you, how one may not experience the threefold suffering pertaining to the self. (NarP 1.46.2)
Sanandana said: O wise one, for this being born here and destined to exist in these states— namely the womb, birth, old age, and so forth— there is this threefold suffering.
The attainment of the Blessed One, whose sole characteristic is the state of bliss consisting of an unsurpassed and extraordinary joy, is considered the medicine and the ultimate oneness.
Therefore, wise men should exert effort to attain that;
O Great Sage, both the knowledge and the action that are the causes for attaining it have been explained.
Thus, knowledge is said to be twofold: that arising from scripture and that arising from discernment;
the former consists of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), while the latter is born of discernment (viveka) regarding the Supreme Brahman.
Manu also, the most excellent of sages, having recollected the meaning of the Vedas, said this;
let it now be heard from me as I speak it clearly. (NarP 1.46.7)
Two Brahmas are to be known: the Brahman of Sound and that which is the Supreme Brahman.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman.
And the Atharvaṇa Śruti says that two kinds of knowledge are to be known:
the supreme, which is the attainment of the Imperishable, and the lower, which consists of the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas.
That which is unmanifest, undecaying, desireless, unborn, immutable,
indefinable, and formless, yet endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs.
The wise indeed behold Him who is all-pervading, omnipresent, eternal, the source of all beings, and the causeless cause; He who, as the pervader, encompasses everything that is to be pervaded.
Understand that supreme abode; it is to be meditated upon by those who desire liberation. That subtle, highest station of Viṣṇu is proclaimed by the words of the Vedas.
That very nature of the Supreme Self is what is denoted by the word "Bhagavat";
the term "Bhagavat" has been designated as the designator of that imperishable Self.
That knowledge by which the true nature of the meaning thus declared is known in its reality is supreme, being other than that which consists of the three Vedas.
O twice-born ones, although that Brahman is beyond the range of words,
the term "Bhagavat" is used for its worship in a figurative sense.
The word "Bhagavan," O Blessed One, resides in the supreme Brahman called Great Splendor (Mahāvibhūti), which is pure and the cause of all causes. (NarP 1.46.16)
The letter *bha* likewise consists of two meanings: "that which is to be known" (*jñeyam*) and "the knower" (*jñātā*).
Therefore, O Sage, this letter *ga* is the progenitor and the creator who has brought down the sacred tradition (*āgama*).
The term *bhaga* is said to denote the sixfold aggregate consisting of complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, as well as knowledge and dispassion. (NarP 1.46.17)
Beings dwell there within that Self of beings, the Self of all;
therefore, the meaning of the syllable *va* is the imperishable One dwelling in all beings without exception.
In this very way, O best of beings, the great sound "Bhagavān" belongs to Vāsudeva, who has become the Supreme Brahman, and goes to no other.
In this context, this word is used in its primary sense as an object of worship, consistent with technical definitions;
it is not used figuratively, for elsewhere it is indeed used figuratively.
He who knows the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of beings,
and who knows both knowledge and ignorance— he is to be called "Bhagavān."
Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor— in their entirety,
and devoid of all qualities and attributes subject to abandonment— constitute the meaning of the word "Bhagavat."
All beings dwell there within the Supreme Self;
because he dwells within all beings, he is therefore remembered as Vāsudeva.
In former times, when questioned by Khāṇḍikya Janaka, Keśidhvaja spoke truly of the etymological explanation of the name of the infinite Vāsudeva.
Since he dwells within all beings and they dwell within him,
Vāsudeva is therefore the Lord, the ordainer and the sustainer of the worlds.
O Sage, he has transcended the primordial nature of all beings, their transformations, and the defects such as the qualities (guṇas);
having passed beyond all veils, he is the soul of all, by whom the entire intermediate space of the worlds is pervaded.

Having abandoned the creation of beings enveloped in extreme suffering, he—who is the essence of all auspicious qualities and whose nature is virtue—assumed at will a vast body according to his desire; thus, he has accomplished the welfare of the entire world.
He is the mass of singular qualities consisting of splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, and the power of his own heroism;
he is the supreme among the supreme, and in that Lord of the high and the low, no afflictions or other defects exist.
He is the Lord, whose nature is both individual and collective, whose form is unmanifest and whose form is manifest;
the Lord of all, the knower of the creation of all, possessing equal power, he is known as the Supreme Lord.

That by which it is known—that form which is free from defects, pure, supreme, and indeed stainless—is both perceived and understood; therefore, that knowledge is said to be distinct from the other. Through the power of self-study and self-restraint, that Supreme Person is beheld.
This Brahman is understood by you as the cause for attaining that [state].
One should turn toward yoga through the study of the scriptures; from yoga, one should direct oneself toward the study of the scriptures.
Through the perfection of both scriptural study and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed.
For the purpose of perceiving that, sacred study is the eye, as is yoga;
he who has become Brahman cannot be seen with the fleshly eye. (NarP 1.46.33)
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to know that yoga; please describe it, so that once it is known, I may behold the Supreme Lord, the support of all. (NarP 1.46.34)
Sanandana said:
Just as Keśidhvaja formerly spoke of Yoga to the high-souled Khāṇḍikya Janaka, so shall I relate it to you.
Nārada said:
O Brahmin, who was Khāṇḍikya, and who was Keśidhvaja? And how did their conversation, which concerned the connection with yoga, come to pass?
Sanandana said: O Janaka, Dharmadhvaja indeed had a son named Amitadhvaja;
his brother was King Kṛtadhvaja, who was ever devoted to the supreme self.
The son of Kṛtadhvaja was the illustrious Keśidhvaja, O twice-born one;
the son of Amitadhvaja was also named Khāṇḍikya-Janaka.
For on the path of action, Khāṇḍikya was deposed from his own kingdom;
joined by his domestic priest and ministers, he possessed but meager means.
Then, having been expelled from his kingdom, he became a wanderer in difficult forests;
relying on knowledge, he also performed very many sacrifices.
O best among the knowers of yoga, once while you were presiding over a sacrifice yourself in order to cross even death by means of the knowledge of Brahman— NarP_1,46.40.
In a lonely forest, a fierce tiger killed his cow;
then the king, having learned that the cow had been slain by a tiger, [informed] the officiating priests.
He asked, "What penance should be prescribed here?
and they replied, "We do not know; let Kaśeru be consulted."
Narada said, "Kaśeru was also told by him, 'So be it,' and he replied accordingly.
O Indra among kings, ask Śunaka; he knows it and will explain it to you."
Having gone there, he questioned him, and he too said to the king, O Sage:
"Neither Kaśeru, nor I, nor anyone else exists on earth at present. (NarP 1.46.44)
"Only one person knows your enemy, Khāṇḍikya, who was defeated by you;
he said to him, 'O Sage, I am going now to ask my own enemy.'"
If that enemy of mine kills me while I am already present at the sacrifice, he will,
when questioned, declare it to be an act of expiation.
"Then, O best of sages, your yoga will become unimpeded.
Having said this, the king, wearing a black antelope skin, mounted his chariot.
He went to the forest where that lord of the earth, Khāṇḍikya, was staying;
and upon seeing his enemy approaching, Khāñjaḍikya [prepared for him].
With eyes copper-red with anger and his bow drawn, he spoke;
Khāṇḍikya said:
"Will you slay us by means of this black antelope skin as if it were armor?"
"O fool, do you not know that he will not strike me while I am wearing the black antelope skin? Tell me, is there no black antelope skin on the backs of deer? (NarP 1.46.50)
Thinking that those fierce, sharp arrows were discharged in vain, I shall slay you; you shall not escape from me alive.
"O evil-minded one, you are a murderous assailant, an enemy who has seized my kingdom!
Keśidhvaja said:
"O Khāṇḍikya, I have come to you to ask about a doubt."
"Either this plan to kill you is being reconsidered, or else he is discharging his arrow in anger.
Then, together with his ministers and his family priest, he went into private.
The high-minded Khāṇḍikya consulted with all his ministers: "This enemy, having fallen into our power, must be executed. (NarP 1.46.54)
"In this world, the entire earth shall come under your control.
Khaṇḍikya said to them all, "It will surely be so; of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.46.55)
But if there is hatred, the entire earth will come under my control;
his victory over the next world is mine, and the whole earth is mine.
If I do not kill him, my victory over the world will be transient; but victory in the next world is infinite, whereas the conquest of the earth is for but a short time. (NarP 1.46.57)
"Therefore, I shall not kill him; whatever he asks, I shall answer that.
Then, having approached his enemy, Khaṇḍikya said to Janaka: ||| NarP_1,46.58 |||
"Ask whatever you wish to ask; I shall tell it to you.
Then, O Sage, he related exactly what had happened regarding the slaughter of the sacrificial cow.
Then he asked him about that very matter regarding expiation;
and the sage explained it to Keśidhvaja according to the proper rule.
Indeed, whatever atonement was prescribed there in its entirety,
he, having understood its meaning, was thus authorized by that high-souled one.
Having arrived at the sacrificial ground, he performed all the rites in their proper sequence;
having completed the sacrifice according to the rules in due order, he bathed in the concluding purificatory rite (avabhṛtha).
Having thus accomplished his purpose, the king reflected:
"All the officiating priests have been honored by me, and all the members of the assembly have been respected. (NarP 1.46.63)
In that very same way, I have fulfilled the desires of those seeking wealth with the objects they longed for;
indeed, I have scrutinized the entire world of mortals.
"Is my mind not yet perfected in action? Why is it not as it should be?
Thinking thus, that lord of the earth fell into deep reflection.
"I did not give the teacher's fee to Khāṇḍikya," [he said];
then that king, mounting his chariot, departed once more.
Svāyambhuva remained where Khāṇḍikya had his impenetrable forest stronghold;
and Khāṇḍikya, seeing him approaching once again, took up his weapon.
Having resolved to kill him, he stood there; but King Khāṇḍikya spoke to him again:
"I have come for no harmful purpose, O Khāṇḍikya; do not be angry."
"Know me to have come here to offer atonement for my preceptor;
by your instruction, the sacrifice has been duly accomplished by me. (NarP 1.46.69)
"I wish to give this to you; choose a teacher's fee.
Being thus addressed, he consulted further with his ministers.
"Desiring to atone for his teacher's offense, what should he be asked by me?
The ministers said to him, "Let him be asked for the entire kingdom. (NarP 1.46.71)

When they requested the kingdom with their troops unexhausted by labor, King Khāṇḍikya, the great lord, laughed and said to them: NarP_1,46.72: "The kingdom is sought after by those who have performed [meritorious deeds], not by those whose soldiers are unweary."
"How could a short-lived sovereignty over the earth be desired by those such as I? This is precisely how you, my minister, accomplish your own self-interest in this matter. (NarP 1.46.73)
"What is the ultimate truth here, and who are you? You are not discerning in this matter.
Having said this, he approached King Keśidhvaja.
He said, "Will you certainly give me the teacher’s fee?
Having been told by him, "Certainly," Khāṇḍikya then spoke to him. (NarP 1.46.75)
O venerable one, you are an expert in the ultimate truth of internal consciousness;
if you would grant me the payment for your teacher.
"Declare that action which is sufficient for the pacification of those afflictions.
Keśidhvaja said:
"Why did you not request from me a kingdom free of thorns?"
"For there is nothing else as dear to kṣatriyas as the acquisition of a kingdom.
Khaṇḍikya said: "O Keśidhvaja, listen to me as to why I have not sought it."
This kingdom is entirely that which the wise do not covet;
for the duty of Kṣatriyas is the protection of their subjects. (NarP 1.46.79)
And the slaying by righteous war of those who oppose my own kingdom—
wherein there is no fault on my part, being powerless, since you have done me no wrong.
For this ignorance, when devoid of the proper sequence, leads only to bondage;
this desire of mine for sovereignty is merely for the sake of seeking the prospect of future births.
He pursues only those qualities born of virtue in others;
begging from kinsmen of the warrior caste is not for the sake of dharma—this is the opinion of the virtuous.
Therefore, this kingdom within the realm of ignorance was not requested by you;
for the wise do not covet a kingdom, as their minds are drawn away by the sense of "mine-ness."
"I am intoxicated by the pride of 'I' and the intoxication of drink; those like me do not [deserve this].
Keśidhvaja said:
"And I, indeed, perform [this] desiring to cross over death by means of knowledge."
"By good fortune, this mind of yours has attained the sovereignty of discernment regarding kingship, various sacrifices, enjoyments, and likewise the exhaustion of merit. (NarP 1.46.85)
And listen also, O delighter of your lineage, to the true nature of ignorance (*avidyā*):
it is the notion of a self in what is not the self, and the perception of one's own domain in what is not one's own. (NarP 1.46.86)
This seed, produced from the tree of ignorance, exists in two ways;
within the body composed of the five elements, the embodied soul remains enveloped by the darkness of delusion.
The person of poor intellect loudly forms the notion, "I am this," even though [the self] exists separately from space, air, fire, water, and earth. (NarP 1.46.88)
Who creates within the body—the abode of the self—an identification with the self, when even houses, fields, and the like are merely objects of enjoyment for the body? (NarP 1.46.89)
For when the Self is bodiless, the wise man thinks "this is mine";
and in this same way, he regards his sons and grandsons, who are produced from that body.
The wise man exercises lordship over his own body, which is not the self;
the human being performs action for the sake of the enjoyment of all bodies.
And whenever a man assumes another body, that [new body] always leads to further bondage;
for just as a house made of clay is smeared with clay and ash.
This body is likewise composed of earth, with its condition sustained by clay and water;
the physical form consists of the five objects of enjoyment through the enjoyments that consist of those five elements.
If one is nourished by that [merit], then what cause for pride is there for a person who has been traversing the path of saṃsāra through many thousands of births? (NarP 1.46.94)
O gentle one, when he who has fallen into the exhaustion of delusion and is shrouded by the dust of latent impressions is washed with the warm water of knowledge, that dust is cleansed away.
Then the weariness of delusion of the traveler on the path of saṃsāra comes to rest;
when the weariness of delusion has subsided, the person possesses a clear internal organ.
Not bestowing any further excellence upon others, one attains supreme nirvāṇa;
for this self consists of nirvāṇa itself, composed of knowledge and stainless.
Phenomena consisting of suffering and ignorance belong to your nature, but not to the Self;
for water has no contact with fire, even though it is in contact with the cooking pot.
Just as a wise man performs actions such as the intensification of sound and other qualities,
so too does the self, through its association with primordial nature (prakṛti), become defiled by egoism and the like.
For that immutable one, having cast aside the pillar [of ego], partakes in the natural qualities (dharmas);
thus, I have described this seed of ignorance to you.
And there exists nothing other than yoga that brings about the destruction of the afflictions.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the second quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanandana said:
He [received] these words of Keśidhvaja, which were rich in spiritual knowledge.
Having heard these words as if they were nectar, Khaṇḍikya spoke again, urging him on.
Khāṇḍikya said:
"Tell me that, O illustrious one, you who are the best among those who know yoga; for you have understood the meaning of the scriptures on yoga within this lineage of Nimi."
Keśidhvaja said: O Khāṇḍikya, listen as I describe the true nature of yoga,
established in which the sage does not fall away even after attaining absorption into Brahman.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; that which is attached to sense objects leads to bondage, while that which is free from sense objects leads to liberation.
Having withdrawn the mind from sense objects, the wise one whose self is consciousness should,
by means of that mind, contemplate the Supreme Lord who has become Brahman for the sake of liberation.
By means of that, one should lead the mind toward the self;
by one's own power, the mind should transform the self, just as a magnet attracts iron.
That distinguished movement of the mind which depends upon one's own effort,
its union with Brahman is designated as yoga.
Thus, one who possesses the practice that characterizes the dharma endowed with absolute excellence is indeed called a seeker of liberation, a yogin.
The yogi who is engaged in yoga is first called "one who is practicing" (yuñjāna);
but when his samādhi is perfected, he is one who has attained the realization of the Supreme Brahman.
If his mind is not corrupted by the fault of obstacles,
liberation from the former [state] arises through practice over successive births.
But the yogin whose meditative concentration is fully perfected attains liberation in that very birth;
having burned away the accumulation of karma by the fire of yoga, he reaches it before long.
Leading his own mind toward the state of yoga, the dispassionate yogi should practice celibacy, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-possessiveness. (NarP 1.47.12)
One should perform the observances (niyamas) of self-study, purity, contentment, and austerity,
and likewise direct the mind toward the Supreme Brahman.
These five restraints (yamas) and five observances (niyamas) have been proclaimed;
they grant distinguished fruits when performed with desire, and bestow liberation upon those free from desire.

Thus, having occupied the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) and other postures, the disciplined ascetic, endowed with virtuous qualities, should practice yoga through those known as restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas).
That which one performs through practice upon the vital breath (prāṇa) situated in the navel is to be known as prāṇāyāma; it is both with seed (sabīja) and without seed (abīja).
When the prāṇa and apāna breaths, being restrained according to the proper method, mutually overcome one another,
that is the third [result] arising from their restraint.
O Lord of enemies, for the yogin who practices, that which possesses a gross form as its object is traditionally taught to be the object of meditation for Ananta.
Restraining the senses that are attached to sound and other objects, the knower of yoga,
devoted to withdrawal (pratyāhāra), should make them follow the lead of the mind.
By that, supreme and unwavering mastery over the self and the senses is born; for one who has not mastered these, the yogi is not a practitioner of yoga. (NarP 1.47.20)
Having brought the vital breaths under control through *prāṇāyāma* and the senses through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*),
one should then make the mind steady upon a virtuous object of focus.
Khāṇḍikya said:
"O highly fortunate one, let that auspicious refuge of the mind be told to me—
that support upon which the entire arising of defects is destroyed."
Keśidhvaja said:
O wise one, the support of the mind is twofold according to its essential nature:
it is both with form and without form, as well as supreme and non-supreme.
Meditation is threefold; this entire universe is said to be of three kinds:
that called Brahman, that known as karma, and likewise that which consists of both.
For the cultivation of existence (bhāvabhāvanā) is threefold: one consists of the nature of karma, another of the nature of Brahman, and likewise yet another consists of both natures. (NarP 1.47.25)
Sanaka and the others are always wise and endowed with the contemplation of Brahman;
others, from the gods down to the moving and unmoving beings, are characterized by the contemplation of action.
And among those such as Hiraṇyagarbha, who are endowed with authority and awakening, there exists a twofold cultivation of being consisting of both Brahman and action. (NarP 1.47.27)
O King, as long as all the specific cognitions and activities remain unexhausted,
this entire universe and that which is beyond it appear divided by the perception of those who see through duality.
That knowledge which has all distinctions subsided, which is pure existence alone, beyond the range of words, and which is realized through self-realization— that is designated as Brahman.
And that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu, who is formless and unborn;
it is the universal form of the Supreme Self, characterized by the absence of specific forms.
O King, since it is not possible for one engaged in yoga to contemplate that [subtle form],
therefore the gross form of Hari, which is within the range of the eyes, should be contemplated.
The Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, Vāsava, and Prajāpati;
the Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, the suns, the stars, and the planets.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, daityas, and all the luminaries of the gods; humans, animals, mountains, oceans, rivers, and trees. NarP_1,47.33 //
O King, all beings without exception, as well as the causes of beings—
ranging from primordial matter (pradhāna) to the specific elements (viśeṣa), and consisting of both sentient and insentient natures— are [contained within this].
Whether one-footed, two-footed, many-footed, or footless—
this embodied form of Hari consists of the threefold nature of contemplation.
All this entire universe, this world of moving and non-moving beings,
is endowed with the power of Viṣṇu, whose essential nature is the Supreme Brahman.
The supreme power of Viṣṇu is declared to be one; likewise, the other is called the individual soul (kṣetrajña);
and a third power is recognized, known as ignorance and karma. (NarP 1.47.37)
O King, O high-minded one, this power of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), when impelled by action born of karma,
is said to exist within this essence-less cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
Through that [power], the one known as the *kṣetrajña* experiences all the afflictions of *saṃsāra*, for its power is obscured by it. (NarP 1.47.39)
O protector of the earth, among all beings, [compassion] is observed to vary in degree;
it is indeed slight in those without breath, and greater than that in stationary beings.
Among reptiles, others surpass them by superior power;
among birds, wild animals surpass them; and among those, domestic animals are superior by their own capacity.
O King, human beings surpass animals by virtue of their superior power;
and even more than them, the deities such as the Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas are preeminent.
Śakra is superior to all the gods, and Prajāpati is superior to him;
Hiraṇyagarbha is superior even to him, being characterized by the power of the Supreme Person.
O King, all these various forms without exception are his own forms,
because they are joined with his power, just as [all things] are joined with space.
O Great-minded One, the second is known as Viṣṇu, the object of meditation for yogis;
it is the formless aspect of Brahman which is called "Being" (sat) by the wise.
O King, that in which all these powers are established is indeed the true nature of Hari;
his great form is not any other form.
O Lord of Men, by his own sport he creates all forms consisting of power, endowed with the activities of gods, animals, humans, and so forth.
For the benefit of the worlds, the activity of that immeasurable one arises from the cause of his past actions; it is all-pervasive and characterized by being unconditioned.
O King, that form should be meditated upon as the Universal Form by one engaged in yoga;
for it serves to purify the self and destroys all sins. (NarP 1.47.49)
Just as fire with its flames raised burns dry grass when fanned by the wind,
so too Viṣṇu, abiding in the mind, consumes all the impurities of yogins.
Therefore, when all powers have reached their state of dullness, one should properly establish the mind there; this is to be known as the pure characteristic.
O King, it is the auspicious basis for the all-pervading self accompanied by consciousness; transcending the cultivation of the three states of existence, it leads to the liberation of yogins.
But others, O tiger among men, whose mental activities are characterized by malice—those gods and others, all of whom have their origins in karma—are impure. (NarP 1.47.53)
The embodied form of the Blessed One, free from desire for any support—
this indeed should be known as *dhāraṇā*, wherein the mind is held fixed.
In that regard, O lord of men, hear what kind of embodied form of Hari should be meditated upon; for concentration is not possible without a support.
With a serene and beautiful face, eyes as long as lotus petals, lovely cheeks,
and a broad forehead shining like a polished slab.
With beautiful ear-ornaments placed evenly upon his ears and shoulders,
he had a neck like a conch shell and a broad chest marked with the Śrīvatsa.
With a belly that has three folds of skin and a curved navel,
he is Viṣṇu with eight long arms, or perhaps with four.
One should meditate upon Him, whose thighs and hips are symmetrical, whose lotus-like feet and hands are perfectly steady,
who is beyond the elements, and who is clad in pure yellow garments.
Adorned with a crown, beautiful armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments,
he was graced by the circle of his radiant bow Śārṅga, conch, mace, and sword.
The yogi, having concentrated his own mind, should contemplate that [object] with total absorption until, O King, the mental retention (*dhāraṇā*) becomes firmly established right there.
Whether speaking, standing still, or performing actions according to one's own will,
when [the mantra] does not depart from the mind, then one should consider it accomplished.
Then, the wise one should contemplate the form of the Blessed One as peaceful, devoid of the conch, mace, discus, Śārṅga bow, and so forth, yet holding a rosary.
When that concentration (dhāraṇā) remains steady in that manner,
one should then meditate upon [the deity] as being devoid of ornaments such as crowns and armlets.
Then, with his mind, the wise man should likewise focus on a single part; thereafter, he should become intent upon the visualization of the whole composed of those parts.
And when there is a single-pointed concentration upon that object, free from longing for anything else, that dhyāna is accomplished through the first six factors, O King. (NarP 1.47.66)
That very apprehension of its own nature which is free from conceptual construction,
accomplished by the mind through meditation— that is designated as *samādhi*.
O King, consciousness is the attainer of the Supreme Brahman, which is the object to be attained;
likewise, the Self is that which is to be attained once all mental constructions have been utterly destroyed.
The knowledge that effects the realization of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the instrument;
having accomplished through that instrument its task of liberation, it indeed ceases once its purpose has been fulfilled.
Having attained the state of being that very essence, he then becomes non-different from the Supreme Self;
and any difference would be produced by ignorance.
When the knowledge that produces differentiation has undergone absolute destruction, who will bring about the non-difference of the self from Brahman, which is already accepted? (NarP 1.47.71)
Thus has the Yoga been explained by me to you, O Khāṇḍikya, as you inquired;
both in brief and in detail. What else shall be done for you?
Khāṇḍikya said: "The true essence of yoga has been explained; everything has indeed been accomplished for me.
By your instruction, all the impurities of my mind have been destroyed."
"What has been declared by me as 'mine'—this is not so, nor is it otherwise; even a king cannot be described thus by those who know what is to be known. (NarP 1,47.74)
"This is 'I' and this is 'mine'"—this is ignorance, and conventional usage proceeds in this manner regarding these two;
however, the ultimate reality is inexpressible, that which is not within the range of words.
Therefore, accept all this that has been done for my welfare by you,
since the imperishable yoga, which is intent upon liberation, has been proclaimed by you, O bull among the Keśins.
Sanandana said:
O Brahmin, having been honored by that Khāṇḍikya with worship as was his due, King Keśidhvaja then returned to his city.
Khāṇḍikya also, having made his son king for the sake of attaining yoga,
went to Viśālā with his mind fully absorbed in Kṛṣṇa.
Having become single-mindedly devoted there and endowed with virtues such as self-restraint (yama),
the king attained dissolution into the stainless Brahman known as Viṣṇu.
Keśidhvaja also, intent on exhausting his own karma for the sake of liberation,
enjoyed sense objects and performed actions without attachment.
Then, O Sage, having exhausted his sins through the enjoyment of auspicious things and being purified, he attained the perfection that utterly destroys the threefold suffering.
All this that you have asked me has been told to you for the purpose of treating the threefold suffering; what else shall I tell you?
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the second quarter of the first part of the Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O illustrious one, I have heard the remedy for the three types of suffering.
Nevertheless, my mind is deluded and does not find immediate stability.
O Brahmin, O giver of honor, tell me how human beings can endure the transgression of their own nature—that conduct practiced by the wicked. NarP_1,48.2.
Sūta said:
Having heard that which was spoken by Nārada, Sanandana, the son of Brahmā,
remembering the deeds of Bhagīratha, spoke while filled with joy.
Sanandana said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history, hearing which your wandering mind will find firm stability once again. (NarP 1.48.4)
O best of sages, in ancient times there was a king named Bharata,
after whose name this land is called Bhārata-khaṇḍa.
Having obtained the kingdom by succession from his father and grandfather,
that king protected it according to dharma, pleasing the subjects like a father.
And in Ṛddha, with various sacrifices, he meditated upon the Blessed One Adhokṣaja,
who is the soul of all gods, his mind intent on diverse ritual acts.
Then, having fathered sons and becoming detached from sense-objects,
that wise king renounced his kingdom and went to the hermitage of Pulastya’s son.
O Sage, having become an ascetic there at Śālagrāma, that great field frequented by those seeking liberation, he performed the worship of Viṣṇu.
O Nārada, having bathed daily in the morning in the pure water, she performed worship with whatever offerings she could obtain, out of a spirit of devotion.
Chanting the supreme imperishable Brahman with devotion, he should worship Draviṇa;
then, having returned to his hermitage, he should worship Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World.
With materials gathered by oneself— fuel-sticks, *kuśa* grass, clay, and so forth—
as well as fruits, flowers, leaves of *tulasī*, and pure water.
Worshipping with a purified mind and overflowing with the expansion of devotion,
that illustrious man, having bathed in the morning with a concentrated mind, once [proceeded].
Chanting his prayers, he remained for three muhūrtas in the water of the Cakranadī;
then, thirsty, she came to that bank to drink the water. (NarP 1.48.14)
O Brahmin, a single female deer, being in her season, fled from the forest;
thereupon, she mated with him when the water had been almost entirely drunk by her.
The roar of the lion was truly great, causing terror to all living beings;
then, because of that lion’s roar, she leapt from the riverbank.
By climbing too high, her fetus fell into the river;
it was carried away with great force, tossed about by a garland of waves.
Bharata took up the young fawn that had fallen from the womb,
distressed by the pain of its premature birth and by its loud, piercing cry.
O Lord of Munis, that doe fell down and died; then, seeing that doe deceased, the royal ascetic— NarP_1,48.19 —
Having taken the young deer with him, the king returned to his own hermitage and cared for the young deer every day, O King.
O Sage, being nourished by him, he grew;
he grazed on grasses in the thickets at the edge of the hermitage.
Having gone far, she returned again out of fear of tigers;
having gone far in the morning, she would then return to the hermitage in the evening.
Furthermore, while Bharata was within his hermitage hut,
that deer continued to move about at various distances from him.
O Sage, his mind was not so deeply attached to Acyuta as it was [to his kingdom],
even though he had abandoned his kingdom and son and cast off all his kinsmen.
He felt a great sense of possessiveness toward that fawn:
"Has it been devoured by wolves? Or has it been struck down by tigers or a lion? (NarP 1.48.25)
When he had gone out and was delaying, his mind thought thus;
and with a face brightened by joy, he remained beside the deer.
His concentration was shattered as his mind was drawn by the sense of "mine-ness";
then, as time passed, that lord of the earth met his end.
Like a father whose weapon was gazed upon by his son who had become a fawn,
he too then beheld only the deer as he was giving up his life.
O Sage, having attained such a state of contemplation, he became a deer;
O best of the twice-born, being one who remembers his former births, he was weary of cyclic existence.
Leaving his mother once more, he went to Śālagrāma,
sustaining himself with dry grass and leaves.
He attained the expiation for the karma that had caused his state as a deer;
having cast off his body there, he was born as a twice-born man endowed with the memory of his former birth.
Born into a pure and preeminent family of practitioners who followed the conduct of the virtuous,
he was perfected in all branches of knowledge and understood the true meaning of all the scriptures.
O great sage, through the knowledge attained by his own self, that best of sages beheld himself as beyond primordial nature (prakṛti) and as transcending the dualities such as pleasure and pain.
That high-minded one beheld all beings with equanimity;
though he had undergone the initiation ceremony, he did not recite the Veda heard from his teacher.
He did not observe ritual acts nor did he take up the scriptures;
even when addressed many times, the fool spoke but a few words.
O Sage, he too possessed qualities that were unrefined, employing the colloquial speech of the village; his body was disfigured, and he wore soiled garments.
With the spaces between his teeth constantly dripping, he was despised by all the citizens;
for by accepting such honor, he brought about the supreme ruin of his yogic power.
The yogi who is despised by people attains the perfection of yoga;
therefore, the yogi should indeed conduct himself so as not to defile the dharma of the virtuous.
Reflecting thus upon the words of Hiraṇyagarbha, the high-minded one considered how people might despise him and not enter into association with him. (NarP 1.48.39)
He manifested himself among the people in the form of one who is dull-witted and insane;
he ate broken grains of millet, cakes, vegetables, wild fruits, and husks. (NarP 1.48.40)
Whatever he obtained, he indeed consumed as it arose in the course of time;
then, upon the death of his father, he was joined by his brothers, nephews, and kinsmen.
He was made to perform field labor and other tasks, nourished on coarse food;
his limbs were rough and stout, and he was dull-witted in his work.
He became a provider for all the world, receiving food as his wages; such was he, lacking refinement, yet possessing the appearance and conduct of a Brahmin.
O twice-born one, the steward of the Sauvīra kingdom considered himself fit for manual labor;
that king, having resolved to go mounted upon a palanquin, set out.
On the bank of the Ikṣumatī, there was the excellent hermitage of the seer Kapila;
[he pondered]: "What is the highest good for men here in this saṃsāra, which is filled with suffering? (NarP 1.48.45)
Urged by the words of the steward, he carried the palanquin of that great sage named Kapila, who was an expert in the dharma of liberation, so that he might question him.
O Brahmin, he too, the sole vessel of all knowledge, was seized by forced labor along with other men who had been taken as corvée workers. 48.47.
Remembering his past lives and desiring the destruction of his evil karma, he took her as his wife; he moved with a sluggish gait, looking only a yoke’s length ahead.
While he, the best among the wise, was acting thus, the others departed in haste;
then that king, beholding the unevenness of the palanquin, [spoke].
"What is this? he asked. "Carriers of the palanquin, proceed evenly!
Having looked again at the palanquin as it was uneven, he laughed. (NarP 1.48.50)

"What is this? the king asked. "You are going in the opposite way. Having heard these words repeatedly as the monarch was speaking, the palanquin bearers said, "This man is walking," without any haste. (NarP 1.48.51)
The king said:
"Are you tired? You have carried my palanquin only a short distance.
Are you not capable of enduring exertion? For you appear stout."
The Brahmin said:
"I am not fat, nor has your palanquin been carried by me;
I am not weary, nor is there any exertion, O Lord of the Earth, for there is another who carries it."
The king said:
"It is seen directly that you are still fat, and the palanquin remains upon you;
for embodied beings certainly experience fatigue when bearing a burden."
The Brahmin said:
"O King, tell me what you have seen before my very eyes;
whether one is strong or weak is a qualification that should be stated afterwards."
"The palanquin was carried by you, and it remains upon you even now;
yet that too is false—listen here to these words of mine."
Then the pair of feet [rests] on the ground; when the two feet are situated, the two shanks are established upon them;
likewise, the thighs rest upon the two shanks, and the abdomen is supported by those.
The chest, the arms, and the shoulders situated upon the belly—since the palanquin rests upon these shoulders, what support have I provided here? (NarP 1.48.58)
This body, which you perceive as standing upon the palanquin, is designated as "you" and "I" therein; otherwise, this [designation] would not occur.
O King, you, I, and others as well are carried away by the elements;
even this entire collection of elements, having fallen into the flow of the qualities (guṇas), passes away.
O Lord of the Earth, these qualities, beginning with *sattva*, are subject to karma;
and through karma, accumulated by ignorance, they exist in all living beings without exception.
The Self is pure, imperishable, tranquil, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature; for it is one and the same in all living beings, and in it there is neither increase nor decrease.
“O King, when there is neither accumulation nor depletion for it, you are still a fool; by what reasoning was this stated by you?
[The consciousness] resides in the feet, calves, hips, thighs, belly, and so forth. (NarP 1.48.63)
When this palanquin was on your shoulder, then the burden was equal for you.
Likewise, O King, it is not only carried by other living beings;
it arises from mountains, trees, and houses, and even from the earth itself.
O King, just as a man’s separation from his natural faculties is a very great burden to be endured, which of these, O King, shall I bear for you? (NarP 1.48.66)
Of whatever substance this palanquin is made, of that same substance is the aggregate of beings;
it has been augmented by you through the equality of this entire world.
Sanandana said:
Having spoken thus, that twice-born man became silent while carrying the palanquin;
the king also, descending to the ground, quickly grasped his feet.
The king said:
"O twice-born one, set down the palanquin and show me favor!
Tell me, who are you that stands here wearing the guise of a fool?"
O learned one, let all that be told by you to me, who am eager to listen— whether you are a lord or a child, and what the reason for your arrival may be.
The Brahmin said:
"O King, it is impossible to say who I am;
moreover, the act of coming here is for a specific purpose."

The experience of pleasure and pain, which gives rise to the body and its like, originates from merit and demerit; in order to experience these, the living being undergoes the acquisition of a body and so forth.
For indeed, O protector of the earth, dharma and adharma are the cause for every living being in all circumstances; therefore, why is the cause being questioned?
The king said:
"There is no doubt that dharma and adharma are the cause in all actions;
and the transition from one body to another occurs for the sake of experiencing [the results of those actions]."
As for that which was said by you—"Who am I?"—this regarding the self cannot be expressed; yet, the desire to hear it arises within me.
O Brahmin, how can it be said that the words "he who exists" and "I" cannot be spoken? O twice-born one, the word "I" used with respect to the Self itself is not a fault.
The Brahmin said:

"The notion 'I am sound' leads to error; it is not so with respect to the Self. Likewise, the cognition of the Self in what is not the Self—whether it be sound or that which is characterized by sacred revelation—is likewise [an error]. (NarP 1.48.77)
"The tongue says 'I am,' O King, as do the teeth, the lips, and the palate;
for by these, I am [produced], since they are all the causes for the accomplishment of speech. (NarP 1.48.78)
Why do you speak with such reasons, saying "I am this very speech"? Even so, it is not proper to say, "I am speech. 48.79.
Since this body, characterized by the head, hands, and so forth, is distinct from the person,
O King, where then can I apply this notion of "I"?
O best of kings, if there were anyone else superior to me, it would be acceptable to say, "I am not this body, and these others are different. (NarP 1.48.81)
When the One Person is established within all bodies, then indeed such words as "Who are you? and "Who am I? are fruitless.
"You are the king, this is the palanquin, we are the bearers and those who precede you, and this is your world; yet, O King, all this that is spoken of is not real."
From a tree comes wood, and from that, this palanquin occupied by you;
O King, where indeed is the notion of "tree" in it, or the notion of "wood"? (NarP 1.48.84)
"This great king is mounted upon a tree," so says this person to you; nor does anyone say that you are seated in a palanquin within the wood.
O best of kings, let the palanquin named Ānanda-dā, which is a mere assembly of wooden parts existing only by its own name, be sought out by you. (NarP 1.48.86)
In this same way, let the separate existence of the umbrella from its ribs be examined:
"Where was the umbrella produced? This principle applies equally to you and to me.
"Man, woman, cow, goat, horse, elephant, bird, and tree—this worldly designation applied to bodies should be understood as having karma as its cause. (NarP 1.48.88)
The Self is neither god, nor man, nor beast, nor tree;
O King, these differences in bodily form have their origin in karma.
That which some call "the king," that which consists of the king's soldiers, and likewise whatever else is called a "king"—all this is not real; it is composed of mental construction.
But that object, O King, which even after a lapse of time does not undergo the perception of destruction— being produced through transformation and so forth— what indeed is that?
You are the king of all sorrow; you are the son of your father, the enemy of your foe, the husband of your wife, and the father of your son. Who are you, O King? Tell me.
"What is this head? But what indeed is your head? What are these feet and so forth? O Lord of the Earth, what are they not at all? (NarP 1.48.93)
O King, having become discerning, reflect deeply upon this: "Who am I?"—for you exist as something distinct from all your constituent parts.
When reality is established in this way, O King, how could it be possible for me to cultivate the notion of "I" as something to be accomplished through separate actions?
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the second part of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first section of the Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanandana said:
Having heard his words, which were endowed with the supreme truth, [the sages...]
Bowing down with humility, the king spoke to that twice-born man.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, regarding these words of yours which consist of the ultimate truth—
upon hearing them, the functions of my mind seem to whirl."
O Brahmin, if this discriminative knowledge regarding all other living beings has been shown by you, then that is the Great Principle (mahat) beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
"I do not carry the palanquin, nor does the palanquin rest upon me;
the body by which this palanquin is supported is distinct from me."
"The activity of beings proceeds from the qualities (guṇas), impelled by karma; these qualities themselves act—'what is it to me? thus you have said. (NarP 1.49.5)
When these words concerning the ultimate truth reached my ears, my mind, having attained the state of realizing the ultimate reality, became overwhelmed with agitation.
O illustrious twice-born one, previously I set out to go and question the seer Kapila regarding what is beneficial in this matter of doubt. (NarP 1.49.7)
And during that interval, because this very statement was uttered by you,
my mind runs toward you for the sake of the ultimate truth.
The venerable sage Kapila, indeed, is a portion of the Lord Viṣṇu, who is the soul of all beings; he has appeared for the sake of destroying the delusion of the world.
"Surely that very Blessed One has manifested himself before our eyes out of a desire for our welfare; thus it is said by you."

O twice-born one, you are an ocean surging with the waves of the waters of all-encompassing knowledge; therefore, tell me that which is the supreme good for the destruction of my delusion. (NarP 1.49.11)
The Brahmin said:
"O King, you ask again what is the highest good; you ask about the ultimate truths, for all the highest goods and ultimate truths are contained within this."
O King, for one who desires wealth and prosperity, or seeks sons and sovereignty, after having performed the propitiation of the deities, that very act is his highest good.
But for the discerning, union with the Supreme Self is the highest good;
whereas rites such as the sacrifice of action are merely a lesser good that bestows the fruits of the heavenly world.
O King, that alone which is not aimed at as a fruit is the primary excellence;
likewise, the Self should always be meditated upon by those engaged in yoga and others as well.
Union with that very Supreme Self is the highest good;
indeed, there are many such goods by the hundreds and thousands.
The ultimate truths do indeed exist here, yet these [worldly things] are not they; hear this from me:
if wealth were the ultimate truth, then why would one abandon this dharma?
O Lord of Men, why was this expenditure undertaken as a sign of attaining one's desire? If it is called the ultimate goal (paramārtha), that too belongs to someone else.
He who has become the ultimate reality is indeed the ultimate reality for another; he is our father.
Thus, there is no such thing as an ultimate reality in this world of moving and unmoving beings.
For the ultimate truth consists of the complete cessation of all effects and instruments;
if the attainment of sovereignty and so forth were here said to be the ultimate truth, [it would be a contradiction].
In this regard, [entities] both exist and do not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth;
therefore, the sacrificial rite accomplished through the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas is what you consider [to be real].
Now, hear from me as I speak regarding that which constitutes the ultimate truth:
whatever effect is produced by means of clay acting as its cause.
O King, it arises from following its cause as something made of clay;
likewise, [the sacrificial fire] is produced by means of perishable substances such as fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and kuśa grass.
That action which is brought to completion must be subject to destruction;
however, the wise accept that the ultimate reality is indestructible.
That which is perishable, without a doubt, and produced by perishable substances—that very action is considered by me to be the ultimate reality. (NarP 1.49.25)
Because it is the means for achieving liberation, the ultimate reality is not itself a means;
rather, meditation alone is designated by the term "the ultimate reality" for the sake of the self, O King. (NarP 1.49.26)
The ultimate reality (paramārtha) is not differentiated from others, yet it is that which causes differentiation;
the union of the ultimate reality and the self is held to be the ultimate reality.
This is false, for this is indeed another substance, since it is not composed of that substance;
therefore, O King, all these other things are superior, without a doubt.
But hear from me in brief, O protector of the earth, the ultimate truth:
it is one, all-pervading, equal, pure, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature.
O King, the omnipresent Self is devoid of birth, growth, and so forth;
it consists of pure consciousness and is pervasive among the wise, transcending names, castes, and the like.
Neither has he been a practitioner of yoga, nor was he disciplined, nor will that king ever become so;
for that [consciousness] is indeed one and the same, existing within his own body and the bodies of others.
This consciousness is the ultimate reality; one who perceives incorrectly does not know it.
Just as the distinction designated as "the six notes" and so forth arises through the differentiation of the hollows of bamboo, [so too does the diversity of phenomena arise from the One].
There is no difference in that great-souled one, who is like all-pervading air;
his oneness and his diversity of forms arise from the engagement in external actions.
He abides in the distinctions of gods and so forth, yet he is indeed without movement;
O King, hear here the ancient account that was sung by Ṛbhu.
To the twice-born Nidāgha, who was generating spiritual awakening,
there was born a son named Ṛbhu, the son of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
O King,
in former times, Nidāgha, the son of Pulastya, became by his very nature a disciple of that [teacher] who had realized the true essence of reality.
With supreme joy, he bestowed upon him complete knowledge;
yet for him, who had attained the reality of knowledge, there was no longer any latent impression of duality.
O lord of men, that Ṛbhu reflected upon the city named Nāgara on the bank of the Devikā belonging to Nidāgha, O hero. (NarP 1.49.38)
O best of kings, he [dwelt] in that city established by Pulastya, which was prosperous, delightful,
and surrounded by beautiful groves.
In former times, there was a disciple of Nidāgha who was skilled in the knowledge of yoga;
when a thousand divine years had passed, his city [was destroyed].
That Ṛbhu went to see his disciple Nidāgha;
he [Nidāgha] was within the range of the doorway while he was performing the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Having been apprehended by him while staying there, he was brought into his own house;
once he had washed his hands and feet and taken his seat, [the king spoke].
That best of the twice-born said respectfully, "Please eat.
Ṛbhu said:
"O foremost of brahmins, whatever may be eaten here in your house, that shall be our food."
"Therefore, let it be told why I have no constant pleasure in coarse foods.
Nidāgha said:
"In my house, there are barley-meal, barley-gruel, rice, and cakes. (NarP 1.49.44)
"O best of the twice-born, eat as much as you please of whatever pleases you.
R̥bhu said:
"O twice-born one, these are poor foods; give me sweet food. (NarP 1.49.45)
"Samyāva, milk-rice, and so forth, as well as sugarcane juices and other flavorful drinks—
whatever is most excellent in my auspicious home, O Nidāgha, all that is in my house. (NarP 1.49.46)
"Prepare sweet food for him from among the delicacies," she was told by her husband; thus addressed, that wife prepared sweet food for the brahmin. (NarP 1.49.47)
Out of respect for her husband’s words, she indeed prepared that food, yet she did not offer the sweet meal to the great sage until he had eaten to his heart's content.
Nidāgha, standing bowed in humility, spoke to the protector of the earth.
Nidāgha said:
"Has supreme satisfaction arisen in you, as well as nourishment?"
"O twice-born one, has your mind been made healthy by this food? O Brahmin, where do you dwell, and where are you prepared to go? (NarP 1.49.50)

"Red," "full," "adorned," "clear," "distinct," "loud," "smooth," "even," "delicate," and "sweet"—these are the qualities therein. Among them, "red" (*rakta*) refers to the unification of the sounds of the flute and the lute; "full" (*pūrṇa*) refers to the fulfillment of notes and intervals, and because it completes the syllables of the metrical feet through their conjunction, it is called "full"; "adorned" (*alaṅkṛta*) refers to that which is joined with the chest, the head, and the throat—this is called "adorned."

*Prasanna* (clear) is that which is free from stammering and hesitation; it is called "clear" because it is manifest. *Vyakta* (distinct) is the correct presentation of words, word-meanings, verbal roots, their modifications, primary suffixes (*taddhita*), compounds, verbal roots, particles, prefixes, accents, genders, modes of expression (*vṛtti*), explanatory notes (*vārttika*), case endings, and syntactical statements; it is called "distinct. *Vikruṣṭa* (loud) is that which is uttered very loudly with distinct words and syllables; it is called "loud. *Ślakṣṇa* (smooth) is that which is recited rapidly yet without haste, through such presentations as the modulation of high, low, and rising tones, and the application of rhythmic tempo (*helatā*) and measure (*laya*).
It is called "smooth" (*ślakṣṇa*) when there is an evenness in the places of sowing and reaping; it is called "even" (*sama*) when there is a leveling of the intermediate positions;

it is called "delicate" (*sukumāra*) when it is endowed with soft words, phonemes, vowels, and articulations; it is called "sweet" (*madhura*) when it is enriched by the excellence of naturally elegant words and syllables. Thus, it is endowed with these ten qualities.

O Brahmin, a word (*pada*) consists of that which ends in a nominal suffix (*suP*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṄ*). There are seven case-endings (*sup*); *su*, *au*, and *jas* are declared to be the first [case], which is essentially the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

In the case of address, when gender and so forth are expressed, the nominal stem—excluding verbal roots and suffixes—is that which possesses meaning, whether it denotes the object or the agent. (NarP 1.52.3)

The second case (dvitīyā) occurs where there is no expressed object (*amauṣaśas*), and it is also used for that which is the object of an action; the second case is prescribed for the direct object (*karman*) when combined with the prepositions *antar* and *antareṇa*.
The third case ending, consisting of *ṭā*, *bhyām*, and *bhis*, is prescribed for the instrumental; it is taught [to denote] both the instrument and the agent.
That by which an action is performed is the instrument; he who performs the action is the agent.

The fourth [case-ending] occurs after the words *ṅe*, *bhyām*, and *bhyas* when there is the sense of giving (*saṃpradāna*) as the grammatical factor; that for whom one has the desire to give, or whom one holds [in mind], or to whom something is pleasing, is the recipient (*saṃpradānaka*). (NarP 1.52.6)

The fifth case ending occurs after [a word] denoting the *apādāna* kāraka, namely that from which one departs, that from which one takes, or that from which one receives; it is used with the suffixes *ṅasi*, *bhyām*, and *bhyas*. (NarP 1.52.7)
The sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) occurs when the primary sense is the relationship between owner and owned;
however, from the suffixes ṅi and os, as well as from the sup-suffixes, the seventh case (saptamī) occurs, and that [seventh case] exists in the sense of location (adhikaraṇa).
O best of Brahmins, that which serves as the basis for the application of protective rites,
whether desired or undesired, is traditionally known as the *apādāna*.

The fifth case [the ablative] is used in connection with *pary-anaṅ* (except), while the second case is used when joined with these karmapravacanīyas: *itarat*, *ṛte*, and words meaning "other than" or "in another direction. (NarP 1.52.10)
The prefix *anu* is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), a state of being so (*itthaṃbhūta*), and a part (*abhāga*); likewise, *pari* and *prati* [are used similarly].
*Antara* is used in the sense of "in between" (*antareṣu*) and "with" (*sahārthe*); while *upa* is said to be used in the sense of "inferior" (*hīne*).
The second and fourth case endings are used for the sense of motion when the action involves movement;
two case endings are used for non-living things; and two case endings are used for the object of the verb *man* (to think) when it expresses disregard.
