The use of the fourth case is prescribed in connection with *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ*; it is also used in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthya*), as well as after words expressing an action (*bhāvavācin*) when they have the sense of the suffix *-tum*.
The third case (instrumental) occurs in connection with "saha" (with), as well as when denoting a limb that is contemptible or a qualifier;
the seventh case (locative) occurs in the sense of time or state; and the sixth case (genitive) also occurs in connection with these [previously mentioned words].
With *svāmī*, *īśvara*, and *adhipati*; with *sākṣin*, *dāyāda*, and *sūtaka*;
in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), two case endings [are used]; and when the word *hetu* is employed, the sixth case ending is used.
Likewise, in the case of a verb meaning "to remember," in the sense of "preparation" (*pratiyatnaka*) for the action of *kṛ*,
and in the employment of verbs meaning "injury" (*hiṃsā*) where there is an object of the action of *kṛ*,
the genitive case is not used for the agent or the object when these are expressed by suffixes such as the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). (NarP 1.52.16)

These ten *lakāras* are indeed to be known as twofold within the case-endings beginning with *su*, and they are traditionally recorded as being contained within the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) beginning with *bhū*.
*Tipta* and *santi* are the first person; *siptha* and *stha* are the middle person; *miva*, *vas*, and *masa* are for the *parasmaipada*; and *mapana* and *idaṃ* are for the feet [of the verses].
"ta," "āte," and "ante" are the first person; "se," "āthe," and "dhve" are likewise the last person.
These are to be known as the forms for the honorific (maha) [first person]; the others in the optative (liṅ) and other moods are to be understood accordingly.
When the personal pronoun *nām* is employed, the first person [of the verb] occurs;
the middle person is prescribed when *yuṣmad* is used, and the highest person when *asmad* is used.

The verbal roots beginning with *bhū* have been declared, as well as those ending in *san* and so forth; likewise, the *laṭ* suffix is prescribed for the present tense and for the immediate past (*anadyatana-bhūta*).
In connection with *mā*, the *laṅ* should be prescribed; after a verbal root, the *loṭ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).
In the sense of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, the *liṅ* occurs; O Sage, the *liṅ* is of two kinds when used for benediction.

The *liṭ* suffix occurs for the past tense when the action is not witnessed by the speaker; *luṅ* occurs for the future; and *lṛṭ* occurs for the future that is not of today, derived from the verbal root.
The *luṅ* [suffix] is prescribed for the past tense (*bhūta*), and *tip* and *ap* are also used; the *ḷṅ* is proclaimed for the conditional (*kriyā*).
Know that the examples of established forms follow the rules of *saṃhitā* and so forth:
"O bull among ancestors, here is the tip of the staff, this curd, and honey-water."
Likewise, this plow-pole is the Hotṛ priest through my wisdom. // NarP_1,52.25 //
O Lord of Sages, *gaṅgodaka* [is the word for] water; *tavalkāra* [is the word for] debt; and *ṛṇārṇa* [is also the word for] debt.
O best of sages, *seṃdra* [is the word for] one afflicted by cold, and *saukāra* likewise [is the word for] a dog. (NarP 1.52.26)
The seat for the bridegroom, the offering for the ancestors, and likewise the leader and the salt—these are for Viṣṇu here; therefore, the respectful offering (argha) is below that for the Guru.
"Hare! O Viṣṇu!"—with these words, they drove away even those who were without Soma;
"O Śauri!"—these two [cried out]; "O Viṣṇu!"—these two; "O Durgā!"—those women; and "O Arjuna!"—they cried to us.
And thus, O best of sages, these six remain by their very nature; here are the six mothers: Vākśurī, Vāgdhasrī, and the others.
Hari lies down; he is the all-pervading one, the object of meditation, and that which remains after him, whether moving or stationary.
Now follows the sixth question: "And Hari, Kṛṣṇa, even when he urinates. (NarP 1.52.30)
"You are the sixth, and there are six existences; those six and their very coating as well—O wielder of the discus, cut them! You are Śauri, you are indeed Śauri. (NarP 1.52.31)
I bow to the Lord of Sages, who possesses a perfectly symmetrical shadow and a dark complexion;
he considers the Gaṅgā to be his splendor, and he is Hari, the destroyer of Mura, and Śiva.
Rāma is desirable, Kṛpa is worthy of honor, and Hari is indeed worshipful and worthy of adoration;
for here the women are seen sleeping, since they are so beloved.
Viṣṇu is the navel, this sun is the fruit; Acyuta is to be praised by devotees in the morning.
O friends, he is the inner self, and likewise, he is Hari.
This is Śārṅgin, this is Rāma; thus has the *Saṃhitā* been proclaimed.
"I shall always do what is commanded by Rāma; I worship Rāma with fervor.
All my evil deeds have been removed by Rāma; salutations to You, O Rāma!
I always desire liberation from Rāma; I am the servant of Rāma."
My mind is deeply delighted in Rāma; O Rāma, salutations to you!
The cowherds, beginning with Sarva, were his friends, and Hari was their lord.
Suśrī, Bhānu, Svayaṃbhū, Kartṛ, Rauhiṇa, Gau, Naur, Anaṅgha, Angodhuk, and Liṭ—these are two, three, and four [syllables] respectively. (NarP 1.52.37)
O Sage, the king, the traveler, the staff-bearer, the slayer of a Brahmin—these five and eight [make thirteen]; this sovereign, O Sage, possesses body, speech, and mind.
Pratyaṅ, pumān, mahān, dhīmān, vidvān, ṣaṭ, pipaṭhīḥ, and doḥ; uśanā, sāvit, and ime are used in the masculine, as are those ending in -rakta, -la, -vi, and -ra-maka.
Rādhā is the refuge of all; she is the cowherd girl, the goddess Śrī, the cow, the bride, and the sister.
She is the earth, the boat, the speech, the sky, the cow, hunger, the quarter of the horizon, and in some places, consciousness. (NarP 1.52.40)

Disease, lightning, splendor, woman, asceticism, lineage, the moon, the eye, the village headman, water, strength, and the thigh—these are the subjects [of comparison], while the agent is expressed as "exceeding" or "surpassing. (NarP 1.52.41)
Svanahuc, Vimaladyu, and likewise Aśvatvārīda;
this Brahmāha, Daṇḍin, Asṛk, Kiñcit, Tyad, and so forth.

This very thing was the speech of Bhidga, the speech of Gavaṅ, the cow, the bull, the lowing, the roaring, the horizontal, the liver, and the excrement; it was the giver, the becoming, the cooker, and the eater. 1.52.43.

I shall state how many words—such as *dīvyaddhanuḥ*, *pipaṭhiḥ*, *payodaḥ*, and *sumumāṃsi*—possess three genders through their connection with qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), and actions (*kriyā*). 52.44.
Śukta, Kīlālapa, Śuci, Grāmaṇī, Sudhī, Paṭu, Svayaṃbhū, Kartṛ, Mātṛ, and Pitṛ are names of Nara. (NarP 1.52.45)

Likewise, for a man who has true speech, no enemies, a steady gait like a bee’s long flight, wealth, the form of the moon, and who is irreproachable, firm, composed, and possesses much gold; NarP_1,52.46.
Alas, everything born from the sequence of the six paths, as well as both the universal and the individual, and all other internal and external things [are likewise]. // NarP_1,52.47 //
Uttara, Uttama, Nemi, Asama, and Samā; then the iṣas; likewise Pūrva, Uttara, Uttarā, Dakṣiṇa, and Uttarādhara.
Furthermore, there are these four others: *yāvat*, *tāvat*, *kim*, and *asau*; then the dual number;
and finally *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, the first person, the last person, the few, and the half.
The negative particle *na*, the numerals *katipaya* (some), *dvi* (two), and *tri* (three), as well as the pure (*śuddha*) and other [particles],
*sva* (own), *ekābhu* (one-landed), *virodha* (opposition), *pari* (around/beyond), *viparyaya* (reversal), and likewise the indeclinables (*avyaya*).
Furthermore, there are secondary derivatives (taddhita) in the sense of offspring, such as Pāṇḍava and Śrautadhara;
likewise Gārgya, Nāḍāyana, Ātreya, Gāṅgeya, and Paitṛṣvasrīya.
For the sake of the deity, this is for the sake of the object; the oblation and the offering belong to Indra and Brahmā.
For the action and the agent, the offering belongs to Dharma, as does the saffron-colored one.
But for the sake of existence and so forth, he is a Kānīna, a Kṣatriya, a Vaidika, and his own;
and in the sense of self, he is a thief, yet he gazes upon the face like the moon in its identical form.

The state of being a Brahmin, the quality of a Brahmin, and likewise Brahminhood; one who possesses cows, one who is wealthy, and one who has riches—these occur in the sense of existence (*astyartha*); and "how much" is used for measurement (*pramiti*). (NarP 1.52.54)

*tuṇḍila* means "one who has a protruding belly" when it denotes birth; *śraddhālu* means "one who possesses faith"; *dantura* means "one who is prominent" in the sense of height; and *sragvin*, *tapasvin*, *medhāvin*, and *māyāvin* likewise mean "one who possesses" [a garland, austerity, intelligence, or illusion] respectively.

*Vācāla* means talkative; *vācāṭa* refers to one who speaks much that is contemptible; *kalpa* is used for "almost" or "nearly complete"; and *deśīya* means "resembling" or "belonging to. (NarP 1.52.56)
*Kavikalpa* and *kavideśya* are used in the sense of expressing a manner; likewise, *paṭujātīya* is used in the sense of censure, while *vaidyapāśa* is used in the sense of praise. (NarP 1.52.57)
O Sage, in former times he was considered a physician who had been seen and experienced;
he was composed of food in abundance, as well as of clay and of women.
O Nārada, [the suffix] *jātī* is used in the sense of "born" (*jāta*), while *atyartham* means "excessively"; *śreyān* and *śreṣṭhaḥ* mean "better" or "best";
*kṛṣṇataraḥ* means "darker," and *śuklatamaḥ* means "whitest"; [these are formed] from the indeclinables (*avyaya*) such as *kim*. (NarP 1.52.59)
Furthermore, it may be even more, or exceedingly so, or even very much higher;
in terms of measurement, it may reach the height of the knees, or even double that.
The word *jānumātram* is used for the depth [of water] when many [people] emerge, while *nirddhāre* is used for two [people] in succession;
*katamaḥ* and *kataraḥ* are used for determining a specific number among many. (NarP 1.52.61)
The second and the third, the fourth, the sixth and the fifth;
the eleventh, the few, the ordinal "how-many-th," and "how many," O Nārada.
O Lord of Sages, the word *viṃśa* means "twentieth," as does *viṃśatitama*; likewise, *śatatama* and so forth. Furthermore, *dvedhā*, *dvaidhā*, and *dvidhā* denote number as well as manner.
In the repetition of an action, one says "five times," as well as "twice," "thrice," and "many times";
for in the case of number, there are indeed the pairs "two" and "three," and also "a pair" and "a triad."
*Kuṭīra*, *śamīra*, and *śuṇḍāra* are considered to have the sense of "small";
likewise, *traiṇa*, *pauṣṇa*, *tuṇḍibha*, *vṛndāraka*, and *kṛṣīvala*. (NarP 1.52.65)
It was filthy, hideous, and infested with cattle; it was filled with the loud cries of *bhauriki* birds, uneven, full of pits, dense with forests, and thick with sugarcane and *śākinī* plants.
Nibirīsameṣukārī, Vittovidyāñcana, Vidyāthuñcu, Bahutitha, Parvata, and Śṛṅgin likewise.
Svāmī, viṣamarūpya, upatyakā, adhityakā, cilla, cipiṭa, cikva, vātūla, and kutapa; // NarP_1,52.68 //
Valla, Himelu, Kahoḍa, Upaḍa,
Ūrṇāyu, Marūta, Ekākī, and likewise Carmaṇvatī.
Jyotsnā, Tamisrā, Aṣṭīvat, Kakṣīvat, Ṛṣamaṇvatī, Āsandīvat, Cakrīvat, Tūṣṇīkā, and Jalpatikā as well. (NarP 1.52.70)
Kaṃbha, Kaṃyu, Kaṃva, Nāradaketu, Kantu, Kantakampa, Śaṃva, as well as Śanta, Śanti, Śaya, Anta, Śayohaṃyu, and Śubhaṃyu.
It has been, it was, it will be, it shall be, let it be, it did not exist, and it may also come to be.
*bhūyāt*, *abhūt*, *abhaviṣyat*—these forms [occur] with respect to the future (*bhaviṣya*) and so forth;
[the forms] *atti*, *jaghāsa*, *āttāt*, *atsyati*, *attvā*, *adat*, *adyāt*, *advit*, *aghast*, and *ātsyat*.
He has offered, he offered, he has performed the sacrifice; the priest will offer, let him offer.
He did not offer, he should offer, he ought to offer; he has sacrificed, he will sacrifice, he plays.
He has played, he is a player, and he will play; he did not play, let him play, he should indeed play.
*adevīt*, *adevīṣi*, *atsunoti*, *asuṣāva*, *sotā*, *soṣyati*, *vai*, *sunotu*, *asunot*, *sunuyāt*, *sūyāt*, *aśāvīt*, *asoṣīt*, and *uttudati*. // NarP_1,52.75 //

He struck (tutoda), has struck (tottā), and will strike (totṣyati); he strikes (tudati), struck (atudat), may he strike (tudet), and let him strike (tudyāt); he has struck (atautsīt), will strike (atsyati), and likewise obstructs (ruṇaddhi), has obstructed (rurudha), is one who will obstruct (roddhā), and indeed will obstruct (rotsyati).
He obstructed, has obstructed, will obstruct; he has obstructed, shall obstruct, and is obstructing.
He extends, has extended, and will extend; let him extend, he has extended, and may he indeed extend.
atanīt, ātānīt, ataniṣyat, krīṇāti, cikrāya, kretā, kreṣyati, "krīṇātu" iti ca;
akrīṇāt, krīṇāt, krīṇīyāt, krīyāt, akraiṣīt, akreṣyan; corayati, corayāmāsa, corayitā, corayiṣyati, "corayatu".
"He would steal from a thief" (*acaurayaccorayet*), "he stole from a thief" (*acūcurat*), "he will steal from a thief" (*acoriṣyat*)—these indeed constitute the ten groups [of verbal forms].

In the case of a causal agent, there is *san* (desiderative) when there is a desire for the action, as in *bhāvayati* ("he causes to be") and *bubhūṣati* ("he desires to be"); but in the sense of the repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), O Sage, the wise man uses *bobhūyate* ("he becomes again and again").
Likewise, when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided, *bobhavīti* is also recited;

and *putrīyati* is used in the sense of desiring a son for oneself (*ātmanīcchā*), as well as in the sense of imitating (*ācāra*), O Nārada; likewise, from a root marked with an *anudātta* or an *it*, it is used in the sense of the exchange of actions (*kriyāvinimaya*).
O Brahmin, understand that for roots such as *niviś*, the ātmanepada is used;
however, the grammarians declare the parasmaipada to be used for the remaining [roots] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.

O Sage, when one wishes to express an excellence of ease, both [the suffixes] *ya* and *yak* should be applied after a root that has three svarita accents, in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). (NarP 1.52.82)
Others maintain that when the agent's activity is not intended to be expressed in the observed usage, they obtain the status of the agent; behold, for "the rice cooks by itself."

"O Sage, [the suffixes] *lap* are used after a transitive root to denote both the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), as in 'the woodcutter cuts' (*sādhu vāsiśchinatti*) or 'the pot cooks' (*sthālī pacati*). (NarP 1.52.84)
O Brahmin, for that [verb] which is otherwise transitive, the [kṛt] suffix is prescribed in the sense of the abstract state (bhāva) or the agent (kartṛ);
it is called "intransitive" (akarmaka) when the fruit and the operation reside in a single locus.
When there is a difference between the two substrata (dharmin) of those two [actions], the verbal root is cited as transitive (*sakarmaka*):

in the case of roots such as *druh* (to bear malice), it is with respect to the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*), whereas for *nī*, *hṛ*, *kṛṣ*, and *vah*, it is with respect to the primary object (*pradhāna*).

In the case of roots meaning "to perceive" (*buddhi*) or "to eat" (*bhakṣa*), and of those whose objects are words (*śabda-karmaka*), the *l*-affixes and others are considered to apply to the object of the agent's own desire when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used; for other [causatives], they are considered to apply to the object of the prompted action. (NarP 1.52.87)
The verbal root is traditionally held to denote both the result and the operation, whereas the suffixes (tiṅ) denote the locus [of the action].
Of these, the result is the primary element, while the operation is subordinate to the meaning of the suffix.
"edhitavya" and "medhanīya" are examples of kṛtya suffixes;
kṛtyas occur in the sense of the abstract state (bhāva) or the object (karman), while those ending in "kṛt" are said to occur in the sense of the agent (kartṛ).

The agent (*kartṛ*), the instrument (*kāraka*), and so forth, are designated as the past tense (*bhūta*) and so on; the object (*gamya*) and so forth are specified for the future (*bhavya*) and so on; and the remainder is considered to be the present (*adyatana*). 1.52.90.

In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, as in *adhiśrīti*, it is cited according to its capacity; in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there are examples such as *rāmāśritaḥ*, *dhānyārthaḥ*, and *yūpadāru*. (NarP 1.52.91)
*vyāghrabhī*, *rājapuruṣa*, *akṣaśaiṇḍa*, and *dvigu* are called *cyanta* (ending in -i);
*pañcagavam*, *daśagrāmī*, and *triphalā* are so designated by convention (*rūḍhitaḥ*).

The *nīlotpala* (blue lotus) and *mahāṣaṣṭī* (great sixth day) are examples of the *karmadhāraya* compound used in the sense of identity; whereas the *abrāhmaṇa* (non-Brahmin) is said not to be a *nañ*-compound, as are terms such as *kumbhakāra* (potter). 1.52.93.
But in a *bahuvrīhi* compound where another meaning [is intended], O twice-born one, "grāmaḥ prāptodakaḥ" (a village that has reached water),
"pañcaguḥ" (one who has five cows), "rūpavadbhāryaḥ" (one whose wife is beautiful), and "madhyāhnaḥ sasutādikaḥ" (midday accompanied by sons and so forth) [are examples].
Use *ca* for conjunction (*samuccaya*) and *tva* or *uta* for disjunction (*anvācaya*).
And for the two [words] in sequence:
"bring alms" and "also bring a cow"—the sentence of these two would be exactly that. (NarP 1.52.95)
But in the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are joined together;
O twice-born one, both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, as well as the two-fold Brahman, are worshipped as one.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Grammar," in the second quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanandana said:
"I shall now declare to you Nirukta, the supreme Veda that is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the ear."
That is declared to be fivefold: Vaidika, Dhātu, and Rūpaka.
In some places there is the addition of a syllable, in others a transposition of syllables;
in some cases a modification of syllables is observed, and in others the loss of a syllable is recognized.
Likewise, O Nārada, that combination of phonemes wherein there is neither modification nor destruction,
and which possesses an excellence of connection with the verbal root, is proclaimed as *saṃyoga*.
By the addition of a letter, *haṃsa* is established; by the transposition of letters, *siṃha*;
by the modification of letters, *gūḍhātman*; and by the elision of letters, *pṛṣodara*.

Indeed, the fifth [type of] *yoga* should be understood in words such as *bhramara* and *udu*; it is stated that "it occurs frequently in the Vedic meters (*chandas*)," and here [the example] to be cited is *punarvasū*.
Furthermore, *nabhasvat*, *vṛṣaṇa*, and those that belong to the *ātmanepada*—
even when separated by other words— are likewise designated as "gati" (particles), as is the case with *ā*.

There was an inversion of case endings, such as "he offers with curd" (dadhnā juhoti), or "we shall drive away the ill-omened one" (abhyutsādayāma ketuḥ), or he made sounds facing forward; likewise, verses were recited that were unfit for sacrifice, such as "grasp it" (gṛbhāya) and others of that sort.

The author of the grammatical treatise intends the transposition of these: case endings, verbal suffixes, voice, gender, number, tense, moods, primary suffixes, secondary suffixes, vowels, agents, and the yaṅ-intensification; and that too is established by means of the principle of "diversity" (bāhulaka).
Rātri, Bimbī, and Kadrū entered [the womb], according to the Vājasaneyins.
"Karṇebhiś ca yaśobhāgya" and so forth are four-syllable [mantras];
likewise, "Devāso atho sarvadevatātitvāvata" is also [a mantra].
The *ubhayāvin*, the *mādyas*, the *pralayas*, and likewise the *stṛcas*;
"apaspṛdhethām," "no avyāt," and "āyo asmān mukhā"—may these protect us. (NarP 1,53.11)
"Of the two pregnant ones, the one with feet; the most extensive among those of the season; the group of fifteen;
and also 'the hero with the golden [chariot] in the highest heaven. (NarP 1.53.12)
With her own wide-spreading speech like a bridegroom’s garment, she milked the waters;
worship him with this oblation, having bathed and gone forth, O you who possess the two worlds as your foundation.
He saw those who had abandoned their oxen, those with distorted gait, those seized by illness, and others; he also saw them measuring out [the land], and those who had caused it to increase.
And *mitrayuśca*, *durasvā vā*, *hātvā sudhitam*—these also;
and *dadhartya* and the following [verses] with *svavadbhiḥ*, and *sasūva* and *dhiṣva*. (NarP 1.53.15)
And he has reached the one who possesses bay horses and the one with the Ikṣu-stalks;
may the charioteer of the two *rathītara*s, who is well-winged, come today to us from within the earth and the atmosphere.
In the case of *brūhi* and so forth, as well as for what follows *ādeḥ*, there is a protracted vowel (*pluta*) in words such as *au śrāvaya*;
likewise in *dāśvān*, *svatavān*, *yāpau*, *tribhiḥ*, and *tvaṃ ca nṛbhiḥ-stutaḥ*. 1,53.17.

The upholders of the cosmic order (ṛtāvāhas) sat down near the reins; they were intent on manly deeds, according to the fourfold application of the rule of abundance (bāhulaka), both through its operation and its non-operation.
Through the Vibhāṣā, by means of transformation, everything pertaining to the Veda is established.
The roots beginning with *bhū* and *vā* are known to be remembered as *parasmaipada*.

O Sage, there are thirty-six roots beginning with *edh*, conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and having acute accents; and there are thirty-eight beginning with *at*, conjugated in the active voice (*parasmaipada*).
Forty-two [suffixes] are said to precede the *loka* [ending], while forty-two are indeed prescribed for the *ātmanepada*;
fifty, beginning with *phakka*, are proclaimed as having the *udātta* accent and its opposite.
Twenty-one roots beginning with *vṛc* are stated to be anudātta (unaccented);
forty-two roots beginning with *gup* are declared to be udātta (accented).
The ten roots beginning with *dhi* are declared by grammarians to be anudātta (unaccented);
likewise, twenty-seven roots beginning with *aṇ* are udātta (accented).
The grammarians have enumerated thirty-four types of *amādayaḥ*;
they number seventy-two, beginning with *mavya* and characterized by elevated (*udātta*) binding.
The root *svāritet* is proclaimed to have only one [vowel accent];
fifty-two roots beginning with *kṣudh* are cited as having anudātta (low-pitched) vowels.
The eighty-eight roots beginning with *ghuṣ* are considered to have an acute accent (*udātta*);
the twenty-two beginning with *dyut* are considered to have a grave accent (*anudātta*).
Sixteen [syllables] beginning with *gha* and ending with *ḍa* are said to be *anudātta*;
thereafter, fifty-two [syllables] beginning with *ja* and ending with *tha* are likewise *udātta*. NarP_1,53.27 //

The roots *svar*, *it*, *drāj*, and *saṃproktas* are stated to be [marked with] the svarita accent; *stan*, *hebhraj*, and *ṛtasrayaḥ* are among those that are anudātta (unaccented) in their verbal forms (*ākhyāta*). From this point on, the roots beginning with *bhā* and ending with *syam* are udātta (accented).
The root *sah* is anudātta-edita and takes only the parasmaipada; *ram*, though single, is also ātmanepadi;
*sad* and *as* are udātta-aita; and *kuc* is udātta-it. (NarP 1.53.29)
After that, there are thirty-five roots beginning with *dhikka*,
followed by four beginning with *chiñ* and *bhṛñ* which have the svarita accent, and after those, [the rest] have the svarita accent.
Forty-six roots beginning with *dheṭ* are declared to be parasmaipada;
however, eighteen beginning with *smiṅ* are considered to be ātmanepada.
Then three beginning with *pū* are proclaimed as having anudātta [indicatory] letters;
*hṛ* takes the parasmaipada endings, while the three beginning with *gup* are ātmanepada verbs.

Those beginning with *rabh* and ending with *yamu* are anudātta-accented; those beginning with *ñi kṣvid* and ending with *tā* are considered to have an udātta accent; likewise, there are fifteen roots beginning with *skaṃbh* that take the parasmaipada endings.

The roots *kit*, *dhātu*, and *udātta* denote giving; *dāna* and *śāna* are of both natures (*ubhayātmaka*); those ending in *svarita* and those beginning with *pac* and followed by *aṅ* are considered to be *parasmaipada*. // NarP_1,53.34 //
These three, beginning with *svarita*, and these two, *vad* and *vac*, which are designated as *paribhāṣin*;
these six classes, starting with *bhū*, are considered to comprise more than a thousand verbal roots (*dhātu*).

The roots *vad* and *han* are also stated to be parasmaipada; furthermore, the four roots beginning with *dviṣ*, which have a svarita accent on their initial syllable, are considered [parasmaipada]. (NarP 1.53.36)
The single root *cakṣiṅ* is declared here to be ātmanepada;
furthermore, thirteen roots beginning with *ir* have anudātta as their indicatory vowel (*it*).
O Sage, the two roots *ṣūṅ* and *śīṅ* are declared by the grammarians to be ātmanepada;
the seven roots beginning with *ṣu* are declared to be parasmaipada.
O Lord of Sages, the verbal root (dhātu) that is designated as having a svarita accent is called "ekāc";
likewise, three beginning with *ghu* are taught as being *parasmaipada*.
O Nārada, the grammarians have declared that the root *stuñ* alone is designated as such in the context of recollection.
The eighteen roots beginning with *rā* are traditionally taught as being conjugated in the *parasmaipada* (active voice);
O Nārada, the root *iṅ* alone is said to be conjugated in the *ātmanepada* (middle voice).
But those four beginning with *vid* are considered to be *parasmaipada*;
likewise, *ñiṣvap*, meaning "to sleep," is designated as *parasmaipada*.
O Sage, those beginning with *syam* which I have mentioned are *parasmaipada*; however, the two roots *dīdhīṅ* and *veṅ*, used in the sense of remembering, are *ātmanepada*.
O best of sages, *prath* and the others, as well as the three roots beginning with *as*, are proclaimed to be udātta; and *carkarīta* and *hnuṅ* are declared to be anudātta.
Seventy-three roots are declared to be in the class beginning with *ad*;
the roots beginning with *dā* are considered to belong to the *parasmaipada*. (NarP 1.53.45)
The root *bhṛ* is indeed declared to be svarita-accented, while *iddhā* is proclaimed to be udātta-accented;
both *māṅ* and *hāṅ* are anudātta-accented among the roots that possess svarita accents.
The twelve beginning with *vāṇiti* and *ādyāśraya*, as well as those ending in *svarita*, are cited; likewise, those beginning with *ghṛmukha* are considered to be *parasmaipada*.
Twenty-two roots have been indicated here in the *bhvādi* class;
twenty-five beginning with *div* are declared to be *parasmaipada*.
O Nārada, both the roots *ṣūṅ* and *dūṅ* are also ātmanepada;
the seven beginning with *pūṅ* are considered to be ātmanepada when marked with the letter *o*.
O Brahmin, those beginning with *dī* and ending with *mukha* are proclaimed here as *ātmanepada*;
those beginning with *syati* are considered *parasmaipada*, like the Vedas.
O Sage, fifteen roots beginning with *jany* are marked for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*);
furthermore, five roots beginning with *mṛṣ* are proclaimed to be *svarita*-accented.
Indeed, the eleven roots beginning with *pad* are considered to be ātmanepada;
however, among those beginning with *svādi* and *curādi*, *rādh* is used only in the sense of "increasing" (*vṛddhi*) when it has an object.
Thirteen roots beginning with *tud* are declared to have an acute accent on the first syllable;
among them, eight beginning with *radh* are proclaimed to be *parasmaipada*.
Sixty-four roots beginning with *sam-ā-dhā* and ending with *ud-ātta* have been declared; furthermore, one hundred and forty roots are considered to begin with *div*. NarP_1,53.54 //

Roots beginning with *svādi*, marked with the *svarita* accent, and ending in the letter *ṅ* are proclaimed [as *ātmanepada*]; however, O Sage, the seven roots designated as *ākhyāta* and the root *dunoti* are *parasmaipada*.
Two roots ending in -aṣṭi and ghu are proclaimed to be anudātta;
among these, fourteen beginning with *ti* are parasmaipada.
O best of Brahmins, thirty-two elements have been declared in the group beginning with *sva*; O most excellent sage, those beginning with *tu* are called the six *tudādi* [roots].

Those roots beginning with *juṣ* that are accented on the first syllable by the Ṛṣi, as well as the ātmanepada roots *ṇu*, *vā*, and those beginning with *vraśca*—these one hundred and five are declared to be accented on the first syllable. (NarP 1.53.58)
O Lord of Sages, only one root beginning with *gūr* has been taught here as being udātta;
furthermore, four roots beginning with *ṇū* are considered to belong to the *parasmaipada*.

The roots beginning with *kuṅ* (to sound) and those beginning with *kuṭ* (to bend), which are marked with the anudātta accent, have reached completion; likewise *pṛṅ* and *mṛṅ*, which are ātmanepada, and six others, including *rip*, are parasmaipada.
The roots *dṛś* and *dhṛ*, as well as *pracch*, have been cited as being ātmanepada;
O Sage, sixteen others are declared to be parasmaipada.
O Sage, six roots beginning with *mil* have been declared to be svaritet, and furthermore,
three beginning with *kṛtī* are also parasmaipadina.
At the beginning of the [section on] *dhātus*, there are one hundred and fifty-seven;
among them, those marked with the *svarita* accent are *rudh*, *nand*, and *kṛt*, which are conjugated in the *parasmaipada*.
Three roots beginning with *ni* and *dhī* are said to be anudāteta;
twenty-five roots, beginning with *śiṣ*, *piṣ*, and *rudh*, are udāteta.
Seven verbal roots beginning with *svar* have been proclaimed as having the svarita accent on their first syllable;
among these, *man*, *van*, and *ātmanebhāṣa* (roots used in the middle voice) are cited, and *kṛñ* is also given as an example.
Then two [classes] are proclaimed, O Brahmin; ten roots are cited by the grammarians;
seven beginning with *ky* are said to be used in both voices; and likewise, there are those beginning with *staṃbhu* which are mentioned in the Sūtras.
O Lord of Sages, all four [groups] have been declared as taking the *parasmaipada* endings;
twenty-two roots beginning with *kruddh* are considered to be udātta-accented.
The root *vṛñ* is ātmanepada, as are the twenty-one roots beginning with *śranth*;
then there are the parasmaipada roots, and the root *grah* is also svaritet.
Among the roots beginning with *kryādi*, fifty-two verbal roots have been proclaimed by the wise;
those beginning with *cur* and ending with *ñi* number one hundred and thirty-six.
O Sage, the eighteen roots beginning with *citya* are said to be ātmanepada;
those beginning with *carca*, however, are proclaimed as belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* class, or alternatively, they are designated as having the suffix *pyant*.
The forty-eight roots beginning with *ad* are likewise [taught];
however, ten roots beginning with *pad* are declared to belong to the *ātmanepada*.
Furthermore, the eight [roots] beginning with *sū* ending in *ñ* have been declared here by the wise;
it is considered that, like the root *iṣ*, they are frequently used after nominal stems (prātipadika) in the sense of the verbal root-meaning.

The suffix *ṇi* is prescribed after a root that possesses a cause (*hetumat*), signifying both "he does that" and "he describes that"; furthermore, roots such as *cit* (to paint) and others are used with the agent or the instrument [as the object] within the meaning of the verbal root itself.
The eight [sections] are declared as the Saṃgrāmas by the wise who are experts in the Anudātta-iccha;
likewise, there are sixteen beginning with the Stomas, and the Andatasya is the illustration.
Likewise, by way of frequent usage (*bāhulaka*), others— whether occurring in the Sūtras, in common worldly speech, or in the Veda—
are all to be included in every grammatical class, and likewise they may express multiple meanings.
"Roots ending in *san* and other affixes, as well as nominal roots (*nāmadhātu*),—in this manner, O Nārada, the infinity of roots should be brought forth here.
This which has been declared is a summary; the detailed exposition is found in various places."

Those roots ending in *ū*, *ṛ*, or *ṝ*—namely *ru*, *kṣṇu*, *śū*, *ṅ*, *snū*, *nū*, *kṣu*, *ci*, *ḍīṅ*, and *śri*—as well as *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, are traditionally recorded as being excluded from the category of monosyllabic roots ending in vowels (*ajanta*). (NarP 1,53.77)

Śaklṛ (to be able), pac (to cook), muc (to release), arc (to praise), vac (to speak), vic (to separate), sic (to sprinkle), pracch (to ask), tyaj (to abandon), nij (to cleanse), ir (the root i), bhaj (to share), bhañj (to break), bhuj (to bend), bhrasj (to fry), matj (to think), yaj (to sacrifice), yuj (to join), ruj (to break), rañj (to color), vij (to tremble), svaj (to embrace), sañj (to adhere), sṛj (to create). // NarP_1,53.78 //
*ad*, *kṣud*, *khid*, *chid*, *tud*, *nud*, *pad*, *bhid*, *vid*, *vyadhi*, *vinad*, *śad*, *sad*, *svid*, *skand*, *hṛd*, *krudh*, *kṣudh*, and *budh*. (NarP 1.53.79)
The roots *bandh* (to bind), *yudh* (to fight), *rudh* (to obstruct), *ṛdh* (to prosper), *ādhī* (to grieve), *vyadh* (to pierce), *śudh* (to purify), *sādh* (to accomplish), *sidhyati* (to succeed);
*man* (to think), *han* (to kill), *āp* (to obtain), *kṣip* (to throw), *chup* (to touch), *tap* (to heat), *tṛp* (to satisfy), and *dṛpyati* (to be proud). NarP_1,53.80 //

The roots *lib*, *lū*, *pū*, *śap*, *svap*, *sṛp*, *iy*, *bhṛ*, *bhaj*, *nam*, *yam*, *rabh*, *kruś*, *daṃś*, *diś*, *dṛś*, *mṛś*, *riś*, *ruś*, *liś*, *viś*, *spṛś*, and *kṛṣ* [are mentioned]. (NarP 1.53.81)
The roots *tviṣ*, *duṣ*, *puṣ*, *piṣ*, *viṣ*, *śiṣ*, *śuṣ*, *śliṣ*, and *yat* [are included];
likewise *ghas*, *vas*, *dah*, *dihi*, *duh*, *nah*, *mih*, *ruh*, *lih*, and *vah*. (NarP 1.53.82)
There are one hundred and two verbal roots ending in consonants that have an anudātta accent;
the particles beginning with *ca*; the word *gavaya*; and those beginning with *pra* which denote direction, place, or time.
For words, O twice-born one, are said to have many meanings and all genders;
likewise, there is the Gaṇapāṭha, the Sūtrapāṭha, and the Dhātupāṭha.
O Nārada, the final dissolution of the nasalized sounds, as well as of Vedic and worldly words, is here described. 53.85.
Therefore, the study of grammar is the means for the collection of words; it is the thorough determination of correct words by way of a concise path.
It is formed by means of roots, suffixes, substitutes, elisions, augments, and so forth.
Thus has this etymology been briefly explained; O Nārada, no one at all is capable of speaking of it in its entirety due to its infinity.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Definition of Etymology," in the second quarter of the Great Narrative within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanandana said:
I shall now proclaim the science of astrology (jyotiṣa), which was formerly declared by Brahmā.
By the mere knowledge of which, the accomplishment of Dharma occurs for men.
The science of the luminaries is said to consist of three sections and four hundred thousand verses;
these are known as Gaṇita, Jātaka, and the section called Saṃhitā, O Brahmin.

In calculation, there are the preliminary operations and so forth, the determination of the mean and true positions of the planets, the inquiry into lunar and solar eclipses, and the calculation of the time of rising. (NarP 1.54.3)

The shadow, the rising of the lunar horns, and the calculation of the *pāta* (node) have been declared; also the divisions of zodiacal signs and the birth-species (*yonija*) of the planets according to their species are described in the *Jātaka*. 1,54.4.
The impregnation, birth, and misfortunes; the allotment of lifespan, the sequence of periods (daśās);
livelihood from karma, the eightfold division (aṣṭavarga), and the celestial royal yogas (nābhasa-rājayogas).
The lunar yogas known as those of renunciation, the nature of the zodiac signs, the results of aspects,
the results of planets and houses, and the miscellaneous [topics] concerning the yogas based on the ascendant.
Unpleasant conjunctions, birth as a woman, and even departure [from life],
the rules for determining lost births, and likewise the characteristics of the decans (dreṣkāṇa).
The form of the Saṃhitā scriptures, the movement of the planets, the characteristics of the year, and those known as the lunar days, weekdays, asterisms, yogas, and half-lunar days; NarP_1,54.8 //
The Muhūrta-upagrahas, the Sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), the planetary course (gocara) in due order,
the Moon’s strength, the strength of the day, and those known as all the Lagna-ārtavas.

The fire-consecration (ādhāna), the male-rite (puṃsavana), the parting-of-the-hair (sīmanta), the naming (nāman), the first feeding (annaprāśana), the tonsure (caula), the ear-piercing (karṇavedha), the initiation with the girdle (mekhalābandhana), and likewise the investiture with the sword (kṣurikābandhana).
The rites for returning home, marriage, consecration, and the characteristics of dwellings; journeys, entries, immediate rain, and the various signs of ritual actions.
I shall now briefly state the entire system of numerical progression:
one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred thousand.
A prayuta, the designation of a koṭi, an arbuda, an abja, a khavaṅkha,
a niravaṅka, a mahāpadma, a śaṅku, and indeed a jaladhi.
Atya, madhya, and parārdha are designations that increase tenfold each;
whether in direct or reverse order, the subsequent calculation is performed in the same manner.

One should multiply the multiplicand by the multiplier; by that [process], starting from the penultimate digit and moving upward, one should divide the divisor, O Sage, and the quotient obtained from the last digit is the result.
The wise say that for an even group, one should take the square root from the last digit;
however, for an odd number, one should subtract the square [of the nearest lower integer] and set the square root aside separately.
O Brahmin, having divided by this [number] doubled, one should place the result under the root; then, subtracting its square, one should divide again by the root.
In this way, O Lord of Sages, the square root of the group arises repeatedly;
the product of three and eight is declared as the cube, and the rule for that is applied to the square root.
The first [digit] is declared to be odd, and the two following it are even;
that which is to be subtracted from the last odd digit is called its root. (NarP 1.54.19)
One should place the square root of the dividend multiplied by three as equal to the root;
one should then multiply that [root] by its own square and subtract the multiplier.
In this manner, from the very uneven [result], the cube-root becomes manifold;
when the divisor and the quotient are multiplied by each other, the portion of eleven is completely eliminated.

O Sage, those who contemplate the meaning of the scriptures should understand that *lava*, *lavaghna*, *hara*, *haraghna*, and *savarṇana* are to be applied in the division of parts (*bhāgaprabhāga*). (NarP 1.54.22)

If, in the sequence of addition or subtraction, one [number] is greater or less than another, those parts are multiplied by the divisor situated at the bottom, increased by its own numerator; then divide [the result] by that same divisor.
One should likewise multiply the wealth or debt by the deficient [value], and one should consider it in that manner;
O Sage, finally, the sum of those [quantities] with equal denominators must be performed.
One should likewise calculate silver in a heap of grain;
furthermore, the result in the multiplication of distinct factors is the product of the numerator divided by the product of the denominator. NarP_1,54.25 //
O wise one, having also subtracted a cheda and a lava from that of Hari, the remainder should be used in the division; the rule for multiplication must then be performed.
O Sage, having squared the two parts of the *hāra* and formed their squares, one should apply the cube-rule to form cubes;
then, for the sake of establishing the square root, one should perform the extraction of the square root from both, everywhere.
One should perform subtraction and addition, square and root, and positive and negative operations, as required, for the successful determination of the quantity. (NarP 1.54.28)
Now, if [the divisor] is less than its own parts by more than one degree, the divisor is not increased by that degree;
however, the numerator remains unchanged there. In the inverse operation, the remainder is as previously stated.
The indicated quantity is divided by the sum of the abridgments; it is then subtracted or added [according to the rule].
This result, multiplied by the desired number and increased by the aspect, is used as the divisor for the quantity that is not desired.
Within the yoga, when two signs have passed and eighty-two thousand [years] remain, the *vargottama* is divided by the interval between signs;
those two are joined with the *yoga-suta*.
The number eight, halved and divided by the desired [quotient], has its square halved and increased by one;
this is considered the first quantity, while the other quantity is the second.
The first term (prāgrūpaka) is the square root of twice the desired quantity; the other (param) is the best.
When the sum and difference of the squares of two numbers are subtracted from each other, these are the squares of those two quantities.
The square of the desired quantity is the *iṣṭavarga*, its cube is the *iṣṭaghana*; the eighth power is the *iṣṭaṣṭama*.
Both of these—square and cube—are known as *eṣī* (powers) of the *iṣṭa* (desired quantity). Furthermore, both [the square and the cube] are indeed manifest (*vyakta*) in calculation (*gaṇita*).
The square root of the product of the multiplier and half [the divisor], increased by the product of the multiplier and the subtractive constant, is the quotient;
and the multiplier is the square of that quotient, decreased by the product of the multiplier and half [the divisor].
When the sine of the latitude is diminished by the visible portion of the moon's disc and divided by the square root of the sum of those two,
then the [lunar] parallax is to be calculated from those two values as in the case of the sun.
When there is a desire for a specific measure among similar quantities, the result is found by subtracting the first and last from the middle;
the desired result is obtained by multiplying the desired quantity and dividing by the first, and in the reverse case, the process is inverted.

In the case of five peaks and so forth, having made mutual sides for the destruction of the result, one divides by the sum of many heaps; the result is obtained through the subtraction of a small portion.
The square root of the desired product of the operations is subtracted from the mixed [square] at the end of the period;
the time multiplied by the measure, divided by the product of the elapsed time and the result, [is the correction].
The results of the months of the smaller zodiac sign should be multiplied by the number of days belonging to its own yoga and divided [by the sum of the days];
for from a large mass of *pala*s, the result of the month of the smaller sign is greater. (NarP 1.54.40)
If the difference between the monthly results is divided by the remainder of the *cedrāśi*, and the additive quantities (*kṣepa*) are multiplied by that [quotient] and then added;
and the additive quantity is divided by the sum [of the results], the results are obtained.
One should divide [the remainder] by those parts of the divisor; the form [obtained] is mixed with time, which completes the calculation.
When it is full, one should proceed; thus, the group of even numbers increases. // NarP_1,54.42 //
Take the square of the sum of the two factors; divide that by the product of the two factors minus one, and subtract the quotient from the square of the sum.
The result is the measure of the smaller factor, while the larger factor is the original sum minus that smaller factor.
The square root of the sum of the squares of the base and the perpendicular is the hypotenuse; the base shall be the arm.
The square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the arm is the perpendicular. 54.44.
From the circumference, that ear-measure [is found] in a triangular or quadrangular field;
when the product of the two quantities, doubled and increased by the square of their difference, [is divided by four], it is the area.

O Sage, the square of the difference between two numbers is obtained by adding their squares and subtracting twice their product; and from the diameter, the circumference is derived through the application of the mathematical form.

The chord is half the diameter diminished by the square root of the product of the sum and the difference of the diameters. The arrow is the square root of the product of the arrow and the diameter diminished by the arrow. (NarP 1.54.47)
The circumference is twice the chord; when the square of half the chord is added to that [square of half the diameter] and divided by five, the result is the diameter.
Thus it has been declared by those skilled in calculation.
The circumference multiplied by the sine of the arc is the *pragula* for the sake of the circumference;
[the result] is divided by the fourth part, the sine of the arrow, the sine of the complement, and multiplied by four.
O Brahmin, one should divide the square of the diameter by the chord; the clear [result] becomes the square of the arrow.
The square of the circle increased by the product of the fourth part of the chord and the square root of the diameter, divided by the chord, [is the result]. 50.50.
The arc is obtained by subtracting half the square root of nine times the square of the mountain (seven) from the square of the radius;
the correction for the middle part is coarse, while the correction for the remainder of the circle's degrees is minute.
The circumference of the base is calculated by multiplying the length by the width;
this is then multiplied again by the depth in finger-breadths (aṅgula). || 52 ||
The pride of Droṇa and the others was shattered by the arrows of Kharva, Indu, and Rāma;
the dimensions of their breadth, length, and depth were measured by fingers multiplied by other nāḍīs.
O twice-born one, the measure of grain in *droṇas* and so forth is obtained by dividing [the number] by six hundred and forty;
however, for other things measured in finger-breadths (*aṅguli*), this does not apply.
One should multiply [the length] by the lords of its own [relevant] axes; from the product, the number of cubits (dres) and so forth shall be obtained.
Thus, the first [measure] in width, multiplied by itself, shall result in the number of finger-breadths (gulās).

O Sage, one should determine the measurement starting from Droṇa as obtained by the arrows (vāṇa), elephants (ibha), and shafts (mārgaṇa); the gnomon (śaṅku) that removes the shadow of the lamp, the stake, and the aperture would thus become the bhava.
The height of the lamp is said to be one *nara*; then, in the forest [of the mandala], it is the height of the lamp minus the *śaṅku*, the man, and the holes.
When joined with the *nara*, the height of the lamp is determined by subtracting those from the base of the human-lamp.

The shadow, divided by the height of the lamp multiplied by twenty, shall be the distance between the lamp and the gnomon; furthermore, the shadow multiplied by the difference between the tips of the shadows [is the result].
The ground for the arising of another means of knowledge would then be non-existent;
once that is attained, it arises like the height of a lamp-flame through the rule of three proportions.
This calculation of the preparatory operations has been declared in brief;
I shall now describe the mean positions of the planets and so forth in the calculation without excessive detail.
O Brahmin, a *yuga* is traditionally reckoned as four thousand years;
its four-tenth part, consisting of four hundred years, is called the *kṛta* age.
Three [units] are proclaimed as Kṛta, two as Dvāpara, and one as Kali;
these constitute seventy-one cycles of the Yugas, together with the years established by Manu.
O best of Brahmins, for Vidhi there are fourteen human days;
O best of Brahmins, his night is likewise proclaimed to be of that same duration.
O Nārada, having condensed the years elapsed since the Self-Existent One, the calculation of the planets should be performed;
or else, it may be done from the beginning of the desired yuga.
In a yuga, the revolutions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus are 4,320,000;
those of Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, and Venus are the same, as they are the first among the sinners who complete their cycles.
For the Moon, [the degrees] are 1, 3, and 7; for Mars, they are 7, 7, 5, 7, 5, 9, and 2.
For Mercury, however, they are 2, 3, 8, 6, 9, 5, and 2.
For Mercury, [the revolutions] are zero, seasons, sky, mountains, three, digits, and mountain-moons;
for Jupiter, they are sky, weapons, eyes, Vedas, weapons, and likewise fire-digits.
For Mercury, the [planetary] years are 31, 29, 21, 14, 7, and 1;
for Saturn, they are 8, 60, 6, 3, 4, and 1.
In the [first] yuga, the left foot [of the mantra] consists of the Moon (1), Fire (3), Void (0), Eye (2), Vasu (8), Serpent (8), and Ocean (4);
and for the right foot, it consists of the Self (1), Fire (3), Yama (2), Aśvin (2), Arrow (1), and Garland (1).
From sunrise to sunrise, by the grace of the Lord, the days in a Yuga are measured as eight, one, eight, seven, one, seven, fifteen, and fifteen. (NarP 1.54.70)
Six, sixty-three, fire (three), fear (eight), and lunar days (fifteen) are the intercalary months;
the lunar day omissions are one, two, three, two, eight, zero, five, and nine.
The four oceans, the eight Kulaparvatas, the six continents, the three fires, the three Vedas, the three fires, and the five moons; these are the months. (NarP 1.54.72)

Prior to the revolution of the Sun’s mandala, there are seven, eight, and three fires (387) kalpas for Mars; four, thirty-four, and twenty (234) for Mercury; and eight, six, and three (368) for Jupiter.
The apogees of Jupiter are 9; those of Venus are 5 multiplied by half (2.5);
and those of Saturn, the slowest planet, are 36; or this is considered the case for the nodes as well.

The lifespan of Manu is eighty-four thousand years; that of the son of Kuja (Mangala) is eight hundred and eight thousand; that of Baudha (Budha) is one hundred and twenty-seven thousand; that of Ajaiva (Brihaspati) is thirty-six thousand; and that of Ravi (Surya) is three thousand six hundred years.
The revolutions of Saturn’s orbit in a kalpa are 3,64,224;
in the current yuga, they are known as the revolutions of the year [of Saturn]. (NarP 1.54.76)
Ten thousand months having been made into [units] by means of the elapsed months starting from the bright fortnight of Caitra (Madhu),
they are separately divided by the months of the Siddhis, the months of the lunar days (grāsa), and the solar months.

Then, having combined the intercalary months with the days and added them to the [current] days, these [values] are placed in two locations; multiplied by the number of elapsed tithis and divided by the lunar days, [they yield the respective results].

Then follow the days and nights devoid of the *lathunā* [intercalary] night, the objects of adornment, the midnight hours, the solar days, the seasons, the years, and so forth, as well as the days, months, and years.
The remainder, diminished by seven, is the lord of the day, beginning with the Sun;
this is multiplied by two or three according to the number of months or years, and increased by one.
Those two, remaining as seven and nine, are to be known as the lords of the month and the year.
The heap of days, multiplied by the revolutions of the moisture [the moon], is divided by the base days.
When divided by the mean motion, the planet becomes [calculated] starting from the zodiacal revolution (bhagaṇa);
thus indeed have the retrograde and slow motions in the accumulation of the apsis (añcaya) been declared by the ancient authorities.
The nodes (pātas) have a retrograde motion; they are subtracted from the [mean] longitudes of the planets in the same manner as the [mean] longitudes are corrected for the equation of the center.
Eight hundred yojanas are known as the diameter of the earth, and twice that is its circumference.
The circumference of the earth shall be the square root of that [value] multiplied by ten;
multiplied by the lambajyā (sine of the colatitude) and divided by its own jyā (sine), it becomes the true circumference of the earth.
The daily motion of the planet as practiced for another location should be divided by that [number];
the resulting quotient, in minutes and so forth, should be subtracted from the previously calculated planets.
One should cast [the points] from one's own location into the position opposite the line;
they shall lie upon the central meridian between the Rākṣasa, Ātapa, and Devauka mountains.
Likewise, Avantikā, Ārohaṭika, and the Sannihita lake;
in the region of Vārapravṛtti-vāk, [the lifespan] shall be more than half of the period of decline.
One should indicate that [longitude] as being less by the nāḍīs of the other place; the motion multiplied by the desired nāḍīs and divided by sixty results in minutes and so forth.
When [the planet] has moved, it should be subtracted; likewise, when it is yet to move, the current position of the planet [should be added].
The maximum [extent of] north-south deviation is one-eightieth part of the minutes of the zodiacal circle.
The cold-rayed moon is displaced from the end of its own course by its own fall;
there, Mars has a residence equal to twice the life-span multiplied by three.
Mercury, Venus, and Saturn are multiplied by four when subtracted by their [mean] anomalies (pātas).
One-eighth of a minute of arc of a zodiacal sign is called the first half-chord (jyārddha).
Then, that second [value] is mixed with the quotient obtained by dividing by two;
it is joined with the first [value] after it has been increased by the quotients obtained from successively dividing the sums.
These segments, which are the sums of the half-chords, are twenty-four in number in their respective order;
the maximum equinoctial sine (paramāpakramajyā), however, is 997.
The arc of that [resulting] sine, divided by the radius (trijīvā), is called the declination (krānti).
Having subtracted the mean apogee from the planet, and likewise having subtracted it from the [mean] anomaly, [the result is the argument].
The remainder is the *kanda*; from that, the sine of the arc (*bhuja-jyā*) and the cosine (*koṭi*) are derived:
in an odd quadrant, the sine is from the traversed portion, and the cosine is from the portion yet to be traversed.
The sine of the arc traversed is equal to the sine of the complement of the arm [multiplied] by the sine of the complement; this, divided by 325, gives the quotient which is the traversed sine-value.
One should divide the distance traversed between the past and future [ascensional differences] by the true observations;
that resulting quotient, having obtained its fruit, should be added to the sine-mass designated as "traversed."

The rule for sequential sines (kramajyā) is thus established, and from it the inverse sine (utkramajyā) is obtained: the minutes [of arc] divided by thirty-seven yield the obtained sine as the traversed integer unit.
One should divide the interval between the traversed and the yet-to-be-traversed by means of the observations of the principles;
that resulting quotient, being the fruit obtained, should be added to the sine-heap designated as "traversed."
The method for sequential sines (kramajyā) is thus; it is also prescribed for inverse sines (utkramajyā):
having subtracted the sine from the total, the remainder is multiplied by twenty-five and divided by the difference between them.
The bow is said to be the product of the number of principles (tattva) and the Aśvins (2), joined with the conjunction;
the degrees of the sun’s slow circumference are the Manus (14), and those of the moon are the Adas (32).
At the end of the even [periods] and at the end of the odd [periods], those two are diminished by two, ten, and five liptās respectively;
at the end of the even [periods], they are seven, thirty-three, thirty-six, twelve, and ninety-nine.
And for Mars and the others [Mercury,
Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn], the values are 2, 7, 9, 6, 1, 4, 5, and 8, respectively, from the beginning of the odd signs up to the end of the even signs.
The qualities, fires, and moons; the sky, mountains, and tastes; the eyes, cows, and peaks; those ending in *ojas*; two, three, and the measure; two, Viśve, Yama, and the mountains. (NarP 1.54.104)
The *khārtuda* (320), *asrāvipat* (1728), and *veda* (4) are proclaimed in the calculation of velocity;
they are divided by the product of the sine of the argument, the radius, and the difference between odd and even [sines].
In the case of even-numbered revolutions, when the positive or negative value is subtracted from or added to the odd-numbered one, the result is the true [longitude].
When that is multiplied by the sine (bhuja-jyā) or cosine (koṭi-jyā) and divided by the degrees of a zodiacal sign (bhagaṇāṃśa), [the result is the equation of the center].
The arc of that sine-result is the manda-phala in minutes and so forth;
when the apogee is in Capricorn and so on, the cosine-result is traditionally held to be additive.
In the case of Cancer and the following signs, the result derived from the cosine (koṭi) must be subtracted from the sine (trijīvā).
The square root of the sum of the squares of that [result] and the sine-result is called the "moving" hypotenuse (cala-karṇa).
The result of the sine (bhujaphala) multiplied by the radius (trijyā) is traditionally held to be positive in the case of Capricorn and so forth;
however, in the case of Cancer and so forth, the result arising from the cosine (koṭija) is to be subtracted from the radius.
The square root of the sum of the squares of that [latitude] and the bhuja-phala is the hypotenuse called *cala*.
That *bhuja-phala*, multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by the *pala-karṇa*, [is the result].
The result obtained in minutes of arc and so forth is known as the velocity (śaidhrya);
this applies at the beginning and in the fourth operation for Mars and the other planets.
Slowness is the single motion of the Sun and Moon; for Mars and the others, slowness and swiftness are stated next. Then again, slowness and swiftness—these four [motions] follow in sequence.
In the case of all [planets], whether in slowness or swiftness of motion, the addition of the degrees and so forth for the planets occurs at Aries and the other cardinal signs;
at Libra and the others, that same value is indeed a subtraction.
Multiplied by the product of twelve and the arm-lengths [of the planet] and divided by the planet's daily motion,
the result in minutes of arc should be applied to the planets as in the case of the sun.
The result for one devoted to a planet should be calculated like that of a planet in the slow-motion (manda) operation;
it is considered to be positive (wealth) when in Cancer and the following signs, and negative (debt) when in Capricorn and the following signs.

The motion of the apogee of the [mean] longitude, multiplied again by the true anomaly and divided by twenty-seven, is then multiplied by its own slow epicycle and divided by the degrees of the zodiacal circle;
these are the minutes of arc.
The mean true motion is subtracted from the motion of the swift apogee;
then, that remainder should be multiplied by the difference between the radius (trijyā) and the hypotenuse (karṇa).

The *cakrakarṇa* is subtracted from the arc; if it is greater than the radius (*trijyā*), it is added [to the arc], and if it is less, it is subtracted. When it is greater, the remainder is the retrograde motion.

The [mean longitudes of] Mars and the other planets are [calculated] by means of the parts of the seasons, the moon, the Vedas, the Indra [eleven], zero, three, one, the qualities [three], eight, the arrows [five], Rudra [eleven], four, the Yamas [two], the rays [twelve], and the Indra [eleven] respectively. (NarP 1.54.119)
By those parts purified by the wheel of the retrograde planet, one determines straightness and curvature;
the sequential sine, multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by twelve, is the terrestrial sine.
Multiplied by the trijyā and divided by the diameter of the day, the result is the arc; and the enemies [of that arc] are the bow.
In the northern transit, that bow is subtracted from the wealth and placed separately. (NarP 1.54.121)
The fourth part of one's own day and night is traditionally known as the halves of day and night;
when the sun moves southward, these are reversed, and they are doubled during the decrease of the day.
The bhā-bhoga is eight hundred liptās; likewise, for the [mean] moon, it is one hundred and thirty-seven.
The liptās of the planet are the bhā-bhoga; the days and so forth are derived from the motion (bhukti) and other factors.
The *liptās* of the conjunction of the sun and moon, divided by the sum of their motions, give the elapsed and remaining [periods];
these multiplied by sixty and divided by the sum of their velocities yield the *nāḍikās*.
The lunar days (tithis) smeared by the sun and moon, divided by their respective [mean] motions, are both past and yet to come;
multiplied by sixty and then divided by the difference between the faster and slower [motions], they are obtained.

The lunar days (tithis), starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, are doubled and increased by one; when not divisible by seven, the remainder corresponds to the karanas: Bava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi.
The Viṣṭi yoga occurs during the latter half of the fourteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight;
the [yogas] Śakuni, Nāga, Catuṣpāda, and Kiṃstughna likewise occur in the bright fortnight. NarP_1,54.127 //
On a surface of stone that is perfectly pure, or as if coated with diamond-paste,
one should draw a circular mandala there using the desired finger-breadths of Śakra.
In the middle of that, one should place a gnomon twelve finger-breadths long according to the prescribed measurement;
wherever the tip of its shadow touches when it is cast during the forenoon and afternoon, [that is the mark].
There, having made two dots at the front and back of the circle,
a line should be drawn between them through their center, extending from south to north.
Between the southern and northern directions, the east and west are established by means of the *timi* fish;
likewise, the intermediate directions are determined by means of the *matsya* fish.
One should make it four-cornered on the outside by means of threads extending from the center;
therein, the desired radiance is considered to be produced by the lines of the arms measured in finger-breadths.
A line extending from east to west is called the equatorial circle (samamaṇḍala);
it is also proclaimed as the celestial sphere (bhamaṇḍala) and the equinoctial circle (viṣuvanmaṇḍala).
The east-west line should be established by means of the meridian line; the shadow at the desired time and the meridian shadow are called the *agra* (the interval) between them.
The square root of the sum of the squares of the gnomon and its shadow is the hypotenuse;
having subtracted the square of the gnomon from the square of the hypotenuse, the square root is the shadow, and vice versa.

In each yuga, the wheel of the suns revolves thirty times in the east; by dividing the number of elapsed yugas by the product of that [number of revolutions] and the number of days, one obtains [the result].
The degrees of the [ascendant] and so forth, diminished by those [corrections], should be understood as the true positions;
from the sum of their products, one should calculate the desired shadow, the gnomon, and other such values.
The trijyās multiplied by the gnomon-shadow and divided by the equinoctial and Cancer [sine] respectively yield the lambajyā and akṣajyā;
their shadows are always the southern lamba and akṣa.

The sum or difference of the direct declination of the sun and that of the planet—depending on whether they are in the same or opposite directions—is the remaining degrees of the sun; from these, the sine (bāhu-jyā) and the cosine (koṭi-jyā) are then derived.
When the sine and cosine of the arm are multiplied by the digits of the hypotenuse in their respective order,
and divided by the cosine of the complement, they are obtained for the shadow-calculation outside the quadrant.

In the case of equality of direction, the difference is taken between the degrees of the sun's altitude and one's own latitude; otherwise, it is the remainder when the directions differ. The sine of that [difference] is multiplied by the radius (trijyā).
The sun, having reached its maximum declination, is in Aries and so forth;
it is subtracted from half the zodiac when in Cancer and so forth, and added to half the zodiac when in Libra and so forth.
Having subtracted the [longitude of the] apogee from the [longitude of the] planet starting from Capricorn (mṛga), the true sun at midday shall be obtained;
its equation of the center, applied repeatedly, is the result, which is the mean sun.
The rising times of the planets, multiplied by sixty and divided by one hundred and eighty, yield their daily motion in *nāḍīs*.
When added to the *ghaṭīs* obtained from the zodiacal circle, these are known as the *ghaṭīs* of their respective solar days.

Multiplied by the radius of the triad (the sine of 90°) and divided by half of their respective day-and-night periods, they are respectively the sines of one, two, and three signs; the arcs of these [sines] are taken separately.
Then, having subtracted [the longitude] from its own [longitude], one should determine the right ascensions (laṅkodayāsavaḥ) for Aries and the others:
The desired rising periods (iṣṭodayāsava) are diminished by the respective degrees traversed in one's own country;
these are then added to those [periods] in direct or reverse order starting from Cancer, and from that [result], whatever [remains].
In reverse order, these six signs beginning with Libra become the desired [periods]; the elapsed and remaining *āsus* should be calculated for the respective suns including precession (*ayanāṃśa*).
The degrees of the portion yet to be traversed (bhogyāṃśa) are divided by their own rising time (svodaya) and multiplied by the elapsed degrees from the beginning of the sign;
one should then subtract these resulting seconds of the portion yet to be traversed from the desired seconds.
In that very same way, the future *lagna*s are pervaded by these [planets] in sequence;
the remainder, cast out in groups of thirty, is divided by the [corresponding] non-cleansed [value].

When Mars is in the ascendant, the portion of the house occupied by it and the portion of the house of expenditure (vyayanāṃśa) are both subtracted from the nāḍīs of the eastern and western natatva; the same is done with the breaths (asus) of the Laṅkā-ascendants.
When the sun has diminished its [daily] motion, one should calculate the midheaven;
then, there will be the remaining minutes of the deficient [arc] and the elapsed minutes of the greater [arc].
In this manner, when the degrees of the arms of the Sun and the Moon are joined within the *sapiṇḍya* period, the calculation of time shall be as follows:
if the degrees of the arms of the Moon are fewer than those of the Sun, the planet [of the Sun] would be less than the Moon.

For them, the destroyers of Śiva are those born of the mountains; the sun is obscured by five hundred and sixty-eight finger-breadths [of shadow], the moon by the earth's shadow, and then the eclipsed one is covered.

Half the sum of the diameters of the eclipsed and the eclipsing bodies, diminished by the arrow (śara) and excluding the portion not eclipsed, is multiplied by ten and divided by one-sixth of the square root of the square of half the sum of the diameters. // NarP_1,54.155 //

The square root of the product of the [longitude of] the Sun, the [longitude of the] Moon, and the [longitude of the] planet minus nine signs, divided by the [longitude of the] Sun, is the duration of the period (sthityardha) in ghaṭīs and so forth, corresponding to the degrees, minutes, and seconds. NarP_1,54.156 //
The [longitude of the] Sun multiplied by six, increased or decreased by the desired palas minus the nadis, is the [longitude of the] Moon;
if it is greater than that, it is otherwise. Thus, when the [Moon] is at the end of the sukha [sign], it is the true [longitude].
When subtracted from the *grāsa* (the eclipse magnitude), these [values] would be the *viśopaka*s;
here, the middle [point] would be at the end of the full moon, while at the end of the new moon, the [true] moon is diminished by three signs (*tri-bhona*).
The degrees of depression (natāṃśa) are obtained by separately correcting those [degrees] with the degrees of obliquity (krānti) and the latitude (akṣa).
When multiplied by three, squared, diminished by two, halved, and added to twelve, it is Hari.
The degrees of the difference between the sun and the tri-bhānāṅga [longitude] are multiplied by nine and divided by thirty-three;
this is the parallax (ālambana), which is positive or negative depending on whether the sun is less than or greater than the tri-bhānāṅga.
Let the [longitude of] the moon, increased by the degrees of parallax (parallactic correction) for all directions and diminished by the lunar day (tithi), be multiplied by six;
let that [result] be increased by its own minutes [of arc] from the point of the non-triple sign (navitribha) minus the parallax. // NarP_1,54.161 //
The ascensional difference (nata) is the difference between the oblique ascensions (tājāṃśa) and the right ascensions (natāṃśa);
it is subtracted from six signs increased by one and divided by fifteen. The direction of the nata is the same as that of the natāṃśas.
The arrow of those two [latitudes], being in the same direction, shall reach its full value;
then, when the portion remaining after subtraction is to be established, it is multiplied by six and three [i.e., eighteen] and divided by the half-duration of the stay.
The portions [of the two] situated in the two [halves] of the interval between them are as before;
by means of those two corrections, the two half-durations become manifest.
The lesser and greater [periods] are joined by those two; the times at the beginning and end of the mouth are seen as intermediate.
Fifteen parts of the nine and five [units], diminished by the sun and so forth, belong to Īśa.

Having first observed the orb of the planet in the sky and having measured its depression below the horizon, one should calculate the sun as diminished or increased by those degrees of time; thus, indeed, the setting and rising of the moon [are determined].

The wise should know that when the portions of the tithis have passed or are yet to come, they are to be understood as having parts, while those within the *talluṃba* and *pāpabiṃba* divisions possess the light of the sun pervading them without obstruction.

When [the latitude] is subtracted from the [ecliptic longitude], and the result is multiplied by two and divided by the lunar days (tithis) plus one, the resulting parallax in digits and so forth is produced clearly according to its direction of correction.

The horns of the moon are white when it is less than half-full; they are prominent when its strength is increasing, and elsewhere they must be described by drawing them according to the measure of its digits.
In the case of five [sides], the sides of the triangle (goṅka) are those remaining when the ears (karṇa) are subtracted from the hypotenuse (śeṣa) individually;
these are multiplied by the square root of the difference between the squares of the sides, divided by three, and then increased or decreased by the quotient obtained.
When the hypotenuse (śravaṇa) is greater than three times the radius (trijyā), the bodies [of the planets] shall be calculated from Mars;
the difference between the two straight and non-straight [distances] is divided by the difference in their velocities.
When the retrograde or direct motion of a planet has passed, one should calculate the elapsed days and so forth;
when the [longitude] is not yet corrected by subtraction, there is a difference in the north-south direction, and their sum is the conjunction.
When the opening of the southern or northern eclipse is small due to the [latitude] correction (mānaukya),
then the difference, parallax, and so forth, are for the sake of clarity, just as in the case of a solar eclipse.
When the sun and the moon are on the same path,
their orbs joined and their declinations equal, that is indeed called *dhṛti*.

When the moon has entered the two *vipaṭītāyana* positions in the form of a crescent, the minutes of arc of its motion are equal; then there is *vyatīpāta*, occurring at the half of the zodiacal circle when joined with austerity (*tapas*).
When the two suns are situated within the zodiacal circle, reaching as far as the midpoint of the circle,
their respective declinations are joined with the degrees and so forth calculated according to the method of direct observation.
Then, when the declination of the Moon— calculated from its [true] longitude and corrected by the equation of the center—
is greater than the declination of the Sun, the node is then past.
If it should be less, then the future [longitude] is that of the left even-footed [sign];
when there is otherwise the declination of the moon, if it is purified by the [lunar] latitude.
The two obliquities, multiplied by the trijyā and divided by the maximum [obliquity], yield the sines of the half-arc intervals between those two;
when the Moon is situated within that arc, [the correction is applied].
When the node has moved past the moon, the [longitude] to be subtracted is multiplied by the velocity of the sun and divided by the velocity of the moon;
the result, in minutes of arc and so forth, is added to the sun. (NarP 1.54.180)
The result of that [longitude] should be added to or subtracted from the Moon's apogee in reverse order;
this operation is to be performed repeatedly until the two [the Moon and its apogee] are equalized.
When the two declinations are equal, there is a node;
then, when the Moon is diminished by the projected degrees, the product of the deficient and the greater [sines] at night is future, while at that moment it is greater.

Having fixed the two halves of the half-night, the minutes of the interval between the two [halves] are divided by sixty and by the [mean] lunar motion; these are the nāḍīs of the time of the eclipse.
One should multiply half the sum of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon by sixty and divide it by the difference between their longitudes;
the result is the duration of the eclipse in units such as nāḍīs and so forth.
The clear middle time of destruction (pātākāla), when subtracted by half the duration (sthityarddha), would be its time of occurrence;
that is designated as "conjoined" (tatsaṃyoga).
The time between the initial and final moments should be known as extremely terrible;
having the form of a blazing fire, it is censured for all ritual actions.
O twice-born one, this much has been declared by Gaṇita in brief;
now I shall speak of the Jātaka according to the tradition, preceded by the designations of the zodiac signs.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Luminaries," in the second quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:
[The parts of the body are] the head, the mouth, the arms, the heart, the chest, the interior, the bladder, the anus, the nails, and the skin.
The pair of knees, shanks, and feet; the limbs; and the ritual actions and so forth.
Mars, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon; the Sun, Mercury, and Venus; Mars; Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and Jupiter are the lords of the signs beginning with Aries.
In this manner, at the time when the moon and sun are in odd signs, the lords of the decans (dreṣkāṇas) are proclaimed to be the first, fifth, and ninth lords [of the signs]. // NarP_1,55.3 //
Five, eight, seven, five, and five degrees are assigned to Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus respectively;
these are declared to be the lords of the thirty-degree divisions (triṃśāṃśa) in odd signs, while in even signs the order is reversed.
Kriyaṇa, Taulika, Rkka, and so forth are the nine divisions (navāṃśakas) in Aries and the other signs;
the lords of the twelve parts from one's own sign are the six signs beginning with the [natal] sign.
The signs born of the earth (Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn) are known as nocturnal because they rise with their backs; the remaining signs are known as diurnal.
Taurus is both [nocturnal and diurnal]; Capricorn is cruel, while the others are gentle and masculine.
Male, female, and neuter; moving, stationary, and dual-natured:
Aries and the other signs are situated in the directions starting from the east, each moving within its own respective location.
From the beginning, the goat, the ox, the woman, the insect, the fish,
and the cricket [are situated] at high degrees by parts of two, three, seven, twenty-seven, five, nine, eight, and twenty.

The first, middle, and final degrees of each respective seventh sign from the exaltation are, in order, the *vargottama* positions; in the half of the signs beginning with movable ones, these correspond to the twelve houses starting from the body (*mūrti*).
The signs Leo, Taurus, and Scorpio are the trines of the Sun;
the fourth, eighth, and twelfth houses are its squares; and the ninth and fifth houses are its trines.

The twelfth, eighth, sixth, third, eleventh, tenth, fourth, seventh, and first houses are the signs of men, quadrupeds, and beasts, respectively; these are rich in strength when situated in the angles (kendras).
After the center [the first house] come the succedent houses (paṇaphara), and after those, the cadent houses (āpoklima).
[The planets are] red, white, resembling a parrot, pale-red, smoky, and pale-white. NarP_1,55.12 //
Variegated, black, yellowish-pink, brown, and clear—these arise from the activity of light; there may be a state of floating known as equanimity and hope when the second [moon] shines like the sun.
The Sun is Time and the Self, the Moon is the Mind, Mars is Vitality, Mercury is Speech, Jupiter is Knowledge, Venus is Happiness, and Saturn is Desire and Suffering.
