O Sage, through white, red, yellow, and black colors, there is affliction for the Brahmins and the other castes;
by two, three, or four colors, they strike the royal people on earth.
With upward-pointing rays that are copper-colored, the commander of the army perishes;
with yellow rays, the king's son; with white rays, the domestic priest; and with variegated rays, the common people.
In the winter, the world is filled with smoke-colored and reddish clouds hanging low;
in the spring, the sun is auspiciously copper-red, possessing the luster of saffron.
In summer he is pale-white, and variegated at the onset of the rainy season;
in autumn he has the luster of the interior of a lotus, and in winter his complexion is red.
O Lord of Sages, it has been stated in due order that a yellow comet portends cold and rain, while one resembling a red mass portends disease and the fear of drought during the summer.
When the sun appears with a form like half a rainbow, it causes hostility among kings;
when the sun resembles the blood of a rabbit, a battle will soon take place on earth.
If the sun resembles a peacock’s feather, it does not rain for twelve years;
if the sun resembles the moon, it shall cause division among kings on earth.
If the sun is dark, there is danger from insects; if it has the appearance of ash, there is likewise danger arising from the kingdom.
When a hole is seen in the solar disc, it portends the destruction of a great king.

A form shaped like a water-jar brings hunger and fear; a form shaped like an archway destroys cities; a form shaped like a parasol brings the ruin of one's country; and a form like a broken sun brings about the end of the king.
If lightning, a meteor, or thunder occurs at the time of sunrise or sunset,
then the death of a king is to be known, or else a conflict with the king.
Surrounding the sun and the moon for a fortnight or half a fortnight, the red clouds at sunrise and sunset cause another king to rule day and night.
At sunrise and sunset, the sun is obscured by clouds resembling weapons;
there is a terrifying battle with asses, camels, and other beings of sinful form.
When the moon has its southern horn elevated, it is auspicious in the signs of Pisces and Aries;
likewise, when its northern horn is elevated, it is most excellent in the signs of Taurus and Capricorn.
The face of Ghaṭotkaca is like that of a bull; that of Karka is like a bow;
that of Śara is like an arrow; that of Kaurma and Hṛdya is like a bow; and that of Tulaka and Karka is like a trident.
The moon rising in an inverted position brings about famine and strife;
when the moon moves toward the south during the two Āṣāḍhas and the asterisms of Mūla and Indrā (Jyeṣṭhā), it portends the same.

When the Moon is in Viśākhā and situated on the right side of the two Maitra constellations (Anurādhā and Jyeṣṭhā), it is a malefic period that causes arson, theft, wandering in forests, and destruction by snakes.

In rites dedicated to the ancestors (pitṛ), the middle [digit] is auspicious; in rites for two deities, the moon in the constellation of Mṛgaśiras is auspicious; and the moon in Revatī, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttarabhādrapadā, Rohiṇī, and Aśvinī is auspicious when it has not yet reached its fullness.
Having passed the right-hand gates of the central enclosure from the ninth dwelling,
there are the deities Yama, Indra, the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), Agni, Varuṇa, and the Maruts, each occupying half a star.
The constellations beginning with Dhruva and those having two deities (such as Aśleṣā) should be one and a half [units]; the others are equal [to one].
When the southern horn [of the moon] is rising, it is not desired; however, the "ant" (pipīlikā) configuration is auspicious during the bright fortnight.
The waning and waxing of one's affairs, as well as their decline and prosperity, follow this sequence:
the broad moon brings about an abundance of food, while the sun destroys the great clouds.
When the horns or the mandala are struck by Mars and the other planets respectively, they become downward-facing, terrifying with weapons, and resemble staffs of punishment.

When Mars is in the *vikrimi* yoga with its own *udaya* (ascendant) during the eighth or ninth lunar mansion from the true [position], there arises security at first, followed by rain and the destruction of kings and people.
That crooked [conjunction] is known as Uṣṇa; it causes suffering for the subjects and arises from fire.
It occurs in the tenth or eleventh lunar mansion, or twelve *rāva*s before the *tīpaya*.
The *kūkra* is to be known as having a curved mouth; it causes the destruction of crops and rain when Mars is in the thirteenth asterism, or when it is retrograde in the fourteenth.
The Bālāsya-cakra is located there; it causes the destruction of rain upon the crops.
At the fifteenth and sixteenth lunar mansions, when retrograde, it becomes Rudhirānana.
The son of the Earth causes famine, fear of hunger, and diseases;
when retrograde in the eighteenth or seventeenth [nakṣatra], it is called Muśala.

When Mars rises in the two Phālguna months and moves retrograde in the Vaiśvadeva constellation, there is famine and it constantly causes fear through the destruction of wealth, grain, and other resources.
When it sets in the constellation of the Four-Faced One (Jyeṣṭhā), it causes the destruction of the three worlds;
when it rises in Śravaṇa or Puṣya, it brings about the loss of speakers, cattle, and horses.
In whichever direction Mars has risen, it brings fear to the king of that region;
and if Mars is situated in the middle of Maghā, it likewise moves in a retrograde course there.

Causing fear through drought and weapons, and bringing suffering to the gods and the destruction of kings, the Gaṇḍa stars of those who hate the ancestors, the gods, and the elements shall be split asunder.
When Mars is situated in any of these— among the three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Svāti, Śravaṇa, or Mṛga— it then causes famine, death, and disease.
When Mars, moving through the southern part while situated in Rohiṇī, does not rain,
yet moves northward across all the asterisms, he bestows auspiciousness.
When Jupiter is in the southern course, it brings about undesirable results for men and causes dissension;
it shall never rise again without an eclipse of the moon.
When Mercury transits through the asterisms of Vasu, Vaiṣṇava, Viśva, Indu, and Dhātṛ, it brings about drought, fear of fire, misfortune, and war with kings.
If Mercury is seen within the asterisms beginning with Ārdrā and ending with Maghā (the Pitṛbhā), it causes fear through the threat of obstructive rain and breaks apart that very star.
At that time, the son of Indu (Mars), causing fear through famine, strife, disease, and drought,
will move through the six lunar mansions beginning with Hasta.
When Mercury moves through the asterisms of Ahibudhnya, Āryaman, Agni, and Yama, he brings about security, abundance, health, and the destruction of disease.
If the Moon, moving through the first three asterisms, pierces the junction star (yogatārā), it brings destruction to physicians, actors, and those engaged in trade.
At that time, for living beings, there is danger from hunger, weapons, fire, and thieves;
the natural course of existence proceeds through the abodes of Yama, Agni, Dhātṛ, and Vāyu.
In the asterisms of Raudra, Indu, Sārpa, and Pitrya, the movement is known as "mixed";
in Bhāgya, Āryaman, Ijya, and Aditi, the movement is said to be "contracted."
Gatitīkṣṇa, Ajacaraṇa, Ahibudhnya, Bhāśrī, Bheṣaja, Yāmātiga, Ativīśva, Abhumūla, Matsya, and Eñjaja. (NarP 1.56.46)
A terrible fate awaits those born under the asterisms of Hari, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vasu, and Varuṇa;
likewise, a destiny called "evil" awaits those born under the asterisms of Indra, Agni, Mitra, and Mārtaṇḍa.
Indeed, whether risen or even set in the paths beginning with that of the common folk (Prākṛta),
for as many days as he is visible, for that long he remains invisible.
The son of the Sun [Mars] moves forty, thirty, and nine degrees respectively;
the son of the Moon [Mercury] [moves] by fifteen and eleven days.
In the *prākṛta* [yoga], the gentle [wind] has gone; it brings security, health, and abundance.
In the *miśra* and *sakṣipta* [yogas], it yields middling results; in the others, it bestows rain.
When Mercury rises during the months of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, Pauṣa, or Āṣāḍha, he bestows the fruit of sin upon the worlds; at other times, he bestows auspiciousness.
When Mercury rises in the months of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika, he brings about fear of weapons, famine, and fire;
however, when he is silver-white or crystal-like in appearance, he is excellent.
For him, the first two months [Māgha and Phālguna] grant fortune; the fifth and eleventh months [Jyeṣṭha and Mārgaśīrṣa] grant auspiciousness; the month of Āṣāḍha yields middling results for men;
Śrāvaṇa is middling; Nabhas (Bhādrapada) is excellent; and Bhādrapada is excellent, though for some men it may be otherwise.
Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa yield evil results for men;
Pauṣa and Māgha bestow auspiciousness; Phālguna and Caitra are middling. (NarP 1.56.54)

Mādhava (Vaiśākha) bestows auspiciousness; Jyeṣṭha yields middling results for men; Śuci (Āṣāḍha) is middling; Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa) is excellent; and Bhādra (Bhādrapada) is excellent in some respects, O man.
The month of Īṣa is declared to be most excellent; such is its fruit.
When the Sun moves through the northern path, it brings about security, health, and abundance of food.
In the southern [direction], the Guru moves in reverse; in the middle, he moves with medium speed.
His colors are, in sequence: yellow, fire-colored (red), dark (blackish-brown), green, and red.
Worshipped by the gods, he brings fear of disease, fire, thieves, weapons, and missiles to living beings,
and causes drought that resembles the end of an eon.
If seen during the day, it portends disease that may lead to the king’s death or the destruction of the kingdom;
Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī likewise constitute the body of the year.
When the navel, the pair of feet, the two thighs, the heart, or the flower [of the body] are afflicted by cruel planets, there is famine, fire, wind, and fear; such is the affliction of the body.
In the Puṣya mansion, there is hunger, thirst, and fear at the navel; there is a complete depletion of roots and fruits;
and for the lord of the heart, there is death. However, if it is conjoined with auspicious planets, it will be favorable.
There will be an increase in crops, health for the people, war, and a lack of rain;
yet, among the twice-born, there will be great happiness for cows, kings, and women.
A rain of thundering serpents brings well-being and great festivals;
yet excessive rainfall is the ruin of the country, even if it brings highly valuable prosperity.

When Jupiter is situated in the lunar mansions beginning with Maghā, there is enmity, disease, and fear; during the rains, there is fear of disease; there is disease and grain; and the sky remains cloudless. (NarP 1.56.64)
The three paths— the gentle, the middle, and the southern—
of Venus should be known as consisting of three tracks each, derived from the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī, occurring in groups of three.
The nine paths (vīthīs) ending with Yāmyā are named Nāga, Airāvata, Vṛṣabha, Uṣṭra, Khara, Mṛga, Añja, Dahana, and Yāmyā. NarP_1,56.66 //
Moving through the three paths on the gentle (saumya) course, Bhārgava indeed brings about the fulfillment of grain, wealth, rain, and crops.
On the middle path, all three [clouds] yield only inferior results;
however, a cloud in the eastern direction brings auspiciousness during the five-day period of the ancestors (pitṛ-pañcaka).
In the three constellations beginning with Svāti, Venus is likewise situated in the western quarter;
however, when the situation is reversed, there is a lack of rain, especially if it is conjoined with Mercury.
When the moon sets on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the fourteenth, or the new moon,
then the earth becomes composed of water.
When Jupiter and Venus are situated in each other’s seventh houses, positioned respectively in the western and eastern paths,
they bestow drought, famine, and war.
If Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, the Sun, and Saturn are positioned ahead of Venus,
they are considered to cause war, famine, and the destruction by water.
In the asterisms of Jala, Mitra, Aryaman, and Āhīndra, there is abundance of food;
in Mūla, there is rain accompanied by weapons; and in Ahibudhnya and Bhaya, there is fear.
When the planet Mars moves through the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Anilaha, Ārdrā, Abharaṇī, Bhāgya,
and Meṣa, it brings about abundance of food and health for men.
One asterism is in the mouth, two in the anus, three in the navel, two in the eyes,
five in the heart, and four in the left hand.
Likewise, there are three lunar mansions on the left foot and three on the right;
there are four on the right hand, which is the position of the birth-moon and the asterism of one's birth.
Sickness, gain, loss, gain, happiness, imprisonment, exertion, a successful journey, and the acquisition of wealth—these are the results in successive order. NarP_1,56.77 //
The planet Jupiter, moving in its direct course, produces such results in many ways;
when it is even, it produces equanimity, and in the case of swift-moving planets, it produces results according to their respective order.
With his head severed by Viṣṇu’s discus, Haṅgu attained immortality by drinking the nectar; he became a celestial being (kheṭa) there, and in that state he was established as a kheṭa.
The sun and moon are the *varaṇa* (obstructing) elements; at every lunar node (*parvan*), they strike [the earth].
Because of their deviation (*vikṣepa*) and descent (*avanati*), and because they have gone far away from them, the *vaṅga* (mercury) and *gāhu* (iron) are produced.
One should purify the [mean] positions of the Sun and Moon by adding six months;
the lords of the parvas (lunar days) are likewise [determined] from the one called Satyadeva in successive order.
On the full-moon day (parvan) dedicated to Brahmā, there is an increase in the prosperity of Brahmā, Indra, Kubera, Yama, Varuṇa, Agni, and Yama, as well as of cattle, crops, and the twice-born.
The result is exactly like that in the Saumya [quarter]; there is affliction by phlegm during the Parvan;
there is conflict among kings and suffering in the Aindra [quarter], and the destruction of crops.
There will be loss of wealth for the wealthy, but an increase in grain for the followers of Kubera;
there will be misfortune for kings, but security for others during the period of Varuṇa.
In the *Hautāśa* parvan there is abundant rain, the growth of crops, and security;
in the *Yāmya* parvan there is drought, the loss of crops, and famine.
If the moon is deficient in its period (velā), there will be loss for kings and a terrible battle;
if it exceeds its period, there will be a loss of flowers, fear, and the destruction of crops.
When there is an eclipse of both the moon and the sun within a single month,
it portends conflict among kings and the destruction of wealth and rain.
When the sun and moon are eclipsed while already risen or while setting, O King, they bring about the destruction of grain;
when both are eclipsed while entirely swallowed, they bestow the fear of famine, disease, and fire.
In the northern course (saumyāyana), it destroys Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas;
in the southern course, it destroys the twice-born in order, when Rāhu has seen it and it is afflicted by the serpent.
In the same way, there are ten divisions of villages and ten divisions of liberations;
even the gods are unable to perceive them, let alone ordinary people.

Having brought those [planets] calculated according to their respective positions, one should consider their day; for we grasp the characteristics of time through other auspicious and inauspicious [signs]. (NarP 1.56.91)
Therefore, for the sake of knowing the [proper] time, a wise person should investigate the forms of portents, the risings and settings of comets, and other signs for human beings.
Celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial [omens], which bestow auspicious or inauspicious fruits,
resemble a sacrificial altar, a banner, a weapon, a palace, a guardian, prosperity, or an elephant.
Those shaped like pillars, spears, and goads are proclaimed as atmospheric;
those situated among the constellations are celestial, while those situated on the earth are terrestrial.
Even a single creature, if its form is divided, will surely not lead to auspiciousness;
for as many days as the comet is seen in its various manifestations, [so shall it be]. (NarP 1.56.95)
They bestow their fruit within as many months as there are years in the eight essential periods;
even those divine comets (ketu) constantly grant the fruits of life.
Short, glossy, and very serene, a white-tailed comet brings abundant rain;
one with a long tail sets quickly and causes drought.
A comet that brings about what is undesirable, possessing a luster equal to Indra’s bow and appearing with two,
three, or four prongs, is considered to bring about the end of the kingdom.
The Maṇihāra, Tuvarṇābha, the radiant Arkasūnu, and the Ketus—
when these appear in the east or the west, they portend the destruction of kings.
Those comets that arise from fire, resembling bamboo shoots, the bimba fruit, the earth, or the parrot's beak, are also traditionally held to yield results.
The sons of Earth (the Bṛhaspatis) resemble water and oil, are circular, and bring about hunger and fear;
the white-complexioned Ketus, the sons of Soma, bestow abundance of food and security.
The son of the Grandfather is Ketu, who possesses three colors and is endowed with the thirty [deities];
from the staff of Brahmā, he is known as Dhūmaketu, the bringer of the end to all creatures.
In the northeast are the sons of Bhārgava, white in form, who grant what is undesirable;
the sons of Paṅgu, known as Viśikhas and Kamakas, are also givers of the undesirable.
The daughters of Guru known as Vikacā and Veṣṭā, though situated in the south, are subtle and white; the daughters of Budha bestow fear from thieves and disease.
Those born from Mars, known as Kuṅkuma, are red and bring about pain and misfortune;
those born from Fire, known as Viśvarūpa, are fire-colored and bestow happiness.
Those that are reddish and dark in appearance are the sons of the Sun (Sūrya) and bringers of evil;
those born of Venus (Śukra) resemble stars and are the Ketus that bestow auspiciousness.
The comet that appeared in the constellation Kṛttikā was surely a sign of the destruction of the people;
having arisen from palaces, trees, and mountains, it brought about the ruin of kings.
The comet named Kaumuda, which brings abundance of food and resembles a white water-lily, is auspicious;
however, the Āvartaketu comet appearing at twilight is not a bestower of desired things.
The measurement of Brahmā, the gods, humans, the ancestors, the sun,
the solar day (sāvana), the moon, the constellations, and Jupiter— these indeed are the nine measurements.
The legal procedure regarding these nine types of disputes is here [established] by means of five [factors];
their respective duties shall be explained according to the legal process.
The entire motion of the planets is determined by the solar measure;
the regulation of rainfall and the conception of a woman's fetus are determined by the civil (sāvana) measure alone.
In the case of rain, the conception [of a child] is not determined by the asterism;
rather, the determination of the lunar day, the year-lord, and so forth applies to journeys, marriages, vows, and hair-cutting ceremonies.
The entire observance of fasting on lunar days and so forth is governed by the lunar month;
however, the definition of the years beginning with Prabhava is governed by the solar measure.
Then, by means of those respective twelve months, there arise those respective eight [periods];
thus, through the medium course of the Guru, the sixty years consist of the Prabhava and the others.
Prabhava, Vibhava, Śukla, Pramoda, Prajāpati,
Aṅgiras, Śrīmukha, Bhāva, Yuvan, and likewise Dhātṛ.
Īśvara, Bahudhanya, Pramāthin, Vikrama, Vṛṣa,
Citrabhānu, Subhānu, Tāraṇa, Pārthiva, and Avyaya.
Sarvajit, Sarvadhārī, Virodhin, Vikṛta, Khara,
Nandana, Vijaya, Jaya, Manmatha, and Durmukha.
Hemalamba, Vilamba, Vikārī, Śārvarī, Lava,
Śubhakṛt, Śobhana, Krodhī, Viśvāvasu, and Parābhava.
Plavaṅga, Kīlaka, Saumya, Sāmāpta, Virodhakṛt, Paribhāvī, Pramādī, Ānanda, Rākṣasa, and Anala. (NarP 1.56.119)
Piṅgala, Kālayukta, Siddhārtha, Raudra, Durmati,
Dundubhi, Rudhirodgarin, Raktākṣa, Krodhana, and Kṣaya.
All sixty-year cycles should be understood as having results corresponding to their names;
five years constitute a *yuga*, and there are twelve such *yugas*.
Their lords, in successive order, should be known as Viṣṇu, the priest of the gods (Bṛhaspati),
Purandara, Lohita, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the one named Ahibudhnya.
Then the Viśvedevas, the Pitṛs, Śaśin, Indra, Agni, Aśvin, and Bhaga;
likewise, in the year of the Yuga, the teachers are Agni, Indu, Vidhi, and Īśvara.

Then, having correctly understood the relative strength and weakness of the lords of the armies who are like grain-eaters, as well as the movement of the planets at that time, one shall obtain the fruit [of victory].
The six-month period beginning with Capricorn (Mṛga), according to the sun's movement, is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa);
that is the day of the gods, while the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) beginning with Cancer (Karka) is their night.
Entering a house, marriage, consecration, and the tying of the sacred thread—
these auspicious rites should be performed during the spring and other seasons, as well as during the northern course of the sun.
Even a censurable act performed during the southern solstice is praised with effort;
the seasons, beginning with Śiśira, consist of two months each, starting from Māgha.
The seasons of Mṛgaśīrṣa, Śiśira, and Vasanta, as well as Grīṣma, occur during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa);
while Varṣā, Śarat, and Hemanta occur from Karkaṭa onwards during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
The lunar month ends with the new moon (darśa), while the solar month is by the transit (saṃkrānti); the civil (sāvana) month is measured by days.
Thirty lunar revolutions constitute a month known as the sidereal (nākṣatra).
Madhu and Mādhava, Śukra and Śuci, then Nabhas and Nabhasya, Iṣa and Ūrja, Sahas and Sahasyaka.
The names of the months beginning with Caitra are derived from the sequence of their penances (tapaḥ),
and [the name of each month] is that in which the full moon (paurṇamāsī) is conjoined with a particular lunar mansion (dhiṣṇya).
The month is named after that lunar mansion, and the full moon day is likewise named after it;
its two fortnights are known as the divine and the ancestral, corresponding respectively to the bright and the dark halves.
Brahmā, Agni, Viriñci, Viṣṇu, and the Daughter of the Mountain are always praised respectively for auspicious and inauspicious rites on the lunar days.
Vināyaka and Yama; Nāga and Candra; Skanda and Arka;
Vāsava and Mahendra; and those called Nāga, Durgā, and Daṇḍadhara.
Śiva, Viṣṇu, Hara, Ravi, Kāma, and Sarva; then Kali, Candra, Viśvedeva, Darśa, Tithīśa, and the Pitṛs are remembered.
Furthermore, the lunar days (tithis) are Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā;
they should be known by repeating this sequence three times. During the bright fortnight, these grant results that are undesirable, middling, and desirable, respectively.
In the dark fortnight, however, the eighth, twelfth, sixth, fourth, and fourteenth days respectively grant desirable, middling, and undesirable results. (NarP 1.56.137)
The lunar days known as the "cavities of the fortnight" (pakṣarandhra) are indeed proclaimed to be extremely harsh;
the nāḍikās are numbered by the ocean (4), the Manu (14), the cavities (9), the limbs (6), and the principles (25).
On those lunar days, five [types of women] should always be avoided in sequence,
with the exception of the new moon (amāvāsyā) and the ninth day, which are designated as "odd" (viṣama).
The lunar days (tithis) are generally auspicious, yet the first day (pratipat) is considered mediocre;
likewise, one should avoid oil on the sixth day, shaving on the eighth, and [certain acts] on the fourteenth day of the month.
One should avoid sexual intercourse with a woman on the full moon and the new moon, as well as on the new moon,
the sixth lunar day, the first lunar day, the twelfth, and on all festival days.
One should never perform the cleansing of the teeth on the ninth lunar day,
nor during a Vyatīpāta yoga, at the time of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the eleventh lunar day, or on the festival days (parva).
On a Sunday or a Tuesday, on the sixth lunar day, during the Vaidhṛti yoga,
or on the tenth day, the man who performs an oil massage and likewise bathes with *āmalaka* fruits [attains great merit].
On the thirteenth day, he suffers the loss of a son;
on the second day, there is no doubt that he suffers the loss of wealth and sons.
On the new moon day, the ninth, and the seventh, there is the destruction of the family.
That full moon day on which the moon is visible during the day is known as Anumatī.
At night, the full moon is of two kinds: Rākā and Amāvāsyā;
likewise, Sinīvālī is considered to possess the moon, while Kuhū is considered to be devoid of the moon.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika is the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga;
the third day of the bright fortnight of Mādhava, known as Puṇya, is the beginning of the Tretā Yuga.
The fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha is declared to be the beginning of the Dvāpara age;
the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa is the beginning of the Kalpa.
The twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, the ninth day in Āśvayuja, and the third day known as the Śukla-tṛtīyā in Caitra and Bhādrapada; NarP_1,56.149 //

The eleventh day of the bright fortnight in Pauṣa, the tenth day of the bright fortnight in Āṣāḍha, the seventh day of the bright fortnight in Māgha, and the eighth day of the dark fortnight in Nabhasya; NarP_1,56.150.
The new moon in the month of Śrāvaṇa, the full moon in the month of Phālguna,
and the full moons in the months of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, Jyeṣṭha, and Caitra.
Manu and others grant extreme merit in the Śrāddha rites for human beings;
on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Moon is in Maghā and the Sun is in Karkaṭa.
At that time, the Gajacchāyā should be known as bestowing exceedingly great merit upon a Śrāddha;
on a single day, there may be three lunar dates, which constitutes a tithi-kṣaya (the omission of a lunar date).
If a single lunar day (tithi) occurs on three weekdays, it is superior; however, if two [lunar days] occur, they are both censured.
That lunar day which extends until the setting of the sun on a particular weekday [is the one to be observed].
If that [lunar day] remains unbroken, it is whole; if deficient, it is designated as "crippled" (khañja).
The fifteenth part of the lunar day constitutes the sequence beginning with Pratipad and so forth.
The *kṣaṇas* are half of those [units], being half their measure;
the Sun is fixed, the Moon is moving, Mars is cruel, Mercury is retrograde, and Jupiter is all-pervading.
Venus is light and mild, while Saturn is sharp; that man who applies [oil] on a Sunday shall become full of suffering.
If Mars is the lord of the lunar mansion, there is luster; if the Moon, illness and good fortune;
if Jupiter, not so; if Venus, loss; and if Saturn, all forms of prosperity.
From the eastern gate of Laṅkā, [the sun] may be above or even below;
by means of the nāḍīs of its own movement through other regions, it becomes [visible] in the west.
Whatever action is performed by a planet endowed with strength succeeds;
that same action, when performed by one devoid of strength, does not succeed even with great difficulty.
The days of the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus yield fruit in all undertakings;
however, the others grant the desired results in cruel deeds.
The Sun and Moon are red in color; Mars is fair and coppery;
Mercury has the hue of dūrvā grass; Jupiter is yellowish-white; and Venus is white.
Kṛṣṇa, the son of Sura, is beneficial on his own days for the performance of duties according to one's respective caste; likewise, [the numbers] seven, five, six, fourteen, seven, and eight.
Bāṇa, Agnilocana, Hya, Vedabāhu, Śilīmukha;
Tryeka, Ahi, Yau, Netra, Gotra, Rāma, Aśva, Dra, Rasa, and Ṛtu. (NarP 1.56.164)
The Kulikas, Upakulikas, and Vāravelās are likewise to be known in succession,
each measuring half a watch (prahara), starting from Sunday.
On whichever day a *kṣaṇa* is observed, its presiding weekday is as follows:
the first [weekday] is the sixth from ours, the second is the second from that, and the third is the sixth from that.
The sixth [planet] is known as the lord of the *kālahorā* for each of the others,
occurring by means of exactly two and a half *nāḍīs* during the day and night respectively.
When an action or task is prescribed for a particular day, it is also auspicious during the moment (kṣaṇa) of that planet;
the lords of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), in order, are Aśvinī, Bharanī, Kṛttikā, and Rohiṇī.
Candra, Īśa, Aditi, Jīva, Ahi, Pitaraḥ, and the one named Bhaga;
Aryaman, Arka, Tvaṣṭṛ, Marut, Śakra, Agni, Mitra, and Vāsava.
Nairṛta, Ap, Viśvedevas, Govinda, Vasu, Toya, Pā,
Ajaikapāt, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan are thus proclaimed.
The three *pūrva* constellations, Maghā, Kṛttikā, Viśākhā, and Mūla—
this group of nine is prescribed as facing downward when the sun is in that [sign].
The calculation of entering anthills, the practice of elemental spirits, writing, as well as the various crafts, arts, wells, and the depositing or extracting of treasures— whatever [is such].

The group of nine known as "those with faces turned sideways" (tiryaṅmukha)—consisting of Maitra, Indu, Tvāṣṭra, Hasta, Indra, Āditi, Bhānti, Aśvin, and Vāyu—is prescribed for the Sun in that [eighth] position. NarP_1,56.173 //
The operation of ploughs and water-wheels, vehicles, leaf-boats, elephants, camels, donkeys, oxen, chariots, ships, lions, and horses; NarP_1,56.174 //
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Ārya, Śata-tārā, Vasu, and Uttara—
this group of nine suns is declared here to be situated in the upper face.
The auspicious rites for the consecration of a king, the elephant, and the banner;
as well as palaces, archways, gardens, ramparts, and so forth—all these are accomplished.
The asterisms Rohiṇī and those called the Uttarās are declared to be fixed; Sūra, Aśvinī, and Puṣya are swift;
and Dvidaivatya and Vahni are proclaimed to be common.
Vasva, Āditya, Vipuṣya, Viṣṇu, Bha, Carasaṃjñita,
Mṛdu, Indu, Mitra, Citrāntya, Ugra, Pūrvā, Maghā, and Trika.

The asterisms Mūla, Ārdrā, and Āśleṣā (the Lord of Serpents) are sharp, yielding results consistent with their own names; while Citrā, Āditya, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇa, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, Anurādhā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are mild.
The piercing of the ears for children is beneficial under the asterisms of Mṛgaśīrṣa, Jyeṣṭhā, Dhanus, Śravaṇa,
Puṣya, Āśleṣā, and the three beginning with Kṛttikā.
All elephant-related tasks should be performed during fixed signs,
and all horse-related tasks should be carried out, especially on Sundays.

One should never undertake a journey or return from one on the Citrā, Ārdrā, Rohiṇī, or the three Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā), nor on the new moon, the eighth, or the fourteenth lunar days, when it concerns cattle.
One should first perform the plowing with oxen under the asterisms Mṛdu, Dhruva, Kṣipra, Cara, Viśākhā, and Pitṛbha (Maghā), as well as under Mūlabha.
To destroy obstacles at the beginning of the rite, one should place three stars starting from the star occupied by the Sun;
three more in front for prosperity; and five on the left side for the sake of Lakṣmī.
In the trident-shaped [configuration], nine is for death; five is for prosperity and nourishment;
three is excellent for the wheel known as the plow.

Sowing seeds under the asterisms Mṛgaśīrṣa, Dhruva (Uttarās), Kṣipra (Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvabhādrapadā, and Revatī), and those belonging to the Pitṛs, Vāyu, and Vasus, as well as under the Samūla asterisms, yields an exceedingly excellent fruit.
If three asterisms from Rāhu’s asterism fall upon the head, there will be a loss of grain;
if three fall upon the neck, it leads to soot (ruin); and if twelve fall upon the belly, it results in prosperity.

One should contemplate the absence of stiffness in the tail, which strikes fear into the four classes of beings; and that there is fire at the navel, which is the fivefold [element] for the sowing of the seed. (NarP 1.56.188)

One should not perform the ritual bath for one who has recovered from illness on the fixed asterisms, nor on Aditi, Āśleṣā, the last [Revatī], the Pitṛs, or the Māruta asterisms; nor during the day, nor under the nakṣatras Śukra and Ārdrā.
The commencement of dancing is recommended under the three Uttaras, Maitra, Aindra, Vasu, Vāruṇa, Puṣya, Ārka, and Pauṣṇa asterisms.
Six constellations beginning with Puṣya are joined to the first half;
then twelve constellations beginning with Indrabha and nine beginning with Navabha are joined to the middle.
Then, for a couple joined in union for a parārdha, there is mutual delight;
the lowest [durations] are those of water, moisture, serpents, wind, fire, and the guardians of heaven.
The subsequent great stars (bṛhattārā), which are equal [in duration] and presided over by two deities, follow in sequence;
their measures in ghaṭikās are thirty, ninety-eight, and eighty-nine.
When the moon has risen in succession, it brings about results equal to the *argha* [offering];
those arising from the north are produced by the deities of the Horse-necked One (Aśvagrīva), the Moon, the Sacrificer (Indra), Nairṛta, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati).
The lunar mansions known as Pitṛ, Dvidaiva, and Vasu are called *kula*;
those presided over by Dhātṛ, Jyeṣṭhā, Aditi, Svātī, Pauṣṇa, Arka, and Hari are [the *yoni*]. NarP_1,56.195 //
The stars Ajāhi, Antya, Kābhaujaṅga, and those called Ākula are the non-kula (akula) stars;
the remaining stars are both kula and akula. Among them, within the kula stars...
If the king sets out when the asterisms known as Bhāni and Upakula are present, he will certainly obtain victory. (NarP 1.56.197)

Or there may be a conjunction or an equality between those two among the groups of *kula* and *akula* stars; if it occurs on a Sunday, Saturday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, and falls on an odd-numbered lunar day (*bhadrā*) and an odd-numbered asterism (*viṣamāṅghribha*).
The *tripuṣkara* configuration bestows threefold merit, while the *yamalāhibha* bestows twofold;
one should perform that [rite] for the destruction of those respective defects, or give three cows or their equivalent value.
If Puṣya is endowed with strength, even if it is pierced or conjoined with a malefic planet, one may give two [gifts] at Dvipuṣkara; there is no fault, even if it is situated in a tree.
Without the taking of hands (marriage), it always grants one's desires in all auspicious rites; [it is also auspicious] when the [year] is 3546 or 3547 [of the Śaka era].
The eyes, arms, arrows, bindus, arms, Vedas, fires, and the combinations; the Vedas, eyes, oceans, fires, hundreds, arms, eyes, and teeth, in sequence. (NarP 1.56.202)
The number of stars for each of the [lunar mansions] beginning with Aśvinī should be known individually;
those bright stars that are seen within their own group are the *yogatārakās*.
In the fire-altar (agni-dhiṣṇya) of Aśvinī, the tree is the Vṛṣa; in that of Bharaṇī, it is the Karaja;
in that of Kṛttikā, the tree is the Udumbara; and in that of Rohiṇī, the tree is the Jaṃbuka.
The *khadira* tree was born from Indubhā, and the black *plakṣa* tree arose from Raudrabhā;
the *vaṃśa* tree originated from Aditibhā, and the *pippala* tree was produced from Puṣyabhā.

The Nāga tree (Ficus religiosa) arises from the constellation Sarpa; the Vaṭa (Ficus indica) is born from Pitṛ; the Pālāśa (Butea monosperma) is produced from Bhaga; and the Akṣa (Terminalia bellirica) originates from Aryaman.
The ariṣṭa tree arises from the portion of the Sun; the śrīvṛkṣa tree originates from Tvaṣṭṛ;
the arjuna tree comes from Svāti and the Bull (Ursa Major); and the vikaṅkata tree arises from the dual-deity asterism (Aśvinī).
The Bakula tree is born from the asterism Maitra (Anurādhā), Viṣṭi is born from the asterism Paurandara (Jyeṣṭhā),
the Sarja tree is rooted in the asterism Mūla, and the Vañjula is born from the asterism Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj).
The jackfruit tree was born from Vaiśvabhāj, and the arka tree from Viṣṇubhā;
the śamī tree arose from Vasudhiṣṇya, and the kadamba tree was born from Vāruṇarkṣa.
From Ajā heśa the mango tree arose, and from Budhnya the picumandaka;
from the constellation Pauṣṇa the honey-tree [appeared]; thus the trees of the constellations are proclaimed.
In whichever lunar mansion the Lord of Śanaiścara (Saturn) resides, that corresponding constellation should be worshipped with great effort;
[the lords of the constellations are] Yama, Viśva, Indu, Dhātṛ, Jīva, and Niśākara.
Indra, Varuṇa, Vāsuki, Agni, Sūrya, Bhūmi, Rudra,
Kārttikeya, Pavana, Gaṇeśa, Rudra, Dhanada, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, and Ṣaḍānana.
Sāvitrī, Kamalā, Gaurī, the two Aśvins, the Pitṛs, Aditi, Vaidhṛti, Vyatīpāta, and both Mahāpātas are always [auspicious]. NarP_1,56.213 //
The first half of the Parigha yoga is censured for all undertakings;
for Viṣkambha and Vajra there are three [periods], and for Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa there are six.

In the case of a tiger-slaying [expedition] or a spear-attack, nine and five *nāḍīs* respectively are indeed censured; likewise, the asterisms of Aditi, Indu, Maghā, Aśvinī, Mūla, Anurādhā, and Puṣya [are to be avoided].
One should draw the various peaks of the letters in their proper sequence;
one line should extend upwards and thirteen lines should run horizontally.
In that regard, it is taught concerning the *ravārjūrika* wheel: one should place the lunar mansion (*bha*) at the head;
[this is done] for the Sun and Moon, which have mutually arrived at their respective positions through the division by the single rays.
The gaze of Ekārgala is indeed devoid of Abhijit;
it lasts for two ghaṭikās, excluding twelve vināḍīs.
The Yoga-prakaraṇa consists of twenty-seven sections in sequence:
Indra, Prajāpati, Mitra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Bhū, Hari, and the beloved of Hari (Lakṣmī).
Kīnāśa, Kali, Rudra, Tithyarddha, Īśa, and Bahirmarut—these six karaṇas, beginning with Bava and ending with Vaṇija, are auspicious. NarP_1,56.220 //
Whether they are limited or contrary, they are desired for auspicious purposes;
five are remembered for the face, one for the neck, and eleven for the chest.
There are four lines at the navel, six at the hips, and three at the channel called the tail;
loss of purpose occurs at the mouth, death at the throat, and poverty at the chest.
Insanity occurs at the hips, emission at the navel, and certain victory at the tail;
the others are stable in the middle, while the four-legged animals are in the middle.
The day-muhūrtas, Rudra, Ahi, Mitra, Pitṛ, Vasu, and Udarka; the Viśvedevas, Vidhātṛ, Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Agni, Vasu, and the Waters. 1,56.224.
Āryamā and Bhaga are to be known as the fifteen [deities];
as well as Īśa, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, Yama, and Vahni.
Dhātṛ, Indra, Aditi, Ijya, Viṣṇu, Arka, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Vāyu—
these constitute the fifteenth part of the day, and likewise according to the measure of the night.
The duration of a muhūrta consists of two ghaṭikās; [the lords of] the watches, the asterisms, and the equal lordships;
likewise Aryaman, the Rākṣasa and Brāhma [lords], those of the Pitṛs and Agni, and Abhijit.
The muhūrtas known as Rākṣasa, Brāhma, and Pitrya— occurring among Bharga, Āja, Aṃśu, and Āvali on the days of the week— should be avoided in auspicious rites.
Whatever action has been described in full for each of these constellations,
that same action— including journeys and other undertakings— should always be performed during the hour (muhūrta) presided over by its respective deity.
An earthquake occurs when [the moon] is in the seventh lunar mansion from the sun; lightning in the fifth;
cholera in the eighth; thunder in the tenth; and then lightning again in the eighteenth.
A meteor (ketu) appearing in the fifteenth [lunar mansion] is a staff (daṇḍa), while one in the nineteenth is a firebrand (ulkā);
that which is known as the fall of a thunderclap (nirghātapāta) should be recognized when it occurs in the fifth of the nine [mansion groups].
The Moon-killer, the Noose, the Thunderbolt, and the Encircler are to be known in their respective order, beginning from the twenty-first lunar mansion. (NarP 1,56.232)
One should not perform auspicious rites when the lunar mansions are conjoined with the Moon;
likewise, one should avoid all ancestral asterisms (pitryarkṣa) as well as those belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, and Pūṣan from the position of the Sun.
When the moon is joined with the hand (hasta) asterism in the poisonous (saviṣa) sub-divisions in successive order, and the lunar mansion is at that same [count],
this evil conjunction (duṣṭayoga) falls there.
In that [period] known as Caṇḍīśacaṇḍāyudha, one should not perform any auspicious rite;
by the count of their conjunction, there would be thirteen lunar days (tithis) and weekdays (vāras). (NarP 1.56.235)
This yoga, named Krakaca, is highly esteemed among auspicious conjunctions;
it occurs when the seventh lunar day falls on a Sunday, or the first lunar day on a Monday.
The conjunction of Saṃvarta should be known as the destroyer of auspicious karma;
likewise Ānanda, Kāladaṇḍa, Dhūmra, Dhātṛ, and Sudhākara. (NarP 1.56.237)
Dhvāṅkṣadhvaja, Śrīvatsa, Vajra, Mudgara, Chatraka,
Mitramānasa, Padma, Lumbaka, Utpāta, and Mṛtyu.
These [yogas] are, in order: Kāṇa, Siddhi, Śubha, Mṛtyu, Muśala, Antaka, Kujara, Rākṣasa, Vara, Sthairya, and Vardhamāna. (NarP 1.56.239)
Twenty-eight yogas that yield their own specific results have been declared; on Sunday they begin respectively from Aśvinī, and on Monday from Ārdrā.
From Āśleṣā comes [the result] for Mars; from Puṣya for Mercury; from Hastā for Jupiter;
from Anurādhā for Venus; and from Śatabhiṣaj for Saturn.
Hasta, Khāti, Mṛgaśiras, and Aśvinī are the asterisms for Mars;
Maitra (Anurādhā) for Mercury; Tiṣya (Puṣya) and Revatī for Jupiter;
Rohiṇī for Venus; and these are called the Siddhi-yogas on Saturday.
Nandā is [auspicious] for the Sun and Mars; Bhadrā is [auspicious] for Venus and the Moon.

When Jupiter is on Jayā and the Moon on Saumyā, when Riktā falls on Saturday and Pūrṇā on Sunday, these are not auspicious; likewise, Nandā on Friday, Bhadrā on Wednesday, and Jayā on Tuesday are not favorable.
Riktā occurs on a Saturday and Pūrṇā on a Thursday; these are called Siddhā.
On the eleventh lunar day there is a Monday, and on the twelfth there is a Sunday.
The sixth lunar day on a Thursday, the third on a Mercury, the eighth on a Venus,
the ninth on a Saturn, and the fifth on a Tuesday are proclaimed as the "burned" (dagdha) yogas.
On a Sunday in the asterism Bharaṇī, on a Monday in Citrā, on a Tuesday in Viśvabhū (Uttarāṣāḍhā), on a Wednesday in Śraviṣṭhā and Āryaman (Jyeṣṭhā), and on a Friday in Jyeṣṭhā; NarP_1,56.247 //
On a Saturday, Revatī destroys the planets and the birth asterism;
likewise, the four groups beginning with Viśākhā are destroyed respectively on Sundays and the other days of the week.
The siddhi-yogas known as utpāta, mṛtyu, and kāraṇa have been proclaimed;
however, those yogas arising from the lunar day (tithi) and weekday (vāra), or arising from the weekday and asterism (ṛkṣa), are not desired.
In the Hūṇa, Vaṅga, and Khasa countries, as well as in other lands, these [rivers] bestow exceedingly auspicious results:
Ghorā, Aṣṭākṣī, Mahodarī, Mandā, and likewise Mandākinī.
The mixed Rākṣasī [is worshipped] on Sundays and the other days of the week respectively,
[yielding results for] Śūdras, thieves, Vaiśyas, the Earth-goddess, kings, and cows, in that order.
And for all those not specifically mentioned, the [planets] beginning with Rāhu (Ghora) are recorded as being auspicious;
they destroy kings in the forenoon, Brahmins at midday, and Vaiśyas in the afternoon.
In the afternoon he [delights] the Śūdras; at dusk, the Piśācas;
at night, the nocturnal wanderers; and in the latter part of the night, the actors.

If the sun’s transit occurs at dawn or during the twilight for cowherds, or as a *liṅgin* (ascetic), it brings misfortune; if the transit of Aries occurs during the day, it bestows strife and discord.
At night there is incomparable abundance, while at the two twilights there is the destruction of rain.
The lion, tiger, boar, donkey, elephant, and buffalo;
the horse, ram, goat, bull, and those with feet as weapons—these are the mounts of the Karaṇas.
The *bhuśuṇḍī*, the mace, the sword, the staff, the arrow, the *vāsa*, the *tomara*, and the *maru*.
In his two hands, he bears spears, nooses, goads, and missiles;
and [he holds] food, milk-rice, alms-food, soup, milk, and curd.
Sweet food, molasses, honey, clarified butter, sugar, and oblations of grain are auspicious for the merchant when he is situated in the *bālava* *gocara*. NarP_1,56.258 //
When the sun is situated in Kaulava, Śakuna, Kiṃstughna,
Catuṣpāda, Tila, or Āga, it indeed causes a solar eclipse while sleeping.
Regarding the rain of Dharma, lifespan, and grain, the results are respectively equal, excellent, or lost;
likewise for weapons, vehicles, food, and whatever the nature of the people may be.
Those worlds shall attain security when they remain seated as if asleep;
[namely] Andhaka, who has dull consciousness, and Sulocana, who has middling consciousness.
The fourfold [transits] beginning with Rohiṇī are known as the *pāpīyāt* (evil) transits;
when the sun’s transit occurs in fixed signs (*sthirabha*), it should be known by the name *viṣṇupada*.
The six signs beginning with Aśvinī should be known as having two natures among the zodiacal signs;
the equinoxes of the sun's transit are to be known in Libra (Tulā) and Aquarius (Ghaṭa).
During the southern solstice, the first [sixteen] moments are auspicious;
during the northern solstice, the latter [sixteen]; and during the equinox, the sixteen moments are declared to be pure and meritorious.
The twilight (saṃdhyā) is measured at three nāḍīs from the moment the sun's disc begins to rise until it sets;
if it occurs in the east, west, south, or north, its merit belongs to the preceding or following day respectively.
Whatever kind of moon causes the sun's transit, a man obtains a corresponding result— whether auspicious or inauspicious— from that sign of the moon.
After the [solar] transit, the sun, having traversed as many degrees as there are until the solstitial transit of the sun,
then [occurs] from the transit into that zodiac sign.
Whether it be a transiting planet or a natal asterism situated on both sides [of the moon] at birth,
both are undesirable in rites such as vows and marriages, according to their respective order.
One should draw a wheel upon a sesame seed— consisting of three tridents and a triangle—
and having placed gold therein, one should offer it for the removal of defects.
The moon is strong by virtue of its strength in the *tārā* (lunar mansion), and the sun is strong by virtue of it;
likewise, the planets are more powerful when they are in transit (*saṃkrama*).
O Lord of Sages, if the Sun is auspicious in the third, eleventh, tenth, sixth, ninth, fifth, or fourth house from birth,
and is not conjoined with or aspected by the Sunless planets (Venus and Mercury), [the native does not suffer].
If the Moon is auspicious from the natal asterism and is situated in the seventh, first, tenth, sixth, third, or twelfth house from the ascendant,
it is not censured by the wise, provided it is not located in the eighth or ninth house as desired.
Mars is most excellent in the third, fourth, and sixth houses, provided he is not situated in the house of birth;
likewise, there is auspiciousness from medicine when Saturn, Mercury, and the Sun are positioned in the twelfth houses.
If one is not born under the eight *svāya* [nakṣatras], he becomes wise;
provided that the auspicious planets, excluding the Moon, occupy the houses from the third through the eighth.

Jupiter is most auspicious when situated in its own sign or its exaltation relative to the natal ascendant, provided it is not eclipsed; O lords of sages, it pierces [the horoscope] when placed in the twelfth, eighth, seventh, fourth, third, or ninth houses.
The son of Bhṛgu (Venus) is auspicious when situated in the birth sign, the fourth, the seventh, the eighth, the tenth, the eleventh, or the twelfth house,
provided he is not pierced by [malefics] occupying the eighth, seventh, first, tenth, first, sixth, or fifth houses.
Nothing auspicious is given when [the planet] is in its domain conjoined with a piercing (vedha);
therefore, having first examined the piercing, one should then declare what is auspicious or inauspicious.
By the application of the method of reversal, even a malefic planet may become a bringer of auspiciousness;
one that yields unfavorable results when aspected by a benefic becomes a giver of good fortune when aspected by a malefic.
Those two planets are fruitless when aspected by their own [sign] or by an enemy; likewise, one situated in its own sign of debilitation, or even in the domicile of its enemy.
Even when set, it would not fail to bestow auspicious or inauspicious results;
therefore, one should diligently perform propitiatory rites when the planets are situated in unfavorable positions.
Decline and prosperity depend upon the planets; therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship.
[Likewise, one should offer] gems such as the pearl, coral, and emerald.
Likewise, the puṣparāga, the vajra, the blue sapphire known as gomedaka,
and the vaidūrya should be worn in their respective order for the satisfaction of the Sun and the other [planets].
If the moon is auspicious on the first day of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), that fortnight brings him good fortune; the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is otherwise inauspicious.
In the bright fortnight, the moon is auspicious when situated in the second, ninth, or fifth houses,
provided it is not pierced by planets moving through the sky while occupying the twelfth, eighth, or fourth houses.
Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enemy, achiever, death,
friend, and supreme friend— these [houses] follow again and again from the house of birth.
The stars known as Janma, Tripañca, and Saptā give undesirable results;
[one should give] vegetables, jaggery, salt, sesame seeds, and gold respectively.
One should give this to a twice-born man for the destruction of undesirable results.
When the Tārā is powerful during the dark fortnight and the Moon is powerful during the bright fortnight—
these are the twelve states of the Moon, occurring in due order in each zodiac sign.
In undertakings such as journeys and marriages, these [planets] bestow results equal to their names.
Multiply the elapsed lunar mansion by sixty, add the ghaṭīs of that time, and divide by four; the remainder from the solar portion indicates the state [of the planet].
Exile, loss, death, victory, laughter, pleasure, joy, the enjoyment of the Śini clan, fever, trembling, and stability—these are the names corresponding to the syllables. (NarP 1,56.289)
The binding of turbans, the employment of fierce ministers, war, ornaments,
mines, and metallurgical works succeed when the Aries ascendant is present.

Auspicious rites, the construction of stable water reservoirs and houses, agriculture, trade, and the tending of livestock—all these succeed even when performed under an unfavorable lagna. (NarP 1,56.291)
In the *mithuna* [period] of the day, one should perform music, knowledge, arts, ornaments, battle, hearing the sacred texts, the mounting of elephants, consecrations, and so forth. (NarP 1.56.292)
During the rising of Cancer, one should construct ponds, wells, tanks, and other water-retaining structures, perform rites for prosperity, and engage in writing and painting. (NarP 1.56.293)
In a stable [ascendant], there is success in sugarcane, grain, trade, commerce, agriculture, service, and so forth; in Leo ascendant, daring deeds, battle, kings, and the like are accomplished.

Knowledge, arts, medicinal herbs, ritual acts, ornaments, moving and stationary objects, maidens, the marriage ceremony, and all auspicious rites for prosperity should be undertaken under the sign of Virgo.
Agriculture, trade, vehicles, cattle, marriage, vows, and so forth—all such activities, as well as those concerning weights and measures, belong to the scale (Tulā). NarP_1,56.296 //
All tasks requiring steady effort, service to the king, consecration ceremonies,
acts of thievery, and stable undertakings should be performed during the rising of Scorpio.
Vows, marriage, journeys, horses, elephants, the arts, crafts, and so forth—
whether mobile, stationary, or mixed— should be undertaken when the bow (Sagittarius) rises.

The binding and releasing of bows, the drawing of weapons, agriculture, cattle, horses, and so forth; as well as setting out on journeys and the acquisition of livestock, servants, and the like—these should be undertaken when Capricorn (makara) is rising.
Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, water-works, the arts, crafts, and so forth,
as well as the making of water-vessels, missiles, and weapons, should be undertaken when the pitcher (kalaśa) rises.
Observing vows, marriage, consecration water, the installation of deities, settling in a new home,
adorning oneself, preparing water-vessels, and the work of horses are auspicious when the ascendant is Pisces.
When the signs beginning with Aries are thus moistened and purified, success is achieved;
however, when they are aspected by malefic planets or conjoined with fierce ones, the result is indeed fierce.
The pairs of oxen (Taurus), Cancer, Virgo, the last of Libra (Libra itself), and those bearing Sagittarius (Sagittarius) are auspicious;
they are auspicious because of their being auspicious asterisms, while the others are inauspicious and are considered evil signs.
Through the observation of planetary conjunctions, a zodiac sign bears the results arising from those planets; deprived of both, it reverts to its own inherent nature.
In the beginning, it yields a full result; in the middle, it yields a middling result;
and at the end, it yields a trivial result—indeed, it is exactly thus for every ascendant.
In all cases, first one must consider the strength of the moon for the performer [of the rite];
then, when the moon is strong, the planets in the seventh house should be considered for their strength.
The moon is the support (ādhāra) and the other planets are the supported (ādheya);
by means of that which serves as the support, the supported is held within its circumference.
The Moon is auspicious, and all the planets bestow auspicious results;
however, if they are inauspicious, they yield inauspicious results—with the exception of the Lord of Wealth (Venus).
A planet situated in those degrees that have risen for the ascendant brings about the results arising from the ascendant;
one situated beyond the second house brings about the results of the second house. (NarP 1.56.309)
In this manner, one should likewise determine the remaining positions;
a lunar mansion endowed with all auspicious qualities is not obtained in just a few days.
A state where defects are few and virtues are abundant is always desired;
for even the Grandfather (Brahmā) strives to wipe away that time which is corrupted by defects.
Even if there is an excess of impurity or other defects,
you should nevertheless perform it on the new moon, the eighth, the sixth, the twelfth, and the first days of the lunar fortnight.

The first menstrual flow is inauspicious if it occurs during the forenoon of the *parigha* yoga, during *vyatīpāta* or *vaidhṛti*, at the twilights, during an eclipse, or under the *viṣṭi* karana. (NarP 1.56.313)

A woman who is sickly, one dear to her husband, one who is miserable, one who has sons, one who possesses enjoyments, and likewise one who is devoted to her husband and has beautiful hair—these correspond respectively to the days beginning with Sunday. (NarP 1,56.314)
The lunar mansions Yāmya, Āgneya, Raudra, Bhāgya, Yāhi, Dvīśa, Indrādi, and Upadviṣ are not beneficial; nor are the months of Madhu, Ūrja, Śuci, and Pauṣa.

Bhadrā, Saṃkrama, Nidrā, Rātri, and the eclipse of the moon and sun; likewise, a woman unfaithful to her husband, sinful enjoyments, an inauspicious asterism, and an inauspicious day [are all to be avoided]. (NarP 1.56.316)
A wise person should offer sesame seeds, clarified butter, and dūrvā grass one hundred and eight times with the Gāyatrī mantra;
he should also give gold, cows, and sesame seeds for the removal of all defects.
The first four nights must indeed be avoided, even by others;
likewise when the moon is situated in an odd sign or degree, and the ascendant is aspected by a masculine planet.
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder and remaining unclothed,
a man desiring a son should approach his wife on even lunar days, avoiding the asterisms of Puṣya, Mūla, Āśleṣā, and Maghā.
When the first pregnancy has become manifest, the *puṃsavana* rite should be performed in the third month, or in the second; and the *sīmantonnayana* should be done accordingly.
In the fourth, sixth, or eighth month, when the lord of that [month] is endowed with strength, and for the couple, the moon and the stars are possessed of power; NarP_1,56.321.
On a day that is not empty or a festival day, on Tuesdays, Thursdays, or Sundays—
excluding the days of sharp and mixed yogas— and when the Moon is in a masculine asterism or division, [one should perform the rite].

When the eighth house from the birth ascendant is pure, and the ascendant of those two is neither in the eighth nor the sixth house, being conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets and devoid of the aspect of malefic planets; NarP_1,56.323 //

When benefic planets are situated in the third, ninth, and tenth houses, and malefic planets are present in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, while the Moon is not in the eighth house or the other aforementioned positions; NarP_1,56.324 //
If even one of the malefic planets, being strong, occupies the twelfth, fifth, or eighth house from the ascendant, it kills either the woman or her fetus; of this there is no doubt.
At that very moment of birth, or even at the end of the period of impurity,
the birth-rite (jātakarman) must be performed for the infant, preceded by the worship of the ancestors.
At the end of the period of birth-impurity, the naming ceremony (nāmakarma) should be performed according to the custom of that family;
the name should be preceded by [an auspicious word] and be well-examined for its auspicious qualities.
When there is a lapse of time due to the affliction of the place, the season, and so forth,
that [rite] should be performed when Venus and Jupiter have not set, and during the northern solstice.
On a day when the stars are fixed, stable, soft, or swift, on an auspicious day,
and on a day endowed with the strength of the moon and the lunar mansions, [the rite should be performed] for the child and his father.
When the auspicious ascendant and auspicious division are present, and the eighth house is endowed with purity;
for men, this occurs in the sixth or eighth month, while for women, it is in the fifth.
Or, in the seventh month, the auspicious ceremony of first feeding with new rice may be performed;
however, one should avoid the Riktā, Dinakṣaya, Nandā, the twelfth, and the eighth lunar days.
On an auspicious day, having set aside other guests, one should partake of the prescribed food during a movable,
fixed, soft, or swift lunar mansion, or under an auspicious *naidhana* asterism.

In the tenth house, conjoined with a benefic, in an auspicious ascendant and an auspicious division, during its first half, and being either conjoined with or aspected by a benefic planet; NarP_1,56.333 //

The first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) is auspicious when malefic planets occupy the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, benefic planets occupy the angles (kendras), the fifth, and the ninth houses, and the Moon is situated in the twelfth, sixth, or eighth house.
In the third or fifth year from birth, the tonsure ceremony (caula) for children should be performed according to their own family tradition or the rules prescribed in their own Gṛhya-sūtra.
During the northern course of the sun, when neither Rāhu nor Ketu are eclipsed,
on days other than the parvan or the riktā tithis, and on the days of Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, and the Moon.
The asterisms of the two Aśvins, Āditi, Jupiter, the Moon, Indra, and Pūṣan are auspicious;
for the rite of tonsure (caulakarma), three asterisms each starting from Hasta and Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa) are likewise favorable.
The birth asterism brings good fortune for the tying of the turban, the tonsure ceremony, the first feeding of solid food, and the initiation ceremony; however, it is inauspicious for other rites.

In the eighth month, when it is joined with purity, in an auspicious lagna and an auspicious navāṃśa, when the moon is not in the eighth house from the birth [ascendant], and is free from the sixth, eighth, and twelfth houses; NarP_1,56.339.
When the auspicious planets are situated in the third, eleventh, tenth, or first houses, while the others are in the third, eleventh, sixth, or twelfth houses;
when it is smeared with unguents, during the two twilights, on a mountain, at night, after eating, or during battle—one should not [perform the rite].
The rite of shaving for kings is not performed on an elevated place, nor on an ornamented vehicle, nor on the ninth day;
rather, it occurs every fifth day.
An auspicious act may be performed even under the asterism Kṣurana, or at its rising;
likewise during a sacrifice by the command of a king or a Brahmin, or upon death, or for the release from bondage.
In marriage, shaving that brings desired results may be performed on any day, asterism, or lunar date;
for the sake of auspiciousness, the application of the razor should be done at the beginning of all auspicious rites.
On the ninth, the seventh, or even the fifth day, or on the third day under a seed-constellation (bījanakṣatra), during an auspicious weekday and at a favorable planetary rising; NarP_1,56.344.
Having properly adorned the houses with canopies, banners, and arches,
one should cause blessings to be recited by virtuous women and others for the sake of merit.
Accompanied by musical instruments, dancing, and other performances, he went to the northeastern direction;
having there taken up soft, middling, and sharp [objects], he returned once more.
Alternatively, one should fill a vessel made of clay or even of bamboo with water joined with many kinds of seeds and adorned with flowers.
For those born of the twice-born castes, the tying of the girdle (mauñjībandhana) occurs in the eighth year from conception or from birth;
for kings (kṣatriyas), in the eleventh year; and for vaiśyas, in the twelfth.
In the fifth year from birth, when he has become proficient in the Vedas and Shastras and is invested with the sacred thread, the illustrious Upanayana ceremony should be performed for him.
For a child, the life-force (jīva) that is weak and unoccupied is a bestower of auspiciousness;
the rite of investiture (upanayana) should be performed in the year as previously stated, but not in one that has not been so specified.
When Jupiter and Venus are visible and the lord of the lunar mansion (the Moon) is in the northern solstice,
Jupiter, Venus, Mars, and Mercury are the presiding deities of the Vedas in their respective order.
For the twice-born, the primary [periods for austerity] are autumn, summer, and spring;
however, their common [periods] occur out of sequence during the five months beginning with the month of Tapaḥ.
In the month of Phālguṇa, he was one who knew the dharma of his own family customs;
in Caitra, he was a knower of ritual procedure, wealthy, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
In Vaiśākha, one becomes wealthy; in Jyeṣṭha, one is an expert in the sciences of the Vedas and a knower of the ritual injunctions, endowed with strength and invested with the sacred thread.
In the bright fortnight, the second, third, fifth,
tenth, thirteenth, and seventh lunar days are likewise [auspicious] for the binding of the sacred thread.
The eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is the most excellent, the sixth and twelfth are middling,
while the other lunar days in the dark fortnight numbering two, three, or five are indeed highly censured.
For the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the asterisms are those of the three Dhīṣṇyas, the three Ārks, Jyeṣṭhā, Rudra (Ārdrā), the Ādityas (Pūrvā-phalgunī),
the three Viṣṇus (Śravaṇa), Aśvinī, Mitrā (Anurādhā), and the lotus-born (Puṣya).
The tenth from the birth asterism is the asterism of action (karma), the sixteenth is the asterism of the aggregate (saṃghāta),
the eighteenth is the asterism of origin (samudaya), and the twenty-third is the asterism of destruction (vināśana).

One should not perform auspicious rites during the two Mānasa constellations or the twenty-fifth asterism; however, the days of the teachers (Jupiter), Mercury, and Venus, as well as those of the Moon and Mars, are recommended.
The two middle watches of the day are indeed for the vow; the other two are considered censurable.
Having divided the day into three parts, one should perform rites dedicated to the gods during the first.
In the second [house], there is human activity; and in the third part, paternal activity.
If [the planet] is in its sign of debilitation, or in that same portion, or in the sign of an enemy, or in that same portion— ||| NarP_1,56.361 |||
If Jupiter or Mars is in the sign of its own lord, yet is devoid of digits (kalās) and good character,
or if it is situated in the house of its own enemy, or in the subdivision (aṃśa) thereof, then the observer of the vow [will suffer].
If the lord of the *śākha*, Jupiter, or Venus is situated in its exaltation, or in its own *navāṃśa*, or in its own sign, or in a [favorable] group of signs, one becomes a perpetrator of great sins.
If the lord of the ascendant, Jupiter, or Venus is situated in a quadrant or a trine,
one becomes exceedingly wealthy and a master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
When Jupiter, or the lord of the *śākha*, or Saturn has reached its highest point in the eighth house,
one who observes vows becomes pure and proficient in the Vedas and the Śāstras.
If Jupiter or Venus, or the lord of the ascendant, is situated in its own house, a friendly house, or its exaltation, or occupies its own navāṃśa,
the native will be endowed with learning and wealth.

The day of the week presided over by the branch-lord (*śākhādhipati*), the strength of the branch-lord for the child, and the ascendant (*lagna*) presided over by the branch-lord—this triad is difficult to obtain during a vow (*vrata*). (NarP 1.56.367)
Therefore, when the Moon is situated in a quadrant (varga) of Jupiter, the observer of vows becomes proficient in learning;
however, if it is in a quadrant of a malefic planet, he is poor and constantly miserable.
When the moon is situated in the Cancer sign during the Śravaṇa and other lunar mansions,
then the observer of the vow shall possess an abundance of Vedic scriptures, wealth, and grain.
When the ascendant is auspicious and in an auspicious division, and the eighth house is endowed with purity;
or when the eighth house from the ascendant is conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets.
When five planets, such as Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon, are strong and favorable;
or when four [planets] are endowed with strength through their positions and other factors and are conjoined with auspicious ones.
Beholding this [time] which is free from the twenty-one great defects,
all the zodiac signs are excellent when conjoined with or aspected by auspicious planets.
Those auspicious signs situated in auspicious navāṃśas should be accepted;
however, Cancer is never to be taken, even if it is aspected by or conjoined with an auspicious planet.
Therefore, the portions of the Gemini and Taurus signs, as well as the portions of Libra and Virgo, are auspicious;
when such a ninth-part (navāṃśa) has reached the ascendant, the vow is prescribed.

When the malefic planets are situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses—excluding the sixth, eighth, and twelfth—and when the benefic Moon is situated in a house other than the sixth, eighth, the ascendant, or the twelfth; NarP_1,56.375 //
Even if the Moon is situated in its own sign, if it occupies the ascendant for one observing a vow,
it does not make the child destitute, nor does it cause him to suffer from consumption in every respect.
When the Sun is in its full splendor in a quadrant, there is destruction of the ancestors for those observing vows;
however, a lagna free from the five defects is auspicious for the initiation ceremony (upanayana).

Except during the spring season, in the dark fortnight, during the seizing of the throat (galagraha), on days unfit for study, and during the Viṣṭi and Ṣaṣṭhī constellations, one does not deserve to perform the sacramental rite.
The four days beginning with the thirteenth, the three days beginning with the seventh, and the fourth are said to be auspicious; these eight are known as the *galagraha* (throat-seizers).
I shall now describe the binding of the *kṣurikā* for kings prior to the taking of their hand [in marriage],
during the months prescribed for wedding, in the bright fortnight, and while the sun has not yet set.

When Jupiter and Venus are in the ascendant, and Mars is endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars, on lunar days prescribed for the tying of the girdle (mauñjībandha), and on days other than Tuesday; NarP_1,56.381.

If the ninth-part (navāṃśaka) of the Moon is not occupied by the lord of the ascendant, and the Moon is pure in the eighth house, while the ascendant is free from the sixth, eighth, and twelfth houses; NarP_1,56.382 //

The girding on of the sword (kṣurikābandhana) should be performed after worshipping the gods and the ancestors, when the auspicious planets are situated in the third, eleventh, tenth, or first houses, and the others are in the third, eleventh, or sixth houses.
One should properly worship the kṣurikā in the presence of the deities;
thereafter, at an auspicious moment, one should fasten it to the waist, provided it possesses the required characteristics.
One should cut it according to the measurement of half its length as the width at the tip;
the resulting segments of that cut shall be the banners for the destruction of enemies.
In the smoke-colored [color], there is death; in the lion, victory; and in the dog, illness.
In the bull, there is the gain of wealth; in the donkey, one becomes exceedingly miserable.
One should measure an elephant with extreme joy, a crow with the destruction of wealth,
and a sword and dagger with pride, using one's own finger-breadths.
One should exclude eleven variations among the units of measurement (mānāṅgula);
the results for the remaining fingers shall be according to their respective order.
The gain of a son, the slaying of enemies, the acquisition of a woman, and auspicious travel; the loss of wealth, the increase of wealth, joy, success, victory, and praise.
If [the bird] is perched on a banner or the tip of a bull's horn, there is a wound in the east;
if on a lion or an elephant, it is in the middle part; but if on a dog or a crow, it is in the rear part.
Neither Dhūmra nor Gardabha ever occupy the final portion of a lunar mansion;
however, during the northern solstice, Śukra and Jīva may be seen occupying it.

For the twice-born who have returned from the house of their preceptor and are self-restrained, [the results are auspicious] during Citrā, Uttarā-phalgunī, Uttarā-āṣāḍhā, Puṣya, Svāti, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Anurādhā, Āśleṣā, and Rohiṇī.

On the days of the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and on the day of the ascendant's degree; and avoiding the first lunar day, the full and new moon parvas, the riktā tithis, the eighth day, and three days [before and after].
Having abandoned other duties on another day, one should perform the shaving for the return ceremony;
for among all stages of life, O best of Brahmins, this householder’s stage is indeed the highest.
Furthermore, happiness resides even in that virtuous woman;
for her, indeed, it is through the power of a favorable conjunction with one of pure character.

Having examined what was spoken by the Grandfather (Brahmā), I shall now declare the purity of the auspicious moment (lagna-śuddhi) for one who is seated comfortably on a holy day, endowed with the proper characteristics, and possessed of a clear mind.
Having prostrated like a deity, one should question the astrologer with devotion,
approaching him with palms full of betel, fruit, flowers, and other offerings.
If a malefic planet is situated in the seventh house from that [ascendant] and Mars is in the seventh from it,
the death of the couple should be predicted before eight years have passed.
If the Moon is situated in the ascendant and Mars is in the seventh house from it, the wise should know that the death of the husband will occur within eight years. (NarP 1.56.399)
If a malefic planet occupying the fifth house from the ascendant is aspected by an enemy and situated in its sign of debilitation,
the woman will undoubtedly have a dead son, or she will be a maiden or an unchaste woman.
Or if the Moon,
aspected by Jupiter, occupies the third, fifth, or seventh house from the ascendant, it establishes a union between the husband and wife.
If Libra, Taurus, or Cancer is situated in the ascendant and is conjoined with or aspected by Venus and the Moon,
then there will be the attainment of a maiden for the men who inquire.
When a female decan is present in a female navāṃśa and a dual sign has ascended,
and this is aspected by the Moon and Venus, then there will be the acquisition of a maiden.

In this manner, for women, the acquisition of a husband occurs when the ascendant (lagna) is a masculine sign and a masculine navāṃśaka, and the ascendant is aspected by masculine planets. ||| NarP_1,56.404 ||| 404 ||

When, during the dark fortnight, the sign from which the query-lagna (praśnalagna) begins is aspected by a malefic or situated in the eighth house, then there shall be no connection [with the desired outcome].
At the time of inquiry, auspiciousness arises for the couple through meritorious signs and omens; however, through these inauspicious ones, misfortune shall prevail on all sides.
On a day when the five limbs [of the lunar day] are pure, endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
or at the rising of the asterism of marriage, the bridegroom’s family should perform the formal selection of the maiden.
With ornaments, flowers, betel, fruits, perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, and so forth;
with white garments, songs, musical instruments, and words of blessing for the removal of obstacles.
The groom should cause [the rites] to be performed in the girl's house preceded by the syllable Om;
then her father should perform the giving away of her with affection. (NarP 1.56.409)
And one should give a beautiful maiden of younger age to a bridegroom who is endowed with noble lineage, good character, youth, beauty, wealth, and learning.

Having worshipped and supplicated the goddess Śacī, the refuge of virtues, who is the most beautiful woman in the three worlds and is arrayed in divine perfumes, garlands, and garments; (NarP 1.56.411)
Endowed with all the primary marks and adorned with every ornament,
she illuminated the quarters of the sky with her priceless garlands of jewels.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should pray to that maiden who is served day and night by thousands of playful women and who is of such a nature as described.
O Goddess Indrāṇī, salutations to you, the beloved wife of the Lord of Gods;
grant me good fortune, health, and the attainment of a son at my marriage.
For women, marriage brings happiness when it occurs in an even year from birth;
for men, it is the same in an odd year. By the reverse of this, there is no eating—that is, no sustenance—for them.
The months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha bestow auspicious results;
Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa are middling, while the others are indeed censured.
Never, from the time the sun enters Ārdrā until the end of Vaśa (Mūla),
should there be a marriage, the consecration of deities, the installation [of images], or the initiation ceremony.
Not when Venus or Jupiter has set, nor when those two are in their states of childhood or old age,
nor when Jupiter is situated in the sign of Leo, or even when he has entered a Leo decan.
Afterwards, Venus, having risen in the east, is a child for thirteen days;
Mercury is so for five days; Jupiter is a child for a fortnight in all respects.
As long as Hṛṣīkeśa is not awakened, there is no auspiciousness;
on the festival day of Vāsudeva, there is no other auspiciousness.
The marriage of a first-born son or daughter should not take place in the month of birth, under the birth asterism, nor even on the day of birth.

There should be no mutual marriage between the eldest daughter and the son of the eldest [brother]; nor should it take place in the month of Jyeṣṭha. If both are eldest-born, it is most excellent; otherwise, it is not.
After the occurrence of a portentous planetary conjunction (*utpāta-grahaṇa*), it is inauspicious for seven days during an eclipse of all the planets;
if not all are eclipsed, it is inauspicious for three days, as well as during the *tridyuspṛk* and *kṣaya* conjunctions.
If [the moon] is eclipsed three days prior, or if it is eclipsed at its rising,
or likewise during the twilight, then for seven days starting from midnight, [there will be no rain].
At the end of the month, one should avoid five days, as well as the *riktā* dates, the eighth day,
the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the *vaidhṛti* yoga, and the first half of the *parigha* yoga.

The taking of a wife's hand is desired when the asterisms of Pūṣan (Revatī), Bharaṇī, the three Uttarās, Anurādhā, Svātī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, and Maghā are not afflicted by their respective *mūla* stars.
In a marriage ceremony, the strength of the Jupiter and the Sun belonging to the couple must necessarily be considered;
if those two planets are weak, worship must be performed for them with great effort.

The strength arising from the *vedha* (piercing), that born of the eight-fold division (*aṣṭavarga*), and that born of form (*rūpa*)—each subsequent one possesses greater strength; the coarse [strength] arises from the path of the *gocara*. (NarP 1,56.428)
Having examined the strength of the moon and the stars, as well as the strength derived from the five limbs,
[one should know that] the lunar day (tithi) has one unit of strength, the day of the week (vāra) has two units, and the asterism (bha) has three units.
Yoga possesses four qualities, while the period known as half-tithi (tithyardha) possesses five;
