beyond that, the manahūrta is more powerful, and the ascendant (lagna) is even more powerful than that.
After that, the *horā* is powerful; after that, the *dreṣkāṇa* is powerful;
after that, the *navāṃśa* is powerful; and after that, the *dvādaśāṃśa* is powerful.
A third part [of the strength] is powerful; therefore, this relative strength and weakness must be examined.
All zodiac signs are auspicious for marriage when they are conjoined with or aspected by benefics.

If five planets, beginning with the Moon, the Sun, and Jupiter, are favorable to a particular zodiac sign, that ascendant bestows auspicious results; likewise, if even four [planets] are endowed with strength, it is so.
[One should choose a time] purified of the *jāmitra* [aspect] and free from the twenty-one great defects;
[herein follow] the names, forms, and results of those twenty-one defects.
I shall now explain this in brief; listen, Nārada, at this time.
The first fault proclaimed is the absence of the purity of the five limbs (pañcāṅga-śuddhi).
The purity of rising and setting, loss, the second solar transit, the third—the group of six malefics—Venus as the sixth, and Mars as the eighth. NarP_1,56.436 //

The junctions (gaṇḍānta), the scissors (kartarī), a planet situated in the sixth, eighth, twelfth, or first house, the eighth sign from the ascendant for both husband and wife, and likewise the fatal minutes (viṣaghaṭī). // NarP_1,56.437 //

The Durmuhūrta, the day-defect (vāradoṣa), the asterism of the Khārjūrika, the one with a broken foot, the asterism of an eclipse or a portent, an asterism pierced by a malefic, and one conjoined with a malefic.
The *kunavāṃśa*, the *mahāpāta*, and the *vaidhṛti* constitute the twenty-first [type of conjunction];
it is the union of the lunar day (*tithi*), the day of the week (*vāra*), the asterism (*ṛkṣa*), the yoga, and the *karaṇa*. // NarP_1,56.439 //
The purity of its five components is called the "purity of the five limbs" (pañcāṅga-śuddhi);
if there is a defect in any of these five limbs within a given lagna, that lagna is useless.
One should also abandon that which possesses five iṣṭas, like milk mixed with poison;
provided that the ascendant and its navāṃśa are both aspected by or conjoined with their respective lords.
Or, if the death of the bridegroom does not occur through mutual infidelity or by a virtuous friend, then the seventh and seventh rising signs from those two [positions] shall be so.
Thus, these two [planets] are not seen in conjunction at the time of the bride's marriage;
likewise, they should be avoided for seven days before and after the sun's transit (saṃkrānti).
In matters such as marriage and other ceremonies, sixteen nāḍīs each [are auspicious];
the sixfold group (ṣaḍvarga) is most excellent for bestowing auspiciousness in marriages, house-consecrations, and so forth.
When Venus is situated in the sixth house from the ascendant, it is called the defect known as Bhṛgu-ṣaṣṭha;
one should always avoid that ascendant, even if Venus is in its exaltation or conjoined with a benefic. (NarP 1.56.445)
Mars in the eighth house is a great defect;
however, if Mars is in its exaltation, one should not abandon a natal ascendant even if it is joined by the three benefics.

When the junction (*saṃdhi*) between the lunar days known as Pūrṇā and Anandā consists of two *nāḍīs*, it is a *gaṇḍānta* that brings death in rites such as birth, journeys, marriages, and vows. (NarP 1.56.447)
The interval between Cancer and Leo, Virgo and Sagittarius, and Pisces and Aries is known as Gaṇḍānta; it lasts for half a ghaṭikā and bestows death.

The junctions of the lunar mansions (*bhasandhi*) are the last quarters of Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Revatī, as well as the sixteenth and first quarters of the [following] asterisms; these are known as *gaṇḍānta*. NarP_1,56.449 //
And there is the formidable *saṃdhitritaya*, the great threefold *gaṇḍānta*, and the *ṛju* and *vakra* configurations of two malefic planets facing the ascendant. (NarP 1.56.450)
That should be known as the "scissors" (kartarī), specifically the "throat-scissors" of the couple;
one should completely avoid a lagna that is afflicted by the scissors configuration.
Even if [the Moon] is joined with benefic planets and endowed with all virtues,
if it is situated in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth house, the defect of the Ascendant known as its own name [occurs].
One should avoid the *tallagna* (the rising sign at the time of birth) in that [calculation], even if it is conjoined with Jupiter and Venus,
whether it is in its exaltation, its fall, in the sign of a friend, or in the sign of an enemy.
Even if endowed with all auspicious qualities, [a marriage] brings about the death of the couple when the Moon is conjoined with a planet; this is the defect known as *saṃgraha*.
One should never perform a marriage during that conjunction of planets known as *saṃgraha*;
if the moon is conjoined with the sun, poverty will clearly result.
If joined with Mars, there is death and disease; with Mercury, childlessness;
with Jupiter, misfortune; but with Venus, one has offspring.
If the Moon is conjoined with Rāhu, the son of the Sun, there is renunciation and the destruction of one's roots;
when conjoined with Ketu, there is constant suffering and poverty.
If the Moon is conjoined with malefic planets, the death of both husband and wife will occur;
however, if the Moon is conjoined with benefic planets, situated in its exaltation, or placed in a friendly sign, [the couple shall live].

The sign of the Sun’s southern course (dōṣāyana) as the ascendant is always for the welfare of the couple, provided it is situated in its own exaltation, its own sign, or even in the sign of a friend.
The Moon joined with a malefic planet causes the death of that couple; likewise, the eighth from the ascendant and the eighth sign itself [do so]. (NarP 1.56.460)
If that [planet] has also gone to the ascendant, it brings about the death of both husband and wife;
however, if that sign is conjoined with a benefic, or if the ascendant is conjoined with a benefic, [the result is otherwise].
One should diligently avoid the ascendant, its degrees, and their respective lords;
likewise, if the twelfth house from the couple's ascendant, or its sign, is situated in the ascendant.
There is a loss of wealth for those two from this; therefore, one should abandon the lord of that portion.
Furthermore, the rising of the birth-ascendant (janmarāśi) and the rising of the natal ascendant (janmalagna) are auspicious.
The place of their accumulation is the Lagna (Ascendant), which bestows ultimate auspiciousness; [the numbers] are five, five, four, and three, and six, five, four, and three. NarP_1,56.464 //
Fire and moon; form and the two Aśvins; desert and the goddesses; sky and arms; twice the goddesses; one’s own and Agni; zero and the two Aśvins; elephants and earths. (NarP 1.56.465)
The forms belonging to the side of Rūpa are fourteen: the sky (0), the eyes (2), the Vedas (4), and the moon (1);
the void (0), the moon (1), the Vedas (4), the moon (1), the six seasons (6), the stars (7), and the arms of the Vedas (4).
From the asterism Aśvinī onwards, in sequence, there are: zero Dastras, zero Candras, one Pūrṇacandra, zero Gatas, six Indravas, six Tarkacandras, two Vedapakṣas, and three Kharāmas. (NarP 1.56.467)
The four ghaṭikās following these are known as "poison" (viṣa);
one should avoid the poison-nāḍīs in rites such as marriage and other ceremonies.

Those muhūrtas which are censured on the days of the week beginning with the Sun (Sunday) should be avoided for marriages and other ceremonies, even if they possess hundreds of thousands of auspicious qualities.
Those days which are designated as having the defect of being "blocked" (nihitāvāra) on Sundays and so forth in succession,
even if endowed with all auspicious qualities, must be avoided for every auspicious rite.
One should avoid that lagna which is like a single bolt on a door, even if it is joined by Venus and Jupiter;
it is like milk mixed with poison. (NarP 1.56.471)
The three seasons following a planetary eclipse or portent should be avoided for auspicious rites;
for as long as the moon has not passed over that constellation and released it, it is like burnt wood.

Among auspicious rites, one should avoid a lunar mansion that is pierced by a planet, conjoined with a malefic, or entirely occupied by one; likewise, one should avoid the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) when it is mixed with a drop of liquor.
An inauspicious lunar mansion is not rendered entirely inauspicious merely by being pierced by auspicious planets in a single quarter;
likewise, a mansion that is pierced or joined by malefic planets is not auspicious in its entirety.
The ninth-parts (navāṃśas) of Libra, Gemini, and Virgo, together with the latter half of Sagittarius—these nine parts are indeed auspicious; the parts of Taurus are not so.

Even those final degrees are givers of auspicious results if they are designated as *vargottama*; other ninth-parts (navāṃśas) are not to be accepted, for they are called "bad ninth-parts" (*kunavāṃśaka*).
One should avoid that day on which there is a *mahāpāta*, even if it possesses all auspicious qualities, as well as the *navāṃśa* and the ascendant (*lagna*) [of that time]. NarP_1,56.477 //
For even that which is endowed with all auspicious qualities brings death to a couple;
likewise, lightning, mist, and rain, though not explicitly mentioned as defects, may cause minor misfortune.
Halos around the sun, rainbows, thundering clouds, the *lattā*, *upagraha*, and *pāta* phenomena, and the lunar day known as *māsadagdha*. NarP_1,56.479 //
The signs are designated as "burnt," "conjoined," "blind," "deaf," "lame," and so forth;
their systematic arrangement is now being established.

These occurrences of lightning, mist, and rain that arise out of season certainly lead to misfortune during an auspicious rite; however, when they occur at the proper time, they lead to no harm at all.
If Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury is situated in a quadrant (kendram), even a single one of them undoubtedly removes the entire accumulation of defects; of this there is no doubt.
One should draw five lines extending horizontally and five extending upwards, with two lines each at the two corners;
then, in the second corner of Śambhu, one should place the fire-pitcher upon the wheel.
Elsewhere it is said that when a single planet pierces a sign with its line of victory,
the planets beginning with the Sun, positioned in front of or behind it, cast a *lattā* upon that sign which contains the day’s asterism.
The asterisms beginning with Arka (Aśvinī) possess the qualities of their respective limbs; they are numbered as five, five, eight, and nine.
Starting from the asterism of the Sun (Aśvinī), these are Āśleṣā, Maghā, Svāti, Anurādhā, and Śravaṇa.

Having calculated the number of days from the Aśvinī constellation, one should avoid a lunar mansion that is afflicted by a fall (pāta) in the Saurāṣṭra or Sālva country, as well as a mansion that has been "struck" (lattita).
Falling in the lands of Kaliṅga and Vaṅga does not bring auspiciousness; however, in Bāhlīka, the land of the Kurus, and other such regions, there is no fault.
In the Middle Country, lunar days that are burnt by the month, as well as those ascendants that are burnt, should be avoided; however, these are not observed in other regions.
The sixth, the eighth, and the twelfth houses, as well as the signs devoid of planets, are to be avoided for those from Gauḍa and Mālava; in other countries, they are not considered reprehensible.
It is never possible to completely wipe away that which is corrupted by defects;
therefore, one should accept even a base metal if it has few flaws and an abundance of virtues.
Thus, at an auspicious moment, one should properly arrange for the mutual gazing of the couple;
[the pavilion] should be four cubits high and four cubits square on all sides.
It had four very smooth pillars on its left side that were slightly curved,
and it was adorned with pavilions and stairs on all four sides.
Sloping toward the northeast, it was adorned with pillars of plantain trees, with swans, parrots, and other birds,
and with variegated water-jars and various arches and sprouts.
Adorned with collections of flowers of the erotic sentiment and with pigments, it was made delightful by the divine and beautiful words of Brahmin blessings, which were like auspicious goddesses.
The couple should thus ascend the auspicious altar of their own fire, which brings delight to the heart with instrumental music, dance, song, and other such performances.
The mountain-heap of the zodiac signs is eightfold; the signs of the sweet lunar mansions, the lords of the signs, their birth-animals, their names, and their seasons bestow sons and grandsons.

The joining of hands (marriage) between a husband and wife when they are in different signs but within the same constellation is excellent; it is middling when their signs are different but their constellations are the same. NarP_1,56.497 //
Indeed, a marriage between those in the same asterism or the same zodiac sign brings about the loss of life;
moreover, a marriage with a woman whose natal asterism falls within the first nine asterisms from her own is highly censured as being far from desirable for the woman.
In the second [navaka] it is middling, in the third it is excellent, and in the ninth it is most auspicious for men.
The three stars beginning with Dhātṛ, followed by Yāmya and Māheśa, are the first [navaka].
Thus, among the host of mortals, the supreme host of immortals should be known;
[they are] Hari, Āditya, Arka, Vāyu, Antya, Mitra, Aśvin, Ijya, Indu, and Tāraka.
Then the hosts of Rākṣasas, Pitṛs, Tvaṣṭṛs, Dvidaivas, Agnis, Indras, and Tārakas, together with Vasus, Vāris, Īśas, Mūlas, Ahitas, and Tārakas [arose].
If the birth asterisms of the husband and wife belong to the same group, there is manifold affection;
if they belong to the groups of gods and mortals, it is middling; if they belong to the groups of demons, it results in their death.
Death occurs in the sixth and eighth [houses]; childlessness in the fifth and ninth;
poverty in the second and twelfth; and in the other houses, there is the highest affection between husband and wife.
If the sole lord [of the seventh house] is in the state of friendship, the marriage is auspicious;
however, it is never so when [the lord] is in the second, twelfth, trine, or sixth and eighth houses.
Horses, elephants, rams, snakes, and cobras; goats, sheep, and mice; rats, cows, buffaloes, tigers, black leopards, and two kinds of deer. NarP_1,56.505 //
Dogs, baboons, tawny-colored animals, monkeys, lions, horses,
lions, and elephants with tusks like those of a cow are the origins of the lunar mansions starting from Aśvinī.
A dog and a female deer, a brown snake and a ram, a monkey and a lion,
an elephant and a cow, a rat and a cat, and a buffalo and a horse— these constitute hostile pairs.
The Jhaṣa, Āli, and Karkaṭa are Brāhmaṇas; those following them are Kṣatriyas and so forth.
When a female sign is joined with a male sign or varga, it is inauspicious according to the degree of disparity.
For a girl born under the signs of Taurus, Aries, and Pisces, [the auspicious times] occur respectively from the third, second, and first lunar mansions,
during the third, fourth, and fifth joints of the lunar day.
One should calculate by number that death occurs within a single nāḍī, not on both sides;
[these apply to] the Prājāpatya, Brāhma, Daiva, and Ārṣa forms of marriage.
However, at the time specified, four [mantras] that bestow fruit should always be performed;
they are known as those of the Gandharvas, Asuras, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas.
The fourth sign from the ascendant and the seventh from the rising asterism constitute the *godhūlika* period;
both of these are conducive to sons and grandsons in marriage.
Among the easterners and the Kalingas, Godhūlika is remembered as the foremost;
however, Abhijit is the foremost in all regions, for it destroys all defects.
When the sun has reached the meridian, there is a moment called Abhijit;
it destroys all defects just as the wielder of the Pināka bow destroyed Tripura.
After the son's wedding, the daughter's marriage should not take place within three menstrual periods;
nor should there be a religious vow for either of them during this time, as one auspicious ceremony supersedes another.
If the marriages of sisters born of the same parents take place within six months of one another,
undoubtedly, within three years, one of them will become a widow.

A marriage in reverse order must never be performed; one should not give two daughters to a single man, nor should two sisters born of the same mother be given to two brothers born of the same father.
A marriage never takes place in this manner, nor do two shavings of the head occur at once;
one born by day [portends death for] the father, but likewise one born at night for the mother.
One who is born under the *gaṇḍa* yoga kills oneself at the two twilights; there is no reversal of this.
A son or a daughter born under *mūla* certainly kills the father-in-law.
One born in the last quarter of that [nakṣatra] does not do so, nor does one born in the first quarter of Āśleṣā;
those born in the last quarter of Jyeṣṭhā kill their elder brother, but a girl does not.

A girl born under the asterisms of Bālika, Ambu, or Mūla does not harm her mother or father; one born under Indrī harms her husband’s elder brother, while one born under Dvidaiva harms her husband’s younger brother.
Starting from the day of the wedding, the entry of the bride should take place on the sixth or eighth day for prosperity,
or on the tenth or seventh day.

Even when Venus is excessively bright, a marriage journey is auspicious provided that two years have passed since birth, and the days of the natal ascendant and the day of birth itself have been avoided.
Bestowing prosperity and establishing all the gods during the northern solstice,
while Atri and the gods— the former gods— are being beheld.
It is auspicious during the months beginning with Māgha, specifically in the five months starting from Caitra,
as well as during the first eight days of both the bright and dark fortnights.
On whichever day a particular deity resides, that deity’s [mantra] is used;
[the deities for the remaining days] follow in order from the second of the first pair and from the third of the second triad, starting from the fifth day.

On the tenth day and so forth, during the four [lunar months], especially on the full moon day, under the three stars beginning with Tryuttarā (Jyeṣṭhā), the Āditya (Pūrvā-phalgunī), the Moon (Mṛgaśiras), the last three Hastas (Hasta, Citrā, Svāti), and when Jupiter is in the asterism; NarP_1,56.527.
It is also auspicious when the Moon is in the signs of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Anurādhā, or Dhaniṣṭhā;
on days other than Tuesday; and when the Sun is bestowing strength upon the doer.
On an auspicious day in the forenoon, endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
at a favorable lagna and in a favorable division, provided that the rising sign does not bring death to the performer.
All the zodiac signs are excellent when conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets;
when the ascendant is auspicious in the *pañcāṣṭaka* configuration, and when it is purified and free from the *naidhana* yoga.
The Moon, Sun, Mars, Rāhu, Ketu, and Saturn, when situated in the ascendant, bestow death upon the doer; others [the remaining planets] bestow wealth, grain, and happiness.
In the second house, malefic planets do not grant what is desired, whereas benefics and the Moon bestow wealth.
In the third house, all the planets grant happiness through sons and grandsons.
In the fourth house, gentle planets bestow happiness while cruel planets cause suffering;
in the fifth house, cruel planets cause exhaustion while gentle planets grant the joy of children.
In the sixth house, benefics will cause enemies, while malefics bring about the destruction of enemies;
in the seventh house, malefics cause disease, whereas gentle planets bestow auspicious results.
All planets situated in the eighth house from the ascendant bestow death upon the doer;
those in the ninth house are sinful and destructive, while gentle ones are auspicious and grant blessings.
Malefics situated in the tenth house cause suffering, while benefics and the Moon bestow fame;
all planets situated in the eleventh house grant abundant gains.
Planets situated in the house of expenditure (the twelfth house) always cause great expense;
like those devoid of wealth who ruin their patron, or like priests devoid of mantras who ruin the sacrificer.
Those devoid of auspicious marks do not attain prosperity; there is no enemy equal to instability.
If the lagna possesses more excellent qualities and its defects are very slight, [it is auspicious].
The installation of deities there bestows the fulfillment of the desired aims of the performer; this applies, in brief, to temples, villages, houses, and so forth. (NarP 1.56.539)
First, one should examine the field by its scent, color, and taste;
its fragrance should be like that of honey, flowers, sourness, and meat, in the order beginning with the Brahmins.
White, red, green, and black in sequence;
sweet, pungent, bitter, and astringent in order.
A boat facing northeast brings ultimate prosperity to men;
if it faces other directions, it brings them perpetual and extreme ruin.
Having dug a trench one *aratni* deep, one should fill it therein;
if [the soil] exceeds [the depth], there is extreme prosperity; if it is deficient, there is loss; if it is equal, there is equality.
Likewise, having performed that at nightfall, one should fill it with water;
if the water is seen to have increased by morning, there will be prosperity, but if it has decreased, there will be loss.
Having thus correctly examined a field endowed with these characteristics,
one should draw a level mandala in its center for the purpose of determining the directions.
Having fixed a gnomon twelve finger-breadths long, one should observe the direction there;
once the field has been made square and purified by the six divisions.
And along the path of the lines, one should construct a very beautiful enclosure wall,
even though there are [other] dimensions in the four directions starting from the east.
There shall be eight doors in each direction in due order;
and their fruits, according to the clockwise sequence, are as follows.
There is loss, the attainment of the wealth of liberation, honor from kings, and a great forest;
there is extreme thievery, excessive anger, and fear in the direction of the Lord of Śacī.
In the southern direction, there is destruction, bondage, fear, the attainment of wealth, the increase of riches,
endlessness, the fear of disease, and a lack of strength.
In the west [of the asterism], there is loss of sons, increase of enemies, attainment of fortune, arrival of wealth, good fortune, extreme misfortune, suffering, and grief. (NarP 1.56.551)
Loss of wife, lack of vitality, loss of grain and the arrival of wealth, prosperity, increase, fear of the month, and disease [occur] in the direction of the Moon. (NarP 1,56.552)
In this manner, one should install a door in a house, rising twice as high as the width of the doorway, either on the western or the southern side.
One should prepare the ground within the enclosure wall so that it consists of eighty-one squares;
in the center, within nine squares, is the station of Brahmā, which is highly esteemed.
If the thirty-two parts surrounding the area equal to the wall are occupied by the Piśāca portion at the commencement of the house, it brings about suffering, grief, and fear.
The remaining directions, when established in the construction, bestow sons, grandsons, and wealth;
these are the channels (śirās) which are the lines of the site arising from the cardinal and intermediate points.
One should recognize that wherever there is a collection of channels belonging to the portions of Brahmā and the portions of the Piśācas, those are the vital junctions (*marmasaṃdhi*) of the site.

The vital points (marmas) and the joints are not desired even when the house is otherwise well-situated; likewise, the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, Māgha, Śrāvaṇa, and Kārttika [are auspicious].
The months [beginning with Caitra] are conducive to the construction of a house, bestowing sons, health, and wealth,
corresponding respectively to the directions starting from the east within the sections beginning with the letter 'a'.
The ass, horse, monkey, dog, goat, sheep, elephant, and hare—these are the sources of the groups of directions; the fifth from one's own group is the enemy.
One should place the class of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in front and the practitioner (sādhaka) behind;
if they are reversed, it leads to his destruction. When the practitioner is between the debtor and the creditor, it is auspicious.

Starting from the asterism of the practitioner (sādhaka) and continuing up to the asterism of the object to be accomplished (sādhya), one should divide that fourfold total by seven; the remainder is then the wealth of the practitioner.
The product of the width and length of the house is called the *pada*.
From that [total], the numbers for the asterism (*nakṣatra*), day of the week (*vāra*), and the divisions (*aṃśa*) of wealth and non-wealth are derived in sequence.
A house with an excess of wealth leads to prosperity; one with an excess of debt is inauspicious.
An odd number of pillars brings about the destruction of good fortune, while an even number leads to poverty.
In the third lunar mansion there is the destruction of wealth; in the fifth, further loss;
and in the seventh, indeed, the destruction of one's very self occurs from the husband.
Twice twelve (twenty-four) is for the one without wealth; the trine (nine) is for the one without sons;
the sixth and eighth houses belong to death; others hold that the auspicious ones reside in the wives' house (the seventh).
The days and divisions of the Sun and Mars bring fear of fire;
other planetary days and divisions grant the fulfillment of all desires and aims.
In the three-month periods beginning with Nabhasya and so forth, respectively, one should lie down facing east, north, west, and south, turning to the left side in a clockwise direction.
The male spirit of the site (vāstupumān), called Cara and Mahodara, moves about in this manner;
in whichever direction the male spirit of the site faces, one should construct the house facing that same direction.
A house with its entrance facing the opposite direction brings about disease, grief, and fear;
however, this defect does not exist for those whose houses face the east.
One should place a small vessel for livelihood, filled with gold dust, grain, and moss, into a pit one cubit deep in the middle of the house for the purpose of consecration.
The navel is half a finger-breadth in extent; three finger-breadths above that is the belly.
One should place a ritual peg (śaṅku) there, which increases one's sons and grandsons.

The measurement of the abdomen for the Brahmins and the other castes is twenty-four, twenty-three, twenty, sixteen, and twelve finger-breadths respectively; it should be adorned with gold, garments, and other ornaments. (NarP 1.56.573)
The yoke-mechanism should be made from trees such as *khadira*, *arjuna*,
and *śāla*, or from *raktacandana*, *pālāśa*, *raktaśāna*, and *viśāla*.
Having divided the bamboo into three parts, one should then [make] a square,
then an octagon, and as the third, an eight-sided piece that is soft and free of blemishes.
Having thus prepared the ground endowed with these characteristics on an auspicious day,
it should be marked out upon the surface of the earth with the thread of the "Purification of the Six Groups."

On days that are soft, stable, swift, and free from the *rikta* and *amā* tithis; when the sun is not present in a movable ascendant; and when the malefic planets are not situated in the eighth house.
In the Naidhana fire, joined with purification, at an auspicious and powerful lagna and in a favorable navamsha,
when the lagna is aspected by or conjoined with benefics, one should plant the sacrificial stake.
With the sounds of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) proclamations, musical instruments, and virtuous women and the like,
[the rite is performed] when auspicious planets are situated in their own signs, exaltations, triplicities, or trines, while others are in the third, eleventh, or sixth houses.

When the Moon is in the eighth or sixth house from the ascendant's navāṃśa, after first performing worship to the astrologer, there are houses with one, two, three, four, seven, or ten rooms. NarP_1,56.580 //
Furthermore, those six types of halls are each of ten kinds:
Dhruva, Dhānya, Jaya, Nanda, Khara, Kānta, and Manorama.
Sumukha, Durmukha, Krūra, Śatru, Svarṇaprada, Kṣaya, Ākranda, the one named Vipula, Vijaya, and the sixteenth house. NarP_1,56.582 //
One should count the houses in this manner according to the variations of their arrangement;
having placed a short syllable beneath a long one, one should set them down as before, starting from the top.
Afterwards, one should fill [the space] with long syllables; this is the rule for all short syllables.
One should construct an *alinda* at the short position, proceeding clockwise from the door of the house.
In the porticoes of the east and other directions, there are sixteen varieties of houses;
the bathhouse is in the eastern direction, and the kitchen is in the south-eastern direction.
In the south is the bedchamber, in the southwest the library,
in the west the dining hall, and in the northwest the storehouse for grain and wine.
In the north is the temple of the gods; in the northeast is the milk-house;
and there should be a bed, a privy, an armory, a place for those skilled in weapons, and a dining hall that is an abode of auspiciousness.
Grain, women, enjoyments, wealth, and the abodes of amorous pleasure.
The construction of their houses, beginning from the northeast (īśānī) in sequence, is auspicious.
These weapons should each be placed in their own positions within their respective directions:
the banner, smoke, the lion, the dog, the bull, the donkey, and the elephants.
These eight, beginning with Dhvāṅkṣa, are the guardians of the directions in order;
they are known as Plakṣa, Udumbara, Cūta, Nimba, and Vibhītaka.
Those trees that bear thorns, milky sap, or are of the *aśvattha* or *kapittha* species, as well as those known as *agasti*, *siṃdhuvāra*, and *tintiḍīka*, are censured.
In the western and southern directions from the front of the house, the pillars supporting the house should be equal in height; they are auspicious when equal and not so when unequal.
The height of the wall should be neither too high nor too low, according to one's preference; one should consider this for all structures, such as houses and the like, upon their rooftops.

The eightfold measurement of houses and so forth is traditionally taught as follows: Pāñcāla, Māna, Vaideha, Kaurava, and Kujñjaka; [along with] Gṛhaśrāva, which is considered the eighth. NarP_1,56.594 //
Māgadha, Śūrasena, Gāndhāra, and Avanti are recorded;
that which is called their height has a width equal to one-fourth of that [measurement].
And from the Pāñcālas and Mātulas onwards, all the measures beginning with the Vaideha should be understood in their respective order according to their progressive increase.
Beyond this, the measurement of Pañcāla is common to all;
the measurement of Avanti is for Brahmins, and that of Gāndhāra is for Kṣatriyas.

For Vaiśyas, the water for rinsing should be drawn from a well, while for Brāhmaṇas and the others, it should be drawn from successively higher sources; this applies as prescribed to houses of two or three stories.
Or on the banner-staff of camel and elephant stables, or on an elephant;
and on the banners of cattle-pens or of other stables, or on an elephant.

I shall describe the ritual for the worship of the site (vāstupūjā) at the time of entering a new house, concerning the doors, beds, seats, food, and banners, as well as those with the lion and bull banners.
One should draw lines one cubit long, ten to the east and ten to the north;
in the center of the house, upon the rice, there shall be eighty-one squares.
One should draw forty-five deities who are about to be described;
thirty-two are to be worshipped on the outside, while thirteen are situated within.
I shall now describe their locations and names in sequence:
these thirty-two gods are situated outside, starting from the northeast corner.
Kṛpīṭayoni, Parjanya, Jayanta, Pākaśāsana,
Sūrya, Śaśin, Mṛga, Ākāśa, Vāyu, Pūṣan, and Nairṛti.
Gṛhākṣata, Daṇḍadhara, Gāndharva, Bhṛgurājaka,
Mṛga, and Pitṛgaṇādhiśa— these are the ones called the Dauvārikas.
Sāma, Sūrya, Aditi, and Diti—these thirty-two gods;
then the four situated in the corners beginning with Īśāna, located near them.
Āpaḥ, Sāvitra, Ghasa, Jaya, and Rudra—
these are recorded as being situated one space apart from Brahmā, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise around him.
Aryaman, Savitṛ, Bimbavivartaka, Vaktrudhādhipa, Mitra, Rājayakṣman, and likewise the one named Pṛthvīdhara.
Āpavatsa is the eighth; these are the forty-five gods:
Āpa, Āpavatsa, Parjanya, Agni, and Diti, in sequence.
And this same group of directions is thus [arranged] completely in the corners;
in their midst are twenty external ones, and they are always two-footed.
Āryamā, Vivasvān, Mitra, and the one called Pṛthvīdhara—
these four are recorded as having three feet, situated around Brahmā in the cardinal directions.

One who knows the ritual of the site (vāstu) should likewise worship Brahmā and the gods of one, two, or three feet with the Vāstu-mantra, using dūrvā grass, curd, unbroken rice (akṣata), and other offerings.
Or, with a Brahma-mantra, one should cause a pair of white garments to be offered,
as well as all the ritual services beginning with the invocation, in their proper sequence.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) consisting of three kinds of food along with musical instruments;
then the performer should offer betel-leaf and pray to the Vastu-puruṣa.
O Vāstupuruṣa, homage be to you, O Lord who delights in resting upon the earth!
Always make my home prosperous with wealth, grain, and other riches.
Having prayed thus, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the worshipper according to one's ability,
and in his presence, provide food for the Brahmins according to one's means.
The man who performs the ritual worship of the site (vāstu) correctly according to this procedure shall obtain health, the birth of a son, wealth, and grain.
He who enters a new house without having performed the worship of the site-deity (vāstupūjā) encounters various diseases, afflictions, and every kind of calamity.
One should never enter a house that is without a door, uncovered, or where offerings have not been made; for such a place is indeed a mine of calamities.
Furthermore, I shall duly explain that journey for kings and others so that their desired fruits may be accomplished, provided they have correctly understood their own birth [horoscopes].
For men whose births are unknown, the attainment of results is like the markings of a wood-boring insect;
yet for them as well, the emergence of results occurs through the occasion of the arising of a question.
A journey on the sixth, eighth, twelfth, or on the new moon, full moon, or the empty (fourth) lunar days leads to poverty and ruin;
likewise, a journey on the first day of the bright fortnight results in destitution and decay.

Journeying under the asterisms of Maitra (Anurādhā), Āditya (Punarvasu), Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Arka (Puṣya), Antya (Revatī), Aśvin (Aśvinī), Hā (Śravaṇa), Iti (Abhijit), Tiṣya (Puṣya), Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā), Uḍu (Uttarāphalgunī), and Ṛkṣa (Uttarāṣāḍhā)— provided they are not the seventh, fifth, third, or first— bestows the desired fruits of one’s journey.
One should not travel toward the east on the day of the new moon; toward the south when Jupiter is present;
toward the west on the days of Venus and the Sun; nor toward the north on the days of Mercury and Mars.
Indra, Agni, the four-faced Brahmā, and Aryaman are the constellations in the east;
at all the gates are the tridents, as well as Mitra, Arka, Bṛhaspati, and Aśvinī.
In sequence, the asterisms belonging to the directions and gates are derived from the seven-times-seven [forty-nine] constellations.
One should cross the *parigha* yoga, but not the *daṇḍa*, nor when the fire and wind are moving toward one's direction.
The southeast is indeed [known] by the sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇya) of the eastern quarter, and the intermediate directions in the same way;
furthermore, the zodiacal signs beginning with Aries are assigned to the quarters in successive order again and again.
When the Lord of the Quarter is situated on the forehead [of the ascendant], there is no returning for the traveler;
the Sun, situated in the ascendant, is on the forehead of the traveler in the eastern direction.
Venus, even when in the twelfth or eleventh house, is situated on the forehead of the traveler in the southeast;
Mars, situated in the tenth house from either the ascendant or the [natal] sign, is likewise situated on the forehead.
Rāhu is situated on the forehead in the southwest when occupying the ninth or eighth house from the ascendant;
Saturn is situated on the forehead in the west when occupying the seventh house from the ascendant.
The sixth [digit] and the moon in the fifth house are in the northwest and on the forehead;
the fourth-positioned Mercury is in the north and on the forehead.
If the vital breath (jīva) is located in two or three places and has reached the forehead in the northeast,
a man who desires to live should abandon the forehead and depart.

If a planet moving in retrograde is situated in the ascendant at the time of a king's departure on a journey, it brings about his defeat; the same applies even if that planetary division (varga) occupies the ascendant.
One should set out when the conjunction of the sun and the moon is favorable and bestows auspiciousness;
in its absence, one may travel by day or night, otherwise there will be the death of the patient.
When Venus is retrograde, there is loss of one's purpose; when it is in opposition (pratiśukra), there is defeat.
Indeed, the planets have no power to remove the evil caused by a retrograde or opposed Venus.
The Vāsiṣṭhas, Kāśyapeyas, Ātreyas, Bhāradvājas, and Gautamas—
among these five lineages, no one is found who is averse to Śukra.
In a single village, at a wedding, during a famine, in a royal conflict,
during an agitation among the twice-born, or during a disturbance involving the king, there is no such thing as an unfavorable Venus (pratiśukra).

Venus, when situated in its sign of debilitation, in an enemy's house, retrograde, or defeated, brings about the defeat of the traveler; however, if it is situated in its own or exaltation sign, it bestows victory.
If the traveler enters the ascendant of Svāṣṭra (Vṛścika), his own natal sign, or his sign of exaltation, or even the eighth house from the sign of an enemy,
or the sign occupied by the lord of those [houses], there is no doubt that death will come to him.
If the lords of the birth ascendant and the eighth house are situated as mutual friends,
the defects arising from the birth sign and the eighth lunar mansion are destroyed by their influence.
Even a dual-natured sign, if aspected by or conjoined with a malefic planet, causes destruction;
it is not desired in a journey when it is a fixed sign at its rising, unless it is itself conjoined with or aspected by a benefic.
During the five asterisms beginning with Ārdrā, one should collect grass and wood;
however, one should not travel toward the southern direction, nor prepare a bed, nor perform the protection of the house.
If [the planets] are in the ascendant at birth, or in the natal sign, or in the sign of the lord of those two,
or in the kendras (angular houses) from those two signs, there shall be the destruction of the enemy for the traveler.
When the head-ascendant (śīrṣodaya) is situated in the ascendant, or when the directional ascendant (diglagna) is also in the ascendant,
or if a benefic varga is in the ascendant, then there is the destruction of the traveler's enemies.
When the ascendant is the rising sign of an enemy’s birth or the eighth house from one’s own birth sign,
or when the lord of either of those two signs is situated in the ascendant, the traveler shall experience the destruction of his enemies.
A crooked path occurs when the ascendant is Pisces, or even when the Pisces portion is rising;
it is censured for all journeys. So too is the ascendant of Aquarius or the Aquarius portion.
The sign occupied by water or its own water-portion brings auspiciousness to Aquarius;
likewise, the first house, the second house, and the vehicle of Sagittarius are known as the mantra.
The path of the enemy, as well as life-force, that which is designated as mental activity,
attainment, and non-attainment— these twelve are the states arising from manifestation.
The cruel Sun and Mars destroy the group of the three acquisitions and the dispositions;
for gentle planets do not engage in such destruction, nor do they nourish the enemy except in specific cases.
Venus does not nourish the body when it has set, nor does the Moon nourish the body when it is in conjunction with death;
this applies to all those traveling in every direction, provided they avoid traveling toward the southern quarter.
This conjunction of the Abhijit moment bestows the attainment of desired fruits;
it yields results even on a day devoid of the purity of the five astrological limbs (pañcāṅga).
I shall now describe those various yogas for journeys from this and that source,
for the attainment of results depends upon the ascendant of the journey for kings and upon the lunar mansion for Brahmins.
For others, [the result occurs] by the power of a moment; for a thief, it is known through omens. Indeed, a yoga is formed by even one of Venus, Mercury, or Jupiter occupying a quadrant or a trine.
If there is *adhiyoga* with two [planets] and *yogādhiyoga* with three,
there will be safety for those traveling during a *yoga*, and victory during an *adhiyoga*.
Through yoga and higher yoga, there is security, as well as the prosperity of victory,
when the Moon, Saturn, and Sun are situated in the houses of business and the enemy.
For a king who has gone to battle, the Goddess of Victory is certain when Venus,
the Sun, Mercury, Saturn, or Mars occupy the ascendant, the seventh house, the third, or the sixth house.
When Jupiter is in the eighth house, the enemy host perishes in fire;
when he is in the fourth house, it dissolves in poison, provided he is joined by other planets situated in the second or eleventh houses.
When Venus is in the ascendant, the Sun is in the eleventh house, and the Moon is situated in the fourth house, the enemy army of the departed king is led to the abode of Yama.
The king goes forth and slays his enemies like a lion a herd of elephants,
when Venus is situated in its exaltation in the ascendant and the Moon is in its exaltation in the eleventh house.
If the benefics are situated in trines or angles and the malefics are in the third, eleventh, or sixth houses, Keśava destroys the enemies whose bodies are unharmed, just as he destroyed Pūtanā.
If the Sun, Jupiter, and Moon go to the sixth, eighth, or twelfth houses from the ascendant, misfortune approaches that person like a woman going to meet her lover.
In his presence, the enemy host was as unstable as the friendship of a villain;
yet, if there were powerful and auspicious Mandāra trees upon the triple-edged swords, [the enemy would not prevail].
During the expedition of that king, the territory of his enemies will come into his hand,
provided that Jupiter is in its own exaltation in the ascendant and the Moon is in the eleventh house.
The king has gone forth to slay his enemies, just as the wielder of the Pināka bow destroyed Tripura,
when Venus is situated in the ascendant at its rising and Jupiter is in the eleventh house.
The king goes forth and slays his enemies, just as Kumāra slew Tāraka,
when Venus is situated in the ascendant, or in a quadrant, or in a trine, while Jupiter is present.
The enemy king, having gone forth, consumes [the foe] like a fire with black trails consuming a forest;
provided Mercury is in its own sign, in a quadrant, or in a favorable asterism or secondary asterism.
Kings wither their enemies as the rays of the sun dry up a lake in summer,
when Venus is situated in a trine or a quadrant, or when the Moon or the Sun is in the eleventh house.
Indeed, when a king has gone forth while Kāla is situated in its own sign, auspicious, and occupying a trine, he destroys his enemies just as the sun dispels the darkness.
The king destroys his enemies like fire consumes a heap of straw;
when the moon is in its own sign and Jupiter is in a quadrant, the mantra accompanied by the *praṇava* has been attained.
Just as the five-syllabled mantra destroys all enemies and sins, so too does the king destroy all enemies when Venus is in Vargottama and situated in this very same ascendant.

Just as the remembrance of Hari destroys heaps of sins, so does the king destroy his enemies when the Moon has gone to a benefic quadrant or trine and is situated in its *vargottama* division. // NarP_1,56.671 //
Just as a mountain-splitter destroys mountains along with their kin, so does one destroy kings of the same lineage;
furthermore, when Jupiter or Venus is in a friendly sign, or situated in a quadrant or a trine.
The king who has gone forth slays his enemies, just as Garuḍa slays serpents,
when [the planet] is situated in a benefic trine and has reached its Vargottama state.
A king destroys his enemies just as the Bhāgīrathī destroys the wicked;
for those kings who go forth to conquer their foes, there are methods known by the name of "kings."
The fire of anger is extinguished by the teardrops of the wives of his enemies;
on the tenth day of the waning moon, when strength has diminished, she is known as Vijayā.
For those who go there, there is victory and no defeat;
for the mind's disposition is more important than omens, auspicious signs, and the like.
Therefore, for the wise, the arousal of the mind is the cause of the fruit through diligent effort,
[whether it concerns] festivals, initiations, marriages, consecrations, ritual purification, or birth-impurity.
A mortal who desires to live should not undertake a journey while these are incomplete:
a fight between a buffalo and a rat, or the distress caused by a quarrel with one's wife.

The king should not proceed if there is a mishap with his garments or other items, nor if he is angry, nor if harsh words have been spoken; likewise, he should not go when there is food with ghee, food made of sesame paste, fish, or rice-pudding with ghee.
Having eaten in the sequence beginning with the east, the king conquers his enemies;
[the favorable omens are] a quiver, supreme rice-porridge, sour gruel, milk, and curd. (NarP 1.56.680)

Having eaten milk and rice mixed with sesame on Sunday and the subsequent days in sequence, one should consume groats, sesame-rice, curd, honey, clarified butter, and milk [on the following days]. (NarP 1.56.681)
The meat of deer, its essence, milk-rice, the flesh of birds and deer,
the meat of hares, rice of the sixty-day variety, priyaṅgu, and cakes.
The flesh of various birds, tortoise, porcupine, iguana, and hare;
sacrificial food (haviṣya), kṛśara-rice, mung-bean rice, and barley flour. NarP_1,56.683 //

Having eaten fish-rice, various kinds of rice, and curd-rice in succession from the Dāsrabha constellation, one travels by means of royal elephants, horses, chariots, and men, and conquers his enemies.
Having offered oblations of sesame seeds into the fire, the king should worship the lords of the directions;
then, having prostrated before the gods and the brahmins, he should proceed with their blessings.
With whatever colors, garlands, perfumes, and so forth [are appropriate], one should [worship] Indra according to the ritual rules with that mantra—
Indra mounted upon Airāvata, resplendent together with Śacī.
Vajrapāṇi, golden-hued and adorned with divine ornaments,
having seven hands, seven tongues, and six faces, and mounted upon a ram.
Svāhāpriya [visualizes] Yama, who is red in color, holding a *sruk* and *sruva* ladles as weapons, armed with a staff, possessing a red bear, and mounted upon a buffalo.
Dark-complexioned, accompanied by those of red hue, with an upward-facing face and auspicious,
he is blue, bearing a sword and a shield, and slaying with his claws— Nirṛti.
With hair standing erect, three-eyed, possessed of a long neck, all-pervading,
holding a serpent-noose, yellow in color, and having a sea-monster as his vehicle.
[He saw] Varuṇa, the Lord of Kālikā, adorned with jewel ornaments,
who is the very form of the life-breath of living beings, possessing two arms and holding a staff in his hand.
One should worship Vāyu, the lord of Añjanī, mounted upon a black antelope;
he has two arms, is golden-hued, and holds a water-pot in his hand while riding a horse.
Kubera, the lord of Citralekhā, the leader of the Yakṣas and Gandharvas;
the wielder of the Pināka bow, mounted upon his bull, the unsurpassed husband of Gaurī.
One should likewise personally observe the king, who is white in complexion, moon-crested, and wears a serpent as his sacred thread, when he is not on a military expedition.
The conclusion of the work consists of the parasol, the banner, weapons, missiles, and vehicles;
it includes the departure from one's own place to another location, as well as two hundred staffs.
Having set out, he himself went for forty or twelve days;
no other person should stay in one place for more than seven or six days.
If lightning, thunder, or rain occurs at an improper time, the king should wait for five nights before proceeding further toward another auspicious conjunction.
During the three types of portents, one should not travel for seven nights;
likewise, one should avoid the cries of a cat, a wall, a jackal, a crow, and a pigeon.

The flight to the left is auspicious for those with voices like the jhañjhā-bird, the bhūka, the peacock, and the cow; the flight to the right is auspicious for the yellow wagtail, the bharadvāja, and the pigeon.
Leaving aside the blue jay, four-footed animals on the left are considered auspicious;
however, at the time of departure, being gazed upon by a lizard while leaving aside a black object is inauspicious.
The mention of boars, rabbits, and iguanas is auspicious for snakes;
however, the mention of monkeys and bears is certainly not desired, as it causes the loss of sight and brings about an irreversible calamity.
The peacock, goat, mongoose, blue jay, and pigeon are auspicious when merely seen during a journey; however, all of these are inauspicious when encountered upon entering a place.
If a corpse is seen that is free from the smell of raw meat, there will be success on the journey;
however, a corpse accompanied by weeping at the time of entry likewise bestows a corpse.
Nor with those who have fallen from their caste, eunuchs, ascetics with matted hair, the intoxicated, those who have vomited medicine, and so forth;
nor with those smeared [with oil], fat, bones, hides, charcoal, wood, or those afflicted by disease.
[One should not travel] with jaggery, cotton, salt, an enemy, an inquiry, grass, or serpents;
nor with a barren woman, a hunchback, one wearing saffron robes, one with disheveled hair, or one who is hungry.
At the time of departure, if naked people are seen, success does not arise;
nor do blazing fires, sons, horses, royal thrones, cities, or women [portend it].
The king [should offer] perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, umbrellas, chowries, and swings;
as well as foodstuffs, sugarcane, fruits, clay, cooked rice, honey, clarified butter, curd, cows, and goats.
Wine, meat, garments washed with nectar, conch shells, and the bull-emblem;
virtuous women, auspicious jars, jeweled water-pots, cows, and twice-born men.
The sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, war-drums, bells, lutes, and the like,
as well as the auspicious chanting of the Vedas, bring success to the endeavors of those who travel.
Having first seen an inauspicious omen, the traveler should remember his chosen deity; then, having performed worship of the Brahmins at the second [crossroads], he should turn back.
A sneeze in any direction is not desired; a sneeze from a cow brings about death.
That which is performed by children, the elderly, the sick, or those afflicted by exhaustion is fruitless.
One should avoid another's wife, the property of the twice-born, or that of the gods; there, one should seek out elephants, horses, and [other] beasts of burden.
Having reached an enemy city, one should not kill women or those who are perpetually unarmed.
The entry into a new house should be performed during the northern solstice,
having first conducted the worship of Vāstu and the offering of oblations on the preceding day.
An entry during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha is auspicious;
it should be known as mediocre during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Kārttika.

In the asterisms of Śaśin (Mṛgaśiras), Jyeṣṭhā, and Antya (Revatī), as well as Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), Mitra (Anurādhā), and the fixed constellations, an expedition is auspicious; it is also auspicious when Jupiter and Venus are visible.
On a Sunday free from the sounds of discord, and on lunar days excluding the *rikta* and the new moon (*amā*),
entry— whether by day or by night— is a bringer of auspiciousness.
On an auspicious day in the forenoon, endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
in a fixed zodiacal sign and a fixed degree, and when the eighth house is pure and conjoined with purification.

When the benefics are situated in the trines and quadrants, while the others are in the third, eleventh, and sixth houses, and when the Moon is not located in the ascendant, the twelfth, the eighth, or the sixth house; NarP_1,56.718 //
If the natal sign of the querent is the ascendant at the time of entry, or if it is in a house of exaltation from those two, there will be prosperity;
if it is in another sign, there will be sorrow and poverty.

Having made the house beautiful and delightful, and having performed the rites with auspicious sounds according to the rules, the wise man should enter while keeping the sun to his left and holding a golden water-pot before him.
If the Moon has entered the rainy season, or even if it is situated in a watery sign,
or if it is in a quadrant during the bright fortnight and aspected by benefics, there will be excessive rain.
If the Moon is in [the sign of] Taurus, endowed with all such qualities, there will soon be little rain during the rainy season when it is aspected by malefic planets.
If the Moon during the rainy season occupies seven white signs and is aspected by benefics,
or if it is situated in the seventh, the trines, or the seventh house from Saturn, it will cause prosperity.
When Venus causes immediate rain while situated near Mercury,
and the Sun is positioned between those two, there shall be a destruction of rain.

When Bhṛgu is situated in the five asterisms beginning with Maghā, there will be rain in the east; when he is in the three asterisms beginning with Svāti, there will be rain in the west. If the opposite occurs, there will be no rain.
If the planets are situated near the sun either in front of it or behind it, they then produce rain; provided they are not moving in a retrograde direction.
If Venus is situated on the left side it brings rain, but if it goes to the south,
there will be rain during the sun's rising and setting at its entry into Ārdrā.
If there is growth of crops during the two twilights, all people will be prosperous;
if it occurs at night, there will be little rain and grain will be priceless; if there is no rain, there will be an abundance of crops.
There is no doubt that at sunrise the [obstacle] will be shattered;
when the Moon, Jupiter, Mercury, or Venus is in a quadrant or the eleventh house, fear perishes.
The sun, having entered Pūrvāṣāḍhā and being surrounded by clouds,
rains daily and visibly from Ārdrā until Mṛgaśīrṣa.
If there is rain during the asterism of Puṣya, it will not rain for ten subsequent constellations;
likewise, if Mars is in Leo, there is rain, and if he is not in Leo, it is the same in Cancer.
If, at the rising of the maiden (Kṛttikā), the clouds break forth, there will always be excellent rain;
Ahirbudhnya is the first constellation for sowing, and Revatī is for subsequent sowing.
Bharaṇī causes the destruction of all crops, while Aśvinī leads to the ruin of everything;
this occurs when Venus stands in the seventh lunar mansion from Jupiter and moves westward.
Then, during the rainy season when the moon is devoid of strength, there shall be a profuse and excessive downpour of rain,
accompanied by a halo around the moon extending as far as the seventh constellation.
Then there will be a rain accompanied by the croaking of frogs filled with lightning,
when Maghā is situated seven degrees above the zenith and its tail is bent downward.
If cats standing on the right side fall down while scratching the ground with their claws during a conjunction involving iron, then rain will occur before long.
In the streets, there will be embankments built by children to cause rain;
rows of ants will be broken, and glow-worms will appear in great numbers.
The climbing of trees and the like by serpents, as well as their delight [in such things], are indicators of drought;
likewise, when at the time of sunrise or sunset the sun or the moon appears discolored.
If there is excessive wind and then excessive rain,
then this earth rests upon the nine limbs of the tortoise facing east.
Having divided it into nine sections, one should draw the mandalas clockwise;
the inner altars and the five-fold movement—this is its navel-mandala.
The regions arising from the east—Māgadha and Lāṭa—constitute its face;
the regions known as Strīliṅga and Kirāta constitute its arms.
Avantī, Draviḍa, and Bhillā are the regions of its side-mandala;
Gauḍa, Kaiṅkaṇa, Śālva, Āndhra, and Pauṇḍra are the regions of its foot-mandala.
Sindhuka, Kāśi, Mahārāṣṭra, and Saurāṣṭra constitute the circle of the tail;
Pulinda, Cīna, Yavana, and Gurjara constitute the circle of the feet.
Kuru, Kaśmīra, Mādreyaka, and Matsya constitute the region of the sides; Khaśa, Aṅga, Vaṅga, Bāhlīka, and Kāmboja constitute the region of the hands. (NarP 1.56.744)

One should sequentially assign the three asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā to each of the nine limbs, starting from the navel; [the body] is afflicted by evils through the malefic planets and becomes auspicious through the benefic ones.
Where the deities dance, fall, and blaze forth;
where they suddenly weep, sing, perspire, and laugh.
Vomiting fire, smoke, fat, blood, milk, and water,
they stand with their faces turned downward and move from place to place.
For such transformations as these are seen even in statues:
the city of the Gandharvas and the appearance of stars during the day. (NarP 1.56.748)
The falling of great meteors, the raining down of wood, grass, and blood, the appearance of smoke from the body in the direction [of the sky], and earthquakes by day and by night. NarP_1,56.749 //
And sparks without fire, and a blaze without fuel; a rainbow at night, a frog on a mountain peak, and a white crow. 56.750.
Sparks are seen [issuing] from the bodies of cows, elephants, horses, and camels;
furthermore, creatures with two or three heads are born into various wombs.
In the morning, four suns appeared simultaneously, scorching the earth;
there was a gathering of people in the village of Jambūka, and comets were seen.
If crows are seen in a state of agitation at night and pigeons during the day, or if trees are seen flowering and bearing fruit out of season; NarP_1,56.753.
Therefore, the cutting down of that [tree] must be performed there; from that, peace is attained by the wise.
Such and other great portents are many, and they bring about the destruction of one's dwelling.
Some grant death, while others bring fear from enemies;
from the middle [of the year] come danger, fame, death, loss, renown, happiness, and unhappiness.
O best of the twice-born, in all such portents as these— including [omens of] sovereign power, loss of wealth, and honey-covered Valmika— [one should perform the rites].
"One should diligently perform an auspicious rite of pacification according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa.
Thus, O Brahmin, this science of astrology has been explained to you in brief.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed science of prosody (Chandaḥśāstra).
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the second quarter of the glorious *Bṛhannala-pūrvabhāga-bṛhad-upākhyāna*.
Sanandana said:
"Metre is said to be of two kinds: Vedic and worldly."
Furthermore, that [language] is again of two kinds, distinguished by its prosodic measures (mātrā) and phonemes (varṇa).

O twice-born one, the two syllables *ma* and *ya*, the two *ta*s, the two *bha*s, and the heavy (*guru*) and light (*laghu*) syllables are declared by those expert in the science of prosody to be the causes in meter.
The *magana* is said to have all [its syllables] light; the *yagana* is remembered as having the first [syllable] light;
the *ragana* has the middle [syllable] light; and the *sagana* is considered to have the final [syllable] light.

O Sage, the *tagaṇa* is known to have a short syllable at the end; the *ja-gaṇa*, beginning with *bha*, has a short syllable in the middle; and the *nagaṇa* is said to consist of three short syllables. These are the three groups of syllables.
The groups [of consonants] are said to be fourfold, with five [vowels] beginning with 'ā' considered as 'ārya';
likewise, a conjunct, a visarga, and an anusvāra followed by a short vowel [are also considered heavy].
A short vowel is said to become long when followed by a conjunct consonant (go), while a long vowel is considered short before a single consonant (lo).
A quarter of a verse is called a *pāda*, and the pause (*viccheda*) is termed a *yati*.
O Nārada, even-metre, half-even metre, and uneven metre are also [defined]:
that which has identical characteristics in all four quarters is called even (sama).
In the first triad [of feet], the second and fourth are equal, while the third is half-equal;
that whose characteristic is thus divided across its four feet is indeed called *viṣama* (irregular).
Beginning with a single syllable and increasing by one letter at a time,
each verse-quarter (pāda) is distinct, continuing up to twenty-six syllables.
Following that, the Daṇḍakas beginning with Caṇḍavṛṣṭi are prescribed;
listen to the definitions of the verses according to their increasing number of three and six feet.
The *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, *bṛhatī*, and *paṅkti* meters are said to be *uktā*, *atyuktā*, *madhyā*, *pratiṣṭhā*, and another preceded by *supratiṣṭhā*. NarP_1,57.11 //
The Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and likewise the Atijagatī are considered [metres];
the Śakvarī preceded by 'Ati' and the Aṣṭi and Atyaṣṭi are recorded thereafter.
Dhṛti, Vidhṛti, Kṛti, Prakṛti, Ākṛti,
Vikṛti, Saṃkṛti, as well as Atikṛti and Utkṛti.

These are the names of the meters, derived from their divisions according to the *prastāra* method: having placed a light syllable (*laghu*) beneath the first heavy syllable (*guru*) in a foot that is entirely composed of heavy syllables; 57.14.
Just as above, so one should also place the remainder at the beginning while proceeding forward;
this is declared to be the expansion (prastāra) until all [the syllables] are light.
If the half-measure is even and lacks a *la*, it shall be a *la*; if it is odd, that same [syllable] is followed by an ascending [consonant].
Having doubled the indicated [values] and added the first [unit], one should sum them together with those positions where a *la* resides.

"Having performed the sprinklings (sekas), state their number," so say those who know the ancient lore; [they are] the vowels, the sprinklings arising from the meters, situated in upper and lower positions.
One should arrange them one by one in ascending order;
then, starting from the penultimate position, one should proceed downward, discarding one by one from above.

In this manner, beginning from the first syllable of the guru, one performs the operation of marking single, double, and so forth; when the collection of marks is combined with their respective numerical values, the total count is obtained. (NarP 1.57.19)
The sum of the indicated figures, increased by one, produces this number;
indeed, that same number doubled and diminished by one is proclaimed by the wise as the "path" (adhvan).
Thus, this brief definition of the meters has been told;
now one should proceed to the names of the various divisions as stated in the *Prastāra*.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "A Brief Description of Prosody," in the second quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Nārada said:
In connection with the discussion on the learned reciters (*anūcāna*), [I shall describe] all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*).
I have heard [these teachings] from the lotus of your mouth, both in brief and in detail.
"O high-minded one, relate in detail the birth of Śuka.
Sanandana said:
"It is said that in ancient times, on a peak of Mount Meru, there was an expanse of *karṇikāra* forests."
The great god dwelt there, surrounded by terrestrial hosts of spirits;
and the goddess, the daughter of the king of mountains, was also present there in ancient times.
There the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana performed divine asceticism,
having entered his own self through yoga and being devoted to the practice of yoga.
Maintaining his vows, that best of sages performed austerities for the sake of a son, [directing them] toward fire,
earth, wind, and the atmosphere on all sides.
"May my son be esteemed for his vigor"—
with this very resolve, he [attained] that which is difficult to obtain by those who have not mastered their selves.
Having undertaken supreme austerity, the lord chose the Lord of the Gods;
indeed, he remained there for a hundred years subsisting on air alone.
There, all the brahman-sages as well as the divine sages were propitiating Mahādeva, the multiformed Lord of Umā.
The world-protectors and the Sādhyas, together with the eight Vasus,
as well as the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the sun and moon.
Viśvāvasu was the Gandharva, and there were hosts of Siddhas and Apsarases;
there, Rudra Mahādeva [offered] a beautiful seat made of Karṇikāra flowers.
Wearing a garland, he shone like the autumnal moon in that divine and delightful forest, crowded with gods and celestial rishis.
Vyāsa, established in the supreme yoga and striving for the sake of his son,
neither lost his complexion nor did any exhaustion arise in him.
That became like a marvel to all the three worlds;
and his matted locks, through their brilliance, resembled the crests of fire.
O Nārada, by such asceticism and devotion, he of immeasurable splendor was seen blazing with light as he remained absorbed in yoga.
Maheśvara, with a serene soul, formed a thought in his mind;
and the Blessed Lord Tryambaka spoke to him, as if smiling.
Just as fire, just as wind, just as earth, just as water,
and just as space, so shall your son become pure.
Sharing in his very being, possessing his intellect, having him as his soul, and taking refuge in him,
he shall attain through his splendor the three worlds and absolute glory.
Having thus obtained the boon, the divine Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī,
then took the fire-drill wood and churned it with the desire to produce fire.
Then, O Brahmin, the venerable sage beheld an Apsaras named Ghṛtācī, who was bearing a supreme form by her own splendor.
O Lord of Sages, upon seeing that apsaras in that forest, the venerable Vyāsa was suddenly deluded by desire. (NarP 1.58.20)
Then, having made Vyāsa’s mind agitated by desire,
the most beautiful Ghṛtācī approached him, having transformed herself into a female parrot.
Having seen that Apsaras, whose beauty was incomparable,
he was pursued by the king of love with an arrow that pierced all his limbs.
But though that sage Vyāsa strove with great effort to restrain his heart's desire, he was unable to control his mind which had already gone forth.
And because of the beauty of Ghṛtācī, who was to be cultivated [by him],
she captivated the sage even as he was striving with effort to restrain himself, out of his desire to achieve this [ascetic goal].
In the forest itself, his semen suddenly fell;
as that semen was being churned within her, Śuka, a man of great asceticism, was born.
The supreme seer and great yogi, born from the womb of the fire-drill (araṇī),
shone like a well-kindled fire that has received the sacrificial oblation.
Thus was Śuka born, as if blazing with splendor,
O best of brahmins, possessing a wonderful and unsurpassed form and complexion.
O Nārada, having approached that Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, who was present in her own form upon the summit of Meru, he bathed her with his own water.
And the black antelope skin fell from the intermediate space onto the earth for the sake of Śuka;
the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsarases danced.
And celestial kettledrums resounded with a great roar;
and the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, as well as Tuṃburu and Nārada [were present].
The two Gandharvas, Hāhā and Hūhū, offered praise to the one born from Śuka;
there, the world-protectors, led by Śakra, had also assembled.
The gods and the celestial sages (*devarṣis*), as well as the brahminical sages (*brahmarṣis*),
[appeared], and the wind rained down all kinds of divine flowers.
The world, both moving and stationary, became filled with joy;
that great-souled one of immense splendor, together with the goddess, [bestowed it] out of his own affection.

Then, as soon as he was born, the powerful Lord of the Gods performed the ritual presentation of the sage’s son according to the prescribed rites, [bestowing upon him] a divine and wondrous appearance.
The gods affectionately gave him a water-pot and garments on all sides,
while thousands of swans, woodpeckers, and cranes [followed].
O Nārada, parrots and blue jays moved clockwise around him,
as did that great sage who had then obtained a divine birth in the forest.
There the wise one dwelt, observant of vows and composed in mind;
as soon as he was born, the Vedas, along with their secret doctrines and compendiums, appeared to him.
They waited upon the best of sages just as they had upon his father;
he, who was learned in the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and their commentaries, chose Bṛhaspati as his preceptor.
O best of the twice-born, reflecting only upon dharma, he studied all the Vedas along with their secret portions (Upanishads) and their compendiums under his preceptor.
Having mastered the Itihāsas in their entirety and the Vedic scriptures in all their aspects,
the great sage, having given the teacher his fee, returned home.
Even in his childhood, that great ascetic, remaining composed as a celibate student, undertook fierce austerities for the sake of the deities and the ṛṣis.
He was worthy of being honored by his kinsmen through both knowledge and asceticism;
yet, O Lord of Sages, his mind found no delight in hermitages.
Among the three roots of the householder's life, Śuka, perceiving the dharma of liberation, reflected upon that very liberation and approached his father.
Then, seeking the highest good and endowed with humility, he saluted him and said:
"May the Blessed One, who is skilled in the dharmas of liberation, speak to me."
"O Sage, just as supreme peace arises for the mind," having heard these words of his son, the great seer spoke to him.
"Study the treatises on liberation and indeed the various duties as well.
At his father's command, Śuka, the best among the knowers of Brahman, undertook this.
O Nārada, he mastered the entire Yogaśāstra as well as the teachings of Kapila,
endowed with a hundredfold Brahmanic splendor and possessing prowess equal to that of Brahmā.
Just as Vyāsa regarded his son as one proficient in the scriptures of liberation,
he then said to Janaka, the lord of Mithilā, "Go."
O lord of men, that king will explain to you the means to liberation in its entirety; by his father’s command, he went to King Janaka of Mithilā.
To inquire indeed into the ultimate limit of Dharma and the final goal of liberation, you were told by the human [being]: "Go thus, without being amazed. (NarP 1.58.50)
You must certainly not travel through the air by means of supernatural power;
you should proceed only by the straightforward path, and not for the sake of momentary pleasure.
Indeed, distinctions should not be observed, for such distinctions lead to attachment;
one should not harbor pride toward that lord of men when he is the recipient of the sacrifice.
You should stay at his residence; he will sever your doubt, for that king is skilled in the Dharma and proficient in the treatises on liberation.
"In whatever manner he may instruct you, that task must be carried out without hesitation.
Having been addressed thus, that righteous-souled sage departed for Mithilā.
At dawn, capable of traversing the atmosphere, he crossed over the earth with its oceans and mountains,
and reached Bhārata-varṣa.
Having traversed various prosperous regions, that great sage reached Videha and met with Janaka.
Having reached the royal gate, he was turned away by the gatekeepers;
there the great yogi remained, free from hunger, thirst, and other such needs.
O Nārada, free from fatigue in the heat and absorbed in meditation,
one of those gatekeepers remained stationed there.
Seeing Śuka standing there like the sun reached its meridian,
he greeted him according to custom and, with palms joined in reverence, paid his respects.
Then he led him into the second courtyard of the royal palace;
there was a great hall connected to the inner apartments, resembling the celestial chariot Caitraratha.
Having shown him that delightful place with its well-arranged water-gardens and flowering trees, and having seated the king upon a throne, he addressed him.
O best of sages, having heard that Śuka had arrived, the king appointed courtesans to attend upon him in order to ascertain his true disposition.
And she was attended by beautiful women with lovely hair— youthful, pleasing to behold,
wearing fine red garments, and adorned with ornaments of refined gold.
Skilled in conversation and discourse, perceiving the inner disposition and proficient in all matters,
more than fifty of them prepared water for his feet and other offerings.
O dear one, having satisfied him with excellent food appropriate to the place and time,
they then led him from there to the city grove once he had finished eating.
O Nārada, they showed themselves one by one in their most beautiful forms;
playing, laughing, and singing, they [presented] themselves to Śuka.
Then all those who knew living beings attended upon that noble-souled one;
he was pure in spirit, born of the fire-sticks, having conquered anger and mastered his senses.
Remaining constantly established in meditation, he neither rejoices nor becomes angry;
having indeed washed his feet and performed the twilight devotions, Śuka remained thus.
He sat upon the auspicious seat and reflected upon that very matter;
there, during the first watch of the night, he became entirely devoted to meditation.
At midnight, the lord took his sleep as was appropriate;
then, having risen in the morning, he immediately performed his purificatory rites.
Surrounded by women, the wise one devoted himself solely to meditation;
by this method, he passed the remainder of that day there as well.
And Nārada spent that night in the royal palace.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Enticement of Śuka," in the second part of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first section of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanandana said:
Then, O best of the twice-born, that king, accompanied by his ministers...
Having placed the family priest at the head, he led forth all the members of the inner apartments.
Taking the water for honor upon his head, he approached the son of the guru,
having brought a great seat adorned with all kinds of jewels.
He gave it to Śuka, the son of his preceptor, who was most worthy of it;
and as he sat there, [the preceptor] honored him with the rites prescribed in the scriptures for a disciple.
Having first offered water for the feet, he presented the guest-offering (arghya) and a cow;
and that best of the twice-born accepted that worship according to the mantras.
The one of great splendor inquired after the king’s inexhaustible welfare; and the king, of noble being and lineage, likewise [inquired] of his venerable son.
Having announced his well-being, he sat down on the ground by his command;
and he, the knower of ritual, having again inquired after the undecaying welfare of the son of Vyāsa,
asked, "For what purpose have you come?"
Śuka said:
"Blessings to you; my father told me that today this king of Videha, renowned by the name Janaka, is an expert in the meaning of the dharma of liberation."
Go there quickly; he will undoubtedly sever for you every doubt in your heart regarding both worldly engagement and renunciation.
Therefore, by my father’s command, I have come here to question you;
thus, O best among the upholders of dharma, you should explain this to me as it truly is.
What is the duty of a Brahmin here in this world, and what is the nature of the goal of liberation?
How is liberation to be achieved—through knowledge or through austerity?
Janaka said:
Listen to what must be done by a Brahmin here from birth onwards;
O dear one, once the initiation ceremony has been performed, he should be devoted to the Vedas.
Endowed with austerity, service to his guru, and celibacy,
he was free from craving for the gods and the ancestors, and devoid of malice.
Having studied the Vedas, being self-restrained, having offered the prescribed fee,
and having obtained permission, the twice-born man should indeed perform the return ceremony (samāvartana).
Having returned home, he should dwell in the householder stage with his wife, self-restrained,
free from malice, maintaining the sacred fires according to the rule, and without negligence.
Having provided for his sons and grandsons, he should dwell in a forest hermitage,
honoring those very same sacred fires according to the rule, being fond of guests.
Having properly internalized all the sacred fires within himself according to the rule, the knower of dharma,
free from dualities and with a self devoid of passion, should dwell in the stage of life dedicated to Brahman.
Śuka said:
"Once direct knowledge and realized wisdom have arisen eternally within the heart,
it is traditionally held that the attainment of such knowledge does not occur without dwelling with a guru."
"O King, must one necessarily dwell in hermitages, or not?
This I ask of you; you ought to tell me that."
Janaka said: Without knowledge and realization, there can be no attainment of liberation;
