likewise, without connection to a guru, there is no attainment of knowledge.
The teacher is the boatman, and knowledge is said here to be the boat;
having understood this and accomplished his purpose, one who has crossed over should abandon both.
For the non-annihilation of the worlds and for the non-annihilation of actions,
liberation is attained here after having performed both auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
Having cultivated the causes through many births in the cycle of existence,
the pure-souled one indeed attains liberation even in the first stage of life.
But for the wise man who has attained that [state], who is liberated, who has seen the goal,
and who desires the supreme— what purpose could there be in the three stages of life?
One should constantly abandon the defects of passion and darkness;
having resorted to the path of goodness, one should perceive the Self by means of the self.
Perceiving the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, one is not defiled at all, just as a water-dwelling creature is not wetted by water.
Like a bird, having ascended from the wind, he enjoys [bliss] thereafter;
having abandoned the body, he is liberated, free from dualities, and endowed with auspiciousness.
In this regard, hear the verses sung of old by King Yayāti,
which, O dear one, are preserved by the twice-born who are experts in the scriptures of liberation.
The light is within the self and not elsewhere; the jewel is likewise right there.
And it is possible for one with a well-concentrated mind to see it by oneself.
He from whom others do not fear, and who does not fear others;
he who neither desires nor hates—he indeed attains Brahman.
When one does not commit any evil toward any living beings,
that is the dharma practiced by the ancients, known as the four stages of life (caturāśrama).
By this sequential yoga, for those who have performed many virtuous deeds through action,
mind, and speech, they then attain Brahman.
Having disciplined the self through austerity, having cast off delusive envy,
and having abandoned desire and greed, one then attains the state of Brahman.
When one becomes equanimous and free from distress toward what is heard and what is seen, as well as toward all beings, being immutable, then one attains Brahman.
When one views praise and blame with equanimity, as well as gold and iron, and likewise pleasure and pain; NarP_1,59.34 //
Cold and heat, likewise gain and loss, the pleasant and the unpleasant,
life and death— when these are equanimous, one attains Brahman.
Just as a tortoise here extends its limbs and then withdraws them again,
so too must the sense-faculties be restrained by the mind of a monk.
Just as a house enveloped in darkness can be seen by means of a lamp,
so too can the Self be perceived by means of the lamp of intelligence.
O best among the wise, I perceive all of this within you;
whatever else is to be known, you know that in its true essence. (NarP 1.59.38)
O Brahman-sage, you are known to have reached the very limit of the sensory realms,
both through the grace of your preceptor and through your own diligent study.
And by the grace of that great sage, divine knowledge has arisen, fully kindled; by that you have been known, indeed, as known to me.
Your knowledge is superior, your understanding is superior, and your sovereignty is superior; yet you do not perceive that.
Whether due to childhood, or from doubt, or even from fear or delusion, even when knowledge has arisen, they do not attain that state. (NarP 1.59.42)
Having had their doubts severed by those like me through pure resolve,
they untie the knots of the heart and attain that state beyond suffering.
O Brahmin, even one who has attained discernment, whose intellect is steady and pure, and who is free from greed, does not reach that state without resolute effort.
There is no distinction for you between pleasure and pain, nor among material objects;
there is no longing for dance or song, and no passion arises within you.
You have no attachment to kinsmen, nor do you have fear in the face of dangers;
O illustrious one, I behold you as one for whom censure and self-praise are equal.
I and other wise men behold you established upon the supreme path, which is imperishable and free from affliction.
That fruit which belongs to a Brahmin here in this world—namely, liberation characterized by the cessation of all calamities—in that very state you abide, O Brahmin; what else do you ask?
Sanandana said:
Having heard these words, he whose mind was composed and who had made his resolve,
established himself by means of the self, having perceived the self by means of the self.
Having accomplished his task, happy and tranquil, he departed silently toward the north;
reaching the Śaiśira mountain, he beheld the son of Parāśara.
And the pure-souled Āraṇeya, radiant with a splendor equal to the sun, was teaching the Vedic collections to his disciples, Paila and the others.
With a joyful heart, he respectfully grasped his father’s feet;
then, the noble-minded one reported everything to his father.
Having heard that dialogue between Śuka and King Janaka concerning the means to liberation, the author of the Vedas was delighted in his inner self.
And Vyāsa embraced his son and drew him close to his side.
Then the brahmins Paila and the others, having studied the Vedas from Vyāsa,
descended from the mountain peak to the earth, devoted themselves to officiating at sacrifices and teaching.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter in the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the Pūrvabhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanandana said: When the Brahmins had descended, Yāja, accompanied by his son, [proceeded].
The wise one sat down in a secluded place, silent and intent on meditation.
An incorporeal voice spoke to Vyāsa, who was accompanied by his son:
"O, O great sage, descendant of Vasiṣṭha, the sound of the Veda is not being recited! (NarP 1.60.2)
"Another sits alone, intent on meditation, silent as if lost in thought;
deprived of the sounds of sacred recitation, this mountain no longer shines."
Therefore, O Blessed One, with a mind always very gracious, study the Vedas together with your wise son, who is himself a knower of the Vedas.
Having heard those words uttered by the voice from the sky,
Vyāsa then engaged in the study of the Vedas together with his son Śuka.
O best of the twice-born, as they were thus practicing for a long time,
a wind blew with excessive force, fanned by the breezes from the ocean.
Then Vyāsa forbade his son, saying, "This is a time unfit for study. But as soon as he was forbidden, Śuka was filled with curiosity.
There he asked his father, "From where has this wind arisen?
You ought to explain to me the entire activity of the wind."
Having heard these words of Śuka, Vyāsa was greatly amazed;
regarding this cause for the suspension of study, he spoke these words.
Divine vision has arisen in you; your mind is healthy and steady.
You are abandoned by both darkness and passion, and are established in truth.
Having personally understood the Vedas within yourself, reflect upon them thoroughly;
for one who travels by the path of the gods goes to Viṣṇu, while the path of the ancestors is characterized by darkness.
These two, having reached their respective conditions, go both to heaven and downward;
for from them the winds blow across the earth and through the atmosphere.
There are indeed seven paths of Vāyu; learn of them in their proper order.
Therein, the hosts of gods known as the Sādhyas, who possess great strength, came into being.
To them also was born a son named Samāna, who was difficult to conquer;
Udāna was his son, and Vyāna was his son.
From him Apāna was born, and after that Prāṇa;
yet Prāṇa, the invincible crusher of enemies, remained childless.
I shall describe their individual functions exactly as they are:
the wind, circulating everywhere within living beings, carries out their various activities separately.
Because it delights all beings, it is called "prāṇa" (life-breath);
likewise, it sends forth masses of clouds born of smoke as well as those born of heat.
In the first path, that wind is named Pravaha;
its supreme radiance surpasses the moisture in the atmosphere and the lightning.
The second wind, named Āvaha, approaches roaring;
it is he who constantly causes the rising of the luminaries, beginning with the moon.
And that which the wise call *udāna* within the intermediate bodies, and that wind which supports the water from the four oceans; NarP_1,60.20.
The wind draws up water from the ocean and gives it to the clouds in the forest;
having joined the clouds together, it delivers them to Parjanya.
The third is the most extensive wind named Udvaha;
it is the ever-moving one by which the vast blue clouds are led in many directions.
Those clouds that have begun their activity for the release of rain are the dense rain-clouds;
it is they that carry the celestial chariots of the gods through the sky.
The fourth wind is named Saṃvaha; it is the crusher of mountains, by whose forceful power the juices produced by trees are broken apart.
The fifth wind is that of great velocity named Vivaha,
in which the divine waters flow through the sky while being tossed about.
And the meritorious water of the celestial Gaṅgā remains,
ever present, wherein even a single ray of the sun is repelled from afar.
It is the source of a thousand rays, by which it traverses the earth;
from it the moon is nourished, and it is the divine treasury of nectar.
The sixth wind is named Parivaha; it is the best among those that sustain life, for at the time of death, it expels the vital breaths of all living beings.
Both Death and Vaivasvata follow his dharma,
by one who observes correctly with an intellect that is tranquil and constantly fixed upon the inner self.
That which leads to immortality for those who delight in the practice of meditation,
and reaching which they swiftly attained the ends of the quarters.
Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, had ten thousand sons,
by whom the rain was overcome and by whom the waters were turned back.
The excellent wind named Parīvaha is difficult to overcome;
thus are these Maruts, the sons of Diti, most wonderful.
Moving everywhere with all their limbs unobstructed—
this is indeed a great marvel, that this best of mountains [is thus affected].
He was suddenly shaken by that purifying wind,
this very breath of Viṣṇu when it is impelled with great force.
"O dear one, when it is recited too loudly, the world then becomes distressed;
therefore, those who know Brahman do not recite the Veda with excessive force."
"For it is said that there is danger from the wind for Vāyu; thus, that Brahman would be afflicted.
Having spoken these words, the lordly son of Parāśara [remained silent].
Having said to his son, "Study," he then departed for the celestial Gaṅgā;
thereafter, when Vyāsa had gone to bathe, Śuka, the best among the knowers of Brahman, remained.
O Brahmin, he who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas performed his private recitation there; O Sage, Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, was deeply absorbed in that recitation.
The venerable Sanatkumāra approached him in seclusion; rising up, the son of Brahmā was indeed honored by that descendant of Kṛṣṇa.
Then the best of Brahmins, the foremost among the learned, spoke to Śuka:
"What are you doing, O highly fortunate one, son of Vyāsa, of great splendor?"
Śuka said:
"O son of Brahmā, I was previously engaged in the study of the Vedas, but now I stand here;
I have come into your presence by some merit of my own."
I wish to ask you something regarding the reality that accomplishes the goal of liberation;
tell me that, O illustrious one, so that I may attain that knowledge.
Sanatkumāra said:
There is no eye equal to knowledge; there is no austerity equal to knowledge;
there is no suffering equal to passion; there is no happiness equal to renunciation.
Abstention from evil deeds, constant practice of virtuous conduct, right livelihood, and proper behavior—this is the unsurpassed highest good. (NarP 1.60.44)
Having attained this human state which is not free from suffering, he who becomes attached is deluded;
he is not capable of liberation from suffering, for attachment is indeed the very mark of suffering.
For one who is attached, the intellect becomes a multiplier of the net of delusion;
enveloped by the net of delusion, one experiences suffering both in this world and the next. (NarP 1.60.46)
One who seeks the highest good must restrain both desire and anger by every possible means, for those two are intent upon destroying one's welfare. (NarP 1.60.47)
One should always protect one's asceticism from anger, one's prosperity from envy,
one's knowledge from honor and dishonor, and one's self from negligence.
Compassion is the supreme dharma; forgiveness is the supreme strength;
self-knowledge is the supreme knowledge; for truth is the supreme benefit.
He by whom everything has been relinquished is a man of true vision and a wise one;
he moves here with his senses under his own control, away from the objects of the senses.
Unattached, with a tranquil self, changeless and composed,
he is both with and without those things that have become his own, yet are not truly his.
Once liberated, he attains the supreme good before long:
namely, constant non-seeing, non-touching, and likewise non-speaking.
O Sage, he who dwells together with all beings attains great excellence;
one should not harm any living beings, but should practice friendliness toward all creatures.
Having attained this human birth, one should not harbor enmity toward anyone;
rather, one should practice poverty, perfect contentment, freedom from desire, and steadiness.
They say this is the supreme good for one who knows the self and has conquered the self: having renounced all possessions, O dear one, become one whose senses are subdued.
Abide in that sorrowless state which is free from fear both here and hereafter; those who are free from desire do not grieve, so one should renounce all personal longing.
O gentle one, by abandoning all worldly blessings, you shall be liberated from the village of suffering;
for this, you must be a sage who is constant in austerity, self-controlled, and of restrained mind.
One who desires to conquer the unconquered should cultivate non-attachment toward attachments;
unattached even to these attachments to virtuous qualities, one should always delight in solitary wandering.
Before long, the brahmin attains unsurpassed happiness;
while other beings delight in pairs of opposites, the sage, though appearing wretched, finds his joy elsewhere.
One who is somewhat satisfied with wisdom, being satisfied with knowledge, does not grieve;
through auspicious deeds one attains the state of a deity, and through mixed deeds, human birth.
And by means of impure actions, one helplessly obtains birth in the lower realms;
there, one is constantly assailed by the sufferings of death and old age.
Living beings perceive this cycle of existence; why then do you not understand it?
You perceive what is harmful as beneficial, and what is impermanent as permanent.
Why do you not realize that you perceive what is worthless as being meaningful,
while you are being entangled by many threads of delusion born of yourself?
Like a silkworm, you do not perceive yourself as being enveloped;
enough with this grasping here, for grasping is indeed fraught with fault.
For the silkworm is bound by its own cocoon;
likewise, living beings who are attached to children, wives, and family perish.
Behold these beings, deeply afflicted, dragged into the snare of delusion like aged wild elephants sunk in the ocean-mud of a lake.
Family, wife, children, the body, and the accumulation of wealth—all this is not one's own and is impermanent; what is truly one's own? Only one's good and evil deeds.
Since one must inevitably depart, abandoning everything,
why are you attached to what is worthless and do not pursue your own true interest?
How will you travel alone along that path which is without rest, without support, without provisions, without a guide, and shrouded in darkness, leading to the maker of gloom?
No one at all will follow behind you as you set forth;
however, your good deeds and your evil deeds will follow after you as you go.
Learning, action, valor, and extensive knowledge—all these are pursued for the sake of wealth; but one who has achieved his purpose is liberated.
This delight in dwelling in a village is a binding rope;
having severed it, the virtuous depart, but the wicked do not sever it.
You behold those of equal birth, age, and beauty snatched away by death, yet there is no weariness in you; indeed, your heart is made of iron.
The river of the mind has form for its banks, touch for its islands, flows with taste,
has scent for its mud, sound for its water, and is difficult to cross on the path to heaven.

One should cross the river by means of the swift boat of the intellect, which has patience as its oar, is composed of truth, is a mine that brings stability to dharma, and has renunciation as its wind-driven course. 1.60.75.
Having abandoned both dharma and adharma, indeed, abandon both truth and falsehood;
abandon dharma through the absence of volitional intent, and abandon adharma through non-violence.
Both truth and falsehood [are perceived] by the intellect through supreme certainty;
[the body is seen as] having bones for its pillars, joined by tendons, and plastered with flesh and blood.
Enveloped by the elements, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement;
it is assailed by old age and sorrow, an unstable abode of diseases.
Abandon this entire universe, which is impure, impermanent, and the abode of the elements—both that which is moving and that which is unmoving. (NarP 1.60.79)
Everything down to the subtle atom consists of the great elements;
likewise, there are the five sense organs, as well as tamas, sattva, and rajas.
Thus, this group of seventeen is designated as the "manifest";
for it is composed of all the sense organs and their objects, both manifest and unmanifest.
This group consisting of twenty-five principles, composed of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
when joined with all these, is designated as impermanent.
The three aims of life, pleasure, pain, life, and likewise death—
he who knows this in its true essence, he knows the origin and the dissolution.
Whatever is grasped by the senses is called the manifest;
on the other hand, that which is to be known as unmanifest is beyond the senses and graspable only through its signs.
With his senses restrained, the embodied being is satisfied as if by streams of water;
he perceives the self established in the world and the world within the self.
The power of one who perceives both the higher and the lower does not perceive the boundary of knowledge,
as they constantly behold all beings in all their states at all times.
For one who has become Brahman, no contact with the inauspicious occurs;
through knowledge, there is cessation of various afflictions, yet not of the body-born [suffering].
Through the illumination of worldly intellect, the path of the world does not perish;
it reveals the living being as beginningless and endless, abiding within the self and immutable.
The Blessed One, the knower of the further shore, declared that one who is neither an agent nor deluded is the being who is perpetually afflicted by those various actions performed by himself.
To counteract their own suffering, living beings kill in many ways;
consequently, they take up yet more new and manifold karma.
Then he suffers because of that, like a sick man who has eaten unwholesome food;
for one whose end is delusion, there is only incessant suffering, yet it is perceived as pleasure.
One is constantly struck and tormented by fearsome arrows;
therefore, one should turn away from the bondage of one's own actions that arise in this world.
Deprived of arms, he wanders through saṃsāra like a wheel;
yet, through his self-restraint, his connection [to the divine], and the power of his asceticism, he attains liberation.
Many have attained the accomplishment that is free from affliction and brings about happiness.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter in the Bṛhad-upākhyāna, in the second quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The Aśoka [treatise] is for the purpose of destroying grief; it is a scripture that brings peace and is auspicious."
Upon hearing it, wisdom is attained; once attained, happiness increases.
Thousands of occasions for joy and hundreds of occasions for sorrow enter the fool day after day, but not the wise man.
And through union with the undesirable and separation from the beloved, those of small intelligence, human beings, are joined with mental sufferings. (NarP 1.61.3)
One should not dwell upon the qualities of things that have passed away;
by disregarding them, one is liberated from the bonds of affection.
One should perceive the defects in that wherein passion arises; by applying the perception of it as undesirable, one will soon shine forth with dispassion.
He who grieves for the past gains neither wealth, nor merit, nor fame;
he becomes joined with non-existence, and that [past object] ceases to exist for him.
Beings are joined with qualities, and likewise they are not joined;
this applies to all, for there is no ground for grief in this alone.
He who grieves over what is dead or lost, having passed away,
gains sorrow through sorrow and falls into great misfortune.
When physical or mental suffering has arisen and cannot be remedied by effort, one should not dwell upon it.
This is the medicine for suffering: that one should not dwell upon it;
for when it is dwelt upon, it does not pass away, but rather increases all the more.
One should destroy mental suffering with wisdom and physical suffering with medicines;
having understood this capacity, one should not equate it with other things.
Life, physical form, youth, the accumulation of wealth, health, and dwelling with loved ones are impermanent; a wise person should never take pleasure in them.
One should not grieve alone over suffering born of ignorance;
rather, without grieving, one should apply a remedy if one perceives a means to do so.
In this life, there is no doubt that suffering is dearer than happiness;
therefore, one should rescue oneself from the sufferings of old age and death.
For physical and mental diseases afflict the body like sharp-pointed arrows discharged by firm archers.
For one who is ill, who fears [death] and desires life,
the body is subjected to strain for the sake of destroying the disease through medical treatments.
Like the currents of rivers, they flow away and do not return;
night and day take away the life of mortals again and again.
This [time] departs utterly during the two phases, the bright and the dark;
it causes the mortal born to age and does not remain still for even a moment.
While those overcome by pleasure and pain grow old, age consumes their lives;
for the sun indeed sets and rises again and again.
Taking with them things never seen before and beyond all suspicion—both desirable and undesirable for men—the nights pass away. (NarP 1.61.20)

Whatever one might desire, whatever objects of desire one might wish for according to one's will, that one would obtain—if the fruit of a person's action were not dependent on something else. (NarP 1.61.21)
Even those who are self-controlled, skilled craftsmen, and wise men are seen to be unsuccessful and deprived of their own merits, despite being virtuous.
Others, being fruitless, devoid of virtue, and the lowest of men,
are seen to be joined with golden hopes while desiring everything.
Another person among living beings, who is constantly intent on violence and deception toward people, perishes even while amidst pleasures.
Fortune attends upon someone who sits idle and does nothing;
yet another performs various actions and still does not attain what is to be gained.
To declare the offenses of a person according to their own nature:
semen produced in one place goes again to another.
For that man who is attached to the womb, a human embryo comes into being;
his rebirth is perceived as being like the flower of a mango tree.
For some who desire sons, who wish for the continuity of their lineage,
and who strive diligently toward that end, no embryo is even produced.
For those who tremble at the womb as if from an enraged venomous serpent, how can a long-lived son be born? How could he be anything other than a corpse, like his father?
Having worshipped the gods and performed austerities for the sake of sons, those wretched men who have carried them for ten months give birth to the disgrace of their lineage.
Others, having obtained wealth, grain, and enjoyments accumulated by their ancestors through those very auspicious rites, are born pure.
When two people have come together for sexual union with mutual intent,
the embryo enters the womb, unobserved by calamities.
Because of attachment to the objects of the senses and through delusion, death is unpleasant;
yet the man who abandons suffering as well as pleasure—both of them—[is not affected by it].
He transcends the Brahman and enjoys supreme, ultimate happiness;
for wealth is indeed abandoned due to suffering, and there is no joy in its preservation.
Upon merely hearing this, one should not think that there is no attainment or that these [wealthy men] will meet with ruin;
for such people, having encountered various and ever-changing states of fortune, become particularly distinguished.
The insatiable go to ruin, while the wise attain contentment;
all accumulations end in depletion, and all elevations end in a fall.
Unions end in separation, for life ends in death;
there is no end to thirst, but contentment is the supreme happiness.
Therefore, the wise praise contentment alone as true wealth in this world;
for he who does not remain even for the duration of a single blink of an eye is one who has attained nothing.
What should one contemplate as eternal within these impermanent embodied beings?
Having reflected upon the nature of all elements, those who perceive with their intellect that which is beyond darkness—[they find the eternal].
Those who have traveled the path do not grieve; they behold the supreme goal.
Yet, one who accumulates this very [wealth] remains unsatisfied amidst desires.
Having seized one like a tiger seizes its prey, death departs;
yet, one might still perceive a means for liberation from this suffering.
One should not grieve; one should indeed undertake [practice], being disciplined and free from addiction, toward sound, touch, taste, form, and likewise smell as supreme.
For one who possesses wealth or lacks it, there is nothing beyond mere enjoyment;
for those who are hired laborers, there is no suffering other than that arising from the use of speech.
And for everyone there is separation, neither by word nor by knowledge;
having withdrawn all affection toward both those who are praised and others alike. (NarP 1.61.44)
He who wanders without arrogance is happy and he is wise;
inwardly turned, withdrawn, indifferent to the world, and free from worldly desire.
One should wander with oneself alone as one's companion; thus one shall be happy, for when the reversal of pleasure and pain occurs, [one must face it alone]. (NarP 1.61.46)
Neither well-disciplined wisdom nor human effort protects one from this [fate];
however, one should apply oneself to one's own inherent nature, for the diligent person does not come to grief.
Like an unwanted affliction, the embryo enters its womb;
those former bodies always belong to this one and the same embodied being.
When the life-force of living beings is obstructed, the activity of flesh and phlegm is consumed; by means of another's body, one's own body—its strength and weakness—is utterly burnt away.
At the end of its destruction, it perishes like an unstable boat [meeting] another boat;
the insentient drop of semen, deposited within the womb through sexual union, [perishes].
By what effort do you perceive the living embryo here,
wherein food and drinks, as well as the foods that have been eaten, are digested?
Why does the embryo not decay like food within that very same belly?
For the movement of urine and excrement within the womb is determined by their inherent nature.
One is not able to act independently regarding either retention or emission;
likewise, fetuses come into being within the womb, and others are born.
For others, great destruction follows by means of this traditional teaching;
therefore, one who is liberated while still living from this connection with the womb [is truly free].
He receives no honor whatsoever, but sinks again into hatred;
such is the seventh stage of the one born from the womb. (NarP 1.61.55)
Consequently, they attain five [senses] and do not live for a hundred years;
there is no doubt that for humans who do not rise up [to practice], there will be no success in yoga.
They are tormented by diseases like small deer by tigers;
even as they are being devoured by diseases and abandon vast wealth, [they suffer]. (NarP 1.61.57)
Even physicians striving with their best efforts cannot remove painful sensations.
And even those various physicians, skilled and proficient in medicines,
are themselves dragged away by diseases like deer tormented by tigers with their bowstrings.
They drink astringent decoctions and various kinds of clarified butter;
yet they are seen broken by old age, like the finest elephants by serpents.
By whom on earth could the beasts and birds afflicted by disease be treated?
For the most part, wild animals and the poor do not suffer from illness. (NarP 1.61.61)
Having assailed even formidable, invincible kings of fierce splendor,
disease seizes them just as a butcher seizes his cattle.
Thus, seeing the world without refuge, overwhelmed by delusion and grief, and being swiftly carried away by a powerful, great current; ||| NarP_1,61.63 |||
Neither by wealth, nor by sovereignty, nor even by fierce austerity can those who are liberated among embodied beings transcend their inherent nature.
Everyone desires to become superior or even supreme in the world;
they strive according to their ability, yet it does not happen in that way.
They would not die, they would not age; all would have every desire fulfilled, and none would encounter anything unpleasant as a result of their exertion.
Intoxicated by the pride of power and by the intoxication of the conceit of honor,
those who are heedless, deceitful, cruel, and yet bold wait upon him.
Griefs turn back for some who lack discernment;
yet for others, they return again and again, never passing over anyone.
And a great disparity in results is observed in the junctions of karma:
some carry the palanquin, while others travel as those seated upon the palanquin.
All those desiring supernatural power, others with chariots at their head,
men whose prosperity had vanished, and hundreds of various women [followed].
Among beings who delight in pairs, men pass away one by one;
behold this other supreme truth, and you shall no longer fall into delusion here.
Abandon even dharma; abandon the mind that discriminates between truth and falsehood.
Having renounced everything, abide in your own true nature and be happy and free from affliction.
This supreme secret has been declared to you, O best of sages,
by which the gods, having abandoned the world of mortals, went to heaven.
Sanandana said:
Having spoken thus to the son of Vyāsa and having taken leave of him,
the great sage Sanatkumāra departed, honored by him with due respect.
Śuka, the best among yogis, having correctly understood that which abides,
went to his father eager to seek the state of Brahman.
Then, having met with his father and bowed down to him, the great sage Śuka circumambulated him and departed for Mount Kailāsa.
Vyāsa, distressed by that separation and overwhelmed by affection for his son, cried out in a dejected state of mind, "Stay for just a moment, my son! (NarP 1.61.77).
Becoming indifferent, free from affection, and released from all bonds,
and contemplating only liberation, he indeed went to the supreme state.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the second quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words, the venerable sage Nārada—
Again, O Brahmin, he questioned that sage regarding the flight of the parrot.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, everything has been narrated by you, whose nature is exceedingly compassionate;
having heard which, my mind has today attained the highest peace."
Furthermore, O Great Sage, instruct me once more in the science of liberation;
for thirst does not reach its end in the ocean of Kṛṣṇa’s qualities.
But those who are liberated from saṃsāra and devoted to the scriptures on liberation—where do they dwell here? This is a great doubt of mine.
"Cut that [doubt], O highly fortunate one; there is no other knower superior to you.
That great sage maintained his self according to the scriptures. (NarP 1.62.5)
Then, knowing the sequential application of the method, that wise man, facing eastward, [performs the practice] gradually upon his limbs starting from the feet, while illuminated by the sun.
Having composed his hands and feet, he sat down like one who is disciplined;
there was no flock of birds there, no sound, and no sight.
When Vyāsa’s son began to yoke himself to that abode,
he beheld his own self as completely released from all attachments.
Then Śuka, having gazed upon the Sun, broke into laughter;
he then once more applied himself to yoga for the sake of attaining the path to liberation.
Having become a great lord of yogins,
the illustrious son of Vyāsa, firm in his resolve, traversed the sky, moving through the intermediate space.
All beings beheld that best of the twice-born as he ascended, possessing a splendor like that of Vainateya and a speed equal to the mind or the wind.
They honored him according to their ability and in accordance with what was right;
likewise, the denizens of heaven showered him with divine rains of flowers.
Seeing him, all the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, as well as the perfected sages, were struck with wonder, saying, "Who is this who has attained such perfection?"
Then, O Nārada, he recounted his own lineage to them;
and that one of great splendor, filled with joy, spoke to those sages.
"If my father should follow me, crying out 'Śuka!',
you must give him an answer with composed minds."
Having been told "So be it" by them, he then abandoned the fourfold worlds,
cast off the eightfold darkness (tamas), and relinquished the fivefold passion (rajas).
Then the wise one abandoned his being; it was like a marvel.
Then, in that eternal state, which is devoid of qualities and honored by its subtle mark (liṅga), [he remained].
Then, upon two incomparable peaks of the Himavat, resembling Mount Meru—
joined together, white and yellow, auspicious, and composed of silver and gold— [he stood].
O Nārada, Śuka likewise descended with a fearless mind upon that [tree] which was a hundred yojanas in extent both horizontally and vertically.
O best of the twice-born, those two horns, which were extremely close together, suddenly became split in two; it was like a marvel that was witnessed.
Then, having suddenly emerged from the two mountain peaks,
that best of mountains could not withstand his course.
Then, traveling above the divine Mandākinī,
the righteous Śuka beheld a forest of trees in full bloom.
While the throngs of Apsarases were sporting and bathing in that [lake], they,
being naked, beheld him who was formless even within his embodied form.
Perceiving that he was departing, his father, filled with affection, followed after him,
having resolved upon the supreme path.
But Śuka, having performed a flight through the atmosphere above the wind,
displayed his own power and then became one with all beings.
Then Vyāsa, the great ascetic, having established himself in the course of yoga,
traveled to where Śuka had flown away in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Having split the mountain peak in two, he beheld Śuka gone;
the sages and Siddhas announced that departure of his son to him.
Then, with the long cry "O Śuka!",
his father himself raised a loud voice that truly made the three worlds resound.
Having become all-pervading, the self of all, and facing every direction, the righteous-souled Śuka replied, making the air resound with the sound "Bho! (Ho!).
Then, uttering the single-syllable sound "Bhoḥ" in this manner,
he caused the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, to respond loudly.
From that time forth, even until now, he has uttered distinct sounds unspoken by others,
addressing Śuka from the ridges and depths of the mountain caves.
Having displayed that power which was previously hidden,
Śuka then abandoned the qualities such as *sattva* and attained the supreme state.
But having witnessed that greatness of his son of immeasurable splendor,
O Nārada, Vyāsa was consoled by the blessed Rudra.
