Thus exhorted, Vyāsa returned once more to his hermitage;
but Śuka, having become one with Brahman, wandered through the worlds.
Then, after some time, O Brahmin, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
went to the hermitage of Badarikā to behold Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Having seen those two gods performing great penance there,
he himself remained engaged in asceticism at that spot, remembering Śuka.
While Vyāsa remained there, Śuka, the supreme knower of yoga,
went to Śvetadvīpa, O dear one, where you yourself had previously gone.
There, the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose power has been witnessed,
was seen— the God of gods, Janārdana, who is indeed sought after by the Vedas.
And being praised by Śukadeva, the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke to Nārada: "O lord of yogis, I have been seen by you while remaining in a secret place from all the gods. (NarP 1.62.40)
"O Vāḍava, you have attained perfection through yoga as instructed by Sanatkumāra;
established on the path of the Ever-Going (Sadāgati), behold the worlds according to your will."
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva,
O Brahmin, he who was born from the fire-drill bowed to him and departed for Vaikuṇṭha, which is worshipped by all the worlds.
O Nārada, it is frequented by the gods dwelling in celestial palaces and is graced by Viraja; all these worlds shine only because that [city] shines.
There, the ponds have stairs made of coral, variegated with gold and jewels,
covered with blue lotuses, and bustling with the play of celestial women.
Resounding with flocks of divine swans and always filled with clear water,
it was guarded there by doorkeepers adorned with ornaments on their four arms.
Accompanied by Viṣvaksena and followed by the Siddhas, Kumuda and others,
he entered the inner sanctum where the four-armed God of gods was present.
He was peaceful, with a serene countenance, dressed in yellow silken garments,
and attended by the personified conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
He was resplendent with Lakṣmī resting upon his chest and with the Kaustubha gem;
he was adorned with a waist-string, a sacred thread, bracelets, and armlets.
He beheld him, whose crown and armlets were radiant, adorned with jeweled anklets,
and being served day and night by the hands of perfected beings (siddhas).
Seeing him, he praised Madhusūdana with a spirit of devotion.
Śuka said:
"Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, the sole witness of all the worlds."
To Hari, whose nature is the seed of the universe, who is perfect, whose self is tranquil, who resides upon Vāsuki, and who dwells in Śvetadvīpa; 62.51.
Salutations to the one who took the form of a swan, to the one who assumed the body of a fish, to the one who bore the form of a boar,
to the man-lion, to the eternal object of worship, and to the Lord of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

Salutations to the four-faced one, to the tortoise, to the broad one, to the self who is his own sister’s husband, to the son of Nabhi, to the sustainer of the world, to the ordainer, and to the one who causes the end.
To Rāma, the lord of the Bhṛgus, and to the supreme Rāghava;
to Kṛṣṇa, the author of the Vedas, who manifests in the forms of Buddha and Kalki.
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who is manifested in four forms, who is to be known and meditated upon, who is named Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and who is the most excellent of men.
To him whose abode is Truth, to the Ordainer, to the Fair-winged One, to the Self-luminous,
to the Rbhu, to the one called of Excellent Vows, to the Abode of Splendor, and to the Unconquered.
To the one of universal form, to the All, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
to the sacrifice, to the enjoyer of the sacrifice, to the most massive, to the subtle, and to the seeker of goals.
To the one whose eyes are the sun and the moon, who possesses power, vigor, and strength;
to the one worthy of sacrifice, the witness, the unborn, and the one with many heads, feet, and arms.
Salutations to the Lord of Śrī, the dweller in Śrī, who is won over by his devotees, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
the sovereign of the eightfold primordial nature, the Brahman, whose attachment is infinite.
To Hṛṣīkeśa, the creator who is to be known through the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Veda,
whose eyes resemble lotuses, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and the self-luminous one.
To Govinda, the creator of the world, the Lord of the world, the yogi,
the truth, the one whose covenant is true, to Vaikuṇṭha, and to Acyuta.
Salutations to Adhokṣaja, to Dharma, to Vāmana, to the one who consists of the three worlds,
to him whose radiance is ghee, to Viṣṇu, to Ananta, and to Kapila.
To Viriñca, who possesses three peaks, whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur,
and Sāma Vedas, who has a single horn, whose fame is pure, and who is the source of the scriptures.
Salutations to Vṛṣākapi, the prosperous one, the source, the architect of all (Viśvakarman),
whose nature is the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, the slayer of the Daityas, and the one who is beyond the guṇas.
Salutations to You, the stainless, the eternal, the immutable, and the imperishable! Protect me, O Lord, who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge.
Thus praised, the Blessed One, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
who is exceedingly affectionate toward those who bow before him, spoke these words to the son of Araṇi.
The Blessed One said: "O son of Vyāsa, highly fortunate one, O you of excellent vows, I am pleased with you.
Attain the knowledge and devotion; you are a knower of truth who bears my own form."
O twice-born one, that very form of mine which was previously seen by you in Śvetadvīpa,
I am that same one, existing as the soul of the universe for the sake of an incarnation.
O illustrious one, you have attained perfection through your constant contemplation of the dharma of liberation,
just as the wind [attains its nature] through the choice of realms, and as the sun [attains its nature] through its radiance.
Your true nature is eternally liberated, yet you are worshipped by gods and men;
for devotion toward me, the ultimate refuge of all, is indeed difficult to find in this world.
Having attained that, nothing further remains to be attained;
until the end of the kalpa, the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa remained established in austerity.
At their command, O Janaka, the virtuous Vyāsa shall compose the Bhāgavata scripture; study that and go to the earth.
He is now performing austerities on Mount Gandhamādana, his soul distressed by separation from you; appease my beloved.
O Brahmin, having been addressed thus, Śuka paid homage to the four-armed one and returned the way he had come, approaching his father.
Then, seeing him nearby and having regained his son, the powerful Pārāśarya, with a joyful heart, desisted from his ascetic penance.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
he returned to his own hermitage accompanied by the two fire-sticks from the forest.
O Lord of Sages, by the command of Nārāyaṇa,
he composed through your mouth this divine compendium, endowed with various narratives.
And he was teaching that Bhāgavata scripture— which is equal to the Vedas and increases devotion to Hari—
to his son Śuka, who was devoted to the path of renunciation.
Even though he delighted in the Self, the Blessed Śuka, son of Pārāśarya,
constantly studied the Saṃhitā which is dear to the devotees of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O sinless one, these duties pertaining to liberation have been declared to you;
they increase devotion to Hari for those who read them or even listen to them.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Dharma of Liberation," in the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the second quarter of the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
And this second quarter is complete.
Śaunaka said:
O virtuous Sūta, may you live long, you who are an expert in all the scriptures;
for we have been made to drink the nectar of the stories of Kṛṣṇa by you, O learned one.
Having heard the teachings on liberation (mokṣadharma) sung from the mouth of Sanandana, what did Nārada, the beloved of the Blessed One, ask thereafter?
The sons of Brahmā born of his mind, Sanaka and the other lords of sages,
wander through the worlds as perfected beings, intent upon the upliftment of the world.
O fortunate one, even Nārada is eternally devoted to Kṛṣṇa; what auspicious and world-purifying discourse could there not be in their assembly? (NarP 1.63.4)
Sūta said:
Well asked, O illustrious one, by you who act for the benefit of the world!
I shall relate all that which was asked by the sage Nārada.
O best of the Bhārgavas, having heard the eternal doctrines of liberation proclaimed by Sanandana, Nārada again questioned those sages.
Nārada said:
Viṣṇu is proclaimed in both the Vedas and the Tantras as the Lord of all gods;
he alone is to be propitiated here by all who desire every goal.
O lords of sages, by which mantras is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu to be propitiated,
and which deities are to be worshipped by those who are devoted to the feet of Viṣṇu?
O Brahmins, let that Bhāgavata Tantra, which involves the preceptor and the disciple,
as well as the initiation and the duties beginning with the morning, be explained.
"O givers of honor, tell me that by which months, by which actions, or by which recitations and offerings of gold and so forth, the Supreme Self is indeed pleased."
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada,
the blessed Sanatkumāra, whose splendor was like that of the sun, spoke.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall declare to you the Bhāgavata Tantra,
by knowing which one may, through pure devotion, accomplish the realization of the imperishable Viṣṇu.
They declare the Great Tantra to consist of three subjects and four feet;
the feet are proclaimed as those called Enjoyment, Liberation, Ritual Action, and Conduct.
The categories of meaning, however, are indeed only three: Paśupati, Paśu, and Pāśa.
Among these, Śiva alone is the Lord (pati), while the individual souls (jīvas) are known as the bound ones (paśus).

O Nārada, behold that as long as there is conjunction with delusion and the like, characterized by a lack of awareness of one's true nature, so long do these beings remain in the state of a bound soul (paśu), as if possessed of duality.
Their nooses are fivefold, and their characteristics are each defined therein;
furthermore, the three kinds of bound souls (paśus), known by the name *kalas*, are fully understood.
They are known by the names Talapāka and Sakala;
among them, the former is joined with impurity (mala), while the latter is joined with both impurity and karma.
The third is proclaimed as being joined with impurity (mala), illusion (māyā), and karma;
whereas the first therein is of two kinds: the contracted (samāsa) and the turbid (kaluṣa).
And "without equal" and "immaculate"—thus the second [category] is likewise;
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds by means of the "cooked" and "uncooked" impurities.
When these two have gone to the pure path, they are the Vijñānākala and the Pralayākala;
whereas this Sakala, constrained by the principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā, wanders about.
In bodies that follow from karma, as well as among those residing in their respective worlds, there are likewise five bonds; therein, the first two are born of impurity and karma.
One [aspect] arises from Māyā, another from the power of concealment (tirodhāna-śakti), and the supreme arises from the Bindu;
though one, it possesses manifold powers, being delicate in its veiling of vision and action.
In this world, for the sake of the body which is like a husk, the karma consisting of merit and demerit belonging to the selves bestows the enjoyment of various fruits. (NarP 1.63.23)
It exists as a continuous flow by way of the logic of the seed and the sprout;
these two are the first [principles], O twice-born one, so now hear those beginning with Māyā.
Victorious is the eternal Supreme Self, the all-pervading Lord, the singular supreme seed and the manifestation of existence, consciousness, and bliss. 1.63.25.
It does not think, nor does it initiate [action], yet it bestows cessation;
that supreme Śāmbhava light revolves in the form of vision and action.
Indeed, Śakti was enjoyed by me in Hari for the sake of the host of bound souls;
they call that primordial, singular Śakti Vidrūpā.
And by her was awakened the Bindu, whose nature is spatial activity and who is named Śiva—
the all-pervading, imperishable cause of the entire multitude of principles.
All the powers of will are latent within this;
they perform their respective functions, and for that reason, O Sage, it is the benefactor of all.
For the sake of favoring those who are to be born, the primordial expansion of Him who desires to emit the universe consists of *nāda*,
and its nature comprises the worlds beginning with Śānti.
O best of Brahmins, that supreme Śakti-tattva is said to possess constituent parts;
from it arise the predominance and subordination of the powers of knowledge and action.
And this expansion, through its non-existence [as a separate entity], is the reality that is Sadāśiva;
therein the power of vision (dṛk-śakti) has become latent, while the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is preeminent.
That principle is indeed called Īśvara, which is the performer of all purposes;
for therein action becomes latent and attains the predominance known as knowledge.
That very reality, called Vidyā, is of the nature of knowledge and illuminating;
both Nāda and Bindu, along with Sakala, are dependent upon the reality known as Sadākhya.
Furthermore, the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) belong to the level of Īśvara, while the mantras are designated as Vidyā;
these principles (tattvas) are proclaimed as the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan).
The Lord is the direct cause here; thus, the Sovereign of the Bindu is the material cause.
It is certain that for these five, because they are devoid of time, there is no sequence.
For indeed, their conceptualization is established based on their functional activity;
however, in reality, the single essence is that which is called Śiva, possessing manifold powers.

Indeed, the Lord, having assumed various forms for the sake of favoring both the conscious and the insentient, has established these conceptual constructions through the differentiation of his functions.
He bestows grace upon the consciousness of all beings who are obstructed by beginningless impurities, and grants them liberation, making them capable in their own respective functions.
Śiva, the benefactor of all, ordains [the world] for the multitude of insentient beings;
for liberation, which is the grace of consciousness, indeed has the nature of Śiva himself.
Since karma is indeed beginningless, it would continue to exist without that respective experience;
therefore, Śambhu is the benefactor who, being the Lord and imperishable, enables its exhaustion for the sake of that experience.
He swiftly brings about the production of subtle instruments and worlds;
for an effect is never seen to exist without an agent, material cause, and instruments.
In this context, the powers (śaktis) are the instrument, and Māyā is held to be the material cause;
for Śivā is eternal, one, and by virtue of her power, she is indeed without beginning or end.
She is indeed common to all men and the cause of the worlds;
by her own nature she generates delusion through the karmas born of one's own consciousness.
The all-pervading, subtle, and supreme Māyā is indeed distinct from its transformations;
having observed the karmas and agitated Māyā with his powers, the Lord of Knowledge [acts].
In the beginning, she who consists of manifold powers creates the principle of time and fashions bodies and instruments for the sake of the enjoyment of living beings. (NarP 1.63.46)
If this world, which is both yet-to-be and already-existent, undergoes dissolution,
then Māyā immediately gives birth to the power whose nature is that of a regulator.
She governs everything; therefore she is known as Niyati (the Ordainer). And immediately following her is Māyā, who is eternal and the deluder of the universe.
The reality that is without beginning or end also generates that which is called *kalā*;
for by means of this, it first imparts *mala* to human beings.
It manifests the power of the agent; therefore, this is called *kalā*.
And by means of *kāla* (time), together with *niyati* (destiny) which has attained the state of an affliction (*upasarga*), [it functions].
Furthermore, she performs her own activity as far as the earth extends,
for the purpose of manifesting objects to the person.
Indeed, it is Kala alone that brings forth the principle known as Vidyā, which is of the nature of light;
for Vidyā, through its own function, pierces the veil of the power of knowledge.
For this [intellect] displays objects by means of its own partial form;
therefore, it indeed makes those objects into things to be enjoyed by means of the supreme instrument.
The Puruṣa, whose power has been awakened, impels the principles beginning with Mahat;
that [power] is indeed the instrument for the experiencer to experience the object of experience, which is directed toward that [Puruṣa].
The manifestation of the object of experience as an object of experience for the enjoyer is called "experience" (bhoga);
in brief, it is the intellect (buddhi) in the form of pleasure and so forth, assuming the form of the object. (NarP 1.63.55)
That instrument called knowledge belongs to both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment;
for although the intellect is luminous like the sun, it is nevertheless an object [of cognition]. (NarP 1.63.56)
And that [power], being dependent on other instruments,
is capable of making him perceive [objects] due to its connection with causes such as the sense organs, and because it is impelled by a longing for his experience.
Moreover, through its connection with the eightfold fruits, its agency is fully established;
for if its lack of agency were accepted, its so-called status as an enjoyer would be in vain.
Furthermore, in that case, all the activities of the Pradhāna would be rendered useless,
since the Puruṣa is devoid of agency and thus provides no motive for the instruments and other factors.
Therefore, since enjoyment is impossible [without it], that very [avidyā] is the impeller here;
its status as the user of the instruments and so forth is held to be due to knowledge alone.
Immediately thereafter, it produces the passion of *kalā*, which brings about the form of the differentiated body (*bhidyaṅgarūpaka*);
by means of this, she is generated for the sake of enjoyment within the person (*puruṣa*) who possesses the differentiated body.
Because activity proceeds from that, it is designated as "passion" (rāga);
and when [the self] is delimited by these principles during the state of being an enjoyer, [it is called the individual soul].
Then this eternal Self receives the designation "Person" (puruṣa);
subsequently, Māyā alone brings forth the unmanifest for his enjoyment.
The cause of the manifestation of the sevenfold qualities is that non-differentiation of the *guṇas* which exists here in the substratum, like the constituent parts of earth and the other elements.
Moreover, that which is their substratum is sung as the Unmanifest (avyakta);
for the three qualities (guṇas) themselves arise from the Unmanifest alone.

Intellect (buddhi) consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; it is characterized by the determination of its functions and has the nature of the ascertainment of objects through the qualities.
That [ahaṃkāra] is also said to be threefold according to its qualities and in accordance with its functions;
from the principle of mahat, ahaṃkāra was born, characterized by the activity of impulsive exertion (saṃrambha).
Through its manifestation, this object attains the state of being fit for conventional usage;
furthermore, it becomes threefold by way of a twofold division of sentient beings.
By name, they are the Taijasa, the Rājasa, and the Tāmasa;
among these, from the Taijasa arise the organs of knowledge together with the mind.
Because they are associated with luminosity (*prakāśa*), they are indeed the means of cognition;
and because they are characterized by activity (*rājasa*) and serve as the cause of action, they are the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
From the *tamas* [quality] itself, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which are the sources of the gross elements, are born;
and therein, the mind indeed possesses the nature of desire and the function of volition.
That mind has a twofold function: it is the enjoyer and the producer of enjoyment, since it always exists externally through its own appropriate state as the sense organs.
Furthermore, by means of the internal activity of volition (saṃkalpa), it brings about the capacity of the senses;
therefore, the mind (manas) is the internal organ. (NarP 1.63.73)
The internal instrument called *manas*, *ahaṃkāra*, and *buddhi* exists in threefold form;
its functions, however, are respectively known as desire (*icchā*), exertion (*saṃraṃbha*), and cognition (*bodha*).
The organs of knowledge are the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose;
and their objects to be grasped, O Sage, are to be known as sound and the rest.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are considered the objects beginning with sound;
while speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are the organs of action.
In the activities of speaking, taking, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure, the instruments are established;
there is no action without instruments.
The activity of the ten organs is brought about by entering into the object;
however, the organs themselves act by taking hold of the object through their pervasive power.

The subtle elements (tanmātras), however, are indeed fivefold: ether, air, fire, water, and earth; from these, the gross elements (bhūtas) arise, each possessing one additional quality [than its predecessor]. // NarP_1,63.79 //
Thus, among these five [senses], this [sense of] sound [perceives] the four primary elements;
touch [perceives] three; form and taste [perceive] two; and likewise, smell [perceives] only the earth.
Their duties are said to be, in due order: providing space, the arrangement of battle arrays, cooking, gathering, and maintaining [the army]. (NarP 1.63.81)
Cold and heat are great instruments of sound; cold and heat belong to water and fire respectively.
In the sun and fire it is bright, in water it is white, and on earth it is manifold, such as white and other colors.
Form resides in the three [elements]; taste is in water and is sweet; on earth it is of six kinds.
Smell is proclaimed to exist in earth, being both unpleasant and pleasant.
That [tanmātra] possesses the quality of that [element], serves as an instrument, and likewise provides nourishment;
however, this is the distinction of the element (bhūta), whereas that [tanmātra] is devoid of such distinctions.
These five elements are situated everywhere;
the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of these five elements.
First, their presence within the body is examined:
in the body, the bones, flesh, hair, skin, nails, and teeth are composed of earth.
The presence of water is observed in urine, blood, phlegm, sweat, semen, and so forth;
fire resides in the heart, the bowels, and the eyes, because their respective properties are perceived there.
And the vital air (vāyu) is established here through the distinctions of its functions, such as prāṇa and the rest;
while space (viyat) resides in all the channels (nāḍī) by virtue of its connection with the activity within the womb.
This means of achieving the purpose of the rod, extending from the instigator to the edge of the earth,
is determined according to the specific enjoyment of each individual.
Indeed, these principles beginning with Kalā, being restricted to each individual soul,
circulate through all bodies according to the power of karma.
And this is the bond of Māyā by which this world is enveloped;
therefore, this impure path extends from the earth up to Kalā.
Therein, that which resides upon the circle of the earth consists of both the immobile and the mobile;
the immobile comprises mountains, trees, and so forth, while the mobile is further divided into three kinds.
Those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and likewise those born from a womb—
among moving and non-moving beings, there are eighty-four hundred thousand species of birth.
Wandering among those [realms], the living being sometimes attains a human body by the power of karma— a supreme form that accomplishes all goals.
Even there, in the land of Bhārata and within families such as those of the Brāhmaṇas, birth occurs only through the power of great merit; it is difficult to attain.
And birth is the union of male and female resulting from the union of semen and blood;
when that single drop enters the womb, it becomes dual in nature.
Then, if the female element (rajas) predominates, a woman is born; if the male element (retas) predominates, a man is born.
Some self (ātman) is constrained by the fetters of impurity, karma, and so forth.
Then, within that [embryo], the whole [being] attains the state of a living soul (jīva).
Thereafter, it is nourished by the portions of food, drink, and other sustenance brought to it.
For here the body grows over the course of weeks, months, and so forth;
it is afflicted by suffering and the like, its form enveloped by the fetal membrane.
Thus situated there in the womb, remembering the auspicious and inauspicious deeds arising from his previous birth, he remains in a state of suffering, being tormented again and again.
In the course of time, even while causing pain to his mother, that infant,
being himself tormented, emerges headfirst from the mechanism of the womb.
For a moment he remains motionless, and then he desires to weep;
thereafter, that infant gradually grows day by day.
Through the divisions of infancy and childhood, one attains youth;
in this manner, the birth of the bodies of embodied beings occurs in this world through a gradual process.
Having obtained this human birth, which is difficult to attain and beneficial to all the world,
who could be more sinful than he who does not deliver himself?
Food, sleep, fear, and sexual intercourse—
these are said to be common to all beings, including even the beasts and other animals.
He who is attached to these four alone is indeed a fool and a destroyer of his own self;
for such is the nature of men, consisting as it does in the cutting of bonds and fetters.
The severing of the bonds of the noose arises through initiation alone;
therefore, for the sake of cutting these bonds, one should perform the initiation of mantra.
For one whose bonds have been destroyed by the power known as initiation and knowledge,
and who is named the pure reality of the self, attains the state of nirvāṇa.
With a vision consisting of his own power, he meditates upon and beholds Śiva;
for the benefit of himself and others, he worships Śiva with mantras.
With the eye of consciousness empowered by the rays of the power of Śiva’s sun,
one whose internal obscurations have ceased perceives [reality] together with Śiva, Śakti, and the others.
The modification of the internal organ known as cognition is not capable of manifesting the Great Lord, because it is a fetter, like shackles and the like. (NarP 1.63.111)
Initiation alone is the supreme cause for the severing of bonds;
therefore, one should perform the initiation into the mantra according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Having been initiated according to the tantric rules and being devoted to the conduct appropriate to his own caste,
he should perform the practice consisting of both the obligatory and the occasional rites.
One should not transgress, even in thought, the conduct prescribed for one's own caste and stage of life;
whatever initiation a person receives while remaining in a particular stage of life, [he must follow its rules].
He should dwell in that hermitage and observe its duties;
for even actions already performed do not lead to bondage.
However, one who has been initiated may desire the enjoyment of whatever worldly pleasures exist, through a single fruit-bearing action arising from the performance of mantras.
By the power of propitiating the mantra, one attains liberation after consuming that [fruit];
however, the man who, having received initiation, does not perform the daily and occasional rites, [does not attain it].
Having attained the state of a Piśāca for some time, he eventually attains liberation;
therefore, one who has been initiated should perform the obligatory, occasional, and other rites.
And by that, the performance of rituals is inferred for this person who, having received initiation,
is a protector of the constant and occasional conduct.
Due to the absence of any deficiency in initiation, immediate liberation arises;
even in that case, this attainment belongs to one who is devoted to the Guru, and not otherwise.
Through initiation, Śiva, who bestows grace upon all, resides within the form of the Guru;
yet for one whose devotion to the Guru is merely artificial, [the Guru] serves as an object of perception and so forth.
Even if he is devoted to his teacher through body, mind, and speech, his atonement for every step he takes will be in vain.
There is no need for expiation, and success is attained at every step,
for a disciple who is devoted to the guru and offers his very self as a gift.
But a teacher who employs mantras incorrectly shall be required to perform penance.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, [I shall describe that which] grants the attainment of desired goals for the purpose of severing the multitude of bonds of the individual soul (jīva).
I shall now proclaim the ritual procedure for initiation, which bestows the power of the mantra.
Because it bestows a divine state and destroys all evils, it is therefore called *dīkṣā* by those learned in all the Āgamas. (NarP 1.64.2)

Because it possesses the nature of reflecting upon all that is to be known, providing protection, and bestowing favor upon those who are to be disciplined, it is called a *mantra* due to its qualities of reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*). (NarP 1.64.3)
These mantras are considered to be of three kinds, consisting of female, male, and neuter natures:
female mantras end with *svāhā*, while male mantras end with *huṃ phaṭ*.
Those who are impotent and devoid of pride are remembered as the classes of mantras;
mantras whose deities are males are considered *mantras*, while those whose deities are females are regarded as *vidyās*.
Those six mantras are praised within the sequences; furthermore, they are of three kinds.
Among them, those beginning with *tāra* (oṃ), ending with *repha* (raḥ), and followed by *svāhā* are declared to be of the nature of fire (*āgneya*).
O Sage, those [mantras] which are rich in the seed-syllables of the nectar of Bhṛgu are said to be gentle;
thus, wise men should understand that mantras are indeed of the nature of both fire and moon.
The fiery [breaths] awaken when the wind has resorted to the Piṅgalā,
and the lunar ones awaken when the wind flows through the left.
All mantras awaken when the vital breath rests in both channels;
however, reciting a mantra during its period of sleep yields fruitless results.
Having uttered each mantra individually, one should utter those of the navigators;
in the case of favorability, they are joined with the nasal drop (bindu), and in the case of opposition, they are joined with the visarga.
If that mantra is recited while the deity is awakened, it bestows swift accomplishment;
even a malevolent mantra becomes effective when recited with this rosary.
The Āgneyas perform cruel deeds, while the Saumyas bestow gentle fruits;
they are endowed with the peaceful knowledge of the most fierce and the peaceful castes.
Even one who is peaceful becomes fierce through the addition of the sprouts *huṃ* and *phaṭ*;
those [mantras] possessed of defects such as being cut do not protect the practitioner at all.
Severed, obstructed, deprived of power, and then turned away; devoid of action, devoid of sight, as well as pinned down and paralyzed.
Burnt, fallen, terrified, soiled, and insulted;
pierced, fast asleep, intoxicated with pride, and fainted.
One whose vigor is destroyed, one with deluded perception, one who is ruined, as well as a child,
a youth, a young man, a mature adult, an old man, and likewise a cruel person.
One who is seedless, devoid of accomplishment, dull-witted, fraudulent, lacking constituent parts,
destitute of essence, squinting, and bereft of seed is considered base.
Embraced and deluded, afflicted by hunger and intensely burning;
deprived of limbs and exceedingly angry, as well as being ashamed in the midst of extreme cruelty.

One whose mind is tranquil, one who has fallen from his position, one who is likewise incapacitated, one who is very old, one who is utterly devoid of affection, and furthermore, one who is afflicted; NarP_1,64.19 //
These faults have indeed been fully described; now I shall state their characteristics, whether they are combined, separate, or joined with their own inherent nature in three ways.
That mantra whose beginning, middle, and end are said to contain the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ) in four or five ways is designated as "broken" (chinnasaṃjñaka).
That mantra in whose beginning, middle, and end the two seed-syllables of the earth (Bhū) are said to be present is known as "Ruddha"; indeed, it bestows accomplishment through extreme hardship.
Lakṣmī consists of three *tāra* syllables; thus, a mantra that is deficient in this regard should be known as lacking power, yielding fruit only after a long time.
The seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*) is at the beginning, *māyā* at the end, and likewise the goad (*aṅkuśa*);
this should be known as the "Averted Face" (*parāṅmukha*), which bestows long-lasting accomplishment upon those who worship it.
If the letter *sa* is seen at the beginning, middle, and end [of a mantra], that mantra is said to be "deaf"; it yields little fruit with great difficulty.
If the five-syllabled mantra lacks the form of the letter *ra*, the *ṛ*-vowel, and the nasal bindu, it should be known as "eyeless"; even with great effort, it does not bestow accomplishment.
At the beginning, middle, and end [of the mantra], there should be *haṃsa*, *prāsāda*, and *vāgbhava*;
or else *haṃsa* and *indu*, or the letter *sa*, or the letter *pha*, or again *varma*.
I bow to that state which is not reached and in which he is pinned;
likewise, there is a pair in the middle, and in the head are the letters *asra* and *lakāra*.
That mantra does not exist; it is paralyzed and acts as an obstacle to success, for the fire conjoined with the wind is situated at the head of that mantra.
That mantra which is seen with the vowel *ṛ* is designated as "burnt" (*dagdha*). An *astra-mantra* is seen to consist of two, three, six, or eight syllables.
That mantra should be known as "terrified" when it is devoid of the syllable *tāra* at its beginning;
for that very mantra is indeed "afraid," whether it begins with the letter *ha* or with *śakti*.
That mantra in which there are four instances of the letter *ma* at the beginning, middle, and end should be known as "defiled" (*malina*); indeed, it bestows accomplishment through extreme hardship.
That mantra in which there is the syllable *dāṛṇ* in the middle, likewise the pair of *krodha* at the head, and the *asra*, is declared to be "tiraskṛta" (suppressed).
If a mantra is split by having two *myo*s at the heart, *vaṣaṭ* at the head, and *vauṣaṭ* in the middle, it should be abandoned, as it yields afflicted results.

That which consists of three syllables and is devoid of the *haṃsa* is proclaimed to be the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*). Furthermore, the *vidyā* or the *mantra* may consist of seventeen syllables.
That mantra which consists of six syllables, five syllables, and so forth, is known as "intoxicated with pride" (madonmatta).
That mantra in whose middle the weapon-syllable (*astra*) is situated is known as "fainted" (*mūrcchita*).
And that blood which resides in the place of rest is said to have its vitality destroyed;
there are four such instances of blood at the beginning, the middle, and the head of the mantra.
It should be known that this mantra which consists of eighteen syllables, or again that which consists of twenty syllables and is joined with the word *smara*, is deluded. (NarP 1.64.38)
That which is enriched with the seed-syllables *hṛllekhā* and *kuṃśa* is called "destroyed. The seven-syllable mantra is that of Bāla, while the eight-syllable one belongs to Kumāra.
A sixteen-syllabled mantra is a youth; one of forty syllables is mature;
those of thirty, sixty-four, and even one hundred syllables are likewise [mature]. (NarP 1.64.40)
The mantra of four hundred syllables is called "the aged" (vṛddha); the nine-syllable mantra joined with the *tāra* is called "the sword" (nistriṃśa). (NarP 1.64.41)
That [mantra] at the end of which the *hṛdaya* is declared, and the *śiras-mantra* is situated in the middle;
that at the end of which the *śikhā*, *varma*, *netra*, and *astra* are seen.
A mantra that is devoid of the syllables *Śiva* (Om) and *Śakti* (Hrīṃ) is known as "seedless" (*nirbīja*).
That mantra in which the sound *phaṭ* is seen six times—at the beginning, the end, and in the middle—is [also considered such].
That mantra which lacks perfection is dull; a mantra of ten syllables is called a *paṅkti*.
A one-syllable mantra is called a *kūṭa*, and it is said to be partless (*niraṃśaka*).
He may have two castes and be devoid of essence; he may be squint-eyed and possess four syllables;
or he may have six syllables and be devoid of seed-syllables, or even possess seven and a half syllables.
Alternatively, that mantra consists of twelve and a half syllables; when it is smoky and marked with a dot, it consists of twenty syllables, joined with three and a half seed-syllables.
That mantra which consists of thirty syllables or twenty-one syllables and is embraced by the *ārligita* is proclaimed to be "deluded" (*mohita*). NarP_1,64.47 //
One who has twenty-four syllables or twenty-seven syllables should be known as afflicted by hunger, and is devoid of mantra-siddhi.
Whether it consists of eleven syllables, twenty-five letters,
or twenty-three letters, that mantra is known by the name Dṛpta.
A mantra that consists of twenty-six syllables, or even one marked by thirty-six syllables,
or one of twenty-nine syllables, is considered to have deficient limbs.
One consisting of twenty-eight syllables or likewise thirty-one syllables should be known as excessively cruel; it is censured for all ritual acts.
That man who has a lifespan beginning from forty years and ending at sixty-three should be known as "ashamed" (vrīḍita); he is not capable for any ritual actions.
Mantras of sixty-five syllables should be known as those that pacify the mind;
they range from fifty-six syllables up to ninety-nine syllables.
O Lord of Sages, those mantras which have fallen from their proper place should be understood as such;
likewise, those mantras that consist of thirteen syllables, and again those that consist of the number of syllables equal to the lunar days (fifteen).
These have been declared as the *vikāsas* by those proficient in all tantras;
they number one hundred, or one hundred and fifty, or even two hundred.
Those mantras whose number of syllables is ninety-two, eighty-nine, or even three hundred are proclaimed to be "without affection" (niḥsneha). (NarP 1,64.56)
O twice-born one, those beginning from four hundred and extending up to a thousand syllables are declared to be excessively large and ineffective in their application.
Those mantras that exceed one thousand syllables are called *pīḍita*;
and those mantras which consist of hymns (*stotra*) are known as being even more than that.
Such are the Manus described as being possessed of defects;
those who, without understanding these defects, mutter these mantras [are likewise flawed]. (NarP 1.64.59)
Success does not arise for them even in hundreds of millions of eons.
I shall now describe the practice of mantras that have been corrupted by defects such as being broken.
Whoever, remaining composed, recites any mantra whatsoever while seated in the *yonimudrā* posture, for him all accomplishments (*siddhis*) shall come to pass.
Placing the left heel at the anus and the right one upon the penis—
this is the binding of the *yonimudrā*, which constitutes the supreme posture (*āsana*).
There is yet another method here regarding the binding of the *yonimudrā*;
I shall explain that to you, along with its secret, O Nārada, in its proper sequence.
Having attained [the teaching] through the lineage succession, devoted to constant practice, intent on the permission of the guru, illustrious, and endowed with initiation; NarP_1,64.64 //
Handsome, pleasant-faced, tranquil, of noble birth, easy to approach, and self-controlled;
he knows the true meaning of mantra and tantra, and is capable of both subduing and favoring others.
The sage is indifferent, self-controlled, a speaker of what is beneficial, and discerning;
he is skilled in extracting the essential truth, disciplined, and well-attired.
One who belongs to a stage of life (āśramin), is devoted to meditation, possesses an intellect that cuts through doubt,
and is engaged in constant practice is proclaimed to be a teacher (ācārya).
Peaceful, disciplined, pure in soul, and endowed with all auspicious marks;
possessed of the means such as tranquility and the like, full of faith, and of very firm resolve.
One whose body is purified by food, drink, and other necessities, who is righteous and pure in mind, firm in the practice of his vows, grateful, and fearful of sin; NarP_1,64.69 //
A disciple should be one whose mind is intent on devotion to the guru, meditation upon him, praise of him, and service to him; otherwise, such a person brings suffering to the guru.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having examined the disciple, the preceptor should perform the purification of the mantra.
One should lay down five lines: eastward, westward, southward, and northward.
In this manner, there shall be four groups of four in the royal chamber;
therein, the first [group] is in the first [cell], and the second [group] is in the first [cell] of the second [row].
The third [syllable] should be in the first of the third [row], and the fourth [syllable] in the first of the fourth;
likewise, the respective fifth syllable is in the fire-pits (āgneya-koṣṭha) of those [rows].
Having written [the syllables] in sequence, the wise one should then purify the mantra,
beginning from the first letter of the name up to the initial letter of the mantra.

In a group of four, where there is a letter of the name, that shall be the first, the "group of four for accomplishment" (siddhicatuṣka); moving clockwise from that, the second is proclaimed as the one called "the goal" (sādhya).
The third is called *siddha* when it occurs in a male [letter], and the fourth is designated as *ari*;
when two letters are in a single square, that is considered to be *siddhasiddha*.
In the second syllable of the mantra, it is proclaimed that the subject is *siddhasādhya*;
in the third, he is *susiddha*; and in the fourth, he is a *siddhāri*.
From the fourth syllable of the name, however, [one should proceed] to the second mantra-syllable;
if it is within that fourth group, then it is where the letter of the name was previously situated.
There, beginning from that very square, one should count in the same sequence as before:
Sādhya, Siddha, Sādhyasādhya, Susiddha, and Tadripu.
If, however, in the third tetrad there should be a description of the mantra,
then this should be understood by the wise in sequence according to the method previously stated.
The Susiddha, Siddha, Sādhya, and Susiddha are the Ṛṣis of that [mantra];
in the fourth group of four, the wise one should count them in this manner.
The enemy-successful (arisiddha), the enemy-to-be-accomplished (arisādhya), its well-accomplished (tatsusiddha), and its enemy (tadripu);
likewise, the accomplished-successful (ṛddhasiddha) and that which has success to be accomplished through double the stated [time]. NarP_1,65.12 //
A *siddha* [mantra] brings success through its excellence; a *susiddha*, by its loftiness; a *siddhāri* destroys those born of the same lineage;
a *sādhya-siddha* achieves results through double the effort; and a *sādhya-sādhya* accomplishes them only with great delay.
A *sādhya* [mantra] becomes well-accomplished (*susiddha*) through double the recitation; a *sādhya-ari* (enemy of the *sādhya*) destroys one's kinsmen.
A *susiddha-siddha* [mantra] is attained by doubling that [recitation], and its *sādhya* counterpart is attained by doubling that [latter] recitation.
From the mere attainment of a Susiddha [planet], one becomes a Susiddhāri who supports his family;
however, an Ari-siddha destroys one's sons, while an Ari-śādhyaka causes the loss of one's daughters.
When that [planet] is well-placed, it destroys the wife; when it is ill-placed, it is remembered as an enemy even to the practitioner himself.
O Sage, indeed there are many other such varieties here as well.
This one called Kathaha is declared by you to be the foremost among all;
having thus purified the mantra, at a pure time and likewise in a pure place—
The Guru shall initiate the disciple; that procedure is now declared. Having performed the daily rites and having prostrated before the Guru’s sandals, [he should proceed].
One should earnestly seek a true guru with devotion for the sake of attaining one's desired goal,
having honored him with garments, ornaments, cattle, gold, land, and other gifts.
Having performed the rites for well-being and the preparation of the mandala and so forth, the Guru, being satisfied and pure, shall enter the sacrificial hall together with his disciple.
Then, having sprinkled the door with the general *argha* water while reciting the *astra-mantra*,
one should dispel the divine obstacles situated in the sky by honoring them with water.
Then, having struck the earth with three blows of the heel, one should perform the ritual action upon the *sarvatobhadra* [mandala] prepared with pigments as previously described.
Having worshipped the fire-maṇḍala and fully honored its constituent digits (kalās),
one should place a water-pot that has been cleansed with the weapon-mantra (astra) and fashioned according to one's capacity.
Having established [the deity] there according to the rules, one should worship a portion of the Sun there,
reciting the root mantra of the reverse-order alphabet while using pure water.
Having filled the water-pot there, one should worship the digits of Soma according to the rules:
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī.
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and Havyakavyavahā—these are declared to be the ten kalās of Agni. Now, the kalās of the Sun are described.
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci,
Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
Then the portions of Indra are to be known as Amṛtā, Mānadā,
Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and the one named Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā,
Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, and Cetī are declared to be the digits (kalās) of the moon.
Having wrapped it with a pair of garments, one should place all the medicinal herbs therein;
having cast in the nine jewels, one should set down five sprouts.
They know them as the jackfruit, mango, banyan, holy fig, and vakula;
and [the gems] pearl, ruby, lapis lazuli, gomedaka, diamond, and coral.
Having thus deposited the gems— ruby, emerald, and sapphire— in their respective order, one should invoke the chosen deity there.
Having worshipped according to the rules, the mantra-practitioner then causes the well-adorned disciple to lie down upon the altar, sprinkling him with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth upon that body according to the prescribed rules,
and having purified it with the network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*), one should place the sprouts upon the head.
Then, having consecrated them with the root mantra one hundred and eight times,
he should sprinkle his beloved disciple while reciting the root mantra in his heart.
Having sipped the remaining water and put on his garment,
the pure child, having prostrated before the teacher according to the rule, should sit down in front of him.
Then, having placed his hand upon the head of the disciple, the guru should subsequently recite the mantra to be imparted one hundred and eight times according to the prescribed rite.
He should utter the syllables "May there be equality," and then the disciple should worship the guru; then, having placed his hand, adorned with sandalwood paste, upon the head of the disciple.
With a concentrated mind, one should whisper the vidyā into his ear eight times;
having received the vidyā, the disciple should also prostrate at the feet of the guru.
Arise, my child; you are liberated. Be one who practices right conduct.
May fame, prosperity, beauty, sons, long life, strength, and health always be yours.
Then the disciple, having risen, should worship the guru with fragrances and other offerings,
and should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), free from any stinginess regarding his wealth.
Having thus obtained the mantra from the guru, from that time forward one should be devoted to the service of the guru with wealth and other means, as well as with one's own body, sons, and wife.
Having offered a handful of flowers in the center to one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva),
one should then worship Agni, Nairṛti, and Vāgīśa in sequence.
When one worships Viṣṇu in the center and Vināyaka, Ravi, Śivā, and Śiva in the outer directions and so forth; or when one worships Śaṅkara in the center [and the others accordingly].
When one worships Ravi, Gaṇeśa, Ambā, Hari, and Śivā, as well as Īśa, Vighna, Arka, and Govinda, with Gaṇanāyaka in the center; 65.45.
When the Sun is situated in the middle [of the zodiac], one should again worship Śiva, Śivā, Ravi, and Viṣṇu;
furthermore, when it is in Gaṇeśa, one should worship Viṣṇu, Ambā, and Śiva, in that respective order.
Thus, having constantly and respectfully worshipped the five deities,
the wise man, rising during the Brāhma-muhūrta, should perform his necessary duties.
Or, while lying on his bed without apprehension, he should meditate upon the white thousand-petaled lotus situated at the crown of his own head, within a circle of light rays.

The Guru is situated in the triangle of Akathādi, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he has two eyes and two arms, and is adorned with white perfumes, garlands, and unguents.
Having meditated upon [the deity] on the left joined with Śakti, and having worshipped him with mental offerings,
the wise one should mutter the Pādukā mantra ten times.

Or [the mantra] is *vā*, *māyā* (hrīṃ), *śrī* (śrīṃ), *bhaga* (bhaga), *indu* (oṃ), and *āḍhyā*; then *viyat* (ha), *haṃsa* (sa), *khakāgni* (kha-ra), *hasa-kṣa-ma-la-va*, *āri* (ya), *agni* (ra), *vāmakarṇa* (u), *idu-yugma* (i-i), and *rut* (sa). 65.51.
Then [the syllables] are BHRŪṂ, Ā, KHĀ, RA, VA, AGNI (RA), BHAGA (LA), INDU (SA), and ĀḌHYA (HA); the final one is PARENTIMA (PHA).
Then MARUT (YA) is joined with SA, KṢA, MALA (MA), TOYA (VA), AGNI (RA), CANDRA (SA), ŚĀNTI (ŚA), and YUTA (HA). NarP_1,65.52.
Then, at the end of "Śrī," [one says] "Nandanātha [Name]," and again at the end of "Devyaṃbā," one worships Śrī Pāṇḍukā with "Hṛt" at the end.
This is the Śrīpādukā mantra, which bestows all accomplishments upon men;
having offered it with the word "guhya," the wise one should then pay homage with these mantras.
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed— the state whose unbroken, circular form pervades all that is moving and unmoving.
Salutation to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge.
Homage be to that Guru, who is the very embodiment of the chosen deity,
whose nectar-like speech destroys the poison known as saṃsāra.
Having thus bowed, one should recite this hymn which produces immediate conviction:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O Lord, the Blessed One, Śiva in the form of the Guru. (NarP 1.65.58)

To the one who has assumed many forms for the sake of successfully bringing about the descent of knowledge, who possesses a youthful bodily form, yet whose true nature is the singular ultimate reality— NarP_1,65.59.

Salutations to You, the Sun who shatters the darkness of all ignorance, the mass of consciousness, whose sovereignty is self-dependent, whose form is fashioned by compassion, and whose nature is Śiva.
Salutations to You, who protect devotees in the hereafter; to You whose nature is pure being; to You who grant discernment to the discerning, and reflection to those possessed of reflective insight.
Salutations to you, who are the illumination of illuminations and the embodiment of knowledge for the wise; salutations to you in front, on both sides, behind, above, and below.
Always establish your seat through your nature as pure existence and consciousness;
by your grace, O Lord, I am one who has accomplished all that was to be done in every respect.
"I am liberated from the great noose of illusion and death; I am Śiva unto you.
Having thus offered praise, one should then present everything to the Guru. (NarP 1.65.64)
O Lord of the World, whatever I do from morning until evening, and from evening until morning, let that be an act of worship unto You.
Then, with the stream of nectar falling from the lotus feet of the Guru,
the wise one should contemplate his own self as washed clean and stainless.
One should contemplate the Root-Vidyā from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Below the root-support (mūlādhāra), there is a circular mandala of wind.
And by means of the wind arising from the seed-syllable of wind situated there,
that upper [space] becomes a triangular mandala of fire, originating from the seed-syllable of fire situated therein.
By the fire that has arisen, she whose form resides in the *mūlādhāra*,
who has the shape of a sleeping serpent, and who encircles the self-existent *liṅga* [is awakened].

Having meditated upon the Kulakuṇḍalinī, who resembles a lotus fiber, who has the luster of ten million flashes of lightning, and who is exceedingly subtle, one should raise her up with the *kūrca* mantra.

The wise one should lead that [consciousness] through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, which pierces the sequence of the six chakras, to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) according to the method taught by the Guru.
Remaining there, one should contemplate oneself as immersed in nectar,
completely pervaded by its mass of radiance— immaculate, consisting of consciousness, and supreme.

Having led her back to her own place while meditating on the deity within the heart, and having beheld her with mental offerings, one should pray with this mantra: NarP_1,65.73: "O Goddess, you who are the supreme power (śakti) of the Lord of the gods, who are the source of all mantras and the bestower of all boons; O Mother, grant me success. O Goddess, you who are the supreme power (śakti) of the Lord of the gods, who are the source of all mantras and the bestower of all boons; O Mother, grant me success."
O primordial God, O Śrīnātha Viṣṇu, who consists of the consciousness of the three worlds, by your very command,
having risen this morning for your pleasure, I shall follow the course of worldly existence.
O Brahmin, in the place where "of Viṣṇu" occurs, a modification must be made for other deities;
thereafter, one should perform the offering of the *ajapā* [mantra] for the sake of attaining all accomplishments.
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times, day and night, the living being constantly mutters the Gāyatrī known as the *ajapā*. NarP_1,65.76 //
The seer is Haṃsa, the meter is said to be Avyaktagātrī, and the deity is Paramahaṃsa; at the beginning and end are the seed-syllable and the power-syllable.
Then one should perform the six-limbed yoga: Sūrya, Soma, Nirañjana, Nirābhāsa, Dharma, and likewise Jñāna.
O best of practitioners, one should sequentially apply these mantras— beginning with *haṃsa* and ending with the ātmanepada suffixes— conjoined with the [six] births, to the six limbs.
The letter *ha*, possessing a splendor like that of the sun, goes outward;
the letter *sa* is likewise described as the meditation during the inward entry.

Having meditated thus, the wise one should offer [the oblation] sequentially into the fires and suns within the four-petaled *mūlādhāra*, which is endowed with the seed-syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*.
To the one who has the luster of a bandhūka flower, who is accompanied by his own power (Śakti), and who is for the sake of his own body;
to the one whose hands display the noose, the goad, the vessel of nectar, and the modaka sweetmeat.
One should offer six hundred [lotuses] to Gaṇeśa, the Lord of Speech,
in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], which is ruby-colored and joined with the letters from *va* to *la*.

To him who is joined with the Śakti on his left side, likewise to the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipati), whose arms are adorned with a sacrificial ladle and a rosary, and who is born from the lotus; NarP_1,65.84.
One should offer six thousand [verses] to Brahmā mounted upon a swan,
on a leaf inscribed with the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, which has the luster of clouds flashing with lightning.
And at Maṇipūra, one should offer six thousand [oblations] to Viṣṇu, who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, and who is accompanied by Śrī.
On the unstruck (anāhata) lotus-petal, joined with the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*,
[he is] white, holding a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, the gesture of granting boons, and a jar.
On the left side, the wise one should offer six thousand [recitations] to Rudra, who is mounted upon a bull, the Lord of Knowledge, and endowed with Śakti.

Then, [one should worship] the Lord of the Senses, who is pure, possesses sixteen petals enriched with vowels, is white and free from blemish, and is the manifestation of great light. // NarP_1,65.89 //
One should offer a thousand [oblations] to the Moving One (Carāya) joined with the power of breath (Prāṇa-śakti),
and a thousand in the lotus of two petals at the Ājñā-cakra, which is joined with the letters *ha* and *kṣa*.
Salutation indeed to the Guru Sadāśiva, who is united with the Supreme Power (Parāśakti),
within the great thousand-petaled lotus endowed with both Nāda and Bindu.
One should offer a thousand [oblations] to the radiant syllables of the Mātṛkās, to the one who holds the best weapon in his hand, and to the supreme, primordial Guru.
Having again taken water in the hollowed palms, [the results] are accomplished by their very nature through twenty-one thousand recitations. (NarP 1.65.93)
"May Viṣṇu, the bestower of liberation through the mental resolve regarding this Ajapā [mantra] numbering six hundred and more, be pleased with me. (NarP 1.65.94)
By the mere resolve of this [mantra], one is liberated from great sins:
"I am Brahman alone, not a transmigrating being; eternally liberated, I am not subject to sorrow. (NarP 1.65.95)
One should contemplate: "I am the Self, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Thereafter, one should perform bodily duties as well as the worship of the deity.
I shall now proclaim that injunction, which is the defining characteristic of right conduct.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.

"May the sages, the gods, the piśācas, and those who are guhyakas depart."
"O all you hosts of ancestors and spirits, I shall perform the release of impurity.
Having said this, he should strike three claps of the palms and cover his head with a cloth.
Facing south at night and facing north during the day,
one should discharge waste and then perform purification with earth and water.

seven on both hands, and three times each on the two feet.

One should not use a tooth-stick that is too rough, nor one that is too smooth. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too uneven, nor one that is too even. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too jagged, nor one that is too smooth. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too thick, nor one that is too thin. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too long, nor one that is too short. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too curved, nor one that is too straight. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too brittle, nor one that is too flexible. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too coarse, nor one that is too fine. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too rough, nor one that is too smooth. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too hard, nor one that is too soft. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too dry, nor one that is too moist. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too hot, nor one that is too cold. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too large, nor one that is too small. One should not use a tooth-stick that is too heavy, nor one that is too light. One should not use a tooth-st
O Lord of the Forest, grant us longevity, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, wealth, prosperity, wisdom, and intelligence.
Having thus made this prayer, the practitioner, being composed, should take a tooth-stick measuring twelve finger-breadths and perform [the ritual] with the Kāma-mantra.

The word for Kāmadeva ending in the suffix *ṅe*, likewise "beloved by all people" (*sarvajanapriya*), with the heart-mantra at its end enriched by the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*); with this, one should purify the teeth. (NarP 1.66.10)
Having cleansed the tongue with the *vāgbhava* syllable and washed the mouth with the root mantra,
one should then go to the temple of the deity and remove the previous offerings (*nirmālya*).
Having put on clean garments, one should perform the auspicious *ārārtika* rite;
having sprinkled the vessel with water while reciting the root mantra, one should kindle it.
Having performed worship and taken up the vessel, he should rise and ring the bell while a lamp of pure cow-ghee is waved all around.
With musical instruments and pleasing songs, the waving of lights (ārārtika) for the God shall take place;
thus, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and having prayed to one's own Lord, [one should proceed]. (NarP 1.66.14)
One should go to a river or similar body of water to bathe while reciting the qualities of the deities;
having reached the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and offered salutations, one should indeed set aside the materials for bathing.
Taking earth consecrated with the root mantra from the region of the waist, one should smear it down to the feet and then wash it off with water from a sacred bathing place.
Then, having washed his feet with the five [substances], he should enter the water again until it reaches his navel, and [take] earth for his left hand.
Having likewise applied [the mantra] to the wrist, the palm of the hand, and again to the tips of the fingers,
he should then take up the Ganges-mud with his finger while reciting the Astra-mantra.
The wise knower of mantras, having rotated it above himself, should cast it away;
he should then smear that which stands on the ground with those mantras upon the six limbs.
Having immersed oneself, one should wash thoroughly; this is called the "impurity bath.
Then, having meditated upon everything as consisting of the Desired (the Self), one should perform the internal bath.

Having meditated upon the Lord, whose form is the mantra, who is infinite, radiant as the sun, and endowed with his own ornaments and weapons, [one should contemplate] that which arises from the water of his feet.
And with that stream entering his own body through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
he should wash away all impurity located within the body.
At that very moment, the mantra-practitioner becomes free from passion and resembles crystal;
then, having bathed according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas, the practitioner remains composed.
Thereafter, one should perform the mantra-bath; its procedure is now described:
having proclaimed the place and time, [one should proceed] with the six ancillaries of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having formed the *muṣṭi-mudrā* from the solar disc, one should invoke the sacred fords (*tīrthas*):
"O Sun, the sacred fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays."
By that truth, O God, O Sun, grant me access to the sacred ford.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters! NarP_1,66.27
Having thus invoked them into the water, one should unite them with the seed-syllable of nectar (*sudhā-bīja*);
having rendered them immortal by means of the cow-seal (*gomudrā*), one should veil them with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).
Having protected it with the weapon-mantra, he should thereafter display the wheel-mudrā;
there, the wise one should visualize the mandalas of fire, sun, and moon.
One should consecrate that water eleven times with the mantra of the Sun, the seed-syllable of nectar (sudhā-bīja), and the root-mantra; having thus consecrated it, one should meditate upon it.
And having invoked the deity from within one's own heart into the worship-diagram (pūjāyantra) in its center,
one should bathe and worship that deity with mental offerings.
Having bowed to her seated upon the lion-throne, the wise man should bow to that water,
which is the support of all beings and of Viṣṇu of incomparable splendor.
"I bow down to those waters which have arisen from that [seed] and possess its form.
Having thus bowed and restrained the seven apertures, the practitioner [proceeds].
Having immersed oneself in that water, one should contemplate the root-form of the deity;
having thus immersed and emerged three times, one should sprinkle [the head] with the *kumbha-mudrā*.
One should consecrate one’s own body three times with the root mantra and four times with the four mantras; O Sage, those four mantras according to the Tantra are now being told.
May the divine waters, the mothers of all beings, purify me— the pure seed of Prajāpati who repeatedly desires to emit the entire universe.
Alakṣmī, who is of the nature of impurity and resides within all beings—the waters, the goddesses, wash her away by their touch; may they purify me.
Whatever ill fortune is in my hair, at the parting of my hair, or on my head;
whatever is on my forehead, in my ears, or in my eyes—may the waters destroy that; salutations to you.
May longevity, health, sovereignty, the destruction of the faction of enemies, auspiciousness, contentment, forbearance, faith, and knowledge be yours; salutations to you!
Having drunk the water from the feet of a Brahmin, one should drink the water from a Śālagrāma stone;
one must not drink [ordinary] water [in their presence], for this is the fixed rule regarding them.
Whatever holy places exist on earth, they reside in the right foot of the Brahmin;
having mentally dismissed one's chosen deity into the orb of the sun, the practitioner [should proceed].
Then, having come to the bank and having diligently washed his garment,
the wise man, having put on two clean clothes, should perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and other rites.
If a person is unable due to illness or other causes, he should perform the expiation for that sin there;
or else, if he is incapable, he may bathe with ashes or with dust.
Then, having sat upon an auspicious seat, he should perform the twilight rites and other duties,
[reciting] with Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, and Mādhava.
Having sipped water, one should wash both hands for Govinda and Viṣṇu;
one should cleanse the lips for Madhusūdana and Trivikrama.
Then one should touch the face with Vāmana and Śrīdhara, and thereafter touch the two hands with Hṛṣīkeśa and Padmanābha; then one should touch the feet.
Then he should touch the head with Dāmodara, the mouth with Saṃkarṣaṇa,
and the two nostrils with Vāsudeva and Pradyumna.
Then one should touch the two eyes with Aniruddha and Puruṣottama;
likewise, one should touch the two ears with Adhokṣaja and Nṛsiṃha.
One should touch the navel with Acyuta, the chest with Janārdana, and the shoulders with Hari and Viṣṇu; this indeed is the Vaiṣṇava sipping of water (ācamana).
With the names beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ), ending in the nasal *ṅ*, and concluding with *svāhā*, starting from Keśava and the others,
[one should touch] the mouth, the two nostrils with the index and ring fingers, and the eyes and ears.
With the little finger, one should touch the region of the navel; in all cases, the joining of the thumbs is prescribed.
This Śaiva rite is said to be performed with the principles (tattvas) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, ending with "svāhā."

One should drink water with the mantras beginning with *dīrgha*, *traya*, *indu*, *yuga*, and *vyoma*, using *ātman*, *vidyā*, and *śiva* as the suffixes, ending with *svāhā*. This is the Śaiva [mantra]. (NarP 1,66.52)

That which is uttered with the words *vāc*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ* at the beginning and ending with *svāhā* is declared to be Śākta; that which is uttered with *vāc*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ* at the beginning is said to be the sipping of water (*ācamana*) by the twice-born, which bestows wealth.
Then one should apply a tilaka mark on the forehead in the excellent shape of a mace (gadā),
the sword Nandaka on the heart, and the conch and discus on the two arms.
The wise practitioner should then place the Śārṅga bow and arrow sequentially upon the head,
at the base of the ears, on both sides, on the back, at the navel, and also on the hump.
In this manner, a Vaiṣṇava should perform [the rite] with earth from sacred fords and the like;
having taken the ashes produced from the *agnihotra* fire, he should do so while reciting the *tryambaka* mantra.
Or else, having consecrated it with the mantra "kiṃ vā agniḥ," one should [consecrate it] in sequence with the five mantras by the names Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and so forth.
One who is a devotee of Śakti should apply three sectarian marks (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, the shoulders, the abdomen, and the heart;
or else, like a woman, one may perform the tri-angled mark (trikoṇa).
Having performed the Vedic twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), one should then perform the Tantric one;
having sipped water according to the rule, the practitioner of mantras should invoke the sacred waters as before.
Then, having sprinkled water upon the ground with a blade of darbha grass three times,
one should consecrate the head with that water seven times.
Then, having restrained the breath and performed the six-limbed ritual assignment (*nyāsa*),
one should take water in the left hand and cover it with the right hand.
The knower of mantras, having consecrated the seeds of ether, air, fire, water,
and earth with the root mantra, [should sprinkle] from that [vessel] with dripping drops using the *tattvamudrā*.
Having sprinkled his own head seven times with that water, the practitioner of mantra should bring the remaining water, which has become that very syllable, to the vicinity of his nose.
Then, having drawn that water consisting of fire within by means of the *iḍā* breath, one should wash away the internal impurity with it;
then that water [is discarded].
One should exhale the black-colored [element] through the Piṅgalā in front of oneself;
thereafter, one should cast it with the Astra-mantra onto a prepared slab of diamond (vajra).
This is indeed declared to be the destroyer of all sins and the remover of evil (aghamarṣaṇa);
then, having washed his hands and sipped water as before, the knower of mantras [proceeds].
Having arisen, the knower of mantras, having placed flowers and other offerings in a copper vessel,
should indeed present the *argha* while reciting the mantra ending with the root syllable.
One should offer the arghya water to the deity residing within the solar disc;
having offered the arghya three times with this [mantra], one should then meditate upon the deity situated in the sun.
One should recite the Gāyatrī prescribed in one's own Kalpa one hundred and eight times,
or twenty-eight times, and offer it with the Guhyeti mantra.
One should meditate upon Brāhmī in a sky marked by stars— she who resembles the rising sun, whose lotus-like hands hold a book and a rosary, and who is clothed in a black antelope skin.
At midday, one should meditate upon the supreme Goddess Pārvatī, the bestower of boons—
white-robed, mounted upon a bull, three-eyed, and situated within the solar disc.
She held a noose and a trident, wore a human skull,
was richly adorned with jewel ornaments at evening, and was clad in yellow silk garments.
The goddess has a dark complexion and four arms; her hands shine with the conch and the discus, and she holds a mace and a lotus, seated upon a solar throne.

Then, having offered libations to the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, one who knows the ritual procedure should satisfy his own chosen deity according to the method of the Kalpa.
Having gratified the lineage of gurus, along with their limbs and retinues, one should perform the libation, saying:
"I gratify Vainateya together with his weapons. (NarP 1.66.75)
A devotee of Viṣṇu should fully satisfy Nārada, Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niśaṭha, Uddhava, Dāruka, Viṣvaksena, and Śaileya.
Having thus satisfied [the ancestors], O best of Brahmins, and having offered the arghya to Vivasvat,
one should enter the hall of worship, wash one's feet, and perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet).
Having diligently offered oblations to and worshipped the fires maintained for the *agnihotra*,
one should go to the place of worship and perform the worship of the door.
One should place Gaṇeśa on the upper branch, Mahālakṣmī on the right,
Sarasvatī on the left side, and Vighneśvara again on the right.
Likewise, one should worship Kṣetrapāla on the left and Gaṅgā on the right;
and Yāmuna on the left and Dhātṛ on the right.

Then the wise practitioner should worship Vidhātṛ, as well as the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures, on the left and right [sides], and thereafter worship the door-keepers as prescribed in their respective ritual manuals.
Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Pracala, Bala,
Bhadra, Subhadra, and others such as these were the Vaiṣṇava door-keepers.
Nandi, Bhṛṅgin, Riṭi, Skanda, Gaṇeśa, Umā, Maheśvara,
Vṛṣabha, and Mahākāla are indeed the Śaiva door-keepers.

The eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, are themselves the Śaktis stationed at the gates; they are remembered as being preceded by their own names and the syllable *a* (with the moon-dot), ending with *ṅe* and *namaḥ*. (NarP 1.66.84)
Then, having sat upon his seat, the wise one, being restrained and pure, should sip water for purification and diligently dispel all obstacles— those of the heavens, the atmosphere, and the earth.
The best of Vaiṣṇavas should indeed install the Mātṛkās beginning with Keśava:
Keśava conjoined with Kīrti, and likewise Nārāyaṇa with Kānti.
Mādhava is accompanied by Tuṣṭi, Govinda is joined with Puṣṭi;
Viṣṇu is united with Dhṛti, and Madhusūdana is joined with Śānti.
Trivikrama is joined with Kriyā; Vāmana is united with Dayitā; Śrīdhara is endowed with Medhā; and Hṛṣīkeśa is accompanied by Harṣā.
Śraddhā is joined with Padmanābha, and Lajjā is accompanied by Dāmodara;
Vāsudeva is united with Lakṣmī, and Saṃkarṣaṇa with Sarasvatī.
Pradyumna is joined with Prīti, Aniruddha with Rati;
thereafter Cakrin is joined with Jayā, and Gadī with Durgā.

The wielder of the Śārṅga bow was endowed with Prabhā; the wielder of the sword was joined with Satyā; the wielder of the conch was united with Caṇḍā; and the wielder of the plow was accompanied by Vāṇī.
Musalī was accompanied by Bilāsinī; Śūlī was joined by Vijayā; Pāśī was united with Virajā; and Kuśī was attended by Viśvā.
Mukunda is joined with Vinatā, and Nandaja with Sunandā;
Nindin is united with Smṛti, and Nara is endowed with Vṛddhi.
Hari is remembered as being endowed with prosperity and joined with liberation;
Kṛṣṇa is endowed with intelligence; Satya is endowed with enjoyment; and Sātvata is endowed with liberation.
Saurikṣama and Sūrarama; Janārdana joined with Umā; Bhūdhara joined with Kledinī; and Viśvamūrti with Klinnā.
Vaikuṇṭha is united with Vasudhā; Vasuda is Puruṣottama;
and Balī is endowed with supreme power, being devoted to the younger brother of Bala.
Bāla is joined with sūkṣma; vṛṣaghnas is joined with saṃdhyā, while vṛṣa is joined with prajñā.
Haṃsa is joined with prabhā, and varāha is joined with niśā.
Vimala is joined with Dhāra, and Nṛsiṃha is united with Vidyut;
the sage Nārāyaṇa is considered the source of the Mātṛkā beginning with Keśava.
The Gāyatrī beginning with "amṛta" is the metre, Viṣṇu is the deity,
and one should meditate upon Hari as being joined with weapons such as the discus and holding a water-pot and a mirror.
One should worship [the deity] who is endowed with Lakṣmī, radiant as lightning, and adorned with many ornaments;
having meditated thus, one should install the Śakti, using syllables encased by the words "Śrī" and "Kāma."
One should recite "That" (tat) for Viṣṇu and his two powers (śakti), and the heart-mantra beginning with the Praṇava;
then one should recite the vital breaths (asūn) for the skin, flesh, blood, muscle, bone, marrow, and semen.
One should place *prāṇa* and *krodha* in the ten locations beginning with the navel;
one at the crown of the head, one in the mouth, two in the eyes, and two in the ears.
Two [marks] on the two nostrils, two on each cheek,
two on each ear, one at the root of the tongue, and one on the neck.
One should place the *ka*-group on the right arm, the *ca*-group on the left arm,
the *ṭa*- and *ta*-groups on the two feet, and *pa* and *pha* on the two sides of the belly.
The syllable *vaṃ* is said to be in the spinal column, *bhaṃ* at the navel, and *maṃ* in the heart;
likewise, the seven syllables beginning with *yā* reside in the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), *haṃ* in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and *laṃ* in the self (*ātman*).
Having sequentially assigned *kṣam* to anger, one becomes capable of worshipping Viṣṇu;
for Śrīkaṇṭha is indeed Pūrṇodarī, accompanied by Ananta and Vijarā.
Sūkṣmeśa was joined with Śālmalī; Lolākṣī was joined with Kṛtrimātaka;
Maheśvara was joined with Vartulākṣī; and Dhīṃśa was indeed joined with Dīrghaghoṇā.
Dīrghamukhya is joined with Bhārabhūti, Tithīśa is joined with Gomukhī,
Sthāvareśa is joined with Dīrghajihvā, and Dhara is joined with Kuṭodarī.
Jhiṇṭīśa is with Urdhvakeśī; Bhautika is with Vikṛtāsyā;
Sadyojāta is joined with Jvālāmukhī, and Anugraha is joined with Ulkāmukhī.
Akrūra is joined with Āsyā, Mahāsena is endowed with Vidyā,
Krodhīśa with Mahākālī, and Sarasvatī with Caṇḍeśa.
Then Pañcāntaka is joined with Siddhagaurī, and Śirottama is joined with Trailokyavidyā; the mantra-power consists of a single Rudra.
