Kūrmeśa is joined with Kamaṭhī; Bhūtamātra has but one eye. Caturvaktra is joined with Lambodarī, and Ajeśa is joined with Drāviṇī.
Sarveśa is joined with Nāgarī; Someśa is joined with Khecarī; Lāṅgalīśa is joined with Maryādā; and Rūpiṇī is joined with Dārukeśa.
With Vāruṇī he is Ardhanārīśa, the beloved of Umā, the lord of qualities;
likewise, with Kākodaryā he is considered to be Aṣāḍhī, joined with Pūtanā.
Daṇḍīśa is joined with Bhadrakālī, Yutrīśa is joined with Yoginī;
Mīneśa is joined with Śaṅkhinī, and Meṣeśa is joined with Tarjayanī.
Lohita is united with Kālarātri, Śikhīśa with Kujanī,
Chalagaṇḍa with Kapardinī, and Dviraṇḍeśa with Vajrā.
Mahābala joined with Jayā, Balīśa with Sumukhīśvarī,
Bhujaṅga joined with Revatī, and Pinākī with Mādhavī.
Khaḍgīśa is joined with Vāruṇī; Bakeśa is united with Vāyavī;
Śvetoraska is joined with Vidāriṇī; and Bhṛgu is united with Sahajā.
Lakulīśa is joined with Lakṣmī, and Śiveśa is joined with Vyāpinī;
in Saṃvartaka, Mahāmāyā is declared to be the Mātṛkā of Śrīkaṇṭha.
Wherever the name of one's own chosen deity is not mentioned, one should apply it everywhere;
the sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī.
The deity is Ardhanārīśa; the application is for the attainment of all goals.
The consonants are said to be the seed-syllables (bījas), and the vowels are declared to be the powers (śaktis).
One should perform the limb-assignment (*aṅganyāsa*) using the syllables situated in the *bhṛgu* (the letter *s*) and in space (*ha*), enriched with the six long vowels;
[one should visualize the deity] whose body is the color of the bandhūka flower and gold, holding a rosary, a goad, and a noose.
One should meditate upon the three-eyed Lord, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament and is worshipped by the gods;
having thus meditated upon Śiva and Śakti, one should [recite] the fourth [mantra] ending with the heart.
One should place the Mātṛkā preceded by its seed-syllable in the location of the Mātṛkās;
Vighneśa is joined with Hrīḥ, and Vighnarāja is joined with Śrī.
Likewise, Vināyaka is endowed with nourishment; Śivottama is joined with peace;
Vighnakṛt is joined with well-being; and Sarasvatī is the remover of obstacles.
Gaṇanātha is with Svāhā, Ekadanta with Sumedhā;
Dvidanta is joined with Kānti, and Gajavakraka with Kāminī.
Nirañjana, Mohinīyukta, Parḍītunaṭīyuta, Dīrghajihva, Pārvatīyu, Jvālinī, and Śaṅkukarṇaka. // NarP_1,66.127 //
Vṛṣadhvaja with Nandī, Gaṇanāyaka with Sureśī,
Gajendra with Kāmarūpiṇī, and likewise Śūrpakarṇa with Umā.
Virocana with Tejovatī, Satya with Lambodara,
and Mahānanda with Vighneśī— she exists in the form of these four manifestations.
Sadāśiva is indeed Kāmada, Āmoda with Madajihvā,
Dumukha joined with Bhūti, and Sumukha joined with Bhautikī.
Pramoda is joined with Sitā; Ekapāda is united with Ramā;
Dvijihva is joined with Mahiṣī; and the one named Śūra is joined with Jabhinī.
The Hero is joined with Vikarṇā; the Six-faced One is endowed with Bhṛkuṭī;
Varada is joined with Lajjā; and Vāmadeva is united with Dīrghaghoṇā.
Dhanurdharya, Vakratuṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Yāminīyuta, Senānī, Rātrisaṃyukta, Kāmāndha, and Grāmaṇīyuta. // NarP_1,66.133 //
Intoxicated and joined with Śaśiprabhā, he was free from intoxication with the restless-eyed woman;
like a rutting elephant with a flickering female, he was matted-haired and endowed with splendor.
Muṃhī is joined with Subhagā; Khaḍgī is joined with Durbhagā;
Vareṇya is joined with Śivā; and Bhaga is joined with Vṛṣaketana.
Bhakṣyapriya is with his sister, Gaṇeśa is joined by his sister,
Meghanāda is with Subhagā, and Vyāpin is joined by Kālarātri.
Gaṇeśvara was addressed by Kāliṅkā regarding the Mothers of Vighneśa;
the group of the Mothers of Gaṇeśa was then proclaimed by the sages.
The meter is Trivṛt-Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śakti-Gaṇeśvara;
having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) with the seed-syllable enriched by the six long vowels, one should then perform the visualization (smaraṇa).
Gaṇeśa should be depicted with a red body and three eyes, holding a goad, a noose, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, while being embraced by his wife who holds a lotus in her hand.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), conjoined with one's own seed-syllable and preceded by the following syllables:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and beyond that, Śāntyatītā.
She is the Illuminator, the Purifier, and the Liberatrix, designated as the Supreme;
likewise, she is the Subtle, the Very Subtle, the Nectar, the Nectar of Knowledge, and the Nourisher.
All-pervading, of the nature of space, infinite, and the source of prosperity is Sṛṣṭi;
then follow Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Sthirā, and Sthiti.
Siddhi, Jarā, Pālinī, Kṣānti, Īśvarīkā, Rati,
Kāmikā, Varadā, or Hlādinī, endowed with Prīti.
Long, Sharp, and likewise Fierce are said to be Sleep and Languor;
Hunger, Anger, and thereafter the Performer of Deeds along with Death.
Yellow, white, and reddish-orange, followed by black, joined with Anantā—thus has the Kalāmātṛkā been described; one who is devoted to those [deities] should practice accordingly.
For the Kalāyuṅmātṛkā, the sage is said to be Prajāpati;
the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is named Śāradā.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) with high-pitched notes situated at short and long intervals;
[one should meditate on the goddess] who bears a lotus, a wheel, and the qualities of a deer, and who is three-eyed.
The wise one should worship that five-faced Bhāratī adorned with pearls;
having meditated upon her thus, preceded by the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ), he should install her together with the final digit (*kalā*).
Then, one should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the root mantra;
having joined the [six] names ending in the dative case with the heart and the other [limbs], one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*).
*Namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* are declared to be the classes [of mantras].
Then, one should meditate upon that desired deity, complete with ornaments and weapons.
Having performed the placement of the six limbs upon that form, one should then begin the worship.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Sandhyā and Other Rites," in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall describe the worship of the deity, which grants the fulfillment of the desires of the practitioner.
Having fashioned either a triangle or a square on the left side, || NarP_1,67.1 ||
Having worshipped [the vessel] with the *sreṇī* mantra and rinsed it, one should place the support upon the heart;
and having likewise rinsed the vessel from its base upwards, one should [place] the fire-mandala there.
Having established the name upon the support, if there is a solar disc there,
one should fill it with water while uttering the *klim* syllable and the *mātṛkā* vowels.
Having worshipped the maṇḍala of catreñju and invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) as before,
one should render them nectar with the cow-mudrā and veil them with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Having washed it with blood, one should recite the *praṇava* over it eight times;
this is declared to be the general *argha*, which brings about all accomplishments for men. (NarP 1.67.5)
Having drawn up some of that water with the *prokṣiṇī* vessel,
the best of practitioners should separately sprinkle himself and the sacrificial materials with it.
One should place a triangle within a hexagon in front of oneself;
having encircled it with a square, one should wash it with the water of the *argha* offering. (NarP 1.67.7)
Then the best of practitioners should immobilize [the obstacles] in the corners starting from the southeast with the conch mudrā,
[placing] the four limbs beginning with the heart-mantra.

Then one should worship the Eye in the center and the [five] weapons in the directions; thereafter, with the three sections of the root mantra, one should worship the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti) located in the middle of the triangle.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, and having established the tripod that has been washed with the heart-mantra, one should worship it with this mantra: NarP_1,67.10.

Then, for the self of the place and time, [one says] "maṃ vahnimaṇḍalāya," followed by "amukārghyāya" at the end of the vessel, and finally with the heart-mantra preceded by *saḥ* and *apahṛ*. (NarP 1.67.11)
This twenty-four-syllable mantra is for the worship of the support (ādhāra).
Having consecrated a bamboo arrow cleansed by one's own mantra, one should install it and perform the worship. (NarP 1.67.12)
*Tāraḥ* (the syllable Om), *Kārma-mahān*, then *jalacarāya*, *varma* (hūṃ), *phaṭ*, *hṛdayam* (namaḥ), and *pāñcajanyāya hṛdayam* (the heart-mantra of Pāñcajanya). || NarP_1,67.13 ||

Therein, for the solar orb (*arkamaṇḍala*), [the mantra] ending with "to the one who delights in the digit at the end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānte kalāramane*), followed by "Obeisance to [Name] Arghya" (*amukārghyai namaḥ*) at the end of the vessel, consists of the syllables of the three-eyed Lord (*tryakṣivarṇavān*). (NarP 1.67.14)
Having worshipped [the vessel] with that, he should there worship the twelve solar digits (kalās) in sequence;
then, reciting the root mantra and the mātṛkā in reverse order, he should [rinse it] with pure water.
One should fill the conch with that [liquid] and worship it with this mantra:
"Oṃ, to the one who is the lunar disc, the sixteenth [digit], whose self is the kalā. (NarP 1.67.16)
"Oṃ amukāya ardhyāmṛtāya svāhā"—this is the heart-mantra for the worship with the *arghya* offering;
therein, one should worship the sixteen digits (*kalās*) of the moon.
Then, having invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) as before with "O Gaṅgā," and so forth,
he should consecrate [the water] with the nectar-gesture (amṛtamudrā) and cover it with the fish-gesture (matsyamudrā).
Then, having enveloped it with the Kavaca mantra, one should protect it again with the Astra mantra;
having meditated upon one's chosen deity, one should then display the mudrās.
Then, the wise one should sequentially display the hand-gestures known as the conch, the mace, and the discus, followed by the supreme Mahāmudrā and the Yonimudrā.
The Gāruḍī and the Gālinī are proclaimed as the two principal mudrās;
there, one should worship the deity while recollecting [it], using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should mutter the root mantra eight times and likewise the *praṇava* eight times;
then, to the south of the conch, one should designate the vessel for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇīpātra*).
Having placed a little of that water in the sprinkling vessel, one should then [recite] three times for oneself:
"Hṛm, obeisance to the Self of the Principle of the Self; obeisance to the Self of the Principle of Knowledge."
With these three mantras— namely *śivatattvātmane*, *haṃ*, and *ca*—
the wise one should sprinkle the mandala with flowers and unbroken rice grains according to the prescribed rule.
Alternatively, one should sprinkle the articles of worship with the root Gāyatrī mantra—
those intended for the water for the feet (pādya), the arghya offering, the water for sipping (ācamana), and also for the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
One should place the vessels, provided with their bases, before [the deity] according to the prescribed rule;
the water for washing the feet (pādya) is traditionally said to consist of water containing śyāmāka grain, dūrvā grass, lotuses, and viṣṇukrāntā.

The *arghya* is said to consist of flowers, unbroken rice, barley, the tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, perfumes, and blades of *dūrvā* grass; after that, the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) is offered.
Nutmeg, kaṅkola,
and cloves, mixed with water and combined with honey, clarified butter, and curd, are declared to be the madhuparka.
Alternatively, one may prepare the water for the feet and other offerings in a single vessel;
however, for the worship of Śaṅkara and the Sun, a conch-shell vessel is specifically recommended.

The powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis) should be meditated upon as white, black, reddish-brown, yellow, dark-green, red, black, and dark-blue; they wear red garments and hold the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhaya).
One should worship [the deity] in a yantra inscribed with gold and other materials, or in a śālagrāma stone, or likewise in a gem, or in an image installed according to the prescribed rite.
An image made of gold or other precious metals, measuring from one thumb-breadth up to a span,
bestows auspiciousness when kept in the home for daily worship.
One should never worship an image that is crooked, burnt, chipped, with a broken head or eyes, or one that is clearly defiled by outcastes and the like.
Or one should worship [the deity] in a liṅga made of bāṇa or other materials, characterized by all the auspicious marks;
having conceived the form with the root mantra and meditated upon the God as described.
On this [day], one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) of her along with her retinue;
however, when she is installed in a Śālagrāma stone, there is neither invocation nor dismissal (visarjana).
Having taken up a handful of flowers and meditated, one should recite the mantra.
O Supreme Lord, I invoke you— who abide within the self, unborn and pure—
into this embodied form, just as one summons the eater of oblations into the sacrificial fire-wood.
For this great form of yours exists here; O Lord, I establish you, who are all-pervading, within it by means of devotion alone, drawing you forth like a lamp.
I prepare a seat for the God who is the inner ruler of all, the auspicious one consisting of all seeds, who abides in the self of the sun, the supreme and pure.
O Lord of Gods, O Master, this power of your form is not different from you;
O bestower of grace upon your devotees, manifest your presence within it.
Even if the ritual manual should be incomplete due to ignorance, lack of application, or deficiency in the means of accomplishment,
nevertheless, remain intent upon it.
O Maheśvara, remain present in this sacrificial seat, filling it with your nectar-showering gaze, or else abide here in bodily form for the completion of the sacrifice.
O you whose splendor is distant to those whose speech, mind, eyes, and ears are devoid of devotion—
be quickly enveloped on all sides by the cage of your own brilliance!
To you, that Supreme Lord whose sight the gods desire for the attainment of their own cherished goals—to you, welcome, and welcome to me! NarP_1,67.44
I have achieved my purpose and am graced; my life has become fruitful.
The Lord of the Gods of gods has arrived; welcome once again to you!
To that supreme lotus-foot of mine, which is pure and from contact with the application of whose devotion the arising of supreme bliss occurs, water for the feet is now offered.
O Lord, for the sake of the Veda of Vedas, for the divine self of the gods, and for the cause of the purity of those already pure, I prepare this rinsing water (ācamana). NarP_1,67.47.
O divine one who removes the threefold suffering and whose nature is supreme bliss,
I offer this arghya to you for liberation from the threefold suffering.
O God, who is free from all impurity and whose nature is perfect bliss, I offer this honey-mixture (madhuparka) to you; be gracious to me.
Even one who is defiled or impure attains purity through the mere remembrance of you; to you, therefore, this water for sipping is offered again.
"O Great-souled Lord of the World, receive this affection with affection!
O Pure-souled One, I bestow upon you the highest affection throughout all the worlds. (NarP 1.67.51)
O Lord, I offer this bath, complete with its primary and secondary limbs, to You whose own form is immersed in the ocean of the awakening of supreme bliss;
I do so with reverence, offering either a thousand or a hundred [prostrations], according to my capacity.
O Lord, one should consecrate the mantras with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
O you whose own secret organ is covered by the garment of illusion, O you whose splendor is concealed,
I prepare a dwelling for your unobstructed consciousness.
To that Supreme Lord, depending upon whom the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) always deludes the world, I offer this upper garment.
Red [garments] are for Śakti, Arka, and Vighna; yellow for Viṣṇu; and white for Śiva.
One should discard that which is defiled by oil and the like, worn out, torn, or soiled.
To you, whose triple power this entire world is devoted,
I offer this sacrificial thread as a sacrificial thread.
O you who are worshipped by the immortals, whose limbs are beautiful by their very nature and who are the locus of various powers, I fashion diverse ornaments for you.
O Supreme Lord, out of compassion, accept this supreme fragrance that fills the quarters of space with the sweet scent of ultimate bliss.

"Let this supreme flower be taken—it is born from the *turīya* forest, enchanting with its various qualities, and possesses intense fragrance. One should never offer *japā*, *akṣata*, *arka*, or *dhattūra* flowers to Viṣṇu. (NarP 1.67.60)
One should not offer the ketakī, kuṭaja, kunda, bandhūka, kesara, japā, or even the mālatī flower to Maheśvara.
One should never offer a citron or tagara to the Sun; when possible, one should avoid offering dūrvā grass, arka, and mandāra to Gaṇeśa, and one should abandon tulasī for him.
Sarojinī, damanaka, as well as marubaka, kuśa, viṣṇukrāntā, nāgavallī, dūrvā, apāmārga, and dāḍima; NarP_1,67.63.
One should perform the worship of the deity with leaves of the *dhātrī* tree combined with those of the *muni* plant;
likewise, the *kadalī*, *badarī*, *dhātrī*, *tintiṇī*, and *bījapūraka*.
The wise man should perform the worship of the deities with the fruits of these trees: the mango, the pomegranate, the citron, the rose-apple, and the jackfruit.
One should not worship the deity with leaves, flowers, or fruits that are dry.
"O Sage, the wise have declared that the leaves of the dhātrī, khadira, bilva, and tamāla are not to be considered defiled, even if they are broken or torn."
The lotus and the āmalaka fruit remain pure for three days;
the tulasī is always pure, as indeed are the bilva leaves.
One should not worship the Mother of the World with palāśa or kāśa flowers, with tamāla or tulasī leaves, nor with chātrī leaves or dūrvā grass.
O Brahmin, one should not offer a flower, leaf, or fruit to the deity with its face turned downwards;
rather, one should offer flowers, leaves, and so forth exactly as they have grown.
O Lord of the God of Gods, please accept with devotion this divine incense from the essence of trees, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, which is fit to be smelled. NarP_1,67.71.
Accept this well-kindled great lamp, which always dispels darkness,
provided with a wick of clarified butter, and offered by me with reverence.
O Lord, accept with devotion this fourfold food, endowed with the six flavors, as my ever-gratifying offering. (NarP 1.67.73)
Accept from me this excellent betel leaf, combined with areca nut and catechu powder, enriched with the fragrant scent of camphor and other spices. (NarP 1.67.74)
Afterwards, one should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) and perform the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇārcana).
When one faces a particular direction and performs worship, that alone should be known as the East; the other ten directions are then the intermediate points.
One should worship the heart-mantra and the others on the filaments, beginning from the southeast corner;
the eye-mantra at the front and the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions, according to the sequence of the limb-mantras.
The powers (śaktis) of the directions, white, bright-white, pale, dark, black, and red-rayed respectively,
should be meditated upon as holding the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness in their hands.
At the end of the [mention of] such-and-such a covering, one should say "the deities";
thereafter, they are described as being adorned with ornaments, together with their limbs, and accompanied by their retinues.
Then, having been fully honored and gratified along with their vehicles and weapons by all the attendants, one should recite this [verse] so that they may become bestowers of boons. (NarP 1.67.80)
Having recited [the mantra] at the end of the root [mantra], one should offer it to the deity:
"O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the attainment of my desired goal. (NarP 1.67.81)
"Out of devotion, I offer to you this worship of the [specific] enclosure";
having uttered this, one should cast a handful of flowers upon the head of the deity.
Then, one should worship those who are to be honored according to the sequence of the enclosures (āvṛtis) as prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa);
thereafter, one should worship Indra and the other deities, together with their weapons, in their respective directions.
Indra, Vahni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, Vidhu,
Īśāna, and Vidhi— thus [are the guardians], and below them, O Lord of Pannagas, is Brahmā.
The wise know that Airāvata, the ram, the buffalo, the preta, the timi fish, the deer, the horse, the bull, the swan, and the tortoise are the vehicles.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace,
the trident, the lotus, and the discus are, in order, the weapons of Indra and the other [guardians].
Having completed the worship of the covering, one should perform the *ārārtika* offering for the deity;
having sprinkled the water from the conch, one should fall to the ground while dancing with arms raised.
Then, rising like a staff and having petitioned his own lord,
he should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south and perform the consecration (saṃskāra) there.
One should gaze at it with the root mantra, sprinkle it with water while reciting the weapon mantra, and strike it again;
then, having sprinkled it with kuśa grass while reciting the armor mantra and performed worship, one should install the Vasu there.
Having caused [the gift] to be given there, one should perform oblations while meditating upon one's chosen deity;
he who performs the fourfold [oblation] with all the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
The best of practitioners should offer oblations with clarified butter, cooked rice, sesame seeds, or milk-rice,
twenty-five times in number, using them together with ghee.
Having offered oblations again with the vyāhṛtis, one should worship the deity once more with perfumes and other offerings;
then, one should unite the deity with the image and subsequently dismiss the fire.
O Agni, O you of great power, accomplisher of all rites!
Even when another rite has arrived, grant your presence with respect.
Having offered [the oblation] to the deity Agni, one should give the water for sipping (ācamanīya);
with the remaining sacrificial food (havis), accompanied by scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should also offer a bali-oblation to the previously mentioned attendants of the deities—
those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce abodes.
For there are yoginīs of fierce form, those who are lords of the hosts,
and others who have become obstacles, dwelling in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
"May they all, with joyful minds, accept this bali offering.
Having thus offered [the bali] in the eight directions, one should again perform the bali for the bhūtas.
Having transformed the water into nectar by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*,
one should offer it into the hand of the deity, and then again offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*).
Having dismissed the deity residing in the image, one should again unite it with that very [image];
then one should offer the food offering (naivedya) to the one who eats the remnants of each [deity].
Caṇḍeśa belongs to Maheśvara, Viṣvaksena to Hari,
Caṇḍāṃśu to the Sun, and Vaktatuṇḍa to Gaṇeśa;
Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī is said to belong to Śakti, who feeds upon remnants.
Then, having recollected the ṛṣis and so forth, and having performed the sixfold root-rite (mūla-ṣaḍaṅga),
one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity and offer it to the deity.
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O God, may accomplishment be mine through your grace, abiding in you.
Then, having offered the water of respect (arghya) with one's face turned away, one should worship with flowers.
Prostration with the two arms, the two feet, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the mind, and speech is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
With both arms, the knees, the head, and also with speech—
this five-limbed prostration is the most excellent of the two types of salutation for worship.
And having prostrated like a staff, the minister should then perform circumambulations;
for Viṣṇu, Soma, Arka, and Vighna, these are four, two-and-a-half, seven, and three respectively.
Then the practitioner of mantra should recite the hymns and other prayers with devotion:
"From this point forward, [I renounce] my life, intellect, body, and all duties, from the standpoint of my authority. (NarP 1.67.106)
In the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, one should declare [one's transgressions] with the mind,
and then with speech, the two hands, the two feet, the belly, and thereafter with the organ of generation.
Whatever was previously remembered, whatever was subsequently spoken, and whatever was performed thereafter—may all that be an offering to Brahman; *ṭha dvayaṃ*. NarP_1,67.108.
"I surrender myself and everything belonging to me to Viṣṇu;
Oṃ Tat Sat, may this be the offering to Brahman"—this is considered the mantra. (NarP 1.67.109)
One whose name begins with the *praṇava* (Om) and consists of eight syllables should indeed offer oneself by means of this [mantra],
whether out of ignorance, negligence, or deficiency in the performance of the rite.
Whatever has been deficient or excessive, all that you should forgive;
whether it was done by me otherwise—lacking in materials, lacking in ritual action, or lacking in mantra.
O Lord, O ocean of compassion, please forgive through Your grace whatever has been done by me,
and whatever action is being performed by me in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
O Lord, may all that be your worship and lead to my prosperity;
for those whose feet have stumbled upon the ground, the ground alone is their support.
O Lord, for those who have committed offenses against you, you alone are the refuge;
otherwise there is no other refuge—you alone are my refuge.
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, out of your compassionate nature,
forgive the thousands of offenses committed by me day and night.
"Thinking of me as a servant, O Lord of the worlds, please forgive me;
I do not know how to perform the invocation, nor do I know how to perform the dismissal."
"I do not know the ritual worship; You alone are my refuge, O Supreme Lord.
Having thus prayed, the practitioner should then recite the verse at the end of the root mantra: NarP_1,67.117 //
Go, go to the supreme abode, O Lord of the World, who pervades the world—
that which even the gods beginning with Brahmā and Sadāśiva do not know.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers, he then, by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*,
placed the deity along with his limbs within the lotus of his own heart.
The wise one, having smelled the flower via the path of the *suṣumṇā*, should dismiss [the deity],
as well as the conch, the discus, the stone, the *liṅga*, the obstacles, and the two suns.
One should not worship the three powers together in one place, for that is a cause of suffering;
[this practice] removes untimely death and destroys all diseases.
The auspicious water from Viṣṇu’s feet brings about the destruction of all sins.
That which has been offered as *naivedya* should be accepted by the devotees of those respective deities;
however, the *nirmālya* of Śiva—consisting of leaves, flowers, fruits, or water—is not to be taken.
Through the touch of a Śālagrāma stone, everything attains purity;
therein, fivefold worship has been described by Nārada and all others. (NarP 1.67.124)

The state of illness, the state of childbirth, fear, the state of practice, as well as the future state, and the state of poor understanding—listen to me as I describe their characteristics in due order. 1.67.125.
One afflicted by disease and the like should neither bathe, nor recite prayers, nor perform worship;
rather, one should simply gaze upon the worship of the deity, or upon the image, or the solar disc.
Then, having prostrated and recited the mantra, he should offer a handful of water (añjali) to Kumāra.
When the disease has ceased, he should bathe, bow down, and worship his guru.
"O Lord of the World, O object of worship for the world, O ocean of compassion! By your grace, may the fault of interrupting my worship not befall me"—thus one should pray to him. (NarP 1.67.128)
Having honored the twice-born and satisfied them according to his ability,
and having received blessings from them, he should then worship the God as before.
This is indeed called impurity due to illness; next, birth-impurity is described.
Birth-impurity is said to be of two kinds: that termed "birth" and that known as "death. (NarP 1.67.130)
Having bathed there and performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) mentally with a concentrated mind,
one should worship the God with the mind alone and mutter the mantra with the mind alone.
When the period of impurity has ceased, having worshipped the preceptor and the twice-born as before,
and having received their blessings from them, one should then perform the daily ritual sequence.
This, however, is declared to be the *sautikī* [rite]; now the *trāsī* is described:
one who has fallen into fear of evil beings [should perform it] with whatever materials for the ritual service are available.
One should indeed worship the God with mental offerings; that is proclaimed as *trāsī*.
This applies when there is a total lack of the materials required for the means of worship.
One should worship the All-pervading Lord with flowers, leaves, or fruits, or even with the mind alone;
for this is the practice for those lacking means—listen now, O Nārada, to the teaching on the lack of understanding.
Women, the elderly, children, and fools—by them, respectively, that [transgression] committed according to their lack of knowledge is proclaimed as *daurbodhī*. (NarP 1,67.136)
In this way, the practitioner should perform worship by whatever means possible;
for he who is devoid of the worship of the deity will certainly go to hell.
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, he should feed the best of the twice-born;
thereafter, he himself should eat with his own attendants what has been offered to the gods.
Having sipped water and performed the purification of the mouth, one should remain for a few moments and listen to the Purāṇas and Itihāsas together with one's own people.

If one who is capable of performing the primary ritual according to all the rules instead performs a secondary substitute, the fruit of that evil-minded person does not arise as it would when the rite is complete with all its constituent parts.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of the Deities," in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Śrī Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall declare the mantras of Gaṇeśa, which bestow all desired objects.
O best of Brahmins, by propitiating whom the practitioner attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The imperishable Viṣṇu’s wife, Śambhu’s consort, the one whose banner is the fish;
Smṛti, rich with flesh, the moon, and Manu—she is again the moon-crested Lord.
"Ṅeṃto gaṇapati toyaṃ bhujaṅgo varada," and at the end of all [the syllables], having uttered "janam," then say "vaśamānaya me. (NarP 1.68.3)
This mantra, ending with the word *priyā*, consists of twenty-eight syllables;
its sage is Gaṇaka, and its meter is Gāyatrī, beginning with the letter *vi*. (NarP 1.68.4)
Gaṇeśa is the deity; the seed-syllable is that which begins with the sixth power (the letter *ṣa*); the application is for the propitiation of the glorious Mahāgaṇapati. // NarP_1,68.5 //

The best of practitioners should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣi on the head, the Chandas on the mouth, the Devatā on the heart, the Bīja on the secret place, and the Śakti on the feet. (NarP 1.68.6)

The knower of mantras should again perform the placement of the six limbs upon this [deity], using the seed-syllable enriched with the six long vowels and beginning with the syllable *yaṃ*, conjoined with the [respective] *jāti* syllables.
The six-limbed mudrā of Śiva should indeed be applied to the six limbs; one should place the [syllables] beginning with *gāṃ* and the world of earth (*bhūrloka*) upon the feet, up to the navel.
One should place the Bhuvarloka, beginning with *gūm*, from the navel up to the throat;
and the Svarloka, likewise beginning with *gūm*, from the throat up to the crown of the head.
This placement, pervaded by the root mantra, is called "of the worlds" (bhuvanābhidha).
Having uttered the root mantra, one should then pronounce the phonemes of the Mātṛkā.
And at the end of that, in the place of the Mātṛkās, there should be the root mantra ending with "namaḥ";
having placed [the letters] up to "kṣaṃ," the wise one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra.
This very sequence of syllables has been declared; likewise, the placement of the words (padanyāsa) is now described, according to the order of five, three, five, three, one, one, two, and four.
With the eight divided words of the root *gāyatrī*, ending with the heart-mantra (*hṛt*),
[one should place them] on the forehead, the face, the throat, the heart, the navel, the thighs, and the knees.
Having placed [the mantra] upon the two feet, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) at the root;
then one should utter the word "vidmahe" after the phrase ending in "tatpuruṣāya."
One should utter "to Vakratuṇḍa" at the end of the word, followed by "we meditate upon" (dhīmahi);
then one should speak again: "may that elephant-faced one (dantiḥ) grant us prosperity" (pracodayāt).
This is declared to be the root Gāyatrī, which bestows all accomplishments.
Having performed the ritual of placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one should meditate thus upon the lotus of the heart.
Resembling the rising sun, the cause of the creation and destruction of the worlds,
he was accompanied by his Śakti, his limbs adorned, and armed with weapons such as a tusk and a discus.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, accompanied by forty-four thousand repetitions, and perform the ten-part offering with eight substances.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations according to the prescribed rule into the consecrated fire:
sugarcane, roasted flour, plantains, flattened rice, and sesame seeds.
Sweetmeats, coconuts, and parched grain are known as the eight substances.
One should worship the pedestal, beginning with the Power of Support (Ādhāra-śakti) and ending with the Supreme Reality (Para-tattva).
One should draw a triangle within a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus outside it; having constructed a square enclosure (bhūpura) beyond that, one should worship Ganeśa there.
The one called Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, Kāmarūpāṇī,
Agrā, Tejovatī, Satyā, and the ninth is Vidhnanāśinī.
This is the seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra), ending with the word "hṛdaya," addressed to the one whose lotus-seat possesses all primordial powers; by means of this, one should offer the supreme seat.
Having invoked the Lord of the Gaṇas there and worshipped him diligently in the center,
one should worship [the other deities] in order in the four directions starting from the east, outside the triangle.
[He saw] Śrī and the Lord of Śrī, Gaurī and likewise the Lord of Gaurī,
Rati and the Lord of Rati, and finally the Earth and the Boar.
One should worship Krama, Ādilva, Vaṭa, Aśvattha, Priyagu, and Adhohari.
Ramā has two lotuses in her hands, and Hari holds a conch and a discus.
Gaurī holds a noose and a goad; Hara holds an axe and a trident. Rati has a lotus in her hand; Smara holds a flower-arrow and a bow.
With the earth holding ears of rice in her hand, and the Boar bearing the discus and mace,
one should worship Vināyaka together with Lakṣmī in front of the deity.
One should worship Āmoda and the others, accompanied by their consorts, in the six corners;
one should worship Āmoda, joined with Siddhi, in front.
One should worship Pramoda together with Samṛddhi in the southeast corner,
and likewise worship Sumukha together with Kīrti in the northeast corner.
In the western direction, one should worship Durmukha joined with Madanāvatī;
and in the south-western corner, one should worship Vighna accompanied by Madadravā.
One should worship the obstructors of the Drāviṇī in the northwest corner,
who hold a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness, and possess a radiance equal to the rising sun.
Adorned by bees greedy for the scent of the ichor trickling from their temples,
they resemble a conch and a lotus respectively on both sides of the hexagon.
Having meditated upon [the deity] together with his two inherent powers, one should worship as before;
the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) on the filaments, and the eight Mothers on the petals.
One should also worship Indra and the others, as well as the thunderbolt and other weapons, within the chamber of the earth;
having thus propitiated Vighneśa, one shall accomplish one's own heart's desires. (NarP 1,68.35)
A wise person, free from sloth, should daily satisfy the elephant-faced deity with forty-four hundred pure waters.
One should subjugate kings with lotuses, their wives likewise with blue water-lilies;
ministers with white water-lilies, and Brahmins with auspicious fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree.

A wise man should subjugate kings with fuel-sticks made from the udumbara tree, vaiśyas with those originating from the plakṣa tree, and the lowest castes with fuel-sticks produced from the vaṭa tree.
Through clarified butter one attains prosperity; through honey there shall be the attainment of heaven;
through cow’s milk there is the gain of cattle; and through curd one possesses all-round abundance.
By offering oblations of food, one obtains food; by oblations of reed-wood (vetasa), water;
and by offering auspicious safflower blossoms, one obtains garments.
Now I shall describe the fourfold libation that grants all desires:
first, one should offer the libation four times with the root mantra, and then offer it individually for each [deity].

Having first satisfied [the deities] four times each with the syllables of the preceding mantras and with mantras ending in *svāhā*, and then having likewise offered satisfaction four times with the root mantras; NarP_1,68.42.
Thereafter, one should likewise fully satisfy the couples and so forth as before;
[one should satisfy] the Śakti together with the Deva, and him (the Deva) together with the Śakti.
And thus there are twenty-six pairs;
one should satisfy them in sequence with seed-syllables consisting of the initial letters of their own names. (NarP 1.68.44)
Altogether, there would be four hundred and forty-four; having thus performed the penance, he should thereafter proceed as before with the ritual services.
Having prayed for all desired objects and bowed down, the wise one should perform the ritual dismissal;
doing so diligently every month, beginning from the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Beginning at sunrise until the moon rises, the practitioner of mantra,
having mastered speech, action, and mind, should not sit upon the ground.
Then, at the rising of the moon, the minister should properly worship Gaṇanāyaka according to the previously mentioned rite, with various offerings of flowers.
One should offer twenty-one sweetmeats and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times before them.
Then, with camphor, saffron, and red flowers mixed with sandalwood, one should offer the *arghya* at the end of the root mantra, followed by "Ṅeṃ Gaṇapataye. (NarP 1.68.50)
"I prepare this arghya within the heart"—this is considered the arghya mantra.
Having praised, bowed, and then dismissed [the deity], one should then worship the Moon once again.
Then, having worshipped the preceptor, one should offer the *arghya* four times;
and when [the food] has been presented, one should give half-portioned sweetmeats (*modaka*) to the Brahmin.
He himself, observing celibacy and having conquered his senses, should consume half [of the food];
he who performs this vow correctly for the duration of a full year, [attains the fruit]. (NarP 1.68.53)
A man who knows the mantra obtains sons, grandsons, happiness, wealth, and health; if he is unable [to begin at sunrise], he may start from sunset until sunrise.
One should perform the vow according to the previously described procedure until the rising of the moon; when this is done, one certainly attains the aforementioned fruit. (NarP 1.68.55)
One should fashion an image of Gaṇeśa from ivory, or even from wood,
from the trunk of an elephant, or from neem, or alternatively from white arka.
Having prepared it and invoked [the deity] therein, preceded by the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇa-sthāpana),
the practitioner of mantras should worship according to the rules while the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu.
Having touched it and remaining without food while carrying it upon his crest-lock,
one shall obtain victory in gambling, dispute, battle, and legal proceedings.
One should utter the seed-syllable (bīja), Varāha, Bindu, Āḍhya, Manu, Indu, Anna, and then Kalī; thereafter, Smṛti, Māṃsa, Indu, Manu, and Āgra, followed by Karṇa, Ucchiṣṭa, and Gaṇa.

"Baka, together with the long breath, is the offering for the great yakṣa; this is declared to be the mantra of the offering, which, even if its syllables are not [perfect], grants all desires. (NarP 1.68.60)
One should write the Praṇava, followed by the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśānī, then the nine-syllabled mantra, and finally "Hastī" and "Piśācī," which is Āgriṃsundarī.
This nine-syllable mantra has been taught as the bestower of all accomplishments to those who worship it;
one should perform the five-fold ritual application (pañcāṅga) using the words of the entire mantra.
O Nārada, everything else shall be the same as the previous mantra;
now I shall duly declare the unsurpassed Vakratuṇḍa mantra. (NarP 1.68.63)
Water (va), the ritual (vi), fire (ra) joined with the moon in the ear (ka), and Hari (ha) likewise;
then the letter 'da' with a long vowel (dā), the son (ra), and wind (ya) ending with armor (va)—this is the six-syllabled mantra.
The sage of this [mantra] is Bhārgava, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is the Lord of the Gaṇas named Vakratuṇḍa; "vaṃ" is the seed-syllable, and the armor is likewise [the same].

Having formed the syllables of the six-limbed mantra with the letters of the mantra adorned by the moon, situated between the *tāra* and the eyes, one should place them between the eyebrows, at the throat, and at the heart.
One should assign [the mantras] to the name, the *liṅga*, and the word, and then perform the pervasive assignment (*vyāpaka*) with the whole;
[he is] like the rising sun in luster, holding in his hands the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
One should worship the elephant-faced one, who wears red ornaments and garments;
having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra ten lakh times and perform the oblation with materials in the tenth part of that number.
One should offer oblations with eight [mantras] upon the pedestal and worship it together with Tīvrā and the others;
having conceived the Form (mūrti) by means of the Embodied One (mūrta), one should invoke it therein and perform worship.
One should worship the six limbs in the six corners, and the eight powers upon the petals:
Vidyā, Vidhātrī, Bhogadā, and Vipraghātinī.
[Nidhipradīpā], Pāpaghnī, Puṇyā, and Paścācchaśiprabhā;
on the tips of the petals are Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, and Mahodara.
Gajānana, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, and likewise Vidhinarāja;
then, outside, those of smoky color together with the world-protectors and their weapons.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas with these five obstructions,
one shall accomplish all desires through the grace of Vakratuṇḍa.
Having received the mantra from the mouth of the Guru preceded by the purificatory rite of initiation,
he should remain a celibate student, eating sacrificial food, truthful in speech, and with his senses subdued.
One should recite the mantra a thousand times for six months, combined with fire offerings;
having overcome poverty, one becomes like the Lord of Wealth.

One should recite the mantra beginning with the fourth case-ending and ending with the fourth case-ending ten thousand times with devotion; by offering oblations one hundred and eight times daily as before, one shall obtain the fruit.
On both fortnights, on the fourth lunar day, the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations one hundred times.
With cakes, one shall attain the supreme state of prosperity throughout the year.
On the fourth lunar day of Aṅgāraka, having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rite, one should offer an oblation consisting of sacrificial food, milk, and boiled rice.
Then, having honored the preceptor, the wise one should feed him according to the rules;
he should perform oblations with the offered substance in the fire-vessel a thousand times according to the prescribed rite.
Having performed this for a year, one shall attain great prosperity.
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I shall describe another means of accomplishment.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa with parched grains, milk-rice, cakes, sweetmeats,
and various fruits, the mantra-practitioner [should then offer] turmeric and rock salt.
One should recite the mantra over vacā weighing half a niṣka, or half of that;
having purified it, one should cast two handfuls of the powder into cow urine.
Having diligently recited the mantra one thousand times with Manu,
[he should approach] her who has bathed on her fertile day, being pure, auspicious, and wearing white garments.
Having placed it before the deity, the wise woman should have her drink the medicine;
even a barren woman obtains a son endowed with all auspicious marks.
Now I shall proclaim another most wonderful secret:
having carefully smeared an area of ground the size of a cow-hide.
Having scattered heaps of grain there, one should place the jar;
having filled it with pure water, one should set it down upon that [grain].
One should light an auspicious lamp in a new, beautiful earthen bowl filled with ghee from a tawny cow, using the two mantras consisting of six and eight syllables.
Having invoked the deity in the lamp, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
or else, the wise person should worship a bathed young girl or a young boy.
Having placed a lamp in front and meditated upon the God, one should recite the mantra;
once the lamp is established, one shall behold Gaṇeśvara in the form of a twice-born brahmin.
When questioned, whether regarding prosperity or what has been lost as well as what is yet to come,
a young girl or a young boy shall thus declare everything.
If the six-syllable mantra ends with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), it becomes an eight-syllable mantra;
there are other mantras as well, O divine sage, belonging to the Lord of the Gaṇas in this Tantra.
However, that which cannot be accomplished here by practitioners in the three worlds,
even that they shall not see anywhere through the twenty-eight [syllables] consisting of rasa and arṇa.
This ritual procedure for the mantras of Gaṇeśa has been declared to you by me;
do not speak it to the dishonest, to the disciples of others, or even to the deceitful.
Thus, he who worships the god Gaṇeśa, the bestower of all accomplishments,
shall obtain every enjoyment in this world and in the end go to the state of liberation.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Gaṇeśa Mantra," in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall describe the procedure for the Lord of the Lotus, who is the embodiment of the three Vedas.
By propitiating the mantras, one shall obtain all that is desired.
The letter *tā* joined with *recikā*, *rati* conjoined with *medhā* and *netra*, *sasarga* augmented by the left ear (*vāmakarṇa*), *bhṛgu*, *vaḍhyāsana*, and *marut*. NarP_1,69.2 //
Śeṣoditya is proclaimed as having eight syllables; he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Devabhaga is the sage, Gāyatrī is the meter, and Ravi is the deity.
*Māyā* is the seed-syllable, *Ramā* is the power, and the application is for the seen and the unseen;
next, the heart is uttered for *Satya*, and the head is declared for *Brahman*.
The *śikhā* and *varman* are proclaimed for Viṣṇu; the *netra* belongs to Rudra; thereafter, the *astra* is declared for Śarva.
The mantras of the Gaṇas are *netro jvālā mano huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, ending with *svāhā*.
Again, having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) for Lakṣmī using the six syllables *hrī* situated within [the mantra].
One should place Śiṣṭāra in the belly and Pṛṣṭha on the back; then, by means of that which is called the *ṅe*-ending [dative case], one should place Āditya, Ravi, Bhānu, and Bhāskara.
One should place the Sun upon the head, in the face, in the heart, in the secret place, and on the two feet;
one should assign the five [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta and the vowels beginning with 'a', ending with the syllable 'ṅeṃ' at the heart.
One should place the eight syllables beginning with *tāra* (oṃ), situated between *hrīṃ* and *ramā*, upon the head, face, throat, heart, belly, navel, genitals, and anus. (NarP 1.69.9)

Preceded by the sound of the moon (the letter *sa*), one should place the syllable *ṅe* within the orb of the cool-rayed moon (*śītāṃśu-maṇḍala*) from the head down to the throat, while reciting the lunar mantra.

Having fully uttered the vowels together with the *sendu* (the nasal bindu), one should place the solar mandala ending in *ṅeṃ* from the throat down to the navel, while meditating on the Radiant One in the heart.
Having pronounced the vowels together with the moon (the nasal bindu) and the letter ṅa,
one should place the circle of fire from the navel down to the feet while recollecting the fire-mantra.
This placement of the mandala, which bestows great splendor, has been declared;
it begins with the letters from 'a' to 'ṣa', ending with the dative case particle *ṅe* and the word *namaḥ*, within the lunar mandala.
The best of practitioners should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) from the crown of the head down to the heart,
beginning with the letter *ḍa* and ending with *kṣa*, which is the solar mandala.
One who is well-composed should perform the placement from the heart to the feet;
this placement, consisting of fire and moon, is said to bestow all accomplishments.

The practitioner of mantra should place the letters of the Mātṛkā, ending with *jaya*, for the sake of the Self of Puruṣa, with "namas" at the end; this is declared to be the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) of the *haṃsa*.
One should then install the nine planets, beginning with Āditya as previously mentioned, assigning eight syllables each to the remaining five, which are measured at five syllables each.
One should place the supports (ādhāra) and the liṅgas in sequence at the navel, the heart, the throat, the interior of the mouth, the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, and the Brahma-aperture.

One should perform the threefold placement (nyāsa) consisting of that called Haṃsa, that called Agnīṣoma, and the three maṇḍalas; then one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra.
Having thus performed the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should meditate upon the Sun in the lotus of the heart—
Ravi, who holds in his hands the pair of gestures of generosity and fearlessness along with two lotuses.

Having thus meditated upon the one who wears earrings, mace, armlets, and a necklace, whose body is the triple Veda, the practitioner of mantra should recite it eight hundred thousand times, with a tenth part as the concluding oblation.
One should perform the oblation according to the rules with red lotuses or sesame seeds during the worship of the Vasus;
first, one should worship Dharma and the others in the locations of the pedestal-worship.
One should worship Prabhūta, Vimala, Śāra, and Samārādhya immediately thereafter; in the center, one should worship Paramādimukha, ending with Khabimba.
One should worship the solar mandala after having worshipped the lunar and fiery mandalas;
likewise, one should worship Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, and Vimalā.
Amoghā, Vidyutā, and Sarvatomukhī are the powers of the seats (pīṭhaśaktayaḥ).
They are produced from the utterance of the three short vowels, are devoid of the neuter gender, and are conjoined with fire (R) and the moon (I).
One should worship those vowels as the seeds of the Śaktis, beginning with that [first vowel];
they are the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and this creation is also accompanied by the remainder.
And thus, at the end, one should utter the heart-mantra for the nature of the Yoga-pīṭha;
this is the Pīṭha-mantra beginning with *Tāra* (Oṃ), and with it one should assign the seat.

The wise one should contemplate the form for the nine-syllable mantra of Dṛṇmanu, which consists of *dhruva*, followed by the sky (*kha*) joined with the *viyat* (the nasal bindu), and then *khakholkāya*. NarP_1,69.28.
Having invoked that witness of the worlds into her [the yantra], one should worship according to the rules;
then, having propitiated the six limbs, one should fully worship the twelve-angled [yantra].
Having worshipped Āditya, Ravi, Bhānu, and Bhāskara in the center, one should worship Sūrya and these others—
Sadyojāta and the rest, along with the short vowels and so forth— in the cardinal directions.
One should worship the powers beginning with the first letter of each of their respective names in the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions;
thereafter, one should worship Uṣā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Saṃdhyā, and then Brahmā and the others.

Having first worshipped Aruṇa, Soma, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus, and having offered sacrifice to the deities beginning with Aryaman in the directions, as well as Mars and Saturn; ||| NarP_1,69.32 |||
One should worship Rāhu and Ketu in the corners as before;
likewise, the wise one should worship Indra and the others, as well as Vajra and the others, as previously described.
Having thus worshipped the Sun, who is affectionate toward his devotees, according to the prescribed rite,
one should, with a concentrated mind, offer the *arghya* to the Lord of Day day after day.
Having restrained the vital breaths and performed the previously mentioned ritual depositions (nyāsa) upon the ground,
one should prepare the mandala of the Sun and worship the pedestal as before.
Having meditated upon the Sun, one should worship him with divine mental offerings;
[one should prepare] a very beautiful vessel made of copper, capable of holding a *prastha* of water.
Having placed [the vessel] within a mandala fashioned from red sandalwood and other substances,
one should fill it with water while reciting the root mantra of the reverse alphabet (vilomamātṛkā).
With streams of nectar emerging from the solar orb,
he manifested saffron, jasmine, sandalwood, and red sandalwood.
One should cast karavīra, japā, rice, kuśa grass, śyāmāka grain,
sesame, bamboo, and barley into the auspicious water.
Having invoked the Sun there along with his limbs and retinue, one should worship him as before with perfumes,
flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, according to the prescribed ritual.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), one should perform the ancillary rites as before;
one should draw the seed-syllable of nectar with sandalwood paste upon the palm of the right hand.
Having covered the vessel for the *arghya* offering with that [cloth], one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind one hundred and eight times; then, having worshipped the Sun once again.
Taking the vessel with both hands and kneeling upon the ground,
he raised the vessel above his head and chose the Sun as his bridegroom.
Having fixed his gaze and honored the Sun with his mind,
the practitioner, through his own singular identity, should mentally recite the root mantra.
One should offer the *arghya* while meditating on the Sun within a circle of red sandalwood;
having offered a handful of flowers once more, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Or, even if he is not present, one should always offer this arghya to Vivasvat;
pleased by that, the Lord of Day shall grant him wealth, fame, and happiness.
This offering of the *arghya* is said to bestow sons, grandsons, and whatever else is desired; it increases both longevity and health. (NarP 1.69.47)
It bestows wealth, grain, cattle, security, fields, friends, and a wife;
it grants splendor, vigor, fame, renown, knowledge, prosperity, and enjoyment. (NarP 1.69.48)
Devoted to the worship of Gāyatrī and intent upon the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā-vandana),
a Brahmin who thus recites this mantra shall never encounter suffering anywhere.
Having thus worshipped [the deity], one should offer the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering) to Vikartana;
it should be accompanied by the syllables *vi*, *yat*, *vahni*, *marut*, *sādyānta*, *arvī*, and *indu*. 69.50.
Indeed, the seed-syllable known as Mārtaṇḍabhairava, which fascinates the three worlds, when encapsulated by the Bimba-seed-syllable, bestows the fruits of all desires. (NarP 1.69.51)
All other [details] here should be understood by the wise as being entirely as before.
[The mantra for] Soma is "Bhṛgu-jalendu-manv-āḍhyaḥ," ending with "hṛdaya" (namas) for Soma.
The six-syllabled king of mantras has Bhrigu as its sage;
its meter is considered to be Paṅkti, and Soma is proclaimed as its deity.
The first syllable is the seed-mantra, "namaḥ" is the power (śakti), and the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of everything.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with one's own seed-mantra extended by the six long vowels.
One should meditate on the Moon, whose face is full and resembles crystal, with a face adorned by dark-blue locks of hair, holding a beloved white water-lily and a garland of pearls.
One should recite the mantra for one hundred thousand seasons and perform oblations with milk-rice mixed with ghee,
amounting to a tenth part of that, upon a pedestal worshipped up to the deity Soma.
Having performed the ritual visualization (saṃkalpa) with the root-mantra of the form, one should worship the Moon according to the rules;
the worship of the limbs (aṅga-pūjā) should take place on the filaments, and these Śaktis on the petals.
Rohiṇī, Kṛttikā, Revatī, and Bharaṇī were in front;
then came Rātri, Ārdrā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Kalā, who possessed a luster like that of a pearl necklace.
Adorned with very white garlands, garments, and pearl necklaces,
all of them were auspicious, burdened by the weight of their breasts, and stood with palms joined in reverence.
With minds attached to their beloveds, languid with the intoxication of passion,
those lotus-eyed women whose faces resemble the full moon are worthy of worship.
On the tips of the petals, the eight planets beginning with the Sun should be worshipped:
Āditya, Bhauma (Mars), Budha (Mercury), Śani (Saturn), Devejya (Jupiter), and Rāhu.
Joined with Venus and Ketu, these planets situated at the tips of the leaves are to be worshipped;
they are red, dawn-colored, white, blue, yellow, smoky, black, and dark.

The wise one should worship the guardians of the directions together with their weapons outside of that [mandala], with their left hands resting upon their thighs and their right hands granting fearlessness.
When the mantra has been thus accomplished, it shall grant one's own desired object;
on the full moon day, having conquered one's appetite, one should offer the arghya at the rising of the moon.
One should first draw three mandalas on the ground, extending from east to west;
standing in the western mandala, one should place the articles of worship in the middle one.
Having established Soma in another mandala provided with a lotus,
one should worship him according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha).
The knower of mantras should place a silver vessel there in front;
having filled it with fragrant milk and touching it, he should mutter the mantra.
Thereafter, the knower of mantras should offer one hundred and eight arghya oblations to the Moon with the Vidyā-mantra for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
By performing this rite according to this procedure every month without sloth, a person on earth attains all his desires within a year.
"O Vidyā, O Mālinī, may there be [success]; O Antacandriṇī, say 'ka';
O Candramukhī, ending with the *dviṭha*—this is declared to be the mantra of Vidyā. (NarP 1.69.70)
Thus, whoever constantly recites this mantra of the Lord of the Night-lotuses (the Moon) will,
before long, obtain wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, and good fortune.

Now I shall declare the mantra of Aṅgāraka, which bestows wealth and sons: Tāra (Oṃ), followed by the long vowel *ī*, the moon (*u*), and the sky (*ha*); that same sequence again, joined with the moon (*u*). (NarP 1.69.72)

Among them, Trailokyamohana is proclaimed as the first;
Śrīkara, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Kṛṣṇa is the fourth here.
The mantra consists of Tāra, Kāma, and Ramā, followed by Puruṣottama ending in the dative case (ṅe);
it includes the armor and weapon mantras, ends with the beloved of Agni (Svāhā), and possesses the number of syllables of fire (three) and the moon (one).
Brahmā is the sage; Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre;
and the deity here is known as Puruṣottama, while the seed-syllable and power reside in the abode of Smara.

Having formed the limbs [of the mantra] through the division of the syllables of the mantra— earth (1), moon (1), single flavor (1), witness (2), eye (2)— one should then meditate upon Puruṣottama according to the prescribed rule.
One should meditate upon Śrī Puruṣottama, who resembles the rising sun, whose hands shine with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and who is clad in yellow garments.
In a pavilion with shimmering archways inlaid with a flood of great jewels, where the canopy was resplendent with a multitude of pearls, self-restraint, and tranquility; NarP_1,70.92.
On a shimmering ruby altar, radiant with the brilliance of ten thousand suns, amidst the tinkling of small bells and anklets from throngs of dancing celestial nymphs; NarP_1,70.93.

One should recite the mantra nine hundred thousand times on that which is adorned by the jewels from the tips of the crowns of the multitude of gods, and one should perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount.
One should worship on the aforementioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal with full-blown lotuses;
by thus propitiating the Lord of Gods, one attains great prosperity.
One obtains sons, grandsons, fame, splendor, worldly enjoyment, and liberation;
this follows the word "uttiṣṭha" (arise), ending with "śrīkara agnipriyā."
Its sage is Vyāsa, its meter is said to be Paṅkti,
and its deity is Hari, known as Śrīkāra, who grants all desired things.
The pair "bhīṣaya" and "dvitaya" should be for the heart; the pair "trāsaya" and "dvitaya" for the head;
the pair "pramarddaya" for the tuft of hair (śikhā); and the pair "pradhvaṃsaya" for the armor (varma).
All the *humantās* are proclaimed to protect the two eyes,
the head, the two eyes, the throat, the heart, and the region of the navel.
One should assign the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon the pair of thighs and the pair of shanks;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual assignment (nyāsa) with the mantras recited in the Puruṣasūkta.
A Brāhmaṇa should place [the mantra] "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth" on the face; likewise, he should place the mantra "The Rājanya was his two arms" on the pair of arms. (NarP 1.70.101)
The thighs of this [Being] are the Vaiśya; the practitioner of mantra should place him upon the two thighs.
The Śūdra was born from the feet; the practitioner of mantra should place him upon the two feet. (NarP 1.70.102)
Then one should place the discus, conch, mace, and lotus upon the tips of the hands;
having thus performed the rite of placement (nyāsa), one should meditate [on the deity] in the previously mentioned pavilion.
Seated upon Tārkṣya, who himself rests upon a seat of red lotuses,
is the God of previously described form, the bestower of fortune and the enchanter of the worlds.
Having meditated thus, the mantra-practitioner should perform worship with one-tenth of eight hundred thousand [recitations],
using red lotuses, sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and wood from *vilva* and milk-exuding trees.
Having offered milk, food, and clarified butter individually with great concentration,
one should know that the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa are the milky trees.
Having conceived the form according to the root mantra upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal,
one should worship the all-pervading Lord together with His limbs, enclosures, guardians of the directions, and weapons.

When the mantra has been thus accomplished, the practitioner should perform the ritual applications as before: first the Tāra (Oṃ), then the Hṛdaya (Namaḥ), then "Bhagavān," followed by the dative suffix "Ṅeṃ" (to), and after that, "Varāha. (NarP 1.70.108)
For form, may there be Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; and those who are devoted to the red [color];
grant me lordship over the earth, O you who are dear to the pure, cause it to be given! NarP_1,70.109
This mantra, Rāmāgnivarṇa, is considered to belong to Bhṛgu as its sage; Anuṣṭubh is declared to be its meter, and the divine Varāha its deity.
The heart is for Ekadaṃṣṭra; the head is remembered as being for Vyomolkāya;
the crest-lock (śikhā) is for Tejo'dhipati; and the armor (varma) is for Viśvarūpa.
One should fashion the weapon for Mahādaṃṣṭra as having five limbs;
alternatively, it may consist of eight syllables, [formed] by the mountains (seven), the sixes, the arrows (five), and the Vasus (eight).
Having divided the excellent mantra into five parts, one should assign them to the five limbs;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the Primordial Boar, who resembles many suns.
Āṃ Hrīṃ: [He is] gold-colored from below the knees to the navel, with a white radiance;
[he holds] the desired objects, protection, the mace, conch, discus, spear, sword, and shield.
And one should meditate upon him holding with his hands the earth shining at the tips of his fangs;
having thus visualized, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, and a tenth part of that with lotuses.
One should offer oblations with [substances] smeared with honey and worship on the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal;
having conceived the form by means of the root mantra, one should worship the Lord within it.
For the accomplishment of the limbs, armor, guardians of the directions, weapons, and machines, one should grant protection through recitation alone;
[the deity] bestows wealth, grain, land, and prosperity.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight during the month of Siṃha, having placed a pure stone into the five products of the cow, one should touch it and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
Then, facing north, the practitioner of mantra should inscribe that stone upon the ground;
this shall ward off afflictions caused by spirits, ghosts, serpents, thieves, and the like.
In the morning on a Saturday, one should fetch earth from a Sādhya site;
having consecrated it with the root mantra, one should then divide it into three parts.
Having smeared one [vessel] with ghee and another cooking pot with oil,
and having thoroughly stirred them in cow’s milk, one should place the purified rice grains therein.
When the hair has been properly cleansed and purified, one should cook the *caru* while reciting the mantra;
having then removed the *caru* from the fire, it should be offered according to the prescribed rite.

Having worshipped with incense, lamps, and other offerings, the wise man should thereafter offer one hundred and eight oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) soaked in clarified butter into the consecrated fire.
In this manner, the mantra-practitioner should perform oblations on all seven days of the week;
thus, opposition within the field, as well as calamities such as enemies and thieves, shall perish.
On a Sunday at sunrise, having again taken earth from the Sādhya field according to the previous rule, and having prepared the oblation as before; ||| NarP_1,70.125 |||
One should diligently offer oblations in a kindled fire according to the previously mentioned number;
in this manner, one should perform the oblation for seven days for the sake of attaining mastery over the sacred field.
One should offer oblations one hundred thousand times with products of the cow and milk-rice;
one obtains the sovereignty over the desired land—of this there is no doubt.
With arms raised like the horizon, possessing divine white fangs whose tips touch the mountains,
and golden-hued, one should remain well-composed within a yellow earthly mandala.
By meditating upon Varāha, one obtains a beautiful land through his grace;
one should meditate on Varāha within the sphere of Varuṇa as having a luster like snow.
There will be the pacification of great calamities for the practitioner, of this there is no doubt;
and for the purpose of subjugation, one should always meditate on [the deity] resembling a peacock within the circle of fire.

One should meditate thus upon the enemy in the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*): as having the luster of blackness within a wind-maṇḍala, situated within a fire-maṇḍala, pure, and in the form of the Boar (*Vārāha*), who grants all accomplishments.
For the pacification of enemies, malevolent spirits, planetary afflictions, poisons, diseases, and other sufferings,
[one should employ] the syllable *bhag* joined with *dhīśa*, its head adorned with the sky (*vyoma*) and the bindu.
The single-syllable mantra of Varāha is another wish-fulfilling tree;
all rites such as worship, the offering of arghya, and so forth, should be performed for this [mantra] as previously described.
The syllable *sa* with the left ear (*vāma-karṇa*), followed by *ni*, *drā*, *si*, and *ya*; for Varāha, the heart-mantra ends with the final syllable;
preceded by *tāra* (Oṃ), this eight-syllabled mantra bestows all sovereignty.
Brahmā is the sage; Gāyatrī is the metre;
the deity is known as Varāha; and it is held that the ritual application of the limbs consists of sixteen, two, four, and three [syllables].
One should also conceive of the application of meditation, worship, and so forth for this [deity] as before;

beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by the word "Bhagavatī" ending in the suffix *-ī*, then the two syllables *dharaṇi*, and thereafter one should utter the two syllables *dhare*. (NarP 1.70.136)
The mantra consists of nineteen syllables and ends with the word *vahnipriyā*.
Varāha is its sage (*muni*), and the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī, beginning with Nivṛt.
The deity is Dharaṇī; the seed-syllable is Tāra; the power (śakti) is Vasupriyā.
The arrangement of the limbs is performed with six, four, three, five, two, two, and two syllables.
[One should meditate on her] as dark-complexioned, richly adorned with various ornaments, seated upon a lotus, possessing full and noble breasts,
holding in her hands a pair of blue lotuses, a stalk of rice, and [the seed-syllable] Śukra.
One should meditate upon the blessed Goddess Earth, who wears variegated garments;
having thus visualized her, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, with a tenth part of that number offered with milk-rice.
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with clarified butter and worship the pedestal of Viṣṇu; having conceived the form by means of the root mantra, he should worship Vasumatī within it.
Having first propitiated the limbs— earth, fire, water, and air—
and having worshipped them in the cardinal petals, one should worship their respective powers in the intermediate petals.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and the kalās of those vidyās;
thereafter, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as Vañca and the rest.
When the mantra has been thus mastered, the practitioner of mantra should accomplish his own desired goal;
likewise, he may enjoy the earth along with cattle, jewels, garments, and other such things.
He shall be beloved by Dharma, happy, and live for a hundred years;
this mantra of the Lord of the World is proclaimed as that which deludes the three worlds. (NarP 1.70.145)
*Tāra*, *kāma*, *ramā*, the seed-syllable, at the end of the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), *puruṣottama*, *śrīkaṇṭha*, at the end of *pratirūpa*, *lakṣmī*, and *nivāsi*. // NarP_1,70.146 //
At the end of *sakala*, one should utter the word *jagatpaścātkṣobhaṇa*;
at the end of *sarvastrīhṛdaya*, however, one should utter the word *vidāraṇa*.
Then, [he praised her] as "the one who causes intoxication and madness" throughout the three worlds,
ending with the description of the most beautiful women among men, after the gods and asuras.
Then there is a pair that torments the mind, a pair that inflames it,
then a pair that withers it, and finally a pair that kills it.
Then again, there are two for paralyzing, two for deluding,
two for causing flight, and then a pair for attracting.
One should arrange the practice of meditation, worship, and so forth for this [deity] as before;
beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should then utter the word "Bhagavatī" ending in the suffix *-ṅi*, followed by two instances of "dharaṇi" and then two instances of "dhare. (NarP 1.70.136)
The mantra consists of nineteen syllables and ends with the word *vahnipriyā*.
Varāha is its sage (*ṛṣi*), and the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī, beginning with Nivṛt.
The deity is Dharaṇī; the seed-syllable is Tāra (Oṃ); the Śakti is Vasupriyā.
The assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpana) is performed with syllables numbering three, four, three, five, two, two, and two.
Dark-complexioned, richly adorned with various ornaments, seated upon a lotus, and possessing full, shapely breasts;
she holds in her hands a pair of blue lotuses, a stalk of rice, and a parrot.
One should meditate upon the Blessed Earth, wearing variegated garments and supporting [all beings].
Having thus visualized her, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, with a tenth part of that number offered with milk-rice.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with clarified butter and worship on the pedestal of Viṣṇu;
having conceived the form by means of the root-mantra, he should worship Vasumatī within it.
Having first propitiated the limbs— the earth, fire, water, and air—
and having worshipped them in the cardinal-petal vessels, one should worship their respective kalās in the corner-petals.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and the kalās of those vidyās;
thereafter, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other weapons.
When the mantra has been perfected, the practitioner should accomplish his own desired goal;
thus, while ruling the earth, he enjoys cattle, jewels, garments, and other such things.
He shall be the beloved of the earth, happy, and live for a hundred years;
this is proclaimed as the mantra of the Lord of the World, which enchants the three worlds.
Tāra, Kāma, and Ramā as the seed-syllables; Puruṣottama at the end of the heart-mantra;
Śrīkaṇṭha at the end of the Pratirūpa; and Lakṣmī, followed by Nivāsin.
At the end of *sakala*, one should utter the word *jagatpaścātkṣobhaṇa*;
at the end of *sarvastrīhṛdaya*, however, one should utter the word *vidāraṇa*.
Then, [the sound] reached the end of the three worlds, causing intoxication and madness; and from the description of the most beautiful women among men, it reached the ends of the gods and demons.
Then there is a pair that torments the mind, a pair that inflames it,
then a pair that withers it, and finally a pair that kills it.
Then again, two for paralyzing, two for deluding,
then two for causing flight, and thereafter a pair for attracting.
One should utter the word *samastaparama* joined with *subhaga*, and at the end of the word *sarvasaubhāgya*, one should say the words *karasarva*. (NarP 1.70.151)
Then Brahmā gave him the Kāmaprada [bow], and thereafter the pair of bows Saindava and Hanu;
after that, he was equipped with a discus, a mace, and subsequently a sword.
Having declared, "Pierce the yoke with all the arrows, the two flanks at the end with the noose,
and [the driver] with the goad," he struck the pair again.
Then, say "Kuru" twice; thereafter, say "tiṣṭha pada," while maintaining one-pointed concentration until the end of the word. Then, having manifested my success, say "bhava ante ca varma phaṭ."
This great mantra, ending with the heart-mantra, is declared to consist of two hundred syllables; Jaimini is said to be its sage, and its meter is declared to be immeasurable.
The deity is proclaimed as the Lord of the World (Jagannātha) for the sake of deluding the worlds;
Kāma is the seed-syllable, Ramā is the power, and the application is for the attainment of everything.

After [the mantra] "O beloved who intoxicates the three worlds, O Supreme Person," the heart-mantra is proclaimed with the words "O agitating of the world" (jagatkṣobhaṇa), followed by "and Agnivarma. (NarP 1.70.157)
The mantra for the head is said to end with "lakṣmīdayitavarma," while the crown-lock (śikhā) follows;
one should then utter the word "maṅgaje" after "manmathas-tama."
Having uttered "kāmadāyai huṃ," one should then place "vama" after that;
at the end of "parama," [one places] "bhṛgukarṇābhyām," and then the word "sarva."
At the end of *saubhāgyakaravarma*, the armor (*kavaca*) is proclaimed;
at the end of *surāsura*, one should utter the word *manujasundarī*.
At the end of *hṛdaya*, one should say *vidāya*; thereafter, one should utter the word *raṇasarvapada*.
Then follows the word *praharaṇadhara*, followed by the word *sarvakāmuka*. 1.70.161.
One should then utter the pair of *hana*s, the heart-mantra, and the bonds;
after that, the two [syllables] for attracting, and then the word *mahābala*.
The armor (varma) and the weapon (astra) have been fully described; thereafter, the eye (netra) should follow. One should then utter "tribhuvana," followed by "cara sarvajan. (NarP 1.70.163)
"O you who have the pair of Hari as your end, tear apart my two minds and bring them under my control; this is declared to be the Netra-mantra at the end of the Varma. (NarP 1.70.164)
The six-limbed mantras beginning with Tārā are proclaimed to end with *phaṭ* and *namaḥ*. After the word *trailokya*, one should utter the word *mohana* preceded by *tāra*. (NarP 1.70.165)
Having addressed him with the name "Hṛṣīkeśa" and other incomparable epithets,
