one should thereafter agitate the hearts of all women.
The word for attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) followed by "go" (*gaccha*) and "come" (*āgaccha*), with the heart-mantra at the end;
having performed the pervasive ritual (*vyāpaka*) with this, the wise one should meditate upon the Lord of the World (*jagannātha*). (NarP 1.70.167)
On the lovely shore of the Ocean of Milk, adorned with celestial trees and creepers,
it possessed the splendor of the rising sun’s rays, illuminating the quarters of the sky with the radiance of its own light.
The air was filled with the fragrance of garlands of flowers and the humming of intoxicated bees,
while the sky was dusted with the pollen of lotuses shaken by a divine breeze.
One should contemplate the forest, delightful with the sweetness of the songs sung by the celestial damsels;
within it, in a pavilion of arches shimmering with an abundance of jewels.
Upon a magnificent canopy shining with profuse, radiant pearls, and adorned with jeweled altars and other ornaments reaching to the very peak of the celestial crown; NarP_1,70.171.
O Brahmin, one should remember the Lord seated upon his divine throne,
holding a conch, a noose, bows, a mace, the sword Nandaka, and a club.
Holding a goad in his arms, he gazes at the Goddess of the Lotus who embraces him upon his chest with her lotus-like eyes shimmering with passion.

Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times; then, with a tenth part of that number, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a half-moon-shaped or lotus-shaped sacrificial pit using *jātī* flowers.
Desiring to worship the Lord of the World, as well as the sacrificial ground, himself, and the sacrificial implements, the wise man should sprinkle them with water while reciting the Gāyatrī.
At the end of "trailokyamohanāya," one should utter the word "vidmahe";
having said "smarāya dhīmahi," [one concludes with] "tanno viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt. (NarP 1.70.176)
This is declared to be the supreme Gāyatrī, which effects all purification;
the wise man should indeed fashion a seat upon the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal.
"Ṭha Ṭha" is declared as the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) for the King of Birds;
thereafter, one should invoke the form [of the deity] into that [seat] by means of the root-mantra of Saṃkalpa.
Then, having worshipped with devotion by means of the pervasive placement mantra (vyāpakanyāsa),
one should worship the Śrīvatsa on the two breasts with that [mantra] which has the Śrīvatsa as its heart.
One should worship the Kaustubha gem on the chest with the mantra ending in *hṛt* (namas) addressed to Kaustubha;
and one should worship the Vanamālā garland on the neck with the mantra ending in *hṛt* addressed to Vanamālā.
Then, one should worship the deities of the limbs according to the rules within the pericarp;
thereafter, one should worship Lakṣmī and the others, along with the attendants and chowries, upon the petals.
Resembling the hue of the *bandhūka* flower, their breasts shone with strings of pearls;
their eyes were like full-blown lotuses, and they moved slowly with the playful intoxication of passion.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Dhṛti, Prīti, and thereafter Kānti, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi—these, beginning with Bīja and ending with Ṅena, are [the goddesses]. NarP_1,70.183 //
The seed-mantra of the Goddess is declared to be BHRŪM, enriched by the moon (the nasal bindu) and the sign of the scorpion (the letter M),
joined with the three short vowels, the neuter vowels, and all the remaining vowels.
One should first apply the seed-syllable of the Goddess to these [petals] in sequence;
then, one should worship the conch, the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the sword, and the mace at the tips of the petals.
The goad, the mace, and the noose, each with its own mudrā and mantra;
then Mahājalacarā, followed by the armor and the weapon, which is the beloved of Fire.
"Pāñcajanya, pratāra, and so forth, ending with 'namaḥ' for the worship of the conch;
'śārṅgāya' ending with 'saśaya' [for the bow]; and 'varmāstra' followed by 'vahnivallabhā' [for the armor and weapon]."
For the worship of Śārṅga, the mantra for the heart is "mahādyaiḥ";
however, in the great Sudarśana [rite], one should utter the words "cakrarāja."

The pair "hayayugmaṃ" (haya-haya), followed at the end by the two "kurus" (kuru-kuru), then the two "chindhis" (chindhi-chindhi), and after that the pair "vidāraya" (vidāraya-vidāraya). // NarP_1,70.189 //
The supreme mantra consists of *grasa* (swallowing) in pairs, followed by *bhakṣaya* (devour) in pairs;
then *bhūka* (earth-element) in pairs, *trāsaya* (terrify) in pairs, and finally *varma* (armor), *phaṭ*, and *suṃdarī* (the beautiful one). NarP_1,70.190 //
The heart-mantra for Sudarśana, used for the worship of the discus, is declared;
one should utter the pair of "Śivis" following the words "mahākhaḍgatīkṣṇa. (NarP 1.70.191)
"Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, and 'salutation to the sword' (khaḍgāya namaḥ) is the mantra for the worship of the sword;
one should likewise say 'O Mahābalā, [you who hold] the great Kaumodakī' at the end."
"O destroyer of all asuras," "subsequently," "gracious one," "pair," and so forth;
ending with the armor, the weapon, the fire-born wife, the Kaumodakī mace, the heart, the kṣa, and the tiṃ. (NarP 1.70.193)
The mantra for the worship of Kaumodakī, which accomplishes all aims, is declared as follows:
from the word "mahāṅkuśa," followed by two "kuṭ" syllables, then "huṃ phaṭ," and "vasupriyā. (NarP 1.70.194)
"Obeisance to the Goad" is declared for the worship of the goad at the neck of the mantra;
at the end of the great dissolution, one should utter the word "Mace."
The mantra for the worship of the mace (musala) is declared as: *yodhaya dvitayaṃ varma phaṭ ante vahnisuṃdarī*, followed by *musālāya namaḥ*. NarP_1,70.196 //
"Mahāpāśa hadādaghaṭaya ākarṣaya dvayam huṃ phaṭ svāhā, and 'namaḥ pāśāya'—this is the mantra for the worship of the noose. (NarP 1.70.197)
These are indeed the mantras beginning with Tārā; thereafter, one should worship Śakra and the others.
Having worshipped even Vajra and the others, one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*);
likewise, by worshipping for just one month with flowers born from the enemy of horses (*hayāri*), [the same result is attained].
Or one should offer oblations with white water-lilies (kumuda) one thousand and eight times;
within just a month, all the best of kings shall become subject to his will.
If one recites the mantra consisting of [the name of] someone ten thousand times,
by the power of this mantra, that person immediately becomes like a slave.
What is the use of saying more here?
By means of this mantra, the practitioner shall accomplish all desires and become equal to Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.70.202)
Thus ends the seventieth chapter in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* in the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the divine Manus of Narahari."
Having propitiated whom, Brahmā and the others indeed performed the acts of creation and so forth.
Saṃvartaka, Candramauli, Manu, and Vahnivibhūṣita—
this mantra known as Ekākṣara is remembered as a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship it.
O best among the wise, Muniratri is the sage, Jagatī is the meter, Nṛhari is declared to be the deity, and the application is for the attainment of all goals. (NarP 1.71.3)
The seed-syllable is *kṣaṃ* and the power (*śakti*) is said to be *ī*; the six limbs are formed by the six long vowels.
[The deity] has the sun, moon, and fire as eyes, possesses the luster of an autumnal moon, and [is endowed] with rays.
One should meditate upon Nṛhari, who holds a bow, a discus, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
one should perform a recitation of one hundred thousand times and an oblation with ghee and milk-rice amounting to one-tenth of that number.

One should worship on the Vaiṣṇava pedestal; the worship of the limbs is performed upon the filaments, while Khageśa, Śaṅkara, Śeṣa, and Śatānanda are worshipped in the directions and intermediate directions.
One should worship Śrī, Hrī, Dhṛti, and Puṣṭi on the corner petals;
one should worship that many Nṛharis in order upon the tooth-edges (the outer petals).
Kṛṣṇa, Rudra, Mahāghora, Bhīma, Bhīṣaṇa, Ujjvala,
Karāla, Vikarāla, Daityānta, and Madhusūdana.
Raktākṣa, Piṅgalākṣa, Añjana, Dīptaruci,
Sughoraka, Suhanu, Viśvaka, and Rākṣasāntaka.
Viśālaka, Dhūmrakeśa, Hayagrīva, Ghanasvana,
Meghavarṇa, Kubhāṅghrikarṇa, Kṛtānta, and Tīvratejas.
Agnivarṇa, Mahogra, Viśvavibhūṣaṇa,
Vighnakṣama, and Mahāsena— these thirty-two lions have been proclaimed.
The wise practitioner should then worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) along with their weapons outside;
when the mantra is thus perfected, the master of mantras shall accomplish all desired objects.
Then Viṣṇu, joined with Pradyumna, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Great One;
then the blazing Viṣṇu, Bhṛgvīśa, and the lotus-seated Jala.
Hari, however, gave to Vāsudeva Vaikuṇṭha, who was joined by Viṣṇu;
and [he gave] the mace-bearer, Nṛsiṃha with the moon, Bhīṣaṇa, and Bhadra as well.
Then Śauri, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, [uttered] Mṛtyumṛtyu from Bhānu;
this twenty-two-syllable mantra of Nṛhari bestows imperial sovereignty.
Brahmā is the sage, Gāyatrī is the metre, and Anuṣṭubh is declared [as another];
Nṛhari is its deity, the bestower of all desired fruits.
The seed-syllable is *haṃ*, and likewise the power is *iṃ*; this is the application for the attainment of all things, [divided] by four Vedas, eight Vasus, six, and six syllables of the Yugas.
Then, having performed the six-fold ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the head, the forehead, and the two eyes;
then upon the mouth, the arms, the joints of the feet, the tips [of the fingers], the belly, and likewise the heart.

The best of practitioners, having interspersed the syllables born of the Manu-mantras with the *praṇava* (oṃ) between them, should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the throat, both sides, the back, and the hump.
The ten-fold ritual placement (*nyāsa*) that brings about the presence of Nṛsiṃha is as follows:
[it is performed] separately on the fingers and toes, beginning with the hands and feet, on the first and last joints of each.
Having placed [the mantras] on all the fingers, one should place the remainder on the two palms,
as well as on the head, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the two eyes, and the two ears.
And on the temples and the roots of the ears, on the chin and the upper and lower lips,
on the throat and the nose, on the two arms, on the chest, and on the region of the navel.
[He should place them] on the soles of the feet, at the waist, the penis, the thighs, the knees, and the calves;
on the ankles, the toes of the feet and hands, at all the joints, and on the body hairs.
The wise one should place the syllables upon the blood, bones, and marrow within the body;
and the syllables upon the feet, ankles, knees, hips, navel, and the region of the heart.
One should place [the syllables] on the two arms, the throat, the chin, the two lips, the cheeks, the two ears, the mouth, the two nostrils, the two eyes, and the head. (NarP 1.71.25)
One should place the syllables on the mouth, the head, the nose, the eyes, the two ears,
the face, the heart, the navel, and all the limbs.
One should place two and a half [syllables] upon the head; from the heart to the feet, one should assign its limbs.
The words beginning with "Ugra" are as follows: "I bow to Mṛtyumṛtyu. (NarP 1.71.27)
Thus, one should place these nine [syllables] in the mouth, the nose, the eyes, the ears, the eyelashes, the heart, the navel, and from the waist down to the feet— these being the nine locations.
The wise one should likewise arrange those very [mantras] beginning with Vīra as before; he should also arrange those very ones beginning with Nṛsiṃha as previously described.
One should sequentially place the syllables of the mantra,
divided according to the numbers one, three, four, six, two, two, ten, and eight, into their respective positions.
From the base to the root, and from the root up to the navel; from the navel up to the heart;
from the heart up to the space between the eyebrows; and then to the three eyes and the crown of the head.
The wise one should perform the placement on the arms, the fingers, and from the head down to the feet by name; this is declared to be the *hari-nyāsa*.
Only Hari himself knows the greatness of this nyāsa;
having thus performed the rite of nyāsa, one should meditate upon Nṛhari within the heart.
With his arms resting upon his chest, his hair touched by them, holding the lotus and the discus,
he pierced the lord of the Daityas with the tips of his nails and was adorned with garlands of flames.
May Nṛsiṃha— blazing-tongued, three-eyed, and bearing a face with fierce fangs—
protect us always, whether he is on land, in water, or in the sky.
Having meditated thus, one should display the mudrā of the Great-souled Nṛsiṃha:
placing both the chin and the lips evenly between the knees.
With both hands pressed against the ground, trembling again and again,
he opened his mouth wide and repeatedly licked his tongue.
This mudrā is proclaimed as the preeminent Nārasiṃhī;
it is formed by binding the three fingers—excluding the little finger—from the thumb of the left hand.
One should form the mudrā associated with Nṛsiṃha like a trident, facing upward;
having likewise pressed down on the two little fingers of both hands with the two thumbs.
Then, for Nṛhari, with the remaining [mudrās] facing downwards,
one should place both hands face down and extend them toward the region of the navel.
One should bring the two shoulders together with the two threatening fingers; this is declared here as the *āntraṇa-mudrā*.
Having turned the hands upward and joined the palms, one places the two middle fingers [together]. (NarP 1.71.41)
One should place the left ring finger upon the right ring finger;
the two index fingers should be joined at their backs, with the two thumbs resting against the index fingers.
This is considered the *cakramudrā* for the presence of Nṛhari;
having formed the *cakramudrā* in that manner, one should [join] the two index fingers with the two middle fingers.
This is the Vaṃṣṭra-mudrā, which destroys all sins;
these mudrās of Nṛsiṃha are esteemed among all mantras.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee into the fire ten thousand times; one should worship on the pedestal as previously described.
Having first worshipped the limbs [of the deity], one should again worship Garuḍa and the others upon the petals of the directions;
the Śrīmukhas in the intermediate directions, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) outside.
Thus accomplished, the mantra shall fulfill all desires;
for a gentle task, the wise practitioner should contemplate the gentle, and for a cruel one, he should contemplate the cruel.
First, having uttered the name of the enemy as if it were the instruction for death, one should personally visualize Hari devouring him with the tips of his sharpened claws and fangs.
One should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times without sloth;
before even a single mandala has passed, the enemy will surely become a guest at the funeral pyre.
Next, I shall describe the various meditations that bestow all accomplishments:
one who desires prosperity should constantly meditate upon the white Nṛhari previously described.
Embraced by Lakṣmī, who stands upon his left side and holds a lotus in her hand,
he is the destroyer of all calamities, such as poison, untimely death, and malignant diseases.
The Greatly Terrifying Man-Lion, whose radiance was like the fire of cosmic destruction,
wearing a garland of entrails, fierce, and adorned with a necklace around his neck.
He has a serpent as his sacred thread and is beautifully adorned by a lion;
he bears the moon upon his crest, is blue-throated, and possesses three eyes in every face.
He was adorned with ten arms resembling iron clubs,
holding a rosary, a mace, a lotus, and a conch shell white as cow’s milk.
Holding a bow, a mace, and an excellent discus,
as well as a sword, a trident, and an arrow— Nṛhari, who possesses the form of Rudra.
Having the luster of an indragopa insect, blue, moon-like, and resembling gold—
from the east up to the north, and including the upward and downward directions— it possesses every color.
Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantras should recite it for liberation from all diseases;
this divine [mantra] removes all death and bestows all accomplishments through mere remembrance. (NarP 1.71.57)
When he meditates upon his great deed, then Nṛsiṃha, the lord of all worlds, adorned with every ornament, appears sixteen cubits in height.
Two have the act of rending as their function, and two are endowed with the extraction of entrails;
two bear the conch and the discus, while two others bear the arrow and the bow.
Two held swords and shields, two bore maces and lotuses,
two carried nooses and goads, and two had the crowns of their enemies placed upon them.
Thus, O Nārada, with undistracted mind, one should meditate upon the omnipresent Lord Nṛhari, who is adorned with sixteen mighty arms, possesses a dark-blue luster, and performs fierce deeds.
In great undertakings, Nṛsiṃha— the lord of all beings, the supreme bestower of all accomplishments— should be meditated upon by the wise as having thirty-two arms.
In his right [hands], he holds a discus, a lotus, an axe,
a noose, a plow, a mace, as well as the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and a goad.
In his left hands, he holds a spear, a bhindipāla, a sword, a mallet, and a tomara;
and in his [other] left hands, a conch, a shield, a noose, and a trident.
Then [he holds] Agni, the bestower of boons, a spear, and a water-pot;
thereafter, a bow, the tarjanī mudrā, a mace, a hand-drum, and a winnowing basket.
With two hands he presses the knees and head of his enemy;
with arms raised upward, the Lord wears a garland of entrails.
With his two lower arms, he performed the rending of Hiraṇyakaśipu—
an act that brings joy to his devotees and inspires terror in the Daityas.
One should thus remember that Nṛsiṃha, who removes the great fear of death;
having meditated in this way, the practitioner of mantras should recite it for the sake of accomplishing all tasks and goals. (NarP 1.71.68)
Now another auspicious meditation is described, which removes diseases of the mouth:
[the deity] is golden-hued, seated upon a beautiful bird, and possesses a mane like a garland of lightning.
He has the complexion of the full moon at its peak, a beautiful face, and three eyes gazing out;
he is richly adorned with yellow garments and great ornaments, possessing a peaceful form as Nṛsiṃha,
holding a discus, a conch, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons with his sprout-like hands.
The practitioner should exert effort in pacifying poisons, diseases, and the like through his own meditations and by bringing happiness,
as well as in the obstruction of the enemy's army.
Having meditated upon the slayer of enemies, the god Nṛsiṃha, and having worshipped him with offerings such as flowers, one should kindle the fire with *akṣa* wood.
One should offer a hundred and ten oblations separately with the *caru* mixed with the roots and the root-mantras;
one should mutter [the mantra] as if devouring the enemy and cast it away as if burning him.
Having performed oblations for seven days, the mantra-practitioner, desiring the conquest of the enemy kingdom, should dispatch the king's desired army at an auspicious moment.
In front of her, having visualized Nṛhari slaying the circle of his enemies,
one should perform the recitation until she returns once more.
Having utterly defeated all enemies along with the splendor of heroism and having attained happiness,
the king, with a joyful mind, should gratify his ministers with wealth.
If the minister is not satisfied with elephants, horses, chariots, jewels, villages, fields, wealth, and so forth, then there will be misfortune for the lord of the earth.
A great danger, even greater than to one's own life, arises for him within his realms;
[this is countered] by means of ashes consecrated with the hundred and eight root mantras.
It destroys poison arising from mice, spiders, scorpions, and the like;
one whose limbs are smeared with it is freed from all diseases—of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.71.79)
Having offered oblations with *sevantī* flowers, one shall attain great prosperity;
by means of *audumbara* wood fuel-sticks, one shall become possessed of an abundance of grain.
By performing a homa of one hundred thousand cakes, one becomes equal to Vaiśravaṇa;
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times in the presence of an angry king.
One immediately attains purity and achieves clarity; with *kunda* flowers there is rising splendor, and with *mocā* flowers there is the destruction of obstacles. (NarP 1.71.82)
By offering oblations of *tulasī* leaves, one shall attain great fame;
by offering oblations of barley-flour (*saktu*) made from *śāli* rice, one shall bring the entire world under one's control.
The desired immobilization [of the enemy] may be achieved with madhūka flowers or with pieces of āmalaka fruit;
likewise, by consuming guḍūcī and caturaṅgula mixed with curd, honey, and clarified butter.
He who offers ten thousand oblations conquers disease and lives for a hundred years;
likewise, by touching an *aśvattha* tree on a Saturday and reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he attains the same result.
Having conquered [obstacles], he who recites this mantra overcomes untimely death and lives for a hundred years.
Now I shall fully describe to you the yantra that deludes the three worlds.
By the mere retention of which all prosperities may arise—
one should write a lotus on white birch bark, accompanied by thirty-two lions.
In the center, upon a lion, one should write one's own seed-syllable just as before;
it should be understood as being joined with three circles by means of the Śrī-bīja.
Having encircled it with nooses and goads, one should worship this supreme yantra named Trailokyamohana, which accomplishes all desires and purposes. (NarP 1.71.89)
By the retention of the Cakrarāja, the Great King, the Lord of all lords of the solar disc, one attains victory; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Now I shall describe another yantra that bestows success; listen, O Nārada!
One should draw an eight-spoked yantra, smooth and provided with a pericarp.
One should write the root mantra there, conjoined with the *praṇava* (oṃ);
and in the center, the single-syllable *nārasiṃha* mantra, together with the name of the person for whom it is intended (*sādhya*).
The wise one should recite the mantra eight thousand times, and having wound it with a thread, he should wrap it outside that with gold, silver, and copper in succession.
Having wrapped it with lac, one should again consecrate it with the mantra;
one should wear this supreme yantra on the neck, the arm, or the topknot.
All men, women, and kings on earth shall come under his control;
moreover, wicked beings—piśācas, serpents, and rākṣasas—will not afflict him at all.
By the grace of the King of Yantras, one shall attain victory everywhere.
Now I shall further explain another yantra that brings all under control.
The wise one should draw the great twelve-spoked wheel as before;
the steadfast one should draw it with petals divided by the twelve measures.
In the center, one should encircle the mantra joined with Śakti using the Śrī-bīja;
this is the wheel named Kālāntaka, which brings about the happiness of the gods.
One should draw the wheel on birch bark as a means of warding off all enemies;
by the mere wearing of it, one shall be victorious everywhere. (NarP 1.71.99)
Now I shall declare the seed-syllable known as Jvālāmālin, which grants all desires: the syllable *haṃ* is the heart, followed by the word *bhagavān*, ending with *ṅe*, and then *narasiṃhāya*.
To Jvālin, Mālin, and Agni of blazing fangs;
to the Protector, the destroyer of all Rākṣasas from the beginning, grant us the state of sovereignty over all beings.
At the end, for the sake of destruction, one should utter "Hari," the destroyer of all fevers;
at the end of the name, one should pronounce two "dahas" and two "pacas."
The pair of protections, followed by the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras ending with *ṭha* and *dū*, beginning with *dhruva* (the syllable *om*),
constitutes this supreme mantra, Jvālāmālī, proclaimed to consist of sixty-eight syllables.
But merit and so forth, as previously mentioned, are [described] by thirteen syllables;
and by eighteen syllables, which consist of five lines (paṅkti) and are numbered after Rudra.
The practitioner of mantra should fashion the limbs with the excellent rays as instruments;
he should meditate upon Nṛhari, who possesses the form previously described and is garlanded with flames.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with the ghee of a tawny cow ten thousand times;
this supreme mantra is the destroyer of Raudra, Apasmāra, Bhūtas, and other such afflictions.
Prāṇa, Māyā, and Nṛsiṃha are declared to be the creation and the Brahmāstra;
this six-syllabled great mantra bestows all desired objects.
The sage is Brahmā, the meter is Paṅkti, and the deity is the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin).
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels.
One should perform meditation and worship according to the very procedure previously described;
by means of this perfected mantra, all success shall be attained by men.
The mantra beginning with the seed-syllable of Ramā consists of thirty-three syllables in the Anuṣṭubh meter;
Prajāpati is the sage, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Lakṣmī-Nṛkesarī.
The assignment of all the deities to the limbs has been described by means of the words;
having thus performed the five-fold placement, one should practice self-protection.
Touching his right arm, he should mutter the mantra of Śarabha:
"Oṃ, to the Heart, to Śiva, to the Noble One, and to the Great Śarabha. (NarP 1.71.112)
The mantra ending with *vahnipriyā* (svāhā) is proclaimed for the purpose of protection;
alternatively, one should recite the two syllables *kṣa-kṣa* at the end of the Rāma-mantra.
Alternatively, one should diligently perform protection by means of Keśava and the others:
"May Keśava protect my feet; may Nārāyaṇa protect my shanks. (NarP 1.71.114)
May Mādhava protect my hips, and Govinda my private parts;
may Viṣṇu protect my navel, and Madhusūdana my belly.
May Trivikrama protect my thighs; may Nara protect my heart;
may Śrīdhara protect my throat, and Hṛṣīkeśa protect my face.
May Padmanābha protect my breasts, and may Dāmodara protect my head;
having thus assigned [the mantras] to the limbs, the practitioner should perform the recitation at the time of japa.
One becomes fearless of ghosts, vetālas, planetary spirits, and rākṣasas;
then, remaining concentrated and performing meditation, one should again install [the mantras] with effort.
May Keśava, bearing the discus and radiant as Jāmbūnada gold, protect [me] from the front; may Nārāyaṇa, bearing the conch and resembling a dark blue cloud, protect from behind.
Above is Mādhava, dark as a blue lotus and bearing a mace;
on the right side is the great Govinda, wielding a bow and possessing the luster of the moon.
In the north is Viṣṇu, the wielder of the plow, resembling the filaments of a lotus;
in the southeast is Madhusūdana, the lotus-eyed one, bearing a mace.
Trivikrama, with sword in hand and glowing like fire, is in the southwest;
Mādhava, the wielder of the thunderbolt, resembling the rising sun, is in the northwest.
In the northeast, may Puṇḍarīkākṣa protect; Śrīdhara, whose weapon is the paṭṭiśa; Vidyutprabha, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Urdhva, who holds a mallet.
And below me is Padmanābha, possessing a splendor equal to the thousand-rayed sun,
the possessor of all weapons, all powers, the primordial of all, facing every direction.
May the unconquered Hari, whose hand holds a noose and who possesses the luster of an *indragopa* insect, protect us; may that Lord, both within and without the body, shield us from fear.
Thus, having entered everywhere this twelve-fold cage called "the flawless," I have no fear whatsoever at any time.
Having thus performed the protection, a man becomes invincible;
this is the prescribed method for all the mantra-groups of Nṛhari.
One should perform all the rites, such as meditation and worship, according to the previously stated method:
"Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one! Homage to you, O creator of the universe! (NarP 1.71.128).
"Salutations be unto you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; salutations to you, O Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa).
Having thus offered this prayer, recited [the mantra], and read [the hymn], one should dismiss the Lord.
When the mantra is thus accomplished, the practitioner becomes a locus of all prosperities;
this supreme eight-syllable mantra begins with "Jaya-jaya Śrī-Nṛsiṃha."
The sage is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī,
and its deity is declared to be the glorious Jaya-Nṛsiṃha, the bestower of all desired objects.

A person of great intelligence should not perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) when the moon is in conjunction with the asterisms of Śravaṇa, Rohiṇī, or Punarvasu, nor when it is joined with the six long vowels.
Then one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Nṛsiṃha, who bears the crescent moon on his crest, within the heart.
O glorious Lord of Men, O tiger among men, sole kinsman of the world; O Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, ocean of compassion, King of the Gods;
O you whose eyes are fire, moon, and sun; O wielder of the Pināka bow; O you who have the moon as your crest-jewel, Lord of Ramā, O Viṣṇu, protect me!

Having meditated thus, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times; then, as a tenth part of that, he should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee, and perform worship as previously described.
One should utter the *tāra* (oṃ), the *māyā* (hrīṃ), and one's own seed-syllable at the end; then one should pronounce Karṇogra Vīra.
Thereafter, one should say Mahāviṣṇu, who is blazing and facing in all directions.

One should utter "sphurad-dvayaṃ prasphura," then the two syllables of the terrible word (*ghora-pada*), then those two even more terrible syllables, and finally the two *ṭha*s in the form of the body.
Having addressed the two *pracaṭas*, the pair of *kahas*,
and the pair of *mads*, one should utter the pair "bind" (*bandha*) and "slay" (*ghātaya*), and then discharge the *varma* and *astra* mantras.
I bow to the auspicious Nṛsiṃha, the terrifier, the death of Death himself;
this mantra of eighty-five syllables bestows desired boons upon those who worship it. (NarP 1.71.139)
For the seers are Aghora and Brahmā, as well as Triṣṭubh and Anuṣṭubh;
likewise, the meters are considered to be Ghorā and Nṛsiṃha as the deity.
A wise person should perform meditation, worship, and other rites for this [deity] according to the *Anuṣṭubh* meter;
especially, this excellent mantra is considered to provide protection against all things.
The seed-syllable is the pair of *jaya*s, followed by the eight syllables "Nṛsiṃha.
Prajāpati is declared to be its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the *anuṣṭubh* is said to be its meter (*chandas*).
Vidāraṇa-Nṛsiṃha is proclaimed as its presiding deity;
*jaṃ* is the seed-syllable, *haṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and the ritual application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of everything.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the long and rich [mantra];
one should meditate upon the fierce Nṛsiṃha as tearing open the chest of the enemy.
Whose weapons are his claws and fangs, who grants fearlessness to his devotees, the abode of Śrī,
with the tips of his hair like molten gold and eyes blazing like fire.
O Divine Lion, whose touch with the claws of your vajra-like nails is supreme, homage be to you!
The Sage is declared to be Brahmā, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh.
The deity of this ocean of mantras is the divine Man-lion (Nṛkesarin);
one should perform the five limbs with all four feet.
O Lord of Sages, all practices such as meditation and worship are declared to be as previously described;
and all the rites mentioned before shall attain accomplishment.

*Tāro namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya hṛñca te / jastejase āvirāvirbhava vajranakhāntataḥ //* 1,71.149 *Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, the Man-Lion! Hrīṃ! To you, the splendor of splendors! Manifest, manifest yourself, O you whose extremities are adamantine claws!* 1,71.149
With "Vrajadaṃṣṭra," at the end of the ritual action, one should cause the two to cry out with fear;
then, with "Tamo grasa," one causes the two to swallow [the darkness], and thereafter, at the end of "svāhā," one grants them freedom from fear.
Ātman and Anta are the most numerous [names]; Dhruva is the last of the seed-mantras (bīja).
This mantra consists of sixty-two syllables; everything beginning with the sage (muni) is declared as before.
The Tāra, the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha, and then "namo bhagavate";
then "narasiṃhāya," the Tāra, and its seed-syllable; when these are joined together [it forms the mantra].
*Tāraḥ* is the seed-syllable for the form of Rūpa; *tārakam* is the seed-syllable for the form of Kūrma;
*tāraḥ* is the seed-syllable for the form of Varāha; and from *nṛsiṃha*, the seed-syllable is [the same].
For the sake of form (rūpa), [one should utter] one's own seed-syllable at the end of *vāmana* and from the perspective of form;
then the three fixed syllables for evil (*pāpa*), the seed-syllable, and "to Rāma" (*rāmāya*) preceded by the Vedas (*nigama*).
The seed-syllable for Kṛṣṇa at the end of Tārā, and then the seed-syllable for Kalki;
then two instances of Jaya, and [the word] "to the Dweller" at the end of Śālagrāma.
Divyasiṃhāya ṅentaḥ, svayaṃbhūḥ puruṣāya hṛt,
and Tāraḥ svaṃ bījam— this [mantra] bestows the great empire.

The mantra of Nṛsiṃha consists of the syllable *khāṃ*; Atri is proclaimed as the sage (*ṛṣi*), Atijagatī is declared to be the meter (*chandas*), and he is said to be the deity (*devatā*) of this mantra.
The ten incarnations, Nṛhari, the seed-syllable (bīja), the void (kha), and the imperishable power (śakti)—
having performed the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) with the seed-syllable enriched by the six long vowels, one should meditate upon Him.
May Nṛhari, who resembles many moons, whose eyes are fixed upon the face of Lakṣmī,
and who is accompanied by his ten incarnations, grant us happiness.
The recitation should be ten thousand times, and the fire-oblation with milk-rice should be one-tenth of that;
one should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal, having mentally conceived the form [of the deity] by means of the root mantra.
First, one should worship the limbs and then the Fish and other [incarnations] on the petals of the directions;
thereafter, by worshipping Indra and the others, as well as the Thunderbolt and the other [weapons], one shall obtain the highest goal.
I shall now declare the great mantra of a thousand syllables, which is concealed within the tantras:
first the seed-syllables of Tāra, Māyā, Ramā, and Kāma, followed by the word of Wrath.
At the end of the word *mūrte nṛsiṃha*, one should utter *mahāpuruṣa*;
at the end of *pradhāna-dharma-adharma*, one should speak the word *nigaḍa*.
At the end of Nirmocana, at that time, a man should set forth;
at the end of Sveśvara, he should see water resembling the waters of the end of time.
Furthermore, it is established as being at the end of all exhaustion, and therefore it is the eternal consciousness of pure awareness;
moreover, it is at the end of all illuminators, eternally arisen, and transcending time and the like.
And [the mantra] "O Great Compassionate One, who pervades rising and setting" is said to be at the heart-lotus; it is situated at the ends of the four petals.
O you whose self is consciousness, O twenty-four-fold one, and beyond that, O twenty-five-fold one at the end! // NarP_1,71.167 //
O Bakō Hari, at the end of a thousand [ages], come, come in embodied form by the sound [of my call];
O Blessed One, Nṛsiṃha, Puruṣa, Lord of Wrath, together with Rasā!

At the end of the *srava* [period], O Mahādeva, there is the sound of the ten classes [of beings] from the words "feet" (*pāda*) and so forth, as well as a thousand fires at the end of the eon (*kalpa*), and a radiance of ten million at the end of the *abhā* [period]. *NarP* 1.71.169.
The ground of the hundred sacrifices is to be known, and from that, the pair of stainless [beings];
Piṅgalekṣaṇa, Saṭā, Daṃṣṭrā, Daṃṣṭrāyudha, and Nakhāyudha.
Then follows the *dānavendrāntaka*, the *avahni*, the *naśoṇita-pada*, and at the conclusion of the conflict between attachment and form, the *bhūta*, *apasmāra*, and *yātudhāna*.
O Blessed One, whose lotus feet are being worshipped by the gods and asuras,
you are the source and the dissolution within the circle of the sky, ending with the Lord of the Sky-Circle (Vyomacakreśvara).
Arise with your form; arise and burn away the accumulation of ignorance.
At the end, burn it and then manifest the pair of knowledge and sovereignty.
Oṃ, O Omniscient One, O You who are without anger at the end, O You who descend through yawning and stretching;
O True Person, at the end of sound, one should utter [the syllable] between existence and non-existence. (NarP 1.71.174)
My fear of bad dreams was settled by the sound of the fetters;
my fear of the sound of the wilderness was dispelled, as was my fear of the venomous footstep.
At the end of a fever, there is fear of ḍākinīs, kṛtyās, and Dhvarevatī;
at the end of a thunderbolt, there is fear of famine and the sound of pestilence.
After the word *mārīca*, there is the word *bhaya*; after that, the word *chāyā*.
After the word *skandāpasmāra*, there is *bhaya*, and after that, *caurabhaya*.
One may experience fear of water, dreams, and fire, or be overcome by elephants, lions, and serpents;
at the end of birth and old age, one utters cries of terror such as "death! and the like.
Then follow the *Bhayam-nirmocana-yuga* and the *Praśamana-yuga*;
at the end of the retention of the form of the object of knowledge, there is the *Nṛsiṃha-bṛhatsāman*.
After the word *puruṣānte*, the phrase *sarvabhayanivāraṇapadaṃ* follows;
then, with sixty-four [syllables] consisting of eight groups of eight, one should utter the fear-dispelling mantra for the female servants (*ceṭikā*).

One should utter the mantra "Vidyāvṛta" (surrounded by knowledge), followed by the sound of thirty-three crores of deities, then "namitānte" (at the end of those who are bowed), and from the word "padapada," one should proceed with "paṅkajānvita" (endowed with lotuses).
Immediately after the word *sravada*, one should utter *ananta*; after *sahasrodara*, one should speak *saṃvadet*; and at the end of the word *sahasrekṣaṇa*, one should pronounce *sahasrapāda*.
Having addressed him with a thousand arms, he spoke with a thousand tongues;
from the earth, with a thousand weapons, he said, "O you whose forehead is at the end of a thousand hands!"
At the conclusion of the destruction of the city by the dispeller of darkness, everything was indeed bestowed;
from the state of the Lord of the King of Mantras, it grants the power of movement through the air.
At the end of the passage leading to the subterranean realm (pātāla), one should utter the "crusher" (yantramardana);
then follows the station that is the abode of the universe, laughing with a terrible, loud laugh.
Then Vāsudeva, then Akrūra, then Hayamukha;
O Viśveśa, you are the supreme haṃsa, yet you are a mockery at the end of the universe.
Then, once the end has been established, the one who effects manifestation should impel Hṛṣīkeśa and Svacchanda; he should then deposit all living beings.
At the end of *grāsakānta*, one should utter *mahāpaścāt piśitāsṛk*; at the end of *laṃpaṭa*, *khecarī*—this bestows the attainment of success. (NarP 1.71.188)
"O unconquerable, immutable, and unmanifest one, within the belly of the cosmic egg!
Then, at the end of a thousand Brahmās, from the sound of "koṭisrag-ruṇḍa," [it arose].
One should utter "Māla Paṇḍitamuṇḍa," then "Matsya" and "Kūrma";
after the end of "Varāha," one should utter "Nṛsiṃha," and at the end of "Vāmana," one should likewise recite.
At the conclusion of the conquest of the three worlds, however, he should utter *pādaśālika*;
then the three *rāmas*, and at the end of the form of Viṣṇu, *dhara* itself.
At the end of the three principles, from the support of the *praṇava*, is that station which is the crest;
it is joined at the end with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), and then likewise *svadhā* and *vaṣaṭ*.
Having recited the *netra*, *varma*, and *astra* mantras, one should go toward the support of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
From the station of the Primordial God (*ādideva*), the *prāṇa* and *apāna* are subsequently established.
At the end of the word *ditija* (son of Diti), he says *pāñcarātrika-vinidhanānte-kare*;
and after the word *daityendra* (lord of the Daityas), he says *mahāmāyā-amoghānte-daryam*.
At the end of the ocean, he is called Dalana; he is Smara, the mass of splendor, fixed as the eternal.
At the end of Tejasvara, at the end of the row of Puruṣas, he is the True Puruṣa.
*Astratāra*, *acyutāstra* and *tāra*, with *vācā sudeva phaṭ*;
*tāramāyāmūrteḥ phaṭ*, and *vaḥ kāmaḥ* preceded by the vowels. 196.
The seed-syllable of the immutable Viśvamūrti is *mūrtistramavyayaḥ*;
for the Māyā-Viśvātman there are six, beginning with *tāraḥ* (*om*), followed by *saucaṃ turātmane*.
*Phaṭ*, *tāra*, *ahaṃ*, *viśvarūpin*, and then the weapon-mantra (*astra*); then *tāra*, *auḥ*, *naipara*, at the end of which is *hraṃsaḥ phaṭ*, and then the *praṇava*.
HRAḤ; at the end of the visualization of the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, PHAṬ DHRUVAḤ;
HRAIṂ; then the weapon-mantra of the one who bears a form beyond comparison, followed by DHRUVAḤ.
KṢAIṂ! O you who assume the form of Nṛsiṃha; OṂ KLAṂ ŚLAŚCA, beginning with the vowels;
O you who bear the form established by the application of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa); and then PHAṬ! NarP_1,71.200.
Hrau, which possesses a single form established by nature, and then Phaṭ;
the Tāra, the three armors, the Saṃkara, Vaṃ, and [the name] with "Amuka" at its head.
"Consume two pieces," "the two," "klīṃ," "bring the one to be accomplished," "the two," and then, O Great-Souled One, "show correctly"—this is the pair. (NarP 1.71.202)
One should recite one's own seed-syllable preceded by the six long vowels, and at the end of the destruction of impurities,
one should utter the two syllables of the North and the seed-syllables of the five arrows.
Then, at the end of "Nṛsiṃha," one should utter "svāhā" for the self whose nature is flame;
then, at the end of "Nṛsiṃha," "svāhā" for the self whose nature is Time, and then the eternal [syllable].
Then follows the seed-syllable of the sky, the seed-syllable of desire, and the two seed-syllables of Lakṣmī;
this is the final mantra of Māyātārā, consisting of one thousand syllables.
Kapila is its sage; the meter is Jagatī;
the deity is Śrī Lakṣmī; Nṛhari is the seed-syllable; and Kṣaiṃ is the power, the beloved of Fire.
The wise have declared that white is the color and the acute (udātta) is the accent;
the field is the Supreme Self, and its application is in the entire path.

*Kṣaḥ*, *sahasrabāhave*, *sahasrāyudhadharāya*, ending with *nṛsiṃhāntam* (the end of the Man-Lion), followed by *vahni-jāyā* (the wife of fire, i.e., *svāhā*) and *astrāya phaṭ*—this is declared to be the mantra. (NarP 1.71.208)
Having performed the purification of the hands with this, one should perform the [ritual] limbs;
at the end of the thousand [repetitions], the syllable *tāra* and *kṣāṃ*, along with the word *kṣara*, cause it to expand.
The mantra for the Heart is said to end with "Nṛsiṃhāya" and "agnijāyā" (svāhā); it begins with "Māraḥ," followed by "kṣīṃ," and ends with "mahātenuṃ" and "vikara. (NarP 1.71.210)
The Śiras-mantra is proclaimed as ending with "to Nṛsiṃha" and "to the one born of fire"; one should utter "Tāra," "kṣūṃ," "to the burner of sins," and end with "the one whose hair is like flames."

O divine lion, you who blaze with a flame that is smokeless, long, and more powerful than a thunderbolt; homage be to you, O Blessed One, Hari, from the mere touch of whose nails [all things are subdued]. NarP_1,71.212.
"To Mahādhvasta-jagadrūpa Nṛsiṃha, [the mantra] twice, twice"—
by this the *śikhā* is declared, and immediately after that, the *kavaca*.
*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), *kṣaiṃ*, *suvarṇaṃ te*, followed by the words *madamattapadaṃ*, and ending with *vihvalitanṛsiṃhāya svāhā*—this is known as the armor (*kavaca*). (NarP 1.71.214)
"Tāraḥ, Ṛkṣau, Sahasrākṣa, Viśvasrākṣa, and one should utter the word Viśvarūpa-padam; ending with Dhāraṇe Agni Priya—this is proclaimed as the Netra-mantra. (NarP 1.71.215)
At the end of a thousand [repetitions], one should utter the word "Tāra-kṣa" with a roar;
then, at the end of another thousand, for the purpose of combat, [one recites] "Nṛsiṃhāya agnisundarī."

The weapon-mantra has been fully declared; thereafter, one should meditate upon the Man-Lion (Narasimha), who possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns, has three eyes, and is adorned with terrifying ornaments.
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the one who shatters the Daityas with staffs whose tips are exceedingly sharp;
having thus visualized him, he should recite the mantra a thousand times, or even more.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter; thus the mantra becomes perfectly accomplished.
Having conceived the form upon the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal by means of the root mantra, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped Nṛhari, one should thereafter worship the limbs first:
the discus, the conch, the noose, the goad, and the thunderbolt.
One should worship the mace, sword, and bell upon the petals;
immediately thereafter, one should also worship the World-Protectors, beginning with Vajra.
When the mantra has been thus accomplished, the practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual applications:
having consecrated ashes with the mantra, he should smear them upon one seized by a planet.
Merely by smearing oneself with ashes, all seizing spirits (grahas) are destroyed;
by this very procedure, [one also subdues] yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras.
Spirits, ghosts, and demons are surely destroyed by this mantra consecrated by Manu; there is no doubt regarding the neutralization of hostile sorcery and magical rites.
One should immediately smear oneself with the ashes; thus the man becomes invincible. On an auspicious day, one should place [the ashes] in a jar within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
Having filled [a vessel] with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
consecrated by that, a person will certainly cross over all calamity.
What is the use of much speaking? This supreme Mantra bestows all that is desired:
"We know Vajranakha; we meditate on Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra;
may Nṛsiṃha impel us toward that [goal] at the end of the recitation. (NarP 1.71.227)
This is the Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī, which bestows all desired objects;
by the mere remembrance of it, the destruction of all sins occurs.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Nṛsiṃha Upāsanā Mantra, Gāyatrī, and Others," in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The Praṇava is the heart; Viṣṇu is the eye; and likewise, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) is the nose."
The mantra ending in "svāhā" for Mahābalā consists of eight syllables.
The Sage is Indu, the Metre is Virāj, and the Deity is Dadhivāmana;
the Seed-syllable is Tāra, and the Power is proclaimed to be Vahnijāyā.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the syllables numbering one, two, three, and five, and those originating from the Manu (seven), on the head, the forehead, and the two eyes; NarP_1,72.3 //
In the ears, the nostrils, the lips, the palate, the throat, and the arms;
on the back, the heart, the belly, the navel, the private parts, and again on the thighs.
One should place the two knees on the two shanks and the feet in sequence;
these are the eighteen [positions] arising from the mantra. Then, one should meditate upon the deity.
White as a pearl, adorned with jewels, seated upon the moon,
her face radiant with locks of hair resembling black bees, she held a pitcher filled with pure water.
One should worship Him holding with both arms a goblet filled with curd-rice;
one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, followed by a tenth part of that number of oblations soaked in ghee.
One should offer oblations according to the rule with milk-rice and curd-rice;
and upon the previously described pedestal fashioned at the end of the lunar phase, one should worship Him.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with the root-mantra of Saṃkalpamūrti,
one should worship the six limbs upon the filaments and likewise upon the petals in the cardinal directions.
[Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha];
and upon the intermediate petals, Śānti, Śrī, Sarasvatī, and Rati.
One should worship the banner, Vainateya, the Kaustubha gem, and the forest garland,
as well as the conch, the discus, the mace, and the Śārṅga bow, upon the eight petals.
Immediately thereafter, having worshipped Keśava and the other guardians of the directions at the tips of the petals, as well as their weapons, one should worship the eight elephants.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda,
Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka are the elephants of the quarters.
The female elephants were, in order: Abhramu, Kapilā, Piṅgalā, Anupamā, Tāmrakarṇī, Śubhradantī, Añjanā, and Vāmanā.
Thus propitiated, the mantra-master shall grant the desired boons to the practitioner.
One who desires prosperity, being wise, should offer a thousand oblations of milk-rice and clarified butter.
One attains great prosperity through the oblation of grain,
and by offering a thousand oblations with seeds produced from the *śatapuṣpā* plant, one gains an abundance of grain.
It shall indeed destroy great fear; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By offering oblations of pure curd-rice, one is liberated from an evil rebirth.
Having meditated upon the form of the Three-Striding One (Viṣṇu), one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind;
even one who is bound will be released from prison through the power of the mantra.
Having fashioned the Lord of Gods on a wall or on a wooden panel, one should worship him daily with fragrant flowers; thus one shall attain great prosperity. (NarP 1.72.19)
Having offered red lotuses, the mantra-practitioner shall bring the entire world under his control;
he should offer oblations of food and clarified butter daily, twenty-eight times in number.
One should duly obtain inexhaustible food, including white rice with clarified butter;
one should offer ten thousand oblations of cakes endowed with the six flavors.
Having overcome misfortune, the practitioner of mantra shall attain great prosperity;
he should offer ten thousand oblations of curd-rice mixed with sugar.
Wherever he may dwell, there too he shall obtain a mountain of food;
a man standing near a *bilva* tree should offer oblations accompanied by the syllables of the *padmākṣa* mantra.
He obtains great fortune in every place, of this there is no doubt;
if he should offer a hundred thousand oblations of milk-rice, he shall become equal to Vācaspati.

Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should offer oblations with *putrajīva* fruits amounting to a tenth part of that number, using wood of that same tree as fuel in a kindled fire; thus, one shall obtain an excellent son.
It should have the practitioner's goal at its center, a radiant pericarp made of gold,
shimmering filaments, and eight petals marked by pairs of mantra syllables.
The final petal of the remaining pair of syllables is encircled by twelve syllables;
outside of that, the yantra is surrounded by the letters of the Mātṛkā, which bestows prosperity upon men.
Having meditated upon the red Trivikrama, the practitioner of mantra should offer ten thousand oblations with red-colored flowers; he shall become victorious everywhere.
One should meditate on [the deity] seated upon a moon-throne and offer ten thousand lotuses;
one shall obtain a kingdom free from thorns, endowed with all auspicious marks.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of cloves smeared with honey, or else with leaves of apāmārga,
enriched with the name of the person to be accomplished, that person will certainly become submissive.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with auspicious apāmārga leaves,
and having likewise recited [the mantra] for seven days, one is liberated from a great disease.
Having uttered the word "Uhirat" preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (Om),
one should then say "Sarvavāgīśvarā," and at the end, "Īśvarā."
At the end of the inconceivable state consisting of all the Vedas, one should impel everything;
this mantra, beginning with Tārā, is proclaimed as that which awakens and brings an end to duality.
The seer is declared to be Brahmā; the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh;
and the deity is the all-pervading Hayagrīva, the bestower of the sovereignty of speech. (NarP 1.72.34)
One should fashion the five limbs of the mantra with the syllable *tāra* as the feet;
[the deity] has a luster like the Snowy Mountain and is adorned with garlands of *tulasī*.
I bow to the horse-faced one, the lofty station of Sarasvatī;
having meditated thus, one should mutter the mantra ten thousand times, and then a tenth part of that [as the fire-oblation].

Having offered oblations of milk-rice mixed with honey, one should worship upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal provided with the *vimalā* and other requisites, having conceived the form [of the deity] through the root mantra.
In the pericarp, one should worship in the four directions, starting from the east in sequence:
Sanandana, Sanaka, Śrī, and likewise Pṛthivī.
Outside of that, in the cardinal directions and in the six corners, one should then worship; after that, one should worship Nirukta and Jyotiṣa, and thereafter Yajurveda and Vyākaraṇa.
One should indeed worship the Kalpa, the Śikṣā, the Chandas, and these Vedāṅgas;
then, at the base of the eight petals, one should worship the eight Mothers.
The practitioner should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Vakratuṇḍa in the middle of the petals,
and thereafter he should worship the eight Bhairavas at the tips of the petals.
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Bhīṣaṇa with blood-red eyes,
Baṭuka, Kāladamana, Dantura, and likewise Vikaṭa.
Outside of that, upon the sixteen petals, [one should place] the ten incarnations of Hari,
as well as the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the sword Nandaka, and the bow Śārṅga.

Outside of that, one should worship the ten lords of the directions, headed by Śakra, along with their vajras and other attributes, in the pavilion; and outside of that, one should worship them at the gates in successive order.
Mahāgaṇapati, Durgā, Kṣetreśa, and likewise Baṭuka,
as well as all the Prakaṭās and other Yoginīs, should be situated outside of that.
Outside of that are seven rivers, and outside of those are nine planets;
outside of those are eight mountains, and outside of those are the lunar mansions.
Having thus worshipped the horse-faced one (Hayagrīva) fifteen times,
one becomes equal to Vāgīśvara in speech and becomes a lord of wealth through riches.
When the mantra has been thus accomplished, the practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual applications;
for instance, one may take one thousand and eight pure drops of water consecrated with the mantra.
The wise man who, having conquered his senses, drinks [this] with the seed-mantra for only a month, will certainly attain mastery of speech, even if he was born mute. (NarP 1.72.49)
The seed-syllable (bīja) is said to consist of the sky, the enjoyer, the earth, the half-moon, and the bindu;
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should cast it into a vessel made of gold.
Then, standing in water reaching up to his neck, the practitioner of mantra, holding milk and *vacā* grass,
should recite the mantra with devotion until he attains liberation through touch.
One should drink all of that, and before long, it will become Sarasvata for him;
likewise, the seeds of the Jyotiṣmatī creeper, increased by one each day. (NarP 1.72.52)
If one should consume [it] consecrated with mantras up to one hundred and eight times,
that person on earth will truly become an incarnation of Sarasvatī.
O best of Brahmins, what need is there for much speaking? By the grace of Manoratha, one becomes possessed of knowledge and a commentator on all the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Hayagrīva," in the third quarter of the Sanatkumāra section of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, the Manus of Rāma, who bestow perfection, shall be described.
By propitiating whom mortals cross the ocean of existence.
Among all the excellent mantras, that which belongs to Viṣṇu is said to be the best;
among those of Gaṇapati, Sūrya, Śakti, and Śiva, it grants one's desired objects.
Even among the Vaiṣṇava mantras, the Rāma-mantras yield superior fruits;
they are many millions of times more efficacious than the mantras dedicated to Gaṇapati and others.
Agni, resting upon the bed of Viṣṇu, with his head adorned by the moon— this [mantra],
which destroys the great mass of sins, is within the heart of Rāma.
Among all the Rāma-mantras, the six-syllabled one is indeed the most excellent;
it destroys thousands of killings of Brahmins, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly.
Stealing gold, drinking liquor, violating the teacher’s bed, and indeed thousands of crores of crores of minor sins— NarP_1,73.6.
By the mere utterance of this mantra, they immediately go to dissolution; of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā is the sage, Gāyatrī is the meter, and Rāma is the deity.
The first seed-syllable is the heart-mantra, and its application is for the attainment of everything;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels.

Having sequentially assigned the syllables of the mantra to the aperture of Brahmā, the space between the eyebrows, the heart, the navel, the genitals, and the feet, one should then duly assign Keśava and the other deities.
Having performed the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) and other rites, one should meditate in the heart upon the best of the Raghus,
who is as dark as a rain cloud and seated upon a hero’s throne (vīrāsana).
He held the *jñānamudrā* in his right hand and rested the other knee upon her; Sītā, with lotus-like hands and radiant as lightning, stood by his side.

Having thus meditated upon her, adorned with various ornaments, beholding the lotus-face of Rāma, the mantra-practitioner should mutter the mantra for one hundred thousand syllables, followed by a tenth part of that as the oblation.
One should offer lotuses into the fire and thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas;
one should worship [the deity] upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal endowed with Vimalā and the other [śaktis].
Having conceptualized the form with the root mantra,
the practitioner should invoke [the deity] into it and worship Sītā, seated to his left, with her own mantra.
The mantra of Jānakī consists of the word *ramā-sītā* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), followed by the word ending in *dviṭha*.
Having worshipped Agni and Śārṅga, one should worship the arrows on both sides.
One should worship the six limbs upon the filaments, and these [four] upon the petals:
Hanumān, Sugrīva, Bharata, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
He was making Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada, Śatrughna, and Jāmbavān read in turn,
while Hanumān stood before him holding a book.
One should worship Bharata and Śatrughna on the two sides holding chowries;
one should worship Lakṣmaṇa behind, holding a parasol with both hands.
Then, on the eight petals, [he placed] Sṛṣṭi, Vijaya while reciting his mantra,
as well as Surāṣṭra, Rāṣṭrapāla, Akopa, and Dharmapālaka.
Having thus fully honored Sumantu and those endowed with the weapons of knowledge in this world,
and having propitiated Rāma in this manner, one becomes liberated while living.
One who is composed should offer oblations with *jātī* flowers smeared with sandalwood for the subjugation of kings; one should use lotuses for the attainment of wealth, grain, and so forth.
One desiring prosperity should offer oblations with flowers produced from the *vilva* tree;
by offering blue lotuses smeared with clarified butter, one shall bring the entire world under one's control.
By means of oblations of red lotuses smeared with ghee, one becomes long-lived and free from disease, and obtains the desired wealth. (NarP 1.73.23)
By offering oblations with *pālāśa* flowers, a man becomes wise;
by drinking water consecrated with that mantra every morning for a year, he shall become a master poet.
One should eat food consecrated with that mantra for the pacification of great diseases;
by means of the medicinal oblation (homa) prescribed for the specific ailment, one is instantly liberated from that disease. (NarP 1.73.25)
On the bank of a river or in a cow-pen, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while subsisting on milk;
by offering oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, one becomes a treasury of knowledge.
One whose sovereign power has been exhausted, subsisting on vegetables and staying within the water,
should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with bilva flowers in a tenfold proportion.
At that very moment, he regains his sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
Having fasted and remained on the bank of the Gaṅgā, a man should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Having offered a tenth part of oblations with lotuses or with flowers produced from the *vilva* tree,
combined with the three sweets and clarified butter, one shall obtain the splendor of sovereignty.
Staying in water during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits,
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with milk-rice in the fire using a tenth part of that amount.
A son or even a grandson equal to Śrī Rāmacandra is born;
there are also many other applications within this king of mantras.
However, there is no world beyond for those who perform the ritual.
One should draw a hexagon with eight petals, and outside of that, twelve petals.
The wise one should write the six syllables of the mantra within the six corners;
likewise, upon the eight-petaled [lotus], he should write the eight syllables containing the *praṇava* (oṃ) at their core.
The seed-syllable of desire is on the solar petal; in the center is the name surrounded by the mantra;
it is surrounded externally by the Sudarśana, and likewise by pairs in the cardinal directions.
This king of yantras is known as the house of the ground shining with the *vajra*, possessing the goads and nooses of Kandarpa, and its corners shining upon the earth.
Having inscribed [the mantra] on birch bark with the eight fragrances, one should worship it according to the prescribed method;
within six corners, one should draw lotuses with eight petals and twelve petals, encircled by two concentric circles.
The wise one should write two pairs of vowels upon the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus;
outside of that, he should write the Mātṛkā and the mantra that is the repository of life.
On an auspicious day, the practitioner of mantras should wear this yantra on the neck, the right arm, or the head; he shall be liberated from all sins.
On an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation, in a suitable location free from thorns,
[one may perform] rites such as subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, driving away, and expulsion.
Likewise, under the two Puṣya constellations, Āditya, Ārdrā, and Maghā, in due order,
a pen made of dūrvā grass is used for subjugation, while one made from karañja wood is used for attraction.
A rosary made from human bone is for killing; one made from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree is for paralyzing;
and [one made from other materials] is for the accomplishment of peace, nourishment, prosperity, and long life, as well as for the pacification of all calamities.
A wise man should engrave [the mantra] upon stone for the purpose of producing delusion;
upon the skin of a donkey for inciting enmity; and upon a banner for the purpose of exorcism.
In the rite for causing fever, torment, grief, and death among enemies,
the most excellent practitioner should draw [the deity] wearing yellow garments and then accomplish the practice.
In rites of subjugation and attraction, one should worship according to the prescribed ritual with the eight fragrances;
likewise, striking, expulsion, and other such acts are performed with funeral ashes and the like.
Through the application of poison, the sun [seed], and milk, death occurs with certainty.
Having thus inscribed this king of yantras, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having encased it in three metals, the best of practitioners should wear it;
"Rāmāya ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ" is this mantra, consisting of six syllables.
The mantra of Mahāsudarśana is said to bestow accomplishment;
it consists of the great word "Sudarśana" and "Cakrarājeśvara."
O you who are the ender of the wicked, the terrifying one for the wicked, and the bringer of fear to the wicked!
Cut through the pair, split the couple, and then tear asunder the two!
Then follows the mantra consisting of the devouring pair of supreme mantras, then the consuming pair,
then the terrifying pair, ending with the armor, the weapon, and the fire-born consort (svāhā).
This [mantra] consisting of sixty-eight syllables is prescribed for the encircling of the yantra:
the Tāra (oṃ), the Hṛdaya (namaḥ), the Blessed One (bhagavate), followed by "ṅe" (ṅe), and then "ṅe" again for Raghunandana (raghunandanāya).
At the end of *rakṣoghnaviśada*, one should utter the word *āyante*; at the end of *madhurādiprasanna*, the word *varadāna*; and at the end of *amita*, the word *tejas*. NarP_1,73.51.
At the end of "Bālāya" and "Rāmāya," followed by "Viṣṇave" and the final syllable of the heart-mantra (Hrīm),
this forty-seven-syllable garland-mantra is thus proclaimed.
The sage is Viśvāmitra; Gāyatrī is said to be the meter;
Śrī Rāma is the deity; the seed-syllable is *dhruva* (om); and the power (*śakti*) is the two *ṭha*s (ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ).
One should fashion the limbs [of the deity] by means of the seed-syllable *Ā* joined with the six long vowels;
one should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship, for this [deity] as previously described.
This mantra, when propitiated, bestows all desires;
it is rich in one's own wishes, truthful speech, and the goddess Lakṣmī-Tārā, and consists of five syllables.
The six-syllabled mantra is of six kinds and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life:
Brahmā, Sammohana, Śakti, and the one known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Agastya is declared to be Śrī Śiva; these are their respective sages in order.
Alternatively, Viśvāmitra is remembered as the sage for the Kāma-bīja and the others.
The meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śrī Rāma;
furthermore, the seed-syllable (bīja) and power-syllable (śakti) are the first and last letters of the mantra, and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are formed by the syllables of the mantra.
Or, one should perform the placement of the mantra-syllables as before using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels;
one should then meditate [on the deity] at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) within a pavilion made of gold.
Within the interior of the celestial chariot named Puṣpaka, upon the furnishings of a lion-throne,
[he saw] the Lord seated upon an eight-petaled lotus, possessing a luster like that of sapphire.
Seated in the vīrāsana posture, adorned with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā),
his left hand resting upon his left thigh, and attended by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having meditated upon the one adorned with jewels, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times;
or else, for the sake of victory over mantras such as those of Smara and others, one should meditate on Hari.

One should perform all rites for desired objects and sacrifices like the six-syllable mantra; it begins with "Rāma," ends with "Candrabhadra," has "ṅena" at the end, and starts with "Dhruva. (NarP 1.73.63)
These two mantras are indeed eight-syllabled; if the final syllables are *tāra* (oṃ), they become nine-syllabled.
The practitioner of mantra should perform all their worship in the same manner as that for the six-syllabled mantra.

This ten-syllable great mantra, beginning with "Jānakīvallabha," ending with two "ṭha"s, and including the armor-verse (kavaca) and so forth, has Svarāṭ as its distinguished sage (ṛṣi). NarP_1,73.65 //
One should perform the six limbs in sequence with desire, the deity, Sītā, the primordial seed-syllable, Svāhā, and Śakti, according to one's wish.
One should place the ten syllables of the mantra upon the head, forehead, between the eyebrows, palate, throat, heart, navel, feet, knees, and toes.
In the city of Ayodhyā, within a pavilion made of gold and variegated with jewels,
where canopies were tied with mandāra flowers and adorned with arched gateways.
Rāghava was seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot on his lion-throne,
surrounded by Rākṣasas, monkeys, and auspicious gods mounted upon beautiful celestial vehicles.
He was being praised by sages who bowed low and attended upon him;
his left side was adorned by Sītā, and he was graced by Lakṣmaṇa.
Having thus meditated upon him as dark-complexioned, with a serene face, and adorned with all ornaments, the practitioner, composed in mind, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
The tenth part [of the ritual] consists of offerings of lotuses and gold; the worship is performed with the six-syllable mantra.
"Rāma" ending in the dative case (ṅe), followed by "dhanuṣpāṇiḥ" ending in the dative (ṅai), and finally "vahnisundarī. (NarP 1.73.72)
This mantra consists of ten syllables; its sage is Brahmā, and its meter is Virāṭ.
Its deity is declared to be Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas.
One should fashion the limbs with the first seed-syllable, the letter *ṭha*, and the seed-syllable of Śakti;
likewise, one should perform the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*), meditation, the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*), worship, and so forth. (NarP 1.73.74)
One should perform [the ritual] as described for the ten-syllable mantra and visualize [Rāma] holding a bow and arrows; [the mantra is]:
*Tāra* (Oṃ), *namo bhagavate*, followed by *rāma*, then *candra* and *bhadra*.
The two mantras consist of the syllables "ṅenta" and "arka"; the visualization of the seers and so forth is as before.
The name of Rāma is likewise twofold: preceded by "Śrī" and preceded by "Jaya. (NarP 1.73.76)
The mantra consists of thirteen syllables; the sage is said to be Brahmā, and the meter is Virāj. The deity is declared to be Rāma, the destroyer of the flood of sins.
One should perform the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) by repeating the three words twice;
for all [rites] such as meditation and worship, one should act as if it were the ten-syllable mantra.
*Tāraḥ*, *namo bhagavate rāmāya*, and at the end *mahāpadam puruṣāya* followed by *hṛt*; this is the eighteen-syllable mantra. (NarP 1.73.79)
Viśvāmitra is the sage-seer, Rāma is its presiding deity, *Tāra* is the seed-syllable, and *Namaḥ* is the power; it consists of six arms, with the moon, eyes, oceans, and fires [as attributes].
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the syllables arising from the mantra,
accompanied by the sounds of drums such as the *niḥśāṇa*, *bherī*, *paṭaha*, conchs, *turya*, and others.
While the dance proceeded on all sides accompanied by shouts of "Victory!
and auspicious blessings, the air was exquisitely perfumed with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and other fragrant substances.
It was filled with breezes carrying the fragrance of various flowers and adorned by the songs of goddesses and celestial nymphs.
Rāghava was seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot on a lion-throne,
accompanied by Saumitri and Sītā, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
[He saw him] dark-complexioned, bearing a bow and arrows, accompanied by Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa,
who had come after slaying Rāvaṇa and had accomplished the protection of the three worlds.
Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantras should recite the syllable one hundred thousand times,
and having offered oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee in ten parts of that number, he should perform the worship as before.
The Praṇava is the heart; thereafter, "to the Lord of Sītā," followed by "to Rāma," at the end of which is the pair "hara," ending with the armor, the weapon, fire, and the beloved.
This mantra consists of nineteen syllables and accomplishes all aims;
Viśvāmitra is its sage, and the Anuṣṭubh is declared to be its meter.
The deity is Rāmabhadra; the seed-syllable is *jaṃ*, and the power is *namaḥ*.
Then, one should meditate as before upon the syllables arising from the mantra in their proper sequence.
His worship, including rites for specific desires and all other such acts, is performed with his six-syllable mantra:
one should recite "Tāraḥ" (Om), one's own seed-syllable, "Kamalā" (Śrīṃ), and "Rāmabhadra. (NarP 1.73.90)

O best of kings, O hero of the Raghus, one should recite: "At the end of the word *maheṣvāsa*, at the end of the word *padānta*, and at the end of the word *daśāsyāntaka*, protect me, grant [me]! (NarP 1.73.91).
At the very end, may there be prosperity for me; this mantra consists of fifty-three syllables, devoid of seed-syllables, and being thirty-two letters long, it bestows fruit. (NarP 1.73.92)
The sage is Viśvāmitra, and Anuṣṭubh is declared to be its meter;
Rāmabhadra is the deity here, with one’s own self as the seed-syllable and Indirā as the power.
The knower of mantras should perform [the rite] with words beginning with the three seed-syllables and with the word *sarva*;
having performed the placement of the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*), he should then place the syllables of the mantra in their proper sequence.

On the crown of the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the pair of cheeks along with the nose, the mouth, the two joints of the arms, and then successively on the breasts, the heart, and the navel; NarP_1,73.95.
One should place the syllables of the mantra on the waist, the penis, the anus, and the joints of the feet;
and one should perform its meditation, worship, and other rites as previously described.
A preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) of three hundred thousand [recitations] is prescribed, along with an oblation (*havana*) of milk-rice (*pāyasa*);
having meditated upon Rāma as yellow in color, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind.
Having offered one-tenth of the portion with lotuses, one becomes a lord of wealth through riches.
The mantra is indeed: *Tāra*, *Māyā*, the pair *Ramā*, followed by *Dāśarathāya* and *Hṛt*.
The mantra consists of eleven syllables; its worship by sages and others is as before.
At the end of "trailokyānta," [the word] "nāthāya" follows, ending with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and possessing eight syllables.
For this [mantra] as well, all [the rites] such as the ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), and worship (arcana) are performed as before;
however, at the end of the word "Āñjaneya," the word "to the Guru" (gurave) follows, ending with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).

The mantra for this [deity] consists of nine syllables; its worship is considered to be as previously described. After the word "Rāma," one should add the heart-mantra consisting of five syllables ending in "-ṅe."
And his worship through meditation by the Sage is said to be entirely like that of the six-syllable mantra:
at the end of "Rāma" are "Candra" and "Bhadra," followed by the two words ending in the dative case (ṅeṃtau), and then the beloved of Agni (Svāhā). (NarP 1.73.102)
The two mantras are declared to be as before, beginning with the worship of the Sage (Muni) and so forth;
likewise, there is Vahni accompanied by Śeṣa, with the moon adorning his head.
The single-syllable mantra of the Lord of the Raghus is like another wish-fulfilling tree;
Brahmā is its sage, Gāyatrī its meter, and Rāma its deity.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantra enriched by the six long vowels,
seated upon a lotus on a mandāra altar-platform at the bank of the Sarayū.
Dark-complexioned, seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), adorned with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), his left hand resting upon his left thigh, and accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
With the sole desire for liberation, he beheld himself as the God of Love of immeasurable splendor, resembling pure crystal and existing in his absolute isolation.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Self and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
all his rites, such as the fire-oblation and daily worship, should likewise consist of six syllables.
The two-syllable mantra is "Vahniḥ Śeṣāsano Bhāntaḥ Kevalaḥ.
All matters regarding meditation, worship, and so forth, are to be understood as identical to those prescribed for the single-syllable mantra. 1.73.109.
The king of mantras consists of two syllables formed by the seed-syllables of Tāra, Māra, and Anaṅga; it may also be three syllables long, and in its sixfold form, it grants all desired objects.
The two-syllable [mantra] ends with Candrabhadra; the four-syllable is of two kinds.
For these, the meditation, worship, and so forth by the sages are as previously stated for the single-syllable mantra.
*Tāra*, *Rāma* ending in the dative case, *varma*, *astra*, and *vahnivallabhā*:
this eight-syllabled great mantra has the same procedure for the worship of the sage and so forth as the six-syllabled one.
The syllable *tāra* (oṃ) should be at the end of the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), followed by *rāmāya*, and ending with the *praṇava* (oṃ).
This eight-syllabled mantra of Śiva-Umā-Rāma bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The sage is declared to be Sadāśiva; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
and Śivomārāmacandra is proclaimed here as the deity.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual with the mantra consisting of six syllables, "ṣaḍvīryayāmāya," which is joined with the five fixed syllables, one should then meditate upon the one worshipped by the gods within the heart.
We worship Rāma, who has three eyes, who bears the crescent moon, who holds a trident, who is most excellent,
whose entire body is smeared with ashes, and who wears matted hair.
One should meditate upon her who is delightful to Rāma, the pinnacle of beauty, adorned with the moon as a crest-ornament,
bearing a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, and possessing three eyes.
