Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then one should perform oblations with *bilva* leaves, fruits, flowers, sesame seeds, or lotuses, accompanied by the three sweets.
Treasures and the perfections desired even by the gods come to him of their own accord;
he is Tāra, Māyā, the elder brother of Bharata, and the mind-born god of love.
The twelve-syllable mantra ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā) is another wish-fulfilling tree;
Aṅgiras is the sage, the Gāyatrī is the metre, and the deity is, moreover, [the same].

Śrī Rāma is proclaimed as the seed-syllable (bīja) of the world, and Svāhā as his power (śakti). The assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) of the mantra is performed with its syllables, which number one, seven, seven, four, and two.
And one should perform all [rites] such as meditation and worship according to the six-syllable mantra: "Oṃ" is the heart [mantra], followed by "Sītāpate Rāma," ending with "ṅe. (NarP 1.73.122)
At the end of the two *hana*s is the armor-weapon mantra consisting of sixteen syllables;
Agastya is its sage, the *bṛhatī* its metre, and [Varuṇa] its deity.

"I am Śrī Rāma," thus the seed-syllable (bīja) is proclaimed; "Rāṃ" is declared to be the power (śakti). The arrangement of the five limbs is performed with syllables numbering four, four, three, four, and two, respectively. NarP_1,73.124 //
One should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship, for this [deity] as in the case of the six-syllable mantra:
one should utter the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), then *hṛt* (namaḥ), and then the word *brahmaṇyasevyāya*.
Bhṛgu, accompanied by his desire, uttered for Rāma the mantra ending with *akuṇṭha-śabda* for the sake of splendor: "To the foremost among those of excellent renown. (NarP 1.73.126)
O beloved, the mantra consisting of the syllables "Rāma-Rāmā" is considered to be entrusted with the staff;
Śukra is its seer, Anuṣṭubh its meter, and Rāma is its deity.
One should perform the five-limbed ritual with all [the mantras] at the feet; the remainder is as in the six-syllable mantra.
The wise one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer oblations of milk-rice in a tenth part of that amount.
For one whose mantra is perfected, there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and the destruction of sins;
at the beginning [of the mantra] one should utter "to the son of Daśaratha," and at the end, one should recite the word "vidmahe."
Then one should utter: "We meditate upon the Beloved of Sītā";
and one should speak: "May Rāma, whose color is proclaimed as red, grant us grace. (NarP 1.73.130)
This is the previously mentioned six-syllabled *magāyatrī*, which bestows all desired fruits; it begins with "padmāsītāpadaṃ," followed by "ṅe," and ends with two "ṭha"s.
The sage is Vālmīki, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is said to be the blessed Sītā;
the seed-syllable is Śrīṃ, and the goddess is Vahnisundarī.
One should fashion the limbs of Śakti with the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels;
then, one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Sītā, who is worshipped by the three worlds.
She possesses the luster of molten gold, holds a pair of lotuses in her two hands, and has a divine body resplendent with ornaments of excellent jewels; she is auspicious by nature.
She was clothed in various garments, moon-faced, lotus-eyed, and joyful in her heart;
she beheld the meritorious Rāghava on his half-made bed, she who was the sovereign of the six qualities.
Having meditated thus, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should perform oblations with ten parts of that number using full-blown lotuses, and worship upon the seat previously described.
Having conceptualized the form with the root mantra, having invoked Jānakī into it,
and having worshipped her, one should worship Rāma to the south and the son of the Wind (Hanumān) in front.
Having worshipped Lakṣmaṇa on the pericarp, one should perform the worship of the limbs in the six corners,
the chief of mantra-holders on the petals, and again the world-protectors on the outside.
Having fully worshipped Vajra and the others as well, one shall become a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhīśvara*).
For the subjugation of kings, one should perform a fire offering (*homa*) with *jātī* flowers smeared with sandalwood.
With lotuses one obtains wealth and grain; with blue lotuses, one subjugates the world;
with bilva leaves, for the attainment of prosperity; and with dūrvā grass, for the pacification of fear.
What is the use of saying more? Through the worship of Sītā, one obtains good fortune, sons, grandsons, supreme happiness, wealth, grain, and even liberation.
Śakra, together with Indra, gave the heart [mantra] consisting of seven syllables to Lakṣmaṇa;
Agastya is its sage, the Gāyatrī its meter, and furthermore, Śakra is its deity.

The great hero named Lakṣmaṇa [should perform] the six limbs with the seed-syllable of the heart (Hrīṃ) enriched by power (Śakti), using that seed-syllable augmented by the six long vowels. (NarP 1.73.143)
Two-armed, with a body possessing the luster of gold and eyes like lotuses,
holding a bow and arrows in his hands, his mind was entirely intent upon the service of Rāma.
Having meditated thus, the mantra-practitioner should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
then, having offered oblations of milk-rice smeared with honey ten times that amount, he should worship at the seat of Rāma.
Indeed, this sacrifice for Rāma bestows all perfections upon him;
for if a man so desires, he shall certainly obtain the complete fruit of the worship of Rāma.
With that effort, one should perform the worship of Lakṣmaṇa with devotion;
for there are many forms of Śrī Rāmacandra that bestow spiritual accomplishments.
Those seeking its accomplishment should always perform the auspicious worship of Lakṣmaṇa with great concentration, either one thousand and eight times or one hundred times.
The *lakṣmaṇa-manu* is to be recited by those seeking liberation without weariness;
those who recite the *rāma-mantras* without having first recited the *lakṣmaṇa-manu* [are unsuccessful].
Success does not arise for them; rather, there is only loss at every step, for one who recites the Lakṣmaṇa-mantra while constantly remaining in solitude.
One is liberated from all sins and shall attain all desires;
this mantra, preeminent in victory, is the sole means for attaining sovereignty.
To regain a lost kingdom, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind;
he shall undoubtedly recover his lost kingdom before long.
Meditating on Rāma in Ayodhyā with undivided mind,
one who has been consecrated shall regain a lost kingdom by reciting the mantra fifty thousand times.
Having meditated with devotion upon Lakṣmaṇa as being liberated from the serpent-noose, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; he will certainly be released from his fetters.
Having become free from pain through the medicinal herbs brought by the son of Vāta,
one who meditates and recites the mantra one hundred thousand times will certainly conquer even minor death.
Meditating upon Meghanāda as being struck down, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
thus, even a formidable and great host of enemies may be swiftly conquered.
Having meditated on one whose mind is intent upon cutting off Śūrpaṇakhā’s nose, one should recite the mantra a thousand times; thus one shall conquer Indra and the other gods. (NarP 1.73.157)
Then, remembering him who has made an effort for the sake of serving the lotus feet of Rāma,
and reciting [the mantra] in a secluded place, one is liberated from a great disease.
For three months, having conquered his appetite, he constantly [offered] seven thousand flowers,
along with one hundred and eight flawless *śatapatra* blossoms.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite and having offered milk-rice with sugar, one should recite the mantra; thus, one is liberated from the disease of leprosy.
In a solitary place, having conquered one's appetite, by this method for six months, one shall be liberated from the disease of consumption; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Having consecrated water with the mantra three times at dawn, one who is composed should drink it daily at the three junctions of the day; thus he is liberated from all diseases.
Poverty and defeat shall not arise; one shall become like the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and never shall there be contact with the defects of poison and the like.
Every day, one should wash the face with water consecrated by Manu;
thus, one shall conquer even the most terrible diseases arising from the mouth, eyes, and other parts of the body.
Having drunk water consecrated with mantras, one will certainly conquer diseases of the stomach;
having fashioned an image of Lakṣmaṇa, one should offer it with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
He is liberated from all diseases; of this there is no doubt.
One who desires a daughter, with his mind intent on the taking of a pure hand in marriage, [attains his wish].
Meditating thus, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with lotuses in the tenth part of that number;
he will obtain his desired maiden very quickly, without a doubt.
Having meditated according to the rules upon the initiated one who is bound by his vows through the mantras of the Jṛmbhaṇa weapons,
he should constantly recite the mantra for three months.
A man who has conquered his senses, preceded by worship, becomes a knower of the reality of all vidyās after reciting [the mantra] seven thousand times.
Meditating upon Viśvāmitra, who performed wondrous feats through his supreme sacrifice, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; thus one is liberated from great fear.
Having performed his daily rites and being purified, he should recite the mantra at the three times of day;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The practitioner of mantras, having been initiated according to the rules, is free from defilement through his virtues;
he is self-controlled, restrained by the discipline of his own conduct, and, though a householder, has conquered his senses.
He who, free from desire, worships the Lord without regard for things of this world,
having burned away all multitudes of merit and sin, becomes pure in mind.
Free from rebirth, he attains the eternal state;
having obtained his desires and enjoyed the pleasures conceived in his mind, he reaches that imperishable station.
Having become immortal for a long time, Jāti goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
thereafter, Nidrā, accompanied by Candra, [goes] to Bharata as his final heart-connection.

The seven-syllable mantra of this [deity] begins with the sage (muni) and so forth, as previously described; it consists of "baka" followed by the moon (indus), then "śatrughna," and ends with "ṅe" at the heart. (NarP 1.73.176)
This seven-syllable mantra, which slays enemies, bestows the accomplishment of all desired goals.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Rāma and Others," in the third quarter of the Sanatkumāra section of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, the mantras of Hanumān, which bestow all desired objects, shall be declared.
O best of Brahmins, by propitiating whom, men come to possess conduct equal to theirs.
The letter *ma* joined with *svara-u*, the sky (*ga*) endowed with *bha*,
and *ha-sa-pha* along with fire (*ra*) and the lord of night (*i*)— this is declared to be the second seed-syllable.
The third seed-syllable is said to be *sva-pha-āgni* augmented by *bhaga-indu*;
the fourth shall be *viyat-bhṛgu-agni-manu-indu*. (NarP 1.74.3)
The fifth [name] is Bhagacandrāḍhyā; vi, yad, bhṛgu, sva, kā, agni;
and man, indvāḍhya, ha, sa—this is the sixth, ending in ṅe; then comes Dhanumān.
This twelve-syllable great king of mantras ends with the word *hṛdaya*;
Rāmacandra is its sage (*ṛṣi*), and the *jagatī* meter is proclaimed for it.
The deity is Hanumān; the seed-syllable is the sixth [letter], and the power is the second.
With the six seed-syllables, one performs the six limbs [of ritual worship] on the head, the forehead, the two eyes, and the mouth.
One should place the syllables in sequence upon the two arms, the neck, the heart, the belly, the navel,
the penis, the two knees, and the two feet.
One should place the six seed-syllables and the pair of feet in sequence upon the crown of the head, the forehead, the mouth, the heart, the navel, the thighs, the shanks, and the two feet.
Then one should meditate upon the Lord of Monkeys, born from the interior of an ointment-box,
resembling ten million rising suns, and the cause of the world's agitation.
One should worship Māruti, who is steadfast in meditation on the feet of Śrī Rāma, honored by Sugrīva and others,
and who terrifies the Rākṣasas with his roar.
Having meditated thus, one who has conquered the senses should mutter the mantra a thousand times;
one should then perform oblations ten times the number of recitations, using grains mixed with milk, curd, and clarified butter.
Having conceived the form upon the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal according to the root mantra,
and having invoked [the deity] there, one should worship it with offerings such as water for the feet (pādya) and other requisites.
The worship of the limbs should take place upon the filaments, and thereafter one should worship upon the petals:
"The devotee of Rāma, of great splendor, the king of monkeys, possessed of great strength. (NarP 1.74.13)
The remover of the mountain of Droṇa, the one who performs worship at the seat of Meru,
the sun of the southern quarter, and the destroyer of all obstacles.
Having thus worshipped [the central deity], one should then worship the names upon the tips of the petals:
Sugrīva, Aṅgada, Nīla, Jāmbavanta, and likewise Nala.
Then one should worship Suṣeṇa, Dvivida, and Mainda as the guardians of the world;
having also fully honored Vajra and the others, the mantra will thus become perfected.
If a man recites the mantra nine hundred times at night for ten days,
his fears arising from royal enemies shall perish.
Having offered a thousand oblations of mātuliṅga, mango, and plantain fruits,
he should feed twenty-two pure brahmins who are students of the Vedas.
When this has been performed, afflictions such as elemental spirits, poisons, planetary influences, diseases,
and the like are destroyed at that very moment, as are those who cause hatred, malevolent planets, and dānavas.
Water consecrated one hundred and eight times with this mantra destroys poison;
likewise, for fevers arising from spirits, epilepsy, or sorcery, [water] consecrated with that same mantra [is effective].
Or one may strike the feverish person with ashes or water while filled with wrath;
within three days that man will be freed from the fever and obtain happiness.
Having consumed either medicine or water consecrated with that mantra, one overcomes all diseases and becomes happy at that very moment. (NarP 1.74.22)
Having smeared his limbs with ashes consecrated by that mantra and having drunk milk over which that same mantra has been recited,
the practitioner who goes forth to fight is not harmed by hosts of weapons.

For scabies, the bursting of sores, and even the eruptions caused by spiders, if they are touched with ashes over which the mantra has been recited three times, they will surely dry up; of this there is no doubt.
One should recite the mantra for seven days, beginning from sunset until sunrise, while taking hold of the ashes and the ritual peg (kīlaka).
Having consecrated it with mantras, one should quickly bury it unobserved at the door of enemies;
those who have fallen into mutual enmity will flee from their foes before long.

The mantra-practitioner, having consecrated ashes, water, and sandalwood with this mantra, gives them mixed with food and other items to whomever he desires; that person then becomes like his servant. (NarP 1.74.27)
Even cruel creatures become thus submissive by taking the root of a *karañja* tree situated at the northeast corner of the lord’s dwelling.

Having fashioned an image of Hanumān the size of a thumb, and having performed the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and worshipped it with vermilion and other offerings; ||| NarP_1,74.29 |||
Facing the house, one should bury it at the door while reciting the mantra;
[thereby,] those arising from planetary influences, malevolent spells, disease, fire, poison, thieves, or kings [shall be averted].
In that house, no calamities ever arise; that household prospers daily for a long time with wealth, sons, and other blessings. (NarP 1.74.31)
At night, in whatever forest, having diligently fashioned an image of the enemy out of ashes or clay, one should inscribe the name in its heart.
Having performed the rites up to the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), one should split [the effigy] with weapons while reciting the mantra;
at the end of the mantra, one should utter the name of the enemy, saying "cut! and "split! (chindhi ca bhindhi ca).
Saying "Kill him! at the end of that [mantra], and having bitten her lip with her teeth and pressed the palms of her hands together, she should then leave him and go to her own home. (NarP 1.74.34)
Doing this for seven days, one shall undoubtedly slay the enemy;
having loosened one's hair with black mustard and salt, one should do so in a cremation ground.
And with the fruits and flowers of the *dhattūra*, as well as the poisons found in nails and hair,
and with the feathers of the crow, the owl, and the vulture, produced from the *śleṣmāntaka* tree.
Facing the direction of Yama, one should offer three hundred oblations at night with *samidh* wood;
by doing this for seven days, one shall cause even a haughty enemy to die.

One should recite [the mantra] six hundred times at night in a cremation ground for three days until one experiences terror; then the vetāla, having arisen, will declare what is to come, both auspicious and inauspicious. (NarP 1.74.38)
Having become a servant, she remains present and carries out whatever is commanded by the practitioner;
furthermore, at night, one should consecrate ashes and water with the mantra one thousand times.
And after that, for three days, one should cast [the remains] into whatever images there may be,
whether they be large or especially small.
Through the power of the mantra, movement certainly occurs; of this there is no doubt—whether on the eighth or the fourteenth day, or on a Tuesday or a Sunday.
One of purified soul should fashion a beautiful image of Hanumān on a cloth using beans soaked in oil, ensuring it is endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Having placed an oil lamp on the left side and a ghee lamp on the right,
the knower of mantras should then invoke [the deity] with the root mantra.
Having performed the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), one should offer water for the feet and other articles;
one should worship with red sandalwood, flowers, vermilion, and so forth.
Then, having offered incense and a lamp, one should present the food offering (naivedya), consisting of cakes,
boiled rice, vegetables, sweetmeats, stuffed pastries, and so forth.
Then, having offered that [oblation] with clarified butter using the root mantra,
the knower of mantras [offers] twenty-seven unbroken leaves of the *ahila* creeper.
Having divided the betel nuts into three parts, one should offer them with the root mantra itself;
having thus performed the worship, the knower of mantras should recite the mantra one thousand times.

Having performed the *ārārtika* offering with camphor and having praised [the deity] in many ways, the wise one should then announce his own desire and dismiss [the deity] according to the prescribed rite.
Having fed seven Brāhmaṇas with the food of the offering,
one should distribute and give to them the leaves that were offered.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to his ability, the wise man should dismiss them;
thereafter, with his speech restrained, he himself should eat together with his beloved kinsmen.
On that day, one should sleep on the ground and observe celibacy;
the mortal who acts in this way will, without doubt, very soon [attain his goal].
By the grace of the Lord of Monkeys, one shall obtain all desires;
one should draw an image of Hanumān on the ground and recite the mantra before it.
The name of the person for whom the rite is performed (sādhya) should be written in the accusative case, preceded by the words "vimocaya vimocaya.
One should first wipe it away with the left hand and then write it again.
Having written it one hundred and eight times in this manner, one should wipe it away once more.
When this is done, one is quickly released from the great prison;
in the same way, one should perform other rites while scraping away the sprouts.
An oblation of mustard seeds effects subjugation; for inciting enmity, one should use horse-dung, saffron, fuel-sticks of *idhma* wood, black pepper, or cumin.
In cases of fever, [one should offer oblations] with dūrvā and guḍūcī along with curd, milk, or clarified butter;
in cases of colic, with the fuel-sticks of karañja and vātāri soaked in oil.
Or, with effort, one may perform it with *nirguṇḍī* fuel-sticks smeared with oil;
for the sake of good fortune, with sandalwood, or with *indralocana* or cloves.
With fragrant flowers for the attainment of garments; with various grains for the attainment of those [grains];
and with the dust from the feet of an enemy mixed with turmeric and salt.
If one performs the fire-oblation for seven nights, the enemy goes to the abode of Yama;
by means of grains, one obtains grain, and by means of food, an abundance of food.
With sesame, clarified butter, milk, and honey, one may achieve abundance of buffaloes and cows;
what need is there for much talk? [These are used] for poison, disease, pacification, delusion, and killing.
In disputes, in paralyzing [enemies], in gambling, in fear of spirits, and in danger;
in subjugation, in battle, in injury, in divine matters, in liberation from bondage, and in the great forest—[these are the times for its use].
This mantra, when perfected, will certainly bestow the highest welfare upon men;
now I shall describe the Hanuman-yantra, which grants all accomplishments.
One should draw three coils joined in the shape of a tail;
in the center, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished, encircled by the *pāśa* seed-syllable.
Having made an eight-petalled [lotus] above, one should write the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) upon the petals;
having drawn a circle outside of that, one should draw a square outside of that.
One should draw tridents at the tips of the lines of the square;
then, one should inscribe the seed-syllable *saiṃ* upon the eight vajras of the earth-pedestal (*bhūpura*).
Having drawn a goad (aṅkuśa) in the corners, one should encircle it with the garland-mantra (mālāmantra);
one should then encircle all of that with three concentric circles of the yantra.
On stone, on a wooden board, on cloth, on a copper plate, or on a wall;
on palm leaves or on birch bark, using yellow pigment, realgar, or saffron—NarP_1,74.67.
Having drawn this yantra, fasting and with senses subdued,
one should establish the life-force of the monkey and worship it according to the prescribed rite.
For the sake of pacifying all suffering without exception, the wise person should wear this yantra;
it destroys all calamities, such as demonic possession, fever, and malevolent spells.
Worn by women and even by children, it captivates the hearts of people;
yet for *bhūtas*, *kṛtyās*, and *piśācas*, it brings destruction at the mere sight of it.
Now I shall declare the garland-mantra: the Tāra, the consort of Viṣṇu (Vāgīśvarī), Māyā endowed with the three long vowels, and the previously mentioned pentad of peaks.
Dhruva, Hṛd, Dhanu, Mān, Nge, Anta, and Prakaṭaparākrama— these,
pervading the ends of the circle of the quarters, proclaim the canopy of his fame.

O you who have whitened the boundaries of all colors, O vajra of the three worlds; O you whose body possesses the radiance of ten million suns blazing with fire, you who are equal in splendor! NarP_1,74.73 //
At the end of the section on his body hair, one should speak of the incarnation of Rudra;
thereafter, the city of Laṅkā, and then the burning of the ocean and the crossing of it.

One should utter the word *daśagrīvaśiraḥ* (the head of the Ten-necked One), followed by the word *kṛtāntaka* (the end-maker). After *sītā*, one should utter the word *śvasana* (the wind), and after *vāyu*, one should pronounce *suta* (the son).
Born from the interior of collyrium, accompanied by Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, he causes delight; at the end of the syllable *kara*, one should utter "sainyaprākāra. (NarP 1.74.76)
"O you who were born from the friendship with Sugrīva; O destroyer of Vālin in battle;
O you whose name ends with the word 'Droṇa' for a specific reason; and O you who uprooted mountains! (NarP 1.74.77)
O Dāruṇākṣa, at the edge of the grove of Aśoka trees, at the end of the cutting, and at the end of the forest guards, gather the multitude! NarP_1,74.78 //
At the end of the analysis, one should say "O Brahma-power, swallow the Brahma-weapon," and at the end of the mark, one should utter the words for warding off the piercing of the power.
At the end of the word *viśalyauṣadhi*, he should recite *samānayan*;
then *bālodita* and *bhānumaṇḍalagrasana*. (NarP 1.74.80)
From the word *meghanāda*, one should utter the word *vidhvaṃsana*; at the end of *indrajit* and *ūdha*, [one says] *ṇa sītā sakṣaka*. (NarP 1.74.81)
At the end of the sound of the host of rākṣasīs, one should utter the word "tearing asunder" (vidāraṇa);
and after proclaiming Kumbhakarṇa and the others, at the end of the slaughter, [one should utter] "supreme resort" (parāyaṇa).
At the end of the description of Śrī Rāma’s devotion, one should utter "tatpare" (intent on that),
and then "vyomadrumalaṅghana" (leaping over the tree in the sky) to describe his great power.
From the sound of the mass of great splendor, he should utter "Virājama," and at the end of Arjuna, having fulfilled the command of his master, he should say "saṃyuga. (NarP 1.74.84)
At the end of "sahāya," one should utter the word "kumāra" and the term "brahmacārin"; at the end of the arising of the deep sound, one should speak of the "dakṣiṇāpatha";
and at the end of the words "mārttaṇḍa" and "meru," one should speak of the "parvatapīṭikā."
At the conclusion of the worship, one should utter the word "ma" at the end of all mantras;
and at the end of the word "mama," [one should say] "O destroyer of all seizing spirits, O Teacher."
O you who drive away all fevers, O destroyer of all poisons,
O preventer of all transgressions, O subduer of all the wicked!
Having recited [the mantra] over all diseases and so forth, one should utter "nivāraṇa" at the end of each "bhaya."
"By the severing of all enemies," thus [he said] for both myself and others. (NarP 1.74.89)
Then, within the three worlds, at the end of all living beings— whether male, female, or neuter—
the pair of *vaśaya* syllables was born.
"First, bring me one who will carry out my command; then, once again, bring a pair.
After that, he shall recite the names of all the kings. (NarP 1.74.91)
At the end of "parivārān mama," form a pair [of mantras] with "sevakān";
at the end of "sarvaśastravī," form two pairs with "ṣāṇi vidhvaṃsaya. (NarP 1.74.92)
Endowed with the three long vowels beginning with *la*, the three *hṛt*s, and the pair *ehi*;
[then] the five peaks in reverse order, and the pair *sarvaśatrūn hana*. (NarP 1.74.93)
The two of them agitated the enemy forces and the armies at the far frontier.
"Accomplish all my business"—these two [words] follow from that. (NarP 1.74.95)
Then, nailing down the mouths of all wicked and evil persons, [one recites] the three *dhe*s, the three *varma*s, the three *phaṭ*s, and the three *hān*s.
This mantra, ending with the word *vahnipriyā*, is known as the *mālā-mantra*; it bestows all desired objects.
This mantra, which has the color of eight arrows of wealth, is the accomplisher of all desired goals.
In times of great fear and great calamity, this [mantra] is remembered as the destroyer of suffering;
it consists of twelve syllables, excluding the six peaks and likewise the initial seed-syllable.
The mantra consisting of five peaks bestows all desires;
Rāmacandra is its sage, and Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter.
Hanumān is declared to be the presiding deity; the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of everything.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the five seed-syllables and the entire mantra.
This son of Añjanī, the messenger of Rāma, the giver of life in the presence of Lakṣmaṇa, the destroyer of Sītā’s grief, and the shatterer of the palaces of Laṅkā; NarP_1,74.102.
These five, beginning with Hanumān and starting with the seed-syllables (bīja), followed by the suffix -ṅe, are indeed the six-limbed mantras; their meditation, worship, and so forth are as before.
The Praṇava, Vāgbhava, Padmā, and Māyā, joined with the three long vowels—
this five-peak mantra consists of eleven syllables and bestows all accomplishments.
All practices such as meditation and worship for this [deity] are also considered to be as previously described.
This mantra, when propitiated, bestows all desired objects.
Homage to the Blessed One, who is infinite behind, whose crest is the moon,
the progenitor of the great Janeya, and at the end of whose power is the beloved of Agni.
This mantra of eighteen syllables is known as Sunirīśvara;
its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Hanumān, the son of the Wind.
The seed-syllable *haṃ* is declared by the wise to be the fire-goddess as its power (*śakti*);
"to Āñjaneya" is the heart, and "to the one whose form is Rudra" is the head.
For the tuft [of hair], it is for the son of Vāyu; for the armor, it is for him whose womb is fire;
for the eyes, it is for the messenger of Rāma; and for the weapon, it is declared to be for the external weapon.

One should meditate upon the son of the Wind-god, who resembles molten gold, whose palms are joined in reverence before Bhīma, whose face is radiant with swinging earrings, and whose eyes are like lotuses.
Having meditated thus and recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds amounting to a tenth part;
then, one should worship on the Vaiṣṇava pedestal according to the method previously indicated.
One who eats only at night, having conquered the senses, and recites [this mantra] one hundred and eight times daily, is liberated from minor ailments; of this there is no doubt.
To ward off a great disease, one should recite it a thousand times every day,
meditating upon the monkey who destroys poverty and slays the hosts of Rākṣasas.
One should recite this ten thousand times daily; before long, one conquers the enemy while meditating on the monkey who made an alliance with Rāma through Sugrīva.
He who would bring about a reconciliation between two adversaries should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
having meditated upon Laṅkā as being on fire, he should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
The wise one shall soon utterly consume the villages of his enemies;
having meditated upon Hanumān at the time of departure, he should recite the mantra.
Whoever goes forth shall soon accomplish his own desired goal and return home;
he who, devoted to recitation, always worships Hanumān in his house [shall do so].
One obtains health, prosperity, and splendor free from affliction;
this is remembered as the "Manu" [protective formula] that guards one in the forest against tigers and thieves.
At the time of falling asleep, one should recite the mantra upon the bed with undistracted mind;
for such a person, there shall never be any fear of bad dreams, thieves, or other dangers.

Then, for Hanumān, who is of the nature of Rudra, there is this great twelve-syllable mantra ending with *varma* and *astra*, which bestows the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*). || NarP_1,74.120 ||
Rāmacandra is the sage (ṛṣi) and the Jagatī meter is declared for this;
Hanumān is the deity, the first seed-syllable (bīja) is "A," and "Hum" is declared as the power (śakti). // NarP_1,74.121 //
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels;
[visualizing it] as having uprooted Mount Mahāśaila and rushing toward Rāvaṇa.
Red as lac-dye, fierce, resembling Yama the Ender at the close of time,
like a blazing fire, victorious, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Surrounded by great heroes such as Aṅgada and others, he stood in the form of Rudra, emitting a terrible roar: "Stay! Stay, O wicked one, in battle! (NarP 1.74.124)
Having worshipped and meditated upon the one who has the form of Śiva, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations of rice grains mixed with milk, curd, and clarified butter, amounting to one-tenth of that number.
Having conceived the form upon the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal endowed with Vimalā and the others, the worship of Hanumān should be performed with the root mantra.
Even for those humans who possess only meditation, success is certain; of this there is no doubt.
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I shall describe its method of accomplishment.
The sādhanā of Hanumān is meritorious and destroys great sins;
it is the most secret in the world and the supreme means for attaining swift accomplishment.
The minister, by whose grace one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds,
should bathe in the morning and sit upon a seat of kuśa grass on the bank of a river.
Having performed the entire six-limbed *prāṇāyāma* with the root mantra, and having offered eight handfuls of flowers while meditating upon Rāma together with Sītā; NarP_1,74.130 //
Then, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with its filaments upon a copper plate using powdered red sandalwood and a stylus made from that same wood.

One should write the mantra upon the ritual diagram (karmikā), and having invoked the Lord of Monkeys there, one should conceive his form by means of the root-mantra; then, having meditated upon him, one should perform the offering of water for the feet and the other rites.
Having offered all the perfumes, flowers, and so forth with the root mantra,
one should then worship the six limbs upon the filaments and the petals.
One should worship Sugrīva, Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada, Nala, Nīla, Jāmbavān, Kumuda, and Kesariśa with petals.
Immediately thereafter, one should also worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and [their weapons] such as the thunderbolt (vajra).
When the mantra has been thus mastered, the practitioner of the mantra (mantrī) should accomplish his own desired goal within himself.
On a riverbank, in a forest, on a mountain, or in a secluded place,
the best of practitioners should accomplish [the rite] after first securing the ground.
Having conquered his food, his breath, his speech, and his senses,
and having performed the binding of the directions and so forth, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditation (dhyāna).
Having performed worship as before, one should recite the king of mantras one hundred thousand times;
then, upon reaching the final day of the hundred thousand, one should perform a great worship.
Having meditated correctly upon the son of the Wind with a one-pointed mind,
one should perform the recitation day and night until his manifestation occurs.
Considering the practitioner to be very firm, the Son of the Wind (Hanumān), becoming well-pleased, then proceeds before the practitioner at midnight.
Having granted the desired boon to the practitioner, the Lord of Monkeys departed;
and having obtained the boon, the moon among practitioners may dwell in his own happiness.
For this meritorious means has been revealed out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
it is indeed a secret difficult to obtain even for the gods.
One should also accomplish other applications that are beneficial for oneself;
subsequently, [one should employ] the syllable "viyat" (the sky) joined with "indu" (the moon), ending in "ṅe", and followed by "pavananandana" (the delighter of the wind).
This ten-syllable mantra, ending with *vahnipriyā* (svāhā), grants all desires;
the [assignment of] sages and so forth, as well as the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), are as previously described.
In battle, one should meditate upon Hanumān, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
seen rising swiftly as he runs to conquer Rāvaṇa.
And seeing the great hero Lakṣmaṇa fallen upon the battlefield,
he gave rise to intense anger and seized a massive mountain.
Making the three worlds tremble with his haughty cries of "Hā!
Hā!", he proclaimed his name throughout the entire universe, assuming a terrifying body.
The wise one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that, as before;
the worship of this mantra is prescribed according to the ritual rules as previously described.
When the mantra has been thus mastered, the practitioner of mantra should accomplish his own welfare;
for this, indeed, is the secret method of accomplishment for this most excellent of mantras.
This is to be strictly concealed among all tantras and must not be given to just anyone.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should perform the daily rites and remain pure.
Having gone to a river and bathed there, having invoked the sacred site (tīrtha) in eight ways,
he should then mutter the root mantra and sprinkle [the water] twelve times, the number of the sun.
Having thus performed the ritual bathing and other rites, either on the bank of the Gaṅgā, or again on a mountain or in a forest, after first securing the ground; NarP_1,74.152.

Inhalation (pūraka) should be performed with the initial letters of the alphabet, retention (kumbhaka) with the five groups of consonants, and exhalation (recaka) again with the initial letters; thus one should restrain the vital breaths.

Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth up to the placement on the pedestal (pīṭhanyāsa), and having meditated upon and worshipped Kapīśvara according to the previously mentioned procedure; NarP_1,74.154.
The practitioner should daily recite this ten thousand times with devotion before it;
when the seventh day arrives, he should perform a great worship.
The practitioner, with a one-pointed mind, should recite the mantra day and night;
having bestowed great fear, it will certainly remain when three parts of the night remain.
During the nights, the son of the Wind-god invariably arrives;
that lord of monkeys shall grant whatever boon the practitioner desires.
Whether it be knowledge, wealth, a kingdom, or the subjugation of enemies, one attains these at that very moment; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed all desires in this world, one shall attain liberation at the end;
one should utter "Hanūman," followed by the pair of Vāyu-mantras (Vāyavya) requested for immediate effect.
Then, at the end of *phala*, one should utter *phakriyānetrayuktā* and *kāmikā*;
thereafter, having said *dhaggante* and *dhagitā*, one should then utter the phrase *āyurāsva*.

The red Garuḍa, whose mantra consists of the syllables *he-ti-bā-ṇa-ne-trā-kṣa-ra*, is Lord Hari, who removes the disease of the spleen; however, the rites beginning with the sages are as previously described. (NarP 1.74.161)
Furthermore, when the deity is designated for a case of abdominal enlargement associated with the spleen (plīhodara),
one should place a betel leaf upon it and then cover it over.
Then the best of practitioners should place an eightfold cloth and a bamboo mat upon it; he should release [the offering] and meditate on the monkey.
One should heat a staff made from the wood of the *badarī* tree over a fire produced in a forest hermitage seven times with this mantra.
With that [instrument], one should strike a bamboo splinter situated in the abdomen seven times; the disease of the spleen (*plīharoga*) will certainly go to destruction.
One should recite: "Tāro namo bhagavate āñjaneyāya," and then utter twice: "Break the chains of [so-and-so]! (amukasya śṛṅkhalāṃ troṭaya). 1.74.166.
"BANDHAMOKṢAṂ KURUYUGAṂ SVĀHĀ"—this mantra is considered to end with *svāhā*.
Its sage is Īśvara, its metre is *anuṣṭubh*, and its deity is [the same]. (NarP 1.74.167)
The glorious Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, is the one who releases from chains; the seed-syllable *haṃ* and the two *ṭha*s are the Śakti, whose function is the liberation from bondage.
One should fashion the limbs with the seed-syllable joined to the six long vowels;
on the left is the mountain [syllable], and on the other side is the pure axe that pierces enemies.
One should meditate upon Hari, who possesses earrings and is the color of gold;
having thus meditated, one should recite the mantra one million times, with a tenth part of that number using mango sprouts.
One should perform the sacrifice as previously described, or the wise may perform his worship; having entered the great prison, a person should indeed recite the mantra ten thousand times.
He will certainly be released from prison quickly and become happy;
and I shall explain to him an auspicious yantra that effects both bondage and liberation.

Within the eight petals, there is a hexagon accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished; in the six corners, one should write the word "Añjaneya" preceded by the eternal syllable (Oṃ) and ending with the dative case suffix "-ṅe".
One should write "Oṃ" and "vātu vātu" within the eight petals;
having thus drawn this supreme yantra with *gorocanā* and saffron.
Having placed it upon one's head, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times for liberation from bondage;
having drawn this yantra on the surface of clay, one should then sweep over it.
The knower of mantras, using his right hand, should perform this daily until the mandala is completed;
when this is done, the practitioner is released from the great prison.
Then, "the sky," "fire," "witness," and "monkey"—these two;
then "water," "in the moon," "in Capricorn," "he releases," and "he releases. (NarP 1.74.177)
Then there is the mantra for Śṛṅkhalikā, consisting of twenty-two syllables;
having written this mantra on the right hand with the left hand, [one should apply it]. (NarP 1.74.178)
Having kept [the object] at a distance, the wise one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
within twenty-one days, he who is bound shall be released—of this there is no doubt.
One should perform all rites for him, such as the worship of the sages and so forth, as previously described;
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with auspicious substances in the tenth part of that number.
On a well-prepared cloth, using a pen made from the tip of a razor, one should draw the beautiful banner of the King of Monkeys with the eight fragrant substances. (NarP 1.74.181)
In the center of that, one should write the eighteen-syllable mantra accompanied by the name of the enemy;
by wearing it bound upon the head after it has been consecrated with the recitation of the mantra, the king [is subdued].
He certainly conquers all hosts of enemies merely by being seen;
one should cause the previously mentioned [emblems] to be depicted on the banner during lunar or solar eclipses and the like. 183. NarP_1,74.183.

Having taken up the banner, the knower of mantras should cause the Mātṛkā to be recited until liberation through touch; thereafter, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part [of that number].
When the sacrificial fire has been consecrated with sesame seeds mixed with mustard seeds,
the king, having raised his banner upon an elephant, should go forth to battle.
Seeing that banner with the elephant upon it, enemies will surely flee;
I shall now correctly describe the protective yantra of Dhanuṣmān.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in its pericarp;
having drawn an eight-cornered figure on the petals, one should encircle it with the garland-mantra (mālāmantra).
Having enveloped that [diagram] on the outside with the Māyā-mantra, one should perform the installation of the vital breath (prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā);
it should be written with a golden stylus upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf.
One should wear on the arm or on the head a yantra prepared by the *sampāta* rite, made with saffron and yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and encased in the three metals.
In battle, at dice, in debate, or in legal proceedings, one shall obtain victory;
one is never overcome by planets, obstacles, poisons, weapons, or thieves.
Having warded off all diseases, one shall live for a hundred years.
[The mantra is] the Sky (ga) joined with the six long vowels, called Fire (ra), encapsulated by the Tāra (oṃ). NarP_1,74.191 //
This great mantra consists of eight syllables; now the garland-mantra (mālāmantra) is being declared:
one should recite "Praṇava," "Vajrakāya," and "Vajratuṇḍa."
At the end of Kapilā is Piṅgalā; the great place of the upward-pointing hair (urdhvakeśa) follows.
Then, at the end of Balaraktamukha, there is Taḍijjihvā Mahā.
Then, with a great and firm blow, he struck the pair of formidable tusks known as Karāla and Utkata,
which were fierce and terrifying, following the slaying of the Lord of Laṅkā.
"Vāyu, the word *mahāsetu*, and again *bandhānte* and *mahā*;
*śailapravāha*, *gaganecara*, and 'come, come'—thus one should speak. (NarP 1,74.195)
O Blessed One, at the end of *Mahābala*, one should utter the word *parākrama*;
then [follow] *bhairava ājñāpaya ehy ehi* and the word *mahāraudra*.
At the end of the [seed] syllable, one should say "dīrghapuccha" (long-tailed one), followed by "veṣṭaya vairiṇam" (bind the enemy).
Having addressed the two words "jaṃbhaya" (devour), the mantra is considered to end with "varma" (armor) and "astra" (weapon). NarP 1.74.197.
The best of the twice-born named Māla consists of the syllables nine, two, and four;
for both the Māla-mantra and the eight-syllable mantra, the worship of the sages and so forth is as before.
Chanted in battle, he bestows victory; in illness, he is the destroyer of disease.
Thus, the practitioner who worships the son of the Wind, the Lord of Monkeys, [attains these fruits].
He obtains all his desires, even those very difficult to attain:
wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, incomparable good fortune, and fame.
It bestows intelligence, knowledge, splendor, sovereignty, and likewise victory in debate;
it grants rites for subjugation and the like, as well as victory in battle.
When worshipped, he who was born from the womb of Añjanā bestows [his blessings] in abundance.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hanuman Mantra," in the third quarter of the Sanatkumāra section of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall describe the ritual for the lamp of Hanumān, together with its secret teachings.
By the mere knowledge of which, the practitioner becomes accomplished.
The dimensions of the lamp-vessel, the measure of the oil,
and the measure of the substance— these indeed are the measurements in their proper sequence.
The specific locations, the mantras, and the ritual for offering lamps are each distinct;
it is considered that [this practice], when performed with oil scented with flowers, grants all desires.
Sesame oil is for the attainment of prosperity; regarding the arrival of travelers, linseed oil is prescribed; and for the rite of subjugation, it is certainly determined.
For the destruction of diseases, mustard oil is prescribed by those skilled in ritual action;
for the purpose of killing, it should be derived from black mustard or from the *vibhītaka* tree.
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), [oil] produced from the *karaja* tree is used; for inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), that produced from the *madhuvṛkṣa* tree.
In the absence of all these oils, oil produced from sesame seeds is the best.
Wheat, sesame, black gram, green gram, and rice—these are declared to be the five grains; they are for the perpetual lamp of the Wind-god.
The flour produced from five grains, well-prepared and very beautiful,
is declared to grant all desires whenever it is offered as a lamp.
For subjugation (*vaśya*), it is proclaimed that [the image] should be made from rice-flour; for killing (*māraṇa*), from black-gram flour; and for eradication (*uccāṭana*), from black sesame-flour.
For the arrival of travelers, it is said that [the offering] should consist of wheat and rice;
for enchantment, it should be made from *āḍhakī* beans; and for causing enmity, it should be made from *kulattha* beans.
In battle, only mung beans are prescribed for the lamp-vessel;
at the junction [of the year], for the sake of prosperity, one made from the three grains or that which originates from musk is recommended.
[He prepared] a mixture derived from cardamom, cloves, camphor, and musk,
for the sake of obtaining a maiden, as well as for a female friend of royal lineage.
In the absence of all other things, five types of grain are considered best;
eight handfuls make one *kiñcit*, and eight *kiñcit* make one *puṣkala*.
Four *puṣkala*s are proclaimed to be one *āḍhaka*;
four *āḍhakas* make one *droṇa*, and four *droṇas* make one *khārī*.
Four *khārīs* are proclaimed to be designated as one *prastha*;
or else, the measurement here is described by another method.
Two *pala*s are considered a *prasṛta*; double that is a *kuḍava*.
Four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*, and four of those likewise make an *āḍhaka*.
Four āḍhakas make one droṇa, and four droṇas make one khārī;
by this sequence they should be known, along with the pātra, in the context of the six ritual acts.
Their measurements are five, seven, and nine respectively; however, in the case of the *saugandha* [type], there is no fixed measurement, as it is accepted according to one's preference.
Regarding the constant vessel for oils, there is a rule arising from the Vārtika:
on Monday, having taken [the oil], one should hold another [vessel] soaked in water.
Thereafter, it should be known by means of the authoritative measure [of its consistency]: the grinding in the hands of a virgin;
that ground substance, placed in a pure vessel, is then kneaded with river water.
Then, being pure and with a restrained mind, one should prepare the lamp-vessel;
while the lamp is being lit in the vessel, one should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) of Mārutī.
Having established [the vessel] upon a pure ground, one should cause a lamp to be offered on the earth;
the syllables of the garland-mantras, combined with the name of the person to be accomplished, [should be used].
The threads to be used for the wick should be made to that same measurement;
alternatively, they may be taken at one-thirtieth of that measure. In rites for the Guru, there should be an abundance of everything.
In the eternal, the universal, and the particular [mantras], those equal to the *kūṭas* are traditionally taught;
the Rudras are declared to be the groups of *kūṭas*, and no restriction regarding the recipient is prescribed.
Twenty-one threads are prescribed for the path;
a red thread is proclaimed for the offering of a lamp to Hanuman.
Black [oil] is for expulsion and hatred; red [oil] is for the rite of killing;
oil weighing one *pala* of equal measure is for important tasks, possessing the qualities of Śiva.
For a permanent [image], five palas are prescribed, or else it is according to one's mental inclination.
One should offer a lamp in the presence of an image of Hanumān,
or one may do so in a temple of Śiva, at a place designated for daily or occasional rites.
There is a certain distinction here regarding Māruta which is described by me.
It is taught that the offering of lamps should be performed with joy before an image, as well as during planetary or demonic seizures, and likewise at crossroads— thus, in these six instances.
The offering of a lamp by Hanumān in the presence of a crystal liṅga and in the vicinity of a Śālagrāma stone is said to lead to the glory of various enjoyments.
In the presence of Gaṇeśa, which destroys great obstacles and calamities,
it is remembered that when there is a terrible fear of poison or disease, one should recite [this] in the presence of Hanumān.
The offering of lamps in the presence of Durgā has been prescribed for victory in battle;
likewise, it is for the destruction of disease at a crossroads and for the removal of evil glances.
It is taught that for the sake of success in all undertakings, one should perform this at the king's gate, upon being released from bondage, in a prison, or at the roots of an Aśvattha or Vaṭa tree.
In subjugation, in fear, in dispute, in the perils of the home, battle, or distress;
in gambling, in the paralyzing of sight, in causing enmity, and likewise in killing.
In raising the dead, as well as in moving an image, and in cases of poison, disease, fever, possession by spirits, and the neutralizing of malevolent magic; NarP_1,75.36.
In a forest thick with thorns, in a vast wilderness, against a fierce tiger, or toward a tusker, and toward all cruel creatures—may there always be liberation from fear. (NarP 1.75.37)

It is proclaimed that [the time for] the arrival of travelers, as well as inauspicious places, the deluding of kings, and both the coming and going at the royal gate, are determined by this. (NarP 1.75.38)
Regarding the gift of the lamp by Hanumān, there should be no doubt in this matter.
The measurement of the mandala is twenty-one piṇḍas for Rudra; it is recorded as being threefold, with the small measurement being five, seven, or likewise nine.
The making of an image for the offering of a lamp to Māruta is prescribed with milk, fresh butter, curd, or cow dung. (NarP 1.75.41)
Having placed the hero, who possesses the prowess of a lion, facing toward the south, [he spoke].
One should depict the auspicious son of the Wind-god on a wall, a cloth, or a pedestal, with his foot placed upon a bear and shining with a diadem.
The offering of a lamp for Hanumān should be given with the *mālāmantra*;
a perpetual lamp (*nityadīpa*) should be maintained with the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Understand that specific distinction regarding the offering of lamps:
on the sixth lunar day and so forth, as well as on the second lunar day and so forth, one should utter this [formula]: "This lamp. (NarP 1.75.45)
One should first utter the word "gṛhāṇa" (take), and afterwards recite the remainder as before;
for the perpetual lamp at the peak and other locations, one should state the mantra consisting of twelve syllables.
There, with the mantra known as Mālā, one should have those various rites performed on ground smeared with cow dung, while keeping the mind fixed upon that [mantra].
One should draw an auspicious lotus on the ground, provided with lines consisting of a hexagon and eight petals; there, one should place a lamp.
One should worship the son of Añjanā on a Śaiva or Vaiṣṇava pedestal;
one should write the six peak-syllables within the hexagon in the intermediate spaces.
One should inscribe the six limbs, joined with their seed-syllables, within the six corners;
the gentle one (Hanuman) situated in the center should be written there, and having worshipped Māruti therein, [one should proceed].
In the six corners, one should worship the six limbs and their names as previously stated;
and on the eight-petaled lotus, these eight monkeys should be worshipped in sequence.
To Sugrīva, Aṅgada, Suṣeṇa, and Nala;
to Nīla, Jāmbavat, and likewise to Prahasta.
Thereafter, for the sake of a beautiful appearance, one should worship the deities of the six limbs;
first to Añjanāputra, and then to Rudramūrti.
Then [he gave it] to the son of the Wind for the sake of Janaki’s life,
to the messenger of Rama, and subsequently for the purpose of warding off the Brahma-weapon.
Having worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), one should proclaim the place and time;
then, taking up water with kuśa grass, one should recite the lamp mantra.
Facing north, the supreme practitioner should recite [the mantra] and accomplish the rite;
having recited that mantra as a *kūṭa*, he should cast water upon the ground. (NarP 1.75.56)
Then, having formed the hollowed palms of the hands, one should mutter the mantra according to one's ability with this excellent lamp, while facing the north.
"O Hanuman, act in such a way that my desires may be fulfilled;
for these are the thirteen materials: cow dung, clay, and soot. (NarP 1.75.58)
Lac, vermilion, red sandalwood, sandalwood, honey, musk, curd, milk, fresh butter, and likewise clarified butter; NarP_1,75.59.
In that regard, cow dung is said to be of two kinds: that derived from cows and that from buffaloes;
subsequently, when the [original] substance has perished, buffalo dung is prescribed.
In the arrival of travelers, in the protection from afar of a great fortress, in the protection of children and others, and in the destruction of fear from thieves and the like; NarP_1,75.61.
In rites for subjugating women and other such tasks, cow dung is recommended in the tradition;
however, that which has touched the ground should not be taken, but rather that which has fallen from the sky into a vessel.
There are four kinds of clay—white, yellow, reddish, and black;
among them are gopīcandana, yellow orpiment, and red chalk.
The ink should be produced from lac juice, or any other [substance] is clearly considered suitable;
having prepared a square enclosure with cow-dung, the wise man [should proceed].
Then, in the middle of that, the practitioner, composed in mind, should fashion the form of Hanumān with buffalo-dung and write the seed-syllable of wrath upon its tail.
One should bathe the image with oil and apply a tilaka-mark with jaggery;
incense produced from the resin of the *śāla* tree is equal to the hundred-petaled lotus.
The best of practitioners should offer an oil lamp provided with five wicks, and he should present an offering of curd and boiled rice.
Reciting this three times at the throat while emitting the remaining poison,
when this is done, even for buffaloes or cows that have perished, [the poison is removed].
Furthermore, the recovery of lost female and male slaves and so forth is proclaimed;
likewise, [it is taught] regarding fear from thieves and other wicked beings, as well as from snakes and the like.
Having constructed a very beautiful house with four doors out of *tāla* wood,
an elephant should be placed at the eastern door and likewise a buffalo at the southern one.
A serpent is at the western gate, and likewise a tiger at the northern;
in this same order, [one should place] a sword, a small knife, a staff, and a mallet.
Having drawn the image in the center with the dung of a buffalo cow,
one should diligently fashion her with a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) and startled eyes.
One should perform a bath with milk, anointing with red sandalwood,
worship with *jātī* flowers, and offer pure incense.
Then, having offered a lamp with ghee, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa);
and before the scripture, one should recite [the mantra] while visualizing the sky as filled with lamps and the moon.
Having performed this for seven days, one is liberated from great fear;
however, one should diligently commence these two on a Saturday.
When fear of an enemy army has arisen, having drawn a mandala with red ochre,
one should draw within it a palm tree that is slightly bent as desired.
And there, one should fashion a standing image with cow dung,
holding the tip of a palm tree in the left hand and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) in the right.
Having constructed a square house one cubit in size on a path made of his own wood at the base of a palmyra tree, he should then draw the image in its center.
Facing southward, with her hands joined in *añjali* at her heart, one should offer her water for bathing, perfumes, and so forth, as available. (NarP 1.75.79)
One should offer her an oblation of thin rice gruel with clarified butter;
thus one should perform the recitation of the two *kili*s every single day.
When this is done, there will soon be a reunion with travelers;
having written [the name] of the king upon a fragment of black stone, [one should place it] at his house.
The rampart was indeed provided with four gates, and at those gates were the three tails of Hanumān, each entwined with the others.
One should fashion an image out of cow dung and worship it with *dhattūra* flowers;
one should offer incense made from *jaṭāmāṃsī* and a lamp fed with ghee and smeared with oil.
The food offering consists of bean cakes mixed with salt and soaked in sesame oil;
Hari should be meditated upon as eating the cake with his right hand.
With his left hand, terrifying the enemy soldiers with stones,
knitting his brows and brandishing them, he stood there frightening and crushing them.
And intent on meditation, one should indeed mutter "bhug-bhug" a thousand times;
by performing the ritual in this manner, one shall destroy the enemy army.
Truth is the protection against difficulties; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Many methods exist therein, but I have described them to you in brief. (NarP 1.75.87)
For one who offers a lamp to Hanumān every day according to the prescribed rite,
there is indeed nothing in the three worlds that remains unattainable.
It should never be given to one of wicked heart, to one whose intellect is inclined toward evil thoughts,
nor to a pupil who is undisciplined or malicious.
One should not give to an ungrateful person, but one should give to one who has been tested;
what is the use of saying more here? The Lord of Monkeys would give everything.
Now I shall declare another mantra that bestows the knowledge of reality:
Tāra (Oṃ), Namo Hanumate, and one should utter the three Jāṭhara [mantras]. (NarP 1.75.91)
Having addressed [the disciple] with the *dana-kṣobha*, one should utter the two *saṃhara*s;
thereafter, one should manifest the *ātmatattva* and then the pair of *yuga*s.
Ending with the word "jāyā" (wife), it consists of twenty-six syllables along with a half [verse];
Vasiṣṭha is its sage, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and furthermore, these are the deities.
Having performed the six limbs [of the ritual] with the mantra-syllables in sequence— namely seven, seven, six, four, eight, and six— the sage Hanūmat should meditate upon the Lord of Monkeys.
With his left arm resting upon his knee and the other hand in the *jñānamudrā* at his heart,
he sat with his mind absorbed in the inner self, situated in the midst of a grove of plantain trees.
One should meditate upon Hari, the bestower of knowledge, who resembles ten million rising suns;
having meditated thus, one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with sesame seeds ten times that amount.
One should worship the Lord as before upon the aforementioned pedestal with offerings of clarified butter;
this [mantra], when recited, certainly destroys the agitation caused by passion. (NarP 1.75.97)
One attains knowledge of reality through the grace of the Lord of Monkeys;
now I shall declare another supreme mantra that causes the flight of all spirits.
One should utter the syllable *tāraḥ*, followed by *kāśīṅkukṣiparavarāhaḥ* and *cāñjanāpadam*;
then, at the end of *vanaputrā*, one should cause the two *āveśi*s to resound.
The seed-syllable is *Tāra* (Om), the deity is the illustrious Hanumān, the weapon is the *Astra*, and the mantra consists of syllables representing the arms;
Brahmā is the sage, Gāyatrī is the meter, and the deity here is once again [Hanumān].
Hanumān is proclaimed as the seed-syllable *kamala*, and *phaṭ* is celebrated as the power (*śakti*).
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable enriched by the six long vowels.

The best of practitioners should meditate upon Āñjaneya, who has a face like a *pāṭala* flower, whose body is equal in splendor to the golden mountain, and who stands at the foot of a *pārijāta* tree. (NarP 1.75.102)
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform an oblation with sesame seeds in ten parts;
the wise one, when sacrificing on the previously mentioned pedestal, should do so as before with the three sweets (trimadhu) smeared upon them.
By means of this mantra, the practitioner should cleanse one seized by a planet;
as the victim cries out, he is liberated, and then the planet quickly flees.
These Manus are always to be guarded and must not be disclosed here or there; they should be given either to a tested disciple or to one's own son.
A wise person devoted to the worship of Hanumān, by especially propitiating Kārtavīryārjuna,
shall obtain the fruit as described.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lamp Ritual," in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Nārada said:
"There were many kinds of kings on earth, beginning with Kārtavīrya..."
They are born and then they dissolve, according to their respective karmas.
How then did this best of kings attain the state of being served by the world, having surpassed all other monarchs? Dispel this doubt of mine.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall speak for the removal of your doubt as to how Kārtavīryārjuna attained the state of being worthy of worship on earth.
He who was the incarnation of the Sudarśana discus on the surface of the earth,
having propitiated Dattātreya, obtained supreme splendor.
O Nārada, by the mere remembrance of that lord of kings,
one conquers enemies in battle and swiftly recovers what has been lost.
Therefore, the mantra-worship and other rites of this [deity], which are concealed in all the tantras, I shall reveal to you—[a practice] that bestows all siddhis. (NarP 1.76.6)
Raudrī is joined with Vahni and Tārā; Lakṣmī is joined with Agni, Indu, and Śānti; [the Lord] is enriched by Vedhā, Adhara, Indu, and Śānti; and Nidrā is joined with Āśā, Agni, and Bindu.
The noose, the illusory goad, the lotus, the armor, and the weapons; the station of Kārtavīrya;
the letter *ra*, the seat of the sky, Ananta, and the two born of fire situated in the ears.
The ram (meṣa), the long [vowel], the wind (pavana), and Manu are said to be the last [syllables] of the heart;
this mantra consists of twenty-nine syllables, beginning with the letter *tā* and ending with the letter *nakha*.
The sage is Dattātreya, its meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh,
the deity is Kārtavīryārjuna, and the seed-syllable, power, and heart-mantra are Dhruva (Om).
One should place the heart-mantra below with the pair of seeds enriched by the remainder (Śeṣa);
the head-mantra with the fourth [vowel] joined with Śānti; and the limb-mantra beginning with Kāma. 1.76.11.

One should place the *śikhā* with [the mantra] enriched by the Moon (I) and preceded by the left ear (U), joined with Māyā (Ī) and Viśa (Ś); one should place the *varma* with the goad (AṂ) and the lotus (HŪṂ), together with Vāgīśvarī (AI). 12. NarP_1,76.12.

The weapon-mantra is released by means of the armor and weapon mantras; it is then pervasive again through the remaining syllables, [placed] in the heart, the belly, the navel, the belly, and from the secret region.
One should place the ten seed-syllables, situated between two *praṇavas*, upon the right foot, the left foot, the thighs, the knees, and the shanks.
Then, from the syllables beginning with *tā* and the remaining letters, [one should place them] on the crown of the head, the forehead,
the two eyebrows, the two ears, likewise the two eyes, the nose, the mouth, the throat, and the shoulders.
Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) on all limbs with the entire mantra,
one who is diligent should meditate upon Kārtavīrya, the lord of men, for the sake of attaining all desired accomplishments.
Resplendent with the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and worshipped by all kings,
he held fifty arrows in his right arms and bows in his left.
One should meditate upon King Arjuna as an incarnation of the Discus of Śrī Viṣṇu, adorned with a golden garland and clothed in red garments.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds, rice grains, and milk-rice in a portion equal to one-tenth [of the recitation]; one should worship him on the Viṣṇu-pīṭha.
In the six corners are the six limbs; then, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, are the Dispeller of the Madness of Thieves and the Dispeller of the Madness of Plague.
The shatterer of the pride of enemies, the shatterer of the pride of the Daityas;
the destroyer of the wicked, the destroyer of suffering, and the annihilator of misfortune and calamity.
In the eight directions, beginning with the east, the eight Śaktis of dark luster are to be worshipped:
Kṣemaṅkarī, Vaśyakarī, Śrīkarī, and Yaśaskarī.
Likewise, the bestower of longevity, the bestower of wisdom, and again the bestower of knowledge;
the eighth is the bestower of wealth—these are the World-Protectors (Lokeśas) joined with their weapons.
When the mantra has been accomplished in this way, it becomes fit for ritual application;
now, the worship diagram of Kārtavīryārjuna is described here.
One should draw the pericarp with one's own seed-syllable, the limbs, and the *dhruva* mantra;
the petals should represent the directions, with the syllables beginning with *Tārā* and ending with *varma* on the petals, and the remaining letters in the intervals between the petals.
The yantra of the Lord consists of a lotus with filaments formed by the semi-vowels and the final vowel, surrounded by the remaining syllables,
and a square earth-mansion adorned at its corners by the elements and their syllables.
Having carefully drawn the yantra with the eight fragrances upon a pure ground,
one should install a water-pot there, invoke the King [of Mantras] into it, and worship him.
Having touched the water-pot, one who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra a thousand times;
he should then consecrate himself with those waters for the sake of attaining all desired goals.
A man consecrated by the Kumbha [consecration] obtains sons, fame, the destruction of disease, long life, the delight of his kinsmen, perfection of speech, and beautiful eyes. (NarP 1.76.29)
When a village or a city is beset by the assault of enemies,
one should install this yantra for the sake of removing the fear of foes.
An enemy is killed with mustard seeds, ariṣṭa, garlic, and cotton;
he is paralyzed by dhattūra, incited to hatred by nimba, and brought under control by lotuses.
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), it is prescribed to use fuel-sticks of *vibhīta* and *khadira*,
along with pungent oil, buffalo ghee, gold, and medicinal ointment.
By offering barley, one attains prosperity; by sesame seeds and clarified butter, there is the destruction of sin.
By means of a mixture of sesame, rice, white mustard, and *jāla* flowers, even a king may be brought under one's control.

An oblation of *apāmārga*, *arka*, and *dūrvā* bestows fortune and removes sin; an oblation of *priyaṅgu* brings women under one's influence, while an oblation of *murā* grants peace from malevolent spirits.
Having offered oblations with fuel-sticks produced from the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Vaṭa, and Bilva trees, one obtains sons, long life, wealth, and happiness.
The destruction of thieves occurs through offerings of snake-skin, gold, white mustard seeds, and salt;
immobilization by means of yellow pigment and cow dung; and the attainment of land through oblations of rice.
In all cases, the number of oblations should be determined by those who know the mantras as ranging from one thousand up to ten thousand, according to the gravity or lightness of the task at hand.
O wise ones, the characteristic of the mantras of Kārtavīrya is now declared:
one should employ "Kārtavīryārjuna" ending in the dative case (ṅe) in all mantras. (NarP 1.76.38)
This ten-syllable mantra beginning with its own seed-syllable consists of nine other syllables of Śiva;
this second mantra is said to be preceded by the first two seed-syllables.
The third [son] was born from his own two desires; the fourth from his own two eyebrows;
the fifth from his own two nooses; and the sixth from his own *māyā*.
The seventh [syllable] is formed by [the two syllables] *svāṅkuśa*; the eighth by *svarama*;
the ninth by *svavāgbhava*; and the final one by *varmāstra*.
In the second through the ninth [syllables], there should be an interchange of the two seed-syllables;
however, in the tenth mantra, the nine syllables are situated within the armor and the weapon.
Among these excellent mantras, one should practice that mantra which is favorable to oneself;
among these, the Virāj meter is declared for the first, while Triṣṭubh is stated for the other three.
When these ten mantras are preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ),
then the first shall consist of the syllable of Śiva, while the others shall consist of twelve syllables each.
The *triṣṭubh* meter is considered for the first [mantra], while the *jagatī* is held to be for the others;
thus, the worship of the twenty mantras is prescribed as before.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual for these [mantras] using the long, wealthy root-seed syllable; the mantra is:
*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), *Hṛt* (Namaḥ), *Kārtavīryārjunāya*, *Varma* (Huṃ), *Astra* (Phaṭ) twice. (NarP 1.76.46)
This mantra consists of fourteen syllables; its worship is considered to be as described previously.
Its five limbs (aṅgas) consist of syllables numbering four, two, three, two, and two respectively.

The Tāra, the heart, the Blessed One, followed by "ṅeṃ," then Kārtavīryārjuna, and the mantra of the armor, weapon, fire, and beloved—this is declared to be the eighteen-syllable mantra. (NarP 1.76.48)
The five-limbed mantra of the Lord consists of forty-seven syllables:
"Namo bhagavate śrīkārtavīryārjunāya. (NarP 1.76.49)
He is the destroyer of all evil, possessing the power and prowess of asceticism;
he is the protector of the seven islands at their borders and the refuge from all calamities.
Then follows the great mantra, beginning with *janyacūḍāmaṇe*, followed by *mahāśaktimate*, then ending with *sahasradahana*, and concluding with *varmāstra*. (NarP 1.76.51)
He is proclaimed as possessing sixty-three forms; by remembering him, all obstacles are removed.
The second is Rājanya-kra-vartin, and the third is the hero Śūra.
The fourth, who is proclaimed as the lord of Māhiṣmatī, was satiated by the waters of the Revā; he was one-eyed and had his hand afflicted.

With the six words beginning with "daśāsya" ending in the suffix -ṅe, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) while [the deity] is being bathed by young women and sporting in the waters of the Narmadā.
One should meditate upon the intoxicated and most excellent of kings obstructing the flood of water with his hands;
having thus meditated, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times, while the rest is as before.
First, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, and the ritual of worship is as before.
There was a king named Kārtavīryārjuna who possessed a thousand arms.
Merely by recollecting it, one may declare what has been taken or lost;
this excellent mantra, consisting of thirty-two syllables, is thus obtained.
With all five limbs [prostrating], the meditation, worship, and so forth are as before;
one should utter the words "vidmahe" after the name Kārtavīrya.
At the end of the word "mahāvīryāya," one should utter the word "dhīmahi"; at the end of the excellent word "tanno 'rjunaḥ," one should pronounce the word "pracodayāt."
This Gāyatrī has been declared for Arjuna; one should mutter it at the beginning of any ritual application.
And for those who mutter the Anuṣṭubh mantra at night, multitudes of thieves [will appear].
They flee far from their homes even at the sound of the *tarpaṇa* libation;
now, therefore, I shall describe the ritual of the lamp which is dear to Kārtavīrya. (NarP 1.76.61)
One should commence the lighting of lamps during the months of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, Mārgaśīrṣa, Kārttika, Āśvina, Pauṣa, Māgha, or Phālguna.

On a lunar day free from the *rikta* tithis, on a weekday other than Saturday and Tuesday, and under the asterisms Hasta, Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā), Aśvinī, Ārdrā, Puṣya, Śravaṇa, and Svātī; NarP_1,76.63.
The commencement of the lamp festival is beneficial when the moon is in the constellation Rohiṇī associated with two deities (the Viśākhā nakṣatra),
as well as during the Carame yoga, Vyatīpāta, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, and Sukarman.

One should perform [rites] during the *prīti* yoga, at times of joy, in [periods of] good fortune, and also during auspicious and long-lived periods; furthermore, when the moon is free from the *viṣṭi* karana, during eclipses, and during the *ardhodaya* and other such [auspicious] conjunctions.
In the yogas, at night, or in the forenoon, the commencement of the lamp is auspicious;
on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, at midnight, it is exceedingly excellent.
If, in that case, a Sunday and the Śravaṇa asterism are difficult to obtain, there is no need for the purification of months and so forth in matters of extreme necessity. (NarP 1.76.67)
Having fasted on the first day, self-restrained and observing celibacy,
he should bathe in the morning with water containing yellow flowers and smear a pure ground with cow-dung water.
Having restrained the breath and performed the ritual intention (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the previously mentioned ritual depositions (*nyāsa*).
One should fashion a hexagon on the ground using red sandalwood and rice grains.
Therefore, having drawn the god of love (Smara) within a hexagon, one should surround it with the nine syllables; outside of that, one should again draw a triangle.
When the yantra has been drawn in this manner, one should place a lamp-vessel there,
made of gold or silver, or, in the absence of those, made of copper.
A bell-metal vessel and an earthen one are for the youngest [son]; at death, one made of iron;
for peace, one produced from mung-bean flour; and at a joint [of the body], one born from wheat flour.
When there are a thousand palas of clarified butter, the vessel is prescribed to be one hundred palas;
when there are ten thousand palas of clarified butter, the vessel is prescribed to be five hundred palas.
When the number is seventy-five, the vessel is known to be sixty palas;
for three thousand palas of ghee, there is a container of one pala of sugar.

In a vessel weighing two thousand [palas], a measure of two hundred is desired; in one weighing one hundred, it is determined by the movement of the axle; one should calculate it similarly for other weights.
In a perpetual lamp, one pala of fire is prescribed, and one pala of clarified butter is likewise remembered as the vessel;
having thus established the vessel, one should insert wicks made from thread.
One, three, or five, seven, and so forth— even odd numbers—
