up to a thousand, have been fashioned as the count of threads according to the measure of the lunar days.
One should add cow’s ghee, purified by a clean cloth,
in a quantity of one thousand palas— or a tenth part thereof, depending on the gravity of the task.
A beautiful probe made of gold or other materials, sixteen finger-breadths in length—
or half of that, or half again— should have a fine point and a thick base.
One should set down the alms-bowl to the south, having placed the fire in the middle and at the front;
and having left a space of four finger-breadths to the south of the bowl’s position.
One should bury a beautiful dagger with its point facing downward and its handle to the south;
there, one should light a lamp preceded by the recollection of Gaṇeśa.
To the east of the lamp, in the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala,
or upon an eight-petaled diagram made of rice, one should duly place the dhūpa.
There, having invoked the sovereign lord of kings, the wise one should worship him as before;
then, taking water and unbroken grains of rice, he should consecrate the lamp.
This mantra for the visualization of the lamp is declared to consist of two syllables and one *bhūmi*:
the *praṇava*, the *pāśa*, the *māyā*, the *śikhā*, and the *kārtākṣara* syllables. (NarP 1.76.84)
For Vīryārjuna, the lord of Māhiṣmatī,
one should utter the word "sahasra" at the end of each syllable, such as "bāhave," followed by the word "sahasra."
To him who has received [the gift] from the hand of one initiated for a sacrifice, who is dear to Dattātreya, the son of Atri, that jewel of a child born to Anasūyā; after that—*NarP_1,76.86*.
Homage! O you who stand upon the neck, the crocodile, and the moon, take this noose;
take the lamp, O so-and-so; protect, protect me! Again, [the word] "pada. (NarP 1,76.87)

The pair "duṣṭān nāśaya" (destroy the wicked ones), as well as "pātaya" (strike down) and "ghātaya" (slay); the two forms of "jahi" (kill the enemies), the *māyā* (hrl-lakṣaṇa), the *tāra* (om), one's own seed-syllable, and the Self-born (AUM). NarP_1,76.88 //
Then, by means of this excellent lamp facing west, [one says]: "O beloved of Agni, protect so-and-so at the end of such-and-such; O bestower of boons! (NarP 1.76.89)
The two syllables *māyā* (h) and *ākāśa* (ha), joined with the moon (*candra*) of the left eye (*vāmanetra*), form *Śivā*.
Then follow *veda* (4), *ādi* (1), *kāma* (e), *Cāmuṇḍā* (ca), *svāhā* (svāhā), *pūṣan* (p), and the *bindu* (m). (NarP 1.76.90)
The Praṇava, the word "Agni-priyā," and the syllables "netra," "bāṇa," and "adhara" constitute the mantra;
Dattātreya is proclaimed as the sage (ṛṣi) of this mālā-mantra. (NarP 1.76.91)
One should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of Cāmuṇḍā using the mantra "Chando 'mitaṃ Kārtavīryarjuno devo 'khilāptikṛt," joined with the six long vowels.
Having meditated upon the deity and then recited the mantra, one should finally cast the water mixed with sesame seeds.
The seed-syllable of Cāmuṇḍā is said to be "halī" (ha-lī) preceded by "govinda" (go) and adorned with the moon (the nasal bindu).
Then, one should first recite the nine-syllable mantra a thousand times:
Tāra (Oṃ), Ananta joined with Bindu (Haḥ), Māyā (Hrīḥ), Sva (Sva), and joined with the left eye (I). (NarP 1.76.94)

The seed-syllables are Kūrma (ha) and Agni (ra), enriched by Śānti (sa) and Bindu (m); then Vahni-jāyā (svā), Aṅkuśa (va), and Dhruva (oṃ). The seer is as previously mentioned; the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the rest is as before.
Having recited the king of mantras one thousand times, one should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Thus, the performer of the offering of lamps obtains everything desired in its entirety.
At the time of awakening the lamp, one should avoid inauspicious speech;
the sight of a Brahmin there is proclaimed to be auspicious.
For Śūdras, the foremost [means of livelihood] is declared to be the killing and binding of Mlecchas;
the sight of rats and cats is inauspicious, whereas that of cows and horses brings happiness.
A flame equal to a lamp leads to accomplishment; one that is crooked brings about night;
sounds that are terrifying bring fear to the performer, while those that are blazing are considered to bestow happiness.
When, during the performance of a lamp-offering, the vessel is seen by fate to have broken, it portends the arising of fear from enemies, the death of cattle, and the destruction of wealth.
If the sacrificer should go to the abode of Yama within a fortnight, he should perform it more urgently;
otherwise, the task will succeed only after a long delay.
If that other lamp is extinguished while it is being made, the performer will become blind;
if there is contact with something impure, disease will occur; and if the lamp goes out, there will be fear of thieves.
If one is touched by a dog, a cat, or a rat, there will be fear of being overthrown from one's position as a king;
however, a lamp lit with cow-dung at the commencement of the rite bestows all desired objects.
Therefore, the lamp should be protected with effort from obstacles;
until its completion, one should observe celibacy and sleep on the ground.
One should avoid even conversing with women, Śūdras, outcasts, and the like;
one should recite the nine-syllable king of mantras one thousand times for each such instance.
He who, standing on one foot before a lamp, recites the hymn of praise daily—especially at midnight—to the Lord of Mantras; NarP_1,76.106 //
If one recites it a thousand times at night, one shall quickly attain one's desired goal; having completed the rite on an auspicious day, one should feed the best of the twice-born.
While sprinkling the performer with water from the jar, one should recite the mantra;
the performer, however, should give a generous sacrificial fee for the sake of satisfaction.
When the guru is pleased, the king, son of Kṛtavīrya, grants what is desired;
he may perform it himself by the guru’s command, or the guru may cause it to be done.
O Nārada, having given wealth and other offerings to him for the purpose of offering lamps,
one who offers a lamp for the sake of attaining his own desired goal without the permission of the Guru [is at fault].
Success does not arise for him; indeed, there is loss at every step.
Cow’s ghee is said to be the best, while that produced from a buffalo is middling.
Sesame oil would be of that same quality, while ghee produced from goats and the like is inferior;
in the case of a disease of the mouth, one should provide a lamp with fragrant oil.
Then, when a lamp was prepared with a thousand palas of oil for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose and for the destruction of enemies, it was not seen.
Then, having accomplished his task, he should perform the rite pertaining to the lamp three times;
at that time, even a task that is very difficult to achieve will be accomplished—of this there is no doubt.
Kārtavīrya is fond of lamps, Mārtaṇḍa is fond of prostrations,
Mahāviṣṇu is fond of hymns of praise, and Gaṇeśa is fond of bilva leaves.
Durgā is surely fond of worship, and Śiva is fond of ritual ablution;
therefore, for their complete satisfaction, one should perform those respective rites with due respect.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Mantra-Lamp of the Greatness of Kārtavīrya," in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, you who are proficient in all the Tantras!"
You have fully explained to me that ritual procedure which is concealed within the Tantra.
But now, O illustrious one, O treasure-house of compassion, I desire to hear of the armor of Kīrtavīrya and Hanumān; please tell me that. (NarP 1.77.2)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O best of Brahmins, I shall declare the most wonderful armor (kavaca) of Kārtavīrya, by which he becomes pleased and brings about the accomplishment of one's goals.
Resembling a thousand suns, blazing with various jewels,
rich with radiant banners and flags, and adorned by ten thousand horses.
Resounding with the terrifying roar of the great ocean at the time of universal destruction,
with the path of the sky overspread by a raised great parasol.
Upon that best of great chariots, resplendent with various blazing weapons,
well-established, vast and noble, adorned with a thousand arms— ||| NarP_1,77.6 |||
Holding a raised bow with his left hands and arrows with the others,
he was adorned with a crown, necklaces, a diadem, armlets, bracelets, and bangles.
Adorned with various ornaments such as finger-rings, waist-bands, girdles,
and anklets— resplendent, exceedingly costly, and of diverse kinds.
The hero, clad in armor, with a lotus-like face beaming with joy,
caused the three worlds to tremble with the lion-roar of his bowstring.
It brings about the destruction of all enemies, the eradication of all diseases,
the bestower of all prosperity, and is attended by the glory of victory.
Bestowing all good fortune, auspicious, granting fearlessness to his devotees,
enriched with divine garlands and unguents, and endowed with all the auspicious marks.
The Lord, standing in the midst of a multitude of chariots, elephants, horses,
and infantry, the bestower of boons, the universal monarch, and the sole protector of all the worlds.
He possessed a splendor equal to a thousand suns rising at once,
and by the fame of his sovereignty born of great yoga, he had pervaded the three worlds.

Having meditated correctly upon the illustrious Maṇḍata, who descended to the surface of the earth from a portion of Hari, according to the distinctions of the self and other categories, one should recite this protection.
May her five limb-forms, brilliant as crystal, protect me—
those beginning with the Heart-mantra located in the corners of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu.
Their forms blazed with garlands on all sides; they held shields, skins, and swords in their hands;
and their bodies possessed unimpeded strength, sovereignty, power, and capability.
May he who is endowed with the power of Kṣemaṅkarī, the destroyer of the hosts of thieves,
and whose weapons are the arrow and the bow, protect the eastern quarter for me.
Accompanied by the Śakti Śrīkarī, the destroyer of the fear of Mārī,
the glorious one bearing the arrow and the bow— may he protect my southern direction.
Endowed with great power, the destroyer of all enemies,
and bearing a mighty bow and arrows, may he protect my eastern direction.
May he who is endowed with glorious deeds and is the destroyer of the hosts of Daityas protect me thoroughly in the south-eastern direction, which belongs to Citrabhānu.
Accompanied by Vidyākara, the destroyer of great suffering,
may the Lord who holds a bow in his hand protect my southwestern intermediate direction.
May he who is engaged in the work of wealth, the destroyer of great misfortune,
and who holds a bow and arrows in his hand, protect my northwestern quarter.
Endowed with the power of longevity, glorious, and the destroyer of great fear,
may he who bears the bow and quiver protect my northwestern quarter for Śiva.
May the all-pervading Lord, who is endowed with the glory of victory, who directly bears the Sahasrāra [cakra],
and who strikes fear into all the wicked, protect my upward direction.
May the Bearer of the Conch, endowed with his great spear, protect the downward direction for me— he who is the sun that pierces the darkness of suffering.
Endowed with the great yoga, his maṇḍala traversing all directions,
may the Lord of Great Yogins, the Holder of the Lotus, protect me from every side.
These forms, however, are red, draped in red garlands and garments;
they possess the appearance of the principal deity and are situated separately upon the excellent chariot.
The Śaktis have lotuses in their hands and resemble blue water-lilies;
they wear white garlands and garments, and are radiant with well-applied tilaka.
May the mighty lords of Indra and the other guardians, each with their respective mounts, weapons, and ornaments, stationed in their own directions, protect me. (NarP 1.77.29)
These have been fully described as the deities of all the enclosures;
endowed with all powers, may they protect me always from every side.
In the heart, the belly, the navel, the stomach, and the secret circle,
they remain in the form of radiant energy, like trees of the wish-granting tree, desiring to protect [the body].
And may others, of great color, in the form of mantras, and most radiant,
protect us by pervading [us] from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
May Kārtavīrya protect my head; may the Lord of the Haihayas protect my forehead;
may Sumukha protect my face; and may he who has pervaded the three worlds protect my ears.
May Sukumāra protect my jaw; may Dhanurdhara protect the pair of my eyebrows; may Puṃṣaḍarīkākṣaga protect my eye; and may Guṇākara protect my nose.
May Brahmajñeya, the seer among the twice-born, ever protect the lower lip;
may the Imperishable One, the repository of all scriptures and arts, protect the tongue and the chin.

May he who is dear to Dattātreya protect my throat; may the Lord of the royal families protect my shoulders; may the destroyer of the pride of Rāvaṇa protect my arms; and may the one of great strength protect my heart.
May the wise one protect my belly; may the conqueror of enemy cities protect my chest;
may the bestower of all aims protect my hands; and may the beloved of the world protect the tips of my fingers.
May he who is intoxicated by the playful grace of the waters of the Revā protect my belly;
may Vīraśūra protect my navel, and may the destroyer of all evil protect my two sides.
The Lord of the seven continents touched his back with his thousand arms;
the Lord of Māhiṣmatī touched his hips; and the Beloved of the Earth touched his thighs and knees.
May Vīrādhipa protect my calves; may Manojava protect my feet;
may he who bears all weapons protect my entire body in all its vital points.
May the Destroyer of all evil protect the body composed of the eight elements;
may He who grants the desires of all the learned protect the ten lords of life, beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa).
May he who has brought the collection of his senses under control protect all my senses—
whatever place is not mentioned, and whatever exists both inside and outside the body.
May the Lord of the lords of all world-protectors protect all of that for me;
and may this body, more solid than a diamond, be covered by this armor.
May I be free from hundreds of afflictions and devoid of fear;
may this divine, impenetrable armor be bound upon me, as it was by the lord of the Haihayas.
I wander by day and by night with a fearless inner self upon the royal highway, that most difficult path crowded with thieves and the like.
In a rugged and terrible forest, in a forest fire, in a mountain cave, in battle amidst a clash of weapons, or in a place inhabited by lions and tigers; NarP_1,77.46 //
In a thicket, in a place crowded with all manner of things, at twilight, in a king's palace, in a dispute, in a vast whirlpool, in the ocean, and on a riverbank; NarP_1,77.47.
In a land crowded with highwaymen and overrun by bands of robbers,
when the seizure of all one's possessions has occurred and a peril to life itself has arrived.
In the onset of various diseases and fevers, in the torment of piśācas and pretas, in afflictions caused by pestilence and bad dreams, and for one distressed by a betrayer of trust; NarP_1,77.49.
In great physical suffering and in the great fever of the mind, in the fear of mental anguish and disease, and even in the calamity of the flames of obstacles; NarP_1,77.50.
Let there be no fear whatsoever for me, who am covered by this armor,
even from all those who desire to harm me and would plunder my wealth.
May the great chariot-warrior ward off with his thousand arms those who are difficult to conquer and bound by the thousandfold noose raised by his own hand.
May the son of Kṛtavīrya, having obstructed their power of movement,
strike them down— pierced by a thousand goads and shattered by a thousand arrows.
May Rājacūḍāmaṇi swiftly reduce our adversaries to a state where they are shattered by a thousand swords and crushed by a thousand maces.
May the lotus-eyed one, who bears a thousand spokes, cause the multitudes of wicked beings such as thieves to be terrified by the sound of his own conch.
May the incarnation of Hari himself protect me in its entirety—
O Kārtavīrya of great heroism, destroyer of all the wicked!
Destroy, destroy everywhere and at all times the wicked thieves! Why do you sleep, O slayer of the wicked? Why do you stand still? Why do you linger? // NarP 1.77.57 //
Arise and protect us from all fears, like your own children—
from those thieves who steal our wealth, from those who hate us, and from those who would harm us.
The wicked who cause fear to the virtuous, those who are deceitful and evil-minded, the malevolent, the corrupt kings, and the sinful ministers; 77.59.

Those who destroy what must be done, those who are wicked and act as adversaries, those who seize all one's possessions, and others who are deceitful—these five; ||| NarP_1,77.60 ||| Please provide the text you would like me to translate. Those barbarians who cause great affliction, the robbers, and the low-born;
those who set fires, administer poison, are deceivers, and carry weapons in their hands—[all these are destroyed].
Those who are sinful, performers of evil deeds, givers of suffering, and possessed of wicked intentions; those who are deceivers, addicted to evil paths, and those who inflict various kinds of fear.
All those who were constantly intent on seeking our weaknesses and prepared to harass us have been struck down by the sound of Kārtavīrya’s great conch shell.
May those Dānavas, Mahādityas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas who are deluded from afar go suddenly to their destruction.
Those who are Piśācas, those great beings (mahāsattvas), those who are Bhūtas, Brahmarākṣasas, those who are Apasmāra-grahas, and those grahas that feed on flesh; NarP_1,77.65 //
The vetālas who consume great quantities of blood, the guhyakas,
the gandharvas, the apsarases, the siddhas, and those born from the wombs of gods and other [divine beings].
The ḍākinīs, the druṇasas, the pretas, the kṣetrapālas, and the vināyakas;
the great tigers, the great clouds, and those with the forms of great elephants.
They have the forms of great elephants, great lions, and those born from great buffaloes;
they take the shapes of bears, boars, dogs, monkeys, and owls.
With heads like those of great camels, donkeys, cats, snakes, cows, and bulls,
these beings of immense size possess various forms and bestow thousands of diverse afflictions.
Causing various diseases— minor, yet possessing great potency and great strength—
they are of the wind-nature (vātika), the bile-nature (paittika), the phlegm-nature (ślaiṣmika), and those arising from the combination of all three (sānnipātika).
The great grahas of Maheśvara, Vaiṣṇava, and Vairiñca;
the Skānda, Vaināyaka, and the cruel Pramathas and Guhyakas.
The slayers of great enemies, the fierce ones, the great plagues, the smallpox, and the great fevers that recur every day, every two days, and every three days; NarP_1,77.72.

Those fevers that recur every fourth day, those occurring every fortnight, monthly, or every six months, as well as those annual ones which are difficult to ward off and extremely terrible; [all these are overcome].

Those great portents occurring in dreams, those malevolent planetary influences in dreams, the *kūṣmāṇḍas*, the *jṛmbhikas*, the terrestrial spirits, the *droṇas*, and those who deceive through their presence; ||| NarP_1,77.74 |||
Those who cause wandering, those who take away life, and the *bālagraha*s and others;
those who seize the mind, intellect, and senses, as well as the *sphoṭaka*s and the great *graha*s.

Those who eat great quantities of food, those who feed on offerings, those who consume corpses, those who roam by day, those who roam at night, and those who are fierce during the twilights; NarP_1,77.76 //
Whether they were heedless or indeed heedful, all those who endeavored to harm me were struck by arrows released from the bow of Kārtavīrya.
May those serpents and great nāgas who dwell in the caves of the great mountains perish by the thousands, their courage, strength, and effort shattered.
The Kālavyālas, the Mahādaṃṣṭras, those known as the Mahājagaras,
Ananta, Śūlika, and others— these are terrifying with the venom of their fangs.
There were fierce leeches with hundreds of heads and severed tails,
as well as highly venomous water-leeches and scorpions with stinging tails.
There were venomous snakes called *kālakūṭa* and *mahāhālāhala*,
as well as water-snakes, aquatic predators, crocodiles, and tortoises.
Fish with poisonous tails and whatever other aquatic creatures there may be—
those born in water, those born on land, and even artificial poisons— all possess great venom.
The guptarūpa, the guptaviṣa, the mouse, the house-lizard, those various terrible poisons known as mahopaviṣas, and others; NarP_1,77.83.
All those who wish to harm us, seeking to destroy our bodies and lives,
shall be torn asunder by the thousands of swords of Kārtavīrya.
May those humans whose senses and courage have perished perish from afar;
likewise may the beasts, bears, and monkeys who roam the forests perish as well.
Lions, tigers, boars, and buffalo— those great wild beasts—
as well as elephants, horses, gayals, donkeys, śarabhas, and wolves.
Dogs, tigers, white cats, mongooses eager for holes,
jackals, hares, hawks, eagles, and other birds.
Bheruṇḍas, crows, vultures, swans, and other species of birds;
those born from sprouts, those born from eggs, those born from sweat, and those born from a womb.
Born into various distinct lineages, diverse and of different kinds,
those who desire to harm us by day and by night shall be subdued.
May they all, their movement and prowess destroyed, be shattered from afar by the thousand maces of Kārtavīrya.
And those who bestow insecurity, those who are deceitful and full of guile, and those who cause killing, destruction, uprooting, hatred, and delusion; // NarP_1,77.91 //

Those who betray trust, the wicked, those men who are treacherous toward their masters, those who are murderous assailants, the evil, and those sinful ones who steal the clothes of women; ||| NarP_1,77.92 |||
They bestow the extreme sufferings of burning, affliction, poison, and the stroke of weapons;
they grant the terrors of seizure of fields and wealth, as well as imprisonment and the like.
Epidemics of various forms, and whatever other evil species there may be, which constantly cause affliction and seek to find a vulnerability in order to harm; NarP_1,77.94.
May they all, their strength and prowess destroyed, go to their destruction from afar, split asunder by the thousand wheels of Kārtavīrya.
Those clouds, those great rains, those winds, and those lightnings;
those blazing great thunderbolts and those terrible portents.
And those terrible falling meteors, as well as the rainbows of Indra and the like;
and the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn.
And Rāhu and the terrible comets, the lunar mansions as well as the zodiac signs, the lunar days, the transits, the months, the years, and the leaders of the ages; NarP_1,77.98 //
The lords of the Manvantaras, the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis who have attained perfection through yoga, the Nidhis, as well as the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, and the Fires; NarP_1,77.99 //
The seasons, the guardians of the world, the ancestors, the assembly of gods, and the sixty-four branches of knowledge that exist within the three worlds; NarP_1,77.100 //
May all those who have been mentioned here, as well as those others who have not been mentioned,
always be gentle toward us and bringers of happiness at all times.
By the command of Kārtavīrya, the lord of yogins of immeasurable luster,
the archer Kārtavīryārjuna became a king of kings and the sovereign of the Haihayas.
The destroyer of the pride of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who is exalted by his playful sport, the very difficult to conquer,
the remover of suffering, the subduer of thieves, the Lord of the Sovereigns of Kings, the Master.

The omniscient one, the giver of all, the illustrious one, the fulfiller of the desires of all the learned, the accomplished one, the crest-jewel of kings, the yogi, the sovereign lord of the seven continents.
Victorious, the conqueror of all, eloquent, possessing a great course, free from greed,
a performer of sacrifices, dear to the Brahmins, learned, to be known through the Veda, and eternal.
The lord of Māhiṣmatī was a warrior of great fame and mighty arms;
he was delicate yet a great hero, a slayer of Māras, with intoxicating eyes.
Śatrughna, the eternal, the hero, the bearer of the conch, the beloved of yogis,
the great devotee of the Lord, the wise one, and the destroyer of great fear.
His divine form is unassailable; his being pervades the three worlds;
he has conquered his senses and subdued his enemies; he is self-willed and possesses infinite valor.
The wielder of the discus, the destroyer of enemy armies, honored by the rules of combat,
the possessor of all scriptures and arts, free from passion, and revered by the world.
A hero, rich in pure essence, possessing great strength and prowess,
highly honored as the glory of victory, the conqueror of enemies, and the leader of mantras.
Wielder of the sword, granter of desires, beloved, destroyer of time, lotus-eyed,
fond of auspicious speech, physician, wise, giver of boons, and self-controlled.
Possessing great wealth, a lord of treasures, a great yogi, and beloved by his guru;
rich in yoga, the destroyer of all diseases, he ruled over the entire surface of the earth.
The wielder of divine weapons, the one of immeasurable soul, the protector of all, the greatly resplendent,
the bearer of all arms, the bestower of desired boons, and the conqueror of the cities of enemies.
Accomplished in yoga, possessing a great body, and lord of hundreds of great assemblies;
he is a treasury of all knowledge and is ever-exerting himself to bestow all spiritual accomplishments.
Thus, by the recitation of these one hundred and eight names, may the ten forms, having fully pervaded the ten directions along the paths of space, protect me forever.
May all my senses be healthy and at peace; may there always be tranquility for me. And may the eight forms, beginning with Śeṣa, be resplendent through their very prowess.
May those situated in the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśa protect me always;
may there be for me unhindered happiness, health, and invincibility.
The destruction of suffering, freedom from obstacles, the increase of progeny, the arising of happiness, the attainment of desires, supreme auspiciousness, impartiality, and health.
Freedom from laziness shall be desired; there shall be the destruction of death, the increase of strength, the removal of fear, fame, beauty, learning, supernatural power, and great prosperity.
The non-loss of one's possessions, the recovery of what was lost,
long life, joy of mind, and the attainment of desired delicacy.
May there be for me the state of being most invincible and indeed great power through the chanting of the name of Kārtavīrya, the lord of the Haihayas.
This armor of Kārtavīrya increases merit,
pacifies all sins, and destroys all calamities.
This secret [teaching] brings about all peace, destroys all fears,
bestows victory and wealth upon men, and grants all auspicious prosperity.
Whether one hears it or recites it, one shall obtain all desires;
even when one sees one's own wealth, such as cattle and so forth, being carried off by thieves.
Then, facing the western direction at night, one should recite it seven times;
within seven nights, one obtains lost property, of this there is no doubt.
Having recited it twenty-seven times while facing the eastern direction, a man can ward off even an enemy army resembling the host of gods and asuras.
In a dispute or a terrible quarrel, he who recites this fivefold [mantra] shall achieve victory; for him, there shall never be defeat.
In times of affliction by all diseases, one should recite it three or five times;
such a person will not be harmed by disease, death, vetālas, bhūtas, or pretas.
One should recite [the mantra] twelve times correctly at night for liberation from bondage; within three days, one is released from fetters—of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.77.129)
By this very procedure, in all ritual practices for accomplishment,
the best of mantra-knowers shall achieve even the unachievable within seven days.
That man who recites this while on a journey and travels upon the road shall have no fear of wicked thieves, tigers, and other such adversaries.
Reciting [the mantra] while sprinkling water upon his body with cupped hands,
he is not afflicted by diseases such as those caused by poison or by eruptions.
Kārtavīrya, the son of Kṛtavīrya, was indeed powerful, a hater of the wicked,
possessed of a thousand arms, a slayer of enemies, clad in red garments, and a wielder of the bow.
Red-scented and adorned with red garlands, the King grants the desires of the one who remembers him;
whoever recites these twelve names of Kārtavīrya, [attains his goal].
Prosperities arise for him and people are always under his control,
O Brahmin, who constantly serves the glorious Cakrāvatāra.
One should always perform protection for that [person] by means of the discus of the high-souled Viṣṇu;
O Brahmin, this armor was obtained by me from Dattātreya, the lord of sages.
What has been spoken to you has been heard; retain it, for it bestows all desired benefits.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Armor of Kārtavīrya," in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Lord of Sages, the armor of Kārtavīrya has been narrated to you."
Listen to the victorious armor of the Son of the Wind (Hanuman), which destroys delusion.
By the mere retention of which all calamities are instantly destroyed;
the suffering born of spirits, ghosts, and enemies goes to its destruction—of this there is no doubt.
Once, I went to see Rāma, the best among those who delight others,
as he sat in the Ānandavana grove meditating on the state of his own Self.
There, having paid homage to Rāma, the lord of Ramā, who was being worshipped by the lords of the thirty gods,
he stood before him on the seat assigned to him.
Thereupon, when asked, the illustrious Rāma himself, the lord of kings, respectfully related everything that had occurred, ending with the slaying of Rāvaṇa.
Then, at the conclusion of the discourse, the Blessed One gave the armor of Māruti to me;
I shall declare that to you, for it must not be disclosed anywhere.
O Nārada, this which was narrated by Śrī Rāma, the son of Añjanā’s son, out of his childhood nature, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
May Hanumān protect me from the east; may the son of the Wind protect me from the south;
may the slayer of Akṣa protect me in the west; and may the one who crossed the ocean protect me in the north.
May the best of monkeys, the beloved son of Keśarin, protect me from above;
may Viṣṇubhakta protect me from below, and Pāvani protect my middle.
May the burner of Laṅkā protect [me] incessantly from all calamities;
may the son of the Wind, the minister of Sugrīva, protect my head.
May the Great Hero protect my forehead continuously between the eyebrows;
and may the Lord of Monkeys, who removes all darkness, protect our eyes.
May the servant of Śrī Rāma protect my cheeks and the roots of my ears;
may the son of Añjanā protect the tip of my nose, and may the Lord of Monkeys protect my face.
May the enemy of the Daityas protect my throat; may the conqueror of the enemies of the gods protect my shoulders;
may the one of great splendor protect my arms; and may he whose weapon is his feet protect my hands.
May he whose weapon is his nails protect [me] from the nails; may the Lord of Monkeys protect my belly;
may he who seizes with his seal protect my chest; and may he whose weapon is his arms protect my sides.
May the destroyer of Laṅkā protect my back incessantly;
may the devotee of Śrī Rāma protect my navel, and may the son of the Wind-god protect my hips.
May the one of great wisdom protect the private parts; may the one fond of guests protect the two thighs; and may the destroyer of the palaces of Laṅkā protect the two hips and the two knees.
May the best of monkeys protect my calves; may the one of great strength protect my ankles;
and may he who resembles the sun and who lifted up Mounts Mandara protect my feet.
May the One Rich in Beings protect my limbs; may he always protect my toes.
May the Great Hero protect the parts of my face, and may the Self-possessed One protect my body hairs.
May Kapi, who moves eternally through the three worlds by day and by night—whether standing, walking, sitting, drinking, or eating—protect us. (NarP 1.78.19)
May the glorious one, possessing supramundane qualities and born from the Three-eyed Lord, protect me—
whether heedless or heedful, whether lying down or in the depths of the water.
Whether on land, in the atmosphere, in fire, on a mountain, in the ocean, or in a tree;
in battle, in terrible distress—may he who assumes a form of infinite splendor protect us. (NarP 1.78.21)
May the All-pervading Lord protect me as I lie down from the ḍākinīs, śākinīs, mārīs, kālarātrīs, and marīcikas, and from the piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasīs.
Bearing a divine body, wise, and the terrifier of all beings, may he who is the protector of the foremost of practitioners forever protect me from every side. (NarP 1.78.23)
May he who, having seen his terrifying form, causes even the fearsome to flee;
he who possesses all forms, the omniscient creator and sustainer of the world—may he protect us.
May he who is himself Brahmā, himself Viṣṇu, and the manifest god Maheśvara,
who dwells within the solar orb and bestows prosperity, protect me throughout the three periods of time.
Upon hearing whose sound, the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as gods, humans, animals, and both the stationary and the moving, [were struck with fear].
Those who follow their own deeds become free from fear even when surrounded by fear;
his many meritorious stories are heard in every kalpa.
Thus he descended upon that best of practitioners, who was ever devoted to Rāma;
for whatever is seen in great abundance, beginning with the Creator Brahmā himself—NarP_1,78.28.
Just as that [space] is pervaded by the form of the monkey which is without collyrium, so am I this All-pervasive One; I am my own self, both subtle and vast.
I bow with self-concentration to him who is the *praṇava*, whose form consists of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* Vedas, and who is the threefold sacrifice; to him, to myself, and to all.
I bow to him who is the very nature of the Self, whose essence is the wind, who sustains many infinite Brahmā-eggs, and who is the true form of Brahman.
Homage to that Hanumān; homage to the son of the Wind-god;
homage to the devotee of Śrī Rāma; homage to the great Dark One.
Homage to the heroic monkey, who formed a friendship with Sugrīva,
who consumed the fire of Saṃkāpa, and who crossed the great ocean.
Salutations to the Supreme Self, who destroys the sorrow of Sītā, who bears the seal of Rāma, and who is the cause of the end of Rāvaṇa.
Salutations again and again to the one who brought about the destruction of Meghanāda’s sacrifice;
to the destroyer of the Aśoka grove, the bestower of victory.
To the heroic son of Vāyu, who moves through the belly of the sky,
who severed the head of the forest-guardian, and who destroyed the palaces of Laṅkā.
Salutations to you, who possess the color of blazing gold, who bear a long tail,
who grant victory to the son of Sumitrā, and who are the messenger of Rāma.
Salutations to the slayer of Akṣa, the warder-off of the Brahma-weapon,
and the destroyer of the wounds inflicted by the great spear from Lakṣmaṇa’s body.
Salutations again and again to the slayer of Rākṣasas, the slayer of enemies, and the slayer of spirits;
salutations again and again to the one who provides a palace for the hosts of heroic bears and monkeys.

Salutations to you, the destroyer of the forces of enemy armies; salutations to the destroyer of weapons and missiles; repeated salutations to the destroyer of poison, the destroyer of enemies, and the destroyer of fear.

To the destroyer of the fear of enemies of the earth, who acts solely for the protection of his devotees, and who brings about the neutralization of the mantras of others, even when those mantras are incited by another; // NarP_1,78.41 //
Salutations again and again to the one who causes milk to cross over stones;
salutations to the remover of suffering, who swallows the orb of the rising sun.
Salutations to you who have claws as weapons, to the terrifying one, to the bearer of teeth as weapons,
to the one who moves through the sky, to the corpse-like one, and to the one with a body of diamond.
O Rāma, salutations to you, who abide in every village, who seek the destruction of *bhūtas* and *pretas*, and whose hand holds a mountain as a weapon.
Salutations to you, who are clothed in a loincloth, who are devoted to the service of Rāma,
who are the sun of the southern quarter, and whose very self is the rising moon for the virtuous.
To the one who destroys the pain of misdeeds and removes all afflictions;
to the one who effects the fulfillment of the Lord’s commands, the attainment of goals, victory in battle, and the winning of friends.
To the one who brings victory to his devotees in divine discourses and in battle,
who utters the sound "kilakilāvuva," and who produces a formidable roar.
To the one who causes the suppression of all fires and diseases, the remover of fear,
who is especially satisfied by a diet of forest fruits at all times.
"Salutations to you who have built a bridge of stone across the great ocean"—
thus, O Brahmin, has this auspicious armor of Māruti been recounted.
It must not be given to just anyone; it should be guarded with great effort. Whoever writes this armor-mantra (*kavaca*) with the eight fragrances should then wear it.
Whether worn on the neck or on the right arm, victory attends him at every step;
what need is there for much speaking? If one respectfully accomplishes a hundred thousand recitations, [the result is certain].
This armor, once consecrated by ritual, shall accomplish even that which is otherwise impossible to achieve.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Hanuman’s Words," in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, [I shall relate] another deed of the son of the Wind-god, which destroys all sins.
This was said by Rāma, who dwells in the Forest of Bliss, to his own [wife].
In the great kalpa Sadyojāta, may there always be devotion for me, Śrī Rāmacandra, in Hanumān, who possesses the power of learning. (NarP 1.79.2)
Listen, O young boy, as I speak to you of the life of Kumāra,
which destroys all sins for those who always hear or recite it.
O Brahmin, I always desire union with him who has the form of a monkey,
in secret and in private, within my own excellent Forest of Bliss.
In this place, my friends and companions, freed from all anxiety,
always sport here, both in public and in private.
However, whatever occurred in secret during one of my incarnations,
I shall now reveal that to you with a joyful heart.
O sage, I previously manifested there in the abode of King Daśaratha as one whose nature consists of four forms, among his three wives.
Then, after some years had passed, the eminent brahmin Viśvāmitra arrived and requested my father, the king, for his daughter.
For the sake of warding off yakṣas and rākṣasas, that righteous-souled one sent me along with Lakṣmaṇa to Siddhāśrama, which is as delightful as Amarāvatī.
Having gone there to the hermitage of Ṛbhu, the two night-stalkers Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras, as well as Subāhu and Mārīca, were destroyed; then the sage became pleased.
He gave me the collection of weapons and likewise made me dwell there for a month;
then the wise son of Gādhi, out of respect, recognized the destined purpose.
He led him to Mithilā and there displayed his formidable bow;
[he showed him] Sītā, who resembled the daughter of a god, as the bride-price for it.
Having divided his bow in the assembly,
he then laughed for a long time at the pride-deluded descendant of Bhṛgu on the road as he departed.
After arriving at Ayodhyā, the city of my father, which was then beset by calamity,
the king— whose mind was intent on the character of his subjects— then recognized me.

O Sage, having consulted with his ministers and having himself chosen him out of affection for the position of crown prince, King Daśaratha was addressed by his beloved wife Kaikeyī upon hearing that news.
With his mind corrupted for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods, he declared:
"Let my son named Bharata be consecrated in the position of crown prince."
"Rāma must be sent away to dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest for fourteen years.
Upon hearing this, I prepared myself to go to the forest accompanied by my wife and younger brother.
Although not commanded by the king to go, I departed for Citrakūṭa;

O twice-born ones, just as he had drunk the water, so too did he drink the fire;

and the organs of action, such as speech, in their own respective locations.
Then, one should place the elements beginning with space (ākāśa) at the head, heart, secret place, and feet;
and subsequently, the lotuses of the heart, the sun, and the moon, in their proper order.
And likewise, it is held that [the mantras] are pervaded by twelve, six, eighteen, and eight kalās;
one should place them in the heart with syllables numbering five, eight, ten, two, and four.
Then, in the locations beginning with space (ākāśa), one should [worship] Vāsudeva and the others;
namely, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
And Nārāyaṇa, along with Parameṣṭhin and the others in succession;
[these are] Parameṣṭhin, Puruṣa, Śauca, Viśvanivṛtti, and Sarvaka.

One should install the element of Wrath (Kopa-tattva), preceded by its own seed-syllable, along with Nṛsiṃha, using the colors of white, wind, fire, water, and earth as before, and with the all-pervading [mantra].
Having arranged [the letters] on all limbs as before, this is declared to be the Nyāsa of the Principles (tattva).
All the initial letters beginning with *ma* should be adorned by the moon (*candra*).
The [mantras] beginning with Vāsudeva should be known by the best of practitioners as ending in the vocative case (ṅe).
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka); NarP_1,80.22 //
The knower of mantras [should perform this] with four, six, and two [repetitions], and again with the root mantra;
some teachers here say that this should be done after breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having performed the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), one should then perform the other placements;
having applied the ten principles (daśatattva) and so forth according to the procedure to be described.

The wise and learned practitioner should perform the placement (nyāsa) of that which was previously described as the "Cage of the Embodiments" (mūrtipañjara), pervading all limbs with the Kirīṭa mantra.
Then, having pervaded the mantra in the tārapuṭa form three times upon the two hands,
one should thereafter perform the placement of the five limbs upon the five fingers of both hands.
One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) three times with the root mantra, from the head down to the feet;
having performed the pervasive placement once with the *tāra* [mantra], one should then proceed with the placement of the mantras (*mantra-nyāsa*).
On the head, the forehead, between the eyebrows, and likewise on the two ears, the two eyes, the two nostrils, the mouth, the throat, the heart, and again at the navel; NarP_1,80.28 //

One should place the mantra syllables ending with the heart-mantra (hṛt) sequentially upon the hips, the genitals, the knees, and the feet; thereafter, one should place the *dhruva* (the syllable Om) upon the head.
Furthermore, one should place the five parts of the mantra, ending with the heart-mantra, upon the eyes, the face, the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
Having again assigned [the mantras] beginning with the Sage (muni), one should assign the five limbs as before.
Now I shall declare the great secret, the most excellent among all supreme assignments.
By the mere knowledge of which a man becomes liberated while living,
he shall undoubtedly become a master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
By propitiating whom the practitioner of mantra attains proximity to Kṛṣṇa,
one should place that mantra encased within the utterances beginning with Tārā and the others.
Then one should place the mantras enclosed by the Praṇava at the beginning;
one should place the mantra enclosed by the Gāyatrī in the location of the Mātṛkās.
The best of practitioners should then sequentially perform the placement (nyāsa) of that Gāyatrī encased by the mantra, and the root-mantra encased by the Mātṛkā syllables.
The wise practitioner should sequentially place the Mātṛkā, encircled by the root mantra,
along with the three Ṛks and the letters of the Mātṛkā, each in its respective location as before.
One should perform the sixfold placement (nyāsa); this is declared to be the sixfold nyāsa. By means of this excellent nyāsa, one becomes directly equal to Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing one who is encircled by the nyāsa, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras—even the gods—bow down to him; how much more so the humans on earth?
Then, one should perform the binding of the directions with the mantra of Sudarśana,
while meditating upon the deity within one's own heart as the bestower of all desired objects.
It was graced by auspicious, excellent trees with branches bent low under the weight of clusters of blossoming flowers,
which were entwined by beautiful creepers bearing masses of flower-clusters as if they were smiling.
The practitioner, composed and concentrated, should meditate upon Vṛndāvana, which has cooled the quarters of the sky with the fragrant pollen falling from the blossoming trees.
It was auspicious with swarms of humming bees whose inner hearts were greedy for the abundance of honey trickling from the clusters of newly blossomed lotuses.
It was repeatedly made resonant by flocks of swans, cuckoos, parrots,
and pigeons, and was beautiful with families of peacocks dancing.
With the auspicious, greyish droplets from the gently flowing, restless waves of the Kālindī, and with the pollen from clusters of blossoming lotuses; (NarP_1,80.44)
Or perhaps it was constantly frequented by those who, intent on tossing about the soft garments of the beauties of the cowherd settlement, were themselves ignited by the fires of passion.
At the end of that, one should remember the most beautiful celestial tree;
beneath it, upon a golden altar, is an unsurpassed jeweled pedestal.
Upon this seat of jeweled mosaic, one should visualize a reddish lotus with eight petals; and in its center, one should visualize Mukunda standing there.
He was as lovely as a full-blown blue lotus, adorned with peacock feathers as his crest-ornament;
he wore yellow garments, possessed a moon-like face, and had eyes like lotuses.
His body was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, marked with the Śrīvatsa, and beautifully adorned;
he was worshipped by the lotus-eyes of the women of Vraja and surrounded by herds of cows.
The wise one should meditate upon Him accompanied by a multitude of cowherds, playing the flute;
having thus visualized Him, the learned practitioner should first recite the mantra twenty thousand times.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer oblations with reddish lotuses ten times that number;
thereafter, for the sake of mantra-perfection, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind.
Having offered oblations with reddish lotuses, one becomes the master of all supernatural powers (siddhis);
having conceived the form [of the deity] according to the root mantra upon the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava seat.
Having invoked Him within that [liṅga], one should worship the Enchanter of the Gopīs;
having worshipped the flute at His mouth, as well as the forest garland and the Kaustubha gem.
Having worshipped the Śrīvatsa on the chest, one should then scatter an offering of flowers;
thereafter, [one should offer] white Tulasī smeared with white sandalwood paste.
The wise man should quickly offer red *tulasī* smeared with red sandalwood paste at the pair of right ankles,
along with a pair of horse-earrings.
With two horse-headed Māras, one should likewise place two lotuses in the heart and on the head according to the rule; thereafter, one should offer them upon the crown of the head.
Two *tulasī* leaves, two lotuses, and a pair of horse-ears (*aśvarī*);
thereafter, one should offer all flowers upon all the limbs.
On the right is the one called Vāsudeva, pure and imperishable consciousness;
and on the left is Rukmiṇī, his eternal consort, red in color and characterized by the quality of passion (rajas).
Having thus worshipped Gopāla, one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇārcana);
one should sacrifice to Dāma, Sudāma, Vasudāma, and Kiṅkiṇī.
In the directions beginning with the east, one should place those beginning with *dāmā*, ending in *ṅeṃ namaḥ*, starting with *dhruva* and so forth;
and in the corners of Agni, Nairṛti, Vāyu, and Īśa, one should place those beginning with *hṛdaya*.
Having worshipped the weapons in the directions, one should worship the queens upon the petals:
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and she known as Nāgnajitī.
Then there were Suvindā, Mitravindā, Lakṣmaṇā born of the Ṛkṣas,
and Suśīlā, adorned with shining, beautiful, and variegated garments and ornaments.
Then, one should worship Vasudeva and Devakī, Nandagopa and Yaśodā, Balabhadra and Subhadrikā, on the tips of the petals.
The cowherds and cowherd-maids had their minds and eyes absorbed in Govinda;
the parents were yellow and pale-white, with hands displaying the gesture of knowledge and the gesture of fearlessness.
Furthermore, the two Mothers, adorned with divine garlands, garments, ointments, and ornaments,
were holding a vessel of sacrificial porridge and a full bowl of milk-rice.
Aruṇa and Śyāmala are adorned with necklaces and jeweled earrings;
Bala is as white as a conch or the moon, wielding a mace and a plow.
Hālālola, Nīlavāsas, Halavāna, Eka-kuṇḍala;
Kalā, Śyāmalā, Bhadrā, Subhadrā, and Bhadrabhūṣaṇā.
Adorned with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, clad in yellow garments, and in the full bloom of youth,
they hold in their hands flutes, lutes, golden staffs, conchs, horns, and other instruments.
Outside that, one should worship the Gopas and Gopīs, whose lotus-hands offer various gifts, as well as the Mandāra trees and other wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas).
The Mandāra, as well as the Saṃtānaka, the Pārijātaka,
and thereafter the Kalpadruma, known as the Dhavari-candana.
Having worshipped [the deities] in the center and in the cardinal directions, one should worship Indra and the others on the outside;
having fully honored their weapons as well, one should worship with the Kṛṣṇāṣṭaka.
And [he praised] Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, the joy of Devakī,
Nārāyaṇa, the best of the Yadus, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, and the protector of dharma.
Then one should worship him who removes the burden of the earth oppressed by the Asuras;
with these enclosures, the worship of the seeker of happiness should be performed.
For the sake of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra and for the attainment of all desires, the wise man should practice thus;
by means of worship and other rites, Vaiśravaṇa and Yama became perfected beings.
And I shall describe its worship at the three times of day, which grants the accomplishment of all aims:
in a magnificent garden pavilion made of gold and jewels, beautifully adorned.
Seated upon a jeweled lotus throne beneath a wish-fulfilling tree,
the child resembled the jewel of the gods, with locks of hair glossy as molasses.
His beautiful cheeks were illuminated by swinging golden earrings; his face was graced with a wonderful smile and a well-shaped chin;
he wore lovely, auspicious, and white nails adorned with gold and bound with shining, pure jewel-encrusted golden threads. (NarP 1.80.77)
With his chest-dust thoroughly cleared by the dust from the cows, his well-nourished body shone with ornaments of gold;
and upon the region of his hips, the pair of his beautiful calves was bound with a girdle of tinkling clusters of small bells.
Laughing, with the noble luster of his lotus-like hands and feet possessing the radiance of blooming bandhujīva flowers,
he holds in his right hand milk-rice and in his left hand fresh butter.
He stood in the midst of a multitude of cows, cowherds, and cowherdesses, his feet worshipped by the gods led by Indra;
he was then intent upon slaying the hosts of enemies of the immortals, including Pūtanā and others, who had become a great burden.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the deity as before with a steady mind;
having offered an oblation of curd and molasses, one should recite the mantra one thousand times.
At midday, one should worship him who possesses such distinguished forms,
and who is honored by hosts of sages beginning with Nārada, as well as by the multitudes of gods.
He was situated in the midst of a multitude of gopas, gopīs, and cows; his beautiful body possessed the luster of thick clouds;
he wore a crest-ornament of peacock feathers, had eyes as long as lotus petals, shimmering eyelashes, and a face like the full moon.
He was beautiful, with the splendor of his cheeks enhanced by swinging earrings, possessing a gentle smile and a fine nose;
he wore garments of excellent gold-hued cloth, divine ornaments, and was anointed with fragrant unguents while the clusters of tinkling bells resonated.

One should worship the son of Nanda for the attainment of wealth (Indirā) by meditating upon him as holding a flute to his own mouth with his left hand, bearing a tusk and a staff, dressed in magnificent attire, and likewise in his right hand, being skillful in granting desired boons.
Having meditated thus, the best of Vaiṣṇavas should worship Kṛṣṇa as before, and he should present an offering consisting of cakes, milk-rice, and other foods.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of milk soaked in ghee,
he should present the bali-offering in its respective directions, and thereafter offer water for rinsing the mouth.
And that best of Vaiṣṇavas who worships Kṛṣṇa in this manner at midday should recite the supreme mantra one thousand and eight times.
All the gods pay homage to that man who is beloved by the worlds;
endowed with intelligence, long life, prosperity, and beauty, he prospers through sons and grandsons.
Regarding the third daily worship, there is a distinction of time;
some learned scholars say it may be performed either in the evening or at night. (NarP 1.80.90)
If one performs it at night with the ten-syllable mantra, or in the evening with the eighteen-syllable mantra,
others have declared that one should perform both rites with both mantras.
In the evening, at Dvāravatī, which was adorned with wonderful gardens and embellished by eight thousand palaces, [he arrived].
In that supreme residence, which was surrounded by lakes of blue water filled with lotuses and water-lilies, and crowded with swans and cranes.
In the glorious circle of jewels, possessing the radiance of the rising sun,
Kṛṣṇa— the enchantment of the three worlds— is seated upon a golden lotus throne.
Surrounded by hosts of sages in the determination of the reality of the Self,
he was bestowing upon those sages his own abode, the supreme imperishable.
Dark as a fresh blue lotus, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
he was glossy, adorned with a crown entwined with locks of hair and a forest garland.
With a beautiful and serene countenance, shimmering makara-shaped earrings,
the śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, and the radiant kaustubha gem, he was most enchanting.
With a chest as dark as Kashmiri saffron, wearing yellow silk garments, and adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and a waist-belt; (NarP 1.80.98)
His heavy burden of supporting the entire earth was removed, his mind was gladdened,
and his four arms shone with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantra should worship; this constitutes the first enclosure with the limbs [of the deity].
The second [enclosure] is with the principal consorts, and in the third, one should perform worship.
He placed Nārada, Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niśaṭha, Uddhava, Dāruka,
Viṣvaksena, Śaineya, and the son of Vinatā at the front in the various directions.
The best of Vaiṣṇavas should worship [the deity] with the world-protectors, Vajra, and the others;
having worshipped thus according to the rule, he should offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having gratified [the deity] here with water, thinking it to be milk mixed with sugar-candy,
the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while meditating upon Puruṣottama.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in all forms of worship, either at midday;
having performed the rites from the seat up to the water-offering (arghya), the wise one should offer praise and bow down.
Having withdrawn his capable self from the lotus of his own heart and having placed it [there],
becoming one with that, he should worship the Self once again.
He who thus worships Vāsudeva every day at the hour of sunset shall attain all his desires and, in the end, go to the supreme goal.
If at night one should worship the Son of Nanda, whose mind is overcome by passion,
who is exhausted from the *rāsa* dance, and who stands in the midst of the circle of cowherd girls.
It was cooled by gentle breezes carrying the grey pollen rising from blossoming *kunda*, *kahlāra*, and *mallikā* flowers.

In the courtyard of the banks of the Yamunā— a place that kindles the god of love, where the edges of the horizon are expanded by the rays of the nectar-rayed moon, which is made charming by the songs of intoxicated bees wandering there after finding an opening in the honey dripping from the rows of blossoming white lilies, and where the jasmine flowers are in full bloom— I see Him with a smiling face, repeatedly playing His flute.
With the brilliance of a mass of clouds gathered near the inner waters, with eyes as long as lotuses flickering like fireflies, with beautiful bimba-fruit lips,
with a crown bound with peacock feathers and a shimmering garland of matted locks, and with his two cheeks illuminated by the radiant rays of his glittering jeweled earrings— NarP_1,80.110.

One should meditate upon Mukunda, who is adorned with girdles, anklets, necklaces, bracelets, and shimmering armlets; who stands gracefully between two cowherd girls wearing garlands of wild flowers; whose arms are entwined by the vine-like arms of his beloveds; who is eager for the playful dance of Rāsa; and who is possessed by the God of Love.

With these [women], his body— adorned with magnificent jewels and clearly manifesting the seven musical notes, which are most charming due to their various distinctions of pitch, modulation, and melodic sequences— is made to whirl about.
In the performance of the rāsa dance, imagined by throngs of women with hands joined together,
he— though possessing a body like a mere stone pillar— assumed his own divine form in many ways through this very body.
Having meditated thus, the mantra-practitioner should perform worship; the first enclosure consists of the limbs [of the deity].
One who desires prosperity, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, should worship with the lotuses of the digits preceded by the vowels.
One should worship the sixteen pairs beginning with Keśava and Kīrti,
and immediately thereafter, one should also worship Indra and the others, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Having fixed a peg into the ground that is broad, well-rounded, smooth, and one span high,
and having stepped upon it with both feet while holding onto each other with their hands— this indeed is the circular dance of the *rāsagoṣṭhī*.
Having thus worshipped with milk, sugar, and ghee,
and having offered the sacrificial food (naivedya) in cups numbering as many as the kings, he should proceed.
The practitioner of mantra should constantly offer [oblations] to the pairs of deities in sequence;
having performed the remaining rites as before, he should recite the mantra one thousand times.
Having praised, bowed, and made his petition, he should complete the remainder of the worship.
He who worships Kṛṣṇa in this manner shall become the abode of prosperity.
He shall become the lord of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed various pleasures here in this world, he shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu at the end.
Thus, when the mantra has been mastered through worship and other means, the wise practitioner should accomplish his desired objects;
he should worship it three times a day for twenty-eight repetitions.
Furthermore, one should satisfy the retinues as prescribed for their respective times:
with curd mixed with molasses in the morning, and again with milk at midday.
Then, at the time of evening, that best of Vaiṣṇavas should again offer libations with milk mixed with sugar-candy and fresh butter.
The word *tarpayāmi* (I satisfy) should be joined at the end of the mantras with their respective names in the nominative case;
however, when the names are in the accusative case, one should again complete the remainder of the worship.
Having sprinkled himself with those pure waters, he should enter the water;
then, having dissolved that which was established there, being absorbed in That, he should mutter the mantra.
Now, the substances for rites performed for specific desires and for libations are proclaimed;
one should resort to whichever among those is prescribed according to the stated rules.

Milk-rice, curd-mixed food, clarified butter, rice cooked with jaggery, sesame-rice, milk, various types of curds, plantains, the *mocā* variety of banana, the *ciñcā* fruit, and likewise a woman in her menses; NarP_1,80.127 //
Cakes, sweetmeats, parched grain, flattened rice, and fresh butter—
this is indeed the sixteenfold set of substances described by Padmajā and others.
Having first offered parched rice and then sugar-candy at the end of the parched rice, whoever should thus satisfy [the deity] seventy-four times every morning; NarP_1,80.129.
Having meditated upon the feet of Kṛṣṇa, the minister shall obtain the desired results from the mandala and other rites;
likewise, fresh butter and curds [are obtained] from milk that is warm while still flowing and has been cooked.
One should worship with nine substances— milk, mango, clarified butter, sugar-candy, honey, and molasses— each repeated eleven times.
Thus, that best of Vaiṣṇavas who performs the libation (tarpaṇa) one hundred and eight times shall obtain the fruit previously described.

What need is there for much speaking? This libation, indeed, bestows all desired things when performed with water, by means of the mental perception that it is warm milk mixed with sugar and candied sugar.
While traveling toward the village of Kṛṣṇa, the practitioner obtains wealth,
garments, and food, along with a multitude of attendants.
The mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra as many times as he performs the libation;
by means of that very libation, he shall accomplish all his objectives.
Now I shall describe the optional oblation (kāmyahoma) for the benefit of practitioners:
a mantra-reciter who desires irreproachable prosperity should offer oblations with *śrī* flowers.
One should offer oblations of food with clarified butter for the prosperity of one's food supply;
one should honor the twice-born with wild flowers and kings with *jātī* flowers.
One should bring Vaiśyas under control with black flowers, Śūdras likewise with blue lotuses, all people with salt, and young women with water-lilies.
The cowherd, the lord of the cow-pen, who performs an oblation with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter in the cow-stalls,
quickly effects peace for the cattle.
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, who wears the dress of a student and is adorned with a network of small bells,
the practitioner of mantra should offer libations with auspicious waters, perceiving them as milk.
Being pleased, he bestows upon him wealth, grain, sons, and fame;
[he does so] with fuel-sticks of the Brahma-tree, or with kuśa grass, or with sesame seeds and rice.
The mantra-practitioner should offer ten thousand oblations into the fire with items smeared with the three sweets;
furthermore, he shall bring Brahmins under his control by using wood produced from the royal trees.

With *prasūna* flowers one should indeed subjugate Kṣatriyas, with *kuraṇḍaka* blossoms likewise the Vaiśyas, and with flowers arising from the *pāṭala* tree, the wise man should subjugate those of the lowest caste.

Having offered ten thousand oblations of white lotuses, red lotuses, campaka flowers, and *pāṭala* flowers, each anointed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one shall bring those excellent women under one's control.

By holding [the powder] made from the flowers of the *hayāri* for eight days, and then at midnight applying it with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), a wise man shall bring excellent women under his control.
For one who offers thirty thousand oblations every night for a month with white mustard seeds soaked in the three sweets, even the Lord of the Gods shall become submissive.
Having brought the garments of a cowherd woman and ascended a *nīpa* tree,
the wise man should meditate on Kṛṣṇa and recite [the mantra] one thousand times at night until the moon has risen.
By force, the practitioner may even quickly attract Urvaśī herself;
what need is there for much speaking here? This mantra brings everything under control.
Now I shall declare the supreme secret that bestows liberation upon men:
one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, the son of Devakī, within the lotus of one's own heart.

I salute the Enemy of Mura, who is as fair as the glorious moon of the Kunda flower, whose eyes are like lotuses, who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his lotus-like hands, and who shines with a beautiful garland of fresh lotuses;

he is the one to be known by the lords of sages, delightful with divine ornaments shining upon his navel, radiant with divine unguents on his limbs, the remover of all fears, and clad in yellow garments.

Having thus meditated upon the Primordial Man seated upon the lotus-throne of his own radiant heart, resembling a wondrous mass of gold with the luster of a dense cloud, one should recite the mantra ten million times—placing one of the two mantras interspersed between two *tārās*.
Then, one should offer a thousand oblations of wood from milky trees as prescribed, mixed with honey, ghee, and sugar, or else with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Thus, meditating daily upon Kṛṣṇa, who is to be propitiated by Lokeśvara, within the lotus of his own heart, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra three thousand times.

Having worshipped according to the rite prescribed for the evening, and having performed the fire-oblation again according to the previously stated rule, the practitioner, with his mind fixed upon that [deity], should proceed.
Thus, the wise person who constantly worships the Delight of the Cowherds crosses the ocean of existence and attains the supreme state.

In the center, within the outer petals of the fire-city enclosure, one should draw Kāmadeva joined with the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the pericarp; in the filaments, the six syllables of the Enemy located in the gaps;

the syllables of the ten-verse mantra preceded by *Śakti* and *Śrī* in the petals; and in the middle of the petals, the syllables of the excellent ten-syllable mantra ending in *daśānta*, each individually placed upon a lotus.

This "cowherd's device" (gopālayantra), which bestows all desired objects, has been described: it is drawn with golden needles upon a cloth smeared with yellow pigment by the God of Love, who is adorned with ornaments of earth; and it is fashioned into a ball within a vessel made of gold.

This [mantra], sprinkled with *saṃyāta* and consecrated by the Great Ones, should be held constantly by those desiring protection, fame, sons, land, wealth, grain, prosperity, and good fortune; it is uniquely skilled in subjugating the three worlds and possesses priceless power.
"Smara, trivikramākrānta, cākrīṣṭyāya, hṛt"—
this is proclaimed as the six-syllabled mantra (manu) that bestows all accomplishments.
The syllable *kroḍa* (krauṃ), enriched by the moon, fire, and peace (*śānti*), is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of Māyā;
the mantra enriched by Govinda, fire, and the moon is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śrī.
From these two [syllables], there may be eighteen kalpas; the mantra consists of twenty syllables.
[It should be recited] at a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, a yantra, a maṇḍala, or before an image.
Worship of Hari should be performed constantly, and not merely upon the bare ground;
he who thus worships Kṛṣṇa attains the supreme goal.
For the twenty-syllable mantra, Brahmā is said to be the sage, Gāyatrī the meter,
Kṛṣṇa the deity, Kāma the seed-syllable, and the dual Ṭha (Ṭha-Ṭha) the power, according to the wise.
The assignment of the limbs (aṅgas) is performed with the syllables six, three, four, four, and two;
having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra, one should then enclose [the syllables] with that mantra.
Being well-composed, one should place the letters of the *mātṛkā* in their respective locations;
having performed the placement of the ten principles (*tattva*), one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*) for the sake of attaining the state of the deity:
on the head, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the two eyes, and likewise the two ears.
In the nose, the forehead, the chin, the throat, the base of the arms, the heart, the abdomen, the region of the navel, the penis, and the root-lotus; // NarP_1,80.166 //
One should sequentially place the mantras ending with the heart-mantra on the hips, knees, shanks, ankles, and feet; this is declared to be the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (the rite of emanation).
In the heart, the belly, the navel, the genitals, the root-lotus,
as well as in the hips, the knees, the shanks, the ankles, and the feet.

One should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the crown of the head, the cheeks, the space between the eyebrows, the two eyes, the ears, the nose, the mouth, the chin, the throat, and the roots of the arms.
Having recited those syllables of the mantra, this is declared to be the placement for stability (sthitinyāsa):
on the two feet, the two ankles, the two calves, and likewise on the two knees.
On the hips, at the base, on the banner, at the navel, in the belly, and again in the heart;
at the base of the arms, in the region of the throat, on the chin, in the face, and on the two nostrils.

One should place the syllables of the mantra on the ears, the eyes, the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, and likewise on the crown of the head; this is declared to be the one called "Withdrawal" (saṃhāra).
Then, having again performed the rites of emanation, maintenance, and re-absorption, that best of Vaiṣṇavas should thereafter install the one named Mūrtipañjara, as before.
Having again performed the six-limbed yoga, one should then meditate upon Kṛṣṇa in the lotus of the heart;
[he is situated] in Dvāravatī amidst supreme palaces as radiant as a thousand suns.
In a jeweled pavilion surrounded by many wish-fulfilling trees,
its pillars, doors, arches, and walls were fashioned from blazing gems.
In the center, there was a variegated canopy of full-blown flowers with hanging pearls, and a ground of rubies shining with clusters of jewels.
Beneath a tree that was auspicious and enriched by streams of jewels flowing incessantly,
the quarters of the sky were illuminated by rows of jewel-lamps.
Acyuta, resembling molten gold, should be meditated upon as seated upon a lotus throne supported by jewels that shine like the rising sun.
Possessing a splendor equal to ten million rising moons, suns, and lightning bolts,
he was handsome in every limb, gentle, and adorned with all ornaments.
Clad in yellow garments, his hands adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
he touched a pitcher from which a stream of jewels surged forth as if struck by an invisible force.
With the tip of his left lotus-foot, which steals the luster of a fresh sprout,
he [placed] Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā upon his head with a stream of a multitude of jewels.
Standing on the right and left, Nāgnajitī and Sunandā sprinkle them with water from jars held in their own hands,
while holding two jars for those two [princes].
And from those two, who were stationed on the right and left [of the Lord], Mitravinda and Sulakṣmaṇa took up two jars filled with jewels from the Jewel River and presented them to the two of them.
Jāmbavatī and Suśīlā, bestowing [their grace], are on the right and left;
outside, there are sixteen thousand beloved ones surrounding him on all sides.
They should be meditated upon as radiant with pitchers from which flow streams of gold and jewels;
and outside of them are the eight treasures, filling the earth with wealth.

Outside of that, one should meditate upon all the Vṛṣṇis as before, along with Svara and the others; having thus meditated, one should recite [the mantra] five hundred thousand times, and its tenth part [as the fire-oblation].
Having offered oblations with reddish lotuses upon the pedestal previously described, one should worship there;
having smeared it with fragrant mud, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
And upon the pericarp, one should draw a hexagon containing the target (sādhya) and the god of love (manmatha);
with the remaining seventeen syllables, one should encircle the vowels.
One should first protect [the deity] in the directions of the wind (northwest) and the corner (southeast), bestowing prosperity; in the remaining [directions], one should bestow wisdom;
and in the six joints and the six petals of the pericarp, one should do so thirty times each.
One should write the Gāyatrī of Smara and the Mālā-mantra upon the eight petals;
having written the six syllables [of the seed-mantra] outside of that, one should encircle it with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
And one should draw the orb of the earth on the outside, as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
the earthly enclosure should be square and adorned with eight vajras.
Having inscribed this yantra on plates of gold or other metals as before, whoever indeed wears it after it has been consecrated is honored even by the gods.
The Gāyatrī mantra for Vāmadeva and Puṣpabāṇa is as follows:
"vidmahe dhīmahī" joined with "tanno anaṅgaḥ pracodayāt," ending with the vocative case (ṅe). NarP_1,80.193 //

The *hṛdaya* mantra for Kāmadeva, ending in *ṅe*, which is "Obeisance to Kāmadeva," is pleasing to all people; it is to be recited at the beginning of the *japa* of the Gopāla mantras. (NarP 1.80.194)
Having thus spoken the words of delusion in the presence of all people, and having uttered "Jvala jvala prajvala" before all the people; ||| NarP_1,80.195 |||
One should say "my heart" (hṛdayam mama), followed by "vaśaṅkuru" twice and "śiraḥ";
thus the Madana mantra is declared to consist of forty-eight syllables.
At the beginning of the recitation (*japa*) and other rites, [one should perform] the subjugation of the three worlds starting with the seed-syllable of Smara;
having worshipped the seat as before and having conceived the form (*mūrti*) by means of the root-mantra.

There, having invoked Acyuta with devotion and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should worship him through the sequence beginning with the seat and ending with the ornaments; furthermore, one should worship according to the order of nyāsa.
[He beheld] the creation, the maintenance, the six limbs, the crown, the two earrings,
the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the garland, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers using the root mantra, the best of Vaiṣṇavas should worship the six limbs in the six corners and in the petals of the directions in due order.

Then, in the corners, the best of practitioners should worship Vāsudeva and the others, followed by Śānti and the rest; furthermore, he should worship the eight queens situated at the tips of the petals.
Then, one should worship sixteen thousand beloved ones all at once:
Indranīla, Mukunda, Karāla, Ānanda, and Kacchapa.
Then one should worship Śaṅkha and Padma, and subsequently the eight treasures (nidhis) starting with Padma in their proper order;
outside of that, one should also worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the [deities] beginning with Vajra.
Having thus reverently worshipped Kṛṣṇa, who is surrounded by seven enclosures,
one should gratify him with milk-rice mixed with curds, sugar-candy, and ghee.
Then, having offered divine services, and having praised and bowed to Keśava,
one should dissolve him into one's own heart along with his retinue of attendants.
Having projected the self and worshipped it thoroughly, the wise one should dwell as one with that;
the jewel-consecration, meditation, and worship are established within the twenty-syllable [mantra].
Thus, he who devotes himself to the mantra shall become the abode of prosperity—
he who recites this mantra through the practices of japa, homa, arcana, and dhyāna.
His house was filled incessantly with jewels, precious metals, and grain;
the earth, abounding in all kinds of crops, remained in his hand.
Endowed with sons and friends, he attains the supreme goal at the end,
having worshipped Govinda in the fire with white flowers and fine rice grains.
Having offered ten thousand oblations with clarified butter, one should apply the ashes to his head;
for him there shall be an abundance of food and other riches, and all women shall be devoted to him.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of red lotuses smeared with the three sweets;
by this, his sovereign power will certainly become like Indra’s, such that even the prosperity of others seems as insignificant as a blade of grass.
He who offers one thousand and eight oblations daily with white flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) shall,
within a month, become the domestic priest of a king.
One should accomplish these and other applications with this mantra;
now I shall declare the ten-syllable king of mantras, which bestows all accomplishments.
Smṛti, Sadyānvitā, Sākṣi, Lohita, Janavallabhā, Pavana, and Agnipriyā—this ten-syllable mantra has been proclaimed. (NarP 1.80.214)
The sage of this [mantra] is Nārada, its metre is Virāṭ, and Kṛṣṇa is its deity;
