Desire is said by the wise to be its seed-syllable, and the wife of Fire (Svāhā) is its power.
Ācakra, Vicakra, and immediately after that Sucakra;
then the wheel that protects the three worlds, and the wheel that is the destroyer of the asuras.
With these wheels ending in the two *ṅeṭha*s, one performs the five-limbed ritual (*pañcāṅgaka*) of the mantra;
then, having pervaded the two hands three times with the mantra enclosed by the *tāra* (Oṃ), NarP_1,80.217.
One should place the syllables of the mantra, beginning with *saṃ* and ending with *hṛt*, interspersed with the *praṇava* (oṃ),
upon the joints of the fingers from the right thumb to the left thumb.
This has been declared as the ritual placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa); now the ritual placement of maintenance (sthitinyāsa) is described.
For the sake of maintenance, the wise one should perform the placement starting from the left little finger up to the [right] little finger.
One should place the right thumb at the end of the left thumb;
likewise, this is the *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) mudrā, which is proclaimed to be the remover of the multitude of faults.
The bestower of knowledge at the end of creation belongs to those of pure mind who follow the stages of life (varṇa);
likewise, the end of their stay belongs to householders, occurring in the form of rites for specific desires and so forth.
At the end of the dissolution of all the lords of sages and those who are entirely dispassionate,
one should again place the phonemes upon the fingers of the mind according to the sequence of the cosmic maintenance.
Furthermore, one should place the five limbs on the two hands using the previously mentioned wheels;
then, one should [place] the letters of the Mātṛkā, accompanied by the bindu and encircled by the root mantra.
The wise practitioner, bowing down, should place [the mantra] in the locations for the Mātṛkā-nyāsa;
thereafter, he should place the root mantra, encapsulated by the Tāra-mantra, as the pervasive [vyāpaka].

One should place the ten principles (tattvas) according to the distinction between withdrawal and emanation; these, ending with "namaḥ," are to be assigned to the self along with the syllables and words of the root mantra.
And the principles ending with the ego, as well as those beginning with earth in their respective order:
earth, water, fire, air, and space. (NarP 1.80.226)
One should properly assign the ego (ahaṃkāra), the great principle (mahattattva), primordial nature (prakṛti),
and the supreme person (puruṣa) to the head, the two eyes, the two ears, and the two nostrils.
One should worship the letters of the mantra, ending with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), interspersed with the *praṇava* (OM) in the face, the heart, the navel, the genitals, the knees, and the feet.
This has been declared as the nyāsa of emanation; now hear, O twice-born one, the nyāsa of maintenance:
[it is performed] in the heart, the navel, the penis, the knees, the feet, and again in the head.
One should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth;
then on the feet, knees, the region of the genitals, the navel, the heart, the face, and the nostrils.
This placement, called withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), is declared for the ears, the eyes, and the head;
it is the end of creation for those in the stages of life (*varṇin*), and the end of maintenance for householders (*gṛhamedhin*).
For the ascetic endowed with dispassion, it is proclaimed to end with the stage of withdrawal;
for those in the [other] stages of life, it is fourfold, and for householders, it is fivefold.
And for ascetics, this auspicious threefold placement (nyāsa) has been declared in due order;
some wise ones know it to extend up to the stage of withdrawal (saṃhāra) even for a householder who is dispassionate.
Then, for the attainment of one's desired goal, one should perform the *vibhūtipañjara* placement (*nyāsa*),
which consists of ten repetitions of the mantra and brings about the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
In the foundation, the banner, the navel, the heart, the throat, the mouth, and the head;
and in the thighs, the neck, the navel, the belly, and likewise the heart.
On the two breasts, on the two sides, on the hips, on the head, and likewise on the face;
on the two eyes, on the two ears, on the two nostrils, and on the two cheeks.
In this manner, [one should assign them] to the joints of the right arm and thigh, to the fingertips,
and then to the head and its preceding directions, as well as to one's own digits.
In the two arms, the two thighs, the head, the eyes, the mouth, the throat, the heart, and the abdomen;
likewise in the *mūlādhāra*, the region of the genitals, the two knees, and the two feet.
One should place [the syllables] on the ears, cheeks, shoulders, breasts, sides, and genitals;
and one should place them in sequence on the thighs, knees, shanks, and feet.
This placement known as the "Cage of Sovereign Powers" bestows the accomplishment of all aims;
by means of this supreme placement, one becomes the very embodiment of Kṛṣṇa.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) known as the "Cage of the Form" (mūrtipañjara), as previously described;
thereafter, one should sequentially perform the two excellent placements of the ten limbs and the five limbs.

The best of Vaiṣṇavas should indeed perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the heart, the head, the crest-lock, all the limbs, the cardinal directions, the two sides, the hips, the back, and likewise the crown of the head.
Furthermore, being composed in mind, one should again perform the placement of the five limbs with the wheels as before;
the other collection of placements mentioned in the eighteen-syllable [mantra] should also be performed.
Then, the wise one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the Kirīṭa mantra;
the best of practitioners should also display the mudrās of the flute, the bilva fruit, and so forth.
Then, one should perform the binding of the directions with the mantra of Sudarśana;
provided that the fingers of the hand are straight and without the thumbs.
This is declared to be the heart-mudrā; the head-mudrā is likewise formed. The fist with the thumbs pointing downward is said to be the crest-mudrā (śikhā-mudrā).
This is declared to be the armor-mudrā (varma-mudrā) when the fingers of both hands are extended.

Holding both arms in the *nārāca-muṣṭi* (arrow-fist) gesture, with the sound produced by the thumb and forefinger, and with the eyes, the forefinger, and the middle finger directed outward on all sides—this is declared the *astra-mudrā*. 1,80.247.
The thumb of the left hand is placed upon the lip;
its little finger is joined with the right thumb, while that [right] little finger is extended.
The index, middle, and ring fingers are slightly contracted and moved;
this is declared to be the *veṇu-mudrā*, well-guarded and dear to Hari.
Because they are already established there, the *mālā*, *śrīvatsa*, and *kaustubha* [mudrās] are not mentioned.

Having joined the left thumb with the thumb of the other hand, and having pressed its tip with the fingers of the right hand as well as those of the left hand, and having bound it firmly, one should place the seed-syllable of Kāma (*kāma-bīja*) within the lotus of one's own heart; having uttered this, it is the *vilva-mudrā*, which bestows all happiness and must be kept secret by the lords of sages.
Whatever evil has been accumulated by means of body, mind, or speech—
all that shall go to destruction through the mere knowledge of the mudrā.
Meditation, recitation, and worship at the three times of the day for the mantra previously mentioned must be performed;
the same procedure prescribed for all applies to both the ten-syllable and eighteen-syllable mantras.
When the mantra has been thus mastered, the practitioner of mantras may perform the ritual applications,
[visualizing] the Lord with his upraised arm and powerful forearm holding Mount Govardhana.
Meditating on Kṛṣṇa, whose face is placed upon a flute with its notes clearly manifested by the fingers of another’s hand, the wise man should recite the mantra while walking without an umbrella.
No fear arises for him even from rain, wind, or thunderbolts; by remembering that Indra of the sky, he would dispel even a multitude of futile masses of lightning.
If ten thousand salt-particles are cast into the waters of the Yamunā while the Sun is sporting there, bathing, or performing other such acts, there will undoubtedly be a drought.
Being sprinkled by beloved women with showers of fine water droplets,
one should meditate for ten thousand [repetitions] and then offer oblations of water, either as water-sprinklings or as water-libations.
Even out of season, there will be heavy rain; of this there is no doubt—for one who is constantly afflicted by delusions of "I" and "mine," and by boils, fevers, and the like.
Remembering this very [mantra] while reciting it over the head, peace shall arise in an instant;
or else, [one should meditate on the deity] mounted upon Garuḍa, accompanied by Pradyumna and Bala.
Having meditated upon Acyuta, who is praised by the fever-demons crushed by his own fever, one should recite the mantra at the crown of the head; thus the sufferer of fever shall be freed from fever.
Having meditated thus and worshipped the fire, one should offer ten thousand oblations of pieces of *amṛtā* (guḍūcī) four finger-breadths long, as prescribed, for the pacification of fever.
Having meditated upon Hari, who removes the suffering of Bhīṣma when he was pierced by arrows,
one should recite [the mantra] while touching the afflicted person with both hands for the pacification of fever.
Meditating on [Viṣṇu] as he gives his son to Sāṃdīpani, one should offer ten thousand oblations with pieces of *amṛta* fruit as prescribed, for the sake of averting untimely death.
One should meditate upon Him as bestowing a son upon the twice-born man whose sons had died, along with Arjuna,
and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for the sake of the increase of sons, grandsons, and other progeny.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of *putrajīva* fruits soaked in sweet juices into a fire kindled with their wood, one shall obtain long-lived sons.
Having worshipped a jar filled with milk, the sap of the *kṣīradru* tree, and other substances at night,
one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times in the morning and sprinkle a woman for six days.
When this is done, even a barren woman shall obtain long-lived sons.
In the morning, one who has restrained speech should take water in a hollow made of *aśvattha* leaves.
One desiring a son should drink [this] for a month after reciting it one hundred and eight times;
even a barren woman obtains a son endowed with all auspicious marks.
Having conquered the *kṛtyā* sent by the King of Kāśī as well as his enemies,
he meditated upon Hari, who was burning the city with his splendor.

If the practitioner, for seventeen days, performs the rite with mustard seeds smeared with excellent oil, the enraged Kṛtyā will certainly destroy the one who commissioned her against him. (NarP 1.80.270)
He was staying in a beautiful, divine hermitage filled with Badarī trees,
touching the body of Ghaṇṭākarṇa with his two lotus-like hands.
Having meditated thus, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets;
even one burdened with great sins becomes purified at that very moment.
Remembering Hari as he causes Rukmi and Bala— who were addicted to gambling— to feel hatred,
one should offer pellets made of cow dung into the fire for the purpose of creating enmity between those two.
By reciting this daily for seven days, one shall cause thousands of enemies to hate one another;
[one shall see] the raining [enemy] mounted upon Garuḍa, with arrows whose tips are blazing fire.
Having meditated upon Acyuta as he pursues a fleeing host of enemies,
one should recite the mantra seven thousand times with undistracted mind.
The eradication of enemies occurs indeed within seven days,
while meditating upon [the deity] as one who has lifted up a monkey carrying a wood-apple fruit.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times; it causes the enemy to vanish at that very moment, while meditating upon oneself as Kaṃsadhvaṃsin (the Slayer of Kaṃsa) cast down from his bed.
While Kaṃsa was dragging the lifeless [Naraka] toward himself,
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times at night using sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the tree belonging to the birth-constellation of the enemy.
By performing oblations in this manner, even a fierce rival shall go to his destruction;
or else, one should offer oblations with wood from the akṣa tree smeared with neem oil.
Reciting ten thousand times at night, one will certainly slay one's enemies before long,
using the hands of a corpse at night, with the three pungent spices (vyoṣa) and cotton seeds offered during the night on a leaf of the *niśā* plant.
For the pacification of an enemy, one should offer oblations in a cremation ground with seeds anointed with castor oil;
however, the rite of killing is not recommended, though if one were to perform it, one should offer ten thousand oblations.
Or, with a peaceful mind, one should offer oblations of milk-rice for the sake of pacification;
meditating upon Kṛṣṇa as he carried away the Pārijāta tree, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
"Everywhere there is victory for him, never defeat;
one should recite [the mantra] while meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, who holds the mudrā of exposition and is seated in his chariot. (NarP 1.80.283)

A noble-minded person, for the increase of dharma, should offer one hundred thousand oblations with *pāvāśa* flowers smeared with honey to Pārtha, who was expounding the meaning of the Gītā for the sake of the growth of righteousness, in order to attain knowledge.
For the protection of kingdoms, cities, villages, dwellings, and even the body,
[he who] assumes all forms possesses a radiance equal to ten million rising suns.
Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is that of Agni and Soma, possesses the luster of molten gold;
his face, feet, and lotus-like arms are illuminated by the sun and fire, and he is adorned with divine ornaments.
Having meditated upon [the deity] who wields various weapons and occupies the entire expanse of space, one should,
being composed, recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the sake of protection.
He who worships Hari at the beginning of the day with wild flowers of red hue, and recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times according to the procedure prescribed for midday; NarP_1,80.288 //
By reciting the mantra one thousand times over a maṇḍala, the practitioner may bring under his control eloquent brahmins;
by visualizing himself wearing the dress of a cowherd, he may likewise subjugate kṣatriyas with jasmine flowers.
Meditating on Kṛṣṇa, who is intent on play, with red *aśvārī* flowers, one shall indeed subjugate those of the Vaiśya caste;
by recollecting him with blue lotuses, one subjugates Śūdras.
Having offered oblations every day for seven days with white flowers, clarified butter, and rice grains, while engaged in song and dance, one should apply the ashes to the forehead and the head.
By wearing these, one shall surely subdue a beloved woman, and she likewise her husband;
namely, betel, flowers, clothing, collyrium, and sandalwood paste.
If one recites this mantra a thousand times and gives it to a man,
that man will soon come under one's control, along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
Meditating on Hari, who dwells in the Vṛndāvana forest together with the cowherd maidens,
one shall bring the world under control by offering oblations of Apāmārga wood.
Having received initiation from a true guru, that best of Vaiṣṇavas who worships Kṛṣṇa according to this rite shall become a master of the eight supernatural powers.
By the mere sight of him, disputants are rendered lusterless;
Sarasvatī shall dwell in the mouth of the speaker and also in the home of the members of the assembly.
Having enjoyed various kinds of pleasures, one shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu at the end.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mantras of Kṛṣṇa," in the third quarter of the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Śrī Sanatkumāra said:
O Lord of Sages, I shall now describe the various divisions of the mantras of Kṛṣṇa.
By propitiating whom, men accomplish their own desired goals.
Śakti-Śrī-Māra-pūrva, Śrī-Śakti-Smara-pūrvaka, and Māra-Śakti-Ramā-pūrva: these are the three ten-syllable mantras.
The sage is Nārada, the meter is Gāyatrī,
and the deity is Kṛṣṇa, known here by the name Govinda, who bestows all desires upon men.
One should assign the limbs of all three [deities] with the *cakras* as before;
then, one should indeed perform the pervasive assignment (*vyāpaka*) with the *kirīṭa-mantra*.
One should perform the binding of the directions with the mantra of Sudarśana;
one should perform the initial meditation, worship, and so forth, as described in the twenty-syllable [mantra].
In the second [chapter], however, one should perform the meditation, worship, and other rites as described in the Daśārṇa;
in the third, the wise man, with a concentrated mind, should meditate upon Hari.
Holding a conch, a discus, a bow, arrows, a noose, and a goad, he is ruddy in hue;
with two arms he holds a flute to his lips, he who is the sun-like Kṛṣṇa.
Having meditated thus, the wise one should recite the mantras five hundred thousand times for each separately;
he should then perform a fire sacrifice with milk-rice mixed with ghee, using one-tenth of that number as the oblation.
When the mantra has been thus accomplished, the practitioner of mantra should perform rites for specific desires as before.
For one desiring prosperity, power, and love, [the mantra] is "To Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda, O beautiful one of fire."
The night, the ocean, the Brahman, the Gāyatrī, and Kṛṣṇa are its seers and so forth;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllables consisting of five, four, four, and two syllables.

Recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, performed twenty times with the utterance of the syllables—what need is there for much talk? This mantra bestows the fruit of all desired objects.
Born from Śrī, Śakti, Smara, and Pūrvaja, he is the one near Śakti and Ramā;
that very ten-syllable mantra is said to be at the beginning, joined with Śakti and Ramā.
One should fashion the two mantras, consisting of sixteen and fifteen syllables respectively, as the limbs by means of the wheels;
[the deity] embraces his own limbs with his two hands, which grant boons and fearlessness, O Beloved.
Having thus meditated on [the deity] whose hands hold a lotus and a blue lotus, who is embraced by those two [consorts], and who is radiant with a discus and a sword,
one should recite the mantra ten lakhs of times, and one-tenth of that for the subsidiary rites.
Having offered oblations with clarified butter, the two leaders of the mantras will then become perfected,
bestowing all desires upon men and granting all prosperity and good fortune.
This mantra of eighteen syllables ending with "Kāma" bestows sons and wealth;
Nārada is its sage, Gāyatrī its meter, and the deity of the mantra is [Viṣṇu].
Kṛṣṇa is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and the beloved of Fire (Ra) is considered the power (śakti).
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable enriched by the six heroic powers (ṣaḍvīrya).
Holding in his right hand milk-rice and in his left fresh butter,
clad in divine garments, may the Son of the Cowherd protect us.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra thirty-two hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations into the fire ten parts of milk mixed with white sugar.
On the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal, one should worship according to the eighteen-syllable mantra;
having worshipped Kṛṣṇa seated upon the lotus, one should offer libations into His lotus-mouth.
One desiring a son should likewise offer libations with milk, ripe plantains, curd, and *haiyaṅgava* butter; in this way, within a year, he obtains a son.
Whatever one desires, all that is accomplished simply through this propitiation (*tarpaṇa*). [The mantra is:
*vāk-kāma-ṅe-yutaṃ kṛṣṇa-padaṃ māyā tataḥ paga-raṃ*. (NarP 1.81.22)

One should utter "Govindāya," followed by "Ramā" and then "Daśārṇam"; these two [syllables] are joined with the vowel of Manu (U) and endowed with the Visarga (Ḥ), and they follow the syllable of Bhṛgu (Bha).
The twenty-two-syllable mantra bestows the state of lordship over speech;
Nārada is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī its meter (chandas), and furthermore, [it is] the deity.
Gopāla is proclaimed as the bestower of knowledge and Kāma is the seed-syllable;
Vāgbhava is the power (śakti), and its application is for the attainment of knowledge. (NarP 1.81.25)
In her upper left hand she holds an excellent book of knowledge,
and in her upper right hand a crystal rosary composed of the Mātṛkās.
He is composed of the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahman), holding a flute in his two lower hands;
he is dark-complexioned with a delicate luster, clothed in the song of the Gāyatrī.

Having thus meditated upon the Lord of the World, who is adorned with peacock feathers, who is omniscient, who is served by the foremost of sages, and who possesses the playful grace of a woman's intoxication; NarP_1,81.28.

The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; having performed the fire-oblation with *kiṃśuka* flowers ten times that amount, he should worship according to the procedure for the twenty-syllable mantra.
Thus, he who worships the mantra shall become the Lord of Speech;
even scriptures not previously seen will flow for him like the waves of the Ganges.
One should utter "Tāraḥ," followed by "Kṛṣṇayugam," and then "Mahākṛṣṇa.
At the end of the words "Sarvajña" and "Tvampraśaṃsa," one should say "Sīda me" and "Agniśca Māram."
"O Lord of Knowledge, quickly bestow this knowledge upon me;
therefore, here is the mantra that grants the Great Knowledge, consisting of thirty-three syllables. (NarP 1.81.32)
Nārada is its sage, the Anuṣṭubh is its meter, and Kṛṣṇa is its deity;
having performed the five-limbed ritual with all the verses, one should then meditate upon Hari.
In a celestial garden, within a pavilion made of jewels resembling the sun, upon a yogic seat in the center, sits Mukunda at the foot of the divine tree composed of all the Vedāntas;

he is surrounded by the Vedas in the form of wish-fulfilling trees, by the four systems of logic which support him like hundreds of mountain peaks, and by Nyāya, Tarka, Purāṇas, Smṛtis, and similar attendants such as the fly-whisks.

May the beloved of the cowherd girls, possessing a body as charming as the god of love, adorned with divine ornaments and fragrant unguents, grant us prosperity—He who, bearing upon the tips of His hands the flute, the flower-arrows, the sugarcane bow, the *anakṣa* dice, the *spṛk*, and the full water-jars;

He who, with His left hand, performs an exposition of the *Śabdabrahman* arising from the flute—the source of all sounds—upon the Mother of the Universe, while manifesting clearly radiant syllables. May He, glowing with a ruddy luster, bestow glory upon us.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with milk-rice (pāyasa) ten times that amount;
the knower of mantras should perform the worship of this [deity] as for the eighteen-syllable [mantra].

One should utter "Tāro namo bhagavate" (Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One), then say "Nandaputrāya" (to the son of Nanda), and immediately thereafter give "Ānandavapuṣe" (to the one whose form is bliss) along with the syllable Ṛ. 81.37.
This twenty-eight-syllable mantra bestows all desired objects;
it contains the word "Nandaputra" ending in the dative case (ṅe), as well as the word "Śyāmalāṅga. (NarP 1.81.38)
Likewise, [the words] "bālavapuḥ kṛṣṇam govindam" again;
from this, the mantra of Daśārṇa consists of thirty-two syllables.
For these two [verses], the seer is the sage Nārada; the meters are Gāyatrī and Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is the Son of Nanda; and the application is for the attainment of everything.
The five limbs [of the image] should be worshipped with the wheels, the limbs, the guardians of the directions, and their weapons;
in the right hand a jeweled goblet, and in the left a golden eye.
One should meditate upon the Lord, embraced by his two goddesses and holding them in his hands;
one should perform a hundred thousand recitations and offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) amounting to one-tenth of that number.
With these two perfected mantras, the practitioner may accomplish whatever he desires.
[The mantra begins with] the Praṇava, Kamalā, Māyā, and then "namo bhagavate. (NarP 1.81.43)
After that, the word *nandaputrāya bālāntavapuṣe* [is added];
this mantra of nineteen syllables is declared by the Sage to be Brahmā.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Kṛṣṇa himself in the form of a child;
this mantra is practiced by the wise for the sake of attaining all perfections.
The mantra consisting of sixteen syllables is proclaimed as beginning with "Tārā" (Oṃ), followed by "Bhagavān Aṅgaja," and ending with "Rukmiṇīvallabhāya Svāhā. (NarP 1.81.46)

Nārada is the sage of this [hymn], the Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and the deity is Manu. One should perform the five ancillary rites (pañcāṅga) using the numbers sixteen, two, four, six, and five; thereafter, one should meditate upon the Lord of the Gods.

May Hari protect us for a long time—He who, with His own left arm, embraces His most beloved, whose complexion is like the *tāpiccha* tree, who possesses a golden luster, and whose arms are uplifted like a garland of lotuses; while she herself embraces Him with her other hand holding a golden staff, He, clothed in pure yellow garments and adorned with various ornaments, fulfills the longing of His own heart.
Having meditated thus, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, with red lotuses constituting the ten-part offering.
One should offer oblations into the fire upon the previously mentioned pedestal with offerings smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), and worship Hari along with His limbs,
Nārada and the other principal attendants, the world-protectors (lokeśas), and their weapons.
Thus perfected, the Mantra bestows all desires upon the practitioner;
even the lotus-foot of Līlādaṇḍa becomes a station for the arms of those devoted to him.
Or at the end of *daṇḍa* [the syllables] are *dha-ra-va-hni*, followed by *adhiśāḍhya*, then *lohita*;
after that, the word *meghaśyāma*, and finally the Lord who resembles water. (NarP 1.81.52)
Having uttered "O Viṣṇu," there are two *ṭha*s; thus it consists of twenty-nine syllables.
Nārada is its sage, the *anuṣṭubh* is its meter, and Manu is its deity. (NarP 1.81.53)
Līlādaṇḍaharī is said to consist of [the numbers] four, four, four, two, seven, four, three, and four;
it is divided into five parts according to the sequence arising from the syllables of the mantra.

May the Lord of vast strides, who has slain Kaṃsa, grant us divine splendor— he who bewilders the cowherd maidens and other exquisite beauties with the playful staff held in his own left hand, while his right hand, resting upon the shoulder of his dear friend, points them out.

One should perform one hundred thousand recitations and offer oblations with sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with the three sweets in ten parts; thereafter, one should worship the limbs [of the deity] along with the guardians of the directions and their weapons.
He who indeed worships Hari, the wielder of the *līlā-daṇḍa*, with constant devotion, is honored by all the worlds; in his home, the goddess Ramā dwells eternally.
The mantra "Sadyārūḍhā smṛtistoyaṃ keśavāḍhyadharāyugam" consists of seven syllables; it is the mantra of Bhayāgnivallabhā and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The seer is Nārada, the meter is Uṣṇih, and the deity is as before; one should fashion the five limbs by means of the wheels. (NarP 1.81.59)
Hari is to be meditated upon as standing in the midst of a multitude of Kapila cows, calling them and holding a flute in his right hand;
in his other [hand] he holds a noose with a staff, he is dark as a rain-cloud, wears yellow garments, and has a peacock feather from the enemy of serpents (Śiva) as his ear-ornament.
One should recite the mantra seven hundred thousand times and then perform the fire oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that amount.
One should worship [the deity] on the pedestal with cow's milk; the first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas).
One that is golden-brown, white-brown, red-brown,
molasses-brown, tawny-colored, and likewise the most excellent Kapila.

Having worshipped eight groups of cows— those that are tawny in four parts, those that are yellowish-tawny, and the most excellent and auspicious ones— one should worship the world-protectors together with their weapons.
Having thus performed worship and once the mantra has been mastered, the knower of mantras should perform rites for specific desires;
he who offers oblations of milk one thousand and eight times every day, [attains his goal]. (NarP 1.81.64)
At the end of the fortnight, he was released along with his troop of gopas; and this is the ritual procedure for Daśārṇa as well:
the Tāra, the Heart, the Blessed One, ending in the dative case (ṅe), and likewise Śrī Govinda.
The mantra is declared to consist of twelve syllables; Nārada is considered its sage (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas), and Śrī Govinda is its deity (devatā).
The ritual arrangement of the five limbs (pañcāṅga) is performed using all the syllables [of the mantra] in groups of one, two, two, and four.

One should meditate upon Him who is seated upon a divine lion-throne shimmering with jewels at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree; who is dark as a rain cloud, clad in saffron robes, exceedingly beautiful, and holding a conch and a lotus in His two hands.

He bears the Lord of the Immortals, who is surrounded by thousands of cows, bathed by streams of nectar trickling from a single jar held in a mature hand, and whose eyes resemble the petals of a fresh lotus.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, performing oblations with milk in a tenth part of that number,
and worship [the deity] as before, whether situated in a cow-pen or within an image and so forth.
Having conceived the form upon the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal according to the root mantra,
one should worship Kṛṣṇa there by invoking him, preceded by the worship of the gurus.
Having worshipped Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā at his two sides, Indra in front,
and Surabhi behind him, one should perform the worship of the limbs upon the filaments.
The eight principal queens, beginning with Kālī, are situated upon the petals of the Vasus;
furthermore, one should likewise bind the Kiṅkiṇīs starting with Baddhā at the corners of the pedestal.
The cords are on his two shoulders, the bamboo flute before him, and the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha gem;
the forest and the rest are likewise situated in the eight directions in front of him.
The Pāñcajanya conch, the mace, the discus, Vasudeva, and Devakī; Nanda the cowherd, Yaśodā, along with the cows, the cowherds, and the gopīs.
Indra and the others are stationed outside, and beyond them are Vajra and the rest;
then there are Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, Supratiṣṭhita, and Viṣvaksena are to be fully worshipped; thereafter, one's own self is to be honored.
The man who worships Govinda once a day or three times a day shall become long-lived, free from disease, and a master of wealth and grain.
The mantra consists of *smṛtiḥ* followed by *sadyānvitā*, *cakrī*, and *dakṣakarṇayutodharā*; ending with *nāthāya*, this great mantra contains eight syllables (*vasuvarṇa*). (NarP 1.81.78)
The Sage is its seer, the Gāyatrī is its meter, and Kṛṣṇa is its deity;
one should assign its five limbs by means of all the pairs of syllables.
Bow down to the cowherd boy, five years of age, who runs about the courtyard with extremely restless limbs and very flickering eyes, adorned with tinkling bells, bracelets, necklaces, and anklets.
Having meditated thus, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times,
and perform a fire sacrifice with a tenth part of that amount using fuel-sticks of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree or with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having conceived the form upon the previously described Vaiṣṇava pedestal according to the root mantra,
the practitioner, with a steady mind, should invoke and worship Kṛṣṇa there.
One should worship the limbs upon the filaments in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions;
[one should worship] Vāsudeva, Bala, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha in the cardinal directions.
In the intermediate directions, one should place Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā, born of the Lakṣmaṇa and Arkṣa lineages;
outside, the world-protectors (lokeśas) with their weapons—thus the mantra becomes perfected.
One should utter "Tāraḥ," then "Śrībhuvanākāmaḥ" ending with "Ṅeṃ," then invoke "Śrīkṛṣṇa," then say "Śrīgovinda," and thereafter the word "Gopījana. (NarP 1.81.85)
Then, for the Beloved (Vallabha), there is the mantra consisting of three lotuses and the syllables of reality;
one should also remember the previously mentioned sage and so forth, as well as Siddhagopālaka.
One should recite while remembering Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, seated in the Mādhavī bower, protected by Garuḍa, and devoted to divine pastimes. (NarP 1.81.87)
The worship of this [deity] should indeed be performed by the best of Vaiṣṇavas as before;
the mantra consists of a single syllable, beginning with the discus, followed by the sound of the chief of sages (Muni), and ending with the word "Sargī."

The two-syllabled mantra is declared to be "Kṛṣṇa"; the three-syllabled one begins with "Kāma" (Ka-ā-ma). That same [mantra] ending in the dative case ("ṅeṃta") consists of four syllables, as does "Kṛṣṇāya namaḥ."
The five-syllable mantra for Kṛṣṇa, followed by another for Kāmarudra,
and ending with the wife of Agni (Svāhā) for Gopāla, is proclaimed to consist of six syllables.
The word *kāma* followed by the dative case-ending of *kṛṣṇa* (i.e., *kṛṣṇāya*), ending with the consort of fire (*svāhā*), is supreme.
The two words *kṛṣṇa* and *govinda*, both in the dative case, consist of seven syllables and bestow all accomplishments.

The supreme seven-syllable mantra for one desiring the power of Śrī and Kṛṣṇa is: *kṛṣṇāya kāmaḥ*. Another nine-syllable mantra consists of *kṛṣṇa* and *govinda* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), with *hṛt* at the end. 1,81.92.
And the two earrings are Kṛṣṇa and Govinda; likewise, the next pair is Kāma and Puṭa.
Kāma is Śārṅgin, situated upon the earth, while Manmatha is enriched by the mind and the moon.
The ten-syllable mantra "To the one with dark limbs, [Oṃ] Hṛdayāya Svāhā" bestows all accomplishments. Another is the mantra ending in "Vapuṣe Kṛṣṇāya," followed by the wife of Agni (Svāhā).
At the end of the two syllables [dvi], one should address Kṛṣṇa, who has the body of a child, as "Kāma";
then, meditating within one's own heart upon Him who captivates the minds of the cowherd women (Gopījanamanohara).

I bow to the youth of Nanda, whose face is like the moon and who possesses the splendor of a gentle rain-cloud; he who sports on the banks of the Yamunā, who is the sole life-breath of Rādhā, and who is served by a fragrant breeze that scatters the internal pollen from the rows of blossoming creepers bowing down at the city-gates of the glorious forest of Vṛndāvana.
O Lord of Sages, their worship should be understood according to the previously mentioned path;
at the end of the name of the son of Devakī, one should utter the word "Govinda."
Having uttered the word "Vāsudeva," he addressed the Lord of the Universe who was increasing [in size], saying:
"O Kṛṣṇa, give me a son; afterwards, I shall praise you."
The mantra ending with "I have gone for refuge" consists of thirty-two syllables.
Nārada is its sage; the meters are Gāyatrī and Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of sons; and the limbs [of the ritual] are assigned to the individual feet and to the whole mantra.
Accompanied by Vijaya and standing upon his chariot, having brought [the princesses] forth from the midst of the ocean,
the son of Vasudeva— who is worthy of being remembered— bestowed his daughters upon the twice-born.
One hundred thousand recitations and ten thousand oblations with palm fruits soaked in honey should be performed;
worship is conducted upon the previously described pedestal with the limbs, world-protectors, and weapons.
When the mantra has been thus accomplished, the practitioner of the mantra obtains a son even from a barren woman:
*Tāra*, *Māyā*, then *Saṃ* with the moon (*i*) and the letter *va* at its end. (NarP 1.81.102)
Thus, this supreme eight-syllable mantra ending with *vahnipriyā* is the sage (*muni*) of this mantra whose essence consists of the five Brahmans, O best of sages.
The seer is Brahmā, and the supreme Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre;
the supreme light, the Supreme Brahman, is proclaimed as the deity. (NarP 1.81.104)
The Praṇava is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and Svāhā is cited as the power (śakti).
"Svāhā" is proclaimed as the heart, and "So 'ham" is considered the head.
The mantra "Haṃsa" is declared to be the crest-lock (śikhā), "Hṛllekhā" is remembered as the armor (kavaca),
"Praṇava" is called the eye (netra), and "Hari-hara" is the weapon (astra).
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, O Brahmin, he is Hari, and he alone is the king of the gods;
he is the form of all, he is named as all, he is the imperishable, supreme self-ruling Lord.
Having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times; the fire-oblation (homa) is considered to be one-tenth of that number.
His worship on the seat of the Praṇava is prescribed with the limbs and the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas).
O Nārada, when the mantra has been mastered in this way, non-conceptual knowledge regarding that which is expressed by such statements as "That art thou" arises for the lord of practitioners.
Kāma is the seed-syllable, Hṛṣīkeśa is the heart-mantra, and Gajāksara is the concluding syllable.
Brahmā is its seer (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī meter is declared to be its meter (chandas).
Hṛṣīkeśa is the deity; its application is for the attainment of everything;
"Kāma" is the seed-syllable, and "Tathā" is declared to be its power.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of the seed-syllable alone, one should practice meditation;
everything declared for Vāsudeva is proclaimed as applicable here as well, according to the mantra of Puruṣottama.
A hundred thousand recitations and ten thousand oblations with clarified butter alone are prescribed;
the libation with the flowers of the *saṃmohinī* is proclaimed for the attainment of all desires.
The seed-syllable of Śrī is "Śaktirāpā"; with this very seed-syllable, the six limbs are likewise formed.
The mantra is declared to be the word "Trailokyamohana" ending with "Namaḥ. (NarP 1.81.114)
The seer is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī, the deity is Śrīdhara;
the seed-syllable is Śrī, and the power is Āpā—by means of this very seed-syllable, one performs the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
Meditation, worship, and so forth, as well as one hundred thousand recitations and a fire-offering (homa) with clarified butter in a tenfold proportion, are prescribed here just as for Puruṣottama.
One should perform worship, fire-offerings (homa), and other rites with fragrant white flowers;
when this is done, O best of Brahmins, Śrīdhara himself will become manifest.
The mantra is "acyutānantagovindapadaṃ ṅeṃtaṃ namontimam";
its seer is proclaimed to be Śaunaka and its meter is Virāṭ.
Parāśara, Vyāsa, and Nārada are remembered as the sages (ṛṣis) of these;
Virāj is declared to be the meter, and Hari, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, is the deity.
The seed-syllable and power of the deity are considered by practitioners to be as previously described;
[one should meditate on] the God bearing a conch and a discus, four-armed and wearing a crown.
He was equipped with all weapons, seated upon Garuḍa,
and worshipped by the lords of sages such as Sanaka and by all the gods.
The god, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, resembled the rising sun;
his earrings were like the orb of the thousand-rayed sun as it rises at dawn.
For the sake of protecting the entire world, he is indeed infinite and eternal;
the God, filled with joy, bestows fearlessness and grants boons.
Having meditated thus, being well-composed, one should worship on the Vaiṣṇava pedestal with the deities of the first enclosure: the discus, conch, mace, and sword.
The second [form] is said to consist of a pestle, a bow, a noose, and a goad;
it was proclaimed by Sanaka and others, as well as by the Śākta teachers Vyāsa, Nārada, and Śaunaka.
The third is [presided over] by the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), and the fourth is proclaimed [by them].
A hundred thousand recitations (japa) are prescribed, with an oblation (havana) of ghee constituting one-tenth of that number.
When the mantra has been thus mastered, the practitioner of the mantra should also perform ritual applications;
meditating on the Lord of Gods at the root of a bilva tree while recollecting him as free from disease.
O twice-born one, by touching [the patient], reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times, or remembering the person to be treated mentally,
the practitioner shall effect the liberation of the sick from disease from the mandala.
One seeking a maiden should offer oblations with parched grains (lāja); for the attainment of wealth, with bilva fruits;
one seeking clothing, with perfumes and flowers; and for the sake of health, one should sacrifice with sesame seeds.
He who, standing in water reaching up to the navel on a Sunday,
should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, will certainly destroy fever.
O Nārada, for the sake of marriage, one should recite [the mantra] for a month while meditating upon Kṛṣṇa situated in the center of the lunar disc; thus one shall obtain the desired maiden.
Having uttered the word "Vāsudeva-pada," followed by the sound of "nigaḍaccheda" (the breaking of shackles),
the mantra ending with "svāhā"— namely, "vāsudevāya varma-astra svāhā"— is proclaimed.
Nārada is its seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī its metre (chandas), Kṛṣṇa its deity (devatā);
the armor is the seed-syllable, the head is the power (śakti), and everything else is as in the ten-syllable mantra.
May Atri—who is joined with the wind-like long *u*, who lies upon a *jhiṇṭī* flower, and who is water—protect me; may the eight-syllabled mantra of Manu protect me. (NarP 1.81.134)
The sage is Brahmā, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is the son of Satyavatī;
the first is the seed-syllable, "Namaḥ" is the power, enriched with the long vowels, and the limbs are accompanied by the Nāda.

For the sake of spiritual accomplishment, one should meditate upon Vyāsa, whose palm shines with the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāmudrā*), who sits upon a yogic seat, holding his other hand upon the surface of his left knee; who is a treasury of supreme knowledge, surrounded by a multitude of Brahmins, serene-minded, possessing the luster of a lotus body, and whose life was exceedingly meritorious.
One should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times and perform an offering of milk-rice with gold;
on the previously mentioned seat, one should first worship the limbs of Vyāsa.
One should worship Paila in the east and other [directions], Vaiśaṃpāyana and Jaimini [in the south],
Sumantu in the corners, and Śrī Śuka and Romaharṣaṇa [in the north].
To Ugraśravas and other sages, as well as to Indra and the rest of the gods,
the practitioner who has thus perfected the mantra attains poetic skill and excellent progeny.
One obtains the power of exposition, fame,
and a multitude of riches by beholding Nṛsiṃha, Mādhava, Lohita, and the first of the Vedas.
The five-syllabled mantra of the daughter of Kṛśānu is the supreme destroyer of poison;
Ananta, Paṅkti, Pakṣīndra, Muni, Chandas, and Surā are considered its seers, meters, and deities.
*Tāra* (Om), *vahnipriyā* (Hrīm), and the seed-syllable (*bīja*) are proclaimed as the powers (*śakti*) of the mantra;
"Jvala jvala mahāmantri svāhā" is declared to be the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). NarP_1,81.142 //
At the end of the word "Garuḍa," [the mantra] "cūḍānana-śuci-priyā" is the head-mantra;
from "Garuḍa" [follows] "śikhe svāhā," which is the crest-mantra (śikhā-manu).
Having uttered the word "Garuḍa," one should say the pair "prabhañjaya";
then the pair "prabhedaya," followed by "vitrāsaya" and "vimardaya."
Then, twice for each [syllable], the mantra of the armor (*kavaca*) is considered to end with *svāhā*, followed by *ugrarūpadharā* and *sarvaviṣahara*. (NarP 1.81.145)

Having uttered "the two terrifying ones" (*bhīṣayadvitaya*), and "burn, burn everything" (*sarvaṃ daha daha*), and then "reduce to ashes, svāhā" (*bhasmīkuru tataḥ svāhā*), this is declared to be the mantra for the eye. (NarP 1.81.146)

The delighter of Devakī, Śauri, Vāsudeva, the younger brother of Balarāma, the elder brother of Gada, the deluder of Kaṃsa, and the deluder of Kaṃsa’s servants.

The progenitor of Dvārakā, the hidden one, devoted to Brahman, true to his promise,

The Lord of Truth, unconquered by Lakṣmaṇa, the worshipful one who brings welfare to Bhadrā,

Murāri, the lord of passion, the destroyer of the earth's suffering;

Worshipped by Indra, the beloved of Ramā, honored by the wife of the wielder of the thunderbolt,

Pradyumna’s father, Sāmba’s grandfather, the moon-like one with many sons,

He is the stealer of Arjuna’s pride, the giver of life to Arjuna,

The charioteer of the white horse, the Truth, the one to be accomplished through truth, the remover of fear,

The conqueror of Mahāsena, the destroyer of Śiva’s army,

He who takes away the weapons of heroes, Time itself, whose hair is dark, possessed of great strength;

Victorious son of Dharma, hero who subdues the pride of Duryodhana,

Rādhā, Rādhikā, Ānandā, Vṛṣabhānujā,

She was bold, clever, full of desire, and a woman who enchanted Hari;
she was graceful, sweet, like honey, a young maiden with the luster of gold.
She who has conquered the moon, conquered the deer, conquered the lion, and conquered the elephant;

The maiden who has conquered the Bimba fruit, conquered the parrot, and conquered the lotus;
the goddess Śrī-Kṛṣṇākarṣaṇā, who eternally possesses a dual form.
She dwells eternally as the beloved, the connoisseur of aesthetic delight, and the favorite of Kṛṣṇa; she is fragrant, full of joy, and adorned by the Son of Nanda.
Clad in divine garments and wearing celestial necklaces, adorned with pearls and gems,
she is fond of forest groves, dwells in forest groves, and is the heroine who leads the lords of the groves.
She of beautiful form, beautiful face, and auspicious, wearing lovely golden armlets;
she who is delighted by the flute-song of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who captivates with her muralī, and who is auspicious.
Bhadrā, Bhagavatī, Śāntā, Kumudā, Sundarī, Priyā,
Kṛṣṇarati, and Śrīkṛṣṇasahacāriṇī.
She who dwells in the beloved places of the bamboo grove and the banyan tree, whose nature is both dual and non-dual,
who resides at Bhāṇḍīra, the radiant one, the mistress of the cowherd girls, and the dear friend.
Divine, the breath of the Vedas, bestowing the nectar of Govinda,
the sovereign prayer to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it grants great bliss.
She is served by the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha, she brings the happiness of millions of Lakṣmīs,
she possesses the beauty of ten million Cupids, and she bestows the delight of ten million Ratis.
Uma is to be grasped through devotion, her very form is devotion, a lake of loveliness;
she is to be propitiated by Brahmā, Rudra, and the others, and is eternally filled with curiosity.
Her pastimes are eternal, her desires are eternal, and she is eternally adorned with amorous passion;
she is the essence of eternal Vṛndāvana, united with the Joy of Nanda.
Always accompanied by circles of cowherd girls and constantly joined by cowherds,
she is a brave distributor of dairy products, full of joy and the giver of bliss.
She is of great playfulness, most excellent, urban, and moving through the city;
she is eternally whirling, full, and adorned with a musk tilaka.
Padmā, Śyāmā, and Mṛgākṣī, who possess the form of Siddhi and bring forth the essence;
Gaurī, whose face is like ten million moons and whose voice is as sweet as ten million cuckoos.
She was the abode of the beauty of virtue, cherished by Nanda and Nandana;
she dwelt in the Aśoka grove and was united with the Bhāṇḍīra forest.
Seated at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree, she is Kṛṣṇā, Viśvā, and the beloved of Hari;
she is inaccessible to the unborn (Ajā) and inaccessible to Bhava, and she has made her abode on Govardhana.
Dwelling on the banks of the Yamunā, she constantly speaks of Govinda;

Praised by Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by Kṛṣṇa, with her abode in the heart of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,

She consists of ten million sacred fords and is the truth; she bestows the fruit of ten million sacred fords;
she is very difficult to attain even through ten million yogas; and she is hard to reach even through ten million sacrifices.

She was Manasā and Śaśilekhā, more fortunate than ten million Lakṣmīs and sinless; she possessed the bliss of ten million liberations, was gentle, and sported with the splendor of ten million goddesses of fortune.
Tilottamā dwells in the three times; she is the sovereign who knows the three times.
She is the knower of the three Vedas and the knower of the three worlds, residing at the end of the fourth state.
She who is difficult to propitiate, she who is propitiated by Ramā, she who is propitiated by the universe, whose nature is consciousness;
she who is propitiated by the gods, she who is propitiated by the Supreme, she who is propitiated by Brahmā, whose nature is the Supreme Self.
She is worshipped by Śiva, won over by love, adored by devotees, and composed of aesthetic rasa;

She is to be propitiated by Kṛṣṇa, attainable through devotion, and served by the multitude of devotees;
she is the support of the universe, the repository of compassion, the sustainer of living beings, and the supreme leader.
She is the crown jewel, eternally perfected, consisting of pure love;
she possesses a divine form, divine enjoyments, and divine attire, and is filled with joy.
She is the essence of a multitude of celestial women, eternally possessed of ever-fresh youth;
she is to be meditated upon as enveloped by the Supreme Brahman, possessing a magnificent form and blazing with great splendor.
Her radiance exceeds that of ten million suns and the splendor of ten million moons;
she possesses speech as tender as nectar and is the primordial source of the Vedas, difficult even for the Vedas to attain.
Attached to Kṛṣṇa, devoted to Kṛṣṇa, served by Candrāvalī,
complete with the sixteen digits, she bears half of Kṛṣṇa’s body.
She whose intellect is black, who sports in the form of the black antelope, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, whose wealth is Kṛṣṇa,
and who causes the enchantment of Kṛṣṇa.
She has black vision, belongs to the black lineage, and is the black goddess who upholds the family;
she is the Self abiding within all beings, honored by all the worlds.
The giver of black [grain], the nourisher of love, the golden-bodied, the delightful,
the supporter of the mountains, the upholder of fame, the great goddess, the bringer of auspiciousness.
The second [form] is Śrīśeṣadevajananī, the mother of the multitude of incarnations; she who is marked by the blue lotus and the lotus, and whose mark is grace.
She has the marks of a chariot wheel, an elephant, and earrings upon her feet;
she bears the marks of a parasol, lightning, and is even adorned with a garland of flowers.
She is marked by the staff and marked by the crown; she is the full moon and marked by the parrot;
she has black bees as her necklace and ripened fruit; she sports in the groves of Vṛndāvana.
She awakens Kṛṣṇa; she eats the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s food;

Her frown lasts until the end of ten million kalpas; she does not fall even when the dissolution has not yet arrived.
She is the treasury of all sentient beings, attended by treasures such as the lotus and the conch.

Mālinī, skilled in dance, made an appointment with Kṛṣṇa at Abhisāra;

Delighting Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she was filled with fear; her every limb was covered in horripilation;
she was intent on embracing Śrī Kṛṣṇa and unable to endure separation from Govinda.
Endowed with infinite virtues, longing for the glorification of Kṛṣṇa,

She is served by Vimalā and others, worshipped by Lalitā and her companions,

Residing in the heart of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she is like a golden tube set with pearls;

Adorned with golden anklets and decorated with golden bells, she—

She is the supreme form, the supreme bliss, and she who sports in the supreme heaven;

A young girl in the bloom of youth, with a crest of blossoming beauty,

Aparājitā is embellished with saffron, lac, and musk.

She is adorned with golden necklaces, rich in flowers, and abounding in pearl strings; she is the very essence of flavor, sweet with sweetness, the goddess Padmā, who holds a lotus in her hand and is renowned throughout the world.

she rests upon the heads of the remaining gods and dwells eternally in the sacred realm.

she is the mother of the Vairāja-sacrifice, the consort of Śrī, and the enchantress of the world.
She is great splendor, great illusion, great beauty, and great mindfulness;

She is praised by the lineage of Viṣṇu, she is the creator, and she is always the protectress of Viṣṇu’s lineage;

She is the abode of joy, eternally established in the machine, residing in Goloka, the bestower of prosperity;

For she is indeed immortal, wonderful, praised by the glorious Nārāyaṇa, imperishable,

To be accomplished through the state of magnanimity, she is both gross and subtle, possessing a form beyond compare;

Her eyes surpassed the blue lotus, she was adorned with a crest of excellent jewels,
she rested upon a couch of love, and she stood in the midst of a circle of splendor.
She is the mistress who conceals the limbs of Kṛṣṇa through her various manifestations;
she is the heroine who veils his divine play, bestowing the flow of nectar that causes the ocean of immortality to swell.

The pastimes of Kṛṣṇa, which remove all impurity, have their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, their minds on the *rāsa* dance, and their minds on divine love; they are dear to Hari, and their multitude of virtues is inconceivable.
She who is the moon for the ocean of the rāsa, the ornament of the rāsa-maṇḍala, whose vows are bowed, whose gaze is like that of a lioness, who is well-praised, and who possesses a beautiful smile.
She is the crest-jewel of the cowherds, adored by the hosts of gopīs, superior even to Virajā;

Gopadhāmā, Sudāmāmbā, Gopālī, Gopamohinī,
Gopabhūṣā, Kṛṣṇabhūṣā, and Śrīvṛndāvanacandrikā.
Delighting in the sound of the lute and other instruments, manifesting in the festival of the rāsa dance,
she was fully known as Kṛṣṇa’s own activity, enchanting ten million gods of love.
She is rich with the ocean of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s virtues, she who deludes even the beautiful goddesses;
she is as pleasing to the mind as the moon-like Kṛṣṇa, and she is the sister of the divine Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇābhilāṣiṇī, who desires the grace of Kṛṣṇa’s love; Kṣemā, who speaks sweetly; Bhruvā, Māyā, and Subhadrikā. (NarP 1.82.203)
Prakṛti, seated beneath the shade of a *nīpa* tree, is supreme bliss;
she has compassionate glances, lips like the *bimba* fruit, and is as beautiful and shapely as a plantain tree.

radiant with the splendor of the golden mountain, full of love and other virtues, and slow-moving due to intoxication.
The thought of Kṛṣṇa, the thought of love, and the thought of delight are given by Kṛṣṇa;
the thought of the Rāsa dance, the thought of ecstatic emotion, and the thought of purity are the great aesthetic flavor (mahārasa).
She severs the continuity of Kṛṣṇa’s glances, she puts to shame the eyelashes of his vision,
she is the mother of Kandarpa, the foremost [goddess], and the bestower of the path to Vaikuṇṭha.
Rāsabhāvā, Priyāśliṣṭā, Preṣṭhā, Prathamanāyikā, Śuddhādehinī, Śrīrāmā, and Rasamañjarī. (NarP 1.82.208)
Suprabhāvā, Śubhācārā, Svarṇadī, Narmadāmbikā,
Gomatī, Candrabhāgā, Ṛṣīkā, Sarayū, and the daughter of Tāmraparṇi.
O Nārada, this thousand-name hymn belongs to the one who possesses a dual form, whose conduct is stainless, who is beyond qualities, and who is untainted.
This, which brings forth the nectar of Vṛndāvana, which pacifies great sins, and which removes the state of barrenness, should be recited with diligent effort. (NarP 1.82.211)
It pacifies poverty, destroys disease, grants great desires,
removes sin, dispels enemies, and bestows devotion to Rādhā and Mādhava.
Salutations to that Blessed One, Kṛṣṇa, whose intellect is unimpeded;
salutations to Him who eternally sports in the ocean of the nectar of union with Rādhā.
Goddess Rādhā is the creator of the world, intent upon the protection of the world, the ordainer of the dissolution of the world, the sovereign of all,
and the mother of all.
O Lord of Sages, I have indeed proclaimed her thousand names, which are divine and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Thousand Names of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa," in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.

she dwells in the midst of a circle of light, her nature being both visible and invisible.
But once, O best of sages, while Kṛṣṇa was standing together with her, Nārāyaṇa himself was born from his left side.
And from the left side of Rādhikā, Mahālakṣmī came forth;
then Kṛṣṇa gave Mahālakṣmī to Nārāyaṇa.
He established him in Vaikuṇṭha for the eternal task of protection;
then, O Sage, from the opening of the cows' mouths, [the Lord appeared] from the Master of Goloka.
At that time, there were countless cowherds equal to him in splendor and age;

From the pores of Rādhā’s body there arose cowherd girls who were equal to Rādhā in every respect, servants of Rādhā, and sweet-spoken.
In that interval, O Brahmin, Durgā— the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu— suddenly manifested from the body of Kṛṣṇa.
The Sovereign Lady is the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) in the form of the seed-syllables of the goddesses;
she is the most perfectly complete radiance, whose essence consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
Endowed with a thousand arms, bearing various weapons, and possessing three eyes,
she is the eternal one who exists in the form of the seed of the tree of saṃsāra.
The Lord of Rādhikā presented a jeweled lion-throne to her;
in the meantime, the four-faced Brahmā arrived there accompanied by his wife.
The illustrious and foremost among the wise, uttering the syllable *Oṃ*,
was born from the navel of Hari as an ascetic bearing a water-pot.
Having praised the Lord of All together with his wife Sāvitrī,
O Sage, he sat upon a beautiful seat by the command of that Lord.
Then, O illustrious one, Kṛṣṇa indeed became twofold in form:
Mahādeva as the left half of his body, and the Lord of the Gopīs as the right half.
Having five faces and three eyes, with the left half of his body being female,
that lord of sages praised Kṛṣṇa and, being commanded by him, sat down before Hari.
Then Kṛṣṇa said to the four-faced one: "O Lord, perform the act of creation;
remain eternally in Satyaloka, and always remember me."
Thus addressed by Hari, he bowed to the Lord of the Universe and departed with his wife; he indeed proceeded to perform the work of creation.
"O best of sages, you are our father; [grant us] a mental body for this kalpa. Thereafter, O high-minded one, he spoke to the five-faced Kṛṣṇa.
"O Lord of the Universe, take Durgā and perform penance in the world of Śiva;
until the end of creation, and at its conclusion, withdraw all worlds from every side."
Having bowed down to Kṛṣṇa, he too went to the world of Śiva.
Then, O Brahmin, after some time, [the following occurred] regarding Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
From his mouth was born Sarasvatī, bearing a lute and a book;
the Blessed One commanded her: "Go to Vaikuṇṭha, O honored one."
"Stay near Lakṣmī, taking refuge with the four-armed one.

[now follows] the mantra, meditation, worship, and so forth, of these who possess the full nature.
