"Oṃ! To the one with great feet, whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs! (NarP 1.83.81).
O Sage, the lion-mantra is said to be *siṃhāya varma astram hṛt*;
with this one should offer the seat, and with the root-mantra one should fashion the image.
Having first worshipped the limbs and the enclosure, one should worship the Śaktis upon the petals:
Jayā, Vijayā, Kīrti, Prīti, and then Prabhā.
One should worship Faith, Intelligence, and Sacred Learning— beginning with the first letters of their respective names—
on the tips of the petals, and then the eight weapons in due order.

Then, outside [the previous circle], one should place the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) holding the conch, discus, mace, sword, noose, goad, arrow, and bow; immediately after them, their respective weapons.

In this manner, once the mantra has been mastered through recitation and other means, the practitioner of mantras who knows the ritual procedures should perform applications with it according to his respective desires.
Having installed nine beautiful jars according to the prescribed rite, filled with jewels, gold, and other precious substances, and placed within those nine jars; ||| NarP_1,83.87 |||
If [the astrological configuration] is neutral, one should worship the Goddess; in other cases, one should worship Jayā and the others.
Having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should consecrate the lord of men.
The king who possesses superior glory of victory conquers his enemies;
he attains freedom from disease, long life, and is entirely free from all ailments.
A barren woman consecrated according to the rite obtains an excellent son;
clarified butter consecrated with this mantra destroys minor malevolent spirits.
Especially for pregnant women, ashes and other substances over which mantras have been recited [are beneficial];
likewise, when Kṛṣṇa has entered the mouth of Irādhikā during her yawning and breathing, [the same applies].
O best of Brahmins, hear now the procedure for that goddess who has arisen bearing a lute and a book, which brings benefit to the world.
The Praṇava, Vāgbhava, Māyā, Śrī, Kāma, and Śakti are proclaimed;
followed by Sarasvatī in the dative case and ending with Svāhā, this is the twelve-syllable mantra.
Manu Nārāyaṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is declared to be the meter (chandas),
and Mahāsarasvatī is proclaimed as its deity (devatā).
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the *vāgbhava* syllable, the wise one should assign the letters;
he should place the *tāra* (oṃ) in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and place the *lajjā* (hrīṃ) between the eyebrows.
Having placed the glorious syllables upon the mouth, nose, ears,
and anus, one should then meditate upon the Goddess of Speech, who holds a lute and a book.
White as camphor and the *kunda* flower, her face radiant as the full moon;
she was mounted upon a swan, adorned with divine ornaments and the crescent moon upon her brow.
The best of practitioners should recite the mantra twelve hundred thousand times, or offer oblations with white lotuses or *nāgacampaka* flowers, numbering one thousand.
One should worship her upon the seat as described by the Mother, according to the sequence to be explained;
one should offer a seat consisting of a lotus of letters and fashion the form with the root mantra.
To the right of the Goddess, the auspicious Vāṅmayī in Sanskrit should be worshipped;
to her left, Vāṅmayī in Prākṛta, the bestower of all accomplishments, should be worshipped.
First, one should worship the six limbs within the hexagon, and outside [of it], one should worship Prajñā and the others:
Prajñā, Medhā, Śruti, Śakti, Smṛti, Vāgīśvarī, and Mati.
Then Svasti is proclaimed, followed by Brahmā and the others;
thereafter, one should worship the world-protectors (lokeśas), and outside of that, their weapons.
Having thus worshipped Vāgdevī, one will become a master of speech in person,
provided one is devoted to celibacy, pure, and has clean teeth, nails, and so forth.
Constantly recollecting all women with the thought that they are deities,
the wise man will certainly attain poetic skill within twelve months.
O Sage, by drinking that consecrated water one thousand times every day,
the practitioner of mantra will undoubtedly become a great poet within a year.
Standing in water reaching only to the chest and meditating upon the orb of the sun,
one should recite the mantra three thousand times daily while focusing on the Goddess stationed therein.
One obtains from the mandala success and incomparable speech upon the earth;
one should offer oblations with palāśa and bilva flowers smeared with honey.
Or, by means of fuel-sticks produced from that [tree], one attains the glory of the Lord of Speech;
likewise, by means of flowers arising from the rājavṛkṣa tree, soaked in honey.
One should offer oblations with six kinds of fuel-sticks and shall obtain incomparable poetic power.
Now, O best of Brahmins, I shall proclaim the Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā.
Having propitiated her, Brahmā created the worlds, both moving and unmoving;
she is Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kāmapūrvā, and Sāvitrī, endowed with the syllable *ṅe*.
The mantra of the Sāvitrī, ending with "svāhā" and containing the word "vasu," is proclaimed;
its seer is Brahmā, its meter is Gāyatrī, and it is declared that she is the deity.
Sāvitrī is proclaimed as the [essence] of all the gods;
she is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, through their respective hearts and proximate forms.
And it is held that the limbs [of the mantra] are to be conceived as being joined with the syllable *ṅe* in their entirety;
she has the luster of molten gold and blazes with the splendor of Brahman.
Her form was like that of a thousand midday suns in the summer heat;
her face was bright with a slight smile, and she was adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
Śivā, who wears garments of many pure silks, who is eager to bestow grace upon her devotees,
and who grants happiness, liberation, and all prosperity.
And the wise man, having meditated thus upon the virtuous goddess born of the Vedas, whose nature is the seed of the Vedas, within the mandala with a radiant triangular pericarp; NarP_1,83.116.
One should worship the Goddess at the Soura-pīṭha with the nine Śaktis beginning with Dīptā;
one should worship the Goddess in the image fashioned with the root mantra.
In the three corners outside, the powers beginning with Brāhmī should be worshipped;
thereafter, the deities beginning with Āditya, together with Uṣā and the others, should be worshipped in sequence.
Then, having worshipped the six limbs according to the rule upon the filaments,
one should worship Prahlādinī, Prabhā, Nityā, and Viśvaṃbharā.
One should then worship Vilāsinī and Prabhāvatī, as well as Jayā and Śāntā;
thereafter, one should worship Kānti, Durgā, Sarasvatī, and Vidyārūpā.
One should worship the pervasive and stainless Īśā, known as Viśālā,
who removes darkness, is subtle, the source of the universe, and brings victory.
Then one should worship the supreme splendor residing in the lotus, which is of the nature of Brahman;
thereafter, one should worship Brahmā and the others, the protectors on the outside, possessing the characteristics previously described.
Then, one should worship the planetary deities outside along with Indra and the others together with their weapons;
in this manner, one should fully honor the goddesses with these ten enclosures.
One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times and offer a thousand oblations of sesame seeds;
liberated from all sins, one attains a long life.
Then, one should offer ten thousand oblations with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets;
within six months, great fortune (Mahālakṣmī) shall be his—of this there is no doubt.
One should offer oblations with the flowers of the Brahma-tree for the sake of external splendor;
what is the use of saying more here? For she, when properly accomplished, [grants all desires].
O Sage, this vidyā shall be a cow of plenty for practitioners;
now I shall proclaim to you a most wonderful secret.
This is the one called the Sāvitrī-panjara, which provides all forms of protection for human beings;
she is adorned with a beautiful crown and attended by Vyomakeśa and Arlaka.
Her eyebrows were arched like clouds, her faces were those of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
Jupiter and Venus were the ends of her ears, and the Moon, Sun, and Fire were her eyes.
She possesses the subtle *iḍā* and *piṅgalikā* channels joined with the nostrils,
is adorned by the two lips of the twilight [mantras], and has the shimmering tongue of speech as her uvula.
[He saw] those whose necks were like sun-gems at twilight, who were accompanied by the arms of the Maruts,
whose hearts were attached to Parjanya, and who possessed circles resembling the Vasus.
The region of the navel was the path wandering through the belly of space;
the hips were known as Prajāpati, and it rested upon the waist of Indrāṇī.
She was graced by her two thighs like the Malaya and Meru mountains, possessing the best of rivers,
with well-formed knees like Jahnu and Kuśika, and she bore the name Vaiśvadeva.
[She] was characterized by the earth, serpents, and trees known as the feet, toes, nails, and body hair;
and she bore the designations of the planets, zodiac signs, lunar mansions, and yogas as the limbs of her form.
[She is] characterized by conventions consisting of lunar days, months, seasons, and fortnights,
and is veiled by the covering known as the twilight of the manifold variety imagined through Māyā.
Resembling the blazing fire of time,
with a luster like millions of lightning-flashes, resembling ten million suns, yet as cool as ten million moons.
She who dwells in the center of the orb of nectar, whose nature is the nectar of intense bliss,
who transcends speech and is beyond the reach of the mind, the bestower of boons, the Mother of the Vedas.

Having meditated upon [Sāvitrī], who consists of the moving and the unmoving, who is eternal, and who is endowed with the imperishable Brahman, one should perform the placement of the *sāvitrī-pañjara* as non-different from one's own self.
I am that seer of the Pañcaratra; my meter is said to be Vikṛti;
and my deity is the Supreme Haṃsa, the primordial deity who is the Supreme Brahman.
The application for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa has been declared;
one should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) with the mantras of the deities of the six limbs.
The wise one should indeed perform the pervasive [meditation] by means of the three roots;
he should meditate upon the previously mentioned deity, possessing form and endowed with qualities.
May she who has three feet, is born from Hari, faces the east, is known as the Brahmāstra,
and is enriched with the twenty-four principles, protect my eastern direction.
Four-footed Brahmadaṇḍā, who is Brahmāṇī with a face turned to the south and endowed with the twenty-six principles— may she protect my southern direction.
Facing westward, consisting of five steps, embodying the fifty principles,
and marked by the Brahmaśiras [mantra], may she protect me incessantly in the western direction.
May she who has a gentle face, who is enriched by the fourth state of Brahman, whose essence is the Atharva-Aṅgirasa,
and who consists of the sixty principles and digits, protect the northern direction with her six steps.
May the hundred-syllabled mantra, composed of fifty letters and consisting of nine feet,
which dwells in the Vedānta and has its head directed upward in the sky, protect me.
Resembling lightning, the twilight of Brahmā, mounted upon a deer, four-armed,
and bearing a bow, arrows, shield, and sword— may she protect my southeastern quarter.
May Brahmī— virgin, Gāyatrī, red-limbed, riding upon a swan,
and bearing a water-pot, a rosary, and the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles— protect [the region of] Nairṛti.
And may Sāvitrī, white in color, youthful, riding upon a bull,
and bearing a skull, a trident, a rosary, and a garland, protect the quarter of Vāyu.
May Śyāmā, Sarasvatī, Vṛddhā, Vaiṣṇavī, and she who is seated upon Garuḍa—
holding a conch, a discus, and the gesture of fearlessness— protect my northern direction.
May the four-armed Mother of the Gods, fair-limbed, riding upon a lion,
and holding the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness along with a sword and shield, protect the downward direction.
Standing at their respective sides, equipped with their own vehicles, weapons, and ornaments,
and stationed in their respective directions, they protect [the world] together with the powers and limbs of the planets.
May the deities who are the presiding forms of the mantras and the deities who empower the mudrās protect us by their pervasiveness, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
This true Sāvitrī-pañjara has been recounted by me to you;
it should be recited with devotion daily at the two twilights, especially at the time of chanting.
One who desires both worldly enjoyment and liberation should recite this with effort;
for speech is the giver of prosperity, the voice of the world, the great earth, and the very ground.
Nandā is the mother of gold, possessed of the visarga, ascetic,
illustrious, virtuous, truthful, consisting of the Vedas, and auspicious.
Viśvā, Turyā, Vareṇyā, Ca, Nisṛṇī, Yamunā, Bhuvā, Modā, Devī, Variṣṭhā, Dhī, Śānti, Mati, and Mahī.
Dhiṣaṇā, Yoginī, Yuktā, Nadī, Prajñāpracodanī,
Dayā, Yāminī, Padmā, Rohiṇī, Ramaṇī, and Jayā.
Senāmukhī, composed of the Sāman, Bagalā, free from defects,
Māyā, Prajñā, Parā, Dogdhrī, Māninī, Poṣiṇī, and Kriyā.
The delightful Jyotsnā consists of sacred fords; likewise, the Saumyā consists of nectar.
There are also the Brāhmī, the Haimī, the Bhujaṅgī, the Vaśinī, the Sundarī, and the Vanī.
She is Oṃkāra, Hasinī, Sarvā, Sudhā, and she who possesses the six qualities;
she is Māyā, Svadhā, Ramā, Tanvī, Ripughnī, Rakṣaṇī, and Satī.
Haimī, Tārā, Vidhugati, Viṣaghnī, Varānanā,
Amarā, Tīrthadā, Dīkṣā, Durdharṣā, and Rogahāriṇī.
She who destroys various evils and cruelty, the six-footed one, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the one who delights in battle;
she is the Yoginī, the stainless, the truthful, the powerless, the giver of strength, and the victorious.
The Gomatī, Jāhnavī, Rajāvī, Tapanī, and Jātavedasā are to be known as Acirā, the bestower of rain, whose essence is the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and who is governed by the cosmic order.
It is the yielder of all desires, gentle, and devoid of the syllable *bhavāh*;
it consists of two feet, four feet, three feet, and six feet. (NarP 1.83.165)
The man who recites the one hundred and eight names of Sāvitrī— which consists of eight lines, nine lines, and a thousand syllables— [attains the supreme goal].
He shall be long-lived, happy, possessed of sons, victorious, and disciplined.
This, O Brahmin, has been described to you as the characteristic of the fivefold nature.
And preceded by the propitiation of mantras, it fulfills all desires.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Five Primordial Natures, Mantras, and Other Principles," in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Brahman, in the interval between the Kalpas, regarding Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest..."
While he was engaged in ascetic penance within the lotus of the world, two [beings] came into being for the purpose of creation.
The two demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha were born from the earwax of Viṣṇu;
as soon as they were born, they were in the waters characterized by the dissolution of the world.
Seeing Brahmā seated upon a lotus, standing at the height of his knees,
and observing that he had begun to eat, [the two] praised the Mother of the Universe.
Then the goddess, the creator of the world, the unsurpassed power of Śiva,
who resides within the eyes of Nārāyaṇa, became pleased as Sleep.
I shall explain her entire mantra and so forth; listen to that.
She is ruddy, wrathful, and peaceful, with her crest adorned by the moon.
The seer (ṛṣi) of the single-syllable seed-mantra is declared to be Śakti;
the meter (chanda) is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Bhuvaneśvarī.

Having performed the placement of the *mātṛkā* upon his body, he should sequentially perform the six limb-protections (*aṅga*) using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels, according to the paths of both withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
Then, one should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) for the sake of attaining the state of the deity:
Hṛllekhā on the head, Gaganā on the face, and [Gaganā] in the lotus of the heart.
One should visualize the red Karālikā at the secret place and Mahocchuṣmā on the two feet;
[and the others] in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, western, and also northern directions.
One should first reside within the elements together with their respective splendors, beginning with the short seed-syllables such as *sa* and so forth;
thereafter, one should sequentially apply the six limbs joined with their respective *jāti*s.
One should place Brahmā, conjoined with Gāyatrī, upon the forehead;
one should place Viṣṇu, accompanied by Sāvitrī, on the right cheek.
One should place Maheśvara, joined with Vāgīśvarī, on the left cheek;
then, having placed Dhanapati with Śrī, one should place him again at the tip of the left ear.
Having placed Rati upon the face of Smara, one should place Puṇya and Gaṇapati;
having placed them above the left ear, one should place them between the ear and the cheek.
The root mantra should be placed in the mouth;
then one should place the *bhūpa* syllables in the base of the throat, on the pair of breasts, on the left shoulder, and in the lotus of the heart.
The instructor [should place the syllables] on the left shoulder, on the pair of sides, at the region of the navel,
on the forehead, on the side and the belly, on the other side and the shoulder, and on the heart.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Brahmāṇīs and the others upon the body according to the prescribed characteristics and the ritual rule, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) on the body with the root mantra, one should meditate upon the Goddess.

Meditate upon her who resembles the rising sun, with towering breasts, three eyes, and a moon as her crown; she holds the boon-granting gesture, the noose, the goad, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and then perform oblations with the ten substances smeared with the three sweets,
using excellent fuel-sticks of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree in a quantity equal to one-tenth [of the recitation].
O Brahmin, grapes, dates, vātāda, sugar, coconut, rice, ghee, and sesame seeds are declared to be the eight substances.
Having meditated there upon Pārvatī, one should offer the arghya to the Sun;
[the mandala] has an eight-petaled lotus on the outside, surrounded by a circle of sixteen petals.
One should draw a very beautiful hexagon in the center of the *kaṇiṅka*;
then one should worship the pedestal (*pīṭha*) endowed with the nine powers (*navaśakti*).
Jayā, Vijayā, then Ajitā and Aparājitā, Nityā, Vilāsinī, Gaurī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā— these are the nine.
Having provided a seat enriched with seed-syllables (bīja), one should fashion the image by means of that very [syllable];
upon it, one should worship the Goddess after having invoked her along with the enclosures (āvaraṇas) in due order.
In the south-east, south-west, north-west, and north-east [corners], the practitioner of mantra should worship the deities of the limbs;
thereafter, he should worship the deities of the couples within the six corners.

In the northeast corner, the practitioner of mantras should worship Gāyatrī, who holds a radiant staff, a water-pot, a rosary, and displays the gesture of fearlessness; he should likewise worship Brahmā in that same form.
In the southwest corner (rakṣaḥ-koṇa), one should worship Sāvitrī, who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus,
is dressed in yellow garments, and likewise worship Viṣṇu in the same manner.

In the northwest corner, one should worship Sarasvatī, who is pure and holds a battle-axe, a rosary, and the gestures of protection and boon; and one should worship Rudra, characterized by the same attributes.
In the southeast corner, one should worship the jewel-pitcher and the jeweled casket,
as well as the yellow, pot-bellied bestower of wealth, who holds them both in his two hands.
One should worship Mahālakṣmī, who is mounted upon the shoulder of Kubera, embracing with her right hand the bearer of betel-leaf on her left.
In the west, one should worship Madana, who is red as a hibiscus flower, adorned with red ornaments, and holding a noose, a goad, and a bow along with arrows.
Embracing her husband with the right hand and holding a blue lotus with the left, one should properly worship Rati, who sits upon the lap of her lover.
In the northeast, one should properly worship Vighnarāja together with his beloved;
he is beautiful, holding a goad and a noose, with the digits of blood from a noble-limbed woman upon his fingers.
He beheld Vighnarāja, naked and clad in the directions, holding a skull-cup filled with honey-wine and a shimmering goblet from which jewels were dripping at his lotus-like hand.
She possessed a form like vermilion, was intoxicated with the playfulness of passion,
held a red lotus in one hand, and touched the banner with the other.
One should worship Puṣṭi, who is embraced by her beloved and is ruddy, and Ārci, who is naked;
then, the two Nidhis are to be worshipped on the sides of the hexagon at the pericarp.
One should worship these limbs upon the filaments; afterwards, one should worship them upon the petals:
first Anaṅgakusumā, and secondly Anaṅgamekhalā.
Then Anaṅgagamanā, likewise Anaṅgamadanāturā,
Bhuvanapālā, Gaganavegā, and after her, the sixth, [Gaganamūrti].
Śaśilekhā and Gaganalekhā—these eight are the Śaktis there;
dark-complexioned and bearing swords and shields, these Mothers are to be worshipped.
Outside the lotus, the attendant Śaktis are to be worshipped:
first Anaṅgadvayāsyādā, and after her, Anaṅgamadanā.
Then Bhuvanavegā, afflicted by love, became Bhuvanapālikā;
she was Sarvaśiśirā, Anaṅgavedanā, and Anaṅgamekhalā.
Holding in their lotus-like hands a goblet, a palm-leaf fan, betel, a radiant parasol, chowries, fine silken garments, and flowers.
One should worship the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), blazing with all their ornaments, outside;
and the Vajra and other [emblems] as well outside of them. In this manner, one should worship the Goddess.

The minister, having offered oblations with the finest fuel-sticks of the Aśvattha tree mixed with the three sweets, shall quickly bring Brāhmaṇas under his control; by means of a lotus-oblation, he shall likewise subjugate kings.
With *palāśa* flowers for his wife and with *kumuda* lotuses as well, the minister should perform a bath day after day with water over which the mantra has been recited twenty-five times.
He who sprinkles himself with water over which [the mantra] has been recited twenty-five times shall possess all good fortune; a man should drink that water in the morning.
Having attained great wisdom, one becomes a leader among poets;
camphor, agallochum, and saffron, when properly prepared together, [yield this result]. (NarP 1.84.46)
Having taken [the powder], one should apply a tilaka; this is the unsurpassed method for subjugating kings.
One should fashion a small image (puttalī) made of rice flour and mixed with honey.
Having recited [the mantra] and established its vital breath (prāṇa) within it, one should consume it on a Sunday;
this brings a king, a woman, or even a man under one's control. (NarP 1.84.48)
Standing in water reaching only to the neck and gazing at the sun risen above the water, one should recite the mantra three thousand times; from that, one shall obtain a desired maiden.
The practitioner of mantra should eat that food over which the mantra has been recited for the sake of attaining prosperity;
meanwhile, he should write the Māyā-bīja together with the name of the person to be influenced (sādhya) upon a wooden board or similar surface using ashes.
At that time, one should display the yantra so that the pregnant woman may give birth easily;
this is known as Bhuvaneśī, born from the thousand-armed [Avalokiteśvara].
O best of the twice-born, she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those men who remember her;
then, O Brahmin, once in another kalpa, there was the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Having conquered the world-protectors, he came to enjoy the three worlds;
then, oppressed by him, the gods went to Vaikuṇṭha for refuge.
Then, O best of sages, by the splendor arising from the limbs beginning with the discus, the goddess Mahālakṣmī became Śrī, embodied and pervading the three worlds.
Having herself slain Mahiṣa and his followers, the Sovereign of the World reached the forest of lotuses, bestowing desired boons upon those who worship her.
O twice-born one, listen as I describe her worship in brief:
she has her head adorned with a dot by the preceptor Mṛtyukrodha.
The seed-mantra of Śrī is declared to be the bestower of desired objects for those who worship her;
Bhṛgu is said to be the seer (ṛṣi), the Nivṛt-gāyatrī the metre (chandas), and Śrī the deity (devatā).
One should perform the six limb-projections (aṅga) in sequence using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels;
thereafter, one should meditate upon Śrī, the bestower of prosperity, who is the object of knowledge for the world.
She, whose radiance was like gold, who walked upon lotuses, was being sprinkled by four white elephants with golden jars of nectar held up by their own trunks.
Holding a boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a lotus, and a garland in her hands, clad in silken garments and wearing a crown—
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for success, and likewise perform one thousand oblations.
Having worshipped with fragrant flowers and lotuses soaked in honey,
one should fashion the form upon the seat arisen from Mahālakṣmī by means of the root mantra.
One should sacrifice as before to the ancillary deities, and then worship Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha on the petals of the directions.
They had the luster of snow, the *tāpī* flower, the *mālatī*, and the sapphire; they were clad in yellow garments and possessed four arms, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
In the petals at the intermediate corners, one should worship the elephants beginning with Damaka:
Damaka, Puṇḍarīka, Guggula, and Kuraṇṭaka. (NarP 1.84.64)
One should worship the deity Śaṅkhanidhi to the right of the Goddess, accompanied by a woman, with faces like pearls and rubies and lotus-faces slightly smiling. (NarP 1.84.65)
Intent on embracing one another, they bear conchs and lotuses;
their heads are marked by two conchs from which showers of jewels are falling.

One should worship him who has a protruding belly and the Kaṃbuka treasure, who possesses thick breasts like a stream of wealth (Vasudhārā), and who, on his left side, is accompanied by his beloved and the Paṅkaja treasure.
Resembling vermilion, their arms were locked together; they held red and blue lotuses, and were marked on their heads by two lotuses from which showers of jewels were pouring forth.
One should worship Tundila, Paṅkajanidhi, and Tattva, as well as Vasumatī, and these [goddesses] beginning with Abalākhyā on all sides at the tips of the petals.

Then, the month joined with the syllable *pra*, followed by *māsa* and *yavana*, and then the heart (*hṛdaya*)—this first mantra, consisting of eleven syllables, is for the worship of Mahāśaṅkha. (NarP 1.85.96)

The *haṃsa* (OM) joined with the Lord of Serpents (*haribhujaṅgeśa*) [HA], joined with the three long vowels and the moon [ĀM], followed by *tāriṇī*, ending with *kapālāya namaḥ*—this is the twelve-syllable mantra. (NarP 1.85.97)

One's own [seed-syllable] followed by the three long vowels, enriched with the breath (*an*), joined with the left tooth (*vāmadaśan*), for the sake of the world-protector (*lokapāla*)—this is the heart-mantra; this third one consists of the syllables of Śiva.

The seed-syllable of the illusory woman (māyāstrībīja), joined with half of ardha-duk, [is] "svaṃ"; [then] "svargakhādimaḥ" for Pāla, the support of all; likewise "sarvaḥ" and "sarvodbhavaḥ. // NarP_1,85.99 //
And "consisting of all purity"—these words ending in the dative case [are addressed] to all the Asuras;
[the names] Rudhirā, Ratidīrghā, Vāyu, Śubhrānila, and Surā [follow].
*Bhājanāya*, *bhagī*, *satyā*, *vikapālāya*, *hṛt*, and *manuḥ*;
this fourth color among the flavors is for the great worship of Śaṅkha.
Having worshipped the orb of the rising sun with water using the root mantra,
one should fill it with the thought that it is nectar, [honoring it] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth.
Having displayed the three-part mudrā, one should worship the lunar maṇḍala;
[the syllable] *repha* (ra), joined with the vowel *u*, the grace-vowel (*anugraha*), and the bindu, resides in the sky of the lotus of truthful speech. (NarP 1.85.103)
The practitioner, being purified, should recite the root mantra— accompanied by the *vipaddhvaṃsa* and *anusarga* [mantras]— over the water eight times.
Having cast the direction of the self through illusion, one should reveal the sky and the source;
there, having meditated upon a circle with eight and six corners, one should contemplate the Goddess.
One should worship her as previously described and then satisfy Maheśvarī with the root mantra using the index, middle, ring, and little fingers.
With the thumb, he recited four times over the water contained in the great conch shell the mantra consisting of the letter *kha*, the syllable *repha* (r), the *anu* (m),
and the *bindu* (ṃ), joined with the letter *bhṛgu* (b) and the moon (*indu*) [the nasal *m*].
One should satisfy Ānandabhairava with the mantra beginning with *dhruva* and ending with *namaḥ*;
then, one should sprinkle the materials for worship with that water mixed with half [the amount of] liquid.
Having displayed the *yoni-mudrā*, one should also prostrate to Bhavatāriṇī;
the ritual procedure for the *argha* offering has thus been fully explained, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).

One should worship the Goddess with delightful offerings upon the previously mentioned beautiful pedestal, which consists of a lotus with a six-cornered pericarp surrounded by the abode of the Earth (Dharāgṛha).
In the Mahīgṛha, one should worship Gaṇeśa and the others in the four directions—
[Gaṇeśa] who holds a noose, a goad, a skull-bowl, and a trident in his hands.
One should first worship Gaṇeśa, who is adorned with a multitude of ornaments,
holding a skull and a trident in his two hands, and decorated with serpents.
One should worship the charming Baṭuka on the right, surrounded by his own retinue,
holding a sword, a trident, a skull-cup, and a hand-drum in his hands.
In the west, one should worship the fierce Kṣetrapāla, who is black and naked,
holding a skull, a hand-drum, a noose, and a phallus in his hands.
One should worship the Yoginīs wearing red garments in the north, preceded by an excellent maiden;
one should worship Akṣobhya upon the head of the Goddess, and the auspicious mantra-ṛṣi.
Akṣobhya, cloth, and flowers are dear to the recipient;
the mantra for the worship of Akṣobhya is the six-pointed [figure]. (NarP 1.85.116)
One should worship Vairācana, Amitābha, the one named Padmanābhi,
and the one known as Śaṅkha-Pāṇḍura on the petals of the directions.
For the sake of attaining one's desired success, one should worship Lābhakā, Mānakā, Pāṇḍurā, and likewise Tārakā upon the lotus petals situated in the intermediate directions.

The names beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the Bindu, likewise followed by the vocative case, ending with "vrajapuṣpam," "pratīccha," and "agnipriyā," and preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ), [are to be used]. NarP_1,85.119 //
The mantras for the worship of Vairācana and the others have been proclaimed;
and Bhūdhara is at the four gates, along with Padmāntaka and Yamāntaka.
Thereafter, one should worship those named Vidyāntaka and Narāntaka;
then one should worship Śakra and the others, as well as the Vajra and the other [weapons], and subsequently perform the recitation (japa).
Thus worshipping the Goddess, one obtains scholarship, wonderful wealth, sons, grandsons, auspicious fame, and mastery over the people. (NarP 1.85.122)
*Tāra*, *māyā*, *śrīmat*, *akajaṭe*, *nīlasarasvatī*, *mahopratāre*, *devāsaḥ*, *sanetraḥ*, and the pair of *gadi*s. (NarP 1.85.123)
May Ramā cut away all gods, piśācas, long-lasting fever, wind-diseases, and dullness, as well as the pair of clouds and trees.
This mantra consists of fifty-two syllables, ending with *māyā* (hrl-lekha), *astra* (phaṭ), *agni* (ra), and *priyā* (svāhā).
With this, one should constantly worship daily and offer a bali-oblation to the Goddess.
When the mantra has been thus perfected, the practitioner performs the ritual applications;
specifically, for a newborn infant, within three days of birth.
The mantra-practitioner should inscribe the mantra upon the tongue with a golden rod, or else with a white blade of dūrvā grass, using honey and clarified butter.
When the eighth year has passed, even a child becomes a marvelous poet;
likewise, he remains unconquerable by other hosts of kings and is honored with wealth.
Having fashioned a peg from human bone as if it were a lotus stalk in water during an eclipse,
one should draw [the diagram] with it using oil, honey, and ghee.
One should encircle the mantra with the letters of the Mātṛkā on a lotus leaf;
having buried that petal in a square sacrificial pit provided with a boundary line (mekhalā), [one should proceed].
Having established the fire there, one should offer a thousand red lotuses, drenched in water mixed with cow's milk, while reciting this mantra.

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), one should offer an oblation (bali) with various jewels and even with pieces of meat, according to the rule, using the mantra for the oblation; that mantra for the oblation is now revealed.
*Tāraḥ*, *padme*, the pair *tandrī*, *viyat* (the sky), and the long *lohitaḥ*;
with *atri* mounted upon the portion of *viṣa*—this declares the word *Padmāvatī*.
The mantra for Bala consists of sixteen syllables: *jhiṇṭīśāḍhya-unila-svāhā*.
Then, at midnight, one should offer the bali-oblation using the previously mentioned mantra.
When this is done, that king shall become victorious among the wise, a preeminent poet,
the abode of the goddess of speech and prosperity, and capable of delighting the people.
If a mantra-practitioner recites [the mantra] one hundred times and wears yellow pigment (rocanā) upon his head,
whomever he looks upon will instantly become like his slave.
Having taken charcoal from a cremation ground on a Tuesday during the morning,
one should wrap it with that mantra and bind it with red threads.
Having consecrated it one hundred times with the root mantra, one should cast it into the house of an enemy;
within seven days, it will drive away the adversary along with his family.
Having written the mantra of Niśā with milk on a human bone,
one should empower it a thousand times on a Sunday at midnight.
Thrown into the enemy's abode, it causes them to fall from their circle;
thrown into one's own field, it destroys the crops and carries away the vigor of the body.
One should write the root mantra within a hexagon; the syllables of the target [mantra] should be on the filaments along with the vowels.
On the outside, there should be petals joined with the eight groups of consonants, surrounded by the ground of the lotus.
One should write the yantra on birch bark with juices of the *jatu* plant, encased in a clean cloth, bound with silk thread, and placed around the neck of a child; this will certainly bring success.
Worn on the left arm, it removes the fear of ghosts for women and grants sons;
worn on the right arm, it bestows wealth upon men who are destitute.
It bestows knowledge upon those who desire knowledge, and it grants victory to kings.

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Different Mantras of the Yakṣiṇīs," in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* in the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said: "Those incarnations of Sarasvatī that bestow success upon men have been described."
Now I shall describe to you the incarnations of Lakṣmī, which bestow the accomplishment of all goals.
The triad of seed-syllables is said to be Vāṇī, Manmatha, and Śakti;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is proclaimed as the meter (chandaḥ).
The deity is Tripurā Bālā; at the middle and the end are the seed-syllables of Śakti.
From the navel down to the feet is the first [part], from the navel up to the heart is the other.
One should sequentially place the third [syllable] from the crown to the heart within the bodies;
the first [syllable] on the left hand, that one on the right hand, and the last on both.
Furthermore, having placed the three seed-syllables on the head, the secret place, and the chest,
one should recite the mantra nine times during the rite known as the "nine-yoni" placement.
One should place [the syllables] on the two ears, the chin, the two temples, the lotus-face,
the two eyes, the nose, the two shoulders, and likewise on the abdomen.
One should place [the syllables] on the two elbows, the navel, the two knees, the penis, the head,
the two feet, the private parts, the two sides, and again on the heart.
One should place [the seed-syllables] beginning with Vāgbhava on the two breasts and the region of the throat, starting from the left side;
[one should place] Rati at the secret place and Prītimatī and the others at the heart.
One should visualize the seed-syllables of desire and so forth, born of the mind, within the center of the earth;
then one should again place the three beginning with the self of speech.
One should place Amṛteśī, Yogeśī, and Viśvayoni— the third—
on the head, in the mouth, at the heart, in the secret place, and also on the feet.
One should place Kāmeśī, enriched with the five seed-syllables, from the heart center onwards in sequence;
likewise, Māyā, Kāma, Vāk, Lakṣmī, and Kāmeśī constitute the five seed-syllables.
Manobhava, Makaradhvaja, Kandarpa, Manmatha, Kāmadeva, and Smara—these five are proclaimed as bestowers of the attainment of the *āsanas*. NarP_1,86.12 //

One should sequentially assign the deities of the arrows—beginning with Drāviṇī and preceded by the seed-syllables of the Mistress of Arrows—to the head, the six faces, the private parts, and the heart. (NarP 1.86.13)
*Drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ jūṃ saḥ*—this is the seed-syllable of the Lord of the Bow (Kāmadeva).
Likewise, there are the powers of attraction (*drāviṇī*), agitation (*kṣobhiṇī*), subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇī*), and summoning (*ākarṣaṇī*).
And Sammohanī—these five deities of the arrows are proclaimed;
with Kāma situated in the middle of the third speech, there shall be the six-limbed [mantra].
Then, one should contemplate the Goddess joined with the six long vowels;
one should meditate upon her as seated upon a red lotus, wearing red garments, and possessing three eyes.

One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, visualizing the Vidyā as resembling the rising sun and bearing a garland, the gesture of fearlessness, and a boon; and one-tenth of that number [of oblations] should be offered with flowers from the *kiṃśuka* tree.
Or one should offer oblations with flowers born from the enemy of horses (lotuses) mixed with sweet substances;
[one should worship] the yantra consisting of nine yonis, surrounded on the outside by eight petals.
One should assign the vowels to the filaments and the eight classes of consonants to the petals;
on the tips of the petals are tridents, and the lotus is encircled by the Mātṛkā.
When the yantra has been drawn in this manner, one should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis):
Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Kāminī, and Kāmadāyinī.
Having worshipped these seat-powers (pīṭhaśakti)— Rati, Ratipriyā, Nandā, and Manonmanī— as impelled [by the deity], one should assign the seat with its respective mantra.
The third [syllable] preceded by *vyoma* (ha) is the great station of Sadāśiva;
ending with *ṅe* and followed by *namaḥ*, this is the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*) for the lotus-seat of the Pretas.
Then, once the form has been fashioned from the sixteen-syllable mantra,
one should invoke the Goddess by means of the root mantra and recite it while offering various kinds of ritual services.
Having worshipped the Goddess in the central womb within the triangle, preceded by Rati—
Rati in the left corner, Prīti in the right, and Manobhavā in front.

From the fire-triangle within the womb, one should place the limbs of Agni; likewise, in the intermediate directions, outside the earth-circle, and from the east onwards, one should also remember the arrows at the tips.
Likewise, the goddesses Vāṇa and Śakti are in the eight wombs;
thereafter are Subhagā, Bhagā, and thirdly, Bhagasarpiṇī.
Bhagamālā, Anaṅgā, Nagādī, Kusumā,
Anaṅgamekhalā, and Anaṅgamadanā— these are the eight Śaktis.
Brāhmī resides in the filaments of the lotus, while the Bhairavas are on the petals;
the Mātṛs beginning with Dīrghā are to be worshipped, as are the eight Bhairavas beginning with Hrasva.
On the tips of the petals are eight seats: the first is called Kāmarūpa;
then Malaya, Kollagiri, Oḍḍiyāna, and Kulāntaka.
Likewise Jālandhara, Unnāsa, and Koṭapīṭha as the eighth;
one should worship Hetuka and Tripurāntaka in the underground chamber (bhūgṛha) in the ten directions.
Vaitāla, Agnijihva, Kamala, Antaka,
Ālina, Ekapāda, Bhīmarūpa, Vimala, and Hāṭakeśvara.
One should worship Śakra and the others, together with their weapons, in their respective directions;
outside of that, in the cardinal directions, one should worship Baṭuka, the Yoginī, and the Kṣetranāyaka.
By worshipping Gaṇeśa, Vidiśāsvara, the Vasus, Sūrya, and likewise Śiva,
as well as the Bhūtas, in this manner, a child shall become a master of wealth and knowledge.
Through oblations of red lotuses, women become submissive; through mustard seeds, kings;
and through *nandyāvarta*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *kunda*, *pāṭala*, and *campaka* flowers.
Through oblations of flowers or even bilva fruits, Lakṣmī becomes stable;
by means of guḍūcī mixed with milk, the practitioner of mantras conquers untimely death.
By performing the homa with dūrvā grass as previously described, one attains health and long life;
by offering oblations of moon-plant, agallochum, and surā, one obtains knowledge and poetic skill.
Through oblations of *palāśa* flowers, one attains success in speech; through oblations of food, one obtains food.
By offering parched grain (*lāja*) mixed with fragrant milk and curd, one shall conquer diseases.
One should apply red sandalwood, camphor powder, agallochum, yellow pigment, sandalwood,
saffron, and spikenard in successive proportions.

In the cremation ground, on the night of the black fourteenth day, amidst the misty waters, [he was found] by those measured by the earth (1), moon (1), joy (9), ocean (4), directions (10), seven (7), and the Vedas (4).
A maiden should grind these [ingredients] and, having consecrated them with the mantra, she should apply a tilaka-mark with it; by its mere sight, she shall bring people under her control.
Having turned back the curse of the Goddess for the sake of accomplishing her purposes, [she summoned] beings such as elephants and lions, as well as Rākṣasas and Śākinīs.
Having first performed the unlocking [of the door], one should thereafter perform the recitation (japa) of this;
whoever should recite the Boar, Bhr̥gu, and Fire within the first seed-syllable.
In the middle and at the beginning, there are the sky and the swan; at the end of the middle, however, is fire.
At the beginning and the end, according to the sequence of the third [syllable], is one's own smoke-bannered [deity].
Having thus recited the mantra one hundred times, the vidyā becomes free from curses and bestows its fruit;
however, one must never separate the letter *ra* from the first or the last seed-syllable.
Or rather, another method for the removal of the curse has been proclaimed by the wise:
the first [syllable] is indeed the third, Kāma, Kāma, and then Vāgbhava.
The mantra consisting of nine syllables, ending with the word *manmathanaṅga*, is proclaimed;
when recited one hundred times, it shall turn back the curse upon the young girl.
The two mantras Caitanya and Āhlādin, when recited, bring about the state of being free from bonds;
the three vowels are the mantra of consciousness, while Dhara, Śānti, and Anugraha are [the mantras of] the earth.
The mantra of Kāma, beginning with *Tārā* (Oṃ) and ending with the *Hṛdaya* (Namaḥ), follows the *Āhlādinī* mantra;
likewise, it is joined with the three illuminating mantras of the three seed-syllables.
Having first made them well-illumined, one should recite them for the attainment of desired success:
the pair of *vada* with long *ambu* (water), followed by *smṛti*, *bāla*, *vana*, and *anaṅga*. (NarP 1.86.49)
The true one with eyes is such for us, or rather, that which illuminates the letters of speech;
in the moist and wetting [state], Vaikuṇṭha is the long *sva*, the final *ga* of the right.
The syllable *nidrā* (pra), together with the moon (*sa*), makes the syllables of Śiva (*śivārṇā*) shine in the middle;
the *tāra* (oṃ) brings about liberation, for this [mantra] does not fail to illuminate the faces of the letters.

A young woman who has been consecrated with the *dīpinī* mantra does not achieve success even if she is practiced; rather, one should cause her to desire the enemy's wealth for the purpose of agitating his enemies. (NarP 1.86.52)
One should recite the seed-syllables of Kāma, Vāk, and Antya for the subjugation of the three worlds; one who is disciplined should recite the seed-syllables of Kāma, Antya, and Vāṇī for liberation.
At the commencement of the worship of Bālā, one should honor the three kinds of gurus:
the divine stream (divyaugha), the perfected stream (siddhaugha), and the human stream (mānavaugha); thus they are threefold.
Paraprakāśa, Parameśāna, and likewise Paraśiva;
then Kāmeśvara, Mokṣa as the sixth, and Kāma, the immortal, as the final one.
These are indeed the divine streams of power (śaktis), ending with the state of bliss:
the one called Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, the one called Aghora, and Vāmadeva.
O Sage, these five known as the Sadyojāta [stream] are remembered as the Siddhaugha;
the Mānavaugha is to be fully understood from the oral tradition of one's own guru.
In the yantra consisting of nine wombs, the most excellent practitioner should inscribe the seed-syllables three times, starting from the central womb and proceeding clockwise.
One should inscribe three syllables each upon the eight petals of the *gāyatrī*;
having encircled this with the *mātṛkā*, one should draw two outer squares (*bhūpura*) around it.

The *traipura* [yantra] is said to be formed by the six corners of the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) intersecting one another; it is accomplished through the application of recitation (*japa*). (NarP 1.86.60)
Held by her arm, she bestows wealth, fame, happiness, and sons;
at the end of desire, one should know the Goddess Tripurā as "vidmahe kaviṣaṃ bhahim. (NarP 1.86.61)
"Bakaḥ," "khaḍgī," "samārūḍhaḥ," "sanetraḥ," "agniḥ," and "dhīmahi"—when these are joined with "klinne" and "pracodayāt," this is proclaimed as the Āditya [Vidyā]. (NarP 1.86.62)
The Gāyatrī of Tripura bestows all perfections and is served by the gods;
now another incarnation of Lakṣmī is proclaimed, which grants success to men.
The beginning of the Vedas, Girijā, Padmā, Manyathu, Hṛdaya, Bhṛgu,
the goddess Māheśvarī ending in the vocative particle ṅe, Annapūrṇā, and Dahanāṅganā.
This vidyā consists of twenty syllables;
its sage is Druhiṇa, its metre is Dhṛti, and its deity is proclaimed to be Annapūrṇeśī.
The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) is performed with the seed-syllable *hṛllekhā* augmented by the six long vowels;
one should place [the mantras] upon the nine locations: the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, shoulders, and anus. (NarP 1.86.66)
There are nine sections, and their respective numbers of verses are now declared:
Then, one should meditate upon the Queen of the Gods, whose form is measured by the number of syllables [of the mantra],
who has a golden complexion, three eyes, and is adorned with garments and ornaments.
One should meditate upon the goddess Bhūramāsā, who is joined [with her consort] and whose lotus-like hands hold a golden vessel;
likewise, one should perform a hundred thousand recitations and ten thousand oblations with sacrificial porridge smeared with ghee.
Worship is prescribed on a pedestal (pīṭha) enriched with the powers of Jayā and the other [attendant goddesses],
consisting of a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a sixteen-petaled lotus.
In the yantra joined with the bhūpura, one should offer the mantra through Māyā;
and in the three corners beginning with the southeast, [one should place] Śiva, Varāha, and Mādhava.
They are called "manus" when recited with their respective mantras;
the *praṇava*, the *manu* [letter] joined with the moon, the sky, the heart, and Śivā. (NarP 1.86.72)
This seven-syllabled mantra of Māruta is for the worship of Śiva;
one should first recite the mantras of Vārāha and Nārāyaṇa. (NarP 1.86.73)
Then, having worshipped the six limbs, one should worship Dharā on the left and Ramā on the right with their respective mantras; O Lord of Sages, those two are now being described.
"O Uṇṇakā, mistress of food, say 'Give me food, give me food!
and cause this man to be given food even at the end of his life, O Analasundarī! (NarP 1.86.75)
O Brahmin, for the desire of land, the twenty-two syllable mantra has *bhūmi* as its enclosure (*saṃpuṭa*);
for the desire of fortune (*lakṣmī*), it has *śrī* as its enclosure; and for the attainment of progeny, it is joined with *candra*.
"Bhuvaḥ" is declared to be the seed-syllable; the "Śrī-bīja" has been previously cited.
One should worship [the deities] preceded by these four seed-syllables situated at the beginning of the mantra.
The four Śaktis are on the four corners of the Veda-diagram, as are Parā and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Kamalā and Subhagā, along with Brāhmī and the others, reside upon the eight petals.
In the sixteen-spoked [wheel] are remembered Māna, Dā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi,
Prīti, Rati, Hrī, Śrī, Svadhā, and then Svāhā as the tenth.
Jyotsnā, Haimavatī, Chāyā, Pūrṇimā, Saṃhati,
and Amāvāsyā— these should be worshipped, preceded by the vital breath (prāṇa), within the Lord of Mantras (mantreśa).
In the *bhūpura*, there should be the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and their weapons in front of them.
When this mantra has been mastered through such means as recitation (*japa*) and the accumulation of wealth, [one attains success].
A minister like Kubera is born, honored by the people.
Now, O best of sages, another incarnation of Lakṣmī is described.
The Praṇava, Śānti, Aruṇā, Kriyāḍhyā, and Candrabhūṣitā; at the end of all [the names] of Bagalāmukha, they are joined with Indhikā and Hrādinī.
The yellow [syllable] *pīta* is established upon *ajarāyuk*, joined again with *dīrghodasa*.
One should utter the word for "speech" (*vācam*), then "mouth" (*mukham*), then "foot" (*padam*), and at the end, one should state the word for "tongue" (*jihvāpadam*). (NarP 1.86.84)
"Kīlaya" (pierce), followed by "and destroy the intellect," ending with one's own seed-syllable;
this is proclaimed as the mantra of Bagalā, beginning with Tāra (Om) and Agnisundarī (Hrīm). // NarP_1,86.85 //
The sage is Nārada, the metre is Bṛhatī, and the deity is Bagalāmukhī; [the worship is performed] with five eyes, five arrows of Kāma, nine, five, and ten syllables [in the respective parts].
Having thus fashioned the limbs [of the mantra], one should then meditate upon her who wears yellow garments,
seated upon a golden throne, possessing a golden luster, the paralyzer [of enemies], and crowned by the moon.
Visualizing her thus, holding a mallet, a noose, a thunderbolt, and a tongue in her hands,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with flowers produced from the *caṃpaka* tree.
One should offer oblations with flowers upon the pedestal and worship this Bālā;
for the sake of worship, one should draw the yantra using sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and other such substances.
One should worship her upon a [mandala] consisting of a triangle, a six-petalled lotus, an eight-sided figure, and a sixteen-spoked wheel;
likewise, one should worship Maṅgalā, Staṃbhinī, Jṛṃbhiṇī, and Mohinī.
Vaśyā, Calā, Balākā, Bhūdharā, the one named Kalmaṣā,
Dhātrī, Kalanā, Kālakarṣiṇī, and Bhrāmikā as well.
And the slow-moving one, the abode of enjoyment, and the future one are remembered as the sixteenth;

The best of teachers should place the root [mantra] beginning with "Siddhalakṣmīpada" upon the foundation mandala, and by means of that very [mantra], he should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*).
Having thus cast off his body, he should meditate upon the deity of the mantra—
dark-complexioned, listening to the speech of a parrot, with one foot placed [upon the other] and her hair disheveled.
Wearing a crescent moon and playing the lute with intoxicating sweetness,
she was clad in red garments, and her crest was adorned with a garland of white water-lilies.

One should recite the mantra ten thousand times for Mātaṅgī, who has conch-shell-like ears and a head shining with variegated colors; and one-tenth of that number [of oblations] should be offered with flowers from the Madhūka tree.
One should offer oblations with flowers mixed with the three sweets for the sake of mantra-siddhi;
one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with a triangular pericarp.
It is surrounded on the outside by eight petals and encircled by sixteen petals;
it is made square on the exterior, captivating to the sight with its splendor.
Upon this seat, one should worship these nine Śaktis in sequence,
beginning with Vibhūti as previously mentioned and ending with Mātaṅgī.
At the very end, "Obeisance to the one seated on the lotus-throne of power" (śaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ);
preceded by the seed-syllables of Speech, Truth, and Lakṣmī, this is declared to be the mantra for the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha).
Having conceived the form by means of the root mantra and having invoked the deity therein,
the knower of mantras should worship according to this procedure that is about to be described.
The wise practitioner should worship Rati and the others in the three corners as before;
the mantra-reciter should worship the five Hṛllekhās in the center and in the cardinal directions.

Then, the knower of the ritual rules should worship the limbs, which possess a radiant luster and hold a noose, a goad, and the gestures of fearlessness and granting of boons, according to the previous procedure.
One should worship the arrows in the cardinal directions and sacrifice the fifth in front;
then, one should worship Anaṅgakusumā and the others in the middle of the petals.

Holding a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons, and possessing ruddy complexions, Lakṣmī and the others, holding lutes in their hands, are to be worshipped again on the tips of the petals.
On the eight outer petals, one should worship Manmatha and the others, who are arrogant with passion;
they have their secondary limbs as quivers and so forth, and they carry flower-arrows, quivers, and bows.
The Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, who possess the characteristics described, are to be worshipped situated upon the petals;
in front of them, the wise one should worship the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga.
Furthermore, sixteen powers (śaktis), beginning with Vāmā, are to be worshipped upon the sixteen petals; they are dark-complexioned and sing with lutes (kalavīṇās).
Furthermore, one should worship four [goddesses] in the four directions of the square:
Mātaṅgī and the others, who are intoxicated with passion and have hands shimmering with lutes.
One should worship Vighneśa in the southeast corner, Durgā in the northwest,
the Baṭukas in the southwest, and Kṣetrapa in the northeast.
The world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped outside together with their weapons, such as the vajra;
when this mantra is joined, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) shall accomplish his own desired goal. (NarP 1.87.145)
One becomes an abode of fortune through *mallikā*, *jāti*, and *punnāga* flowers,
or by offering oblations with the fruits or leaves produced from the *bilva* tree.

Through lotuses, one attains the acquisition of a kingdom for a prince; through blue lotuses, one obtains prosperity; with alkaline substances mixed with honey, one shall subjugate the entire world; and [with the same] one shall win over a woman.
The smoke from fuel-sticks of *vañjula* quickly spreads rain;
with pieces of *amṛtā* smeared with milk, one destroys fever and gains gold and food.
Through *dūrvā* grass one obtains long life; through rice grains one becomes wealthy;
and through *kadaṃba* flowers, all things come under one's control when they are soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhura*).
Gold, when offered with flowers produced from the *nandyāvarta*, bestows the perfection of speech;
one should offer oblations with *nimba* blossoms for the sake of attaining desired prosperity and abundance.
By means of *palāśa* flowers, a man becomes endowed with golden luster;
likewise, sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, saffron, and gorocanā [yield these results]. (NarP 1.87.151)
Offerings made of *nirguṇḍī* roots, when sacrificed into the fire or applied as a forehead mark (*tilaka*), bring about subjugation and endearment; by such a homa, a man is released from fetters.
Gold mixed with salt and neem oil destroys enemies;
gold mixed with salt and powdered turmeric can paralyze the world.
O best of the twice-born, this Mātaṅgī-siddhavidyā has been declared to you;
listen further as I describe another incarnation. 1.87.154.
If the mantra of Dhūmāvatī, which consists of eight syllables, is further colored in two ways— namely, enriched with Dīpaka, Aprīti, and Candra,
and likewise with Vati and Vahni— it is the beloved of Fire.
The sage is Pippalāda, the metre is Nivṛt, and the sovereign goddess is Dhūmāvatī;
one should contemplate [the mantra] with the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels. (NarP 1.87.156)
Then one should meditate upon Dhūmāvatī, the subduer of enemies—
discolored, flickering, fierce, tall, and clad in soiled garments.
With disheveled hair, slender, a widow with sparse teeth,
mounted upon a chariot bearing the banner of a heron, and with pendulous breasts.
She had hands like the sun, held a skull in her hand, was clothed in space,
possessed excessively thick hair, and had extremely crooked, curved eyes.

Having thus contemplated her as one who is constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, who causes fear, and who delights in quarreling—one should recite the mantra ending with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and *phaṭ*. (NarP 1.87.160)
Having placed the seed-syllable upon the object to be accomplished and having positioned the corpse upon it, one should recite the mantra;
then, having seized the corpse by the name of the enemy, one should recite the mantra.
Wearing a turban and a tunic, the wise man, while Kṛṣṇa is present day and night,
should remain fasting in a cremation ground, a forest, or an empty temple.
Restraining his speech and meditating on the Goddess incessantly for the sake of the mantra’s accomplishment,
an enemy who rises up against him more than a thousand times is seized by fever.
Peace for fever may be achieved by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or even by milk;
having first written the mantra and so forth, one should then write the name of the enemy.
One should likewise write the second letter of the name of Manu followed by the name of the enemy;
through the recitation of the mantra ten thousand times in that direction, the death of the corpse shall occur.

Having burned a heron in the cremation fire and taking its ashes, one who knows the mantras should recite the name of the adversary eight hundred times; this brings about the eradication of the enemy.
Having prepared [an image] with cremation-ground ashes, one should place a corpse upon it;
during the dark fortnight, one should recite [the mantra] while obstructing those who are hostile.
And one should offer incense made from buffalo milk, which causes the ruin of enemies;
thus has the fourfold descent been briefly described.
What more do you wish to ask of Durgā, the Mother of the World?
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Fourfold Mantra of Durgā," in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, having thus heard about the sacrifice preceded by mantra-recitation and meditation...
Among all those who have entered [the spiritual path], Nārada is the one who beholds the gods.
Filled with humility, he inquired about the worship of Śrī Rādhā, the primordial mother of the world, as well as of her various incarnations and portions.
Nārada said: "O Sage,
by your grace I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, and I have been born anew,
having heard the majesty of the mantras of the Mother of the Universe."
Just as the incarnations of the faces of Lakṣmī have been proclaimed,
so too do I wish to hear the majesty of the incarnations of Rādhā.
O best among the wise, tell me truly the number, the forms, and the powers of those incarnations of Rādhā that grant all perfections.
Having heard these words of Nārada,
Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā, meditated upon the lotus feet of Rādhā and spoke.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Brahmin, I shall proclaim the most secret of secrets—
the account of the incarnation of Rādhā, which bestows the fulfillment of desires upon those who worship her.
Candrāvalī and Lalitā were her two very dear friends;
Candrāvalī is remembered as the sovereign of the eight women headed by Mālāvatī.
Lalitā is considered the sovereign of the eight [goddesses] headed by Kalāvatī;
those headed by Mālāvatī are said to be for the worship of Rādhā’s feet.
Now hear the names of the mistresses of Lalitā:
Kalāvatī, Madhumatī, Viśākhā, and she named Śyāmalā.
Śaibyā, Vṛndā, and she named Śrīdhara— all of whom possessed forms identical to her—
along with others headed by Suśīlā, were declared to be the thirty-two companions.
Listen to them, O highly fortunate one; I shall proclaim their names to you:
Suśīlā, Śaśilekhā, Yamunā, Mādhavī, and Rati.
Kadambamālā, Kuntī, Jāhnavī, Svayaṃprabhā,
Candrānanā, Padmamukhī, Sāvitrī, and Sudhāmukhī.
Śubhā, Padmā, Pārijātā, Gauriṇī, Sarvamaṅgalā,
Kālikā, Kamalā, Durgā, Virajā, Bhāratī, and Surā.
Gaṅgā, Madhumatī, Sundarī, Candanā, Satī,
Aparṇā, and Manasānandā— these thirty-two are the beloveds of Rādhikā.
Once, the goddess Chhalilā, in male form with a body as dark as Kṛṣṇa,
created sixteen kalās, all of which possessed a splendor equal to his own.
O best of sages, I shall describe their mantra, as well as their meditation, the sequence of yantras and worship, and the secret found in all tantras.
Vāta, Marut, Agni, Vahni, Dharā, Kṣmā, Jala, Cāriṇī, Vimukha, Cara, Śuci, Vibhu, Vanaspati, Śakti, and Svara are the vowels. 18.18.
Prāṇa, Tejas, Sthira, Vāyu, and likewise Vāyu, Prabhā, Jyakūmabhra, Nāda, Dāvaka, and then Pātha. NarP_1,88.19 //
Space, fire, earth, water, and the light of the void-impulse; earth, taste, the bow, pervasion, burning, and also taste and water.
Viyat, Sparśa, Hṛt, Haṃsa, Halāgrāsā, Halātmikā,
Candrāvalī, Lalitā, and Haṃselā are considered the heroines in the Nāyaka [system].
Rādhā herself, abiding as the morsel of food, is the very embodiment of Śakti;
the remaining sixteen digits (kalās) are known as her thirty-two constituent parts.
O Lord of Sages, the entirety of verbal expression is pervaded by these alone;
among them, she who is headed by Lalitā has attained the state of being the Sixteenth.
The goddess Śrī Rādhā Sundarī is proclaimed by the Tantrikas as Kurukullā, Vārāhī, and both Candrā and Lalitā. (NarP 1.88.24)
I shall now declare to you, exactly as it is, the collection of mantras born from them:
[the mantra] uttered playfully by the heart (ha), the vital breath (sa), the earth (la), the swan (ha), the sun (sa), and fire (ra).

Listen now to the threefold classification according to the *haṃsa-bheda*, in its proper order: the first begins with *haṃsa*, the middle begins with *yā*, and the one in which *haṃsa* stands at both the beginning and the middle is the last.
That very third nature is the fourth by means of the final Māyā;
among these, three others exist for the sake of liberation through the attainment of the fourth, while the [remaining] three are for prosperity.
Thus has the Vidyā of Tripurasundarī been proclaimed by Sarumata; the seed-syllable of Vaśinī is said to consist of the letters *da*, *ha*, *bhu*, *mi*, *ra*, *sa*, *akṣa*, and *mā*.
The vital breath (prāṇa) joined with the power of essence (rasa-śakti) is the great syllable of Kāmeśvarī;
through its union with the void (śūnya), water (ambu), essence (rasa), and fire (agni), it becomes the mantra of Mohanī.
The mantra of Aruṇa is said to consist of the pervasive one (vyāpaka), followed by rasa (6), akṣi (2), and svaya (3), then the pure seed-syllable (vimalabīja);
it is joined with jyā (1), nabha (0), dāha (3), and vahni (3). (NarP 1.88.30)
This mantra, which consists of *kaṃ* joined with *nabhoda* (the sky) and is pervaded by ten earths (*kṣmā*), is declared to be victorious and the bestower of victory everywhere. (NarP 1.88.31)
The mantra of Kaulinī, which bestows all perfections and is proclaimed as the supreme sovereign of all, consists of the *grāsa* (the devourer), the sky, fire, and the letter *sva*. (NarP 1.88.32)

With these eight mantras, joined with the [eight] groups and ending with the goddesses of speech (vāgdevatās), there should be a ritual placement (nyāsa) by which one becomes identical in nature with the Goddess.

One should place [the seed-syllables] in the aperture, on the forehead, at the *ājñā* center, in the throat, and in the heart; likewise in the navel, the *ādhāra*, and in both feet, from the base up to the tips.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) with the seed-syllable enriched by the six long vowels;
[one should meditate on] Lohitā Lalitā, who holds in her hands an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a goad.
One should contemplate her as holding the King of Desire (Kāmarāja) on her lap, bound by a cord;
the Goddess in the center is indeed one alone, yet she abides in sixteen forms.
Therefore, one should worship fifteen other goddesses upon her body;
Śiva is said to be the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas) is declared [to be the same], and the deities (devatās) are Lalitā and the others.
In the collection of names for all the eternal obstructions,
I shall hereafter explain the ritual applications in detail within this chapter.
Now, O Nārada, listen to that second among the sixteen Nityās who has been described as Kāmeśvarī, the bestower of all desires.
The first [syllable] is *śuci* joined with its own [consonant]; the second would be *lalitā*.
Then there is *śūnya* joined with fire (*agni*), followed by that which is conjoined with the pervader of the mountains (*rayovyāpta*).

The vital breath (prāṇa), together with the fire of essence (rasāgni) and the pair of voids (śūnyayugma) accompanied by the mobile (cara); furthermore, this [vital breath] is joined with the burning of the lineage of space (nabhogotra).

The syllable *aṃ* joined with the mobile (*ca*) and the heart (*hṛt*) conjoined with the nine powers (*navaśakti*)—this is the eleven-syllabled eternal Kāmeśvarī, the sole bestower of desires. (NarP 1.88.42)
One should perform the six limbs in sequence using the very syllables of the root-vidyā:
the heart with one, the head with that many, and then two each for the remaining two.
In the same way, the weapon is proclaimed to be with four [syllables] for the eyes,
and with one for the sight, ears, and pair of nostrils, as well as for the tongue, heart, navel, and private parts.
Thereafter, one should install the syllables of the Vidyā upon all the limbs, from the head down to the tips of the toes, by means of pervasion in these locations.
One should perform the pervasive [protection] with the entire [mantra] according to the stated sequence.
Now I shall explain the meditation (dhyāna) as enjoined for the daily worship (nityapūjā).
By which the Goddess, being well-pleased, grants one's desire without effort—
she who resembles ten million rising suns and is radiant with a crown of rubies.
Adorned with necklaces, neck-ornaments, girdles, rings, anklets, and the like, she was dressed in red garments and beautified by jeweled ornaments.

she held a noose and a goad, as well as a bow made of sugarcane and arrows of flowers.
Then, once the mantra has been mastered, the practitioner should perform the ritual applications, [visualizing the goddess] holding in her hands a jewel-bowl filled with wine and granting boons.
Now I shall describe the third [vow], named Bhagamālinī. It begins with Kāmeśvarī and so forth; it consists of six [syllables] and ends with the syllable *rasa*. NarP_1,88.52 //
After *dharā* and *yuk*, *cara* follows; thereafter, *rasa* is said to be stable (*sthira*).

The syllable *sthirā* is joined with *bhū*, *gotrā*, *sadāha*, *agni*, and *rasa*;
it is *sthirā* again, followed by *nabhas* joined with *marut*, and endowed with *rasa* and *varṇa*.
Then the mercury (rasa) is joined with sthirā and subsequently with marut;
then, sprinkled with ambahaṃsacara, the mercury shall again become stable.
The Haṃsa is endowed with Sthirādhara, along with Vyāpta and Cara;
then Rasa, Sthirā, Vyāpta, and Bhū, joined with Śūnya and Agni.

Rasa, Sthirā, then Sāgni (Sā with Agni), Śūnyaṃ (Śūnya) joined with Tavi (Ta), Marut (Ra), Rayaḥ (Ya), Śūnyaṃ (Śūnya) joined with Agni, and after that, Hṛt (Ha), Ahaṃ (Sa), and Sā (Ca). // NarP_1,88.57 //
Rasa, Sthirāmbu, Viyat joined with Svaya, and Prāṇa;
Dāha, Agni, Ugrasas, Tasmāt, Sthira, Kṣmā joined with Dāha,
and Sacara— these are the Javī-vidyās in sequence from the third onwards.

Then there is a group of four vowels, followed by the sixth [vowel] (rasa), then the stable one (sthirā) joined with the heart-vowel (hṛd) and water (ambu), then burning (dāha) with earth (kṣmā), then the moving one (sacara) which is swift (javī) and the heart (hṛt).
Dāha is joined with water and wind; in the sky, it is joined with fire and taste.
Sthira is joined with wind; Śūnya is joined with fire and the two moving [elements] of space.
The *haṃsa* [breath] is joined with the pervasive wind; from that, the void (*śūnya*) and water (*ambu*) are pervasive.
Burning (*dāha*) is joined with the syllables of the lineage (*gotra*), and likewise burning as well as speed (*raya*).
The heart (hṛd) together with the earth (dhara), the burning (dāha) and the fire (raya) joined with the two moving ones (cara);
then the taste (rasa) and the firm one (sthirā), and thereafter the vital breath (prāṇa) accompanied by taste and fire (agni). // NarP_1,88.62 //
A pair of zeros joined with the letter *ca* (cha), then preceded by that [same], and a pair of zeros with *go* (ga) and *tra* (ta), joined with water (*va*) and the letter *ca* (cha). (NarP 1.88.63)

after Gotra comes Āhamarud-yuktā, which constitutes the water-assignment (ambunyāsa). NarP_1,88.64 //
Water conjoined with fire, or conjoined with air;

O Brahmin, the *grāsa* (the morsel) is conjoined with the earth (*bhū*), and the *rasa* (the essence) is pervaded by that; then the heart (*hṛt*) follows, as well as burning (*dāha*), water (*ambu*), and subsequently the fire (*agni*) accompanied by water and air (*marut*).
Śūnya and Kevala, Rasa, and that which consists of the moving and the stationary; Viyat joined with Ambu, Dāha joined with Agni, and Śuci joined with Sāyu.

These, in order, are: Jya, Sacara, Rasa, Bhu, and Nabha-yuta; then Hamsa twice joined with Cara, and finally Prana joined with Rasagni.
The pair of voids (śūnya) joined with the letter *ca* (carayuta) is "heart-burning" (*hṛddāha*); it is joined with water (*ambu*), wind (*marut*), and sky (*vyoma*).

possessed a beautiful smile and a radiant countenance, and was adorned with divine ornaments.

she was endowed with eight arms, and she was resplendent with ornaments of rubies.
The sky was reddened by the mingling rays from her ruby crown;
she wore yellow silk garments and jeweled anklets and a girdle.
She was radiant with ornaments of clusters of blossoms interspersed with red pearls,
and she held a jewel-lotus, a conch, a *puṇḍra* mark, a sugarcane bow, and the orb of the full moon.
Holding a white lotus and a golden-horned vessel with her left arms,
she holds the flower-arrowed god (Kāmadeva) and a citron with her right hands.
Having thus meditated upon Vahnivāsinī, who is surrounded on all sides by Śaktis bearing their respective names, one should worship her within the form of the fire.
O Sage, she by whose mere remembrance the three worlds become subject to one's will is the seventh eternal goddess, Mahāvajreśvarī.
I shall proclaim its vidyā, which bestows perfect accomplishment upon practitioners:
the second [syllable] of Vahnivāsinī and the fourth of Nityaklinnā.
The fifth begins with Bhagamālā; the second belongs to Bheruṇḍā;
the second [syllable] of Nityaklinnā is the third; and the sixth and seventh [syllables] are [the fourth and fifth].
The eighth and the ninth should likewise be at the beginning; then the last one again;
then two, then one by one, then two by two, and finally two.
Having enveloped [the body] with Māyā, one should perform the six limbs in sequence;
one should install each [limb] with ten syllables of the mantra, each encased by Śakti.
In the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, chest, navel, and private parts, respectively,
[one should meditate on] her who is red, clad in red garments, and adorned with red garlands and ornaments.
Four-armed and three-eyed, radiant with a crown of rubies,
she holds a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and likewise an arrow with a pomegranate seed as its tip.
Holding [the weapons] with her arms and eyes that are cooled by compassion and great love,
she gazes upon the practitioner within the six-angled star, the lotus, and the city of the earth.
Seated comfortably in the center of the wheel, her lotus-face smiling,
she is surrounded by Śaktis who are identical in form to herself, and she resides in the midst of yellow.
She was surrounded on all sides by Śaktis seated in swaying boats upon the lion-throne,
who were constantly engaged in diversions such as coming and going.
One should meditate on the Mistress of Mantras as she acts within the crimson ocean;
this is declared the seventh [dūtī], and now hear also of the eighth messenger.
The first [syllable] shall be Vajreśvarī and so forth; then follows that joined with space (viyat) and fire (agni);
then water (ambu) joined with wind (marut), and then the lineage (gotrā) joined with earth (kṣmā).
Thereafter, one should be joined with the pure *rayovyāsa*;
then the *dūtīs* of the *atyārṇas* residing in fire are proclaimed as the eternal (*nityā*) ones.
The six-limbed [protection] of the vidyā should be performed with the mantra joined with the six long vowels;
one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the five [senses], beginning with the ears, using the syllables encased by that very [mantra].
Having placed the sixth [syllable] upon the nose, one should place the pervasive [syllable] with the Vidyā,
which possesses a radiance equal to the midday sun during the summer season.
She wears a crown of nine jewels, has three eyes, and is clad in crimson garments;
her body shines with a splendor enhanced by various ornaments.
She has a pure smile and eight arms, being praised by great sages;
with her left hands she holds a noose, a shield, a mace, and a jeweled goblet.
Holding in her right hands a goad, a sword, a small knife, and likewise a lotus,
she is intent upon granting the desired objects of the practitioner.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess, the messenger who destroys misconduct.
Thus has this [mantra] been described to you, which wards off all calamities. (NarP 1.88.127)
O Nārada, she is the bestower of fortune, the cause of the abiding in Śiva-hood, and the giver of all perfections; now hear of your ninth eternal goddess, named Tvaritā.
I shall proclaim [the mantra] which bestows fame, knowledge, wealth, health, and happiness;
first is that of Vahnivāsinī, and immediately after that, the Dūtīs and the others.
The Haṃsa is the Earth itself, joined with the moving radiance;
the Vāyu is endowed with the movement of light and possessed of the power of grasping.
By means of the burning of the heart, there is likewise the eighth [syllable] of Vahni (Agni);
*Haṃsa* joined with earth (*kṣma*) and ether (*kha*) is the first [syllable], and that same [syllable] joined with *cara* is the second.

One should perform the assignment of the limbs upon the hands and the body using pairs of syllables in the sequence of six:
on the head, forehead, throat, heart, navel, and likewise the base (ādhāra).
