Listen now to the meditation on the mantra-syllables— those situated in the second, penultimate, and middle positions, as well as the others— preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ) and so forth, which bestows all accomplishments.
She was of a dark complexion and auspicious form, radiant with the beauty of fresh youth,
and adorned with eight serpents arranged in pairs, their ornaments brilliant.
With earrings, armlets, girdles, and anklets—
[all] belonging to those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, who possessed terrifying forms.
Clad in a garment of young shoots,
her arms adorned with beautiful bracelets made of peacock feathers, she shone with a crown of rubies.
She wore a chaplet made of peacock feathers, possessed that very umbrella and those same banners;
her chest was adorned with a string of *guñjā* berries, and the saffron paste on her breasts was shimmering.
She has three eyes and a beautiful face; her lotus-like mouth bears a gentle smile, and her four arms shine with the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having thus meditated upon the goddess Totalā, who is surrounded by her powers (śaktis), one should worship her;
standing before her is Lu-phaṭkārī, radiant with arrows and a bow in her hands.
"O Lord of Sages, this ninth eternal [form] is called Tvaritā; she is intent on bestowing fruits upon practitioners with great haste."
It pacifies obstacles and evil dreams and bestows all desired objects.
It is pure, joined with its own [seed-syllable], beginning with the first [letter], and endowed with the letter *ra* and the fire [the letter *ra*]. (NarP 1.88.143)
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the second, joined with itself and the supreme powers of the forest;
thus is described this eternal *Kulasundarī*, known as the three-syllabled one.
By the mere recollection of which omniscience is produced—
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) with those three root syllables thus uttered.
At the beginning, middle, and end, according to the sequence of the ritual for worship and recitation,
one should perform each with those three seed-syllables conjoined with the long vowels.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands, limbs, and faces as prescribed by rule,
[using the syllables] for the zenith, east, south, north, west, nadir, and fire.
Residing within the well-sounding interior, they sequentially sound themselves within the base,
the apertures, and the heart as the first, and in the three eyes as the second.
The third [mark] is on the ears and the chin; the fourth is on the nose and the palate;
the fifth is on the shoulders and the navel; and thereafter, on both hands and feet.
One should place [the mantra] ninefold from the root to the middle to the tip with the root-syllables;
[one should worship] the red goddess, whose form is red, who is served by the Bṛhatī.
She was adorned with red garments, ornaments, garlands, and unguents; she had six faces and lotus-like eyes, and she shone with a crown of rubies set with priceless gems.
Her auspicious chest was adorned with shimmering clusters of jewels;
she was the supreme bliss of compassion, seated upon a seat of red lotuses.
She is endowed with twelve arms, representing all the various branches of knowledge for everyone,
and holds a coral rosary, a lotus, and a water-pot fashioned from jewels.
She holds in her right hands a cup filled with jewels, a loincloth, and a seal-ring for exposition; and in her left hands, a book and a beautiful blue lotus.
With her arms she held a golden pen, a garland of jewels, and a choice conch shell,
while being praised on all sides by gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras.

Having meditated thus, one should worship her constantly by means of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Daityas, Ṛṣis, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others, for the sake of attaining eloquence, fortune, beauty, and spiritual accomplishments.

One should visualize her as white for the attainment of mastery over speech alone; as having the luster of gold for the sake of prosperity; as smoke-colored for the purpose of inciting hatred among enemies; and [as black] for death and for subjugation.
And one should contemplate her as blue for the purpose of silencing;
this is the tenth daily [deity], O Kulasaundari, who has been described to you.
Now I shall speak of the tenth [mantra], Trikuṭā, which is both eternal and non-eternal:
it consists of the Haṃsa (haṃsaḥ) joined with the heart (hrīṃ), the vital breath (praṃ), the essence (rasaṃ), the burner (dāṃ), and the ears (karṇau). (NarP 1.88.159)
Joined with the Kulasundarī-vidyā according to the oral tradition,
this [Vidyā] consists of three syllables— eternal and non-eternal— and is endowed with six peak-syllables (kūṭākṣara).
It is considered to have seventy-two divisions through forms such as *pratiloma* and others;
by partaking of her, a man becomes a perfected being who moves through the sky in happiness.
One would be capable of performing both restraint and grace throughout the three worlds;
by means of the two syllables "haṃsa" joined with long vowels, the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) is formed.

One should sequentially place the syllables of the Vidyā, joined with the nasal bindu, in the middle of the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, the navel, and the secret foundation (guhyādhāra) respectively.
Having again pervaded [the body] entirely according to the prescribed rite,
one should meditate upon Śivā, who is the soul of all, for the sake of attaining all prosperity.
She has the luster of the rising sun’s orb, is radiant with a crown of rubies,
wears ornaments made of ruby, and is clad in garments of crimson silk.
She was resplendent with six lotus-like faces adorned with beautiful, smiling expressions,
each face possessing three eyes, and she was endowed with twelve arms.
And she holds in her left hands a noose, a rosary, a lotus, a bow of sugarcane, a shield, and a trident, as well as a goad and a book.
With single-minded devotion, one should meditate upon the Goddess as holding a flower-arrow, a lotus, and likewise a human skull and the gesture of fearlessness in her right hands.
Thus has this eleventh [chapter] been declared; now hear the twelfth, O Nārada.
The *Tvaritā* [mantra] consists of the final [letter], the first, the *yuti*, *doha*, *cara*, and *sva*. NarP_1,88.169 //
Then the letter *ha* joined with the burning [fire] and earth, likewise the fifth of the Vajreśīs;
joined with the winds and enriched by the center, this is after the tenth.
The eighth [syllable] is *vajreśī*, following the sequence of *bhūmī*, *rasā*, *kṣmā*, and *svayutā*;
then there are six syllables for *tvaritā*, and immediately after that is the third [mantra].
The first [mantra] immediately following this is called Nīlapatākā; it is radiant by its nature of burning and is a constant mantra of seventeen syllables. (NarP 1.88.172)
The assignment of the limbs [of the deity] arises from the mantras consisting of two, two, one, two, one, and six syllables,
respectively, in the ears and so forth, the pair of nostrils, the speech organ, the throat, and the heart.
Furthermore, one should sequentially place all seventeen mantra-syllables upon the navel-base and then, in order, upon the joints of the feet.
And one should perform the pervasive rite with the entire [mantra] according to the rules,
[visualizing her] resembling a sapphire and resplendent with a crown of shining jewels.
She has five faces and three eyes, wears crimson garments,
possesses ten hands, and is adorned with glittering ornaments of pearls and gems.
Her body was adorned with clusters of jewels, her face possessed a beautiful smile,
and she held in her hands a noose, a banner, a shield, a Śārṅga bow, and a boon-granting gesture.
She holds [these] on her left side, adorned with all ornaments:
a goad, a spear, a sword, an arrow, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness.
Seated upon a lotus throne, she held [objects] with her right hands;
she was endowed with an excellent form, complexion, attire, face, hands, weapons, and ornaments.
In the sequence of daily worship, one should meditate upon the Goddess surrounded by hosts of Śaktis;
[one should visualize] an eight-petaled lotus joined with three hexagons, and beyond that—
That pair of cities is octagonal, surrounded by two sets of earth-fortresses (bhūpuras),
provided with four gates in the cardinal directions, and endowed with side-arches.
Having performed the name-enclosure (*nāmāvṛta*) of the Śakti, one should worship Śivā there with the Gaṇas.
This twelfth daily rite of yours, Nīlapatākinī, has been proclaimed.
It grants victory in battle and bestows the supernatural powers of the sword, sandals, and collyrium;
it accomplishes the mastery of Vetālas, Yakṣiṇīs, servants, Piśācas, and other such beings.
She who bestows treasures, subterranean wealth, and the accomplishment of food, and is impelled by desire—now I shall speak of the thirteenth Nityā; listen, O Nārada! (NarP 1.88.184)

O Sage, the syllable *rasa* (ra), followed by *nabhaḥ* (na), then *dāha* (da), preceded by the pervading earth (*kṣmā*)—that is, *va*—and joined with space (*kha*), becomes the eternal, single-syllabled *vijaya*. NarP_1,88.185.

One should form the four [syllables] of the Vidyā with the consonants joined to the long vowels, and the remaining two with the other [consonants]; thus one should perform the six limbs upon the hands and the body.
Then, one should place the syllables, joined with the nasal bindu, in sequence upon the sense organs beginning with the ears, and also upon the mind; the rest is as before.
She has five faces and ten arms, with three eyes in each face,
and she is resplendent with a radiant crown set with a crescent moon.
Adorned with all ornaments, radiant in yellow garments,
her bodily luster equal to the rising orb of the sun, she possessed a pure smile.
With his left arms, he holds a conch, a noose, a shield, a bow, and a white lotus;
likewise, with his right arms, he holds a discus, a goad, a sword, an arrow, and a mātuluṅga fruit.
Holding [weapons] with her right hands in a terrifying display during combat,
yet gentle in appearance when in attendance, she sat upon a lion throne.
She is surrounded on all sides by Śaktis mounted upon tigers;
in battle, in worship, and in other rites, she is seated upon a comfortable throne.
And the Śaktis also, seated upon comfortable thrones during the worship,
are all goddesses who possess identical forms, faces, hands, and weapons.
Having constructed two squares adorned with four gates and provided with eight pillars, one should worship there as previously described.
Having fashioned an eight-cornered figure within that, with a pair of lines inside it, and likewise a sixteen-petalled lotus within that; NarP_1,88.195 //
In the same manner, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus and invoked her there, one should duly worship her with offerings, surrounded by her respective Śaktis.
This Trayodaśī has been declared to bestow victory in debate and in battle;
now I shall describe the Caturdaśī, which is eternal and indeed auspicious in every way.
The syllable Kha (Khaḥ), joined with Hṛd (Hrīṃ) and Ambu (Vaṃ), is the eternal Sarvamaṅgalā.
One who has attained perfection through the method of the Single Syllable (Ekākṣarya) becomes a sky-walker (khecara) in an instant.
One should then duly assign the root-mantra, enriched with the six long vowels, to the six limbs.
Eternal, with the luster of gold, adorned with pearls and rubies,
wearing a crown of rubies, her two eyes overflowing with flickering compassion.
She has two arms and holds the teaching [scripture] upon a lotus with eight, sixteen, or thirty-two petals, situated within a pair of earth-palaces provided with four gates.
Holding a mātuluṅga fruit in her right lotus-hand,
she bestows wealth and other blessings with her left hand upon her own devotees.
She was surrounded on all sides by powers equal to herself,
and accompanied by another sixty-seven [powers] born of the Apsarases.
In ritual applications at other times, she is always intent on worship according to her stated power;
this is declared to be the fourteenth [day], and now hear likewise about the fifteenth.
Earth with ether is empty; earth and water, then stable water;
speed joined with fire, fire joined with water, water joined with air, and air joined with water. NarP_1,88.205 //
The sky joined with the wind, the sap joined even in the void,
the lineage together with the moving one, and likewise the letter preceded by water.
Ambu, Agni, and Hṛt; Dāha, Ambu, Rasa, Kṣmā, Ravi, and Hṛt joined with Sva; Haṃsa joined with Marut; and Dāha joined with Marut; and Prāṇa joined with Marut. (NarP 1.88.207)

Burning (dāha) occurs with fire (agni), life-force (prāṇa), and the car (cara); the bowstring (jyā) and wind (marut) together with the enemy (ari); water (ambu) with the car (cara); the clan (gotra) and the heart (hṛt) with fire (agni); and the bowstring (jyā), water (ambu), and taste (rasa) joined with itself (sva).
The king is fire; these others are water and essence; then there is speed.
Through this burning, you shall become ashes twice over, joined with the fire and the wind.
The *haṃsa* always consists of fire (*a*), and it is joined with earth (*la*) and its own burner (*ra*);
thus there are seven burners for this [mantra], while those beginning from the eighth are five.
Situated below the penultimate [letter] and immediately following the blue banner (nīlapatākā) is Tvaritā; you (Tvaṃ) and Bheruṇḍā are the eighth, and likewise the ninth is Navanā.
That Jvālāmālinī-nityā is proclaimed to consist of sixty-three syllables,
[arranged] by means of one, two, four, five, four, and ten syllables.
One should perform the assignment of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) for both the hands and the body using the root syllables from the beginning;
with the remaining syllables, one should perform the pervasive assignment (vyāpaka). Then, one should meditate upon the Eternal One (Sanātanī).
Resembling a blazing fire, radiant with a crown of rubies,
she has six faces and twelve arms, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Holding a noose and a goad, a sword and a shield, a bow and arrows, a mace and a discus,
a trident and fire, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her ten lotus-like hands.
She was surrounded on all sides by her own powers (śaktis) equal in measure to herself;
her lotus-face shone with a beautiful smile, and she was endowed with three eyes.
Having meditated thus, one should worship her constantly with those ritual offerings;
having constructed two squares provided with four gates.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with its stalks, then a triangle within it,
and a hexagon with a triangle in the center, one should worship Śivā there.
This fifteenth [mantra] has been declared; now hear the sixteenth, O Nārada:
it consists of the two syllables *citrā*, together with the principles of Vāyu and Praṇava.
That which is established for the attainment of wealth, grain, and the discovery of hidden treasures—
one should perform it with the mantra beginning with "vidyā," joined with long vowels in sequence.
One should assign the six limbs as before, and the Mātṛkā along with the Vidyā;
[the goddess] has the luster of the rising solar disc and is adorned with ornaments of the nine gems.
She wears a crown of nine jewels and is radiant with variegated silken garments;
she has four arms and three eyes, her face shining with a pure smile.
She consists entirely of bliss, is eternal, and bestows all that is desired; she has four arms, holding a noose and a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should worship her who bestows auspiciousness, who resides in the center of the womb of the lotus-pericarp,
and likewise perform worship upon that wheel with her powers.

Prāṇa (ha) and Dāha (ra) conjoined with Dharā (la); then again, the first (a) and Marut (ya) in the Rasa (va) group; Vyāsa (ma) conjoined with Marut (ya) and Śakti (ī); then Bhūḥ (la) conjoined with itself (la), and then the triad [of these].

The first [syllable] of this [mantra], joined with a foot, is followed by a pair of *rasas* (liquids); then comes *haṃsa*, conjoined with *dāha* (fire) and the two *vahni-śaktis* (powers of fire). NarP_1,88.226 //
The sky (ha) and so forth, with the heart (sa), the fire (ra), the lotus (va), the void (kha) joined with itself (ha),
then water (va) joined with poison (sa), and wind (ya) joined with the sky (ha).
The void (ha), pervaded by the earth (la), and the *haṃsa* (ha-ka-sa); these are the first and last [letters] of the three mantras.
The five syllables beginning with the sixth of this [mantra] are said to have the face of the Daitya (da) as their first.
The second section is said to consist of eleven syllables ending with the final [syllable], and the third consists of twenty-five syllables; thus the mantras are declared in sequence. (NarP 1.88.229)
The young girl, marked with six limbs by two or three mantras beginning with the three seeds,
has disheveled hair, a youthful form, is red in color, and is the embodiment of bliss.
One should meditate upon her holding [these], or else one may visualize goddesses identical to her in weapons, form, and color, with hands bearing arrows, bows, nooses, and goads.
"Those who have given birth in season, whose wombs quiver, and whose eyes are ever-joyful and reddish—thus was Candrāvalī herself described at the end [of the section] on Kurukullā. (NarP 1.88.232)
I shall describe Vārāhī, the supreme body of Lalitā:
pure by its own nature, it is empty, like the sky, possessing the essence of a cloud, and stable.
Ambu, followed by Rayaḥ Sāgni; then Marut, Ambu, and Rayaḥ; then Ilasāyuta, Agni, and these again joined with Ambu and Marut. (NarP 1.88.234)
Fire is composed of burning, water, wind, and the *haṃsa*; again, by means of fire, these three [are formed].
Water and burning are joined with wind, and then the *haṃsa* with the earth becomes space (*nabhas*).
Furthermore, by means of the fire of *tejas*, the five [elements] are joined with their own [corresponding element];
first, water is joined with its own [element], and thereafter, water is joined with fire.
The void is conjoined with the pervasive and the pure; the void is joined with power (śakti) and space (nabhas).
Fire is earth together with its own greenness; water is endowed with the mobile (caras).
This has been declared as the first group of four; hereafter follows the one joined with the name Jya, along with Cara and Rabha, which precedes this.
Then the Essence (Rasa) was addressed by Agni: "Depart from here with the fourfold [group].
Then Haṃsa, together with Śubha, Udbhra, and Cāra, departed with his own [retinue] as before.

First, the *haṃsa* (ha-sa) with fire (ra), then the triad (tri-ta) joined with its own [vowel] in the heart (*hṛdaya*), then *rasa* (sa) with the moving one (*cara*, ya), preceded by that, and *rasa* (sa) joined with fire (ra). // NarP_1,88.240 //
Afterwards, the triad of Vāta together with the earth and space was spoken;
then Prāṇa joined with its own [element], and finally Rasa joined with the heart.
This triad is subsequently pervaded by burning and conjoined with water;
it is endowed with the weight of the earth-element, joined with touch, accompanied by sound, and possessed of speed.
With *dāha* (fire), each preceding one is joined with the preceding wind (*marut*);
the void (*śūnya*) is accompanied by the winds, and the mobile (*cara*) is formed by the heart-fire (*hṛddāha*) and water (*ambu*).
The syllable *sparśa* (kṣa) is conjoined with wind (*marut*, y); *hṛd-dāha* (ṭa) is conjoined with water (*ambu*, v);
*jyāgni* (ra) is conjoined with itself; and *haṃsa* (ha) is likewise conjoined with water and wind (*ambu-marut*, vy).
The *rasa* is joined with its own [element] in the form of the heart;
the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and heat (*dāha*) are joined with earth (*dharā*), and those two again with fire (*vahni*) and space (*viyat*).

The water [of the syllable] should be joined with the fire [of the letter *ra*], conjoined with the sixty-second vowel [the long *ī*], and likewise the two previously mentioned letters; purity is thus conjoined with its own [vowel].

The syllables *sthirā*, *rasā*, and *vatasvena* [form one part]; then *dāvau*, *haṃsau*, and *dharā* with its own [consonant] (*svayuk*); then *yutiḥ* followed by *nādavatī*; and finally that which is joined with *hṛt*, *ambu*, and *marut*. (NarP 1.88.247)
And Haṃsa, Marutā, Vidya, the one of one hundred and ten syllables, Vārāhī, the fifth Viśvavijayā, and Bhadrakaumudī. (NarP 1.88.248)
She is renowned as Vārtālī, the bestower of all desired things such as the rites of immobilization (staṃbhana) and so forth;
one should perform the ritual assignments (aṅga) with the seven or six syllables of the mantra.
Divided into ten, seven, and seven-fold sections,
it is provided with a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and two circles.
Having fashioned a wheel right there and having written his own name upon it, he should worship it; then he should meditate on the Goddess, whose face is like a stake and who resembles gold.
[He saw her] up to her neck in the form of a woman, with blazing tawny lotuses,
three eyes, and eight hands, holding a discus, a conch, and a goad.
One should contemplate her seated comfortably upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, holding a noose, a pestle, a head, as well as granting protection and bestowing boons.
O Sage, in daily worship one should remember her powers as equal to herself;
in ritual applications, one should remember the Goddess as seated upon a lion or even mounted on a tiger.
Mounted on an elephant, mounted on a horse, and mounted on a chariot with her power-staffs;
she may be dark, ruddy, yellow, or black, with a body like a blue lotus.
In those respective applications, one should meditate accordingly for the attainment of those specific results:
one should visualize the fifth [syllable] as reddish for subjugation, and yellow for immobilization.

The practitioner, the best of the twice-born, should meditate on her as dark-green when on a difficult path, as white for the destruction of enemies in battle, and as smoke-colored for the purpose of eradication.
These sixteen Nityās have been briefly proclaimed to you;
they grant the desires of those who worship them and instantly effect the destruction of all sins.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mantras of Rādhā and Others," in the third quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, regarding these Śaktis who abide in the enclosures, and according to their convention (*samaya*)—
I shall proclaim the thousand names, preceded by meditation upon the Guru.
O Nārada, know that the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva are proclaimed as nine, starting from Nātha and ending with Subhaga. 1,89.2.
The festivals beginning with the Guru’s birthday and ending with the New Moon—these seven indeed the best of practitioners should contemplate with the activity of the mind. (NarP 1.89.3)
One should also recite the *Guru-stotra* with an inner self absorbed in Him:
"Salutations to You, O Lord, Blessed One, Śiva in the form of the Guru. (NarP 1.89.4)
To the one who has assumed many forms for the sake of the successful entry into knowledge,
who is ever-new, whose form is ever-new, and whose sole nature is the ultimate reality.
Salutations to you, the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance, the mass of consciousness,
the independent one whose form is fashioned by compassion, the very self of Śiva.

To the one who is dependent upon his devotees, who is auspicious for those destined for liberation, and who takes the form of the auspicious; to the discernment of the discerning, and to the investigation of those capable of investigation.
To the light of lights, to the one whose form is knowledge for the wise—
to him I offer salutations in front, on both sides, behind, above, and below.
"Always establish your seat in the palace of my mind.
Having thus praised the Guru with devotion, one should contemplate the Supreme Goddess. (NarP 1.89.9)
I bow to the Goddess who consists of mantra, who takes the form of Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, and the zodiac signs, and who is the embodiment of the seat of the Mātṛkās.
I bow to the Great Goddess, the Mother, the Supreme Sovereign,
who brings about the destruction of the waves of the surging and turbulent fire of Time.
If a man competes with Ravi, Tārkṣya, Indra, and Kandarpa, or with Śaṅkara, Anala, and Viṣṇu, even when only a single syllable has been mastered; NarP_1,89.12 //
I bow to the Goddess Sarveśvarī, the Great Śrī Siddhamātṛkā, by whose syllables the three worlds are adorned with the moonlight of the moon. NarP_1,89.13 //
I bow to that Siddhamātṛkā, upon which these three worlds—from the cosmic egg down to its outer shell—are strung like beads on the great thread of the Imperishable (akṣara). NarP_1,89.14 //
That seed-syllable which arises from the three corners as the eleventh support is seen even today as the entire world, from the cosmic egg down to the shell of the universe.
She whose [mantra] consists of the letters beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *na*, *ḍha*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *kṣa*;
she who dwells in the head, the arms, the heart, the throat, the hips, and the feet.
I bow to the Great Goddess, whose form is supreme bliss, who is extracted from the syllable *naumīkāra*, who is the essence of essences, and who is higher than the highest.
Moreover, even the deities do not know in the slightest who she is,
from where she comes, where she is, or by what means she exists— whether as one possessing form or as one devoid of form.
I bow to that imperishable Goddess, whose form is the letter *kṣa*, the supreme Śivā who shines forth amidst the surging waves of the Kula lineage. 1.89.19.
I bow to that Īśvarī who, by the sequential order of the classes [of consonants], has the name Umāṣṭaka established for her, and who is the source of the great siddhis arising from the eight groups.
I bow to the venerable Tripura, who dwells within the supreme seat known as Kāmapūrṇaja, and who is the treasury of the four commands. NarP_1,89.21 //
Whoever, being well-composed, recites this hymn at the beginning of worship and other rites for the Nityā goddesses, all of them will undoubtedly be granters of boons to him.
Now I shall declare to you the armor of the Goddess, consisting of nine jewels,
by means of which the practitioner shall always be victorious over gods, asuras, and men.
May Lalitā, who is omnipresent, protect me from all sides and at all times;
may Kāmeśī protect me from the front, and Bhagamālī immediately thereafter.
May [the deity] protect the direction; likewise, may Nityaklinnā always protect my right side;
and may Bheruṇḍā protect the direction of the ghouls (Nairṛtī) for me.
Likewise, may Vahnivāsinī protect the western quarter;
may the eternal Mahāvajreśvarī always protect me in the northwest.
May she who is thus invoked protect my left side;
may Māheśvarī, the swift bestower of success, protect the northern direction.
May the beautiful woman of the Daivataka clan protect me perpetually from above;
may she known as Vijayā, whose banner is blue, protect me from below and on all sides.
May she who is the embodiment of Jvālāmālinī, the source of all auspiciousness, always bestow blessings upon me, as well as upon my body, senses, mind, and vital breaths.
O Mind, protect my mind incessantly; may it guard me at all times from desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and even arrogance.

May they always protect me from evil, from grief on all sides, from total decay, from untruth, from cruel thoughts, from violence, from thieves, and likewise from lethargy, while impelling me toward what is auspicious.
May the sixteen eternal goddesses, mounted upon elephants with their own Śaktis, protect me;
likewise, may they, mounted upon horses, always protect me from all sides.
May they protect me, mounted upon lions, and may they also protect me while seated on bears;
and may they protect me from all sides at all times in battle, even when mounted upon chariots.
May they who are mounted upon Tārkṣya protect me, as well as those who move through the sky;
may those who dwell on the earth and those who go everywhere protect me, and may the goddesses protect me at all times.
May the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, by means of their own powers, ornaments, and weapons, drive away my diseases caused by the spells of others and the like.
May the countless goddesses Śaktis, mounted upon elephants, horses, leopards, lions, and Garuḍas, and bearing all weapons, protect me always from every side. (NarP 1.89.36)
Reciting daily at dawn and dusk this armor that provides all protection,
one shall never behold anything inauspicious, remaining forever established in bliss.
Thus has been proclaimed this auspicious armor of Lalitā,
by the mere retention of which a mortal becomes fearless, victorious, and happy.
Now, O Sage, I shall declare to you the thousand names along with the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇas),
consisting of the respective sequences for each of the sixteen [deities].
Lalitā, Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī,
Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī are proclaimed.
Vajreśvarī, likewise Dūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Saṃvit, as well as Nīlapatākā and the one named Vijayā. (NarP 1.89.41)
Sarvamaṅgalikā, she known as Jvālāmālinī,
and Citrā— these are the sixteen eternal goddesses, whose forms are to be worshipped in sequence.
Kurukullā and Vārāhī—these two possess beautiful forms; likewise Vaśinī, Kāmeśī, Mohinī, and Vimalāruṇā. (NarP 1.89.43)
Tapinī, likewise Sarveśvarī, and also Kaulinī;
she whose body is the end of all mudrās, whose form is the color of gold, and whose physical structure is without parts.
She has a body the color of a noose, yet she bears a beautiful form the color of a lotus;
she is the three-segmented one, the establisher, the restrainer, and the veiler.
Among those [mudrās] kept close at hand are the one called Cāpa (the Bow), as well as those named Pāśa (the Noose) and Aṅkuśa (the Goad);
likewise, there are Namaskṛti (Homage), Saṃkṣobhaṇī (Agitation), and Vidrāvaṇī (Driving Away).
Ākarṣaṇī is renowned, as well as Āveśakāriṇī; Unmādinī preceded by Mahā, and then Kuśā is considered Khecarī.
The arousal of power from the seed-syllable is designated as gross, subtle, and supreme;
likewise, there are *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *mahimā*, and *garimā*.
Attainment, as well as the state of being desired, sovereignty, and mastery; likewise enjoyment, accomplishment, and the accomplishment of will are proclaimed.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and she whose nature is Mahālakṣmī.
Desire, intellect, ego, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, knowledge, and likewise fortitude; NarP_1,89.51 //
Nābhabījā, Amṛtā, Smṛti, Dehātmarūpiṇī,
Kusumā, Mekhalā, Madanā, and Madanāturā.
Rekhā, Saṃveginī, Aṅkuśā, and Mālinī;
likewise Saṃkṣobhiṇī, Vidrāviṇī, and Ākarṣaṇarūpiṇī.
She is called Āhlādinī (the Delighting), as well as Samohinī (the Enchanting); likewise Staṃbhinī (the Paralyzing), Jambhinī (the Devouring), Vaśaṅkarī (the Subduing), and Rañjinī (the Pleasing).
She is likewise proclaimed as Unmādinī and Arthasādhinī;
she is full of prosperity, composed of mantra, and the destroyer of duality.
Siddhi bestows prosperity, brings about what is dear and auspicious,
is declared to grant all desires, and likewise liberates one from suffering.
The pacifier of death, likewise the warder-off of obstacles,
the one with beautiful limbs, and likewise the bestower of good fortune.
The fifth is Jñānamayī, who bestows knowledge and sovereignty;
she dwells in the Vindhya mountains, possesses a formidable form, and removes all sins.
Likewise, there is the protection consisting of bliss (Ānandamayī), which bestows desired fruits;
then the Victorious One (Jayinī), the Stainless One (Vimalā), the Mistress of Desire (Kāmeśī), the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Vajriṇī), and the Goddess of Fortune (Bhagā).
She is the enchantress of the three worlds, the fulfiller of all hopes,
the one who has attained the state of universal agitation, and she is established as the bestower of good fortune.
She is the abode that accomplishes all aims, she who dwells as the remover of all diseases;
she is the place that provides all protection, she who dwells as the bestower of all attainments.
It consists of Śiva, who is the nature of the station of the *bindu* that is the support consisting of all bliss;
it is known as preeminent, likewise secret, and even more secret.
It is the very nature of the oral tradition, residing within the heart of Kulakaula;
it is the secret, the non-secret, the natural, and likewise the most profound secret.
Tripurā, Tripureśī, and likewise Puravāsinī; Śrīmālinī, Siddhāntā, and Mahātripurasundarī.
She is adorned with nine regions consisting of islands made of the nine gems;
she dwells in the Kalpa grove and worships the senses in the form of the seasons.
The Seal of Time (Kālamudrā) is known as Mātṛkā, the instructor of the Jewel-land;
she is the embodiment designated as the Supreme Reality and likewise the subduer of the dualities of the sense objects.
The Yoginī of Melodious Union has the nature of place, time, form, and sound;
she is joined with the entire wheel of secret and manifest Siddha-Yoginīs.
She is known as Fire, Sun, Moon, and Earth; likewise, she is called by the name of the Eight-Syllabled Self;
she is the fivefold nature of the vowels, and she is invoked by the names of various vows.
Free from prohibited conduct, possessing the nature of the signs of accomplishment (siddhacihna),
she resides in the four parts of the tortoise (kūrmabhāga) and has the nature of the eternal worship (nityārcā) and so forth.
The worship of *damanaka* and other [plants] bestows success in the six rites (*ṣaṭkarma*);
worship with specific substances on particular lunar days and weekdays brings auspiciousness.
From Vāyu [were born] Anaṅgakusumā, likewise Anaṅgamekhalā,
Anaṅgamadanā, and she named Anaṅgamadanāturā.
Madadeginīkā, as well as Bhuvanapālinī,
Śaśilekhā, and she who is designated Gatilekhā are thus enumerated.
Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Dhṛti, Kānti, Manoramā,
the one known as Manoharā, and likewise Manorathā.
Madanonmādinī, Modinī, Śaṅkhinī, as well as Śoṣiṇī, Śaṅkārī, Siñjinī, and Subhagā.
Pūṣan, Vāsumanas, Rati, Prīti, Dhṛti, as well as Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, and likewise Aṃśumālinī.
Śaśinī, Aṅgirā, Chāyā, as well as Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalā, Tuṣṭi, and the one called Amṛtā— she is the Ḍākinī and likewise the world-protector.
Durgā is the radiant form of the *baṭuka*, the embodiment of the Lord of the Field (*kṣetreśa*),
the very nature of Kāmarāja, and likewise the form of Manmatha.
She is the very form of Kandarpa, as well as the one whose banner is the sea-monster;
she is the essential nature of Manobhava, and Bhāratī in the form of the phonemes.
Madanā, Mohinī, Līlā, Jambhinī, Codayā, Śubhā, Hlādinī, Drāviṇī, Prītī, Ratī, Raktā, and Manoramā. (NarP 1.89.79)
She is the intoxication of all, the face of all, indeed unbreakable and of immeasurable exertion;
her power is vast and unmanifest, and she possesses various forms of agitation and conflict.
She is the power of passion, the power of hatred, and likewise she who takes the form of sound and the other sense objects;
she is eternal, stainless, moist, the one who causes moisture, and afflicted by love.
She is celebrated as Madadravā, Drāviṇī, and Draviṇī;
she is Madāvilā, Maṅgalā, Manmathānī, and Manasvinī.
Mohā, Modā, Mānamayī, Māyā, Mandā, Mitāvatī, Vijayā, Vimalā, Śubhā, and likewise Viśvā. // NarP_1,89.83 //
Vibhūti, Vinatā, and various other Vinatās in succession;
Kamalā, Kāminī, Kirātā, and Kīrtirūpiṇī.
The Kuṭṭinī is designated, as well as the Kulasundarī,
the Kalyāṇī, the Kālakolā, and likewise the Ḍākinī and the Śākinī.
Lākinī, Kākinī, Rākinī, and likewise Kākinī;
she who is known as Icchā, Jñānā, and Kriyā, and who bears the eight weapons.
Kapardinī is likewise designated, as well as Kulasundarī,
Jvālinī, Visphuliṅgā, Maṅgalā, and Sumanoharā.
The science known as Kanakākinavā is proclaimed to be manifold;
it consists of the signs called Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and likewise Cancer.
Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio,
Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Sārā, and likewise Sarvabhakṣā.
She is proclaimed as the soul of the universe, possessing various and manifold forms;
she is without rival, free from fear, and her majesty is inconceivable through prayer.
Then Raktā is proclaimed, as well as Vidyāprāpti, Svapinī, Hṛllekhā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Kṣobhiṇī, and Madanāturā. (NarP 1.89.91)
Nipandanā, Rāgavatī, likewise Madanāvatī,
Mekhalā, Drāviṇī, and Vegavatī are proclaimed.
Kamalā, Kāminī, Kalpā, Kalā, and the one of wondrous form (Kalitādbhutā),
Kiratā, as well as Kālā, Kadanā, and Kauśikā.
Kaṃbuvādanikā, Kātarā, Kapaṭā, as well as Kīrti, Kumārī, and Kuṅkumā are likewise proclaimed. (NarP 1.89.94)
Bhañjinī, Veginī, Nāgā, Capalā, Peśalā,
Satī, Rati, Śraddhā, Bhogalolā, Madonmattā, and Manasvinī.
Vihvalā, Karṣiṇī, Lolā, as well as Madanamālinī, Vinodā, Kautukā, Puṇyā, and Purāṇā are proclaimed [as the forms of the goddess]. (NarP 1.89.96)
Vāgīśī, Varadā, Viśvā, Vibhavā, Avighnakāriṇī,
Bījavighnaharā, Vidyā, Sumukhī, and likewise Sundarī.
Sārā, Sumanā, and likewise Sarasvatī are proclaimed;
Samayā, Sarvagā, Viddhā, Śivā, and Vāṇī are also celebrated.
She is likewise declared to be Dūrasiddhā, and is considered to be Vigrahagavatī; she is Nādā, Manonmanī, Prāṇapratiṣṭhā, and Aruṇavaibhavā.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna are proclaimed;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
Phaṭkārī, Kiṅkarārādhyā, Jayā, and likewise Vijayā;
Huṅkārī, Kheṭacarī, Caṇḍā, Chedinī, and likewise Kṣapiṇī.
She who utters the "huṃ" of a woman, the bringer of well-being, whose form consists of four syllables;
she whose limbs are the letters of the Śrīvidyā mantra, Kālī, the southern one, and the bestower of kingship.
Speech is Sarasvatī, the supreme refined language;
she is multiform, the form of the mind, delightful, blissful, and full of wonder.
She is known as the Triad and also as the Supreme Self;
she is of immeasurable power, consisting of the nature of speech, and likewise of the nature of the Bindu and the emission (sarga), being the soul of the universe.
Likewise, that which is called Traipurakaṇḍā consists of the threefold nature beginning with the knower;
it bestows longevity, prosperity, fame, enjoyment, beauty, and health. (NarP 1.89.105)
She is proclaimed as consisting of knowledge pertaining to this world and the next;
she is known as Jīvā, Vijayā, and likewise Viśvavinmayī.
The Vidyās beginning with Hṛdā, whose forms are radiant with color and other qualities, pervaded the world;
they are Viśvamohanikā and the one known as Tripurāmṛtā.
She is described as the form of universal nourishment, as well as the deluder, the agitator,
the moistener, and likewise the great source of prosperity.
Saṃpatkarī consists of six syllables; Sīmāmātṛtanū is Rati;
Prīti is also said to be Manobhavā, as well as Vārādhipā.
She who possesses three peaks, six peaks, and five peaks is of pure body;
she has reached the unstruck (anāhata) and is established in the maṇipūraka.
Seated in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, established in the Ādhāra, and stationed in the Ājñā;
she consists of the thirty-six peaks and is composed of the fifty pairs.
The mistress of accomplishments such as the magic sandals, likewise the bestower of victory,
the giver of forms at will, the Vetāla-form, and the Piśācikā.
Vicitrā, Vibhramā, Haṃsī, Bhīṣaṇī, Janarañjikā, Viśālā, Madanā, Tuṣṭā, Kālakaṇṭhī, and Mahābhayā.
Māhendrī, Śaṅkhinī, Aindrī, Maṅgalā, Vaṭavāsinī,
Mekhalā, Sakalā, Lakṣmī, Mālinī, and Viśvanāyikā.
Sulocanā, Suśobhā, Kāmadā, Vilāsinī, Kāmeśvarī, Nandinī, Svarṇarekhā, and Manoharā. (NarP 1.89.115)
Pramodā, Rāgiṇī, Siddhā, Padminī, Ratipriyā,
Kalyāṇadā, Kalādakṣā, and thereafter Surasundarī.
Vibhramā, Vāhakā, Vīrā, Vikalā, Korakākavi, Siṃhanādā, Mahānādā, Sugrīvā, Markaṭā, and Śaṭhā. (NarP 1.89.117)
Biḍālākṣā, Biḍālāsyā, Kumārī, Khecarī,
Bhavā, Mayūrā, Maṅgalā, Bhīmā, Dvipavaktrā, and Kharānanā.
Mātaṅgī, Niśācārā, Vṛṣagrāhā, Vṛkānanā, Sairibhāsyā, Gajamukhā, Paśuvaktrā, and Mṛgānanā. (NarP 1.89.119)
Kṣobhakā, Maṇibhadrā, Krīḍakā, Siṃhacakrakā,
Mahodarā, Sthūlaśikhā, Vikṛtāsyā, and Varānanā.
Capalā, Kukkuṭāsyā, Pāvinī, Madanālasā,

Sumukhā, Paṇḍitā, Kruddhā, Varāhāsyā, Saṭāmukhā,
Kapaṭā, Kautukā, Kālā, Kiṅkarā, Kitavā, and Khalā.
She is proclaimed as Bhakṣakā, Bhayadā, Siddhā, and Sarvagā;

Ambikā, Vāmadevī, she whose nature is Mahāmāyā,
Vidārikā, Viśvamayī, Viśvā, and Viśvavibhañjitā.
The Heroine, the Agitator, the Knowledge, the Delighter, whose form is the seed-syllable;

She is known as Māninī, Madhurā, Māyā, and Mohinī; likewise as Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Bhavyā, Viśālākṣī, and Śucismitā.

Nityā, Amṛtā, Jīvitā, and likewise Dayā.

Kāminī, Khecarī, Garvā, Purāṇā, Aparameśvarī,
Gaurī, Śivā, Ameyā, Vimalā, Vijayā, and Parā.
She is the purifier, the lotus-like knowledge, the sovereign of the universe, the beloved of Śiva;
she is indeed of infinite forms, the blissful lotus-eyed one, and the irreproachable.
The granter of boons, the giver of speech, the manifold voice whose body is the Vedas,

Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci,
Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bādhinī, Dhārinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī,
Suśrī, Svarūpā, Kapilā, and likewise Havyakavyavahā.
Voracious, devouring the universe, with restless eyes and a flickering tongue,

The Vaṃśā, Pippalā, Nāgā, Rohiṇā, and Palāśakā;

Nimbā, Madhūka-saṃjñā, Aśvatthā, Gajāhvayā,

Having performed the ritual and recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should then offer oblations; thus, a fire sacrifice performed on the first lunar day brings about great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*).
Likewise, on Fridays for a year, he shall become equal to a king;
especially on the fifth lunar day, he should perform the fire-oblation as previously described.

On that lunar day, one should offer oblations of white flowers such as jasmine, anointed with the three sweets (trimadhu), along with food and clarified butter; by performing these offerings regularly, a man shall become wealthy in food.
For whatever object one desires, all that is indeed obtained at all times through oblations of ghee, and likewise by means of sesame seeds and rice.
By offering golden lotuses drenched in the three sweets,
one obtains great fortune from the mandala, possessing a praiseworthy form.
From today until that day, one should daily offer with devotion a thousand blossoming white water-lilies (*kahlāra*), sprinkled with honey, as the first oblation.
He shall obtain fame, wealth, and sons; of this there is no doubt, through the certain performance of a thousand oblations with *caṃpaka* flowers sprinkled with honey.
O Nārada, by offering one hundred *pāṭala* flowers sprinkled with ghee as oblations for a month, one likewise obtains a hundred gold *niṣkas*, and by three thousand such offerings, three thousand.
From the month of Darśa onwards, he obtains variegated garments,
and from the month [of Citrā] onwards, fragrant substances such as camphor and sandalwood.
One obtains other delightful objects useful for enjoyment by offering a hundred oblations on the seventh lunar days with rice grains sprinkled with milk. (NarP 1.90.127)
By that, there will undoubtedly be an abundance of rice within six months;
and by offerings of sesame seeds, one shall obtain health within a year, day by day.
Likewise, a man who offers oblations with *dūrvā* grass on the three lunar days corresponding to his own birth star becomes free from affliction,
enjoys great prosperity, and lives for a hundred years.
Or one may offer oblations with *guḍūcī*, sesame, and *dūrvā* grass for three births;
by that, one shall possess longevity, prosperity, fame, enjoyments, merit, hidden treasures, and so forth.
By offering oblations of ghee, milk-rice, and milk respectively into those three fires,
the king’s minister shall likewise come to possess long life, health, and great wealth.
On the seventh lunar day, by performing oblations of plantain, one obtains good fortune daily;
likewise, by using three pieces of *dūrvā* grass, each the length of a span (*prādeśa*) and combined with the three sweets.
One should offer oblations daily during a severe fever caused by the combination of humors (sannipāta),
and on those days, one should constantly recite the mantra while touching water.
One should perform bathing and drinking with its water one thousand times;
one may even cook food and so forth with it for the sake of liberation from disease.
The powdered wood of the tree belonging to the victim's asterism, along with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), mustard, and sesame,
should be ground together and mixed with the dust raised from the footprints of the person to be targeted.
Having properly fashioned a doll with the name attached to its heart,
one should strike that doll with sharp iron weapons as previously described.
In this manner, within seven days, the one to be accomplished will certainly become submissive.
Then, having buried such a doll in the middle of the sacrificial pit, [one should proceed].
Having placed a fire above, one should then offer oblations daily with the Vidyā three thousand times during the third watch of the night, using mustard seeds soaked in its juice.
One may forcibly bring a woman even from a distance of a hundred yojanas;
one may bring a woman under control by means of owls mixed with honey.
One shall obtain prosperity by offering coconut fruits together with jaggery;
likewise, by offering *kahlāra* lilies sprinkled with clarified butter, or red lotuses smeared with milk.
By offering oblations of *caṃpaka* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*),
as well as flowers produced from the *bakula* and *madhūka* trees, one shall obtain a daughter.
By offering oblations of *punnāga* flowers and clarified butter, one obtains garments;
by offerings of buffalo meat, one obtains buffaloes; by offerings of goat meat, goats; and likewise, by offerings of beef, cattle.
By means of oblations of clarified butter and jewels, the practitioner obtains a jewel;
then, having fashioned an effigy out of rice-flour mixed with sugar, he attains his goal.
Having placed the syllables of the name upon the region of the heart, one should cook [the substance] in oil and clarified butter at night;
with a mind focused on that, one should consume it day and night after having recited the vidyā.
By practicing this for seven nights, a man, a woman, or even a king will come under one's control like a slave and surrender their mind, life-force, and so forth. (NarP 1.90.145)
Likewise, one should offer oblations with red or white flowers of the *hayāri* plant;
after twenty-one nights, a man attains great prosperity.
By offering goat meat smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) from a golden vessel, one obtains gold;
by offering it smeared with milk, one obtains land abundant with crops for the extent of a *maṇḍala*.
By performing oblations with lotus seeds for three days, one obtains prosperity;
in the practice of recitation, one should offer oblations of bilva fruits ten times the number of mantra repetitions.
Thus, one whose mantra is fully perfected shall, by sprinkling water from cupped palms consecrated with mantras into the mouths of those bitten by a serpent and seemingly dead, restore them to life.
Reciting the vidyā over his ears, or striking his head suddenly with a staff empowered by recitation, one shall raise the dead back to life.
Having formed the *yoni* in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should duly offer oblations into the fire there with sesame,
mustard, wheat, rice, grain, and barley.
For the sake of prosperity, one should offer bakula, campaka, lotus, kahlāra, and red lotus flowers, either individually or combined with the three sweets (trimadhu). NarP_1,90.152 //
With white water-lilies, jasmine, *kunda*, and *madhūka* flowers;
with *aśoka*, *pāṭala*, *bilva*, white *jātī*, and *vikaṅkata* flowers, for the attainment of Indirā.
Through oblations of fresh blue lotuses, white water lilies, and *karṇikāra* flowers, one shall obtain fortune, good luck, a treasure, long life, and fame. (NarP 1.90.154)
Having offered oblations of dūrvā grass, guḍūcī, aśvattha, vaṭa, āragvadha,
as well as those produced from white arka and plakṣa, one shall be freed from disease after a long time.
By consuming [food] combined with sugarcane, rose-apple, coconut, plantain, jaggery, and sugar, one attains unshakable fortune and will certainly become an enjoyer [of prosperity]. (NarP 1.90.156)
When mustard seeds and clarified butter are offered into a fire of wood for the death of an enemy,
the fourfold army of the foe perishes along with its gold, born from [the power of] the four-fingered [mantras].
Within seven days, the pain and suffering of disease will surely arise; of this there is no doubt.
One should perform daily worship at all times, as well as fire-offerings with clarified butter.
To attain that [state], one should drink water consecrated with mantras in the morning,
[water] mixed with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, musk, and gorocanā.
And for the sake of accomplishing all goals, one should worship Śivā with these fragrances: Kāśmīra saffron, black agallochum, and even those produced from the sweat of deer.

One should drink water that has been consecrated by reciting all the eternal [mantras] together with the *mātṛkā* at dawn three times; likewise, this is auspicious for the attainment of mastery over speech.
One should perform the preparatory rite as before, observing a milk-vow for one hundred thousand recitations of the syllables;
then, one should perform the fire-oblation with red lotuses sprinkled with the three sweets.

A person who has perfected the mantra through recitation, libation, fire-offerings, worship, and sprinkling may perform the prescribed ritual applications; otherwise, the deities of that mantra will not grant success.
O Sage, his vital breaths are indeed swallowed up by them in an instant when they are enraged;
there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished through this lore.
At the foot of a banyan tree in the forest, in mountain peaks and caves, in the midst of gardens or in the wilderness, and at the root of a mother-tree.
On the shore of the Sindhu river, in the forest Caita, a man should propitiate these yakṣiṇīs with lotuses,
white water-lilies, red and white fragrant utpalas.

By means of a row of fragrant roots (*sugandhiśiphā*) smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), through oblations performed according to the rule over seven days from that very mandala, [the desired result is attained]. (NarP 1.90.167)
One attains victory in a duel, in hand-to-hand combat,
in wrestling, in battle with weapons, in debate, and even in gambling.
In all legal proceedings, one certainly attains victory;
by means of flowers produced from four-finger-widths of gold, one may paralyze one's enemies.
Likewise, [one should worship] with flowers arising from the *karṇikāra*, the *punnāga*, the *nameru*, the *caṃpaka*, the *ketaka*, the *rājavṛkṣa*, and those produced by the *mādhava*.
As before, one should offer oblations at the gates in sequence with seven flowers;
in the cases mentioned, the certain paralyzing or breaking of the enemy occurs.
By performing oblations in the fire of the enemy’s birth star and tree using fuel-sticks soaked in mustard oil and clarified butter, they will indeed bow down at one's feet.
One should properly offer oblations into the fire of the wood of death with the leaves, flowers, and fruits of the tree of death as fuel, preceded by the worship of the deity on its day.
The fourfold army of the enemy shall be afflicted by disease;
by that means, his victory shall come about, even through his own destruction.
On a Sunday, when the fire has been kindled with fuel-wood produced from the sun (arka) tree,
one should offer oblations in sequence with the leaves, flowers, fruits, stalks, and roots arising from that same tree.

Having turned away from the direction of the enemy, one should perform the rite according to the rules in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) using oblations of ghee poured from a vessel containing a calf of the same color as the cow.
Whether the one afflicted by disease flees or bows down filled with fear,
[one should perform the rite] in a fire fed with *palāśa* fuel, using his five limbs soaked in ghee.
On a Monday, by means of an oblation, it shall be as before; of this there is no doubt.
With fuel-sticks of *khādira* wood in the fire, he should offer its five parts soaked in that clarified butter.
By performing an oblation on Tuesday with *apāmārga* wood, one certainly attains that [result];
on Monday with *saumya* [wood], and on Thursday with *pippala* wood.
For one born under the Uduṃbara tree, on a Saturday during the day of Śamī, with cow's ghee,
those of bright, yellow, white, dark, and other complexions [should be worshipped] as before.
One attains that fruit by means of a fire kindled with those same [substances], starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) and proceeding in sequence until the fifth. NarP_1,90.181 //
By performing oblations with rice, chickpeas, mung beans, barley, and black gram,
soaked in buffalo ghee, one shall obtain those [results] on those lunar days.

Furthermore, by using goat's milk, ghee, and so forth— prepared as previously described from gold that has been freed of husks— one shall obtain the aforementioned fruit, starting from the sixth [day] up to the seventh.
That [offering] increases fivefold when performed with all these together, along with two sesame seeds,
white rice, milk-porridge, sprinkled offerings, and sheep's ghee.
One obtains from the oblation that same fruit which was described at the outset;
likewise, by offering those various substances soaked in honey into a fire produced from the tree of a lunar mansion, one attains the corresponding result.
The attainment of that indeed occurs even through the *havana* sacrifice; there is no doubt about this.
However, having first accomplished the *vidyā*, one should afterwards perform all the aforementioned rites without exception.
The wise one should accomplish the ritual applications through the grace of Maṅgalā,
after having worshipped the deity, a young Brahmin boy, or a maiden.
Having established an auspicious young maiden with beautiful limbs, who has bathed and wears clean garments,
or likewise a young boy, one should worship them with the vidyā-mantra.
Having touched the head [of the image], one should recite the vidyā a hundred times and likewise worship it with flowers that are reddish,
white, or even richly fragrant.
One should offer guggulu incense until the conclusion of the ritual;
then, once the deity has entered that [person], one should worship him with devotion.
Then, while reciting that vidyā, the observer of the vow should question her with those aforementioned services; and she shall tell him his desired object.
Whatever has been, is, or will be, and whatever else resides in the mind,
as well as all past lives— she, when worshipped, shall declare it all.
Then, having worshipped her as before and dissolved her into one's own self,
one who is steady-minded and full of the Self should recite that mantra a thousand times and wander about happily.
By offering red lotuses sprinkled with the three sweets, one attains prosperity;
and by offering white ones through the fire-oblation (homa), one attains great fame.
By offering oblations for the prescribed period with red sprouts smeared with honey,
one obtains gold, or a treasure, or even the earth itself.
By offering white water-lilies smeared with milk upon a golden vessel, as prescribed, one shall obtain all desires;
that man shall quickly become fortunate and possess various kinds of grain.
One shall obtain one's desire by offering blue lotuses smeared with clarified butter; likewise, by offering white water-lilies smeared with that same substance, one becomes a favorite of the king.
By performing oblations at that time with *palāśa* flowers combined with the three sweets, the fourfold state of scholarship is surely attained; of this there is no doubt.
By offering parched grain mixed with the three sweets at that very time,
one indeed obtains a maiden as a wife, endowed with every virtue.
Likewise, one who offers powdered coconut fruit mixed with sugar or molasses, along with honey and grapes, becomes like the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) without effort. (NarP 1.90.200)
In the same manner, [one should perform the rite] with oblations of food and clarified butter, as well as with rice grains and sesame seeds,
and likewise with reddish flowers, such as those produced from the bandhūka plant.
Through oblations of white flowers, one shall obtain success in speech;
through oblations of white and red flowers mixed together, one shall obtain long life and health.
By offering oblations of three types of *dūrvā* grass smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one shall conquer them;
likewise by an oblation of *guḍūcī*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and sesame seeds.
By performing oblations with hundred-petaled lotuses mixed with sandalwood paste and camphor,
one obtains prosperity that shall endure as long as one's lineage lasts.
Having ground saffron with snow-water and mixed it with camphor,
he [anointed himself] with that paste and with blossoming golden *kahlāra* flowers.
May the royal ordinance abound in prosperity; may he live for a hundred years on earth, without rivals, free from affliction, free from enemies, and pure in intention.
By offering oblations with pieces of sugarcane stalks, one shall obtain clothing;
likewise by means of red or white flowers originating from the *karavīra*.
By offering oblations of *pāṭala* flowers smeared with honey, one shall subjugate a young woman;
likewise, by means of lotuses, one shall bring a goldsmith’s wife under one's control.
By performing white oblations with milk from a cow that has a calf of the same color and is black,
even one whose mind is most sinful attains incomparable fortune.
O Sage, by offering cotton seeds smeared with *sauvīra* salt at that very time into a crescent-shaped sacrificial pit (*ardhendu-kuṇḍa*), one's enemies will certainly be brought under control.
By offering oblations into the fire with their leaves and seeds,
and likewise with those seeds of death sprinkled with neem oil, they destroy those [enemies] of gold.
Likewise, horses afflicted by disease are certainly cured by oblations of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*);
and gold, when smeared with oil and offered with *akṣabīja* seeds, is the destroyer of all [evils].
By sprinkling *karañja* seeds with golden water, one becomes free from piśācas;
likewise, by offering the five limbs of a tree grown from unbroken grains (*akṣata*). (NarP 1.90.213)
By performing a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with seeds of the *akṣadruma* tree mixed with neem oil on that very day, the enemy will certainly become possessed by epilepsy. (NarP 1.90.214)
When fire is present in the birth asterism, tree, or fuel of an enemy,
the offering of flesh from his own womb and those very substances into that fire brings about the death of the foe.
Likewise, by performing oblations with lotus seeds soaked in mustard oil,
enemies arise who inflict leprosy and other diseases that destroy the body.
If one uses red phlegm (marica), mustard seeds, and gold smeared with oil in the middle of the royal circle,
the enemy will certainly be seized by a burning fever on that very day.
Thus, during rites of suppression and for one's own protection,
one should daily cause the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and so forth to be performed by those who are affectionate and have attained true knowledge.
Either by means of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, or by means of those very vidyās employed for their respective purposes, one shall quickly destroy this mantra that has been otherwise established.
Three hundred thousand [years] are said for the Kṛta age; likewise, it is double that for Tretā;
it is said to be triple for Dvāpara, and fourfold for the Kali age.
The fire sacrifice (havana) should be performed with one-tenth [of the recitation], the libation (tarpaṇa) with one-tenth of that;
the sprinkling (mārjana) should be one-tenth of that, and the feeding of Brahmins (dvijabhojana) one-tenth of that.
In this manner, one should perform the recitation for all [mantras] according to their respective numbers for the sake of success; thereafter, one should perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*).
O Lord of Sages, the recitation for Kāmeśvarī should indeed be performed twice as much;
once the mantra is mastered, one may then apply it in various ritual practices as desired.

O Lord of Sages, for the sake of attaining perfection in the *vidyā* of Bhagamālā, one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) are prescribed, and the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites should be performed according to a tenth part of that number.

The recitation of the Nityaklinnā mantra is prescribed as one hundred thousand times, and the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed at one-tenth that number for the sake of attaining success in the Vidyā; thereafter, one should accomplish the ritual applications.
Then, observing silence and subsisting on milk, he should mutter nine hundred thousand times the Bheruṇḍā mantra as prescribed; he should perform the remainder of the rite with great care.
A recitation of three hundred thousand for Vahnivāsinī has been prescribed;
all else should be performed by the best of practitioners just as previously described.
The recitation of the mantra of Mahāvajreśvarī is considered to be three hundred thousand;
the fire-oblation and other rites should indeed be performed according to the prescribed sequence, with one-tenth of that number.
O Sage, one should recite the mantra of the messenger (dūtī) one hundred thousand times without weariness;
then, by the rule of the tenth part of that number, the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites should be performed according to the prescribed path.

O Lord of Sages, one should recite the *Tvaritā* mantra ten million times, and having performed all the rites such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number, one attains the perfection of the *vidyā*. (NarP 1.90.230)

O best of the twice-born, it is declared that for the Vidyā Kulasundarī, one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣa) should be performed, and the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites should be done with a tenth part of that amount.
The recitation of the *Nityānityā* mantra is considered to consist of three hundred thousand repetitions;
the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites are prescribed to be one-tenth of that number, according to the stated injunctions.

O Lord of Sages, fifty-three hundred thousand recitations of the Nityapatākā mantra must be performed according to the rule, and the fire oblation (homa) and other rites should be performed with one-tenth of that number.
O Nārada, victory for Vijayā has been proclaimed as occurring at the measure of one hundred thousand [recitations];
the rest has been explained as before, as the means for the accomplishment of the vidyā.
One should recite the entire *Aṅgālikā* mantra one hundred thousand times;
it is taught that the fire oblation (*homa*) and other rites should be performed according to the sequence of one-tenth of that number. (NarP 1.90.235)
One who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the Jvālāmālinikā mantra eight hundred thousand times;
the fire-oblation and other rites are prescribed to be performed with the aforementioned substances in one-tenth of that number.

O Lord of Sages, for the sake of attaining mastery over the Vidyā, one hundred thousand recitations of the *citrā* mantra, followed by fire offerings (*homa*) and other rites, should be performed according to the prescribed rule.
This first chapter on the Nityās has been declared in brief; everything herein, including the preliminary practice of the yantras, must be understood. (NarP 1.90.238)
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nityāpaṭala," in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall declare the mantra of Maheśa, which accomplishes all aims.
By propitiating whom a person attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The heart-mantra is *sa-ba-ka*, subtle (*sūkṣma*), ending in *la* (*lānta*), and joined with the infinite wind (*anantānvito marut*).
This five-syllabled mantra, preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ), is declared to be six syllables.
Vāmadevī is the seer, Paṅkti is the metre, and Īśa is its deity;
the instructor should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with this mantra using six syllables.

One who has the mantra as their very form should assign the syllables of the mantra and so forth in due order to the index finger, the middle finger, the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb. (NarP 1.91.4)
These [faces] are known as Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Bhava, and Vāmeśa;
they are located in the mouth, heart, feet, and private parts, and furthermore, [the fifth] is on one's own head.
Thereafter, one should sequentially assign the six limbs of the mantra, conjoined with their respective seed-syllables, to the five faces— the eastern, southern, western, northern, and the central.
Immediately thereafter, for the sake of protection, one should perform the *golaka*-nyāsa:
in the heart, the mouth, the two shoulders, the two thighs, the throat, the navel, and on both sides.
Immediately thereafter, one should place [the syllables] on the back, the heart, the head, the mouth, the eyes, the nostrils, and at the joints of the arms and legs, including their tips.
Furthermore, [the syllables] are placed on the head, face, heart, belly, thighs, and both feet;
then, on the heart and the lotus-face, [the syllables] Ṭaṅka, Mṛga, Bhaya, and Vara.
The best of teachers should duly place the six syllables of the root mantra in sequence upon the face, shoulders, heart, feet, thighs, and belly.
The wise one should then place them on the crown of the head, the forehead, the belly, the shoulders, and the heart; thereafter, with this mantra, he should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka).
Salutations to Śambhu, who possesses infinite forms, whose essence is the nectar of the light-linga,
and whose limbs are illuminated by the shadow of the body of the fourfold manifestation.
Having thus surrendered his body, he should contemplate the Lord of Pārvatī;
he should constantly meditate upon Maheśāna, who resembles a mountain of silver.
He has the beautiful moon as his crest-ornament, his limbs radiant with jeweled ornaments,
holds an axe, the gesture of fearlessness, and a deer in his hands, and possesses a gracious countenance.
Seated upon a lotus, praised on all sides by hosts of celestial flowers,
wearing the skin of a tiger, he is the primordial source of the universe and possesses a universal form.

One initiated according to the Śaiva path should mutter the mantra of Śiva— who has three eyes, five faces, and who removes all fears— until one hundred thousand recitations of the reality (tattva) have been completed.
One should offer as many thousands of auspicious milk-rice oblations;
then the mantra becomes perfected, bestowing the desired accomplishments upon the practitioner.
One should worship the God upon a pedestal consisting of the nine Śaktis beginning with Vāmā:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Kalapadā, and so forth. (NarP 1.91.18)
Vikāriṇī is proclaimed first, then Vikariṇī, Balapramathanī,
and then Sarvabhūtadamanī.
These are proclaimed as the Śaktis of the Śaiva-pīṭha, beginning with Manonmanī.
After [saying] "Obeisance to the Blessed One" (namo bhagavate), one should then say "sakalādi."

Then, [one should offer] salutation again to the infinite one who is devoted to the power whose nature is the qualities (guṇa), who is beyond that, and who is the essence of the seat of yoga; this is the mantra beginning with "Tārā. (NarP 1.91.21)
With this mantra, one should offer a seat to the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain;
having conceived the form with the root mantra, one should invoke Śiva there and worship him.
In the pericarp, one should worship the Mūrti-Īśa, the elephant of the northeast direction, resembling pure crystal; in the cardinal directions are those beginning with Tatpuruṣa.
Yellow, black, white, and red, bearing weapons similar to those of the principal deity and endowed with four faces— one should worship them according to the prescribed rule.
In the corners, one should worship the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, which are of the nature of light, in their proper order;
one should worship the limbs situated on the filaments, as well as the Vighneśas and the serpents.
Then Ananta, named Sukha; then Śivottama, who is without interval;
then Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and thereafter Trimūrti.
Afterwards, [he gave birth to] one named Śīkaṇṭha and then Śikhaṇḍin in succession;
[their complexions were] red, yellow, white, reddish, black, red, collyrium-colored, and dark.
They wore the crescent moon upon their crowns, were seated upon lotuses, adorned with ornaments,
possessed three eyes, held tridents, thunderbolts, bows, and other weapons in their hands, and were enchanting to behold.
Thereafter, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Uttarā, then Rudra, and again Caṇḍeśvara;
then Nandin and Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and again the Bull.
Then [he saw] Bhṛṅgin, Riṭi, and Skanda, these seated upon lotus-thrones,
[colored] respectively golden, water-like (white), ruddy, dark, pearl-white, lunar (white), and pale-red.
Then Indra and the others, joined with their weapons such as the thunderbolt, are to be worshipped;
having thus worshipped the God, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times daily.
Completely liberated from all sins, one shall obtain the desired prosperity;
by reciting [the mantra] two thousand times, one is freed from diseases—of this there is no doubt.
By reciting the mantra three times, one shall obtain long life; by reciting it a thousand times more, one shall obtain all desires. (NarP 1.91.33)
One should reverently offer a hundred thousand oblations with pure sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter;
this will destroy the afflictions born of portents—of this there is no doubt. (NarP 1.91.34)
By reciting it one hundred thousand times, a human being becomes Śiva himself in person.
The six-syllabled mantra, conjoined with Śakti, is declared to be the eight-syllabled mantra (manu).
The seer (ṛṣi) was proclaimed of old as [the Ṛṣi] Chandas, and the deity (devatā) should be Umāpati.
The ancillary parts (aṅga) have been stated previously; one should meditate upon the gentle Īśa. 1,91.36.

Resplendent like the bandhūka flower, three-eyed, the all-pervading Lord wearing the crescent moon, with a smiling face, he holds in his own hands a trident, a skull-cup, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should meditate in the heart with the mind upon Him who is richly adorned with beautiful ornaments, His body embraced by the arm of the Daughter of the Mountain seated upon His left thigh.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule,
and then perform a fire sacrifice with one thousand of the finest *āragvadha* wood sticks, duly sprinkled with honey and ghee.
One should worship the Lord of Umā upon the previously described pedestal with perfumes and flowers;
outside, Hṛllekhā and the others should be worshipped with the limb-enclosures as before.
In the middle and in the east, south, north, and west,
one should worship Vṛṣabha and the others in sequence upon the petals starting from the east, according to the prescribed rule.
Then one should worship Caṇḍeśa, who has three eyes, a red appearance, and whose hands shine with a trident, an axe, a rosary, a bracelet, and a water-pot.

One should worship Durgā, who holds a discus, a conch, and the gestures of fearlessness and granting of boons, who possesses the luster of emerald, is gentle, three-eyed, and adorned with beautiful ornaments.
Then one should worship the lovely six-faced child, who possesses twelve eyes, has the luster of the rising sun, and holds a bell upon the tip of a branch of the *kalpa* tree.
And one should worship Nandita in the north, adorned with jewel ornaments,
having a dark-complexioned body, and holding an axe, a boon-granting gesture, and a trident.
One should worship Vighnanāyaka, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who has the luster of saffron, and whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon.
Then one should worship the General, who is dark-complexioned, holding a red lotus in his hand, with that same hand placed upon his left lap, having two eyes, and adorned with red garments.
Then the eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī and possessing the characteristics previously described, are to be worshipped;
one should also worship the world-protectors, Indra and the others, in their respective directions.
One should worship the weapons, beginning with the vajra, in succession outside of that;
thus the mantra-practitioner who worships the god Śambhu, the lord of Umā.
He shall become the locus of good fortune and welfare for all the worlds;
joined with the *sāṃta* and *sadyānta*, his head is adorned with the *bindu*.
The mantra known as Prāsāda is proclaimed to bestow all perfections upon those who worship it;
the ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is declared using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels.
O Nārada, the sages and others have declared that this [mantra] also consists of six syllables;
the preceptor should assign the forms beginning with Īśāna to the thumbs and the other fingers.
They know them in sequence as Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, the one called Vāmadeva, and the seed-syllable Sadyojāta. (NarP 1.91.53)
Furthermore, one should place those respective directions with the five short vowels beginning with *u* in reverse order, joined with the corresponding fingers.
In the regions of the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet, respectively, and in the faces directed upward, eastward, southward, northward, and westward; NarP_1,91.55.
Then the wise one should properly assign the thirty-eight kalās upon his body,
beginning with Īśāna, correctly upon the fingers in their proper order.
The best of instructors should perform the placement [of the fingers] starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger;
then he should place them again on the head, the mouth, the lotus of the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
Having placed [the mantras] on the face, the head, and so forth, one should again assign the limbs;
having uttered the five *tāras*, the heart-mantra "to the Omniscient One" is recited.
Then the word "amṛte tejo mālini tṛptāya," followed by "brahmaśirase" at its end, and then the blazing [syllable] located at the head (the *śiras*). NarP_1,91.59 //
To Śikhin for his crest, to the one beyond [all] for primordial awakening—that is his crest;
to the Vajra-holder, the one with a vajra in hand, the independent one—for his armor.
Having uttered "Saiṃ Saiṃ Hauṃ," [one should say] "Toṃ" for the secret power (guhya-śakti);
the eye-mantra is declared as "Ślīpaśuṃ Huṃ Phaṭ" at the end for the power (śakti).
Having thus discharged the weapon, one who is composed should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) in the five directions:
east, south, west, north, and the center.
One should place the five digits (kalās) of Īśāna in the faces in sequence:
"Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" is the first digit, Śaśinī.
Īśvara is the auspicious one of all beings; immediately after that is Maṅgalā;
then Śabdānta, the lord of Brahmā, and again the lord of Brahmā.
The third [digit] bestows the desires of Brahmā; may Śiva be intent upon that for me.
O Brahmin, the fourth is said to be Marīci, and it belongs to Sadāśiva.
Then, after that, there is another [mantra] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and joined with *namaḥ*,
[to be placed] in the eastern, western, southern, and northern faces respectively.
The practitioner of mantras should sequentially assign four parts of the Puruṣa;
the first is declared to be "Tatpuruṣāya Vidmahe," which is called Śānti.
After "mahādevāya śabdānte," one should say "dhīmahi";
then follows the second Vidyā, which is "syāt," and after that the word "tanno rudraḥ."
The *pratiṣṭhā* kalā is said to follow next; it consists of the third [syllable] ending with *pracodayāt*.
Beyond that is the *nivṛtti* kalā, which is entirely preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) and joined with *namaḥ*.

The practitioner of mantra should duly assign the eight kalās in the heart, the two shoulders, the navel, the belly, the back, and then the chest, and finally the breast, according to the prescribed rite.
First, the initial portion was uttered as "aghorebhyaḥ";
then, immediately after that, from the mouth of Moha, came "atha ghorebhyaḥ" at the end.
After Aghora comes Kṣamā; the third is proclaimed as Parā.
After all the Ghorataras comes Nidrā, who is entirely devoted to Sarva.
The fifth is declared to be Disease, after which follows Death as the sixth; thereafter, obeisance to You. (NarP 1.91.73)
Hunger is said to be the seventh [offering] to those in the form of Rudras, and thirst is said to be the eighth;
these, beginning with Dhruva, are accompanied by the word "namas."
One should then place the thirteen left digits upon the secret parts, the pair of thighs, the knees, the shanks, the buttocks, the waist, and both sides. (NarP 1.91.75)
The first [kalā] is for Vāmadeva; it should end with "namas," and its power is Ruja.
The second is proclaimed to be for Jyeṣṭha; it ends with "namas," and its power is Rakṣā. (NarP 1.91.76)
The fifth [deity] is Kalakāmā, and after that, for the sake of the Vikaraṇa;
then immediately following that, Saṃyamanī is declared as the sixth, preceded by the word "namaḥ."
The seventh is desired as Balakriyā for the sake of transformation;
the eighth is Vṛddhi, and at the end of Bala is the firm (sthirā) kalā.
After "namo pramathanāya," "rātri" is uttered;
at the end of "namo sarvabhūtadamanāya," the syllable "bhrāmaṇī" follows.
"Salutation to Mohinī"—this is declared by those who know the mantras as the twelfth digit (kalā);
"Salutation to Manonmanī," followed by [the name] Jvarā, is declared as the thirteenth.
These [mantras], beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava), ending in the dative case, and concluding with "namas," are proclaimed [to be used];
one should place them on the feet, arms, breasts, nose, head, and the pair of upper arms.
The eight mantras originating from Sadyojāta are correctly the kalās in sequence:
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta"—this is the first kalā, Siddhi.
Furthermore, "Salutation to Sadyojāta" is declared to be *vṛddhi*;
the third would be *dyuti*, and immediately after that, *abhava*.
Lakṣmī is declared the fourth; from her, the state of non-existence does not arise.
Medhā is said to be the fifth; O Kalā, may you be born from me once again.
The sixth, called Samīritā, is Prājñā; at the end of existence, there is the radiant digit (kalā).
After that, "Salutation to Udbhava," and the eighth digit is Sudhā.
