All the thirty-eight kalās, beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending in the dative case, are joined with "namaḥ"; these are declared to be the five [sets] beginning with the word Brahman.
Having thus disposed his body [into the mantra-deities], he himself shall become Gaṅgādhara;
then, becoming composed, he should meditate upon Sadāśiva in this manner.

With five faces having the luster of white, yellow, black, and pale-white *japā* flowers, adorned with eyes, wearing a crown marked with *glauṃ*, and possessing the radiance of ten million full moons; NarP_1,91.88 //
Holding in his hands a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, fire,
and the lord of serpents, he is radiant with ornaments, and [carries] a bell, a noose, the gesture of boon-giving, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times; one should then perform oblations with *karavīra* flowers soaked in honey, consisting of a tenth part of that number.
One should worship on the pedestal previously described;
one should fashion the image with the root mantra and, having invoked it, worship that image together with its enclosures.
One should worship Īśāna, who is three-eyed and white, holding in his hands a trident, a hand-drum, a gesture of fearlessness, and a boon-granting mudrā, in the northeastern direction.
One should worship Tatpuruṣa in the east, who holds a battle-axe, a boon-granting gesture, and a shield, who is as radiant as lightning, four-faced, and three-eyed.
Holding in his hands a rosary of seeds, the two nooses of the Vedas, a staff of a seer, a hand-drum, a skull-topped staff, a sharpened trident, and a skull-cup.
The best of mantra-knowers should worship Aghora in the southern direction— he who has the luster of collyrium, four faces, fearsome teeth, and three eyes, and who inspires dread.
Vāmadeva has four faces colored like saffron and possesses three eyes;
with his four hands he holds a deer, a bowstring, protection, and a boon. NarP_1,91.96 //
In the west, one should worship Sadyojāta, who has a crown shining with the crescent moon as its crest,
who resembles camphor and the moon, who is gentle, and who possesses three eyes.
One should properly worship the graceful one with a smiling face, who holds in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a rosary, and an axe. NarP_1,91.98.
One should worship the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, which consist of the nature of light, in the corners in due order;
one should worship the lords of obstacles, beginning with Ananta, on the petals all around.
Then, outside [the circle], one should worship Umā and the others, along with Śakra and the rest together with their weapons;
thus, endowed with supreme devotion, one should worship the Lord of Gods.
One should lead [the rite] with dances, songs, and other captivating hymns of praise.
The *tāra* (Om), conjoined with *māyā* (Hrīṃ), the ether (Ha), the bindu (M), and the nasal vowel (Ū), [forms the mantra]. (NarP 1.91.101)
The mantra consisting of eight syllables is considered to be joined with five syllables;
the wise one should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and other rites as prescribed for the five-syllable mantra.

Having the luster of vermilion, wearing a crown of shimmering jewels, with the moon upon his crest, adorned with divine ornaments and unguents, and having a serpent as his sacred thread; NarP_1,91.103 //
One should meditate upon Śiva, the Lord of All, who holds his beloved’s hand resting upon her breast as she sits on his left thigh, and who dispels the fear of the Vedas, mountains, and serpents.

One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with milk-rice mixed with ghee one thousand times, having first conceived the form [of the deity] upon the pedestal according to the root mantra.
First, the enclosure with the limbs [of the deities] such as Ananta and others; immediately following that, the third is taught by the leaders of the world with Umā and the others.
The fourth and fifth [mudrās] of these are proclaimed to be with weapons;
thus should the best of practitioners worship the God every day.
Having obtained wealth that extends to his sons, grandsons, and others, he rejoices here in this world. [The mantra is:
*Tāraḥ* (Om), *Sthirā*, *Sa-ka-ṛ-indu-bha-ghṛguḥ* (sa-ṛ-u-ma-la-va-ya) conjoined with *sargaḥ* (the visarga). NarP_1,91.108 //
The mantra, consisting of syllables and having the nature of Mṛtyuñjaya, has been proclaimed;
its seer is Kahola, and the meter is said to be the Gāyatrī of the Goddess. (NarP 1.91.109)
Mahādeva, the Conqueror of Death, is declared to be its deity;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual with the [mantra] joined with the long [vowel] by Bhṛgu.
With eyes like the moon, the sun, and fire; with a smiling face; seated upon a pair of lotuses;
with hands radiant with mudrās, a noose, a deer, and a rosary; and possessing the luster of the moon.

One should meditate upon him who deludes the entire universe, his limbs bathed in nectar trickling from the crescent moon on his forehead, adorned with necklaces and other ornaments, and radiant with his own innate luster.
The wise one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount,
using pieces of *amṛtā* soaked in pure milk and clarified butter.
In the Śaiva [tradition], one should worship the form upon the pedestal starting from the root of the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa);
having propitiated the limbs and the enclosures (āvaraṇas), one should thereafter worship the lords of the world (lokeśvaras).
Then, O best of sages, once this mantra has been perfected through recitation, worship, and other rites, the most excellent practitioner should worship the weapons on the exterior.
One should perform the rites prescribed for the auspicious time in order to achieve one's desired results,
having offered oblations daily with devotion using pieces of *sudhā* plant soaked in milk.
One shall obtain a lifespan of up to a thousand months, as well as wealth and sons,
by drinking milk, ghee, milk, or clarified butter from the eastern *sudhāvaṭa* tree.
One should offer one hundred and seven oblations in sequence for each of the seven substances on their respective days;
furthermore, one should daily feed seven brahmins with sweet foods.
One should give a sacrificial fee to the officiating priests consisting of a reddish-brown, milk-yielding cow;
thereafter, one should gratify the preceptor with wealth and other gifts, regarding him as a deity.
By this method, one who has been afflicted by sorcery,
malevolent spirits, fever, and the like shall be liberated and live for a full hundred autumns without difficulty.
In cases of sorcery, fever, paralysis, terrible insanity, diseases of the head, incurable illnesses, suffering from poison, delusion, burning sensations, and great fear; NarP_1,91.121 //
This man is declared to be a bestower of peace, a giver of fearlessness to all;
one should offer oblations with these substances according to the rule throughout three lifetimes.
One should feed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas with sweet foods;
one thereby attains long life and obtains desired prosperity.
A wise person should daily offer eleven oblations with *dūrvā* grass;
this shall indeed conquer untimely death and increase longevity and health.

A fire sacrifice performed with the finest sacrificial fuel produced from the nectar-creeper (*sudhāvallī*), saffron (*kāśmīrī*), and *bakula* flowers over three lifetimes removes all death and disease.
An oblation performed with *siddhārtha* seeds destroys even great fevers;
an oblation of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks is the destroyer of all diseases.
First, [one should utter] "to Dakṣiṇāmūrti," then immediately after that, one should speak the word "to the dweller" at the end of the word "at the root of the banyan tree. (NarP 1.91.127)
One should subsequently utter the word "namaḥ" to him whose limbs are solely devoted to meditation;
this is declared to be Rudra, the source of bliss, conjoined with the power of the Savior (Tārā).
The mantra consisting of thirty-six syllables bestows the fruits of all desires; Śuka is declared to be the sage, and the meter is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh. (NarP 1.91.129)
The deity is Śambhu, proclaimed by the name Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
he is to be worshipped with mantras produced from the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* at the beginning and end, preceded by those joined with the power of *tāra*.

The assignment of the limbs, beginning with the heart, is performed using the six, six, six, and eight syllables [of the mantra] upon the head, forehead, eyes, ears, the pair of cheeks, and the nose. (NarP 1.91.131)
One should place the syllables of the mantra upon the mouth, the joints of the arms, the throat, the breasts, the heart, the navel region, the hips,
the private parts, and again upon the joints of the feet.
Thereafter, one should pervade the body with the two powers of *tāra*;
[then one should meditate] upon a beautiful slope of the Himalayas, frequented by *siddhas* and *kinnaras*.
The heat was warded off on all sides by the branches of various trees,
while flowering trees were embraced by networks of creepers laden with beautiful blossoms.
In a place cooled by the breezes from waterfalls emerging from rock crevices, where throngs of celestial nymphs were singing and flocks of peacocks were dancing; (NarP 1.91.135)
In that place, the quarters of the sky were made resonant by flocks of warbling cuckoos,
and it was frequented by deer who had abandoned all mutual jealousy.
It was adorned with fragrant flowers born of both water and land,
and was constantly frequented by the ancient sages, such as Śuka and others, for their perpetual happiness.
It was beheld by the gods, headed by Purandara, together with their consorts and attendants—
a banyan tree of great height, radiant with fruits of ruby.
It was adorned with dense leaves made of emerald and decorated with hanging ornaments fashioned from the nine precious gems.
At its base, upon a beautiful and auspicious lion-throne fashioned from jewels, stood [the Buddha], possessing a wondrous, virtuous shade that cuts through the torments of saṃsāra.
Seated, adorned with dark ornaments, his face resembling the autumnal moon,
like Mount Kailāsa, three-eyed, and with matted hair marked by the crescent moon.
Intent on gazing at the tip of the nose, seated in the vīrāsana posture, with his hands resting upon his knees in the *bhadrāṭaka* position, he was richly adorned like a deer.
One should meditate upon Hara, who is exceedingly serene and has serpents bound around his arms;
one should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times, augmented by ten thousand repetitions.
One should offer oblations with pure sesame seeds mixed with milk, numbering one-tenth of that [total],
and worship according to the prescribed rite upon the pedestal (pīṭha) described in the Pañcākṣara[-tantra].
Subsisting on alms, with his senses subdued, one should recite this mantra eight hundred and fifty times daily for a month; he attains supreme excellence of speech.
Having recited this mantra three times, one should drink milk;
by meditating upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one becomes an expounder of the scriptures. (NarP 1.91.146)

First, one should utter the Praṇava, then the word "Hṛdaya," followed by the word "Bhagavate" joined with the suffix -ṅe (dative case), then "Dakṣiṇāmūrtim," and finally one should pronounce "Mahyam medhām. (NarP 1.91.147)
"Bestow [this]: this mantra consists of twenty-two syllables ending with two *ṭha*s;
its sage is Caturmukha, its meter is Gāyatrī, and its deity is declared [to be Brahmā]. (NarP 1.91.148)
One should fashion the six limbs with the six long vowels conjoined with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
Alternatively, one may do so with the words derived from the mantra; the visualization and other rites are considered to be as previously described.
First is the red, fierce seat, immediately followed by the one possessing the *bindu*;
then the second [syllable] situated in the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*), long [in vowel], and adorned with the moon of peace (*śānti*).
The third is the Lāṅgalīśārṇa mantra, endowed with three seed-syllables;
it is declared to be the essence of Nīlakaṇṭha and the supreme remover of the two kinds of poison.
The two syllables "hara" followed by the fire-born wife (svāhā) are proclaimed as the heart-mantra;
"kapardine" followed by the pair of feet (namaḥ) is declared to be the head-mantra.
"Ṭha Ṭha" for Nīlakaṇṭha—this is declared to be the Śikhā-mantra;
at the end of the word "Kālakūṭa," one should add "viṣabhakṣaṇam. (NarP 1.91.153)
"Hūṃ phaṭ" is designated as the armor (kavaca) mantra for Nīlakaṇṭhin; "svāhā" at the end is the weapon (astra) mantra. The wise know these to be the five limbs of the mantra.
One should sequentially place the three seed-syllables on the crown of the head, the throat, and the heart-lotus;
[the deity] possesses the brilliance of ten thousand rising suns and is adorned with a mass of matted hair beautified by the moon.
One should meditate upon Hara, who has three eyes and holds in his hands a serpent-ornament, a rosary, a trident, a skull-cup of Brahmā,
and a khaṭvāṅga staff.

One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and then properly offer oblations into the consecrated fire with clarified butter and sacrificial ghee in quantities amounting to one-tenth of that number.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship the Lord Nīlakaṇṭha on the seat according to the Śaiva tradition,
by means of the ritual for conquering death, which destroys the two kinds of poison.
Agni, Saṃvartaka, Āditya, Ra, Anila, and the sixty Bindus—
this is known as the Cintāmaṇi seed-syllable, which bestows all prosperity.
The sage is declared to be Kaśyapa; the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is proclaimed to be Ardhanārīśvara, the Lord of the worlds.
One should perform the six limbs in sequence with the six consonants beginning with *repha* (r):
[the deity] has three eyes, resembles a sapphire, and holds a trident, a noose, and a skull-cup.
One should meditate upon the Lord who is half-female (Ardhanārīśvara), holding a red lotus in his lotus-like hands, adorned with beautiful ornaments, and wearing a crown bound with the crescent moon.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform three hundred oblations with sesame seeds soaked in honey; one should worship on the Śaiva pedestal together with the limbs and the enclosures.
One should then recite the mantra beginning with Vṛṣa and the Mothers, followed by the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and their weapons,
ten thousand times for the pacification of disease.

This seed-syllable, revolving with the utterance of *svāhā*, dripping supreme nectar and situated upon the lunar disc at the crown of the head, when meditated upon, removes poison and disease. (NarP 1.91.165)
It is enriched with vowels in reverse order, and the seed-syllable resides within the house of fire;
it is surrounded on the outside by a hexagon shining with consonants beginning with the letter *ra*.
When recited over the head of one afflicted by a spirit, it quickly destroys that spirit;
when recited over the afflicted limb, it certainly pacifies that specific pain.
First the Praṇava, then the heart-mantra, then Paśupati ending in the dative case (ṅe), then again the Tāra, then "namo bhūtebhyaḥ," and then "adhipataye" followed by the eternal syllable "dhruvaṃ."
"Namaḥ rudrāya," followed by the pair "khaḍgarāvaṇa," then the pair "vihara," and subsequently the pair "narīnṛtya" separately.
Then, after "to the one who has gathered the ashes of the cremation ground," [one should say] "to the refuge," and again the word "to the one who bears the bell, the skull-garland, and so forth."
After the word "vyāghracarmapada," [the word] "paridhānāya" follows;
after the word ending in "śaśāṅkakṛtaśabda," [the word] "śekharāya" follows thereafter.
One should say after the word "kṛṣṇasarpa-pādāt": "yajñopavītine," "balayugmam," "calāyugmam," and "anivartaka-pāline."
Then there are the two jaws, which again terrify the two classes of beings;
thereafter, within the center of the mandala, there should be the two hips.
Then, pacify with the Rudrāṅkuśa mantra and cause entry with the *yuga* mantra;
afterwards, cause possession and utter the *Caṇḍāsipada* mantra.
This Rudra, the lord of Dhārā, together with Agnisundarī,
proclaims this Khaḍgarāvaṇa mantra consisting of one hundred and seventy syllables.
"Obeisance to the Lord of Beings, svāhā"—this is declared to be the mantra for worship;
this accomplished mantra is said to be perfected through recitation alone. (NarP 1.91.176)
After two tens of thousands, it is capable of grasping the elements and so forth;
then there is *māyā*, which is the pair of *sphurat*, and again the pair of *prasphurat*.
With the two syllables "ghātaya" at the beginning and "varma phaṭ" at the end,
this great mantra of fifty-one syllables is known as the Aghora-weapon (Aghorāstra).
Aghora is declared to be its seed-syllable, and the *trivṛt* meter is cited as its meter;
Aghora Rudra is designated as the deity, the leader of the mantra.
The heart is said to consist of five [syllables], the head is declared to consist of six;
the crest-lock is described as having ten, and the armor is considered to consist of nine.
The eye is said to consist of eight syllables (vasu), and the weapon is declared to consist of ten syllables (daśārṇa);
[these are to be placed] in sequence upon the head, the eyes, the mouth, the throat, the heart, the navel, and the thighs.
One should assign [the mantras] to the pair of knees, shanks, and feet using the Rudra-bhinnākṣara syllables, numbering five, six, eight, four, six, two, four, three, six, and two respectively.
One should meditate upon Sadāśiva, known as Aghora, who is dark-complexioned, has three eyes, possesses eight arms, wears red garments and red unguents on his limbs, and holds various weapons.
This is the mantra for the destruction and subjugation of bhūtas, vetālas, and the like, as taught by Manu:

the syllable *tāra* (OM), followed by the syllable *vānta* (PHA), situated upon the earth (*dharā*)—that is, the letter *la*—and adorned with the left eye (*vāmanetra*), the moon (*indu*), and the earth (*bhū*). (NarP 1.91.184)

The six-syllable mantra of Pāśī Baka, consisting of the ear, the eye, armor, and weapons, is known as the Pāśupata weapon; it wards off evil planetary influences and minor afflictions. (NarP 1.91.185)
With six syllables ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and accompanied by their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), one should meditate on the six limbs;
[the deity] is as radiant as the midday sun, fearsome, three-eyed, and adorned with serpents.
One should meditate upon Hara, the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), who possesses various weapons and four faces;
one should recite the mantra for one hundred thousand times and perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number.
In the fire consecrated with cow’s ghee and the sacred mantra,
one should worship on the Śiva-pīṭha with the limbs [of the deity], the Mothers, the World-Lords, and the weapons.
One should sprinkle water consecrated with this mantra into the mouth of one possessed by a spirit;
by the power of the great mantra, that person immediately releases their cries.
The man who releases arrows consecrated with this mantra in battle will conquer all enemies in an instant, like a second Pārtha.
The final letter of the alphabet joined with a bindu is the heart-mantra for Kṣetrapāla.
This [mantra] beginning with *tārā* and consisting of eight syllables is proclaimed as that of Kṣetrapāla;
having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels, one should meditate [upon him].

One should meditate upon him who has the luster of a blue mountain, who is clothed in the directions, adorned with serpents, and three-eyed; who bears tawny hair standing erect, and carries a skull and a mace.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with clarified butter-drenched *caru* in its tenth part; thereafter, one should worship in the sacred field (*kṣetra*).
Upon the seat imagined as Dharma and the other [elements], one should respectfully offer this oblation (bali) to him, together with his limbs, his retinue, and his attendants.
First, he strikes the two thighs; then, he breaks the two parts of the hating man;
again, he shatters the pair, and once more, he makes the two dance.
Then [one should recite] the pair of feet of Vighna, followed by Mahābhairava,
and the two [mantras] "gṛhṇa" and "pāvakasundarī" for the bali offering to the Kṣetrapāla.
This is declared to be the *bali* mantra, which bestows the fruits of all desires;
having performed it with the oral instructions upon a large sacrificial cake during the nights, the practitioner [attains his goal].
Having recollected the Lord of the Field as previously described, one should offer the oblation into his hand;
satisfied by this oblation, the Protector of the Field bestows [his favor].
One should recite "Kāntim medhām balāyogyam tejaḥ puṣṭim yaśaḥ śriyam" ending with "baṭukam" in the dative case, as well as "Āpaduddhāraṇam. (NarP 1.91.200)

After that, one should utter two *kuru*s, followed by *vaṭuka* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*); this twenty-two-syllable mantra begins with the *dhruva* and is conjoined with power (*śakti*). (NarP 1.91.201)
The body of Manu consists of two, four, seven, four, and one syllables;
it is a child, resembling crystal, with a face shimmering with longing.

One should remember with devotion Him whose limbs are radiant with divine ornaments, who has three eyes, who wields the staff and the trident, who is exceedingly gracious, and who grants fearlessness to his devotees.
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should then perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with honey in a tenth part of that number.
Upon a most beautiful lotus-throne imagined from the *dharmas* and other elements, which is joined with a sky-lotus situated within a triangle inside a hexagon; NarP_1,91.205 //
One should worship the god Baṭuka, together with his limbs and retinue, in due order:
"Day by day, consume the blood and flesh of the enemy faction along with your Gaṇas and accompanied by dogs! NarP_1,91.206 //
This is declared to be the bali-mantra, interspersed with the name of the enemy;
delighted by this offering, Baṭuka [destroys] the enemy army.
Having cut [the food] from the groups, one who distributes the meat with an angry mind is said to be like an elephant-hook, a flame-peak, or a lānta-dānta. (NarP 1.91.208)
This Caṇḍa mantra, ending with *phaṭ*, is declared to consist of three syllables;
Trita is said to be its sage (*ṛṣi*), and the *anuṣṭubh* meter is proclaimed for it. (NarP 1.91.209)
Caṇḍeśa is declared to be the presiding deity; now the arrangement of the limbs will be described.
"Dīptaphaṭ" is declared as the heart, and "Jvalaphaṭ" is said to be the head.
"Śikhājvālini Phaṭ" is proclaimed; "Vahaphaṭ" is considered the armor (kavaca);
"Halaphaṭ" is declared the eye (netra); and "Sarvajvāliniphaṭ" is supreme.
Having thus assigned the six limbs, one should then meditate upon the god Caṇḍeśvara,
who is red-bodied, three-eyed, and clothed in red garments.
And holding a trident, a rosary, a staff,
and a water-pot, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that amount.
With pure sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with the three sweets,
one should fashion the form upon the pedestal described for the five-syllable mantra using the root mantra.
Kūrmeśa joined with the Bindu, followed by "Caṇḍeśvarāya," is declared to be the Heart-mantra for the worship of Caṇḍeśa.
The enclosure should consist of the limbs, the Mothers, and all the [deities] beginning with Vajra;
one who is proficient in the Śaiva mantras should recite the mantra of Caṇḍeśvara.
One obtains all desires and rejoices both in this world and in the next;
listen, O Nārada, as I shall recite the divine hymn to Maheśvara.
By the recitation of which, all mantras become perfected in worship.
Salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, who dwells within all beings and whose forms are earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the sacrificial fire, the moon, and the sun.
Salutations again and again to Him who dwells within the Vedas, who is the Veda itself, and from whom the Vedas are born;
to the Great One, beyond the senses, eternal.
Salutations again and again to Śambhu, who cannot be defined through the divisions of gross and subtle;
salutations to Bhava, the destroyer of the suffering born of worldly existence.
Homage again and again to the All-Knowing One, who is far beyond the path of logic, who bestows the fruits of austerities, and who is generous with the four aims of human life.
Salutations again and again to the Great One, who is empty of beginning, middle, and end; to Him who has cast away all fear; who is the object of meditation for yogis; and who is devoid of qualities.
Salutations again and again to the soul of the universe, who is solitary, whose crest is the shimmering moon, who destroys the pride of Kandarpa, and who is the destroyer of Time.
Salutations again and again to the one who dwells as a consumer of poison, who has attained the shoulders of a bull,
and whose noble feet are bound together like a garland of rivers.
Salutations again and again to the pure one, whose nature is purity, the inner self of the pure, the destroyer of cities, the full, and the one of meritorious name.
Salutation to the one who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon his own devotees,
to the one who is without clothing yet is the dwelling place for all, and to the Lord of the universe.

Salutations again and again to the one who is the root of the triple form, the three-eyed, the wielder of the trident, the abode of the three worlds, whose nature is the light of the abodes, and the giver of birth.
Homage again and again to Him whose feet are reddened by the crest-jewels in the crowns of gods and asuras; to the Beloved who has given half of Himself to His own beloved.
O Brahmin, this hymn of Maheśa has been proclaimed as the destroyer of all sins; it bestows the presence of Śiva and illuminates the serpent-tantras.
This is that very great tantra, which illuminates all the gods and is joined with the means for accomplishing the fulfillment of the world's desires.
O twice-born one, those mantras which have been described in this tantra in general should be understood as bestowing accomplishment for the benefit of the world. (NarP 1.91.232)
Those Vaiṣṇava mantras which are especially the most excellent of all should indeed be practiced for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
The mantras of Rāma, the mantras of Kṛṣṇa, the mantras of the Lord of the Rāsa dance along with their ancillaries,
those of Śakti, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and Śiva are declared to be bringers of auspiciousness.
Among them, one should worship those who bestow the fruit of liberation for the sake of illuminating one's own self.
O Sage, all this that you requested has been explained to you:
the propitiation of the deity with devotion. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Maheśa Mantra," in the third quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Thus ends the third quarter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Kumāra, Nārada, desiring to know the highest good, spoke again with joy and great delight.
Nārada said: Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one! You have proclaimed this great tantra, which benefits all the worlds and is the most supreme among all tantras.
Now I wish to hear the supreme narrative of the Purāṇas;
O Sage, tell me all those various accounts that exist within each Purāṇa, for you are considered omniscient.
Sūta said:
Having heard those auspicious words of Nārada concerning the inquiry about the Purāṇas, Kumāra replied to him. 1.92.4.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Brahmin, this narrative known as the *Pārāṇa* arises from various kalpas;
it is joined with diverse stories, wonderful, and very extensive."
This sage is eternal, and as he knows it, so does no other; therefore, you should ask him, the best among those who know many kalpas.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Kumāra, Nārada,
bowing with humility, then spoke to the Eternal One.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, best among those learned in the Purāṇas, devoted to knowledge and realization,
recount to me in its entirety the classification of the Purāṇas.
When this is heard, everything is heard; when this is known, everything is known; when this is performed, everything is performed.
He will attain direct realization of the dharma consisting of the conduct of the castes and stages of life;
and how many Purāṇas are there, and what is their number according to measure?
O Lord, tell me those accounts joined with various narratives,
as well as stories concerning the four castes and the various vows and so forth.
"O Lord, reveal thoroughly the accounts of the lineages according to the order of creation;
for there is no one else superior to you who is a knower of the Purāṇic narratives."
"Therefore, tell me that which shatters all doubts.
Sūta said:
"Then, O Brahmins, having heard what was spoken by Nārada, the Eternal One (Sanātana)..."
Having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa for a moment, the best among the learned then spoke.
Sanātana said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of sages! [This work] is beneficial to all the worlds."
I shall fully declare to you that which was spoken by Brahmā in the past— the definitive understanding regarding the knowledge of the Purāṇic narratives that has arisen within you.
Once, however, the son of Brahmā, the renowned sage named Marīci, his mind enveloped by affection for his son, [spoke] to Marīci and the other sages.
Endowed with the study and hearing of the scriptures, and having mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary branches,
he approached his father, Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
Having bowed with devotion, O Lord of Sages, he asked this very same thing—
the stainless ancient narrative— which you yourself ask me, O giver of honor.
Marīci said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, source and dissolution of the worlds,
omniscient one, source of all auspiciousness, sovereign over all— salutations be unto you!
O Father, tell me, who am eager to hear, about the ancient seed,
as well as its characteristics, its measure, the authority, and likewise the speaker and the questioner.
Brahmā said:
Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the compendium of the Purāṇas, by the knowledge of which all that consists of speech— the entire world of moving and non-moving beings— becomes known.
O giver of honor, in all kalpas there was but one Purāṇa, the seed of the four aims of life, extending to a hundred crores [of verses]. (NarP 1.92.22)
From that Purāṇa, the activity of all the Śāstras originated; however, seeing that over time there was a failure to grasp this Purāṇa, the one of great intelligence [acted].
And in every age, Hari is born in the form of Vyāsa,
always with a work measuring four hundred thousand verses in every Dvāpara age.
Having divided it into eighteen parts, he pointed it out even in the earthly realm (bhūrloka);
yet even today, in the world of the gods (devaloka), its extent is one hundred million.
Its essence indeed exists, and it is described as consisting of four hundred thousand [verses]:
the Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, and likewise the Vāyavīya.
The Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, and Mārkaṇḍeya are proclaimed, as well as the Āgneya, the Bhaviṣya, the Brahmavaivarta, and the Liṅga.
Likewise, the Vārāha, the Skānda, the Vāmana, that which is named Kūrma,
the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and similarly the one called Brahmāṇḍa— these are the eighteen [Purāṇas].
I shall relate in brief a single narrative, a sūtra that calls together both speaker and listener; listen with a concentrated mind.
In the beginning, for the welfare of all the worlds, the ancient Brahman was indeed fully proclaimed there by the high-souled Vyāsa, the knower of the Vedas.
That indeed is the foremost of all Purāṇas, bestowing dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation;
rich with various narratives and histories, it is said to consist of ten thousand verses.
O Lord of Sages, it is there that the origin of the gods and the asuras, as well as that of the Prajāpatis such as Dakṣa and others, is proclaimed.
Then follows here the meritorious recitation of the lineage of Lokeśvara, the Sun, the Supreme Self, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
In this [chapter], the descent of the illustrious Rāmacandra— who is of the nature of supreme bliss and who manifests through the fourfold emanation— is described.
And thereafter, the glorification of the Lunar dynasty is described,
wherein the life-story of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World, which removes all impurities, is recounted.
In it, there is seen a description of all the continents and regions without exception, as well as of the netherworlds and the heavens.
The description of the hells, the narrative of the hymn to the Sun,
and likewise the birth and marriage of Pārvatī are recounted.
Then the narrative of Dakṣa was proclaimed, followed by the description of the Ekāmraka sacred field; O Nārada, this is declared to be the first part (pūrvabhāga) of this Purāṇa.
In its northern section, however, the description of Puruṣottama has been fully recounted in detail,
according to the procedure for pilgrimage.
In this very section, the life of Kṛṣṇa is narrated in detail,
as well as the description of the realm of Yama and the ritual for ancestral śrāddha offerings.
In it, the duties of the social classes and stages of life are proclaimed in detail,
as well as the narrative of the Viṣṇudharma-yuga and a description of the dissolution of the world.
Therein is the exposition of the Yoga systems and the description of the Sāṃkhya;
the summary of the discourse on Brahman and the praise of the Purāṇas.
This Brahma Purāṇa, consisting of two parts,
has been described as the destroyer of all sins and the bestower of all happiness.

Having written down this Purāṇa, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and having offered it together with gold on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, [one attains the highest state]. (NarP 1.92.44)
Having honored a reciter of the Purāṇas with garments, food, and ornaments, one should also devotedly give a water-cow to a twice-born man.
O twice-born one, he who recites or even hears this *Brāhmānukramaṇī* shall dwell in the world of Brahmā as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars endure.
He too shall obtain the fruit of every Purāṇa, both as a listener and as a speaker;
for he who listens to the entire Purāṇa, O Brahmin, having conquered his senses, [attains that same reward].
And by eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) according to the rule, he shall attain the state of Brahman.
What is the use of speaking much here, my child? Whatever a human being desires, all that he obtains from the recitation of this Purāṇa.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the History of the Brāhma Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Brahmā said:
"Listen, my son, I shall proclaim the Purāṇa known as the Padma."
It bestows great merit upon men who listen to it or recite it with joy.
Just as every embodied being is called "one with active senses," so too this [work],
which destroys sin, has been proclaimed in five sections.

O twice-born one, it is there that Pulastya, for the sake of Bhīṣma, expounded the expansion of dharma according to the sequence of creation and so forth, through various narratives, histories, and other means.
And the greatness of Puṣkara has been proclaimed in detail,
as well as the procedure for the Brahma-sacrifice, characterized by the recitation of the Vedas and so forth.
In this [section], there is the glorification of various gifts and the description of various vows,
as well as the marriage of the Mountain-born goddess and the great narrative known as the Chātaka.
The majesty of cows and other beings, which bestows all merit, has been proclaimed,
as well as the various slayings of the Daityas, such as the Kālakeyas.
O best of the twice-born, that section in which the worship and the giving of gifts to the planets is proclaimed is designated as the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa by the great-souled Vyāsa.
In the past, there was the story of Śivaśarman regarding the worship of one's father, mother, and other elders;
afterwards, the story of Suvrata, as well as the slaying of Vṛtra.
Then follows the narrative of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, as well as the story of Sunīthā; likewise the tale of Sukalā, and after that, the discourse on Dharma.
Then follows the narrative of service to one's father, the story of Nahuṣa, the life of Yayāti, and the description of the preceptor as a sacred site.
The dialogue between the King and Jaimini, filled with many wonderful stories,
as well as the account of Aśokasundarī accompanied by the slaying of the demon Huṇḍa.
Therein is the narrative of Kāmoda, joined with the slaying of Vihuṇḍa,
and the dialogue of Kuñjala with the high-souled Cyavana.
Then the narrative of the Siddhas was proclaimed, which describes the fruit of this section;
this is remembered as the Bhūmikhaṇḍa, consisting of the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
The origin of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) was described there by the sages and Sauti;
thereafter followed the configuration of the earth and the worlds, and the narrative of the sacred fords (tīrtha).
The narration of the origin of the Narmadā, the individual accounts of its sacred fords,
and the meritorious stories of Kurukṣetra and other holy sites have been proclaimed.
The narration of the merits of the Kālindī, the description of the majesty of Kāśī,
the majesty of Gayā, and the merit of Prayāga.
The exposition of the yoga of action according to the castes and stages of life;
the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini, accompanied by accounts of meritorious deeds.
Then follows the narrative of the churning of the ocean, the narrative of the religious vow,
the greatness of the five days of Kārttika, and the hymn that removes all offenses.
O Brahmin, this first section, known as "Heaven," which destroys all sins,
concerns Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice and the consecration of Rāma’s kingdom.
Then follows the arrival of Agastya and others, the glorification of the lineage of Paulastya,
the instruction on the horse sacrifice, and thereafter the conduct of the horse.
Virtuous discourses on various kings, a description of the Lord of the World, and the majesty of Vṛndāvana, which destroys all sins. (NarP 1.93.21)
Therein is the recounting of the eternal pastimes of Him who descended as Kṛṣṇa,
the greatness of the Mādhava bath, and the fruit resulting from bathing, giving gifts, and worship.
The dialogue between the Earth and the Boar, the story of Yama and Brahmā,
the conversation with the king’s messengers, and the description of the hymn of praise to Kṛṣṇa.
Then follows the narrative of Dadhīca, the union of Śiva and Śambhu,
the incomparable majesty of the sacred ash, and the supreme majesty of Śiva.
The narrative of Devarāta’s son, the praise of those who know the Purāṇas,
the story of Gautama, and then the Śivagītā are recorded.
In another kalpa, this account of Rāma, situated in the hermitage of Bhāradvāja, was told;
for those who always hear or read this Pātālakhaṇḍa, [it brings great merit].
The narrative of the Mountain, which pacifies all sins and bestows the fruit of all desires, was indeed previously proclaimed by Śiva for the sake of Gaurī.
After that, the story of Jālandhara, followed by the glorification of Śrīśaila and other sites;
thereafter, the meritorious story of Sagara was proclaimed.
The supreme merit of the Gaṅgā, Prayāga, Kāśī, and Gayā;
the greatness of giving food and other gifts—this is that Great Dvādaśī vow. (NarP 1.93.29)
The greatness of the twenty-four Ekādaśīs has been proclaimed separately,
as well as the Viṣṇudharmasamākhyāna and the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu.
Then follows the majesty of the Kārttika vow, the fruit of the Māgha bath,
and the sin-destroying majesty of the sacred fords (tīrthas) of Jambūdvīpa.
The majesty of the Sābhramatī, the description of the manifestation of Nṛsiṃha, the narrative of Devaśarman and others, and the description of the majesty of the Gītā. (NarP 1.93.32)
And there is the narration of the greatness of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata through devotion,
as well as the majesty of Indraprastha, which contains accounts of many sacred fords (tīrthas).
Then follows the description of the Mantraratna, the detailed account of Tripādbhūti,
and thereafter the meritorious stories of the incarnations beginning with the Fish.
O Vāḍava, [I have told you] the divine hundred names of Rāma, their greatness, the testing by Bhṛgu, and the majesty of Śrī Viṣṇu. (NarP 1.93.35)
This fifth section, which bestows all merit, is the conclusion; that best of men who hears this *Padma* consisting of five sections, [attains the highest state]. (NarP 1.93.36)
Having enjoyed his desired pleasures here, he shall indeed attain the abode of Viṣṇu;
this is the fifty-five thousand [verse section] known as the Padma.
He, who recites or likewise hears this *Padmānukramaṇī*, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, saluted by all the gods.
He too shall obtain the fruit arising from hearing the Padma Purāṇa.

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Table of Contents of the Padma Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
The glorious Brahmā said:
Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the great Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa.
This [work] consists of twenty-three thousand [verses] and is the destroyer of all transgressions.
O Maitreya, in that first section where six parts have been introduced by Śaktija, there [is] the introductory summary of the Purāṇa.
The primary creation and the origin of the gods and others,
the narrative of the churning of the ocean, and thereafter the lineage of Dakṣa and the rest.
The life-story of Dhruva, the life-story of Pṛthu,
the narrative of the Pracetasas, and the account of Prahlāda.
The first part is declared to be the description of the separate sovereignty [of the sons];
the second is the narration of the lineage of Priyavrata and the delineation of the continents and regions.
The narrative of the netherworlds and hells, the description of the seven heavens,
and the account of the days of the week beginning with the Sun, each endowed with its distinct characteristics.
The conduct of Bharata and the instruction on the path to liberation,
as well as the dialogue between Nidāgha and Ṛbhu, are proclaimed as the second section.
Following that, the narration of the Manvantaras, the incarnation of Vedavyāsa,
and the deeds that deliver beings from hell were recounted.
In the dialogue between Sagara and Aurva, there is a definition of all dharmas;
likewise, the ritual for ancestral rites (śrāddha) is prescribed, as well as the regulations concerning the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama).
The conduct of the virtuous has been told, followed by the narrative of Māyāmoha;
this third section is proclaimed as the destroyer of all sins.
O best of sages, in the fourth section is the meritorious account of the Solar dynasty, the recitation of the Lunar dynasty, and various stories concerning kings.
The inquiry concerning the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, followed by the story of the inhabitants of Gokula;
the slaying of Pūtanā and others in his childhood, and the destruction of Aghāsura and others in his youth.
In his youth, there was the slaying of Kaṃsa and likewise the deeds performed in Mathurā; thereafter, in his prime, the divine sports occurring in Dvāravatī are described.
Wherein occurred the slaying of all the Daityas and various kinds of marriages;
wherein Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe and the Sovereign of the Lords of Yoga, took his stand.
The removal of the earth's burden was accomplished through the slaying of enemies and other means;
this narrative concerning Aṣṭāvakra is declared to be the fifth book.
The conduct of Kālīja has been proclaimed, as well as the fourfold nature of dissolution;
the exposition of the knowledge of Brahman and the account of Khāṇḍikya have been described.
And this sixth part was proclaimed by Keśidhvaja;
after that, however, it was [proclaimed] by Sūta with reverence for Śaunaka and the others.
When questioned and repeatedly urged, [the sages] spoke various meritorious discourses on dharma known as the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, including vows, observances, and restraints.
The Dharmaśāstra, the Arthaśāstra, Vedānta, as well as Jyotiṣa; genealogies and narratives according to their sections, hymns, and likewise the Mantras.
Likewise, various sciences have been proclaimed that are beneficial to all the world;
indeed, this Viṣṇu Purāṇa is a compendium of the meaning of all the scriptures.
The account of the Vārāha-kalpa has been narrated here by Vyāsa;
the man who reads it with devotion and he who hears it with respect [attains the highest goal].
Indeed, both of them, having enjoyed their pleasures, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu;
and he who, having had this written, should give it away on the full moon of Āṣāḍha along with a cow of ghee, [shall likewise attain that state].

O twice-born one, he who possesses this [text] and knows the meaning of the Purāṇa for the sake of devotion to Viṣṇu goes to the abode of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot with the splendor of the sun.
O twice-born one, whoever shall recite or even hear this table of contents of the Viṣṇupurāṇa shall obtain the fruit of the Purāṇa.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Table of Contents of the Viṣṇupurāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Brahmā said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, I shall proclaim the Vāyavīya Purāṇa."
Upon hearing which, one attains the abode of Rudra, the Supreme Self.
That Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of twenty-four thousand verses;
herein, Māruta, in connection with the Śveta Kalpa, expounds the Dharmas.
O Brahmin, that which is unarisen, consisting of two parts, and characterized by creation and so forth, was explained there in detail as the Vāyavīya.
In this [section], the lineages of kings that are proclaimed throughout the Manvantaras,
as well as the slaying of the demon Gaya, are described in detail.
Furthermore, the greatness of the months has been declared, with the excellence of the fruit of Māgha specifically mentioned;
likewise, the duties of giving and the duties of kings have been expounded in detail.

In this [section], the first division has been proclaimed, which provides a definitive determination of the vows and other practices for those who move upon the earth, in the netherworld, in the quarters, and in the sky.
O Lord of Sages, in its northern section, the description of the Narmadā tīrthas and the Saṃhitā of Śiva are indeed told in detail.
That eternal God who is difficult for all gods to comprehend stands perpetually upon her bank with his entire being.
This water of the Narmadā is Brahmā, this is Hari himself, and this is the supreme Hara; this formless Brahman, this absolute liberation, is the water of the Narmadā.
Surely, for the sake of the welfare of the world, Śiva has caused this certain power to descend from his own body as a river.
Those who dwell on the northern bank are indeed the attendants of Rudra;
those who dwell on the southern bank go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Starting from Oṃkāreśvara as far as the western ocean,
there are thirty-five confluences of rivers that destroy all sins.
There are twenty-one [tirthas] on the northern bank and twenty-three on the southern;
the thirty-fifth is declared to be the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
Indeed, there are four hundred well-known sacred fords (tīrthas) existing on both banks of the Revā, together with their confluences.
O Lord of Sages, there are sixty thousand and sixty million sacred fords on both banks of the Revā, at every single step.
This compendium is of great merit, concerning Śiva, the Supreme Self,
wherein the life-story of Narmadā has been proclaimed by Vāyu.
Having written down this Purāṇa and accompanied it with a cow made of molasses, he who gives it with devotion to a Brāhmaṇa householder on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa— ||| NarP_1,95.17 |||
That man who causes this Vāyavya [section] to be heard, or who hears it himself, shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
He who regularly eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt.
And he who hears this table of contents (anukramaṇī), or likewise causes it to be heard, [attains the same state].
He too shall obtain the fruit arising from hearing the entire Purāṇa.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Table of Contents of the Vāyu Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
O Marīci, listen; I shall tell you what was composed by Vedavyāsa.
The Purāṇa named Śrīmadbhāgavata is equal to the Veda.
That work, consisting of eighteen thousand verses, is proclaimed as the destroyer of sins;
it has the form of a celestial tree and is endowed with twelve chapters (skandhas).
O best of Brahmins, the Blessed One himself is proclaimed to be the one whose form is the universe;
this occurred there, in the first book, during the assembly of the Sūta and the ṛṣis.
The meritorious life story of Vyāsa and likewise that of the Pāṇḍavas,
as well as the narrative concerning Parīkṣit— this is what has been proclaimed here.
In the dialogue between Parīkṣit and Śuka, there is the description of the two-fold creation;
and in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, the nectar of the deeds of the deities.
The definition of a Purāṇa and the origin of the cause of creation—
this second book has been compiled by the wise Vyāsa.
Then follows the life story of Vidura and his meeting with Maitreya,
and subsequently the section on the creation of Brahmā, the Supreme Self.
The Sāṃkhya system of Kapila is also included here; this is cited as the third [topic].
First is the account of Satya’s conduct, and after that, the account of Dhruva.
The meritorious narrative of Pṛthu, and then that of Prācīnabarhis—
thus has this fourth and excellent section (skandha) regarding creation been recounted.
Then follows the account of Priyavrata’s life, which bestows merit upon those of his lineage,
as well as a description of the worlds situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
This fifth section, concerning the abode of hell,
is considered to be the description of Ajāmila’s life and the account of Dakṣa’s creation.
Following that, the account of Vṛtra and the merit-bestowing birth of the Maruts;
this sixth book has been proclaimed by Vyāsa for the sake of nourishing [the work].
The meritorious account of Prahlāda and the description of the social classes and stages of life have been narrated as the seventh chapter, O child, in this discourse on latent impressions and karma.
The narrative of the liberation of the lordly elephant, the description of the Manvantaras,
the churning of the ocean, and the binding of Bali’s power.
This eighth [chapter] is proclaimed as the account of the deeds of Matsyāktāraka;
it contains the narrative of the Solar Dynasty and the description of the Lunar Dynasty.
O high-minded one, this ninth chapter, concerning the lineage and the life of the ancestors, has been declared;
it contains the childhood deeds of Kṛṣṇa, his youth, and his residence in Vraja.
Childhood at Mathurā, youth with the residence at Dvārakā,
and the removal of the earth's burden— this is recorded as the tenth [section] within the Nirodha.
The conversation between Nārada and Vasudeva has been proclaimed,
as well as that between Yadu and Dattātreya, and between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Uddhava.
The mutual destruction of the Yādavas, the liberation of the eleventh [Viṣṇu], the description of the future Kali age, and the liberation of King Parīkṣit; NarP_1,96.19 //
The arrangement of the Vedic branches, the ascetic practice of Mārkaṇḍeya,
the solar manifestation, and thereafter the Sātvata [manifestation] were proclaimed.
"I take refuge in the narration of the number of Purāṇas; this is indeed the twelfth.
Thus, O child, has the Śrīmad Bhāgavata been told to you.
It has been declared that [this teaching] bestows devotion, enjoyment, and liberation upon the speaker, the listener, the instructor, the one who approves,
and even the one who provides assistance.
On the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, this [gift], together with a golden lion,
should be given with affection to a twice-born devotee of the Bhāgavata.
Having honored [the teacher] with garments, gold, and other gifts by one desiring devotion to the Blessed One,
whoever causes this table of contents to be heard or likewise hears it,
obtains the supreme fruit born from hearing the Purāṇa.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Table of Contents of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata," in the fourth quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Śrī Brahmā said:
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall proclaim the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
It consists of twenty-five thousand [verses] and is based on the narrative of the *Bṛhatkalpa*.
The dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka, a description of the summary of creation,
and various meritorious discourses on dharma have been set forth herein.
In the first quarter of the initial section, by the high-souled Sanaka,
in the second [section] called Mokṣadharma, there is the exposition of the means to liberation.
And the exposition of the Vedāṅgas, as well as the birth of Śuka in detail,
was narrated by Sanandana to the high-souled Nārada.
In the Mahātantra, the liberation from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu-pāśa) is taught,
as well as the purification of mantras, initiation, the extraction of mantras, and worship.
The ritual applications consist of the armor-verse, the thousand names,
and the hymns of Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śakti, in their proper sequence.
In the third [chapter], the sage Sanatkumāra explained to Nārada the characteristics of the Purāṇas, as well as their authoritative measure and the nature of giving.
Each has been specified individually, preceded by the appropriate time for giving,
for all the months beginning with Caitra, and for each of the lunar days (tithis) separately.
The vow for the first lunar day and the others, which destroys all sins,
was proclaimed by the eternal sage Nārada to Nārada on the fourth [day].
This first part, known by the title *Bṛhat-ākhyāna*, has been proclaimed;
in its subsequent section, however, is the eleventh-day vow (*ekādaśī-vrata*) inquiry.
Then the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Māndhātṛ is proclaimed,
as well as the meritorious story of Rukmāṅgada and the account of the birth of Amohinī.
The curse of Vasu upon Mohinī, the subsequent act of her deliverance,
the most meritorious narrative of Gaṅgā, and the glorification of the pilgrimage to Gayā.
The incomparable majesty of Kāśī, the description of Puruṣottama, the ritual for visiting the sacred field, accompanied by many ancient narratives.
Then follows the majesty of Prayāga, after that the majesty of Kurukṣetra,
the narrative of Haridvāra, and likewise the narrative of Kāmodyā.
The majesty of Badarītīrtha and likewise that of Kāmākṣā,
the majesty of Prabhāsa, and then the narrative of Puṣkara.
Then follows the narrative of Gautama, followed by the hymn to the feet of the Vedas,
the majesty of the Gokarṇa sacred field, and likewise the narrative of Lakṣmaṇa.
The narration of the majesty of Setu, the description of the holy sites along the Narmadā,
the majesty of Avantī, and after that, that of Madhurā.
The greatness of Vṛndāvana, the attainment of even a beast in the presence of Brahman,
the deeds of Mohinī, and likewise the account of Nārada— thus indeed [it is told].
The man who hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard while composed in mind, goes to the abode of Brahmā; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
But he who, on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina, should give this [manuscript] along with seven cows to a venerable Brahmin, shall indeed attain liberation.
Whoever describes this table of contents of the Nārada-purāṇa,
or listens to it with a one-pointed mind, shall also attain the state of heaven.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Table of Contents of the Nāradīya Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Śrī Brahmā said:
"Now, O Sage, I shall fully declare to you that which is named the Mārkaṇḍeya [Purāṇa]."
This great and most meritorious Purāṇa is for those who always read or listen to it.
That Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, which describes all dharmas by means of birds, is said to consist of nine thousand verses.
The question of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya was previously addressed by Jaimini;
thereafter follows the discernment of the dharma of birds and the description of their birth.
This is the account of their previous births, the transformation of the Lord of Heaven (Indra),
the pilgrimage of Balarāma, and then the narrative concerning the sons of Draupadī.
The meritorious story of Hariścandra, the battle known as Āḍībaka,
the narrative of the father and son, and then the account of Dattātreya.
Then follows the account of Haihaya, accompanied by a great narrative;
the story of Madālaka is told, along with the life of Alarka.
The meritorious proclamation of creation has been recounted in nine ways:
the description of the time of the end of the Kalpa, and the exposition on the creation of the Yakṣas.
The creation of Rudra and others has been described, as well as the glorification of the conduct on the islands;
and various stories of the Manus, which destroy sins, have been recounted.
Among them, the story of Durgā is exceedingly merit-bestowing in the eighth interval;
following that is the origin of the Praṇava, which arises from the splendor of the three Vedas.
Then follows the account of the birth of Mārtaṇḍa, together with his majesty, as well as the lineage of Vaivasvata and the life-story of Vatsaprī.
Then the meritorious story of the high-souled Khanitra was told,
as well as the life of Avikṣit and the proclamation of the Kimicchaka vow.
Then follows the life-story of Nariṣyanta and the life-story of Ikṣvāku; thereafter the life-story of Nala and the excellent narrative of Rāmacandra.
The narration of the lineage of Kuśa, the proclamation of the Lunar dynasty (Soma-vaṃśa),
the meritorious story of Purūravas, and the wondrous tale of Nahuṣa.
The meritorious life-story of Yayāti, the genealogy of the Yadu dynasty, the childhood exploits of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and thereafter his deeds in Mathurā.
Then follows the account of the deeds at Dvārakā and the narrative concerning all the incarnations;
thereafter is the exposition of Sāṃkhya and the proclamation of the unreality of phenomenal expansion.
The life story of Mārkaṇḍeya and the fruit of hearing the Purāṇa:
that man who listens to this Purāṇa with devotion and respect.
O child, he who recites this [work] named Mārkaṇḍeya shall attain the supreme goal;
and he who explains this Śaiva [text] attains that very state.
He who, having written it down, bestows it upon an excellent brahmin on the full moon day of Kārttika together with a golden elephant, shall attain the station of Brahmā.
Whoever hears or even causes others to hear this table of contents of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa shall obtain their desired fruit.

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Table of Contents of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
The glorious Brahmā said:
Now, therefore, I shall duly proclaim to you the Āgneya Purāṇa.
Agni related the account of the Īśāna-kalpa to Vasiṣṭha.
That [work], consisting of fifteen thousand verses and containing various wonderful deeds,
removes all sins for those men who read it or hear it.
First is the question, then the narrative of all the incarnations of the Ancient One (Purāṇa),
followed by the section on creation, and thereafter the worship of Viṣṇu and so forth.
Thereafter follows the fire-ritual (agnikārya), characterized by mantras, mudrās, and so forth;
then the procedure for all initiations (dīkṣā) and the description of consecration (abhiṣeka).
The characteristics of the mandala and so forth, then the cleansing with *kuśa* grass;
the ritual for the investiture of the purifier (*pavitrāropaṇa*), and thereafter the ritual for the temple (*devālaya*).

Then follow the worship of the Śālagrāma and other [liṅgas], the specific characteristics of the various forms, the procedure for the ritual placements (nyāsa) and so forth, and finally the consecration and completion of the rite.
The worship of Vināyaka and others, the supreme procedure for various initiations,
the consecration of all the gods, and the description of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The majesty of sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, a description of the continents and regions,
the arrangement of the upper and lower worlds, and the exposition of the celestial sphere.
Then the science of astrology was proclaimed, as well as the treatise known as the *Yuddhajayārṇava*;
thereafter, the six types of ritual action (*ṣaṭkarma*) were taught, along with the collection of mantras and medicinal herbs.
The worship of Kubjikā and others, the sixfold ritual of placement (nyāsa),
the procedure for the ten-million-fold fire sacrifice (koṭihoma), and the description of the Manvantaras.
Then follow the duties such as celibacy (brahmacarya) and the ritual rules for ancestral rites (śrāddha);
thereafter, the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña) is proclaimed, as well as Vedic and Smārta rituals.

The exposition of expiatory rites, the vows and so forth pertaining to lunar days, the description of vows for the days of the week, and the glorification of vows for the lunar mansions. // NarP_1,99.12 //
The instruction on the monthly vows, the ritual for offering lamps,
the worship of the Ninefold Array, and the description of the hells have been proclaimed.
In this [work], the exposition of vows and gifts has been declared,
as well as the description of the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) and the unsurpassed ritual for the junctions of time (saṃdhyāvidhi).
Then follows the exposition of the meaning of the Gāyatrī, the hymn of praise based on its indicative marks,
the recitation of the mantra for royal consecration, and the religious duties of kings.
Then the chapter on dreams was proclaimed, followed by the determination of omens and the like;
next, the instruction on mandalas and so forth, and then the ritual for the initiation into the jewels.
Then follows the instruction on the policy taught by Rāma, followed by the characteristics of gems; thereafter the science of archery is proclaimed, and finally the exposition of legal procedures.
The account of the conflict between the gods and asuras, the exposition of Ayurveda,
the medical treatment of elephants and other animals, and thereafter their pacification.
Then follow the medical treatment for Gonarādi and various forms of worship;
thereafter are the diverse rites of pacification (śānti), and after that, the science of prosody (chandaḥśāstra).
After that, there is literature, followed by those [treatises] called Ekārṇava and so forth;
then the instruction on established grammar, and the lexicon consisting of the sections on creation and the rest.
Then follow the characteristics of the dissolutions, the description of the body,
a depiction of the hells, and thereafter the system of Yoga.
After that, the knowledge of Brahman is the fruit of listening to the Purāṇa.
This, O Brāhmaṇa, is proclaimed as the Āgneya Purāṇa. (NarP 1.99.22)
Having transcribed [this], whoever should give it on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa according to the prescribed rite, together with a golden pen and a cow made of sesame seeds; ||| NarP_1,99.23 |||
He who knows the meaning of the Purāṇa is then glorified in the heavenly world.
This table of contents of the Āgneya [Purāṇa], which bestows liberation, has been declared to you.
For men who hear and likewise read it, both in this world and in the next.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Table of Contents of the Agni Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Śrī Brahmā said:
Now I shall fully declare to you the Purāṇa that bestows all perfections.
It shall be for you a future bestower of all that is desired by the world.
There, where I arose as the primordial creator of all the gods,
I was formerly born as Manu Svāyambhuva for the purpose of creation.
Having bowed to me, he asked about the Dharma that accomplishes all goals;
then, being pleased, I spoke to him the teaching connected with Dharma.
When the high-minded Vyāsa, the arranger of the Purāṇas,
had composed [the work], the sage then divided that entire collection into five parts.
The account of the Adhōraka Kalpa, filled with various wonderful narrations—
therein the first section is known as the Brāhma Parva, wherein the commencement [of the work] is found.
In the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka, there is the transition of the inquiry concerning the Purāṇas,
which consists primarily of the deeds of Āditya and is endowed with all narrative accounts.
Endowed with the characteristics of creation and so forth, he is the embodiment of the entire essence of the scriptures; thereafter follows the description of books, scribes, and writing.
And here the characteristics of all the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have been proclaimed;
the seven kalpas of the lunar fortnights and the initial lunar days (*tithi*) have also been proclaimed.
The remaining kalpas, beginning with the eighth, are recorded in the Vaiṣṇava Parvan;
in the Śaiva Purāṇa they are divided according to their bodies (kāya), and in the Saura Purāṇa they follow the sequence of the final narrative.
The fifth book, which includes the dissolution of the world, is called the Pratisarga; it is endowed with various narratives and contains the conclusion of the Purāṇa.
Among these five, in the former [Vedas], the greatness of Brahmā predominates;
but in dharma, desire, and liberation, that of Viṣṇu and Śiva also prevails.
The second and third [sections] consist of four groups of verses;
the last one is called Pratisarga, and it contains all the narratives.
The wise Vyāsa has described this section concerning the future;
this Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of fourteen thousand verses.
The Śruti declares that Brahman is equal to all the gods, where their equality is proclaimed despite the gradations of their qualities. 1.100.14.

Having written that [text], the wise man who, free from envy, should give it on the full moon day of Pauṣa, together with a cow made of molasses, along with gold, garments, garlands, and ornaments; ||| NarP_1,100.15 |||

Having worshipped the reciter and the book according to the prescribed rite with perfumes and other offerings, as well as foods and edibles, and having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and so forth; ||| NarP_1,100.16 |||
Indeed, one who has conquered the senses, having fasted and being composed in mind,
or else eating only a single sacrificial oblation, should either recite or even listen [to this].
He who recites this table of contents (anukramaṇī) as it has been set forth for the future is liberated from terrible sins and proceeds to the station of Brahmā.
Whoever recites or hears this attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Table of Contents of the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Śrī Brahmā said:
"Listen, my child, I shall proclaim to you the tenth Purāṇa."
The work named Brahmavaivartaka reveals the path of the Vedas.
There, the venerable Sāvarṇi, standing in person before the divine sage Nārada, spoke all the extraordinary meaning of the Purāṇas.
The essence of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is love for Hari;
for the purpose of establishing the non-difference between those two, the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa is supreme.
The knower of the Vedas has related here in brief that account of the *Rathantara-kalpa* which I have previously described in the *Śatakoṭi-purāṇa*.
Vyāsa, having divided that which is known as the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa into four parts, proclaimed it to consist of eighteen thousand verses.
It is endowed with the Brahma-prakṛti, Vighneśa, and Kṛṣṇakhaṇḍa;
therein, following the dialogue between the Sūta and the Ṛṣi, follows the introduction to the Purāṇa.
The first section is on cosmogony; following that is the great dispute between Nārada and Brahmā, wherein both suffered defeat.
Thereafter, there was the attainment of the world of Śiva and the acquisition of knowledge by the self of Śiva;
following that, by the word of Śiva, [the same occurred] for Marīci and Nārada.
And the journey of Sāvarṇi for the sake of knowledge to that most meritorious hermitage, frequented by the Siddhas, which causes wonder throughout the three worlds.
For this section on Brahmā, when heard, destroys all sins;
following that, the dialogue between Sāvarṇi and Nārada is proclaimed.
It is joined with the greatness of Kṛṣṇa, followed by various narratives and stories,
and it also describes the portions that have become parts of Prakṛti.
The majesty [of the Lord] and the manner of worship and so forth, as they truly exist in detail—this Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, when heard, bestows prosperity. (NarP 1.101.12)
The inquiry concerning the birth of Gaṇeśa, along with the great meritorious vow;
and the origin of Vighneśa together with Pārvatī and Kārttikeya.
The deeds of Kārtavīrya and the wondrous life of the son of Jamadagni [Paraśurāma] are told;
there was a very great dispute between the son of Jamadagni and Gaṇeśa.
This section on Vighneśa indeed destroys all obstacles;
it contains the inquiry regarding the birth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, followed by the wonderful narrative of his birth.
The journey to Gokula and the wondrous events such as the slaying of Pūtanā are described there, along with the various pastimes of his childhood and youth.
The autumnal *rāsakrīḍā* with the cowherd girls has been proclaimed;
in the *Rahasya*, the play with Rādhā is described in great detail.
After that, following Akrūra, there was Hari’s arrival in Mathurā;
once the slaying of Kaṃsa and the others had occurred, Kṛṣṇa performed the sacraments for the twice-born.
Following this, the wondrous acquisition of knowledge from Kāśya Sāṃdīpani,
the slaying of the Yavana, and Hari’s subsequent journey to Dvārakā occurred.
In that place, O Brahmin, the wondrous slaughter of the inhabitants of hell was carried out by Kṛṣṇa;
this is the "Kṛṣṇakhaṇḍa," which shatters the cycle of worldly existence for men.
This Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa, which is truly transcendent, has been recited, heard, meditated upon, worshipped, and saluted. NarP_1,101.21 //
By reciting or hearing this work spoken by Vyāsa, which originated from the beginning, one is liberated from the terrible ocean of saṃsāra through the pacification of both knowledge and ignorance.
And whoever, having written this, should give it on the full moon day accompanied by a cow,
attains the world of Brahmā, liberated from the bondage of ignorance.
And whoever should recite or even hear this table of contents,
he too, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, obtains his desired fruit.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Table of Contents of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa," in the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the Pūrva-bhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. // 101 //
Brahmā said:
Listen, my son, I shall proclaim the Purāṇa known as the Liṅga,
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who read it and those who hear it.

And that which is called the *liṅga*, which Hara taught to me while standing upon the fire-liṅga for the sake of attaining dharma and other goals, is based on the narrative of the Fire-born One (Agni).
That very Purāṇa, consisting of two parts and embellished with many narratives, was proclaimed as the Liṅga by the venerable Vyāsa.
That [work], consisting of eleven thousand verses, indicates the greatness of Hara;
it is the supreme among all Purāṇas and the very essence within the three worlds.
At the beginning of the Purāṇa, there is the question; then, in brief, the account of creation;
after that, the narrative of Yoga is proclaimed; and beyond that, the narrative of the Kalpa.
Then the origin of the Liṅga and its Mother (Ambā) were proclaimed;
thereafter follows the purifying dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Śailādi.
Then follows the account of Dadhīca and the description of the duties of the Yugas;
thereafter, the narrative of the Cosmic Egg (Bhuvanakośa), and then the genealogies of the Sun and the Moon.
Then follows the detailed account of creation, as well as the narrative of Tripura;
thereafter, the installation of the Liṅga and the liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa).
Likewise, the vows of Śiva, the description of right conduct,
expiations for misfortunes, and the glorification of Kāśī and Śrīśaila.
After that, the narrative of Andhaka; then again, the account of the Boar incarnation;
after that, the account of the Man-lion incarnation; and then the slaying of Jalandhara.
Then follows the *Sahasranāma* of Śiva, the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the burning of Kāma, and subsequently the taking of the hand of Girijā.
Then follows the narrative of Vināyaka, the narrative of the King, and the story of Śiva, as well as the account of Upamanyu; this is declared to be the first part.
