Saṃgameśa, Nahuṣeśa, Mokṣaṇa, Pañcagopaka,
Nāgaśāva, Siddheśa, and the two Tīrthas of Mārkaṇḍa and Aṅkrūra.
At the places known as Kāmoda, Śūlāropa, and Māṇḍavya, and at Gopakeśvara, Kapileśa, Piṅgaleśa, Bhūteśa, Gāṅgeya, and Gautama; 131.
Āśvamedha, Bhṛgukaccha, Kedāreśa— the destroyer of sins—
as well as Kalakaleśa, Jāleśa, Śālagrāma, and Varāhaka.
Candraprabhāsa, Āditya, the one called Śrīpati, Haṃsaka,
Mūlyasthāna, Śūleśa, the one called Ugra, and Citradaivaka.
Śikhīśa, Kāṇṭitīrtha, Daśakanya, Suvarṇaka, Ṛṇamokṣa, Bhārabhūti, Puṅkhā, Muḍi, and Ḍiṇḍima.
Then there are Āmaleśa, Kapāleśa, and that which arises from Śṛṅga and Eraṇḍī;
thereafter Koṭitīrtha, Loṭaṇeṣa, and beyond that, Phalastutirata.
Then follows the story of Rohitāśva within the majesty of Dṛmijaṅgala; next is the narrative of Dhundhumāra, and then indeed the means for his slaying.
After that was Vadhū, then Citravāha, then his son Mahimā,
then Caṇḍīśaprabhāva, and then Ratīśvara.
Then Kedāreśa, Lakṣatīrtha, and the Viṣṇupadī-born [site];
then Mukhāra, Cyavana, Andhāsya, and the lake of Brahmā.
The place called Cakra, the narrative of Lalitā, the holy ford (tīrtha) abounding in cow dung,
Rudrāvarta, and the Markaṇḍa tīrtha which destroys all sins.
The Lord of Hearing, Śuddhapaṭa, Devāndhu, Pretatīrthaka,
Jihvodatīrtha, Saṃbhūti, Śivodbhanda, and the Praise of Fruits.
This section, known as Avanti, indeed destroys the sins of those who hear it;
hereafter, the sixth section, called Nāgara, is now being described.
The account of the origin of the *liṅga*, the auspicious story of Hariścandra,
the majesty of Viśvāmitra, and likewise the ascent of Triśaṅku to heaven.
In the *Hāṭakeśvara-māhātmya*, there is likewise the slaying of the Asura Vṛtra,
the description of Nāgabila, Śaṅkhatīrtha, and Acaleśvara.
The narrative of Camatkārapura, which is supremely wondrous;
Gayaśīrṣa, Bāla, Vālamaṇḍa, and that called Mṛga.
One should take refuge in Viṣṇupāda, Gokarṇa, Yugarūpa,
Siddheśvara, Nāgasaras, Saptārṣeya, and indeed Agastyaka.
Bhrūṇagarta, Naleśa, Bhaiṣma, Vaiḍura, Arkaka,
Śāramiṣṭha, Somanātha, Daurga, and Ātarjakeśvara.
The narrative of the slaughter by the son of Jamadagni, the account of the extermination of the Kṣatriyas,
Rāmahrada, Nāgapura, the six liṅgas, and the sacrificial ground.
The Muṇḍīrādi-trikārka, the one called Satīpariṇaya,
Rudraśīrṣa, Yāgeśa, Vālakhilya, and Gāruḍa.
The curse of Lakṣmī, the twenty-seventh, the temple of Soma,
that which was bound by Ambā, the one called Pāṇḍuka, the Āgneya, and the Brahmakuṇḍaka.
Gomukha, the one called Lohayaṣṭi, Ajāpāleśvarī,
as well as Śānaiścara, Rājavāpī, Rāmeśa, and Lakṣmaṇeśvara.
The Liṅga known as Kuśeśa and the one known as Laveśa are the most excellent of all;
they are celebrated as the sixty-eighth and the triple birth of Damayantī.
Then indeed, Revatī, Bhaktikā born at the tīrtha,
Kṣemaṅkarī, Kedāra, and Śuklatīrthamukhāraka are located here.
The narrative of Satyasandheśvara, as well as the story of Karṇotpala;
Aṭeśvara, Yājñavalkya, Gaurī, and likewise Gāṇeśa.
Then follows the description of the site-plan (vāstupada), the narrative of Ajāgṛha,
the well of good fortune (saubhāgyāndhu), the Lord of the Spear (śūleśa), and the narrative of Dharmarāja.
Then follows the narrative of Miṣṭānnada and Aśva, followed by the three [accounts] concerning Gāṇāpati;
then the life-story of Jābāli and the story of Makareśa.
The account of Kāleśvarī and Andhaka, as well as the Kuṇḍa of five flavors;
Puṣyāditya, Rauhitāśva, and the proclamation of the origin of the Nāgas.
Then follows the Bhārgava-carita, and after that the Vaiśvāmitra;
then the Sārasvata, the Paippalāda, the Kaṃsārīśa, and the Paiṇḍaka.
The account of Brahmā’s performance of sacrifice, joined with the narrative of Sāvitrī;
the [account of] Raivata known as Bhartṛyajña, and the inspection of the principal sacred fords.
The three sacred fields (kṣetra) are remembered as Kaurava, Hāṭakeśa, and Prabhāsa;
and the three forests (araṇya) are Pauṣkara, Naimiṣa, and Dhārma.
The three cities are Vārāṇasī, the one called Dvārakā, and the one called Avantī;
the three forests are Vṛndāvana, the one called Khāṇḍava, and the one called Aḍvaika.
Kalpa, Śāla, and likewise Nandigrāma— these three unsurpassed places,
known as Asi, Śukla, and Pitṛ, are declared to be a triad of sacred fords (tīrthas).
The three excellent mountains are Ṛśya, Arbuda, and Raivata;
and the triad of rivers are the Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, and the Sarasvatī.
Among these, each is proclaimed to yield the fruit of three and a half crores:
Kūṣikā, Śaṅkhatīrtha, Āmaraka, and Bālamaṇḍana.
The fourfold group consisting of Sāmbāditya, Śrāddhakalpa, Yaudhiṣṭhira, and Andhaka is said to bestow the fruit of the Hāṭakeśa field.
The four-month vow of lying upon the waters with Śiva as one's bed (Aśūnyaśayana), Maṅkaṇeśa, Śivarātri, and the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa. NarP_1,104.165 //
The gift of the earth, Vānakeśa, Kapālamocaneśvara,
Pāpapiṇḍa, Māsalaiṅga, and the glorification of Yugamāna and others.
The section on Niṃveśa and Śākaṃbharyā, the glorification of the eleven Rudras,
the narration of the greatness of giving, and the glorification of the twelve Ādityas.
Thus has been described this urban section known as Prabhāsa;
therein is Someśa, Viśveśa, and the greatly merit-bestowing Arkasthala.
The narrative of Siddheśvara and others is proclaimed here separately;
[then follow] Agnitīrtha, Kapaddarśin, and Kedāreśa, which bestows liberation.
Bhīma, Bhairava, Caṇḍīśa, Bhāskara, Indu, Kujeśvara,
Budha, Ijya, Bhṛgu, Saura, Aṅgu, Śiravīśa, and Haravigraha.
There reside five other Rudras, beginning with Siddheśvara;
they are Varārohā, Ajāpālā, Maṅgalā, and Laliteśvarī.
Lakṣmīśa, Vāḍaveśa, Urvīśa, Kāmeśvara,
as well as those known as Gaurīśa, Varuṇeśa, Durvāseśa, and Gaṇeśvara.
Then [the stories of] Kumāreśa, Caṇḍakalpa, and the one known as Śakulīśvara were told, followed by the excellent narratives of Koṭīśa, Bāla, Brahmā, and others.
Then follows the account of Narakeśa, Saṃvarteśa, and Nidhīśvara;
then that of Balabhadreśvara, Gaṅgā, and Gaṇapa.
The sacred narrative of the river named Jāmbavatī and of the Pāṇḍu-well;
likewise, the accounts of the hundred sacrifices, the hundred thousand sacrifices, and the ten million sacrifices.
The narrative of Durvāsas, Arka, Ghaṭasthāna, and Hiraṇyāsaṅgama;
[the accounts] of Nagārka, Kṛṣṇa, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the ocean.
The accounts of Kumārī and Kṣetrapa, of Brahmeśa, of Piṅgalāsaṃgameśa, and of Śaṅkara, Arkaghaṭeśa, and [the others] are told separately.
There is the glorification of the Ṛṣitīrtha, the Nandārka, and the Tritakūpa; and the wonderful account of the Sasopāna, the Parṇārka, and the Nyaku and Matī rivers.
The account of the history of Vārāhasvāmin at the two ankles known as Chāyāliṅga,
as well as the story of Kanakanandā, and likewise that of Kutī and Gaṅgeśa.
Then follows the account of Camasodbheda and Viduratha, the Lord of the Three Worlds; likewise, the accounts of Maṅkaṇeśa, Traipureśa, and Ṣaṇḍatīrtha.
Likewise, there were the stories of Sūryaprācī, Trīkṣaṇa, and Urumānātaka; as well as those of Cyavana and Arkeśa at the sites of Dhāra and Śūlasthala.
The narrative of Ajāpāleśa, Bālārka, and Kubera-sthala;
the meritorious story of Ṛṣitoyā, and the glorification of Saṅgāleśvara.
The narration of Nāradāditya, the description of Nārāyaṇa, the majesty of Taptakuṇḍa, and the praise of Mūlacaṇḍīśa. (NarP 1.104.183)
The story of Caturvaktra and Gaṇādhyakṣa, and of Kalaṃbeśvara; the story of Gopālasvāmin and Vṛkulasvāmin, and of the Maruts.
Then follow the accounts of Kṣemā, Arka, Vinatā, Vighneśa, Jaleśvara,
Kālamegha, Rukmiṇī, Durvāsas, Īśvara, and Bhadra.
The account of Śaṅkhāvarta, Mokṣatīrtha, Goṣpada, Acyutasadman,
Jāleśvara, Huṅkāreśvara, and Caṇḍīśa.
The wondrous account of the small sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of Vighneśa located at Āśāpura,
as well as the stories of Kapileśa and Jaradgavaśiva.
The narrative concerning Nalakarkeṭeśvara and Hāṭakeśvara;
that concerning Nārada, the bed, the ornament, Durga, Kūṭa, and Gaṇeśa.
The narrative concerning Suparṇailā and Bhairavī arising from the Bhaḷḷa-tīrtha;
the glorification of Kardamāla and of Guptasomeśvara.
Then follows the account of Bahusvarṇeśa, Śṛṅgeśa, and Koṭīśvara;

Svarṇarekhā, Brahmakuṇḍa, Kuntī, Bhīmeśvara,

The wonderful narrative of Durgā, Bhilleśa, Gaṅgeśa, and Raivata;
then the story of Arbudeśvara and the glorification of Acaleśvara.
Then follows the account of Nāgatīrtha and the description of Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage;
thereafter, the majesty of Bhadrakarṇa and of the Three-eyed One (Trinetra).
Then follows the majesty of Kedāra and the glorification of the pilgrimage to Tīrthāṅgama,
as well as the accounts of the Koṭīśvara-rūpa-tīrtha and Hṛṣīkeśa.
The glorification of Siddheśvara and Śukreśvara; the description of Maṇikarṇīśa, Paṅgutīrtha, Yamatīrtha, and Vārāhatīrtha.
Then [the greatness of] Candraprabhā, Sarpīḍodā, Śrīmātā, and the Śuklatīrtha,

Then follows the account of Kanakhala, as well as the stories of the Cakra and Mānuṣa tīrthas, and likewise the narrative of the Kapilāgni-tīrtha arising from the Raktānubandha.
[The tirthas] Gaṇeśa, Pārtheśvara, Yāntra, Ujjvala,
Caṇḍīsthāna, Nāgodbhava, Śivakuṇḍa, and Maheśaja.
Then follows the story of Kāmeśvara and the birth of Mārkaṇḍeya;
thereafter, the account of the various holy sites (tīrthas) located at Uddālakeśa and Siddheśa.
The origin of Śrīdevarāvāta, and [the accounts] of Vyāsatīrtha and Gautamatīrtha;
the majesty of Kulasaṃtāra, and of the two tīrthas named Rāmakoṭi and Āhvatīrtha.
The wondrous account of the emergence of Candrodbheda, Īśānaśṛṅga, and Brahmasthāna;
and the auspicious narrative of Tripuṣkara, Rudrahṛda, and Guheśvara.
The majesty of Avimukta and Umā-Māheśvara,
the power of Mahaujas, and a description of Jambū-tīrtha.

and in the majesty of Dvārakā, there is the narrative of Candraśarman.
The observance (vrata) pertaining to Ekādaśī, known as the worship beginning with vigilance;
the narrative of Mahādvādaśikā; and the meeting between Prahlāda and the sage.

The narrative of Durvāsas, the proclamation of the commencement of the expedition, the account of the origin of the Gomatī, and the fruit arising from bathing and other rites therein. (NarP 1.104.205)
The majesty of Cakratīrtha, the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean,
the narrative of the lakes of Sanaka and others, and thereafter the story of Nṛgatīrtha.
The meritorious account of the cow-pastures, the arrival of the gopīs at Dvārakā,
the narrative of Gopīsaraḥ, and the glorification of Brahmatīrtha and other sacred sites.
The narrative known as the Pañcanadyāgamākhyāna, which contains various legends and recounts the worship of Śiva-liṅgas, the gift of sacred waters, and the adoration of Kṛṣṇa.
The manifestation of Trivikrama, the narrative of Durvāsas and Kṛṣṇa, the slaying of the Daitya Kuśa, and the fruit arising from specific modes of worship. 104.209.
The glorification of visiting the sacred fords at Gomati and Dvārakā;
the beholding of Kṛṣṇa’s temple and the ceremonial bathing at Drāravatī.

Having written this out in the *Skānda-sarvottara-kathā* during the description of the majesty of Śibi, whoever should give it along with a golden trident— *NarP_1,104.212*
Having honored a Brahmin at midday, he rejoices in the state of Śiva.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Table of Contents of the Skanda Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the Great Narrative (Bṛhad-upākhyāna) in the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the Purāṇa named after Vāmana."
Rich with the deeds of Trivikrama, it consists of ten thousand verses.
The narration of the Kūrma-kalpa, containing the stories of the three sections and consisting of two parts,
brings auspiciousness to both the speaker and the listener.
First is the inquiry regarding the Purāṇas, then the severing of Brahmā’s head,
followed by the narrative of the liberation of the skull, and the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Then follows the account of Hara assuming the form of Time (Kāla) and the burning of Kāma,
as well as the battle between Prahlāda and Nārāyaṇa and the war between the gods and the asuras.
Then follows the narrative of Sukeśī and Arka, then the Bhuvanakośa,
then the account of the optional vows (kāmyavrata), and after that, the life-story of Śrī Durgā.
Next follows the life story of Tapatī, a description of Kurukṣetra,
the incomparable majesty of Satyavatī, and the glorification of Pārvatī’s birth.
Then her penance and marriage, followed by the narrative of Gaurī;
then the narrative of Kauśikī, and after that, the life of Kumāra.
Then follows the narrative of the slaying of Andhaka, followed by the episode of Sādhyā;
thereafter comes the life of Jābāli, and then the wonderful story of Arajas.
The battle between Andhaka and Īśvara, the incorporation of Andhaka into the ranks of the Gaṇas,
the account of the birth of the Maruts, and thereafter the life-story of Bali.
Thereafter, the account of Lakṣmī’s three strides is told;
following that, auspicious stories concerning Prahlāda’s pilgrimage to sacred fords are narrated.
Then follows the account of Dhundhu’s deeds, then the narrative of the hungry ghosts (preta),
then the narrative of the Man of the Stars (Nakṣatrapuruṣa), and after that, the life of Śrīdāman.
At the conclusion of the account of Trivikrama’s exploits, there is the supreme hymn proclaimed by Brahmā; and in the dialogue between Prahlāda and Bali in Sutala, there is the praise of Hari.
Thus, this first part of this Purāṇa has been recounted to you;
now hear its latter part, known as the Bṛhad-vāmana.
The Māheśvarī, Bhāgavatī, Saurī, and Gāṇeśvarī—
these four Saṃhitās here consist each separately of a thousand verses.
In the Māheśvarī [section], there is the glorification of Kṛṣṇa and his devotees;
in the Bhāgavatī [section], there is the wonderful narrative of the Mother of the World (Jaganmātṛ).
In the *Sauryā* [chapter], the greatness of Sūrya, which destroys sins, has been told;
and in the *Gāṇeśvarī*, the life-story of Gaṇeśa, the Great Lord, [is recounted].
This most wonderful Purāṇa, named Vāmana,
was narrated by Pulastya to the high-souled Nārada.
From Nārada it was obtained by the great-souled Vyāsa;
and from Vyāsa, his disciple Romaharṣaṇa received this.
And he shall relate it to the Brahmins of Naimiṣa;
thus the auspicious Vāmana Purāṇa has been handed down through tradition from of old.
Those who read and those who hear it also go to the supreme goal;
moreover, he who, having written this Purāṇa, should bestow it upon someone during the autumnal equinox, [attains the same].
To a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, he who gives a cow filled with ghee shall rescue his own ancestors from hell and lead them to heaven.
At the end of the body, having experienced his enjoyments, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Table of Contents of the Vāmana Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"Listen, O child Marīci, to the Purāṇa known as the Kūrma."
In this [section], there is the account of Lakṣmīkalpa, wherein Hari assumed the form of a tortoise.
And out of compassion, he recounted to the sages, in connection with the story of Indradyumna, the distinct greatness of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
O Sage, that auspicious collection consists of seventeen thousand well-composed verses,
wherein the various kinds of Brahma-dharmas were formerly proclaimed.
They do not grant a good rebirth to men through the diversion of various discourses;
rather, in that [work], in the first section, there was formerly the commencement of the Purāṇa.

The dialogue between Lakṣmī and Indradyumna, the discourse with the host of tortoise-sages, the account of the conduct of the social classes and stages of life, and the proclamation of the origin of the world. 1,106.5.
The enumeration of time in brief, and the praise of the All-pervading Lord at the end of the dissolution.
Then follows, in brief, the account of creation as well as the life-story of Śaṅkara.
The description of the thousand names of Pārvatī and of Yoga,
followed by the narrative of the lineage of Bhṛgu and that of Svāyambhuva.
Then follows the origin of the gods and others, the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the account of Dakṣa’s creation, and subsequently the glorification of Kaśyapa’s lineage.
The narration of the lineage of Atri, the auspicious life-story of Kṛṣṇa,
the dialogue between Mārtaṇḍa and Kṛṣṇa, and the discourse between Vyāsa and the Pāṇḍavas.
The narration of the duties of the ages (yugas), the glorification of Vyāsa and Jaimini,
the majesty of Vārāṇasī, and thereafter that of Prayāga.

thereafter, the greatness of various kinds of sacred fords (tīrthas) was described individually.
The description of secondary creation is known as the Brāhmī Saṃhitā;
hereafter follows the exposition of the meaning of the Bhāgavatī Saṃhitā.
In this [work], the distinct conduct of the social classes has been declared;
therein, the established order of the Brāhmaṇas is proclaimed in the first quarter.
"O child, this [profession] is always selfless and increases the happiness of enjoyments;
thus, the second livelihood for Kṣatriyas has been correctly proclaimed. (NarP 1,106.15)
By resorting to which one shakes off evil in this world and goes to heaven—
thus has the fourfold livelihood of those born in the Vaiśya caste been described in the third [chapter].
By practicing this conduct, one correctly attains the supreme goal;
likewise, in its fourth quarter, the livelihood of a Śūdra is described.
By means of which the Lord of Śrī, who increases the welfare of men, is satisfied;
therefore, in its fifth foot, the mixed meter (saṃkara) is declared as the mode of occurrence.
"By practicing which one attains the supreme future state"—thus, O Sage, is this second compendium consisting of five verses. (NarP 1,106.19)
The third [digit] here is that of the Sun; it accomplishes the tasks of men and awakens those with desires to the success of the six types of ritual action.
The fourth, named Vaiṣṇavī, is proclaimed as the bestower of liberation;
consisting of four feet, she is the very embodiment of Brahman for the twice-born.
These are proclaimed, in order, to consist of six, four, and two thousand islands.
This Kūrma Purāṇa bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life;
for men who read or hear it, it grants the most excellent state of existence.
Having written this down and offered it with devotion, together with a golden tortoise, to a Brāhmaṇa, he goes to the supreme goal. (NarP 1.106.24)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Sequence of the Kūrma Purāṇa," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Brahmā said:
"Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim to you the *Matsya Purāṇa*."
In which the history of seven kalpas is stated in brief upon the surface of the earth.
In the description of the Man-Lion (Nārasiṃha), Vyāsa, the knower of the Vedas,
having commenced it, designated that [work] as consisting of fourteen thousand [verses].
Then follows the dialogue between Manu and Matsya, the narration of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
the origin of Brahmā, the gods, and the asuras, and likewise the origin of the Maruts.
Then the Madanadvādaśī, likewise the worship of the world-protectors (Lokapālas),
the exposition of the Manvantaras, and the description of the Vaiśya kingdom.
The origin of Sūrya Vaivasvata, as well as his union with Budha,
the narration of the lineage of the ancestors, and likewise the time for performing ancestral rites (śrāddha).
The practice of the sacred sites of the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha), the origin of Soma,
the glorification of the Lunar dynasty (somavaṃśa), and likewise the life-story of Yayāti.
The recounting of the lineage of the ancestors, the celebration of the lineage of creation,
and likewise the curse of Bhṛgu upon Viṣṇu for his tenfold birth upon the earth.
The glorification of the lineage of Puru, the lineage of the descendants of Hutāśana, then the yoga of action (kriyāyoga), and finally the proclamation of the Purāṇa. 1,107.8.
The Nakṣatrapuruṣa vow, the Mārtaṇḍaśayana vow,
the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow, and likewise that known as the Rohiṇī-candra vow.
The procedure for constructing a pond and its greatness, as well as the ritual of planting trees,
the bed of good fortune, and likewise the Agastya vow.
Likewise, there is the Rasakalyāṇinī vow on the third day of the endless [fortnight],
and similarly the vow of Anantā, and again the Sārasvata vow.
Likewise, the eclipse-empowerment (uparāgābhiṣeka), the lordship of the seventh (saptamīśana),
the one called Bhīmā-dvādaśī, and similarly the bed of Ananga (anaṅgaśayana).
Likewise is the Aśūnyaśayana vow, as well as the Aṅgāraka-vrata;

May my householder life not come to ruin; O bestower of dharma, artha, and kāma!
The gift of the half-moon is prescribed here as bestowing all accomplishments;
on the second day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should assume the form of Śakra, the creator of the world.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
for in the month of Āśvina, the second lunar day of the bright fortnight is indeed meritorious.
A gift bestowed upon this [tithi] is said to yield infinite fruit;
for in ancient times, on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, Yama was [honored] by Yamunā.
He was fed by him in his own home; this is the second invitation to Yama, and here at home is the meal for nourishment provided by my sister. (NarP 1,111.19)
Thereafter, however, clothing and ornaments should first be given to him.
On the lunar day on which Yamunā fed the god Yamarāja from her own hand out of sisterly affection,
he who eats here from the palm of his sister’s hand obtains unsurpassed jewels, wealth, and grain.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, by performing a Śrāddha rite and honoring the ancestors,
one obtains health as well as a lineage of sons and grandsons.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the ritual cleansing with water from a cow’s horn and the sight of the crescent moon grant all desires to men.

Having offered the arghya water and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), one who has conquered the senses should worship the young moon with ghee and flowers for the sake of attaining dharma, kāma, and artha. (NarP 1.111.24)
On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, having worshipped Prajāpati in the form of the Sun according to the prescribed rule, one should honor him with red flowers.
Having fashioned a golden image according to one's means with red pigments and scents,
one should then prepare a full copper vessel filled with rice grains smeared with cow's ghee.
Having offered it with devotion to the God, he should present the image to a brahmin;
when the vow has been performed in this manner, O Brahmin, he becomes like the sun risen in person.
A man born on this earth becomes difficult to approach and difficult to overcome;
having enjoyed his desired boons here, he goes at the end to the station of Brahmā.
Constantly praised by all the gods and seated upon his excellent celestial chariot,
the best of the twice-born [then appeared] on the second day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna.
Having worshipped Śiva with very white and fragrant flowers, and having fashioned a canopy with flowers and auspicious floral ornaments; ||| NarP_1,111.30 |||

Having propitiated [the deity] with various food offerings, incenses, lamps, lustration rites (nīrājana), and so forth, one should prostrate with the eight-limbed salutation (sāṣṭāṅga), falling upon the ground.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, a mortal becomes free from disease,
endowed with wealth and grain, and shall certainly live for a hundred years.

Whatever procedure has been prescribed for the second lunar days occurring in the bright fortnight, that very same should be performed on those in the dark fortnight by those skilled in the ritual rules.
Indeed, it is Agni himself who, assuming various forms, is worshipped separately on the second lunar days; the rules regarding celibacy and so forth are as previously stated.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow for the Second Day of the Twelve Months," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:
"Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the vows for the third day to you."
By performing these correctly and promptly, a woman shall attain good fortune.
Having worshipped according to the rules with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as auspicious garments and ornaments, and with blades of *dūrvā* grass, the maiden should remain fasting.
A woman seeking a boon— specifically one desiring good fortune, sons, or a husband—
as well as the wives of twice-born men who have husbands, or a maiden endowed with auspicious marks.
Having gratified [the deity] with vermilion, collyrium, garments, and other offerings, she, with a delighted mind,
should perform a night vigil out of a desire for the completion of the vow.
Then, O Brahmin, one should present that image—
whether made of metal or clay— to the preceptor, or else cast it into a body of water.
Having thus performed the auspicious Gaurī-vrata for twelve years,
one should give twelve cows as a formal dedication for the successful completion of the rite.
What is the use of saying more in this regard? Just as Gaurī is the bestower of good fortune for women, no other such [goddess] exists in the three worlds.
By worshipping Gaurī with devotion, one obtains wealth, sons, a husband, knowledge, the fulfillment of commands, fame, happiness, and indeed every desired object.
The third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha is proclaimed as the inexhaustible lunar day; it is the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, which renders acts performed on it imperishable.
The wise know that there are two white and two black beginnings of the yugas;
on the white ones, the morning part is to be observed, and likewise on the black ones, the time for austerity.
Indeed, the Dvāpara and Kali ages have set in during the month of Bhādra;
therein, on the third day of the bright fortnight, [one should worship] the Teacher of the World together with Śrī.
One should worship Nārāyaṇa with flowers, incense, and ointments;
or else, having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, one is liberated from all sins.
A man should worship Viṣṇu with unbroken grains (akṣatas), he should bathe with unbroken grains as well;
he should feed the brahmins with roasted barley flour (saktu) and he himself should consume it.
Having thus performed the rite, O Brahmin, the man who is devoted to Viṣṇu and is honored by all the gods attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Now, the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is known by the name Raṃbhā;
on that day, one should duly worship an excellent Brāhmaṇa together with his wife.
O Brahmin, a woman desiring good fortune has duly undertaken this Rambhā-vow with perfumes, flowers, garments, and other offerings.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one clad in white garments bestows wealth, sons, and a mind inclined toward dharma that brings auspiciousness. (NarP 1.112.18)
One should worship Keśava together with Lakṣmī, along with the twice-born and their wives,
with meals, gifts of fragrant perfumes, garments, and ornaments.
A woman, greatly delighted by these pleasing words and desiring good fortune,
having observed this vow, becomes endowed with wealth and grain.
By the grace of the God of gods, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, one should perform the Svarṇagaurī vow.
One should worship Bhavānī with the sixteen types of offerings, saying:
"O you of noble vows, grant me sons; grant me wealth; grant me good fortune."
"And grant me all other desires; homage be to you!
Having thus prayed to Bhavānī, the Goddess of the Gods, who is united with Bhava, [he spoke].
Desiring the fulfillment of her vow, she should likewise cause a windmill to be given;
thus, having performed this auspicious vow for sixteen years, the woman [attains her goal].
One should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth;
in a pavilion or a pure mandala, one should worship the deities beginning with Gaṇeśa.
Having fashioned a copper vessel, one should place it upon a water-pot;
there, one should worship a golden image of Bhavānī.
Then, having properly worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the fire oblation (homa) using sixteen bamboo vessels filled with cooked food.
Having offered the food-offering (naivedya) to the Goddess, one should present it to the twice-born;
thereafter, one should give the ancestral offering (vāyana) to one's relatives and kinsmen.
Having given an image to the preceptor as well as a sacrificial fee to the twice-born,
a woman who is devoted to the performance of the vow shall obtain the full fruit.

On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should devoutly perform the Hāritālaka vow according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the offering of water for the feet and the arghya.
Then, having placed the food along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) into a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bamboo, or even clay— NarP_1,112.31.
One should bestow [the image] together with its fruit and its cloth upon a brahmin;
at the conclusion of that, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) along with beloved kinsmen.
A woman who has thus observed this vow, having enjoyed delightful pleasures,
shall become a companion of Gaurī through the power of this vow.
Articles of good fortune, garments, and sixteen bamboo vessels should be diligently given to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite.
And with great effort, he should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to other eminent Brahmins, and even more than that, to the Brahmins for the satisfaction of the gods.
Thus, whatever woman performs this vow that increases good fortune, she certainly attains good fortune through the grace of the Goddess. (NarP 1.112.36)
When the third lunar day of the month of Bhādrapada coincides with the asterism Hasta,
that is indeed designated by Śauri as the vow known as Hastagaurīvrata.
Likewise, the vow named Koṭīśvarī was proclaimed by the wielder of the Pināka bow; and the procedure for Lakṣeśvarī, which is of the same nature, is now being declared.
In this [observance], the vow should be undertaken for a period of four years;
it should be performed by means of fasting year after year, O Nārada.
O Lord of Sages, having purified one hundred thousand unbroken grains of rice or sesame seeds, one should then cast them into flowing water.
Having fashioned a very beautiful image of the Goddess from that cooked [flour],
he should place it upon a heap of perfumes and flowers, adorned with garlands of blossoms.
Having installed Pārvatī there, one should worship her, permeated by devotion,
with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food offerings.
O Brahmin, having offered various fruits and paid obeisance, one should ask for forgiveness; then one should dismiss the Goddess into the midst of the water and offer the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"Having given [the offerings] to Brahmins who know the ritual rules, one should eat on the following day.
Thus, O Brahmin, has the Koṭilakṣeśvarī vow been described to you. (NarP 1,112.44)
By the power of this vow, one goes to the world of Gaurī at its conclusion;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should perform the Bṛhadgaurī-vrata.
O Nārada, for five years according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should worship the preceptor at the conclusion with wealth and other gifts, as well as other Brahmins.
Five married women should be honored with garments, ornaments, sandalwood paste, bodices, earrings, and necklaces— [those who are] dear to Hari.
Five bamboo vessels, wrapped with threads, together with vermilion, cumin, and the substances for auspiciousness; NarP_1,112.48.
One should give them and feed them godhūma flour preparations, fresh cakes, fruits and the like, as well as the five types of *vāyana*. NarP_1,112.49 //
Having offered the *argha* and the sacrificial threads (*vāyana*), one should eat while restraining one's speech;
one should wear that fruit around the neck for the fulfillment of all desires.
Then, having risen at dawn, adorned with ornaments and accompanied by her female companions and the sounds of song and instrumental music, she should dismiss that image of Gaurī into the river.
"O auspicious lady, you have been summoned by me and honored according to the prescribed rite; go wherever you wish for the sake of bestowing good fortune upon me. (NarP 1,112.52)
Having thus performed this vow with devotion, O twice-born one, by the grace of the Goddess,
one shall enjoy pleasures and, at the end of the body, attain the world of Gaurī.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the Viṣṇu-Gaurī vow,
having worshipped her— who is worthy of homage by the entire world— with various kinds of ritual offerings.
Having fed the married woman who has been honored with auspicious articles,
one should dismiss her after bowing to her for the pleasure of Viṣṇu and Gaurī.

On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having performed the auspicious Haragaurī-vrata according to the previously prescribed rite, one should worship the Mother of the Universe.
By the power of this vow, having enjoyed delightful pleasures and attained the world of the goddesses, he rejoices together with her.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, O best of the twice-born, one should perform the Brahma-Gaurī vow,
even though she has already been worshipped according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Through the grace of Brahmagaurī, she rejoices there in union;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, Saubhāgyasundarī is to be worshipped.
Through the previously mentioned procedure, by the offering of a coconut as an *arghya*,
she, being pleased and gratified by the vow, bestows her own world.
The third day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna bestows happiness upon one's family;
when worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, it shall grant all auspiciousness.
And in all the third [lunar days], O Sage, the procedure is common:
the worship of the Goddess, the worship of Brahmins, giving gifts, the fire-oblation, and the dismissal.
Thus have these observances of the third lunar day been described to you here;
when performed with devotion, they indeed grant the desires that dwell in the heart of the worshipper.

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Vow for the Third Day of the Twelfth Month," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, I shall proclaim to you the vows for the fourth day."
By performing which, men and women shall obtain their desired objects of longing.
On the fourth day of the month of Caitra, having properly worshipped Gaṇapa in the form of Vāsudeva and having given a gift of gold, ||| NarP_1,113.2 |||
On the fourth day of Vaiśākha, having offered prayers to the one named Saṃkarṣaṇa, a brahmin, honored by the gods, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having given a conch shell to the foremost of householders and the twice-born,
one who knows the ritual procedure attains the world of Saṃkarṣaṇa and rejoices there for many kalpas.
By worshipping the one in the form of Pradyumna on the fourth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
and giving fruits and roots to the ascetics, a man shall attain heaven.
On the fourth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, by worshipping Aniruddha and giving gourd bowls to ascetics, a man shall obtain his heart's desire.
Having thus performed the vows of the four forms for twelve years,
one who desires the fruit must perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) according to the prescribed rule.
Furthermore, by performing the unsurpassed Satī-vrata on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha,
one shall rejoice in the world of Gaṇapati’s mother, equal to that [merit].
Likewise, on the fourth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, there is another auspicious vow,
since that day is the very beginning of the ritual procedure known as Rathantara.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa according to the prescribed rite with a mind purified by faith, a person shall also obtain even that fruit which is difficult for gods and others to attain.
O Sage, on the fourth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, at the rising of the moon, his birth occurred.
And the best among those who know the ritual rules should offer the *arghya* oblation to Gaṇeśa—
[visualizing him] as having a protruding belly, four arms, three eyes, and a red complexion.
One should meditate upon him as richly adorned with various jewels and possessing a serene countenance;
one should worship him with all the ritual services, beginning with the invocation.
One should offer sweetmeat (modaka) as an oblation that grants pleasure to Gaṇeśa;
having thus performed the vow and then eaten the sweetmeat itself.
Having performed his worship, he should sleep comfortably on the ground alone during the night;
by the power of this vow, he shall obtain the desires conceived in his mind.
Having obtained [this] in this world and even in the next, one shall attain the state of Gaṇeśa;
there is no other vow like this in the three worlds.
Therefore, one who desires all objects of longing should exert effort toward this task;
specifically, on this very day, the Dūrvā-Gaṇapati vow [should be observed].
Some desire it thus, O celestial sage; I shall describe that procedure to you:
having fashioned a golden image of Gaṇeśa placed upon a copper vessel.
Wrapped in a red cloth within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala,
one should worship it with red flowers and five leaf-stalks.
Having worshipped with bilva leaves, apāmārga, śamī, dūrvā, and other flowers dear to Hari, as well as with fruits and sweetmeats; ||| NarP_1,113.20 |||
Having prepared an offering, one should respectfully present it to the preceptor who knows the ritual rules;
then, being prepared, one should offer the *argha* water.
Thereafter, O Sage, having made a formal prayer, one should give the image of Vighneśa along with its appurtenances.
Having thus served for five years according to the prescribed rule, one should respectfully present oneself to the teacher who is knowledgeable in the ritual procedure.
Having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, one shall go to the realm of Gaṇapati;
furthermore, on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, [one should worship] the cow known as Bahulā.
One should worship him here with effort using garlands, perfumes, barley, and so forth;
then, having circumambulated him, one should perform an act of giving if one is able.
If one is unable [to perform the full rite], one should bow to her and dismiss her;
she may be five years old, twelve years old, or even sixteen years old.
Having performed the vow and completed it, one should give a milch cow;
by the power of this vow, having enjoyed delightful pleasures, [one attains liberation].
Honored by hosts of deities, he shall attain Goloka;
furthermore, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, there is the Siddhavaināyaka-vrata.
Having worshipped with all the ritual services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana),
one should meditate upon Siddhivināyaka with a one-pointed mind.
The god who has one tusk, ears like winnowing baskets, and an elephant’s face, who possesses four arms and holds a noose and a goad, resembling molten gold.
One should offer twenty-one leaves with twenty-one names, endowed with devotion; hear now those names. (NarP 1,113.30)
One should offer a leaf of the *śamī* tree to Sumukha, a *bhṛṅga* flower to Gaṇādhīśa,
a leaf of the *bilva* tree to Umāputra, and *dūrvā* grass to Gajamukha.
One should offer a jujube fruit (*badarī*) to Lambodara, a thorn-apple (*dhattūra*) to Harasūnu,
a *tulasī* leaf to Śūrpakarṇa, and a *śiṃbija* fruit to Vakratuṇḍa.
One should offer Apāmārga to Guhāgraja, Bārhatika to Ekadanta,
Sindūra to Heramba, and Patraja to Catuḥhasta.
Then, having taken two blades of dūrvā grass together with sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice— a leaf for Agastya, the Lord of All, which increases his delight.
Endowed with devotion, one should offer five *modaka* sweets as worship;
having provided water for rinsing the mouth, having paid obeisance, and having made a prayer, one should then dismiss [the deity]. (NarP 1,113.35)
O Sage, one should present a golden image of Vināyaka, complete with its accessories,
to the preceptor, and give sacrificial fees to the twice-born.
O Nārada, having thus performed worship with devotion for five years and having practiced this meditation,
one obtains auspicious desires pertaining to both this world and the next.

On this fourth lunar day, one should never look at the moon; for by looking at it, one incurs a false accusation—of this there is no doubt. Now, to destroy that fault, one should recite the following Puranic mantra: NarP_1,113.38: "Obeisance to you, O Lord of the Night, who are the abode of all the worlds, the source of all the luminaries, and the dispeller of the darkness of ignorance. NarP_1,113.39: "Obeisance to you, O Lord of the Night, whose form is the moon, who are the cause of the world's creation, preservation, and destruction, and who are the supreme Brahman. NarP_1,113.40: "Obeisance to you, O Lord of the Night, who are the witness of all beings, the bestower of boons, the remover of all sins, and the refuge of the virtuous. NarP_1,113.41: "Obeisance to you, O Lord of the Night, who are the master of the three worlds, the remover of all calamities, the granter of all desires, and the embodiment of all auspiciousness. NarP_1,113.42: "By reciting this mantra, which destroys all sins and grants all desires, one is released from every evil deed and attains the highest state. NarP_1,113.43: "Even if one has committed a great sin, by reciting this mantra three times with devotion on the fourth lunar day, one is liberated from all transgressions. NarP_1,113.44: "Therefore, one should always recite this mantra with a focused mind on the fourth lunar day; by doing so, one obtains the fruit of a thousand lunar fasts. NarP_1,113.45: "Having thus spoken, the Grandfather (Brahmā) vanished on the spot; and the gods, having heard this, were filled with joy. NarP_1,113.46: "Thus, O King, I have told you the entire procedure regarding the fourth lunar day, which destroys all sins and grants the fruit of all desires. NarP_1,113.47: "By listening to this account, which is auspicious and destroys all sins, one is freed from every evil deed and attains the highest state."
"The lion killed Prasena; the lion was slain by Jāmbavān.
Do not weep, my child; for this Syamantaka belongs to you."
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should worship Vināyaka as Kapardīśa.
One should worship with the *pauruṣa* hymn using ritual offerings:
unhusked rice grains held in the fist and cowrie shells, given without a specific motive.
One should give rice grains intended for the Viśvedevas, mixed with those dedicated to Hara, to a Brahmin boy who has been honored with perfumes and flowers.
May this Kapardin Gaṇanātha be pleased with those offerings presented by them;
on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, the vow known as Karaka is prescribed.
In this matter, the qualification belongs to women alone; their procedure is now proclaimed:
having bathed and being well-adorned, a woman should worship Gaṇādhīśa.
In front of that, one should place ten bowls filled with cooked food;
having offered them to the God of gods with devotion and a disciplined mind.
Having thus uttered, "May the God be pleased with me," one should then respectfully offer [the gift] to married women and to Brahmins according to their desire.
Then, at night during the rising of the moon, having offered the *argha* according to the prescribed rite,
one should eat sweet food for the complete fulfillment of the vow.
Or else, O Sage, one should present to a twice-born man a water-pot filled with milk or water, enriched with betel nut, unbroken rice, and gems.
Having performed this vow for sixteen or twelve years, the woman,
after making an offering, should then conclude this vow.
Or rather, for as long as she lives, a noble woman desiring good fortune should perform this vow;
there is nothing equal to this for women that bestows such auspiciousness.
"There exists nothing else in the worlds that is eternal; such is the established doctrine.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, the Nāga-vrata is proclaimed."

Having made the formal resolve for the morning vow, and having drunk the pure fluid from the udder and throat of a cow and bathed, he should then at midday worship the serpents, beginning with Śaṅkhapāla.
One should worship the remainder with offerings preceded by invocations;
one should perform nourishment with milk—this is known as the Nāga-vrata.
O best of Brahmins, when this auspicious Nāga-vow has been performed by men in this manner,
poisons are destroyed without delay, and serpents do not bite.
O lords of sages, from the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa until the end of the year,
one should subsist on a single meal, and on the second [day], at night.
By means of the *ayācita* and *upavāsa* fasts on the third and fourth days respectively,
a man should thus perform this according to the rule in sequence for four years.

Having completed that, at its conclusion, one who has performed the ritual bath after the vow and observes the great vow should have a chariot made of gold fashioned in the form of a rat with a multitude of serpents.
If one is unable [to provide the full materials], one should instead make a bright lotus with beautiful petals using colored powders;
having placed a water-pot upon it, it should be joined with a copper vessel.
One should fill [the vessel] with bright rice and place Gaṇeśvara upon it;
having covered it with a pair of cloths, one should worship him with perfumes and other offerings.
One should prepare sweetmeat as an offering, saying, "May Gaṇeśa be pleased," and one should keep vigil with the playing of cool-toned instruments and the recitation of Purāṇic narratives.
Having bathed at dawn in the clear light and performed the fire-oblation according to the rules with sesame, rice, barley, white mustard seeds, clarified butter, and sugar-candy; NarP_1,113.61.
Gaṇa and Gaṇādhipa, Kūṣmāṇḍa and Tripurāntaka, Lambodara and Ekadanta, Rukmadaṃṣṭra and Vighnapa.
Brahmā, Yama, Varuṇa, Soma, Sūrya, Hutāśana,
Gandhamādin, and Parameṣṭhin— thus by these sixteen names.

One should offer oblations into the fire one hundred and eight times for each [name], beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *ṅeṃ namas*, starting with "Vakratuṇḍa" followed by *ṅeṃ* and ending with the armor-mantra (*varma*). NarP_1,113.64 //
Then, having offered oblations according to one's ability with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, one should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
After worshipping the guardians of the quarters, one should then feed the Brahmins.
Then, one should give to the preceptor twenty-four sweetmeats and milk-rice, as well as a cow with her calf, along with a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having bowed down, honored with a ceremonial gift, and dismissed those best of the twice-born, he should give even more to others according to his ability.
One should eat together with one's kinsmen, being joyful in mind oneself;
having performed this vow, a man enjoys the most excellent pleasures here.
"By the grace of Gaṇeśa, one attains union with Viṣṇu;
O Nārada, some call this the 'Excellence Vow' (Varavrata)."
This very procedure and its fruit here are likewise equal;
one should pray with devotion to Vighneśa on the fourth lunar day of the month of Pauṣa.
One should feed even a single Brahmin in this manner and give sweetmeats as a sacrificial fee;
when this is done, O Sage, the observer of the vow shall become a vessel of prosperity.
On the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, the Saṃkaṣṭavrata is prescribed;
there, the observer of the vow, having made a formal resolve for fasting, should proceed according to the rules.
One should remain with a restrained mind until the rising of the moon;
then, when the moonrise has arrived, [one should worship] the earthen Gaṇanāyaka.
Having prepared [the deity], one should place it upon the pedestal along with its weapons and vehicle;
having worshipped it according to the rules with the sixteen types of offerings.
One should also offer a sweetmeat (modaka) as an oblation, along with jaggery and crushed sesame;
then, one should present the arghya water in a copper vessel mixed with red sandalwood.
Having prepared kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, śamī leaves, and curd, one should cause these to be offered to the Moon.
O jewel of the ocean of the sky, O moon, O Lord of the daughters of Dakṣa,
O you who possess the form of Gaṇeśa, accept this water offering given by me.
Having thus offered divine *arghya* that destroys sins to Gaṇeśa,
one should feed the most excellent Brahmins according to one's ability and then eat oneself, following their permission.
O Brahmin, by performing this vow known as Saṃkaṣṭa, which brings about auspiciousness,
one shall become prosperous with wealth and grain and shall never encounter distress.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, however, there is the unsurpassed Gaurī-vrata;

By men and especially by women, [one should worship] with kunda flowers mixed with saffron,

With incense, lamps, and offerings of food including jaggery, ginger, milk, milk-rice, salt, and *pālaka* vegetables; ||| NarP_1,113.82 |||
Widowless women and most auspicious Brahmins should be honored;

O Sage, bathing, giving gifts, chanting, and fire-offerings—

having fed the twice-born with sesame-based sweets, the person should then eat himself.
Devoted to the worship of Gaṇeśa through acts of giving, fire-offerings,

Having fashioned a golden elephant-faced [image] and having worshipped it with diligence,
it should be given to an eminent brahmin for the sake of the prosperity of all riches.
O best of Brahmins, on whichever month it may be, if the fourth lunar day (caturthī) falls on a Sunday or a Tuesday,
it bestows special fruits.
And on all fourth lunar days, whether in the bright or the dark fortnights,
the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa), the Lord of Gods, should be worshipped by those intent on devotion.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fourth-Day Vow of the Twelve Months," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:

By steadfastly adhering to these with devotion, one may attain all desires.
The Matsya-jayantī is declared to be the fifth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu;
on this day, devotees should perform the worship of the Fish Incarnation with great festivities.
This is called Śrīpañcamī; on that day, the worship of Śrī should be performed with offerings such as perfumes and other services, as well as with food offerings such as milk-rice (pāyasa).
Lakṣmī indeed never abandons one who worships her here;
likewise, there is the Pṛthvīvrata, the Cāndravrata, and the Hayagrīvavrata.
Those desiring various specific accomplishments should perform each respective rite according to its prescribed method.
Then, on the fifth day of the month of Vaiśākha, a person, having worshipped Śeṣa, [should proceed].
Endowed with all the hosts of Nāgas, one obtains the desired fruit;

Indeed, the attainment of all desired fruits comes through feeding Brahmins;
furthermore, O Sage, on the fifth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, [one should worship] Vāyu, who is omnipresent.
Having gone out from the village and sat down upon the surface of the earth,

One should place the raised [liṅga] in the center upon the prepared lotus;

Having duly worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should perform the examination of the wind;
for whichever wind prevails during the first and subsequent watches of the night, [that is the indicator].
One should properly perform worship for each of those lords of the directions;
having remained there without food for four watches of the night, one should do so.
Having returned to his own home in the evening and eaten a small amount with a composed mind,

"Whatever dream arises during that night in the fourth watch, that very one shall surely come to pass," so indeed said Śiva.
But when an inauspicious event has occurred, one devoted to the worship of Śiva,

Having fed eight twice-born men, one shall thereafter obtain auspicious fruit;

This vow, observed on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, generates good fortune for men both in this world and in the next, and indeed bestows an abundance of food.
On the fourth day, at the end of the day, O Nārada, the wise man, having placed all the foods in separate vessels, should drench them with water.
Then, having removed that [mixture] into another vessel, one should set it in water;

Having worshipped the gods and performed a ritual bath, he should place the food offering (naivedya) before them and,
with a joyful mind, give that food to beggars.
Having spent the entire day in this manner, one should go to a temple of Śiva at the onset of night and worship the Lord in the form of the Liṅga.
Having properly worshipped Maheśvara with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should recite the five-syllabled mantra a hundred or even a thousand times.
Having offered the recitation to the god Bhava, who is the very form of worldly existence,
and having praised him with all the Vaundika and Paurāṇika hymns, he remained undisturbed.
One should constantly pray to the Lord Īśāna for the attainment of all kinds of food—
both the autumnal grains and those of the rainy season.
"May I be endowed with all those things in birth after birth.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, he indeed returned to his own home.

Having given food to Brahmins and others, one should eat cooked food while restraining one's speech; this is the vow regarding food, O Brahmin, which has been practiced by men according to the prescribed rule.

On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, men who are devoted to faithfulness should perform [this rite], which produces an abundance of all kinds of food and grants a favorable rebirth in the next world.
On both sides of the door, one should draw fierce venomous serpents with cow dung;
one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings, and immediately thereafter, Indrāṇī.
Having performed worship with gold, silver, and other materials, with curd, unbroken rice, kuśa grass, and water,
as well as with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and various offerings of food.
Then, having circumambulated that object and bowed down to it,
and having made a prayer with a spirit of devotion, one should offer it to the foremost of Brahmins.
Whatever substance such as gold or silver has been offered here to the Brahmins,
may that yield infinite fruit for me in birth after birth.
O Nārada, when one gives wealth in this manner with a spirit of devotion,
the Lord of Wealth becomes pleased and bestows prosperity such as gold and other riches.
Having performed this vow and having fed the Brahmins with devotion,
the man should afterwards eat himself, accompanied by his wife, children, and friends.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should satisfy the nāgas with milk.
He whose family, up to the seventh generation, shall be entirely free from fear of snakes,
should worship the best of ṛṣis on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada.
Having bathed in a river or similar body of water at dawn and performed his daily rites without sloth,

Jamadagni and Vasiṣṭha—these seven are remembered as the sages (ṛṣis).

Having performed this vow dedicated to Gaṅgā and enjoyed his desired pleasures, he shall,

On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, there is the Upāṅgalalitā vow.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Fifth Day (Pañcamī) in Each of the Twelve Months," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* in the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ṣaṣṭhī Vow Observed on the Sixth Day of Each Month," in the fourth quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanātana said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe to you the vows pertaining to the seventh day (Saptamī).
By performing these with devotion, a person shall attain union with the Sun.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, however, one should perform an external bath on a sacrificial mound smeared with cow dung and strewn with white clay.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus and visualized it,
one should place two deities who have mastered the elements upon the eastern petal.
And one should place the two Gandharvas who have performed their task upon the southeastern petal;
likewise, one should place the pair of Rākṣasas upon the southern petal.
O best of sages, one should place two [deities] on the leaf in the south-west;
the two great Nāgas, the sons of Kadrū, who have performed their service, are in the west.
O best of the twice-born, one should place two Yātudhānas in the northwest, two sages in the north, and one Graha in the northeast upon the pedestal.
Their worship should be performed with perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
with lamps and incense, along with food offerings, betel, areca nuts, and other such items.
Having thus performed the worship, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with ghee one hundred and eight times;
for the Sun, one should offer eight oblations, and for the others, eight each, in due order.
Then, with the name-mantra, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) upon the altar;
thereafter, O twice-born one, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the brahmins according to one's capacity.
Having performed this rite, one shall obtain all happiness;
at the end of the body, having beheld the mandala of the Sun, one shall go to the supreme state.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Jahnu himself drank up the Gaṅgā out of anger, and then released her again from his right ear-canal.
Having bathed there in clear water at dawn,
one should worship her with all the ritual services, including perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth.
