On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the sun named Vivasvat was born; having worshipped him there individually with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, [one should proceed].

O best of Brahmins, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one performs the auspicious vow known as A-vyaṅga; by doing so, one attains union with the Sun—of this there is no doubt.
The cotton garment of the Lord of the Cows is indeed four cubits long and one and a half cubits wide.
At the conclusion of the worship, this auspicious vow should be offered for the sake of joy.
If this [tithi] is joined with a Tuesday, it shall be the destroyer of sins;
on this day, charity, recitation, and burnt offerings—all shall become inexhaustible.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, however, is the Amuktābharaṇa-vrata;
here, the worship of Soma and Maheśvara is proclaimed.
Having worshipped with the sixteen services beginning with *gaṅgā*, and having prayed and prostrated, one should dismiss [the deity] for the fulfillment of all desires. (NarP 1.116.33)
This is the "Fruit-Seventh" (phalasaptamikā); its procedure is now proclaimed:
the coconut, the eggplant, the orange, and the citron.
Having placed seven fruits— namely the kūṣmāṇḍa, the bṛhatī, and the pūga—
in front of Mahādeva, one should fasten the other cord.
O best of the twice-born, having worshipped with supreme devotion a [rosary] made of seven threads and possessing seven knots, one should wear it on the left hand.
Whether it be a woman or a man, for as long as the year lasts,
one should feed exactly seven Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa) and then dismiss them.
The wise man should eat them himself for the sake of fulfilling his vow;
those fruits should also be given to seven brahmins.
Having thus performed and observed [this] for seven years according to the rule,
O Brahmin, that practitioner of the vow attains union with Mahādeva.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, the auspicious Saptamī should be known;
on that day, having performed one's ablutions and worship, and having caused the best of the twice-born to recite [the scriptures].
Having begun with a tawny-limbed cow and having worshipped her, he should then pray:
"O auspicious one, I give you; may Aryaman himself be pleased. (NarP 1,116.41)
"Protect the entire world, for you are born of Dharma.
Having spoken thus, she gave [the earth] to the knower of the Vedas and offered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having personally paid homage, O Brahmin, he should dismiss [the guests] and quickly cause [them] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having thus performed the vow, on the following day, he should [entertain] the best of the twice-born.
Having fed [the guests], one should then eat that food which remains from the twice-born;
for this, O Brahmin, has been declared as well-spoken by those endowed with faith. (NarP 1.116.44)
By the grace of the God of gods, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, there is the vow known as Śāka-saptamī.
In that [rite], one should give seven vegetable dishes and golden lotuses to seven Brahmins; thereafter, one should oneself subsist on a diet of vegetables.
On the second day, having fed the twice-born and given them food and sacrificial fees,
he should dismiss them and, restraining his speech, eat together with his kinsmen.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Mitra-vrata is proclaimed;
it is that very thing which Viṣṇu’s right eye performed here.
O twice-born one, the sun-god named Mitra was born to Aditi from Kaśyapa;
therefore, his worship should be performed according to the prescribed rite.
Having prepared [the offerings] and fed seven brahmins with sweet foods and other delicacies,
having given gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and having dismissed them, one should then eat oneself.
Having performed this according to the prescribed rule,
a twice-born man certainly goes to the world of the Sun, while a Śūdra likewise attains birth in a noble family.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, having fasted and observed the vow known as Abhaya,
one should worship the Sun at the three junctions of the day while remaining seated upon the ground.

Having given to a twice-born man a sweetmeat (*modaka*) the size of a *prastha*, prepared from rice soaked in milk, and having provided other foods and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to seven or eight others; ||| NarP_1,116.53 |||
Having given away either land or gold, one may then eat for oneself;
this is known as the vow called "Fearlessness," remembered as the giver of fearlessness to all.
Other twice-born ones declare that the vow named Mārtaṇḍa is indeed one alone,
as it is proclaimed by the wise to have a single deity.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, having fasted on that day and worshipped the orb of the Sun, one should perform the vow known as Sarvāpti.
Having fashioned [an image] of gold and performed a night vigil with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should feed seven Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa) on the following day.
Having given coconuts as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to them, he should then give to the Guru a golden disk of the Sun, accompanied by a proper sacrificial fee.
Having offered [the gift], having entreated [the recipient] earnestly, and having dismissed him, one should then depart oneself.
This is proclaimed as the rite named "Bestower of All Attainments," which fulfills all desires.
By the power of this vow, duality shall indeed be resolved in every way.
The vow known as Acala is prescribed for the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha.
This Trilocanajayantī is remembered as the remover of all sins;
and this Saptamī known as Rathā bestows the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Having worshipped a golden image of Savitṛ in this [rite], one who is endowed with devotion and sincere intent should give a golden chariot yoked with horses together with an elephant;
he indeed goes to the world of Śambhu and, having enjoyed pleasures here, rejoices even there.
This seventh [tithi] is Bhāskarī, resembling ten million suns;
bathing is prescribed during this time at the hour of dawn.
Having placed seven leaves each of the *arka* and the *badarī* upon his head, he should bathe for the pacification of the sins of seven lifetimes.
And regarding this, the Lord Āditya himself has declared a vow that bestows sons:
Being greatly pleased, I shall become his son through my own portion;
therefore, having become one who has conquered the senses, you should fast day and night.
On another day, having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should worship the twice-born and then feed them with curd-rice, milk, and milk-porridge.
He who performs the Putrasaptamī rites according to this procedure obtains a virtuous son who is long-lived and free from disease.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Tapasya, one should observe the Arkapuṭa vow.
One should worship the Sun with *arka* leaves and consume *arka* leaves as food.
One should constantly recite the name of the Sun; such is the vow of the "Sun-enclosure.
This bestows wealth, grants sons, and destroys all sins. (NarP 1.116.70)
"O twice-born one, some call this vow the 'Bestower of the Three Aims' (trivargadā); others, however, call it the 'Vow of Sacrifice' because of the performance of oblations according to the rules."
O best of the twice-born, it is declared that the worship of the Sun on every seventh lunar day throughout all months fulfills all desires; this is sufficient.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Saptamī Vow Observed in the Twelve Months," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* in the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, the birth of Bhavānī is proclaimed.
Having performed a hundred circumambulations, a great festival of pilgrimage should be celebrated.
The sight of the Mother of the World bestows all bliss upon men;
herein alone is the consumption of the Ashoka bud proclaimed.
Those who drink eight buds of the Aśoka tree under the asterism Punarvasu on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra shall never encounter sorrow.
It is proclaimed as the Mahāṣṭamī because of the prescribed ritual for the worship of the Goddess;
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should fast here, subsisting only on water.
Having bathed and then having bathed the goddess Aparājitā with water from meat and young mangoes,
one should worship her with perfumes and other offerings, and present an oblation consisting of sugar.
On the ninth day, before the breaking of the fast, one should also feed young maidens;
[the devotee] shall shine, resplendent like the sun, in a celestial chariot composed of light.
O Brahmin, by the grace of the Goddess, one may wander through the worlds after having worshipped the Three-eyed Lord on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
That man who worships the Goddess on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa, honored by all the gods.
Having bathed with the water of the night on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, he travels by means of a celestial chariot accompanied by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
With that very [substance], one should bathe the Goddess and worship her according to the prescribed rite;
then, having bathed her with pure waters, one should anoint her with moon-fragrant sandalwood paste.
Having offered the food offering accompanied by sugar, one should present the water for sipping (ācamana);
then, having fed the Brahmins and given gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
And having first offered [the food] thereafter, he should eat himself while restraining his speech;
by performing this vow, a man shall attain the world of the Goddess.
Likewise, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rite and bathed her with milk, one should offer sweet food.
Then, having fed the twice-born on the following day and having himself also eaten,
he should complete this vow which increases one's progeny.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, one should undertake the vow known as Daśāphala;
having made the formal resolve for the fast, one should bathe and perform the daily obligatory rites.
One should worship Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Ananta, Govinda, and Garuḍadhvaja with ten leaves of black Tulasī.
One should constantly worship the divine Kṛṣṇa with these names: Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Hari, and Prabhu.
Then one should perform prostrations accompanied by circumambulations;
in this manner, for ten days, one should observe this supreme vow among all vows.
One should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule at the beginning, middle, and end;
one should offer the sacrificial porridge one hundred and eight times with the Kṛṣṇa-mantra.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the wise man should properly worship the preceptor according to the rules,
using a vessel made of gold, copper, clay, or bamboo.
Having had an auspicious Tulasī leaf fashioned out of gold,
and having made a golden image, one should worship them according to the prescribed rite.
Having placed the image in a vessel, one should present it to the preceptor;
a cow, together with her calf and adorned with garments and ornaments, should also be given.
For ten days, one should offer ten *pūrikā* cakes to Kṛṣṇadeva;
the observer of the vow should either give them to one who knows the ritual rules or eat them himself.
O best of the twice-born, a bed should also be given according to one's ability;
then, on the tenth day, one should present an image along with ritual materials to the preceptor.
At the conclusion of the vow, having performed this unsurpassed observance for ten years, one should indeed give ten *pūrikā* cakes to each of ten Brahmins.
Having observed the fast according to the prescribed rite, one shall become endowed with all desires;
at the end, one attains union with Kṛṣṇa—of this there is no doubt.
This Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī is remembered as the remover of the sins of men through the mere act of fasting on that birth-day of Hari.
One who fasts and bathes with sesame seeds in the pure water of a river or similar body of water is liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
In a well-located place, within a prepared pavilion, the wise man should fashion a mandala;
having placed a water-pot made either of copper or clay in its center, [he should proceed].
Upon that, one should place a copper vessel, and upon that,
a beautiful golden image of Kṛṣṇa, covered with a pair of garments.
With a devoted heart, one should worship Devakī, Vasudeva, Yaśodā, and Nanda with offerings such as water for the feet and other ritual services.
One should worship Vraja, the cowherds, the cowherd women, and the cows in all directions;
then, having performed the *ārārtika* ceremony, one should ask for forgiveness and bow down with devotion.
He should remain standing in that same manner at midnight and bathe Hari once again;
he should worship him again with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), pure water, fragrances, and other offerings.
O Nārada, one should offer as an oblation cumin, bishop’s weed, ginger, and sugar-candy, placed in a silver vessel with clarified butter. (NarP 1.117.34)
Having performed the ārārtika rite once more, while meditating upon the one who assumes ten forms, he should offer the arghya water with devotion to the Moon.

Then, having asked the Lord of Gods for forgiveness, the observer of the vow should pass the remainder of the night with the recitation of Puranic hymns and various kinds of songs and instrumental music.
Then at dawn, one should feed the foremost of Brahmins with sweet foods;
having given them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should dismiss them with a satisfied mind.
Then, having given that image of Viṣṇu, together with the golden cow and its accessories,
as a sacrificial fee to his preceptor, he should dismiss him and partake of the food himself.
Having thus performed this vow for his wife, children, friends, and servants,
a man attains the world of cows in person, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
There is no other vow similar to this in the three worlds by the performance of which the fruit of eleven crores may be obtained.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, a man should perform the Rādhā-vrata;
as before, he should worship a golden image of Rādhikā placed within a water-jar.
Having worshipped her at midday, one should conclude with a single meal;
or, if capable and devoted, one should observe a fast on the following day according to the prescribed rule.
Having fed the married women and presented a ritual image to the preceptor, he himself should eat; thus he should complete the vow.
O brahmin sage, by performing this vow according to the prescribed rule, the practitioner,
having attained the secret [knowledge] born of the cow-pen, shall dwell in the retinue of Rādhā.
And here the Dūrvāṣṭamī vow is described; listen to that from me, O best of the twice-born, when the dūrvā grass has grown in a pure place.
Having installed the liṅga, one should then worship it with devotion using perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, curd, unbroken rice, fruits, and so forth.
At the conclusion of the worship, being well-composed, one should offer the *arghya* with these two mantras:
"O Dūrvā grass, you are born of nectar; you are saluted by gods and asuras."
Grant me good fortune and progeny; be the accomplisher of all my undertakings, just as you are spread across the surface of the earth with your branches and sub-branches.
"Likewise, grant me also an expansive lineage that is free from old age and death.
Then, having circumambulated them and indeed having fed the brahmins there, [he departed].
Having eaten himself and having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins, he should go home,
taking with him excellent fruits that are sweet and fragrant.
Thus, O twice-born one, the Dūrvā-aṣṭamī is meritorious and removes the sins of men—
especially for women of all four castes.
That woman who, out of delusion, does not worship dūrvā grass according to the prescribed rite,
will undoubtedly suffer widowhood for three lifetimes.
O twice-born one, when the constellation Jyeṣṭhā is conjoined with the month of Jyeṣṭha, it should be known as Jyeṣṭhā by name; when worshipped, it destroys all sins.
Then, beginning from this [day], a vow for sixteen days is prescribed for Mahālakṣmī, which increases all forms of prosperity.
"Devoted to you, I shall perform the Mahālakṣmī vow;
by your grace, may it reach completion for me without obstacle."
Having recited this, he then tied a cord on his right hand,
provided with sixteen knots and endowed with sixteen strands.

Then, day by day, the practitioner of the vow should worship Mahālakṣmī with perfumes and other offerings until the eighth day of the dark fortnight; there, the wise one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having constructed a pavilion of cloth within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala,
and having properly consecrated a water-pot, one should then illuminate a lamp.
Having removed the cord from his arm, he should present it beneath the water-pot;
having fashioned four golden images identical in form to him.
One should cause them to perform the ceremonial bathing with water and likewise with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
having worshipped them according to the prescribed rite with the sixteen types of offerings.
A vigil should be observed there with the sounds of singing and musical instruments;
then, when midnight has arrived and the moon, the source of nectar, has risen.
Having offered the *arghya* and bound [the image] with substances such as sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*) according to the prescribed rite,
one should present these to Mahālakṣmī, who is seated within the lunar disc.
O you who were born from the ocean of milk, brother of Mahālakṣmī,
abode of nectar, together with Rohiṇī, accept this water offering from me.
O lotus born from the ocean of milk, O lotus-dweller,
O you who reside upon the chest of Viṣṇu, be the granter of all my desires.
O sole mistress, mistress of the world, beloved of Jamadagni, imperishable one!
O Goddess Reṇukā, mother of Rāma, protect me and grant me auspiciousness.
Having prayed to Mahālakṣmī with these mantras, one should properly worship the wives of those learned in the Vedas,
honoring them well with perfumes, lac-dye, and collyrium.
Having fed [the guests], one should offer oblations into the fire with bilva, padmaka, and milk-porridge;
O Brahmin, in the absence of those, one should offer clarified butter, sacrificial fuel-wood, and sesame seeds from various households.
And for the supreme victory over death and for the pacification of all diseases,
[one should offer] sandalwood, palm leaves, flower garlands, and likewise unbroken grains (akṣata).
Durvā grass, safflower thread, a pair [of garments], or even a bilva fruit,
as well as various kinds of food— sixteen of each item should be placed in a new winnowing basket.
Covering it with another winnowing basket, the observer of the vow should offer [the gift] accompanied by the mantra:
"Lakṣmī, born from the Ocean of Milk, the sister of the Moon... (NarP 1,117.70).
"May the beloved of Viṣṇu be satisfied by this vow;
one should then present those four images to those learned in the Vedas."
Then, having fed four Brahmins and sixteen married women with sweet food, he should dismiss them along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The rule for completion follows, conjoined with the desired results;
having performed this vow of Mahālakṣmī according to the prescribed rite, O Brahmin, [one attains these fruits]. (NarP 1.117.73)
Having enjoyed his desired worldly pleasures, he shall dwell for a long time in the world of Lakṣmī;
this is called Aśokāṣṭamī, on which the vow of Ramā is fully completed.
In this regard, there should be worship of the Aśoka tree, and likewise a single meal is prescribed;
for by performing the Aśoka vow, a woman indeed becomes free from sorrow when sorrow arises.
O Brahmin, wherever this Mahāṣṭamī occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, no deliberation need be made regarding its validity. (NarP 1,117.76)
In that regard, the worship of Durgā is proclaimed with all the ritual services (upacāras),
having performed fasting or a single meal on the Great Eighth Day (mahāṣṭamī).
Having attained prosperity in every respect, he rejoices for a long time like a god.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the vow known as Karaka is prescribed.
Therein, Śambhu accompanied by Umā should be worshipped with great effort;
and at the rising of the moon, the offering of the arghya water must always be performed by those observing the vow.
For those desiring a son endowed with all virtues and manifold happiness,
the Gopāṣṭamī is proclaimed to be observed on the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
There, one who desires all forms of prosperity should perform worship of cows, offer morsels of food to cows, circumambulate cows, follow after cows, and practice giving.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should [worship] a pair made of darbha grass—
an Anagha and an Anaghā— accompanied by many sons.
Having placed it in an auspicious location smeared with cow dung,
one should worship it with various kinds of services such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having fed a Brahmin couple and dismissed them after they have received their sacrificial fee,
a man or a woman who has performed this vow according to the prescribed rule [attains the fruit].
One obtains a son endowed with auspicious marks; of this there is no doubt.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, by fasting and keeping a vigil in the presence of Kālabhairava, one is liberated from great sins.
Whatever unwholesome karma has been committed during a human birth,
all of that goes to destruction upon seeing Kālabhairava.
Now, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, there is the Śrāddha known as Aṣṭaka,
which grants satisfaction to the ancestors for a year and increases the lineage of the family.
Having worshipped Śiva with devotion on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa,
one who practices exclusive devotion attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, one should worship Bhadrakālī with devotion—
the goddess who slays hosts of enemies and bestows all desires.
O twice-born one, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should satiate Bhīṣma,
desiring an uninterrupted lineage as well as invincibility.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, O Brahmin, one intent on the vow should worship the goddess Bhīmā for the fulfillment of all desires. (NarP 1.117.92)
O twice-born one, by properly worshipping Śiva and Śivā with perfumes and other offerings on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, one should worship Śītalā with all kinds of cooked foods prepared according to the rules on the seventh day.
O Śītalā, you are the mother of the world; O Śītalā, you are the father of the world;
O Śītalā, you are the protectress of the world; salutations again and again to Śītalā!
I pay homage to the goddess Śītalā, who is mounted upon a donkey, naked,
holding a broom and a water-pot, and the destroyer of eruptive boils.
And those who, standing in cool water, recite this [mantra] "Śītale Śītale," for them the goddess Śītalā shall grant the pacification of eruptive boils.
O twice-born one, for him who thus worships with the mantras of Śītalā,
there shall be peace for a year through the grace of Śītalā.
On the eighth day of every month, during both fortnights,
by worshipping Śivā or Śiva according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the desired fruit.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Aṣṭamī Vow Observed in the Twelve Months," in the fourth quarter of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna in the first part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:
Now, O best of Brahmins, I shall indeed describe the vows pertaining to the ninth day (Navamī).
By performing which deeds, men in this world obtain their desired fruit.
During the bright fortnight of Caitra, on the ninth lunar day, is the Śrī Rāmanavamī vow;
there, a devoted and capable person should perform the fast according to the prescribed rules.
And if he is unable [to do more], he should certainly observe a single meal after the midday festival,
and having fed the Brahmins with sweet foods, he should well practice that which pleases Rāma.
He who likewise performs the Śrī Rāmanavamī vow with devotion, offering cows, land, sesame seeds, water, gold, and so forth, as well as garments and ornaments; ||| NarP_1,118.4 |||
Having shaken off their sins here, they shall go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu in Vraja;
and here the vow of the Mother was proclaimed by Bhairava, which they should observe together.
With garlands, perfumes, garments, and food offerings, one should worship the sixty-four Yoginīs;
here indeed is Bhadrakālī, the most powerful among the Yoginīs.
The best of Brahmins is consecrated to the sovereignty over all of them;
therefore, one who has conquered his senses should worship her there while observing a fast.
O Rādhā, he who worships Caṇḍikā on the ninth day with both petals according to the prescribed rite rejoices together with the gods in a celestial chariot.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, that best of men, having observed a fast,
should worship Umā according to the rules and feed young maidens and brahmins.
Having given a sacrificial fee with his own devotion, he should eat rice mixed with milk;
O Brahmin, that man who performs this Umā-vow according to the prescribed rule [attains the fruit].
O best of Brahmins, he who performs this during both fortnights in the month of Āṣāḍha shall enjoy excellent pleasures here in this world and, at the end, attain the path to heaven. (NarP 1.118.11)
And at night, one should worship the white goddess Aindrī seated upon Airāvata;
he shall indeed become a partaker of enjoyments in the world of Indra, traveling in a celestial vehicle.
O best of Brahmins, he who observes the practice of eating only at night or fasting during both fortnights of the month of Śrāvaṇa should worship the maiden Caṇḍikā.
Thus, one should worship her, the remover of sins, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps,
various kinds of food offerings, and likewise by feeding young maidens.
Thus, he who performs this supreme vow of Kaumārī with devotion shall indeed travel by celestial chariot to the eternal world of the Goddess.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada is proclaimed as Nandā;
on that day, he who worships Durgā according to the rules with the ritual offerings, [attains great merit].
Having obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina is proclaimed as the "Great" (Mahā) Navamī.
O twice-born one, in the afternoon, the worship of the Śamī tree should be performed in the eastern direction;
then, during the first watch of the night, [one should worship] the sword, the bow, the arrows, and the mace.
A trident, a spear, an axe, a small sword, a shield,
an umbrella, a banner, an elephant, a horse, a bull, a book, and a balance.
Having worshipped the staff, the noose, the discus, and the conch with offerings such as perfumes and other services, one should there offer a buffalo to Bhadrakālī.
Having thus performed the bali offering and eaten only cooked food,
and having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born, one should there conclude the vow.
Thus, whoever worships Durgā, the destroyer of the misfortunes of men,
shall enjoy excellent pleasures here in this world and, at the end, attain the state of heaven.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika is proclaimed as the inexhaustible (akṣaya) day;
on that day, one should indeed properly perform the libation at the root of an Aśvattha tree.
O Nārada, one should then offer the arghya to the Sun with the mantras prescribed in one's own Vedic branch for the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors as well.
Then, O Lord of Sages, having fed the twice-born with sweet food,
he himself should eat and enjoy himself after giving sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the brahmins.
Thus, for one who performs recitation, giving, worship of the twice-born, and fire-offerings with devotion, all of it becomes inexhaustible; such is the teaching of the sacred ordinance.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the day is proclaimed as Nandinī;
he who fasts on that day and worships the Mother of the World [attains great merit].
By worshipping with perfumes and other offerings, he becomes a partaker of the fruit of the horse sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, one should worship Mahāmāyā.
O Brahmin, intent on eating but a single meal for the sake of attaining the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice,
one should observe the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, which is honored by the world.
She is called Mahānandā because she always bestows supreme bliss upon men;
bathing in her, as well as giving gifts, reciting prayers, performing fire-sacrifices, and fasting [therein], [yield great merit]. (NarP 1,118.30)
Everything becomes inexhaustible; no doubt should be entertained in this matter, O best of the twice-born, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
O best of the twice-born, that Ānandā is remembered as greatly meritorious and the remover of all sins; he who, having fasted, worships you there, O Ānandā.
He shall obtain his desired objects; this is the truth, the truth that I have spoken.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Vow of the Ninth Day Occurring in Each of the Twelve Months," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:
Now, I shall indeed proclaim to you the vows pertaining to the tenth day.
Having performed these with devotion, a person shall become dear to Dharmarāja.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship Dharmarāja with flowers,
fruits, perfumes, and other offerings available at that time.
Having fasted, or having eaten but a single meal, and having fed the best of the twice-born,
he should then give them fourteen [gifts] as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability.
O Brahmin, he who thus performs the worship of Dharmarāja shall,
by the command of Dharma, attain the state of the gods and remain undecaying.

On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava, a person, having worshipped Viṣṇu with fragrant substances and other offerings, as well as with white and sweet-smelling flowers; 119.5.
Having performed one hundred circumambulations and having diligently fed the Brahmins, one attains the world of Viṣṇu; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, Jāhnavī, the best of rivers, descended from heaven to the earth; therefore, she is remembered as the bestower of merit.

The month of Jyeṣṭha, the bright fortnight, the Hasta nakṣatra, Wednesday, and the tenth lunar day (daśamī); the Garā, Ānanda, and Vyatīpāta yogas; and Virgo, the Moon, and Taurus as the signs of the Sun. NarP_1,119.8 //
O twice-born one, this is declared to be the ten-fold yoga, most meritorious;
it removes ten sins, and therefore it is known as the "Ten-remover" (Daśahara).
He who, with a joyful mind, bathes according to the prescribed rite in the waters of the Jāhnavī upon reaching this [place],
goes to the abode of Hari.
The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha is remembered as auspicious by Manu and others;
on that day, bathing, recitation, giving gifts, or burnt offerings bestow the attainment of heaven.
The tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa fulfills all hopes;
on this day, the worship of Śiva with offerings such as perfumes is highly recommended.
In that regard, fasting, eating only at night, feeding the twice-born, the recitation of mantras, and the gift of gold, cows, and so forth, destroy all sins. (NarP 1.119.13)
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhasya,
one should perform the vow known as the Daśāvatāra, including bathing in a body of water.
Having performed the observances of the twilight prayers and the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors,
he should then, with a concentrated mind, worship the ten incarnations.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, Trivikrama, Rāma, Paraśurāma, Kṛṣṇa, the Buddha, and indeed Kalki.
Having worshipped ten golden images according to the prescribed rite,
O Nārada, one should respectfully present them to ten eminent Brahmins.
Having observed a fast and taken only a single meal, and having fed the brahmins,
he should afterwards eat himself together with his loved ones, remaining composed in mind.
Having performed this vow with devotion and having enjoyed excellent pleasures here,
one shall at the end go by celestial chariot to the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is proclaimed as Vijayā;
having placed four balls of cow dung in the courtyard of the house in the morning, [one should perform the rite].
In the form of the Cakravāla mountains, one should indeed worship all four— Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, as well as Bharata and Śatrughna— in the midst of them.
Having placed cleaned grain together with silver inside four earthenware vessels that have lids, and having covered them with washed garments; NarP_1,119.22.
Accompanied by his father, mother, brothers, sons, wife, and servants,
he should be honored according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and food offerings.
Having paid homage and having fed and honored the twice-born,
a man who performs this rite for a year shall be endowed with the splendor of the gods.
O twice-born one, he will certainly be born prosperous in wealth and grain;
then, at the time of the afternoon on the ninth day, she was invited.
O Brahmin, having gone to the east toward a *śamī* tree and taken the earth from its root,
he should return to his own home amidst the sounds of singing and instrumental music.
Having worshipped her according to the prescribed rite and prepared his own forces,
he emerged undisturbed through the eastern gate from the village.
Then, [he should strike] an image of the enemy made from leaves and such materials,
or even one conceived in the mind, with a golden arrow shaped like a male organ.
"Thinking 'I shall pierce [him],' being greatly delighted, he would reach his own home at night;
or even one who has performed the ritual in this manner may go forth for the subjugation of enemies. (NarP 1,119.29)
O Brahmin, this very tenth [lunar day], when always observed according to the prescribed rite,
bestows wealth, victory, sons, cattle, elephants, horses, goats, and sheep.
O Nārada, one who performs the Sārvabhauma vow on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika shall attain a heavenly state at the end of this life. NarP_1,119.31 //
Having observed a fast and eating only once a day, at midnight he should offer oblations with cakes and other foods in the ten directions— at the door of his house and outside the city.
O best of the twice-born, having prepared an eight-petaled maṇḍala on a ground smeared with cow dung, one should perform worship beginning with Gaṇeśa using these mantras.
Whatever evil has previously entered into me through this sinful deed here,
may Indra, the king of the gods, who grants all desired boons, destroy it today.
Whatever sin has entered into me here through my own evil deeds,
may Vahni, the king of splendor, who grants all desired objects, destroy it.
Whatever sin has entered my right side through evil deeds performed here in this world,
may Yama, the King of the Departed, who grants all desired boons, truly destroy it.
Whatever evil has entered me through my own wicked deeds in this world,
may Nairṛti, the king of the Rākṣasas and the bestower of all desired things, destroy it.
May Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures and the bestower of all desired things, destroy that evil which has followed after me here through my sinful deeds. (NarP 1,119.38)
Whatever evil has entered into my breath through sinful deeds here on earth,
may Vāyu, the king of the Maruts and the granter of all desired boons, destroy it.
May Soma, the lord of the Ṛkṣas and Yakṣas, who grants all desired things, destroy whatever sin has entered me through evil deeds in this world.
Whatever sin has come upon me through evil deeds in this world,
may the Lord, the Master of beings who grants all desired boons, destroy it.
May Brahmā, the Lord of Prajāpati, who grants all desired objects without exception, destroy whatever upward-moving evil has come upon me here through my own sinful deeds.
May Ananta, the king of the nāgas, who bestows all desired things, destroy that evil which resides within me below due to my sinful deeds in this world.
Having thus offered the bali-oblation in the ten directions, being composed and unwearied, he should cast the bali for the Kṣetrapāla outside of that.

Having thus performed the prescribed rites, the wise man should spend the remainder of the night with songs mostly auspicious in nature, with the recitation of hymns, and with prayers and other such practices.
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped the guardians of the world and the best of the twice-born,
one should worship twelve [of them], feed them according to one's ability, and give a sacrificial fee.
Having thus performed this vow, O Brahmin, one enjoys auspicious worldly pleasures;
and after experiencing the bliss of heaven for a yuga, one becomes a sovereign king.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should observe the Ārogyaka vow;
one should honor ten Brahmins with perfumes and other offerings, and drink the water from their feet.
Having drunk [the water] and then given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should abandon the single meal;
having performed this vow, O Brahmin, one indeed attains health upon the earth.
By the grace of Dharmarāja, he rejoices in heaven like a god;
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, one should worship the Viśvedevas.
Keśava is established in those ten forms: Ṛtu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, Muni, Guru, Vipra, and Rāma.
Having caused them to sleep upon seats made of darbha grass,
O Nārada, they were honored with perfumes, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to each one individually and having bid them farewell,
he should offer that dakṣiṇā to the foremost of the twice-born or to his preceptor.

Having thus performed the ritual, O brahmin-sage, one who enjoys pleasures while observing the vow with a single meal per day shall attain both worlds; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, having fasted and subdued his senses...
One should properly worship the ten gods named Āṅgirasas.
Having fashioned them out of gold, O Brahmin, and having honored them with offerings such as perfumes and the like,
[one should worship] the Self (ātman), longevity (āyus), the mind (manas), skill (dakṣa), intoxication (mada), and likewise the vital breath (prāṇa).
Barhiṣmān, Gaviṣṭha, Datta, and Satya—these ten, O Nārada, [attained their goal] after feeding ten Brahmins with sweet food. (NarP 1.119.57)
One should offer those images to them in sequence for the attainment of the heavenly world;
on the final tenth day of the bright fortnight, however, one should worship the fourteenth Yamāni.
Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, Antaka, Vaivasvata, Kāla, and Sarvabhūtakṣaya; ||| NarP_1,119.59 |||
Audumbara and Dadhnas, two Nīlas and two Parameṣṭhins,
Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta— these are the fourteen.
Having worshipped them with offerings such as perfumes and the like,
one should then satisfy them with three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass for each individual.
And then, O Nārada, one should offer the arghya to the Sun with a copper vessel,
using water mixed with red sandalwood, sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and barley.
Come, O thou who possessest the rays of a thousand suns, mass of splendor, Lord of the World!
Accept this water-offering given by me with devotion; have compassion upon me.
Having offered the *arghya* with this mantra and fed fourteen Brahmins, and having given a silver *dakṣiṇā*, he should dismiss them and then eat himself. (NarP 1.119.64)
O Brahmin, having thus performed his duties through the grace of Dharmarāja,
he enjoyed worldly pleasures for the sake of his sons, which are difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot at the end of the body, he becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Tenth Day (Daśamī) Observed in Each Month," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first part of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:
On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), however, being composed and abstaining from food on both [the preceding and following] lunar portions (*tithi*), [one should observe the vow].
O Sage, having constructed a beautiful and variegated pavilion with various kinds of flowers.
Having bathed according to the correct ritual procedure, fasting and with his senses subdued,
he should worship Viṣṇu with faith and a well-composed mind in accordance with the rules.
With various kinds of services, recitations, offerings of gold, circumambulations, diverse readings of hymns, and captivating songs and instrumental music; (NarP 1,120.3)
By prostrating like a staff, with enchanting shouts of "Victory!",
and by keeping a vigil at night, one goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, that best of men, having observed a fast and undertaken all the observances to be described for the three days, [should proceed].
On the twelfth lunar day, one should worship the eternal Vāsudeva with devotion using the sixteen types of offerings, and thereafter feast one's kinsmen.
And having given a sacrificial fee to them and dismissed them, one should eat oneself.
This [river], however, is named Kāmadā, the destroyer of all sins.
O Brahmin, when properly observed with devotion, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one should fast according to the prescribed rite on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha.
On the following day, one should worship Varūthinī and the Slayer of Madhu;
here, the gift of gold, food, maidens, and cows is highly praised.
Having performed the Varūthinī vow, a man devoted to his observances is liberated from all sins and attains the station of Viṣṇu.

Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, and having bathed on the following day, one should worship Puruṣottama with perfumes and other offerings after honoring the Mohinī.

O King, by fasting on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha and feeding the Brahmins, one is liberated from sins; of this there is no doubt. ||| NarP_1,120.12 |||The final answer is: By fasting on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha and feeding the Brahmins, O King, one is liberated from sins; of this there is no doubt. ||| NarP_1,120.12 |||From the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati": Furthermore, son of good family, what is the bodhisattvas' skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom? Having performed the daily rites on the twelfth day and having worshipped Trivikrama,
he should then feed the foremost of the twice-born and give them sacrificial fees.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha by abstaining from water, a man, liberated from all sins, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, from sunrise until the next sunrise,
having performed his daily rites at dawn on the twelfth day, he should worship with ritual offerings.
Having worshipped the Lord whose hair is like a dark blue lotus and having fed the Brahmins with devotion,
one shall obtain that same fruit which belongs to twenty-four Ekādaśīs.

Having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha for the sake of the Yoginī, and having worshipped Nārāyaṇa on the twelfth day after performing his daily obligatory rites; NarP_1,120.17 //
Then, having fed the foremost of Brahmins and given them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
he obtains the fruit of all possible gifts and rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu.
Listen now to the procedure for the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha;
having fasted on that day according to the rules in an auspicious pavilion.
One should install an excellent image of Viṣṇu, made of gold or silver, possessing four resplendent arms adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
O twice-born one, [he should place her] wearing yellow garments upon a bright, well-spread couch;
then, having bathed her with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with pure water accompanied by mantras.

One should perform the ritual services with the *puruṣasūkta* itself, including the offerings beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with the waving of lights (*nīrājana*); thereafter, one should pray to Hari.
O Lord of the World, when you are asleep, this entire world is asleep;
and when you are awakened, the whole world, including all that is moving and unmoving, becomes awake.
Having thus prayed before the deity, a devoted man should undertake the observances enjoined for the four-month period according to his capacity.
Then, on the morning of the twelfth day,
he should worship the one who reclines upon Śeṣa with the sixteen types of offerings, and thereafter feed the Brahmins.
Having gratified [the deity] with curd and honey, one should eat oneself while maintaining silence;
from that time forward, O best of Brahmins, one should worship daily with perfumes and other offerings.
O Brahmin, by performing the vow of the Lord’s sleep according to this rite,
a mortal shall become endowed with both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the grace of Viṣṇu.

O best of the twice-born, O most excellent of men, having fasted according to the prescribed rules on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one attains the fulfillment of all desires.
On the twelfth day, having performed his daily obligatory rites, he should worship Hari as Śrīdhara with the sixteen types of offerings, and then indeed feed the twice-born brahmins.
And having given a sacrificial fee to them, he should dismiss them and eat together with his kinsmen;
thus does one perform this supreme vow for the fulfillment of the desires of Brahmins.
Having obtained all desires here in this world, he indeed goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu after fasting on the sacred Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas.
Having become self-restrained on the twelfth lunar day, one should worship Janārdana with the sixteen types of offerings; then,
having fed the Brahmins and given them sacrificial fees, one obtains here a son endowed with excellent qualities.
He goes directly to the abode of Viṣṇu, being saluted by all the gods.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhas,
one should indeed worship Upendra on the twelfth day with various kinds of ritual offerings.

Having fed the Brahmins with sweet foods and having bestowed the sacrificial fees upon them, he who has thus fulfilled his vow, being composed and devoted to the Brahmins and his wife, [attains success].
Having enjoyed all pleasures here, he indeed goes to the abode of Viṣṇu after fasting on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, specifically on the fast known as Padmā.
O best of the twice-born, having performed the daily worship there, one should then carry out the gift of the waist-band for the image that was previously installed.
Having led her to the reservoir with the performance of a festive ceremony, and having performed the ritual sipping of water there, he worshipped her according to the prescribed rites.
Having brought him there, one should have him lie down on his left side in that pavilion;
then, when the twelfth day has arrived, one should worship Vāmana with perfumes and other offerings.
Having fed the Brahmins and given them sacrificial fees, he should dismiss them;
O Brahmin, he who performs this unsurpassed Padmā-vrata in this manner [attains the fruit].
Having obtained worldly enjoyment here, one indeed attains liberation at the end through this elaborate rite;
having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Īṣa, one truly worships Indirā.
O Brahmin, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony at midday before a Śālagrāma stone; this brings pleasure to Viṣṇu, and therefore it should be done in the morning on the day of Hari.
Having worshipped the lotus-navelled Lord and fed the Brahmins,
the wise man should dismiss them after giving them sacrificial fees, and then he himself should eat.
Thus, the mortal who has fulfilled his vow, having enjoyed his desired pleasures here and having delivered ten million ancestors, goes at last to the abode of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin, having fasted according to the prescribed rules on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight— the day of Viṣṇu known as Pāśāṅkuśā— one should worship Viṣṇu.
Then, having fed the foremost of the Brahmins and given them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he should bow with devotion and dismiss them, and thereafter he himself should eat.
Thus, the man who performs the Pāśāṅkuśa vow with devotion,
having enjoyed excellent pleasures here in this world, goes to the same realm as Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, having fasted according to the rules on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, one should worship Rāmā on the morning of the twelfth day.
One should then feed the Brahmins— Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, the God of gods, the eternal— and then dismiss them after they have received their sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
O Brahmin, having thus fulfilled his vow and enjoyed his desired pleasures here on earth,
he attains proximity to the Lord of Ramā by means of a celestial vehicle.

Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, known as Prabodhinī, one should awaken Keśava at night while he is asleep with auspicious songs and other such offerings.

With mantras from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and with various kinds of musical instruments, as well as with grapes, sugarcane, pomegranates, and others such as plantains and śṛṅgāṭakas; NarP_1,120.52 //
Then, after the night has passed and on the following day,
having bathed and performed his daily rites, he should worship Gadā-Dāmodara.
Having fed the Brahmins with the sixteen services and also with a hymn dedicated to Puruṣa, he should dismiss them after they have been fully satisfied with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
Then, one who performs the Bodhinī vow with devotion and respect should present that golden image, together with a cow, to the preceptor. Thus it is said: NarP_1,120.55.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures here in this world,
he attains the station of Viṣṇu by fasting on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
On the twelfth day, one should worship Kṛṣṇa with offerings such as perfumes and other services;
then, having fed the most eminent Brahmins and given them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having first served [the food] to others, he should afterwards eat himself, composed and together with those dear to him;
thus should one who has undertaken the vow practice it with a spirit of devotion. (NarP 1.120.58)
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, which is known as Mokṣa, he indeed ascends a celestial chariot and goes at the end to the station of Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped Ananta, who possesses a universal form, on the morning of the twelfth day with all ritual offerings, the twice-born man should feed the Brahmins.
Having bestowed the sacrificial fee and given gifts, he should eat together with his kinsmen;
having thus performed the vow, O Brahmin, he shall enjoy his desired pleasures in this world.
Having uplifted ten ancestors and ten descendants,
one shall go to Hari by fasting successfully on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa,
and by worshipping Acyuta on the twelfth day with all ritual services.
Having fed the Brahmins with sweet foods and having dismissed them after they have received their sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
one should perform this vow, O Brahmin, according to the rules for the Saphalā rite.
Having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, one indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu by fasting on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, which bestows sons.
On the twelfth day, one should worship the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) with offerings such as the arghya,
and then, having fed the most eminent Brahmins, give them sacrificial fees.
Having set aside [the remainder], he himself should eat the leftover food together with his beloved kinsmen;
thus, O Brahmin, having fulfilled this vow, he shall enjoy his desired pleasures in this world.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha while consuming six sesame seeds, they indeed ascend an excellent celestial chariot and go at last to the abode of Hari.
Having bathed, given gifts, offered libations, performed oblations, eaten, and worshipped—
with sesame seeds alone, O best of the twice-born— on the morning of the twelfth day indeed.
Having properly worshipped Vaikuṇṭha with all the ritual offerings,
he should feed the twice-born, give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and then bid them farewell.
Having thus performed the vow according to the rule, O Brahmin, being well-composed,
one shall enjoy desired pleasures here in this world and, at the end, attain the abode of Viṣṇu.

O twice-born one, having fasted on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) called Jayā in the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should worship Hari, the Lord of Śrī and the Supreme Person, in the morning on that day of Hari.
Having fed them, given the sacrificial fee, and dismissed the Brahmins, he himself,
being purified, should eat the remainder of that meal together with his own kinsmen.
O Brahmin, he who thus performs this vow for the gratification of Keśava shall enjoy excellent pleasures here in this world and, at the end, go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having fasted on the Vijayā Ekādaśī of the dark fortnight of the month of Tapas,
one should worship the Lord of Yogins with perfumes and other offerings on the morning of the Dvādaśī.
Then, having fed the brahmins and satisfied them with sacrificial fees,
and having dismissed them, he himself should eat together with his kinsmen while maintaining silence.
A mortal who has thus fulfilled his vow, having enjoyed his desired pleasures here,
goes at the end of the body to the world of Viṣṇu, highly honored by the gods.
O best of the twice-born, having fasted with devotion on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should worship the Āmalakī tree in the morning on the twelfth day.
Then, having fed the twice-born with all ritual offerings and excellent food for the sake of the lotus-eyed one, he should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Having thus performed the worship and other rites with this ritual procedure at the Āmalakī tree on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, one who undertakes the austerity shall go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, which liberates from sin,
one should likewise worship Govinda on the morning of the twelfth day.
Having fed the twice-born with the sixteen types of offerings and having given them a sacrificial fee,
he should dismiss them and then eat himself together with his kinsmen.
O Brahmin, he who performs this vow of liberation from sin goes by means of a radiant celestial chariot to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Brahmin, the vow pertaining to Ekādaśī, whether observed on the dark or the bright fortnight, has been proclaimed as bestowing liberation; there is no doubt whatsoever regarding this.
Since it is accomplished in three days, brings renown, destroys sin, and is the best of all vows, O Brahmin, it should therefore be known as yielding great fruit. (NarP 1.120.84)
O Nārada, one should abandon four meals during those three days:
one at the beginning and one at the end, and indeed two in the middle.
Now, I shall declare the rules for this three-day vow:
one must avoid bell-metal, meat, lentils, chickpeas, and kodrava grain.
On the tenth day, a Vaiṣṇava should always avoid these ten things: leafy vegetables, honey, food from others, eating a second time, and sexual intercourse. (NarP 1,120.87)
Gambling, sleep, betel-leaf, cleaning the teeth, speaking ill of others, backbiting, theft, violence, and likewise sexual pleasure; 120.88.
On the eleventh day, one should indeed avoid anger, false speech,
bell-metal, meat, liquor, honey, oil, excrement, and speaking with barbarians.

On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one should avoid these twelve things for twelve years: physical exertion, travel abroad, eating a second meal, sexual intercourse, and touching those who are untouchable.
Thus, a wise Brahmin who has made a formal vow should observe the fast; however, if he is incapable, he should instead eat only one meal a day, but not eat at night.
Or even if one must wander for alms without asking, one should not abandon such a vow.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Vow of Ekādaśī in the Twelve Months," in the fourth part of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* within the first section of the glorious *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sanātana said:
Now, O sinless one, I shall describe to you the vows of the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*).
By performing which deeds a man shall become most beloved of Viṣṇu in this world.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should observe the Madana-vrata;
one should set up a flawless jar filled with white rice.
Likewise, it should be provided with various fruits and accompanied by stalks of sugarcane,
covered with a pair of white cloths, and anointed with white sandalwood paste.
One should place a copper vessel filled with various kinds of food and accompanied by gold according to one's capacity, together with molasses, upon it.
There, fasting on the following day, one should worship the god Acyuta, who can assume any form at will, with offerings such as perfumes and other ritual services.
Having worshipped again at dawn, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa;
one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having thus observed this vow for a year, one should give a bed, together with a cow of ghee and all necessary furnishings, to the preceptor.
Having honored a golden image of Kāmadeva, a conch shell, a milch cow, and a pair of Brahmin couples with garments, one should present them as offerings.
"May Hari, who can assume any form at will, be pleased with me"— uttering this very prayer,
whoever performs the Madanadvādaśī vow according to this rite, [attains the fruit].
Having consumed all his sins, he attains equality with Hari;
in this very [context], the Bhartṛdvādaśikā-vrata has been prescribed.
Having prepared a well-spread bed there and having installed the glorious Hari upon it,
one should arrange a canopy of flowers over it.

Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, the observer of the vow should keep a vigil at night with dance, instrumental music, song, and so forth; thereafter, on the following day at dawn—
One should present a golden image of Śrī Hari, together with His bed, to an eminent brahmin;
then, having fed the brahmins and satisfied them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), one should bid them farewell.
Even for one who has performed this vow in this manner, his marital union becomes stable;
and for seven births, he enjoys the pleasures desired in both worlds.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, having fasted and subdued his senses,
he should worship Mādhava with devotion using offerings such as perfumes and other services.
One should give cooked food that is satiating, sweet, along with a water-pot to a Brahmin according to the prescribed rule, saying, "May Mādhava be pleased."
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, having worshipped Trivikrama with perfumes and other offerings, one should present a water-pot filled with sweet food.
After that, the observer of the vow should practice eating only one meal a day for the sake of a twice-born man;
by this vow, Trivikrama, the God of gods, is fully satisfied.
O Nārada, it bestows abundant enjoyments and, in the end, liberation;
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should feed twelve brahmins.
Having honored them with sweet food and fragrant substances such as perfumes individually and in due order,
he should give them garments, staffs, sacred threads, and rings.
And one should devoutly offer alms-bowls, saying, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, the observer of the vow should worship Śrīdhara.
Being devoted to that [deity], he should, with devotion, feed the best of the twice-born with curd-rice and perfumes and other offerings;
having given silver sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and bowed down, he should dismiss them.
"May Śrīdhara, the Lord of Gods, be pleased by this vow," thus saying,
the observer of the vow, having worshipped Vāmana on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, [should proceed].
In front of that, one should feed twelve Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa) and give a golden gift; thus one becomes a bringer of pleasure to Viṣṇu.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should worship Padmanābha with offerings such as perfumes and other services, and feed the twice-born in his presence.
O best of the twice-born, one should give a golden image adorned with garments as a sacrificial fee along with sweet food; by this vow, Padmanābha becomes well-pleased.
The Govatsadvādaśī vow, observed during the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, bestows access to Śvetadvīpa as well as the desired enjoyments of the body.
There, having drawn a cow together with its calf using fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like, one should worship it in a copper vessel with flower garlands.

Having prepared the *arghya* offering in a vessel with flowers, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds according to the prescribed rule, one should present it at her feet with this mantra, O Nārada. (NarP 1.121.29)
O Goddess born from the ocean of milk, saluted by gods and asuras, composed of all the gods, and adorned by all the gods! NarP_1,121.30 //
"O Mother, O Mother of cows, O Mother, accept this water offering; salutations be unto you!
Then, one should present vaṭakas prepared with black gram and other ingredients.
Thus, five, ten, or even one [lamp], according to one's own means:
"O Fragrant One, you are the Mother of the World, eternally situated in the station of Viṣṇu."
O you who consist of all the gods, devour this morsel offered by me;
O Goddess who consists of all the gods, adorned by all the gods!
"O mother, O daughter of Nanda, make my desire bear fruit;
on that day, [prepare] food fried in oil and food cooked in a pot, O best of the twice-born."
O twice-born one, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should avoid cow’s milk, cow’s ghee, curd, and buttermilk before the deity Dāmodara.
Having worshipped with ritual offerings such as perfumes and the like while remaining well-composed, he should feed twelve Brahmins with cooked food in their presence.
Then, with affection, he should present to them water-pots filled with water, covered with cloths, well-adorned, and accompanied by betel nuts, sweets, and gold.
When this is done, one becomes dear to Viṣṇu and enjoys all pleasures;
at the end of the body, one attains union with Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt.
And the Nīrājana vow is also prescribed here; listen to that from me:
having adorned the Lord of the World when He has arisen from sleep at the onset of night.
O Sage, having adorned himself and kindled a new fire, he worshipped it with mantras and offered oblations therein once it was fully ablaze, using a silver lamp.
One should cause Hari to be honored with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings by the people, and then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for him;
likewise for Lakṣmī, Brahmāṇī, and Caṇḍikā who follow after him.
One should perform the nīrājana rite in due order for Āditya, Śaṅkara, Gaurī, the Yakṣas, Gaṇapati, the Planets, the Mothers, the Ancestors, the Mountains, and all the Nāgas.

One should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for the cows and the circular rite (*maṇḍala*) for the buffalo and other animals, accompanied by the sounds of "Salutation! and "Victory!", as well as the ringing of bells and conch shells.
When the great festival of *nīrājana* had commenced, amidst the clamor of cows whose horns were smeared with vermilion and whose bodies were adorned with various pigments; 1,121.44.
Horses endowed with auspicious marks, elephants overflowing with rut, and all the royal insignia, such as the parasol and others, O Nārada. (NarP 1.121.45)
The king, together with his domestic priest and devoted to his ministers and servants, honored the lake according to the rules and personally cleared it with great care.
Amidst the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, he should stand properly adorned upon a new lion-throne fashioned from various jewels.
Then, either a courtesan endowed with auspicious marks or a woman of noble family should slowly perform the *nīrājana* rite over the head of the king.
In this manner, this Great Peace (Mahāsānti) should be performed every year by a wealthy king or another person desiring health for the coming year. (NarP 1.121.49)
O Brahmin, in whose kingdom, city, or village this supreme peace-rite called *nīrājanā* is performed, their diseases go to utter destruction.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform the unsurpassed Sādhya-vrata;
likewise, Manobhava, Prāṇa, Nara, and the heroic Yāta [are to be honored].
Citi, Hayo, Nṛpa, Haṃsa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa,
Vibhu, and Prabhu— these are proclaimed as the twelve Sādhyas.
One should worship these [images] fashioned from rice with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
then, having fed the foremost of the twice-born, one should give twelve excellent sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) here.
Having given [the offerings] to them, he should dismiss them with the words, "May Nārāyaṇa be pleased.
It is known that within this very [rite] is the one designated as the Twelve Ādityas.
There, the wise man should worship the twelve Ādityas according to the vow:
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Śakra, Aṃśa, Varuṇa, and Bhaga.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu are proclaimed as the twelve;
having worshipped them with effort on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in each month, one should proceed.

At the conclusion of the vow, one should spend a year; moreover, having worshipped twelve golden images according to the prescribed rite and having fed the best of the twice-born, [one attains the fruit].
Having honored each one with sweet foods, the observer of the vow should offer them;
thus, having performed this vow known as the Dvādaśāditya, a man [attains the fruit].
Having reached the world of the Sun and enjoyed pleasures there,
he is then born on earth as a righteous soul among humans, free from disease.
Then, by the merit of his vow, he shall regain the vow once more;
O best of the twice-born, having shattered the mandala by that merit, he shall ascend.
One shall attain the stainless, formless, and beyond-dual Brahman;
O best of the twice-born, it is here that the vow known as Akhaṇḍa is declared.
Having fashioned a golden image named Janārdana and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should feed the twice-born in its presence.
For twelve months, one who has conquered the senses should eat only at night; then, at the end of the year, having worshipped that image according to the prescribed rite, ||| NarP_1,121.63 |||
One should give a cow along with [other gifts] to the preceptor and likewise offer this prayer:
"Whatever incomplete vow has been performed by me throughout a hundred lifetimes... (NarP 1.121.64).
"O Blessed One, by your grace, may that [fruit] remain unbroken for me here.
Then, having fed the foremost of the brahmins with milk-rice enriched with pieces of sugar-candy, ||| NarP_1,121.65 ||| he [proceeded].
"Indeed, one should give twelve golden [coins] as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to him.
Having thus performed the vow and having gratified Janārdana, O Brahmin, [one attains the fruit]. 121.66.
By means of a golden celestial chariot, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
this is declared to be the Rūpavrata on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa.
On the tenth day, having bathed according to the rules, the observer of the vow should take cow dung from a white or single-colored cow that has been standing in the open air, O twice-born one.
O Nārada, having prepared one hundred and eight small cakes (piṇḍikās) with that [mixture],
one should dry them by placing them in a vessel made of either copper or clay in the sun.
Having observed a fast on the eleventh day and worshipped according to the prescribed rules,
one should perform a vigil at night before a golden image of Viṣṇu.

Then, on the morning of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), [the image] should be placed upon a vessel of sesame seeds amidst auspicious songs, instrumental music, the recitation of hymns, prayers, and other such rites.
Having placed [the deity] in a jar filled with water, one should worship it with ritual offerings;
then, having generated a new fire by means of friction of wood and other methods.
Having worshipped that according to the prescribed rule, the wise man should offer each individual small sacrificial cake (piṇḍikā),
along with sesame seeds and clarified butter, using the twelve-syllable mantra.
Then, with a very affectionate mind, he should joyfully feed one hundred and eight brahmins milk-rice (pāyasa) while reciting the Vaiṣṇavī and Pūraṇa hymns.
The preceptor should cause him (or her) to drink the image together with the water-pot;
having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins according to his ability, and having bowed, he should dismiss them.
Whether it be a man or a woman, having performed the vow thus with devotion, [he or she attains the goal]. (NarP 1.121.75)
One obtains beauty and good fortune; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Sahasya, one should observe the Sujanma-dvādaśī vow.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite and having drunk the water from the horn of a bull and so forth, one should undertake the annual vow after circumambulating it.
Thereafter, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight every month, one should perform a gift:
a prastha of ghee, and then four prasthas each of rice and barley in succession.
Two *raktikas* of gold, half an *āḍhaka* of sesame seeds, a jar of milk, and a single *māṣa* of silver—these sweet cooked foods bring satisfaction. (NarP 1.121.79)
An umbrella made of gold weighing half a māṣa, a prastha of excellent molasses, a pala of sandalwood, and a fine garment measuring five cubits; NarP_1,121.80 //
Having thus performed the monthly gift and consumed [the food] in due order,
one should cook cow’s urine, water, or clarified butter, along with the four kinds of vegetables.
The monthly fast-breaking meal consists of barley mixed with curd, sesame and ghee, along with sugar, darbha grass, water, and milk. NarP_1,121.82 //
Having thus performed his vow for a year, he should fashion a golden image of the Sun,
place it within a copper vessel, and install it after worshipping according to the prescribed rite.
Having returned the gift along with the cow to the preceptor, one should prostrate before him;
having fed twelve Brahmins, one should also give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Brahmin, one who has thus fulfilled his vow attains birth in an excellent family;
he shall be free from disease, rich in wealth and grain, and possess unimpaired senses.
O twice-born one, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, having worshipped a Śālagrāma stone according to the rules with devotion, one should place gold in its mouth.
Having placed it in a silver vessel and covered it with a pair of white cloths,
one should give it to a knower of the Vedas and then feed him a meal.
Having thus performed the single meal with beneficial milk-rice mixed with sugar and ghee, he should remain intent on meditating upon Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed his desired enjoyments here, he attains the abode of Viṣṇu on the final twelfth day of the bright fortnight, having offered a golden image of Hari.
O twice-born one, having honored those who know the Vedas with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should feed twelve Brahmins and give them a sacrificial fee.
Having given [the gift], he should afterwards dismiss [the recipient] and then eat himself along with his kinsmen.
[The auspicious days are] Trispṛśā, Unmīlinī, Pakṣavardhinī, and likewise Vañjulī.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā—
these eight Dvādaśīs, when observed with a fast, are destroyers of sin.
Śrī Nārada said:
O Brāhmaṇa, what are the characteristics of these [vows], and what is their fruit?
Tell me all that, as well as those other meritorious ones.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by Nārada, the eternal sage, the best of the twice-born,
having praised his brother, the great devotee of the Lord, spoke.
Sanātana said:
"O brother, you have asked well, cutting through the doubts of the virtuous.
I shall describe the characteristics and the specific fruits of the various Mahādvādaśīs."
If the Ekādaśī has ended before the rising of the sun, then that Dvādaśī is named Trispṛśā; it yields great fruit.
O Nārada, he who fasts on this day and worships Govinda certainly obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
When the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is pierced by the tenth lunar day (daśamī) at sunrise,
one should completely abandon that [eleventh day] and observe the fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
Having worshipped there the one named Vāsudeva according to the proper ritual procedure for worship,
one obtains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices upon the opening [of the eyes].
But when the eleventh lunar day touches the southern solstice at sunrise,
one should always observe a fast on that day known as Vañjulikā, setting aside the other.
In this [mandala], one should constantly worship with devotion the god Saṃkarṣaṇa, the supreme bestower of fearlessness upon all, using offerings such as perfumes and other services.
This Mahādvādaśī bestows the fruit of all sacrifices;
it is declared to be the remover of all sins and the granter of all prosperity.
O Brahmin, when both the new moon and the full moon fall on a Sunday,
that twelfth lunar day is known as Pakṣavardhanikā, and it yields great fruit.
On that [day], one should worship the god Pradyumna, the Lord of the worlds,
who directly bestows all sovereignty and increases sons and grandsons.
But when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) occurs during the bright fortnight conjoined with the Maghā asterism,
it is called Jayā by name, which destroys all enemies.
On this [day], O Lord, one should worship Maniruddha, the husband of Ramā,
who grants all desires to men and bestows all forms of good fortune.
If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight should be conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa, then it is named Vijayā; on that day, one should worship the Mace-bearer (Gadādhara).
O Brahmin, by fasting on that day, a man shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), which eternally bestows all happiness and is devoted to all enjoyments.
And when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight is conjoined with the constellation Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī), it is remembered by the name Jayantī as being of great merit.
O best of Brahmins, on this day one should worship the god Vāmana, who grants success to men; when observed as a fast, it bestows the fruit of all vows.
It yields the fruit of all gifts and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
this is especially so when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) occurs during the bright fortnight and is conjoined with Jupiter and the Sun.
Then Aparājitā is proclaimed, the bestower of omniscience;
on this day one should worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment.
O Brahmin, by the mere fasting of this [vow], even one who eats [meat] would become liberated, having severed the bonds of saṃsāra and [reached] the ocean of knowledge.
But when the Maitra constellation (Anurādhā) occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, then both vows should be performed; there is no fault here, as they share a single deity.
On the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada when it is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
and on the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika when it is joined with the last asterism (Revatī), one should observe these two vows.
O best of Brahmins, among these, the vow of eating but one meal on the twelfth lunar day is naturally prescribed as the destroyer of sins.
Since the vow of Ekādaśī is obligatory when joined with Dvādaśī, no concluding rite (udyāpana) is prescribed here; it should be observed as long as one lives.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dvādaśī Vow of the Twelfth Month," in the fourth quarter of the first part of the *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*, within the *Bṛhadupākhyāna*.
Sanātana said:
Now, therefore, I shall describe to you the vows of the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*).
By performing these with devotion, a person becomes fortunate on earth.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Madhu, having fashioned an image of Madana out of sandalwood and having worshipped it with diligence, one should fan it with a fan.
Then Kāma, who increases sons and grandsons, became intensely agitated;
O Lord of Sages, listen now to the worship of Anaṅga that is prescribed therein.
