One should paint the bodiless god of love (Anaṅga) upon a smooth wooden panel with the dyes of vermilion and turmeric,
accompanied by Rati and Prīti, and bearing a flower-bow and quivers.
At midday, one should worship with devotion Kāmadeva, Vasanta, Vājivaktra, and Vṛṣadhvaja, using perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and garments.
And with various kinds of incantations, O Nārada, one should use this mantra:
"Homage to Māra, to Kāma, to the embodiment of the god of love."
One should worship the Lord of Women with devotion before him, who indeed causes the minds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Indra to tremble.
One should reflect, "This is Kāma," by means of garments, garlands, ornaments, and the like;
and having honored a Brahmin couple with perfumes, clothing, and decorations.
O Brahmin, he who thus celebrates this great festival every year when the spring season has arrived,
shall always remain joyful and well-nourished.
Or one should worship month by month until the year is completed—
the Madana born from the heart, Kāma, Manmatha, and the beloved of Rati.
One should worship Anaṅga, Kandarpa, Makaradhvaja,
and then, thereafter, Manobhava, who is known as Kusumāyudha.
Likewise, O Brahmin, on uneven ground one should offer a garland and say "I am dear";
furthermore, it is taught that one should give a goat after bathing in a river according to the prescribed rite.
One should give milk-yielding goats to a poor householder;
moreover, by this gift, he is not born again in this world.
If this [day] is joined with Saturn, it is known as Mahāvāruṇī;
if it occurs on the Gaṅgā, it is superior to ten million solar eclipses.
When there is an auspicious conjunction (*śubhayoga*) and one hundred asterisms (*ṛkṣa*) coincide on a Saturday during the month of Vaiśākha in the bright fortnight,
it is renowned as the *Mahāmahā*, which grants liberation to ten million members of one's lineage.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, the vow of Kāmadeva is prescribed;
there, one observing the fast should worship Kāma with perfumes and other offerings.
Thereafter, every month on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, this very vow should be performed; at the end of the year, a decorated cow [is to be given].
One should give to a Brahmin with due honor for the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the vow;
this is the vow for the pacification of misfortune, to be observed on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Having bathed there in the river water, one should worship a white mandāra flower, or an arka, or a red karavīra, grown in a pure place.
Then, having gazed at the sun in the sky, one should pray with this mantra:
"O Mandāra, Karavīra, and Arka, you who are born from the rays of the Sun!"
"May you, when worshipped, destroy my misfortune; homage be to you!"—he who thus worships these three trees with devotion year after year.
His misfortune perishes; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
On the pure and bright thirteenth lunar day, one should observe a single meal.
Having worshipped the two Lords of the World, Umā and Maheśvara,
one should fashion their forms out of gold, silver, or even clay, according to one's capacity.
Having placed it in a temple, a cow-pen, or the house of a Brahmin— where a lion or a bull resides— and having consecrated it with divine mantras, O Nārada.
Then, for five days, there shall be worship, as well as the vow of eating but one meal a day;
on the morning of the third day, having bathed and worshipped them again.
Thereafter, every year, they should be entrusted to a Brahmin who is proficient in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; after that, a period of five years should be observed.
At the conclusion of that, one should cause those two [the donor and the recipient] to be presented with a pair of cows;
thus, whether a man or a woman, having performed this auspicious vow...
One never suffers the separation of husband and wife for seven births by performing the auspicious Ratikāma-vrata on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas.
O best of the twice-born, whether it be a maiden or a woman who has observed the fast, this [rite] wards off widowhood for women and likewise increases their progeny.
Having fashioned Rati and Kāma in either copper, or earthenware, or likewise in gold or silver, one should worship them properly with perfumes and other offerings.
Then, having invited a brahmin couple on the fourteenth day,
and having honored and fed them, one should give those two images along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having thus performed this unsurpassed vow for fourteen years,
a pair of cows should be given for the sake of completing the vow.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Gotrirātra vow is prescribed;
having fashioned an image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa out of gold or even silver.

Having bathed [the image] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and placed it upon a seat adorned with cloth within an auspicious eight-petaled mandala, one should worship it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings.
Then, having performed the *ārārtika* rite, one should offer a jar of water with rice;
having done this for three days, and having worshipped for a month at the conclusion of the vow.
O Nārada, having accomplished the correct purpose, one should give [the gift] with the mantra:
"Five cows were produced when the great ocean was being churned."
Among them, to that cow named Nandā, salutations again and again;
having circumambulated her, one should then give her to a Brahmin with the sacred mantra.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows be at my sides; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Then, having properly honored a brahmin couple, one should feed them;
and having treated them with respect, one should present to them [an image of] Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices,
that same fruit is obtained from the vow of the three nights for the sake of the lineage (gotrirātravrata).
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should fashion a golden Aśoka tree and worship it according to the prescribed rite; this is the Trirātra-aśoka-ka-vrata.
O Brahmin, a woman devoted to fasting should daily perform one hundred and eight circumambulations with reverence, using this mantra.
O Aśoka, you were created long ago by the compassionate Hara for the sake of benefiting the world; therefore, be gracious, O beloved of Śiva!
Then, on the third day, having worshipped the bull-bannered god (Śiva) upon that tree according to the prescribed rite, one should feed a brahmin and cause [gifts] to be given.
A woman who has observed this vow shall never encounter widowhood;
accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others, she shall be very dear to her husband.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, having taken a single meal with a concentrated mind,
one should diligently light an oil lamp at twilight and perform worship.
One should give [the offering] outside at the door of the house, saying, "May Yama be pleased with me. O best of Brahmins, when this is done, no affliction from Yama arises.

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, O best of the twice-born, having eaten but a single meal and having bathed again at twilight, one should remain silent and well-composed.
O twice-born one, one may illuminate Śiva with a thousand lamps, or even with a hundred,
or else with a garland of thirty-two lamps.
One should illuminate the lamps with ghee and worship Śiva with perfumes and other offerings,
as well as with various kinds of fruits and food offerings, O Nārada.
Then one should praise Śiva, the Lord of Gods, with a hundred names;
indeed, those names are proclaimed as bestowing all desired objects.
Homage to Rudra, the Terrifying, the Blue-throated, the Creator;
homage indeed to the one with matted hair, the Lord of Gods, whose hair is the sky.
Salutations indeed to the bull-bannered one, to Soma, to the Lord of Soma;
to the sky-clad one, to Bhṛṅgin, to the beloved of Umā, and to the Increaser.
Salutations indeed to the one consisting of austerity, to the all-pervading Śipiviṣṭa;
salutations to the one fond of serpents, to the serpent, and to the lord of serpents.
Salutations to the upholder of the earth, to the sky, and to the lord of beasts;
salutations to the destroyer of Tripura, and to the lion, the tiger, and the bull.
Salutations indeed to the measured one, to the protector of the measured, to the perfected one, to the supreme being,
to him who is sung in the Vedas, to the hidden one, and to the secret of the Vedas.
Homage to you who are long-lasting, of long form, and of long purpose;
homage to you, the great one, the foundation of the world, whose form is indeed like space.
To the auspicious one, the distinguished one, the disciplined one, the Supreme Self;
to the wearer of the elephant hide and the slayer of the demon Andhaka.
To the one who is blue, red, and white; to the beloved of Caṇḍamuṇḍa;
to the God who loves devotion; to the end of sacrifice; and to the imperishable.
Salutations to you, the Great Lord; salutations to Mahādeva, the destroyer of Hara;
salutations again and again to the three-eyed one, to the triple Veda, and to the limbs of the Veda.
Salutations indeed to the one who is the object, whose nature is the object, and who is the ultimate reality;
salutations indeed to the one whose form is the universe, who is the universe, and who is the Lord of the universe.
Salutations indeed to Śaṅkara, to Time, to him whose form consists of the divisions of time, to the formless, to the multiformed, and to the subtlest of the subtle.

Salutations to you who dwell in the cremation ground; salutations to you who are clothed in animal skins; salutations to the one whose crest is the moon, and to the one who rests upon the earth as Rudra.

Salutations to Durgā, who carries one across difficulties; to the witness of the limbs of Durgā; to the one whose form is the *liṅga*, to the *liṅga* itself, and to the lord of those who possess the *liṅga*.
Homage to the one whose form is power; indeed, homage to the one whose purpose is power.
Homage, repeated homage to you, the cause of all causes; to the conqueror of death, whose nature is the self-manifested being;
to the three-eyed one, the blue-throated one who wields the trident; to the consort of Gaurī, the source of all auspiciousness; homage!
O Brahmin, having recited these one hundred names which proclaim the virtues of the wielder of the Pināka bow,
and having performed a circumambulation, he departed for his own abode.
O Brahmin, having thus performed this vow through the grace of Mahādeva,
one shall enjoy all pleasures here in this world and, at the end, attain the state of Śiva.
He who, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, worships Anaṅga according to the prescribed rite—
whether three times a day or once— attains the state born of union with Śiva.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with offerings such as perfumes and the like,
one should feed a Brahmin couple at the water-pot or upon an auspicious cloth.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he himself should observe eating only once a day;
by performing it thus according to the rule, the observer of the vow becomes a vessel of good fortune.
O best of Brahmins, he is born on earth through the grace of Mahādeva.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, having worshipped Acyuta Hari,
one should offer a vessel of ghee to an eminent brahmin for the sake of attaining all perfections.
O Brahmin, beginning on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha and continuing for three days,
the vow of the Māgha bath brings about the fruits of various desires.
The fruit that one obtains by bathing for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha cannot be attained on earth even by a thousand horse-sacrifices.
There, bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, and charity attain infinity.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should fast.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, one should begin the vow of Dhanada by worshipping the Great King,
the Lord of Yakṣas, with offerings such as perfumes and other articles.
O best of the twice-born, one should worship [this] written on a cloth with pigments with a spirit of devotion, in this manner every month on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight.
A man should worship [the deity] while fasting, or by eating but one meal a day;
then, at the conclusion of the vow, he should again offer a golden image of the Lord of Wealth (Dhananāyaka).

O best of the twice-born, having performed [the rites] together with the treasures that are golden in appearance, along with the sixteen types of services and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for the ablutions; NarP_1,122.79 //
With various offerings of food, one should worship with devotion while remaining composed;
then, having adorned a cow with garments, garlands, perfumes, and ornaments.
O Brahmin,
having fed twelve or thirteen Brahmins with sweet foods, one should cause a beautiful cow along with her calf to be given to a knower of the Vedas.
Having worshipped the guru with garments and other offerings, one should present that image to him;
then, having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born according to one's ability, and having bowed and taken leave of them, one should depart.
The wise man, being composed, should eat himself together with those who are dear to him;
O Brahmin, when this vow has been performed in this manner, even one who is destitute shall attain great wealth.
Renowned on earth, he rejoiced like another Rājarāja.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Trayodaśī Vow Observed on the Thirteenth Day of Each Month," in the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the first part of the Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanātana said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe to you the vows pertaining to the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī).
By performing these in this world, a person shall obtain all their desires.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, O Śivā, a great festival for the Noble One (Āryā) should be performed with saffron, agallochum, sandalwood, perfumes and the like, garments, and jewels.
Having offered canopies, banners, and umbrellas, the Mothers should be worshipped;
having performed this worship, O Brahmin, one should remain fasting or eating but a single meal.
A man on earth obtains merit greater than that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
right here, he should perform the worship of Damana with fragrant flowers.

On the fourteenth day of the month of Rādhākṛṣṇa, having observed a fast, one should offer [the gift] at the arrival of night to Śiva, who is of the nature of Śiva, when [the lunar day] is fully complete.
Having bathed and wearing clean garments, the wise man should likewise worship the Liṅga with perfumes and other offerings, and with bilva leaves on all sides.
Having given the mantra to the foremost of the twice-born, one should eat on the following day;
and in this very same manner, O best of the twice-born, on all the Kṛṣṇa days.
One who desires wealth and progeny should perform the Śiva-vrata;
on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should observe the Śrī-Nṛsiṃha-vrata.
Whether capable or incapable of observing the full fast,
one who eats but once a day should worship Nṛsiṃha, the slayer of the Daitya, at the arrival of night.
Then, O Nārada, one should propitiate the deity with the sixteen services, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and other offerings, using this mantra: NarP_1,123.10.
O you whose hair-tufts are like refined gold, whose eyes are like blazing fire,
and whose divine lion-claws have a touch harder than a diamond— homage be to you!
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, the observer of the vow should sleep upon the bare ground,
with senses conquered, anger subdued, and entirely renouncing all enjoyments.
O Brahmin, he who thus performs this supreme vow according to the rules year after year attains the abode of Hari after having enjoyed all worldly pleasures.
O Lord of Sages, the pilgrimage to Oṃkāreśvara must be performed right here;
for worship there is difficult to attain, yet its sight destroys all sins.
What is the use of saying much more here? Whatever consists of worship, meditation, and recitation has been taught as that which bestows knowledge and liberation upon men.
In this regard, the vow of the Liṅga, which destroys sin, should also be performed;
having bathed the Liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and smeared it with saffron.
Whoever thus worships this linga made of flour with food offerings, fruits, incense, lamps, garments, and ornaments, shall obtain the fulfillment of all goals.
He obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the grace of Mahādeva,
by performing the penance of five fires during the day on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, a person, having worshipped Śiva while remaining pure, should place a honey-cow in their mouth; this is known as the Rudra-vrata.
One shall obtain all prosperity through flowers produced in various places and seasons;
the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is prescribed for the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas.
O best of the twice-born, it should be performed according to the ritual prescribed in one's own Vedic branch;
having consecrated it with a hundred recitations of the mantra, one should then offer it to the Goddess.
Whether it be a man or a woman, by performing the Pavitrāropaṇa rite,
one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the grace of Mahādevī.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the supreme Ananta-vrata should be performed;
indeed, one meal consisting of a prastha of wheat flour should be taken.

Having roasted it and anointed it with sugar and ghee, one should offer it to Ananta after first worshipping him with perfumes and other offerings; [the offering] should be made of either cotton or silk.
Having fashioned a very beautiful thread provided with fourteen knots,
one should then remove the old [thread] and cast it into a body of water.
A woman should bind it on her left arm and a man on his right;
having cooked it with flour and boiled it, one should give it accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
From this very day, one should personally observe this most excellent vow for a period of fourteen years;
thereafter, the wise person should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
O Sage, having fashioned a Sarvatobhadra mandala with grains of various colors, one should place a very beautiful copper jar there.
Upon that, one should place an auspicious golden image of Ananta, covered with a yellow silk cloth; there, one should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship Gaṇeśa, the Mātṛkās, the Kheṭas, and the World-Protectors individually;
then, having performed the fire-oblation with sacrificial food, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
O best of the twice-born, one should devotedly give to the preceptor a bed with its furnishings, a cow, and an image, as well as fourteen other brahmins.
Having fed him with sweet, cooked foods, one should satisfy him with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). He who thus performs the Ananta-vrata with direct devotion [attains the fruit]. (NarP 1.123.32)
He too, through infinite faith, becomes a partaker of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
now hear from me the procedure for the Kadalī-vrata as well.
Whether it be a man or a woman, having bathed, one should worship Rambhā standing in the grove with perfumes, flowers, grains, sprouts, and other offerings.
Having thus worshipped with curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken grains (akṣata), lamps, garments, and cooked food, one should then pray to the Goddess with this mantra: NarP_1,123.35 //
O Goddess, worshipped by the daughters of the Apsaras, the Marut-gods, and the Nāgas, grant me health of body and beauty; homage be to you!
Having thus made this prayer, one should feed four young women who have recently given birth,
and who are adorned with parrot feathers, sidvaraka seeds, collyrium, and lac.
Having paid obeisance and completed the observance, one should go to one's own home;
O Brahmin, when the vow has been performed in this manner, having attained supreme good fortune, [one attains the highest state].

In this world, one shall go to the supreme heavenly realm by means of a celestial chariot on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, provided one does not die by poison, weapon, water, or fire.
For those killed by snakes, wild beasts, thunderbolts, and the like, as well as for those who have slain a Brahmin,
one should perform the *kriyā-śrāddha* on the fourteenth day according to the rules of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
One should feed a group of Brahmins with sweet, well-cooked foods;
one should also provide libations for the cows, mouthfuls of grass, and an offering for the dogs and crows.
Having performed the ritual rinsing, he himself should afterwards eat together with his kinsmen;
O Brahmin, he who performs the Śrāddha in this manner, providing it with the prescribed sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), [attains the highest reward].
Having delivered his ancestors,
O best of the twice-born, he shall go to the eternal world of the gods on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Īṣa, [worshipping] Dharmarāja.
Having properly worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should give him a golden vessel or one made of bell-metal;
O Nārada, Dharmarāja protects such a person on earth.
Thus, he who performs this supreme gift of a Dharma-image, having enjoyed excellent pleasures here in this world, shall go to heaven by the power of that merit.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, having performed an oil massage at the rising of the moon and then bathed, one should worship Dharma; thus one shall obtain freedom from fear of hell.
At twilight, with a concentrated mind, one should light oil lamps for the satisfaction of Yama at a crossroads, outside the house, or in a sacred place (brahma-pradeśa).
In the year known as Hemalamba, in the glorious month of Kārttika,
on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, at the break of dawn.
O lord of sages, having bathed in the Maṇikarṇika tīrtha along with the gods, the god Viśveśvara applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes.
Having worshipped his own self by himself, he undertook the Pāśupata vow;
thereafter, he performed a great worship there at the liṅga with perfumes and other offerings.
With *droṇa* flowers, *bilva* leaves, *arka* flowers, and *ketaka* flowers;
with blossoms, fruits, sweet ripe offerings, and various kinds of food oblations as well.
By performing this vow of eating only once a day, which pleases the Lord of the Universe,
one obtains all desired objects both in this world and the next, O Nārada.
One who desires prosperity should also perform the Brahmakūrca vow here;
having fasted and subdued his senses, he should drink the five products of the cow at night.
Cow’s urine from a tawny cow, likewise cow dung from a black cow,
milk from a white cow is prescribed, and similarly curd from a red cow.
Having taken the ghee from the variegated cow, one should mix it together;
then, having bathed at dawn with a bunch of *kuśa* grass, one should offer libations to the deities.
Having gratified the Brahmins, he himself should eat while remaining silent;
for this is the Brahmakūrca vow, which destroys all sins. (NarP 1.123.56)
Whatever sin has been committed in childhood, in youth, or even in old age,
it perishes at that very moment through the fast of the *brahmakūrca*.
The Pāṣāṇavrata is also prescribed here; listen to that, O Nārada:
having fasted during the day, one should consume at night a cake made of flour shaped like a stone.
Having worshipped Gaurī with perfumes and other offerings, one should present a vessel of ghee;
having performed this vow as prescribed, O best of the twice-born.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, by eating only one meal, a man shall obtain sovereignty, happiness, good fortune, and beauty, as previously described.
Having fasted and worshipped a golden bull, one should give it to a twice-born man;
then, having risen early on the following day and bathed, [one should worship] Soma Maheśvara.
One should worship with lotus flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
having fed the twice-born with sweet food, one should satisfy them with sacrificial fees and other gifts.

O Brahmin, this Śiva-vrata bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who perform it, those who instruct others in it, those who assist in it, and those who rejoice in it. (NarP 1.123.63)
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the Virūpākṣa vow is prescribed;
having reflected upon it, I shall attain the presence of Kapardīśvara here.
O Brahmin, having bathed in deep water, one should worship Śiva Virūpākṣa with perfumes,
garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food.
Having given that [image] to a twice-born man, one rejoices in heaven like a god;
the libation to Yama is prescribed for the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha.
At a time when the sun has not yet risen, having bathed,
one should satisfy Yama by reciting the twenty-eight names that have been proclaimed, for the sake of liberation from all sins.
One should perform the libation with sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water, as well as the feeding of brahmins;
one should also eat that very same kṛśara-rice oneself, remaining silent.
O twice-born one, on the final fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having observed the Śivarātri vow by fasting without water, one should worship here during both day and night.

With a concentrated mind, one should worship a self-manifested (svayambhu) linga or an earthen (pārthiva) linga with offerings such as perfumes and the like, as well as with bilva leaves and other materials.
Then, on the following day, having worshipped once again with incense, lamps, food offerings, the recitation of hymns, mutterings of mantras, and other such services; NarP_1,123.71.
Having fed the Brahmins with sweet foods and having dismissed them after they have received their sacrificial fees,
a mortal who has thus performed the vow, by the grace of Mahādeva, [attains his goal].
Having worshipped Durgā with devotion on the fourteenth day of the final bright fortnight, one obtains the enjoyments of the immortals, highly honored by the deities. (NarP 1.123.73)
Then, O Brahmin, one should feed the Brahmins with offerings of perfumes and other articles;
having thus performed the vow, O Brahmin, one should eat only a single meal for the sake of Durgā.
O Nārada, by observing a fast on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, one obtains all desired objects both in this world and in the next.
By drinking the water of Kedāra, one obtains the fruit of eloquence and intelligence;
however, the procedure common to all [concluding rites] is stated for the final completion (udyāpana).

In this rite, there shall be exactly fourteen jars, made of either copper or clay, which are new, without cracks, accompanied by betel nuts, unbroken rice, and sweetmeats, along with sacrificial fees and fine garments.
One should indeed prepare that same number of staffs of authority, purifiers, seats, vessels, and sacrificial threads.
One should perform the remainder as previously described, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Vow of the Fourteenth Day Observed in Each of the Twelve Months," in the fourth part of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna within the first section of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sanātana said:
Now, O Nārada, I shall describe to you the Pūrṇā vows; listen.
By performing which, a man or a woman shall obtain a continuous succession of happiness.
O best of Brahmins, the full moon day of Caitra is declared to be the beginning of a Manvantara;
on this day, one should offer a jar filled with water and rice for the satisfaction of Soma.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha as well, a gift given to anyone bestows everything;
whatever substance one gives to a Brahmin, one certainly obtains that very thing.
And here the vow of Dharmarāja is described; listen to that:
on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should indeed give cooked food and a water-pot to an excellent brahmin.
One should give [this] for the satisfaction of Dharmarāja, yielding the fruit of the gift of a cow;
herein one should give a black antelope skin together with its hooves and its horns.
Having covered it with sesame seeds, cloths, and gold, he who gives a black antelope skin to a twice-born man, honoring him according to the prescribed rite; ||| NarP_1,124.6 |||
He who knows all the scriptures and bestows the earth with its seven islands indeed rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
He who gives water-pots filled with clear water and accompanied by gold to the foremost of the twice-born never grieves at any time.
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should observe the Vaṭasāvitrika vow;
fasting, she should water the banyan tree with waters comparable to nectar.
One should wrap it with a thread, performing one hundred and eight circumambulations to the right;
then, one should pray to the divine Sāvitrī, who is devoted to her husband.
O Sāvitrī, worshipful to the world, Mother of the World, whose deity is your husband;
O you who abide in the banyan tree, grant me non-separation from my husband—salutations to you!
Having thus made this prayer and having fed married women on the following day,
the woman who then eats herself shall be a partaker of good fortune.
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, the Gopadmavrata is prescribed;
[one should worship] the four-armed, massive-bodied [deity], possessing a radiance like that of gold.
Adorned with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, Lakṣmī, and Garuḍa,
it was attended by sages, gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
Having bathed there, one should perform worship of Hari of such a kind with the Puruṣasūkta and with offerings such as perfumes and the like.
With a heart full of affection, one should satisfy the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and other gifts;
and one should feed the twice-born and others with sweet cooked foods according to one's ability.
O Brahmin, by performing the vow in this manner through the grace of the Lord of Kamalā, one obtains all desires pertaining to this world and the next; there is no doubt about this.
The Kokilā-vrata is also prescribed here; its procedure is now stated:
having commenced on the full moon day, one should perform the vow and bathe in water outside [the village].
Until the end of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Kokilā in the form of Gaurī,
with golden wings, jewel-like eyes, and a lotus-face of coral.
She was endowed with the hue of musk, born in the Nandana grove,
perched upon mango and campaka trees, and uttering sweet, melodious songs.
One should meditate upon the goddess Pārvatī, who has assumed the form of a cuckoo;
one should worship her daily with perfumes and other offerings, as she is depicted in colors upon a cloth.
Then, at the conclusion of the vow, O twice-born one, he should devoutly give to a Brahmin an image made either of gold or of sesame flour, along with a gift of gold, while reciting the mantra.
"O Goddess, having been born from the Caitraratha grove as a cuckoo beloved by Hara, you have been given to a brahmin after being fully honored; may you become the bringer of all happiness."
Then, one should feed thirty or one brahmin and a married woman;
having given gifts such as clothing according to one's ability, one should bow and dismiss them.
O Nārada, that woman who thus performs this supreme Kokilā-vow shall obtain happiness and good fortune for seven births.
Now, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, the commencement of Vedic study is prescribed;
there, the libation to the gods, sages, and ancestors should be performed with the Yajus formulas.
One should also perform the worship of the sages according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch:
by the Bahvṛcas on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, and by the Sāmagas during the month of Bhādrapada.
And likewise, the protective rite should be performed according to the prescribed rules.

Having washed white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), unhusked grains (*akṣata*), and black mustard seeds (*rājikā*) with water, and having purified them with safflower-dyed cloth, white cloth, saffron-colored thread, or water, one should worship the hosts of gods beginning with Viṣṇu with perfumes and other offerings. Then, having made a prayer and bowed down, one should joyfully bind them to one's own forearm from the hand of a twice-born man.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born, he should perform the lesson;
and having dismissed the seven sages, he should maintain the sacred thread (brahmasūtra).
Having personally fashioned a new [image] colored with saffron and other pigments,
one should feed the foremost of Brahmins according to one's ability and then perform the rite after they have eaten.
O Brahmin, when this vow has been performed, whatever Vedic ritual was forgotten, performed incorrectly, or not done at all during the rainy season shall become a meritorious act.
On the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, one who observes the Umā-Maheśvara vow,
eating but a single meal and diligently worshipping Śiva on that day, [attains his goal].
With palms joined in reverence, he should pray: "O Lord, I shall perform the vow tomorrow.
Having thus informed the deity, he should undertake this supreme vow.
Having slept near the deity during the night and risen during the latter watch,
he should then remain constantly engaged in the rites of benevolence and so forth, wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
One should worship Śaṅkara properly with various kinds of ritual offerings:
with bilva leaves rich in fragrance, with food offerings, incense, and lamps.
Then the wise man should fast until the end of the day at the rising of the moon;
having worshipped again in that very place, he should perform a vigil during the night.
Having thus performed the vow untiringly until the end of fifteen years,
he should perform its formal conclusion every year according to the prescribed ritual.
There were two golden images of Umā and Maheśa,
as well as fifteen excellent jars made of gold, silver, and clay.
There, two images together with their cloths should be placed in a single jar;
having bathed them with the five nectars, one should then worship them with pure waters.
Then, with sixteen types of offerings, he should feed fifteen twice-born men with sweet foods and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should present a single water-pot enriched with the [image of] the Lord’s form to the preceptor;
having thus performed the vow known as Umāmāheśvara.
He is born renowned upon earth as a treasury of all prosperity;
furthermore, on this very day, the Śakra-vrata is also prescribed.
Having bathed at dawn according to the prescribed rule, he should worship the Lord of the Gods with offerings such as perfumes and with heaps of food oblations.
Then, O twice-born one, having fed the invited Brahmins according to the prescribed rites,
he should likewise feed others who have assembled there— the poor and the helpless.
O Brahmin, this Śakra-vrata must be performed annually by a king, a wealthy man, or anyone else who desires a bountiful harvest of grain. (NarP 1.124.46)
In the month of Āśvina, on the full moon day, one should perform the vow known as Kojāgara;
having bathed according to the prescribed rite, fasting and with senses subdued.
Having worshipped Lakṣmī, one should place her golden image in a vessel made of copper or clay, covered with cloth, and honor her with various kinds of ritual offerings.
Then, at the time of evening when the lord of stars has risen,
one should light lamps filled with ghee, made of gold, silver, or clay.
Having cooked a large quantity of milk-rice mixed with ghee and sugar, [in amounts of] one hundred thousand, half that, ten thousand, one thousand, or even just one hundred.
Having placed [the offerings] in many vessels during the Kaumudī festival of the cool-rayed moon,
when only one watch of the night has passed, he should present them to Lakṣmī.
Then, he should devoutly feed the Brahmins with that [food], and thereafter,
together with them, he should keep a vigil accompanied by dancing, singing, and auspicious rites.
Then, having bathed at sunrise, one should offer that image to the Guru.
During this night, Mahālakṣmī remains with her lotus hands granting boons and fearlessness.
"At midnight, who wanders through the world on this earth?
To that one who stays awake, I shall grant wealth, for he is my worshiper."
This vow, which gratifies Lakṣmī, should be performed year after year;
it bestows prosperity in this world and, at the end of this life, that which pertains to the next world.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one should perform the viewing of Kārttikeya for the sake of further attaining the status of a Brahmin and for victory over all enemies.
O best of the twice-born, right here, at the onset of night, the festival of Tripura should be observed by offering lamps; it brings happiness to all living beings.
Insects, moths, mosquitoes, and trees, as well as those living beings that move in water or on land—
even they, upon seeing lamps, are no longer subject to birth and indeed attain liberation once more.
O Brahmin, here at the rising of the moon, the six Kṛttikās are to be worshipped.
Likewise Kārttikeya, Khaḍgin, Varuṇa,
and Hutāśana [should be worshipped] with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and extensive food offerings.
Having thus worshipped the gods with offerings of excellent rice, fruits, and vegetables that satisfy the fire and the Brahmins, a lamp should be placed outside the house.
Likewise, near the edge of the lamp, a charming square pit should be made, measuring fourteen finger-breadths; it should then be sprinkled with sandalwood water.
Having filled [the vessel] with cow's milk, one should place therein a golden fish,
beautiful in all its limbs and joined with pearls for eyes.
Uttering the mantra "And salutation to Mahāmatsya," one should worship there with perfumes and other offerings and present [the image] to a twice-born man.
The gift of the ocean of milk has been described to you by me, O best of the twice-born;
by the power of this gift, one rejoices in the presence of Hari.
O Nārada, having performed the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) and the *nakta* vow here, one attains the world of Rudra; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
On the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should give a vessel of salt enriched with gold to a peaceful Brahmin for the fulfillment of all desires.
Formerly, this world was abandoned by Lakṣmī; thereafter, Hari, Purandara, Soma, as well as Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati [were likewise forsaken].
On the full moon day conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, these five, by the power of the world,
once again adorned it with festivals of good fortune and playful delights.
Therefore, for the increase of all good fortune, a man, during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism,
should anoint his own body with a paste of white mustard seeds.
One should bathe with water infused with all medicinal herbs and wear new garments;
having seen auspicious objects, touched them, and bowed, one should thereafter perform worship.

Having performed the fire sacrifice with offerings such as incense and other perfumes on the days of Hari, Indra, the Moon, Puṣya, and Jupiter, one should gratify the brahmins by feeding them milk-rice.
O Brahmin, having performed this vow which increases the pleasure of Ramā and destroys misfortune, one rejoices both in this world and in the next.
Then, on the full moon day of Māgha, [one should give] sesame seeds, cotton, and blankets;
or else jewels, a tunic, a turban, sandals, or wealth.
Having given a gift according to one's wealth, one rejoices in heaven;
likewise, he who worships the god Śaṅkara here according to the prescribed rite [attains the same].
Having obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
On the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, the worship of Holikā is prescribed.

He should cause a heap of all kinds of wood and stones to be prepared; there, having kindled the fire according to the rules with extensive mantras that destroy demons, ||| NarP_1,124.77 ||| He should cause a heap of all kinds of wood and stones to be prepared; there, having kindled the fire according to the rules with extensive mantras that destroy demons, ||| NarP_1,124.77 |||
“You were made [a deity] by foolish people, O Holi, out of fear of blood-drinking [demons].
Therefore, I shall worship you; O Bhūti, be the bestower of prosperity.”
Having kindled it with this mantra, one should then perform a circumambulation by throwing pieces of wood and other materials,
while holding a festival accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
This Holikā is a Rākṣasī who caused fear to Prahlāda;
therefore, they burn her with wood and other materials while chanting auspicious songs.
"O best of Brahmins, know this: according to another view, this burning of the year is the burning of desire; thus, O lord of sages, the state of affairs in the world is manifold."
At the end of each fortnight, there are two [observances] performed separately;
therefore, O Brahmin, listen to me as I describe the vow for the new moon (Amāvratam), which is exceedingly dear to the ancestors.
There, on the new moon day of Caitra and Vaiśākha, one should perform the worship of the ancestors with a Śrāddha according to the Pārvaṇa rite, in accordance with one's wealth.
Since providing food for the twice-born and especially the gift of cows and other such things on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) in all months bestows great merit; NarP_1,124.84 //
O Nārada, for whom was this vow of Sāvitrī proclaimed on the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha? Its ritual procedure has also been fully described here.
O twice-born one, in the pure months of Nabhas and Bhādra, at the end of the full moon,
one who performs the ancestral śrāddha, gives gifts, offers oblations, and worships the gods, attains infinite merit.

O twice-born one, in the afternoon of the new moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, having addressed the kuśa grass grown in a sesame field with the mantra of Viriñci, [one should say] "huṃ phaṭ" and cut them.
One should always employ others for all tasks at once;
however, on the day of the new moon, one should specifically perform the ancestral Śrāddha and libations for the ancestors.

The offering of lamps in the waters of the Ganges, at the sacred site of Gayā which grants liberation, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, and in the houses of the gods— these are duties to be performed.
Likewise, the worship of Lakṣmī should be performed at rivers, groves, ponds, shrines, cow-pens, and marketplaces, using gold and silver, whether fashioned into images or not.
And gambling, which yields results according to the year, [is performed] with victory or even defeat;
here, the worship of cows is prescribed by means of anointing their horns and other limbs.

Even on the road, the worship of the ancestors may be performed by those endowed with faith through gifts of fodder, grain, and the like, as well as through prostrations, circumambulations, and the feeding of Brahmins.

O best of Brahmins, when the ancestral śrāddha is performed during the months of Pauṣa and Māgha with observances such as celibacy, and with recitations, fire-oblations, and worship, its fruit is especially great.
On the new moon day conjoined with the asterism Karṇapāta and the sun, the merit at Gayā is especially great;
likewise, in the month of Phālguna, one should perform the Śrāddha rite alone and feed the twice-born.

"O Sage, I have thus briefly explained to you the duties pertaining to the lunar days (tithis): that acts such as giving charity yield all fruits, yet on the new moon (darśa) and the full moon (soma), the fruit is especially great."
There is a distinction in every case as well; it is found in another Purāṇa.

Thus, in the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, in the first part, in the Bṛhad-upākhyāna, in the fourth quarter, is the narration of the vows for the full-moon and new-moon days occurring in each of the twelve months, titled "The One Hundred and Twenty-fourth [Chapter]. Sūta said:
Having been thus addressed by the sage Nārada, those Kumāras were indeed questioned by him.
Having been honored by him, those most eminent among the knowers of the scriptures, having performed their daily rites, departed for the world of Umāpati.
There, having bowed to the fierce one whose feet are worshipped by the lords of sages such as Śrī Vāmadeva and others who resemble the foremost suns of the lords of the quarters,
and who is saluted by the lords of gods and asuras, they sat upon the ground at his command.
Then, having heard there the Śivāgama— the essence of all scriptures and the means of liberation from the bonds of Paśu— they,
whose nature was now a mass of gnosis, bowed to the Enemy of Tripura and departed for their father’s abode.
Having prostrated at his lotus feet, they were honored and welcomed by their father;
having received his blessings, they still wander today through the worlds as living sanctuaries, ever-present holy sites.
Then they went to the edge of the Badarī forest, where they beheld [Viṣṇu] being served by hosts of the lords of the gods—
the imperishable lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, which ascetics free from passion meditate upon for a long time.
O Brahmins, having then received from the Kumāras the desired knowledge along with its practical realization, Nārada became exceedingly joyful in his heart.
Having returned from the banks of that river of gold and having prostrated before his father,
he was honored by his father, Brahmā, and sat down.
Having heard from the princes that knowledge which is conjoined with discernment,
he described it according to its true nature, and having heard it, he too rejoiced.
Then, having bowed his head and received blessings, that best of sages went to Kailāsa, which is frequented by sages and perfected beings.
It was eternally filled with various wonders, with trees bearing flowers in every season,
such as mandāras, pārijātas, campakas, aśokas, and vañjulikas.
It was surrounded by various other trees filled with flocks of diverse birds,
their crests tossed by the wind as if beckoning to travelers.
It was crowded with various herds of wild animals and teeming with perfected beings (*siddhas*) and *kiṃnaras*,
and it possessed lakes of clear water with shimmering golden lotuses.
It was graced by cranes, swans, ruddy geese, and other birds, resounded with their cries,
and was frequented by throngs of Apsarases sporting there, who had been rubbed by the falling waters of the celestial river.
In the waters of the Alakanandā, which were tawny with the saffron from their breasts,
the elephants, delighted by the fragrance, raised up lotuses with their trunks and sprayed them with water.
Then, on that mountain peak resembling a white cloud, the area was crowded with female elephants and young calves being bathed by their keepers.
He beheld a banyan tree resembling a dark cloud, extending for a hundred yojanas;
beneath it sat [the Lord], situated in the midst of a circle of yogis.
To the one with matted hair, the odd-eyed one, clothed in a tiger skin,
whose every limb is adorned with ashes and decorated with serpent ornaments.
O Brahmins, having seen that moon-crested Lord, who was perpetually adorned with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, Nārada bowed his neck in devotion.
Then, with his head bowed at the feet of that Lord of the World,
he praised the bull-bannered god with words from a mind full of devotion.
Honored by the yogis, he then sat down at the command of Sthāṇu;
thereafter, the Teacher of the Worlds inquired after Nārada’s welfare.
And he said with courtesy, "O Brahmins, through your favor I possess everything," while all the best of yogis were listening there.
He inquired about the knowledge pertaining to Śambhu, which brings liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
Śiva, his mind fully satisfied by his devotion, [responded] with respect to him.
He who is compassionate toward those who bow before him taught the yoga endowed with eight limbs;
he, having obtained the knowledge of Śambhu from Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
With a deeply serene mind, he bowed and went into the presence of Nārāyaṇa;
there too, Nārada remained constantly intent on coming and going.
Served by yogins and perfected beings, he gratified Nārāyaṇa.
This great Nāradīya [Purāṇa], O brahmins, has thus been recounted to you by me.
This narrative is equal to the Vedas, an illustration of all scriptures, endowed with the four quarters, and increases the knowledge of those who hear it. (NarP 1.125.26)
O Brahmins, whoever should recite this Nārada-portion in a temple of Śiva, in an assembly of eminent twice-born men, or likewise in a temple of Keśava; NarP_1,125.27 //
In Mathurā and Prayāga, in the presence of Puruṣottama, at Setu, Kāñcī, Kuśasthalī, Gaṅgādvāra, and Kuśasthala; NarP_1,125.28 //
Whether at Puṣkara, on a riverbank, or anywhere else, the devotee shall obtain the great fruit of all branches of knowledge and all sacred fords.
Whether among all forms of giving or all types of asceticism without exception,
one who is devoted to fasting, who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya), and has conquered his senses [is superior].
Both the listener and the speaker, being devoted to Nārāyaṇa—
or even one who delights in devotion to Śiva— shall attain perfection while listening.
The arising of all perfections and the inexhaustible accumulation of merit has been described;
it destroys all sins for those who always read or hear it.
This [work] removes the defects of the Kali age for men, increases all prosperity, fulfills the desires of all, and illuminates all knowledge. (NarP 1.125.33)
O twice-born ones, [this applies] to the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śāktas, and those devoted to the Sun,
as well as to the Gāṇapatyas and to the twice-born who follow the system of castes and stages of life.
It is the illuminator of austerities, vows, and their fruits,
as well as of mantras, yantras, and the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (vedāṅgas), each according to its specific division.
Likewise, whoever recites with devotion or listens with a concentrated mind to this compendium of the Āgamas, the Sāṃkhya, and the Vedas— ||| NarP_1,125.36 |||
Having heard this Nārada Purāṇa, which is equal to the Vedas, one shall obtain all desired objects, even those difficult to attain among the gods and other beings.
One should worship the reciter with devotion by means of wealth, jewels, garments, and the like, and constantly with gifts of land, gifts of cows, and gifts of gems. (NarP 1,125.38)
O Brahmins, one should constantly gratify the teacher with gifts of elephants, horses, and chariots—
especially him who expounds the Purāṇa, which is a compendium of Dharma.
Who else is a teacher like him, who bestows the fourfold aims upon men,
[serving them] constantly with body, mind, speech, and even with wealth and other means?
One should do what is pleasing to that preceptor who instructs in the Dharma,
having heard the Purāṇa according to the rules and having performed the fire-oblation and the worship of the gods.
Afterwards, one should feed a hundred Brahmins with sweet foods and milk-rice (pāyasa);
one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, for through such devotion Mādhava is pleased.
Just as the Gaṅgā is the best of rivers, as Puṣkara is the best of lakes, as Kāśī is the best of cities, as Meru is the best of mountains, so is Hari Nārāyaṇa the supreme deity.
The Kṛta Yuga, the Sāmaveda, the cow, the Brahmin, food, and water;
the path, the king of beasts, the Puruṣa, the Aśvattha tree, and Prahlāda as the mouth.
Uccaiḥśravas, Vasanta, Japa, Śeṣa, Aryaman, Dhanu,
Pāvaka, Viṣṇu, Indra, Kapila, Vākpati, and Kavi.
Arjuna, Hanumān, Darbha, Citta, Citraratha, and Urvaśī are like lotuses made of gold; for they are the most excellent among their own respective species.
In the same way, the Nārada Purāṇa is proclaimed among the Purāṇas:
"May there be peace, may there be auspiciousness for all of you, O best of the twice-born! (NarP 1.125.47).
"I shall go to the presence of my preceptor Vyāsa, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Having spoken thus, Sūta was honored by the high-souled ones, headed by Śaunaka.
Commanded by all of them, he went once more to see his guru;
and those best of the twice-born, Śaunaka and the others,
being composed and having properly performed what they had heard, remained there engaged in the sacrificial session.

He who employs the ritual of recitation and worship as a medicine for Hari, the destroyer of the poison of the Kali age’s impurities, attains a mind free from poison; having reached that state, he indeed obtains the sacrifice and the world most desired by the virtuous.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Purāṇas," in the fourth quarter of the *Bṛhannāradīyapurāṇa*, within the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna*.
This concludes the first part of the *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīyapurāṇa*.
May the Lord who deludes Madana with Śrī Rādhā be ever victorious!
